NOBILITATE AC PRVDENTIA ORNA- tiffimis viris, Consulibus, atque Sena- tui, Ecclefiæq; Imperialis Reipub. Col- mariensium, Dominis suis plurimum obseruandis, fauorem & pacem à Deo patre per Iesum Christum, optat Ioannes Brandmil- lerus.
units.tr: To the most distinguished men, adorned with nobility and prudence, the Consuls and Senate, and the Church of the Imperial Commonwealth of Colmar, their most respected lords: John Brandmuller wishes favour and peace from God the Father through Jesus Christ.

units.la: ST HOC NON solum in more positum, institutoq; maiorum viri præstantissimi, sed etiam hodie in communi vsu ac confuetudine, vt, quando matrimonia contrahuntur & confirmantur, imo ante nuptiarum celebrationem in ipsis sponsalibus, mortis fiat mentio, tum viri, tum mulieris, hoc est, ambarum personarum, quæ in matrimonio collocantur. Testatur hoc præter quotidianam experientiam & D. Chrysostomus, qui in hunc modum, in Sermone de Fide & Lege natura, & sanctò spiritu scribit: Eapropter Deus vbiq; sepulchra fieri voluit, ut illis nostra ipsorum infirmitatis memores fieremus. Ideo omnis civitas, omne castellum ante ingrefsum sepulchra habet, ut contendens intrare in civitatem qua imperat & floret diuitiis & potentatu, aliisq;[?] dignitatib. priusquam videt, quod secum concipit, videat primum quod sit. Ante portas sunt sepulchra, ante agros sunt sepulchra. Ubique ante oculos est nostra humilitatis schola, & docemur in quid desinamus tandem, et videmus qualia futura sint phantasmata: neque hic solum, sed & ingressuri ad communionem vitae, docemur vilitatem summam naturae. Sæpe vir quando uxorem ducere vult, meminit in desponsatione, & scribit in dote.
units.tr: It is not only the custom of the most excellent men and the institution of our ancestors, but also the common practice and usage today, that when marriages are contracted and confirmed, and indeed even before the wedding in the betrothal itself, mention is made of death, both of the man and of the woman, that is, of both persons who are being joined in marriage. Besides daily experience, St. Chrysostom also bears witness to this, who writes in this manner in his sermon on Faith and the Law of Nature and the Holy Spirit: "Therefore God wanted tombs to be made everywhere, so that we would remember our own weakness. So every city and every fortress has tombs before its gates, so that one who is about to enter a city that rules and flourishes with riches, power and other dignities, sees first what he is. Before the gates are tombs, before the fields are tombs. Everywhere before our eyes is the school of our humility, and we are taught what we shall come to in the end, and we see what the phantoms will be like. And not only here, but also those about to enter into the fellowship of life are taught the utter worthlessness of nature. Often a man, when he wishes to take a wife, thinks of death at the betrothal, and writes of it in the dowry.

units.la: Nondum introducta est, & mors statim describitur: nondum convixerunt, neque nuptia habita, & mortem statim definit.
units.tr: She has not yet been brought in, and death is at once described. They have not yet lived together, nor has the wedding been held, and at once death is set down as a limit.

units.la: Nondum nuptam vidit, et mortis aduersus illam calculos proponit, Scribit in hunc me[?]dum: Si mortuus fuerit vir ante mulierem, si mulier ante virum, hoc & hoc dispensatur[?]. Sic formata sunt patria leges. Ubique omnibus naturae sunt monumenta: & non solum eorum qui sunt & vivunt, mortis feruntur sententia: sed & eorum qui nondum nati. Quid enim ultra dicit? Quod si natus fuerit filius, & mortuus fuerit: nondum fructus & sententia lata est, &c.
units.tr: He has not yet seen the bride, and he sets before himself the calculations of death against her. He writes in this manner: "If the husband dies before the wife, or the wife before the husband, this and this is provided for." Thus the laws of the fatherland are formed. Everywhere there are monuments of nature for all: and the sentence of death is pronounced not only on those who are and live, but also on those not yet born. For what does he say further? "But if a son is born and dies, the fruit is not yet, and the sentence is passed," etc.

units.la: Hæc cum itafint[?], & hodie sic fiant, atque olim similiter facta fuerint: neminem esse, aut fore arbitror, cui vel mirum, vel absurdum videatur, quod ego (ante aliquot annos) in uno eodemq; libro seu volumine coniunxerim & Funebres & Nuptiales conciones: quarum illa quidem habentur, quum moriuntur, hæ vero quando coiugio devinciuntur mortales.
units.tr: Since these things are so, and are done so today, and were done similarly in the past, I think there is no one, or will be, to whom it seems either strange or absurd that I (some years ago) have joined in one and the same book or volume both funeral and nuptial sermons: of which the former are delivered when people die, and the latter when mortals are bound together in marriage.

units.la: Quod vero præmissis funebres, atque iis demum adiunxi nuptiales, & illarum plures, quam harum posui: multa sunt rationes, quas reddere possem.
units.tr: As for why I have placed the funeral sermons first, and only then added the nuptial ones, and why I have set more of the former than of the latter, there are many reasons I could give.

units.la: Principio nouerunt omnes qui aliquot annos in ministerio Ecclesiæ fuerunt, nunquam fere plures nuptias conciliari ac confici solere, quàm eo tempore, quo pestilentia abiit. Atq; Utinam quidam possent continere tantisper a nuptiis, donec illa quidem sauire[?] in ipsorum medio cessaret. Experiuntur quoq; idem, plus semper materia sibi offerri faciendi sermonem de morte quam de nuptijs. Quam doquidem[?] illa potest esse singulorum hominum: ha vero non nisi duorum.
units.tr: In the first place, all who have been some years in the ministry of the Church know that almost never are more weddings arranged and performed than at the time when the plague has passed. Would that some could abstain from marriage for so long, until that plague had ceased to rage in their midst. Also, people find that there is always more material offered to them for preaching about death than about marriage; since death can concern each individual person, whereas marriage concerns only two.

units.la: Deinde sentimus omnes in tota hac vita nostra semper plus fellis, quam mellis, plus tristitia quam laetitia inesse. Credimus autem qui vere Christiani & vocantur & sumus, longe multoq; melius esse prius gustare amara, quam dulcia: prius flere, quam gaudere. Dicit enim Christus Dominus noster (quem & super ciuitatem fleuisse, & in orationibus pernoctasse legimus: risisse vero aut iocasse nusquam, ut scribit Bernard. Sermon. 4. de Aduen[?]. Domini: quem etiam prius passum esse, quam in gloriam suam intrasse, nouimus ex Luc. 24. & 1.Pet.1.) Beati qui fletis nunc, quia ridebitis. & alibi: Pusillum & non videbitis me, & iterum pusillum, & videbitis me. Amen amen dico vobis, plorabitis & lamentabimini: vos mundus contra gaudebit. Vos autem mœrore afficiemini, sed mœror vester vertetur in gaudium. Mulier cùm parit, dolorem habet, quia venit hora eius. Cùm autem peperit puerum, iam non meminit anxietatis, propterea quòd gaudeat hominem esse natum in mundo. Et vos igitur nunc quidem mœrorem habetis, sed iterum videbo vos, & gaudebit cor vestrum, & gaudium vestrum nemo tollet à vobis. Sed de his satis.
units.tr: Next, we all feel that in the whole of this life of ours there is always more gall than honey, more sadness than joy. We believe, however, that those who are truly and rightly called Christians, and are so, it is far better to taste bitter things first than sweet: to weep first than to rejoice. For our Lord Christ says (whom we read to have wept over the city and to have spent nights in prayer, but never to have laughed or joked, as Bernard writes in Sermon 4 on the Advent of the Lord; whom we also know to have suffered before entering into his glory, from Luke 24 and 1 Peter 1): "Blessed are you who weep now, for you shall laugh." And elsewhere: "A little while and you will not see me, and again a little while and you will see me. Truly, truly I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice. But you will be grieved, yet your grief will be turned into joy. When a woman gives birth she has sorrow, because her hour has come. But when she has borne the child, she no longer remembers the anguish, because she rejoices that a man has been born into the world. So you too now indeed have sorrow, but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you." But enough of these things.

units.la: Porrò quoniam spero has quoque qualescunque conciones, à me in nuptijs quondam habitas, nonnihil facturas ad ecclesiæ Christi cùm institutionem, tum consolationem: volui eas, sicut & funesbres aliis (quibus collectanea mea placent) communicare. Si lectores in istis quædam bona, pia & utilia reipub. Christianæ repererint, non cupio, ut mihi (qui sum malus, & servus inutilis) pro his gratias agant aut habeant: sed ei à quo omnis donatio bona & omne donum perfectum, hoc est, Deo & patri Domini nostri Iesu Christi, accepta referant. Sin vero aliquid male, perperam, inutiliter, pernitiosæue scriptum viderint, velim mihi imputent, ac Deum orent, ne mihi imputet, sed ignoscat, propter filium suum dilectum, ut pote qui hoc nec volens nec sciens, sed profectò ignorans fecerim. Interea si quis amicus & frater in Domino alicuius erratí me admonuerit, equidem haud inuitus, sed libenter id corrigam & emendabo.
units.tr: Moreover, since I hope that these sermons, of whatever kind they are, which I once delivered at weddings, will be of some use both for the instruction and for the consolation of the Church of Christ, I have wished to share them, as I did the funeral sermons, with others (who take pleasure in my collected writings). If readers find in them anything good, pious and useful for the Christian commonwealth, I do not wish them to give thanks to me (who am a wicked and unprofitable servant) or to hold me in regard for these things; rather let them refer it to him from whom every good gift and every perfect gift comes, that is, to God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ. But if they see anything written wrongly, amiss, uselessly or harmfully, I would have them impute it to me, and pray to God that he not impute it to me, but pardon it for the sake of his beloved Son, since I have done this neither willingly nor knowingly, but certainly in ignorance. Meanwhile, if any friend and brother in the Lord has admonished me of some error, I will gladly, and not unwillingly, correct and amend it.

units.la: Caterūm mihi dubitanti ac circumspectanti, quos velim his oratiunculis, ad nouos coniuges & nuptiales homines paratis & dictis, deligere patronos: venite vos, amplissimi viri, mihi in metem[?]. Sic enim ipse mecum cogitaui. Ecce Deus Opt. Max. qui cunctos homines vult saluos fieri, & ad agnitionem veritatis peruenire, pro sua bonitate et gratia nuper Colmariensibus ita illuminatos oculos mentis dedit, tantumq; robur Christiana fortitudinis, ut abolitis superstitionibus, & reiectis doctrinis prohibentium contrahere matrimonium, quod inter omnes honorabile est, teste D. ◡Apostolo, puriorem euangelij doctrinam amplexi sint, & ecclesiam suam reformationem (quod felix & faustum sit) instituerint. Vix igitur nunc fideliores hisce ac magis strenuos patronos nancisci poteris. Est enim illis adhuc recens quasi, cogitare quàm impium sit ac nefarium diligere magis fcortationem à Deo vetitam & damnatam (vt in Antichristi regno fit) quàm contrahere matrimonium à Deo institutum, probatum & honoratum.
units.tr: Now, as I was doubting and looking about whom I should choose as patrons for these little speeches, prepared and delivered for new spouses and for those entering marriage, you, most distinguished men, came into my mind. For I thought to myself thus: behold, God, the best and greatest, who wills that all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth, by his goodness and grace has recently given such enlightened eyes of the mind to the people of Colmar, and so much strength of Christian courage, that, having abolished superstitions and rejected the doctrines of those who forbid marrying, which among all is honourable, as the Apostle bears witness, they have embraced the purer doctrine of the gospel, and have established the reformation of their Church (may it be fortunate and prosperous). Hardly, therefore, could you now find more faithful or more vigorous patrons than these. For it is still, as it were, fresh to them to consider how impious and wicked it is to love fornication more, a thing forbidden and condemned by God (as happens in the kingdom of Antichrist), than to contract marriage, which is instituted, approved and honoured by God.

units.la: Quoniam autem de hoc diuino instituto seu ordine Dei, id est, de coniugio, nec non de officio coniugum plurima tractantur in his concionibus: ideo placet eas Colmariensibus dedicare. Quapropter viri præstantissimi, vobis hunc meum laborē offero, & sub nomine vestro in publicum emitto, submisse rogans, vt eo animo excipiatis eum, quo veritatis euangelicæ doctrinam recepistis: de qua vobis læta mente gratulor, inq; ea constantiam & perseuerantiam opto. Atque huius gratulationis lætitiæq; aliqua significatio hic libellus esto. Valete, clarissimi Domini, in Christo Iesu, vnico verae salutis vitaq; authore.
units.tr: Since many things about this divine institution or ordinance of God, that is, about marriage, and also about the duties of spouses, are treated in these sermons, it has therefore pleased me to dedicate them to the people of Colmar. Wherefore, most distinguished men, I offer you this my labour, and send it out to the public under your name, humbly asking that you receive it with the same mind with which you received the doctrine of the evangelical truth: for which I gladly congratulate you, and I wish you constancy and perseverance in it. And let this little book be some sign of this congratulation and joy. Farewell, most illustrious lords, in Christ Jesus, the sole author of true salvation and life.

units.tr: The text to be expounded.

units.la: DIXIT quoq; dominus Deus: Non est bonum hominem esse solum: faciam ei adiutorium quasi coram eo. Formatus igitur dominus Deus de humo cunctis animantibus terræ & uniuersis volatilibus cæli, adduxit ea ad Adam, vt videret quid vocaret ea. Omne enim quod vocauit Adam animæ viuentis, ipsum est nomen eius. Appellauitq; Adam nominibus suis cuncta animantia, & uniuersa volatilia cæli, & omnes bestias terræ. Adæ vero non inueniebatur adiutor oportunus. Immisit ergo Dominus deus soporem in Adam: cumq; obdormisset, tulit vnam de costis eius, & repleuit carnem pro ea. Et adificauit Dominus deus costam, quã tulerat de Adam, in mulierem: & adduxit eam ad Adam. Dixitq; Adam, Hoc nũc os ex ossibus meis, & caro de carne mea. Hac vocabitur virago, quoniam de viro sumpta pta est. Quamobrem relinquet homo patrem suum & matrem, & adhærebit uxori suæ[?], & erunt in carnem unam. Erat autem uterque nudus, Adam scilicet & uxor eius: & non erubescebant.
units.tr: And the Lord God also said: It is not good for man to be alone; I will make him a helper as it were before him. So the Lord God, having formed out of the earth all the beasts of the field and all the fowls of the air, brought them to Adam, to see what he would call them. For whatever Adam called each living creature, that is its name. And Adam gave names to all cattle, and to all the fowls of the air, and to all the beasts of the earth. But for Adam there was not found a suitable helper. So the Lord God cast a deep sleep upon Adam; and when he was asleep, he took one of his ribs and filled up the flesh in its place. And the Lord God built the rib, which he had taken from Adam, into a woman, and brought her to Adam. And Adam said: This now is bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh. She shall be called Virago, because she was taken out of man. Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and they shall be one flesh. Now both of them were naked, Adam and his wife, and they were not ashamed.

units.la: TEXTUS EXPLICATIO.
units.tr: EXPLANATION OF THE TEXT.

units.la: MOses fidelis Domini servus in opere sexti diei perseverans hoc loco, formationem fœminæ, & coniugii institutionem explicat: ubi hæc ordine nobis expendenda proponuntur.
units.tr: Moses, the faithful servant of the Lord, still engaged in the work of the sixth day, here explains the forming of the woman and the institution of marriage, where the following points are set before us to be weighed in order.

units.la: Primum, formans fœminæ causa: fecundò, ratio formandæ fœminæ: tertiò, usus fœminæ: quartò, modus formationis fœminæ: quintò, autor coniugii: sextò, descriptio coniunctionis viri & uxoris: septimò, utriufque nuditas.
units.tr: First, the cause that forms the woman; second, the reason for forming the woman; third, the use of the woman; fourth, the manner of forming the woman; fifth, the author of marriage; sixth, the description of the union of husband and wife; seventh, the nakedness of both.

units.la: I Formans causa atque autor est Deus ipse. Ita enim scribit Moses: Et rursum dixit Dominus deus, Faciam homini adiutorium. item: Et ædificauit Dominus deus costam, quam acceperat de homine, in mulierem. Unde fœminæ & matrimonij dignitas æstimatur. Solent enim opera ex suis causis ponderari. Contemnunt igitur Deum, qui vetant coniugia. Matrimonium etiam locus ipse in quo institutum fuit, paradisus videlicet, & ipsa tempóris vetustas, co-[?] mendat. Vide etiam hic, quanta optimi architecti Dei potentia, quæ ex tantilla particula, tanquam ex trabe extruxit hoc ædificium, hoc adiutorium, id est, mulierem, quæ typum prætulit ecclesiæ super petram ædificatæ, & ex costa, tam elegantia membra cōcinnauit, tantos formauit sensus, & perfectū & integrum, & absolutum animal fecit, quod posset & colloqui, & communione substantiæ viro multa afferre solatia. Sed qui de nihilo produxit materiam, multo magis potuit facere de modica materia magnam, non per additionem materiæ aliunde sumptæ, sed per multiplicationem eiusdem materiæ in seipsa.
units.tr: The cause and author of the forming is God himself. For so Moses writes: And again the Lord God said, I will make a helper for man. Likewise: And the Lord God built the rib, which he had taken from the man, into a woman. From this the dignity of woman and of marriage is judged. For works are usually weighed by their causes. Those therefore who forbid marriage despise God. The place in which marriage was instituted, namely paradise, and the very antiquity of the time, also commend it. Observe here too how great was the power of God, the best of architects, who from so small a particle, as if from a beam, built this structure, this helper, that is, the woman, who foreshadowed the Church built upon the rock; and from a rib he fashioned such elegant limbs, formed such senses, and made a perfect, whole and complete living being, able both to converse and, by sharing a common life, to bring the husband many comforts. But he who brought matter out of nothing could much more easily make something great out of a small quantity of matter, not by adding matter taken from elsewhere, but by multiplying that same matter within itself.

units.la: 2 De ratione & impellente causa formationis fœminæ Moses ita scribit: Dixitque Dominus, Non est bonum (bonitate solitudinem non ferente) vt Adam, id est, homo effictus ad imaginem nostram, sit solus: postulat enim caput corpus, maritus sponsam.
units.tr: 2. Moses writes thus about the reason and impelling cause of forming the woman: And the Lord said, It is not good (since goodness does not tolerate solitude) that Adam, that is, man made in our image, should be alone; for the head requires the body, the husband his bride.

units.la: Ratio itaq; formationis mulieris fuit multiplicatio generis humani, quæ non poterat esse per solum masculum: & hoc est quod dicitur, Non est bonum hominem esse solum, quia tolleretur multiplicationis bonū.
units.tr: The reason, then, for forming the woman was the multiplication of the human race, which could not be achieved by the male alone. And this is what is meant by: It is not good for man to be alone, because the good of multiplication would be taken away.

units.la: Etsi autem hæc verba dicta sunt de primo homine siue terreno: tamen intelligi possunt etiam de secundo siue cœlesti homine, id est, domino Christo, cuius typum gessit Adamus, teste apostolo Ephe. 5. Neque id solum, verùm etiam de cæteris cùm terrenis, tum cœlestibus hominibus.
units.tr: Although these words were spoken of the first man, who was earthly, they can also be understood of the second man, who is heavenly, that is, the Lord Christ, whose type Adam bore, as the apostle witnesses in Ephesians 5. And not only this, but also of the other men, both earthly and heavenly.

units.la: Quomodo igitur non fuit bonum, id est, conueniens vel commodum, vt Adam esset solus? hoc est absque adiumento sibi simili, id est vxore propria, quæ est viri bonum, auxilium, gaudium, donum, benedictio, corona, corpus. Hæc enim omnia prædicantur in scriptura de muliere bona. Quia primùm simpliciter [?] & per se non fuisset bonum, pulchrum & decorum, cùm cætera animantia omnia habuerint sua socia atque adiutoria. Quoniam ergo inter cuncta animantia iam formata non inuentum est pro homine adiutorium, quod esset coram eo & simile ei, <bl>(ein gehülff / der zu nächst bey im stunde / oder vmb ihn were / der ihm hülffe sich mehren vnd</bl> <bl>nehren [?] /</bl> βοηθὸς κατ᾽ αὐτὸν, ἢ ὅμοιος αὐτῷ [?]) in illis ipsis vero animantibus ratione carentibus sua paria licuit cognoscere: quomodo non quàm optimè conueniisset etiam Adæ facere adiutorium simile eius? qui tanquam Dominus omnibus imposuit nomina, & vnicuique bestiarum & volucrum & brutorum omnium generi, suum vocabulum iuxta cōcessam sibi sapientiam & illustrem rerum cognitionem distribuit, & hoc rationis & sermonis munere, in quo non postrema pars imaginis diuinæ cernitur, Sirac. 17. Habebat quidem multa adiutoria Adam, veluti omnes creaturas, iumenta, bestias, volucres: sed hæc licet homini ministrent, & nos adiuuent cooperando nobiscum, irrationabilia tamen sunt; & homine longe inferiora, neq; illi similia vel substantia, vel dignitate.
units.tr: How, then, would it not have been good, that is, fitting or convenient, for Adam to be alone? That is, without a helper like himself, namely his own wife, who is a good thing for a man, a help, a joy, a gift, a blessing, a crown, a body. For all these things are said in Scripture of a good wife. For at first it would not have been good in itself, simply and of its own nature, nor beautiful and fitting, since all the other animals had their own companions and helpers. Since, therefore, among all the living creatures already formed no helper for man was found, one that would be before him and like him (<bl>(a helper who stood nearest to him, or beside him, who would help him to multiply and to nourish</bl> βοηθὸς κατ᾽ αὐτὸν, ἢ ὅμοιος αὐτῷ [βoēthos kat' auton, ē homoios autō]), yet in those very creatures lacking reason it was possible to recognise their counterparts. How could it not have been most fitting to make for Adam too a helper like him? He who, as lord, gave names to all, and assigned to each kind of beast and bird and every brute its own appellation, according to the wisdom granted to him and his clear knowledge of things, and by this gift of reason and speech, in which no small part of the divine image is seen (Sirach 17). Adam indeed had many helpers, like all the creatures, beasts of burden, wild animals, birds; but although these serve man, and assist us by working with us, they are nonetheless irrational, and far inferior to man, nor like him either in substance or in dignity.

units.la: Deinde non fuisset Adæ bonum vt solus maneret, quia non fuisset ei iucundum, cum nullum confabulatorem haberet: est autem homo animal sociabile, vt ille ait: adeo vt etiam in coelo nullus cupiat esse solus. vnde quidam vetus Hebræus: Aut societas, aut mors. Et Cicero: Solem è mundo tollere videntur, qui tollunt amicitiam. Et alius Hebræus [?] Id est, Cuicunque non est vxor, is non est homo. Et Mimnermus: [?] q. d. vitam non esse vitam sine dulci coniugio. Item Philippus, [?] Id est,
units.tr: Next, it would not have been good for Adam to remain alone, because it would not have been pleasant for him, having no one to talk with; and man is a sociable animal, as one says: so that no one would even wish to be alone in heaven. Hence an old Hebrew: either fellowship or death. And Cicero: those who take away friendship seem to take the sun out of the world. And another Hebrew saying: whoever has no wife is not a man. And Mimnermus says, in effect, that life is not life without a sweet marriage. Likewise Philippus:

units.la: Dulce merum, dulcis coniunx; mens conscia recti: Nil tribus his cunctis dulcius esse potest.
units.tr: Sweet wine, sweet wife, and a mind conscious of what is right: nothing can be sweeter than these three things.

units.la: Præterea nō fuisset bonū homine mansisse[?] solū. Si enim hoc factū fuisset, vnde nancisci potuissemus Immanuele, qui feinen mulieris existit benefices nos? imo, quomodo potuissemus nos omnes nasci? Nonne enim mulieres genuerunt regè, & omnem populū, qui dominatur mari & terræ, & ex illis nati sunt, & ipsæ educauerunt eos, qui plantauerunt vineas, ex quib. vinū fit: & ipsæ faciunt stolas omnium hominū, & ipsæ faciunt gloriam riam[?] hominibus, & non possunt homines separari à mulieribus: quemadmodum Zorobael ait. 3. Esd. 4.
units.tr: Moreover, it would not have been good for man to remain alone. For if this had happened, from where could we have obtained Immanuel, who was born of a woman for our benefit? Indeed, how could we all have been born? For women bore kings, and every people that rules over sea and land, and they were the ones who nursed those who planted vineyards, from which wine is made; and they make the garments of all men, and they bring glory to men, and men cannot be separated from women; as Zerubbabel says in 3 Esdras 4.

units.la: Sed quomodo hoc dictum, Non est bonum hominem esse solum, ad Christū referri potest? Ioan. 12. ipsemet inquit: Amen amen dico vobis, nisi granum frumenti deiectum in terrâ mortuum fuerit, ipsum solum manet: si vero mortuum fuerit, multū fructū affert.
units.tr: But how can this saying, It is not good for man to be alone, be referred to Christ? In John 12 he himself says: Verily, verily I say unto you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.

units.la: Quomodo ad terrenos homines. 1. Adæ filios? Apostolus dicit, 1. Cor. 7. Satius est matrimonium contrahere, quàm uri[?]. Item: Qui elocat nuptum, bene facit. & 1. Tim. 5. Volo igitur iuniores nubere, liberos gignere, domum administrare, &c. Item, Eccle. 4. Melius est duos esse simul quàm vnum: habent enim emolumentum societatis suæ: si vnus ceciderit, ab altero fulcietur, &c.
units.tr: How does it apply to earthly men, the sons of Adam? The apostle says, 1 Corinthians 7: It is better to marry than to burn. Likewise: He who gives his daughter in marriage does well. And 1 Timothy 5: I desire therefore that the younger women marry, bear children, and rule the household, etc. Likewise, Ecclesiastes 4: Two are better than one, for they have a good reward for their labour; if one falls, the other will lift him up, etc.

units.la: Quomodo ad cœlestes & Christianos homines? Ioan. 15. ait Dominus: Non vos me elegistis, sed ego elegi vos & constitui vos, vt eatis & fructum afferatis, & fructus vester maneat. & Apostolus Heb. 10. Consideremus nos inuicem in hoc, vt prouocemus ad charitatem & bona opera, non deferentes aggregationem nostri mutuam, sicuti mos est nonnullis.
units.tr: How does it apply to heavenly men, that is, Christians? In John 15 the Lord says: You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain. And the apostle in Hebrews 10: Let us consider one another, to provoke one another to love and good works, not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is.

units.la: Porrò dictum illud iam sæpe repetitum, (Non est bonum hominem esse solum) videtur pugnare primùm cum isto Ioann. 6. Secessit Iesus iterum in montem ip.e solus. Deinde cum illo Pauli 1. Cor. 7. Bonum est homini uxorem non attingere. Quod ad primum attinet, sciendum, quod pater filium suum Christum etiam à vulgo hominū discedentem, non reliquit solum, quia quæ placita sunt ei, fecit semper, Ioan. 8. Adhæc nonnunquam expedit uersantibus in hoc mundo, à turba hominum abesse, & secedere cum Christo ad desertum locum seorsim, Matth. 6.14. Quod ad alterum attinet, obseruandæ sunt circumstantiæ rerum & personarum. Deus enim dixit, Non est bonum hominem esse solum, in principio, cum adhuc nullus esset homo in rerum natura præter Adamum solum, in paradiso, in statu innocentiæ, propter propagandum humanum genus. Dei autem seruus Paulus scripsit, Bonum esse homini uxorem non tangere, in ultima hora, in mundo, in statu hominū corrupto, quorum iam magnus erat numerus, propter declinandam afflictionem. Item tamen mox addidit, ne quis putet eum damnare coniugium, Attamen propter stupra uitanda, suam quisq; uxorem habeat, & suum quæque virum habeat. Qua correctione Apostolus seipsum exponit, & docet cui homini bonum sit non tangere mulierem: non omni, sed illi qui non habet opus fornicari: nemo autem opus non habet, nisi qui dono castitatis donatus est. Unde & Origenes Hom. 11. in Exod. Bonum est homini mulierem non tangere, saluo tamen remedio his qui pro infirmitate sua remedio indigent nuptiali. Denique initio bonum absque exceptione viro fuit habere uxorem sibi adiunctam: nunc etiam eatenus bonum, ut interim amarum dulci permixtum sit propter Dei maledictionem.
units.tr: Moreover, the saying that is so often repeated, It is not good for man to be alone, seems first to conflict with John 6, "Jesus again withdrew into the mountain by himself alone," and then with 1 Cor. 7, "It is good for a man not to touch a woman." As to the first, it should be noted that the Father did not leave his Son Christ alone, even though he withdrew from the common crowd, because Christ always did what pleased him (John 8). Moreover, sometimes it is useful for those living in this world to be away from the crowd of men and to withdraw with Christ apart into a desert place (Matt. 14). As to the second, the circumstances of the things and persons must be observed. God said, It is not good for man to be alone, at the beginning, when as yet there was no man in existence except Adam alone, in paradise, in the state of innocence, for the propagation of the human race. But the servant of God, Paul, wrote, "It is good for a man not to touch a woman," in the last hour, in the world, in the corrupted state of men, of whom there was already a great number, in order to avoid distress. Then, however, he at once added, lest anyone think that he condemns marriage: "Nevertheless, because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband." By this qualification the Apostle explains himself, and teaches for which man it is good not to touch a woman: not for everyone, but for the one who has no need to commit fornication; and no one is without this need except the one who has been given the gift of chastity. Hence also Origen, Hom. 11 on Exodus: "It is good for a man not to touch a woman, yet with the remedy of marriage kept for those who, because of their weakness, need that remedy." Finally, at the beginning it was good for the man, without exception, to have a wife joined to him; now too it is good to this extent, that for the time being what is bitter is mixed with what is sweet, on account of God's curse.

units.la: 3 Usus fœminæ & coniugij exponitur his verbis: Faciam ei adiutorium, quod præstò sit illi: quæ loquutio obsequia prompta & expedita in uxore declarat. Huc[?] respexit Apostolus, cùm mulierem propter virum factam dicit, quæ viro obsequiens esset, & ut corpus capiti suo parêret, 1. Corinth. 11.
units.tr: The use of the woman and of marriage is set out in these words: "I will make him a helper who is suitable for him." This phrase declares a ready and useful service in the wife. The Apostle had this in view when he says that the woman was made on account of the man, to be obedient to her husband, and that she should obey her head as the body does (1 Cor. 11).

units.la: Primus igitur usus est, qui cernitur in opera & studijs, quæ uxor marito præstat tanquam corpus capiti. Sciebat enim Deus, hominem per peccatum in labores & omnis generis ærumnas prolapsurum.
units.tr: The first use, therefore, is seen in the work and labours that the wife performs for her husband as the body does for its head. For God knew that man would fall through sin into labours and every kind of hardship.

units.la: Alter in augenda sobole ad conseruandū genus humanum: de quo Genef. 1. Crescite & multiplicamini. Atque is sanè usus sontem administrationis domesticæ, civilis, ecclesiasticæ continet. Est igitur coniugium officina procreandi & multiplicandi generis humani, propter ecclesiam Dei.
units.tr: The second is for increasing offspring, to preserve the human race; of this Gen. 1: "Increase and multiply." This use certainly contains the source of domestic, civil and ecclesiastical government. Marriage is therefore the workshop for producing and multiplying the human race, for the sake of the Church of God.

units.la: Tertius adhibetur ad vitanda stupra & probrosas libidines, 1. Corinth. 7. Prou. 5. Hæc utilitas medicinę loco post vitiatam naturam coniugio accessit: idque aduersus omnes inordinatas & illicitas commixtiones. Bonæ igitur nuptiæ, vt inquit Damascenus lib. 4. de Orthodoxa fide, cap. 25. ob fornicationes, quas præscindunt, rabiem concupiscentiæ per legitimam cōmixtionem[?] non finentes ad iniquos furere actus.
units.tr: The third is employed to avoid fornication and shameful lusts (1 Cor. 7; Prov. 5). This benefit was added to marriage as a kind of medicine after nature had been corrupted, and it works against all disorderly and unlawful unions. Good marriage, therefore, as Damascene says in Book 4 of On the Orthodox Faith, chapter 25, cuts off the fornications, and by lawful union does not allow the raging of concupiscence to rush into wicked acts.

units.la: Quarrus usus mysticus est, qui versatur in contemplatione arctissimæ societatis, quæ inter Deum & populum suum exstitit, seu coniunctionis Christi & ecclesiæ, quam nobis arctissimum hoc vxoris & mariti vinculum repræsentat, de quo Ephes. 5. Nam in pio & casto coniugio præcipuè florent ac dominantur 1. amor mutuus, verus, ardens: 2. fides coniugalis, vt in mutuo amore acquiescant, nec appetant alios, vel alias. 3. societas bonorum & ærumnarum: 4. generatio. 5. defensio. 6. ἐπιείκεια[?] tolerans infirmitates & næuos concordiæ causa. Hæ sex res, quas merito neruos atque artus coniugij possumus nominare, teste Dauide Chytræo, & coniugij adiuncta, (vt Mathias Flacius vocat) etiam in filio Dei & ecclesia simili fœdere copulatis perspicuè lucent.
units.tr: The fourth use is mystical, and it lies in the contemplation of the most intimate fellowship that existed between God and his people, or of the union of Christ and the Church, which this most close bond of wife and husband represents to us (Eph. 5). For in a pious and chaste marriage six things especially flourish and prevail: (1) true, mutual, ardent love; (2) marital faithfulness, so that the spouses rest in mutual love and do not seek others, either men or women; (3) fellowship in goods and in hardships; (4) generation; (5) defence; (6) forbearance [ἐπιείκεια], enduring infirmities and faults for the sake of harmony. These six things, which we may rightly call the sinews and joints of marriage, according to David Chytraeus, and which are joined to marriage (as Matthias Flacius calls them), shine out clearly also in the Son of God and in the Church, who are joined by a like covenant.

units.la: 4 Modum formandæ fœminæ exponit Moses, quum ait: Et fecit illabi Dominus deus soporem in Adam )(.[?]i.somnum profundum: quia vnam ex costis illius ablaturus erat: vt ne sentiendo dolorem, mulieri ex se formatæ, postea doloris memor, infensus fieret: & vt diuinæ simul potentiæ opus mirabile ostenderetur, quæ hominis dormientis
units.tr: 4. Moses sets out the manner of forming the woman when he says: "And the Lord God caused a deep sleep [soporem] to fall upon Adam," that is, a profound sleep, because he was about to take one of his ribs, so that the woman formed from him would not feel pain and, remembering the pain later, become hostile; and so that the wonderful work of divine power would be shown at the same time, a power that opened the side of a man asleep, and yet did not rouse him from the rest of sleep.

units.la: Notes: the rest of the sentence aster "dormientis" continues on the next page as the catchword latus aperuit,nec eum tamen à quiete soporis excitauit.
units.tr: The rest of the sentence, after "asleep," continues on the next page, with the catchword "opened his side, yet did not rouse him from the rest of sleep."

units.la: Et obdormiuit ) Si alterum Adam spectes, ex hoc dum in cruce interquiescit, cœlestis Eua expromitur.
units.tr: And he fell asleep. If you regard the other Adam, then from this, while he rests on the cross, the heavenly Eve is brought forth.

units.la: Tulitque vnam ex costis illius ) Necessarium erat ( vt scribit Glycas par. 1. Annal. ) Euam non itidem,vt in Adamo factum erat, è terra prouenire, sed ex ipsa potius Adami essentia: quo hac ratione mutuus amor coniugibus inderetur. Pars autem robustior in hoc ędificium sumitur,quod quantum onus erat laturum,non fugiebat architectum. Genef. 3. enim dicit, Cum dolore paries filios. Non formauit Dominus mulierem de pede, quia non erat serua,& quia maritus non debet esse tyrannus erga vxorem (vt etiam habetur Dist. 18. lib. 2. Sentent.) ὡς λέων ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ αὐτῆς, Ecclesi. 4. nec de capite,quia non erat viri domina: & quia mulier non debet αὐθεντεῖν ἀνδρός 1. Timoth. 2. sed de costa, quia erat viri socia futura, ἡ συγκληρονόμος χάριτος ζωῆς, 1. Pet. 3. Porrò sicut vnam costarum tulit Dominus,sic vna tantum est ecclesia, vnumque corpus, 4. Efd. 5. Ephef. 4.
units.tr: And he took one of his ribs. This was necessary (as Glycas writes in Part 1 of his Annals), so that Eve would not come from the earth in the same way as had happened with Adam, but rather from the very substance of Adam, so that by this means mutual love would be implanted in the spouses. The stronger part is taken for this building, and the architect did not shrink from the burden it was going to bear. For Gen. 3 says, "In pain you shall bring forth children." The Lord did not form the woman from the foot, because she was not to be a servant, and because a husband ought not to be a tyrant towards his wife (as is also found in Dist. 18, Book 2 of the Sentences), like a lion in her house (Ecclus. 4), nor from the head, because she was not to be the lord of the man, and because a woman ought not to usurp authority over a man [αὐθεντεῖν ἀνδρός] (1 Tim. 2), but from the rib, because she was to be the companion of the man, a fellow heir of the grace of life [ἡ συγκληρονόμος χάριτος ζωῆς] (1 Pet. 3). Moreover, just as the Lord took one rib, so there is only one Church and one body (4 Ezra 5; Eph. 4).

units.la: Et clausit carnem pro ea ) vt ne posset discusso somno, quod factum erat, ex vacuitate sentire : & ne ob ablationem tristitia assiceretur. In Adamo altero parem commutationem reperias. Quid is communicat vxori suæ? quam firmitatem? quod robur? Nos legimus Iesa. 53. Si posuerit pro peccáto animam suam. &1. Corinth. 1. Qui factus fuit nobis sapientia à Deo, iustitia, & sanctificatio, & redemptio. Sed quae vicissim reddit sponsa: Legimus in eodem Prophetae capite, Vere languores nostros ipse tulit, & dolores nostros ipse portauit. Poterat Deus (Augustino teste tract. 15, in Ioan.) posse os reddere, poterat ad faciendam mulierem nō costā, sed carnem detrahere: sed detraxit os, & detracto osse, formata est mulier, & in locum osis caro adimpleta est. Quid igitur significauit? Facta est mulier in costa tanquā fortis: factus est Adam in carne tanquam infirmus. Christus est & ecclesia. Illius infirmitas nostra est fortitudo.
units.tr: And he closed up the flesh in its place. This was so that, once the sleep was broken, she could not feel from emptiness what had been done, and so that she would not be affected with sadness because of the removal. In the second Adam you will find a similar exchange. What does he share with his wife? What firmness? What strength? We read in Isaiah 53: "If he shall give his soul for sin," and in 1 Cor. 1: "who was made to us wisdom from God, righteousness, sanctification and redemption." But what the bride gives back in return? We read in the same chapter of the prophet: "Surely he has borne our infirmities, and carried our sorrows." God could (on the testimony of Augustine, Tract. 15 on John) have restored the bone; he could have taken flesh rather than a rib to make the woman; but he took the bone, and with the bone taken, the woman was formed, and in the place of the bone the flesh was filled up. What, then, did this signify? The woman was made from the rib as the strong part; Adam was made in flesh as the weak part. Christ is the head, and the Church is his body. His infirmity is our strength.

units.la: Et ædificauit Dominus deus costam, quā acceperat de homine in mulierem) Ædificata autem Heua dicitur à costa maritali, quae instar ædificij sic parata fit, ut ad concipiendum fœtum, & eum gestandum, pariendum que apta esset. Eodem tropo liberi בנים[?] dicuntur, quasi parentum structura & ædificium: & fulturę generis, familiam ædificantes. Deinde quia figura fuit ecclesiae Christi, cui Ædificandi verbum non raro attribuitur, ut Matth. 16. 1. Corinth. 3. Ephes. 4. Quanquam hoc verbo significatur etiam ex illa coniunctione maris & fœmellae, ædificari familias, ex familijs ciuitates, & inde regna. Rerumpublicarum. n. & imperiorum feminarium est coniugium. Sunt autem nunc in utroque latere viri & mulieris costæ duodecim. Ideò antea verisimile est in Adamo tredecim iuga costarum fuisse, ex quo Heua ædi-ficata est: iuxta quorundam sententiam.
units.tr: And the Lord God built up the rib that he had taken from the man into a woman. Eve is said to be built up from the husband's rib, which is prepared, like a building, so as to be fit for conceiving, carrying and bearing the offspring. By the same figure, children are called "sons" [בנים], as it were the structure and edifice of their parents, and the supports of their stock, building up the family. Further, because this was a figure of the Church of Christ, to which the word "to build" is not seldom applied (Matt. 16; 1 Cor. 3; Eph. 4), although by this word is also signified that from that union of male and female families are built up, from families cities, and from these kingdoms. For marriage is the seedbed of commonwealths and empires. Moreover, there are now twelve ribs on each side of the man and woman. Therefore it is likely, according to the opinion of some, that in Adam, from whom Eve was built, there were formerly thirteen pairs of ribs.

units.la: 5 Author coniugij siue causa efficiens fœderis coniugalis indicatur his verbis: Et adduxit eam ad hominem illum. Quis? Dominus deus. (à quo uxor bona teste etiam Salomone, Pro. 19.) quam? mulierem Heuam. ad quem? virum Adamum: ostendens quòd propter illum istam condiderit. Hæc sunt sponsalia & sacra fœdera, quibus Deus fœminam tanquam paranymphus seu nymphagogus & pronubus (ita enim Theodoretus Deum vocat in Epito. diuin. decretorum) cum marito coniunxit, commendans illam Adamo, ut futuram generandæ, educandæque sobolis coniugem. Non enim legitur hic: Et rapuit ad se Adamus Heuam: sed, Adduxit Deus: quod significans Dominus dicit Matth. 19. Quos Deus coniunxit, homo ne separet. Est igitur coniugium indissolubilis coniunctio vnius maris & vnius fœminæ, quæ legitimè coniungi possunt, instituta diuinitus, ut agnoscamus Deum esse mentem castam, & in castitate ei seruiamus, & hoc modo propagato genere humano colligatur æterna ecclesia Deo.
units.tr: 5 The author of marriage, or the efficient cause of the marriage covenant, is indicated by these words: "And he brought her to that man." Who? The Lord God (from whom a good wife comes, as Solomon also testifies, Prov. 19). Whom? The woman Eve. To whom? The man Adam, showing that he created her for his sake. These are the betrothal and sacred covenants by which God, as the paranymph or matchmaker and bridesman (for so Theodoret calls God in the Epitome of the Divine Decrees), joined the woman to her husband, commending her to Adam as the future partner for begetting and rearing offspring. For it is not read here, "And Adam snatched Eve to himself," but "God brought her." The Lord signifies this when he says in Matthew 19: "What God has joined together, let not man put asunder." Marriage is therefore an indissoluble union of one male and one female, who may lawfully be joined, instituted by God so that we may acknowledge God to be a chaste mind and serve him in chastity; and in this way, with the human race propagated, the eternal Church is gathered to God.

units.la: 6 De coniunctione & arcta familiaritate viri & uxoris, & communione omnium rerū inter ipsos, Adamus ita loquitur, accepta prophetica gratia: Hac vice) id est, nunc facta est ex viro mulier, posthac non sic erit: sed ex muliere vir, imo non ex muliere, sed ex utriusque cooperatione, 1. Cor. 11. vel, hac vice, subaudi, deprehendo ac video, vel agnosco Deum mihi fecisse auxilium simile mihi, per q; omnia mihi respondens. Est enim os, &c.
units.tr: 6 Concerning the union and close intimacy of husband and wife, and the sharing of all things between them, Adam speaks thus, having received prophetic grace: "This time" (that is, now a woman has been made from a man; from now on it will not be so, but a man from a woman, or rather not from a woman but from the joint cooperation of both, 1 Cor. 11). Or "this time" should be understood as: I perceive and see, or I acknowledge, that God has made for me a helper like myself, answering me in all things. "For she is bone of my bones," etc.

units.la: Os de ossibus meis) Sed unde aut quomodo Adam cognovit eam pro osse suo? utique doctrina Spiritus sancti afflatus.
units.tr: "Bone of my bones." But whence or how did Adam know her to be his own bone? Surely by the teaching of the afflatus of the Holy Spirit.

units.la: Et caro de carne mea) Costa enim illa, de qua formata est mulier, non fuit sumpta de latere Adami nuda, sed cum aliqua carne. Quemadmodum autem Adamus agnovit Evam ꝑ carne sua: ita Christus seipsum per persecutione pati dicit, cū patitur ecclesia. Act. 9.
units.tr: "And flesh of my flesh." For that rib from which the woman was formed was not taken from Adam's side bare, but with some flesh. Just as Adam recognised Eve as his own flesh, so Christ says that he himself suffers through persecution when the Church suffers (Acts 9).

units.la: Haec vocabitur virago) Mulierem ut in ceterarum rerum, ita etiam in nominis viri venit communionem, quae ab אִישׁ, id est, viro אִשָּׁה quasi vira, vel virissa, ἀνδρίς, ut Aquila vertit, denominata fit.
units.tr: "She shall be called woman." The woman, as with other things, so also in the name, shares in the man's; she is named from ish, that is, "man" (אִישׁ), ishshah (אִשָּׁה), as it were "maness" or "female man," androis (ἀνδρίς), as Aquila translates.

units.la: Eo quod de viro sumpta sit ipsa) iterum ablationem costae insinuat. huc spectans Apostolus, dicit: Non enim est vir ex muliere, sed mulier ex viro. Hinc quoque illa viri gloria, quem veneretur, dicitur, ut vir Dei gloria quem honoret, & cuius maiestatem praedicet.
units.tr: "Because she was taken out of man." He again points to the removal of the rib, to which the Apostle looks when he says: "For man is not from woman, but woman from man." Hence also that glory of man which she venerates, as the Lord's glory which she honours and whose majesty she proclaims.

units.la: Propterea deferet vir patrem suum & matrem suam) privatim habitaturus, nec non incestam libidinem vitaturus. Relinquet enim maritus parentes, non quantum ad dilectionem, quia filius non potest denegare parentes: sed quantum ad cohabitationem, quia filius cum est vxoratus, statim est emancipatus, & necesse habet prouidere sibi & vxori & familiae.
units.tr: "Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother," that he may live privately and avoid unchaste lust. For the husband leaves his parents, not as regards love, since a son cannot deny his parents, but as regards living together; for a son, once married, is at once emancipated and must provide for himself, his wife and his household.

units.la: Et hærebit cum vxore sua) atque adeo fidem seruabit vxori suae. Non dicit cum vxoribus: nec nisi vna Heua exprompta est ex Adami costis. videris Chrysostom. Tom. 2. pag. 130. Hom. 38. de Inuent. sanctæ crucis. Verbo autem Adhærendi, intima viri & vxoris coniunctio significatur, de qua Sapientia Ecclesi. 25. Tribus rebus exornor, & apud Dominum & apud homines venusta efficior: eæ sunt, fratrum concordia, propinquorum amicitia, & vxor atque vir inter se consentientes: vel, vt Græcus textus habet, ἀνὴρ ἑαυτοῖς συμπεριφερόμενοι [?] & Ecclesi. 40. Amicus & socius commodè conueniunt: sed vtrumque antecellit vxor iuncta viro. Hinc de Isaaco & Rebecca legitur, Gene. 24. Qui introduxit eam in tabernaculum Sarae matris suae, & accepit eam vxorem: & in tantum dilexit eam, vt dolorem, qui ex morte matris eius acciderat, temperaret. Vt autem nullum in humanis arctius vinculum coniugio, cuius causa parentes quoque homo relinquere iubetur: ita non arctum modo, sed inseparabile est fœdus, quo nos sibi deuinxit Deus, à cuius dilectione nihil nos separare potest,
units.tr: "And he shall cleave to his wife." And so he will keep faith with his wife. He does not say "to wives," nor was more than one Eve taken from Adam's ribs. See Chrysostom, vol. 2, p. 130, Homily 38, on the Invention of the Holy Cross. By the word "cleave" is signified the closest union of husband and wife, of which Ecclesiasticus 25 says: "Three things I am adorned with, and I am made lovely before the Lord and before men: the concord of brothers, the friendship of kinsfolk, and a wife and husband agreeing with one another"; or, as the Greek text has it, "husband and wife conducting themselves together" [?]. And Ecclesiasticus 40: "Friend and companion meet fittingly, but a wife joined to a husband surpasses both." Hence it is read of Isaac and Rebekah, Genesis 24: "He brought her into the tent of Sarah his mother, and took her as wife, and loved her so much that he eased the sorrow which had come upon him from the death of his mother." And as there is no closer bond among men than marriage, for the sake of which a man is commanded to leave even his parents, so the covenant by which God has bound us to himself is not only close but inseparable; nothing can separate us from his love.

units.la: Eruntq; in carne unam) vel,in carne una: id est,officia dilectionis mutua exhibebunt. Vir igitur si diligat uxorem, carnem suam dilexerit:& eam si odiat, se oderit. Qui igitur inuisam[?] Christus sponsam suam odio habeat? in quo typi corpus & veritas cernitur. Notandum autem quod haec verba, ἔσονται εἰ[?] δύο εἰς σάρκα μίαν (Sic.n.L X X. verterunt)in Euangelicis scriptis inueniantur ad diuersas causas translata. Primum quidem Christus ea usurpat Matt.19. ad probandum,quòd nō liceat uxorem quavis de causa, more Iudaeis recepto, repudiare,& alteram in matrimonium ducere. Haec insignis doctrina est. Exijsdem verbis Apostolus ad Eph.5. ratiocinatur,arctissimam esse mariti & uxoris coniunctionem,charitatemque indissolubilem. Ubi sanè egregia institutio commendatioque est vitae coniugalis proposita. At 1. Cor. 6. colligit ex'illis verbis,eum qui scortatur, membra sua facere membra meretricis. Faciunt igitur eadem verba ad morum correctionem. Hoc autem pacto, ex quacunque historia, multiplex & varia eruditio spiritualis, ab ijs qui diligentes sunt,colligi potest.
units.tr: "And they shall be one flesh," or "in one flesh," that is, they will show one another the duties of mutual love. If a husband loves his wife, he has loved his own flesh; and if he hates her, he hates himself. How then does Christ hate his spouse, whom he has not hated, in whom the body of the type and the truth is discerned? It should be noted that these words, "They shall be two in one flesh" (for so the Seventy translated), are found in the Gospel writings applied to different purposes. First, Christ himself uses them in Matthew 19 to prove that it is not lawful, for any cause, to put away one's wife, as the Jews commonly did, and take another in marriage. This is a remarkable teaching. The Apostle reasons from the same words in Ephesians 5 that the union of husband and wife is most intimate and their love indissoluble; there, surely, an excellent instruction and commendation of married life is set forth. But in 1 Corinthians 6 he infers from those words that he who joins himself to a harlot makes his members the members of a harlot. These words therefore serve for the correction of morals. In this way, from any history whatever, a manifold and varied spiritual instruction can be gathered by those who are diligent.

units.la: 7 Porrò de nuditate Adami & Euae in paradiso Moses ita loquitur: Fuerunt autem ambo illi nudi, homo, inquam, ille, & uxor eius,& non erubescebant:vel, non confusibi les se reddebát. Peccato enim & præuaricatione nondum præsente, gloria, quæ supernè venerat, vestiti erant: & quasi angeli versabantur in paradiso, non concupiscentijs flagrantes, non ab aliis affectionibus infestati, non naturæ necessitatibus obnoxij: sed prorsus incorruptibiles & immortales conditi, neque vel vestimentorum amictu ibi egebant, ut Chrysostomus scribit. Præclarus sane fructus innocentiæ est bene sibi conscia nuditas, & animus pudoris nescius. Ac quoniam hodie videmus neq; pueros ex iua nuditate erubescere, demus operam ut quoque simus pueri, non quidem sensibus, sed malitia, ne pudefiamus, quando cuique reddet secundum opera sua Dominus Iesus, qui discipulis suis dixit, Matthæi decimo octauo: Amen dico vobis, nisi conuersi fueritis, & efficiamini sicut pueri, non ingrediemini in regnum cœlorum: de cuius possessione vtinam nostrūm nullus depellatur, Amen.
units.tr: 7 Moreover, Moses speaks thus of the nakedness of Adam and Eve in paradise: "Now both of them were naked, that man, I say, and his wife, and they were not ashamed" (or, "they did not make themselves confused"). For, sin and transgression not yet being present, they were clothed with the glory which had come down from above; and they moved about in paradise like angels, not burning with lusts, not troubled by other passions, not subject to the necessities of nature, but created utterly incorruptible and immortal, and they had no need there even of the covering of clothes, as Chrysostom writes. Surely the fruit of innocence is a nakedness conscious of itself and a mind ignorant of shame. And since today we see that even children do not blush at their nakedness, let us take care that we too be children, not indeed in our senses but in malice, so that we are not put to shame when the Lord Jesus renders to each one according to his works, who said to his disciples in Matthew 18: "Truly I say to you, unless you turn and become like children, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven." May none of us be cast out from the possession of that kingdom, Amen.

units.la: CONCIO II.
units.tr: SERMON II.

units.la: Genes. 3.
units.tr: Genesis 3.

units.la: MVLIERI quoque dixit: Multiplicando multiplicabo ærumnas tuas, & conceptus tuos. In dolore paries filios, & ad virum tuum desiderium tuum, & ipse dominabitur tui. Ada vero dixit, Quia audisti vocem vxoris tuæ, & comedi disti de ligno, ex quo præceperam tibi ne comederes, maledicta terra propter te, in laboribus comedes ex ea cunctis diebus vitæ tuæ: spinas & tribulos germinabit tibi, & comedes herbas terræ. In sudore vultus tui vesceris pane, donec reuertaris in terram, de qua sumptus es: quia puluis es, & in pulverem reuerteris.
units.tr: To the woman also he said: I will greatly multiply your pain and your conception. In sorrow you shall bring forth children, and your desire shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you. But to Adam he said: Because you have listened to the voice of your wife, and have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you that you should not eat, the ground is cursed for your sake; in toil you shall eat of it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles shall it bring forth to you, and you shall eat the herbs of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread, until you return to the ground from which you were taken, for you are dust, and to dust you shall return.

units.la: 1 Est hoc in more positum institutoque maiorum, vt testari volentibus coram ecclesia Christiana, se coniuges esse, præleguntur quædam capita ex verbo Dei, ne videlicet illud vitæ genus honestum & laudabile ingrediantur absque scientia & intellectu Dei & verbi eius, quemadmodum infideles facere solent: de quibus Raphael angelus Tob. 6. Hi namque qui coniugium (inquit) ita fuscipiunt, vt Deum à se & à sua mente excludant, & suæ libidini ita vacent, sicut equus & mulus, quibus non est intellectus, habet potestatem dæmonium super eos.
units.tr: 1 It is the custom and practice of our ancestors that, when those who wish to declare themselves married stand before the Christian congregation, certain chapters of the Word of God are read beforehand. This is so that they do not enter upon that honourable and praiseworthy way of life without the knowledge and understanding of God and his Word, as unbelievers are wont to do. Of such people the angel Raphael speaks in Tobit 6: "Those who take marriage in such a way that they shut God out from themselves and from their minds, and give themselves over to their lust like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding, the demon has power over them."

units.la: 2 Sunt autem sex capita, quæ illis potissimum proponuntur: idque à ministris Ecclesiæ: quos ante 1000. [?] annos publico ritu nouos coniuges coniunxisse, ex Nicephoro lib.14.cap.55 apparet. vbi Synefius dicit, Deum & leges, & sacram Theophili manum, vxorem sibi dedisse. Idem constat ex Martini decreto Distin. 24. capite Sponsus. Vbi iubentur sponsi & sponsæ in templum venire, & à sacerdote benedictionem accipere.
units.tr: 2 Six chapters are chiefly set before them, and this is done by the ministers of the Church. That ministers used to join newly married couples in a public rite about 1000 [?] years ago appears from Nicephorus, book 14, chapter 55, where Synesius says that God gave the bride to the bridegroom through laws and through the sacred hand of Theophilus. The same is evident from the decree of Martin, Distinction 24, the chapter Sponsus, where bridegrooms and brides are ordered to come into the temple and receive a blessing from the priest.

units.la: Primum est de institutione matrimonij, cuius author Deus existit, teste Mose, Genesis secundo cap. Idem est qui & amorem mutuum in cordibus nubentium excitat, Gen.24. Prou. 18.19.Tob.3.Ecclesi.26.
units.tr: The first concerns the institution of marriage, whose author is God, as Moses testifies in Genesis, chapter 2. He it is who also kindles mutual love in the hearts of those who marry: Genesis 24; Proverbs 18–19; Tobit 3; Ecclesiasticus 26.

units.la: Alterum de arctissima & indissolubili familiaritate & coniunctione mariti & vxoris: cuius Christus meminit contra Pharisæos, Matthæi 19.
units.tr: The second concerns the closest and indissoluble fellowship and union of husband and wife, which Christ mentions against the Pharisees, Matthew 19.

units.la: Tertium de præceptis Dei indicantibus officium, quod vterque coniugum facere tenetur: qualia habentur, Exod. 20. Ephes. 5. Colos. 3. 1. Pet. 3.
units.tr: The third concerns the precepts of God that set out the duty which each of the spouses is bound to perform. Such precepts are found in Exodus 20; Ephesians 5; Colossians 3; 1 Peter 3.

units.la: Quartum de benedictione, qua benedixit Dominus masculo & fœminæ, Genes.1.
units.tr: The fourth concerns the blessing with which the Lord blessed the male and the female, Genesis 1.

units.la: Quintum, de cruce & afflictione, quam post peccatum imposuit Deus in matrimonio collocatis: de qua hoc loco, & 1. Corin. 7. vbi dicit Apostolus: Attamen afflictionem in carne habituri sunt huiusmodi. Et Genes. 25. Vbi Rebecca grauida inquit, Si sic mihi futurum erat, quid necesse fuit concipere?[?]
units.tr: The fifth concerns the cross and affliction which God laid upon those joined in marriage after sin. Of this we speak in this place, and in 1 Corinthians 7, where the Apostle says: "Yet such people shall have affliction in the flesh." Also Genesis 25, where Rebecca, being pregnant, says: "If it was to be so with me, why was it necessary to conceive?" [?]

units.la: Sextum, de consolatione, quam sub cruce positi accipere debent, ne sub ea despondeant animum atqz pereant. Christus enim peccatum, propter quod onus afflictionū nobis incumbit, in fe suscepit, & sua cruce nostrâ, siquidem credimus in eum, benedixit & fanctificauit. Vnde Dauid Psalmo centesimo vigefimooctauo: Beati omnes qui timent Dominum, qui ambulant in vijs eius: Labores manuum tuarum manducabis, beatus es, & bene tibi erit. Vxor tua sicut vitis fructifera, &c. Item Paulus, 1. Timoth. 2. Mulier seducta, obnoxia facta est transgressioni: salua tamen fiet per generationem liberorü, fi manserit in fide ac dilectione, & sanctificatione cum castitate. Hinc Chryfoftom. Hom. 5. de Poenitent. O magnum donum, quod in poenam dedit Deus, in salutem vertit: peccatum tristitiam peperit, tristitia peccatum contriuit: & quemadmodum vermis in ligno natus idipsum comminuit: sic tristitia de peccato nata, peccatum comminuit per poenitentiam inducta.
units.tr: The sixth concerns the consolation which those placed under the cross ought to receive, so that they do not lose heart under it and perish. For Christ took upon himself the sin on account of which the burden of afflictions rests upon us, and by his cross he blessed and sanctified our cross, provided we believe in him. Hence David in Psalm 128: "Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways. You shall eat the labour of your hands; you are blessed, and it shall be well with you. Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine," etc. Likewise Paul, 1 Timothy 2: "The woman, having been deceived, was made subject to transgression; yet she shall be saved through the bearing of children, if they continue in faith and love and holiness with chastity." Hence Chrysostom, Homily 5 on Repentance: "O great gift, which God gave as a punishment and turned to salvation! Sin brought forth sorrow, and sorrow crushed sin; and just as the worm born in the wood crushes the wood itself, so sorrow born of sin crushes sin, when it is brought on through repentance."

units.la: Cæterum penultimi capitis hic præcipuè fit mentio, nempe necessitatis & afflictionis, quam habituros coniuges Scriptura prædixit. Mulieri enim multa sunt patienda ante partum, in partu, & post partum. Viro, in colenda terra infelici: quæ aut spinas proseret, aut victum quidem, sed non sine labore & sudore: & in quam tandem fit conuertendus. Ad mulierem enim, inquit Dominus: Multiplicando multiplicabo dolorem tuum) id est, Ego quidem volebam te citra dolore & ærumnam viuere, liberam ab omni moerore fore & tristitia, omnique voluptate affluere:at quia non usa es ut oportet tanta prosperitate, sed affluentia bonorum eo te ingratitudinis adduxit: propterea tibi frenum impono, ut ne amplius lasciuias, ad tristitias & gemitus te condemnans. Anadiplosis Hebraica certitudinem & ærumnarum vim declarat, quibus hucusque nihil decedit, constanter durante muliebri dolore per menses, conceptus, partus, & liberorum educationem. Proponitur autem primo summa, more Hebraico: quam deinde sacra narratio per partes exponit.
units.tr: Moreover, it is chiefly the last of these chapters that is mentioned here, namely the necessity and affliction which the Scripture foretold that the spouses would have. For the woman must suffer many things before childbirth, in childbirth, and after childbirth. The man must suffer in cultivating an unfruitful earth, which will either put forth thorns or yield food, but not without labour and sweat, and into which he is at last to be turned back. For the Lord says to the woman: "I will greatly multiply your sorrow." That is: I indeed wished you to live without pain and toil, free from all grief and sadness, and abounding in every pleasure; but because you have not used such great prosperity as you ought, and the abundance of good things has led you into ingratitude, therefore I put a bridle upon you, so that you may no longer indulge in wantonness, condemning you to sorrows and groans. The Hebrew anadiplosis declares the certainty and the force of these troubles, which have not lessened up to now, since the woman's pain constantly endures through the months, the conception, the birth, and the upbringing of children. The sum is first stated, in the Hebrew manner, and then the sacred narrative sets it out part by part.

units.la: Et conceptum tuum) τὸν γεννησμὸν σου [?]:dolorem ex conceptu natum. Totum tempus significatur nomine conceptus, quo in utero fœtus fertur: omnisque angustia, quam habet mulier à conceptu usq; ad partum. Tempus sanè plenum molestia & cruciatu. Declarant hunc capitis dolores, deliquia animi, lassitudines, oculorum vertigines, fastidium in cibis, redundantia stomachi, crurum & inguinum tumor, &c. Gravior tamen fœminæ, quàm maris conceptus. Hæc sunt initia generis humani post casum.
units.tr: "And your conception": [τὸν γεννησμὸν σου] [?]: the pain arising from conception. The whole time is signified by the word "conception," during which the foetus is carried in the womb, and all the distress that a woman has from conception to birth. It is indeed a time full of discomfort and torment. These are declared by headaches, fainting fits, weariness, dizziness of the eyes, loathing of food, overflow of the stomach, swelling of the legs and groin, and so on. Yet the conception of a woman is more burdensome than that of a man. These are the beginnings of the human race after the fall.

units.la: In dolore paries filios) Conceptum partus sequitur, altera miseriæ pars, cuius magnitudinem res ipsa declarat: & reliqua scriptura, quæ maximam quamque afflictionem cum parturiendi labore comparat, ut Iesa. 13. Ierem. 6. 48. Ezech. 30. Hose. 13. Mich. 4. 5. Iohan. 16. Itaque apud Græcos, ὠδὶν[?] dolor & partus est.
units.tr: "In sorrow you shall bring forth children": After conception follows the second part of misery, the greatness of which the thing itself declares. The rest of Scripture also compares every great affliction with the labour of childbirth, as in Isaiah 13; Jeremiah 6 and 48; Ezekiel 30; Hosea 13; Micah 4–5; John 16. Hence among the Greeks [ὠδίν] means both pain and childbirth.

units.la: Et ad virum tuum erit appetitus tuus) id est, pendebis à viro tuo: sub viri potestate eris: viro obedies explens eius cupiditates. Loquutio Hebraeis frequens, desiderium sive appetitum alicuius ad alterum esse, pro alterius arbitrio subiectum esse. Significatur item mulieri omne praesidium in viro, ad quem velut ad portum confugiat, positum esse. Huc spectasse videntur & Graeci in vo-ce ἀποστροφή[?]. Tertia igitur divinae sententiae pars est, ut ὑπάνδρος[?], i. viro subdita sit mulier, non libera aut proprij iuris, ut sequitur.
units.tr: "And your desire shall be toward your husband": that is, you shall depend upon your husband; you will be under the power of your husband, obeying him and fulfilling his desires. It is a common expression among the Hebrews that a person's desire or appetite is toward another, meaning to be subject to the other's will. It is also signified that for the woman every refuge lies in her husband, to whom she may flee as to a harbour. The Greeks also seem to have had this in view in the word [ἀποστροφή]. The third part of the divine sentence, then, is that the woman should be [ὑπάνδρος], that is, subject to her husband, not free or of her own right, as follows.

units.la: Et ipse dominabitur tibi) Ciuili, non tyrannico imperio: cum scientia, ut caput. Contra naturae igitur legem, & hanc in mulierem latam sententiam, foeminae imperium, sive publicum, sive privatum obtinent.
units.tr: "And he shall rule over you": by civil, not tyrannical, government, with knowledge, as the head. Against the law of nature, then, and contrary to this sentence pronounced upon the woman, women hold dominion, whether public or private.

units.la: Ad Adam vero dixit(qui nullam veniam; culpa in mulierem reiecta, assequutus est.) quia audisti vocem) qui meam audire debebas, ut gloria & imago mea.
units.tr: "But to Adam he said" (who obtained no pardon, since he threw the blame upon the woman): "Because you have listened" (you ought to have listened to me, as my glory and image).

units.la: Uxoris tuae) quam verbo meo regi à te oportebat, non ei tibi contra mandatum meum obsequendum.
units.tr: "To the voice of your wife" (whom you ought to have ruled by my word, and not obeyed against my command).

units.la: Et comedisti de arbore, de qua praecepi tibi, dicens: Non comedes ex ea) Indicatur causa miseriae, qua Dominus etiam afficere solet eos, quibus peccata ignouit, ut discant se & peccasse, & peccata odisse.
units.tr: "And have eaten of the tree of which I commanded you, saying, You shall not eat of it": the cause of the misery is pointed out, with which the Lord is also accustomed to afflict those whose sins he has forgiven, so that they may learn both that they have sinned and that they should hate sin.

units.la: Maledicta est humus propter te).i. propter inobedientiam tuā. Explicatur pœna talionis, terrā rebellē fore Adamo, qui se Deo rebellem præstitisset. In dolore comedes eam) id est, quicquid ex ea natum fuerit.
units.tr: "The ground is cursed for your sake": that is, on account of your disobedience. The punishment of retaliation is explained: the earth would be rebellious to Adam, who had shown himself rebellious to God. "In sorrow you shall eat of it": that is, whatever is produced from it.

units.la: Omnibus diebus vitæ tuæ) Explicat ordine partes maledictionis. Complectitur hæc sententia Dei, molestias & labores, dolores varij generis, infirmitates, morbos, senium, & id genus mala, quæ opponuntur voluptati Edenis. Sed tolerabilem reddere debet hanc calamitatem, partim æqua sententia Dei in peccatum pronunciata, partim suturi seculi, quam expectamus, gloria & integritas, quæ his malis succedet, veluti Dominus his verbis promittit, Beati qui lugent, quoniam ipsi consolationem accipient.
units.tr: "All the days of your life": he sets out in order the parts of the curse. This sentence of God comprehends troubles and labours, pains of various kinds, infirmities, diseases, old age, and evils of this sort, which are opposed to the pleasure of Eden. But this calamity ought to be made tolerable, partly by the just sentence of God pronounced upon sin, and partly by the glory and wholeness of the age to come, which we await and which will succeed these evils, as the Lord promises in these words: "Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall receive comfort."

units.la: Et spina atque tribulū)ꝓ fructiferis arboribꝰ.
units.tr: "And thorns and thistles will spring up among the fruit-bearing trees."

units.la: Faciet crescere tibi: & manducabis herbas agri) Huc referuntur olera & legumina, pisum, fabæ, milium, far, triticum, hordeum. Cum hac sententia dei, voluptuariorum luxus pugnat, ut quæ nos ad frugalitatem inuitet, & curam de lautiore victu eximat.
units.tr: "It will make grow for you, and you will eat the herbs of the field." Here belong pot-herbs and pulses: peas, beans, millet, spelt, wheat and barley. This saying of God stands against the luxury of the pleasure-seekers, since it invites us to frugality and removes anxious care for a more sumptuous diet.

units.la: In sudore vultus tui vescéris pane) latissimé patet is sudor & labor. Non.n.unum muneris genus viro imponitur. Nullum autem munus caret suo sudore & molestia, quæ præbeatur ijs qui illo utuntur. Facessant igitur hic ociosi ventres, aduersus quos Apostolus, 2.Thef.3. Qui non laborat, non manducet. Donec reuertaris in humum) q. d. efficiâ ut nihil promoueas absque sudoribus. ut his exercitatus perpetuam doctrinam habeas modestè agendi, tuamque ipsius naturam agnoscendi. Neque hoc ad breue tempus, sed omni tempore vitæ durabit: donec in terram resoluaris, liberatus ærumnis. Ex ea enim sumptus es: quandoquidem pulvis sis, & in puluerem reuersurus sis) corpore scil. Mens enim interitu caret, & ad Deum redit, unde proficiscitur, Ecclesiastici duodecimo.
units.tr: "In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread." This sweat and labour extends very widely, for not one kind of work is laid upon man, and no work is free of its own sweat and trouble, which falls to those who engage in it. Let idle bellies therefore be banished from here, against whom the Apostle says, 2 Thess. 3: "If anyone does not work, neither let him eat." "Until you return to the ground": that is, as if to say, "You will achieve nothing without sweat," so that, trained by this, you may have a lasting lesson in acting with moderation and in recognising your own nature. Nor will this last only for a short time, but for the whole of life, until you are dissolved into the earth, freed from your hardships. For you were taken from it, since you are dust and will return to dust, namely in body. For the mind is not subject to death and returns to God, from whence it came, Ecclesiasticus 12.

units.la: 4 Porrò tametsi hoc in loco videatur tantum caput quintum tractari, tamen tertium simul quoque tangitur. Officium. n. suum cum fœminæ, tum viri hinc discere possunt. Unde Apostolus, 1. Cor. 14. Mulieres vestræ, inquit, in ecclesijs sileant: nec enim permissum est illis ut loquantur, sed ut subditæ sint, quemadmodum & lex dicit. & Ephesior. 5. Sic debent viri diligere suas uxores, ut sua ipsorum corpora. Qui diligit suam uxorem, seipsum diligit. Nullus enim unquam suam ipsius carnem odio habuit, imo enutrit ac fouet eam, sicut & Dominus ecclesiam. Ita ergo (dicit Augustinus lib. 2. de Genesi contra Manich. cap. 18.) quæ videntur maledicta, præcepta sunt, si non carnaliter spiritalia legamus. Lex enim spiritalis est. Dominus autem Deus noster qui legem dedit, addat etiam gratiam omnibus & singulis coniugibus, ut iuxta illam viuere possint in Christo Iesu seruatore nostro, Amen.
units.tr: 4 Moreover, although in this place only the fifth chapter seems to be treated, the third is touched upon at the same time. For both wife and husband can learn from it their duty. Hence the Apostle, 1 Cor. 14: "Let your women keep silence in the churches, for it is not permitted to them to speak, but they are to be subject, as the law also says." And Ephesians 5: "So ought husbands to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. For no one ever hated his own flesh, but rather nourishes and cherishes it, just as the Lord does the Church." Thus, as Augustine says (book 2 of On Genesis against the Manichaeans, chapter 18), "those things which seem to be curses are precepts, if we read them not carnally but spiritually. For the law is spiritual." May the Lord our God, who gave the law, also grant grace to all and each of the spouses, so that they may live according to it in Christ Jesus our Saviour. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO III
units.tr: CONCIO III

units.la: Genes. 6.
units.tr: Genes. 6.

units.la: Vmq̃[?] cœpissent homines multiplicari super terram, & filias procreassent sibi, videntes filij Dei filias hominum, quòd essent pulchrę, acceperunt sibi vxores ex omnibus quas elegerant. Dixitq̃ Deus: Non disceptabit spiritus meus cum homine in æternum, quia caro est: eruntque dies illius centum viginti annorum.
units.tr: When men had begun to multiply upon the earth and had begotten daughters for themselves, the sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were fair, and they took wives for themselves from among all whom they had chosen. And God said: My spirit shall not contend with man for ever, because he is flesh; and his days shall be a hundred and twenty years.

units.la: 1 Fatentur ferè omnes instare diem Domini magnum: idque haud immerito. Nam si Apostoli suo tempore dicebant: Scripta verò sunt propter admonitionem nostri, in quos termini ætatum inciderunt, 1. Corint. 10. Ecce iudex ante ianuam assistit, Iac. 5. Porrò rerum omnium finis imminet, 1. Pet. 4. Filioli, nouissimum tempus est, 1. Ioan. 2. quantò magis id hodie dicere licet. Adhæc non solùm Apostoli, sed Christus ipse de signis extremum diem praecursuris vaticinatus est, quæ quotidie fieri & videmus & audimus. Inter hæc verò signa & hoc unum est, de quo Dominus Matth .24. & Luc. 17. vbi ait: Sicut erant dies Noe, ita erit & aduentus filij hominis. Sicut enim erant in diebus, qui præcesserunt diluuium, edentes & bibentes, contrahentes matrimonium, & nuptum dantes, vsque ad eum diem, quo intrauit Noe in arcam: & non cognouerunt, donec veniset diluuium, & sustulisset vniuersos: ita erit & aduentus filij hominis. i. ante Christi aduentum regnatura est summa securitas, 1. Thess. 5. regnaturi item sunt carnales affectus edendo, bibendo, nubendo, &c. id quod Christus videtur innuisse quoque Luc. 21. vbi dixit: Cauete autem vobis, ne grauentur corda vestra crapula & ebrietate & curis huius vitæ, subitusque vobis ingruat dies ille. Quid ista admonitio aliud indicat, quàm regnatura ista vitia ante mundi finem?
units.tr: 1 Almost everyone admits that the great day of the Lord is at hand, and not without good reason. For if the Apostles said in their own time: "Now these things were written for our admonition, on whom the ends of the ages have come" (1 Cor. 10); "Behold, the judge stands before the door" (Jas. 5); "The end of all things is near" (1 Pet. 4); "Little children, it is the last time" (1 John 2); how much more may we say so today? Moreover, it was not only the Apostles but Christ himself who foretold the signs that would precede the last day, signs which we both see and hear of every day. Among these signs is also the one about which the Lord speaks in Matthew 24 and Luke 17, where he says: "As were the days of Noah, so will the coming of the Son of Man be. For as in the days before the flood they were eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage, until the day Noah entered the ark, and they did not know until the flood came and swept them all away, so will the coming of the Son of Man be." That is, before the coming of Christ there will reign the greatest security (1 Thess. 5); and there will likewise reign carnal desires of eating, drinking, marrying, etc. This Christ also seems to hint at in Luke 21, where he said: "But take heed to yourselves, lest your hearts be weighed down with dissipation and drunkenness and the cares of this life, and that day come upon you suddenly."
