What else does this warning indicate than that these vices will reign before the end of the world?

units.la: Cæterum cùm Christus coniunctionem marium & fœminarum ponat inter reliqua signa aduentus sui: nec tamen nubere & nuptum dare, sicut nec edere aut bibere malũ sit, cùm ista omnia sint à Deo ordinata: videndum erit quatenus ea res improbetur à Domino, & quomodo in ea peccari possit, ne rem ipsam, eiusque legitimum vsum cum abusu damnemus ac reijciamus.
units.tr: But since Christ lists the union of men and women among the other signs of his coming, and yet to marry and to give in marriage is no more evil than to eat or to drink, since all these things have been ordained by God, we must consider in what respect this matter is condemned by the Lord, and how sin can be committed in it, so that we do not condemn the thing itself and its lawful use together with its abuse and reject it.

units.la: 2 Quomodo olim peccatum fit, docemur hic per Mosem, qui primùm facit quidem mentionem multiplicationis generis humani, sed non piorum ac fidelium hominum. Sic etiam sub finem mundi, abundabit iniquitas & refrigescet charitas multorum, Matth. 24 ac filius hominis cùm venerit, vix reperturus est fidem in terra, Luc.18.
units.tr: 2 How sin came about in former times we are taught here through Moses, who first indeed mentions the multiplication of the human race, but not of pious and faithful men. So also at the end of the world, "iniquity will abound and the love of many will grow cold" (Matt. 24), and "when the Son of Man comes, he will scarcely find faith on the earth" (Luke 18).

units.la: Secundò meminit ἀποστασίας[?] fidelium, de qua Paulus quoque, 1 Tim. 4. 2 Thes. 2. & corruptionis magistratus & iudicum. Dicit enim: Videruntq; filij Dei filias hominum quòd elegantes essent. Nam filij Dei hic dicuntur non angeli, neque dæmones, vt quidam fingunt: sed vel homines iusti ac pij, qui videl. à parentibus suis in vera religione ac cultu vnius Dei probè instituti erant, quiq; ex linea ac gente illa erant, vnde promissum ac benedictum illud semen futurum erat. i. prognati ex Seth (quem sui virtutis causa Deum appellauerunt, teste Cyrillo) & Enos: vel, iudices & potentes, magnates & proceres.
units.tr: Secondly, he mentions the apostasy [ἀποστασίας] of the faithful, of which Paul also speaks (1 Tim. 4; 2 Thess. 2), and the corruption of magistrates and judges. For he says: "The sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were fair." For the sons of God here are called not angels, nor demons, as some pretend, but either men who were just and pious, who had been rightly instructed by their parents in the true religion and worship of the one God, and who were from that line and race from which the promised and blessed Seed was to come, that is, those born of Seth (whom, on account of his virtue, they called God, as Cyril testifies) and Enos; or else judges and the powerful, magnates and nobles.

units.la: Mos enim scripturæ est, vt homines filios Dei vocet, præsertim illi dilectos, illumque colentes, vtpote ab illo creatos, factosq;[?] veluti deos, futurosque si Deum coluerint, vt Exod. 4. Deut. 14. Iesa.1. Hosc. 11. Psal. 82. Ioan. 1.Ioá. 3. Sic vocabantur eluuionis tempore filij sanctorum patriarcharum: sed hi auertentes aures à veritate, aspexerunt vanitate. i. pulchritudine filiarum hominum, genitarum à fratricida Caino. Fallax enim gratia, & vana est pulchritudo, teste Salomone Pro.vlt. Familiare quoque est Scripturæ, vt illud quod est magnificum, vocet diuinum, sicut montes Dei, cedri Dei. i. magni montes, altissimæ cedri: & in propheta Niniue dicitur ciuitas magna Deo. i. ciuitas magnificentissima. Apud magnates ergo & hominum potentissimos, quorum officij erat vitia ac flagitia arcere atque punire, tempore Noe, omnis honestas, iustitia & æquitas in pessum iuerat. Nam & hi viderunt, libidinis animi, non timoris dei oculis, filias hominum, quòd essent pulchræ, non quòd timentes Deum: & pulchritudine earum capti acceperunt sibi, non Deo, vxores ex omnibus, quas elegerant, non eas quæ Domino placebant, sed quas libebat, & quot quot libebat, sequuti suam libidinem, non Dei metum, non sanctorum parentum voluntatem, non legem coniugiorum, quæ mutuum præsidium, & sobolis procreationem p.ob[?], incestum & promiscuam libidinem improbat atque damnat.
units.tr: For it is the custom of Scripture to call men the sons of God, especially those who are beloved and who worship him, since they are created by him and, as it were, made gods, and will be such if they worship God (Exod. 4; Deut. 14; Isa. 1; Hos. 11; Ps. 82; John 1; 1 John 3). Thus in the time of the flood the sons of the holy patriarchs were so called; but these, turning their ears away from the truth, looked upon the vanity, that is, the beauty of the daughters of men, who were born of the murderer Cain. For "charm is deceitful and beauty is vain," as Solomon testifies (Prov. 31). It is also a familiar practice of Scripture to call what is magnificent divine, as "the mountains of God" and "the cedars of God," that is, great mountains and very lofty cedars; and in the prophet Nineveh is called "a great city to God," that is, a most magnificent city. Among the magnates and the most powerful men of the world, whose office it was to restrain and punish vices and crimes, at the time of Noah all honesty, justice and fairness had gone to ruin. For they too looked upon the daughters of men with the eyes of lust and not of the fear of God, because they were fair, not because they feared God; and captivated by their beauty they took for themselves wives, not for God, from among all whom they had chosen, not those who were pleasing to the Lord, but whom they wished, and as many as they wished, following their own lust, not the fear of God, not the will of their holy parents, not the law of marriages, which condemns and forbids incest and promiscuous lust, although marriage was instituted for mutual help and the procreation of offspring.

units.la: Tertiò meminit Moses pulchritudinis filiarum hominum. Habuerunt ergo maiorem rationem formæ crp[?] oris, quæ teste Poeta, bonum fragile est, & teste Bione Borysthenite, bonum alienum, quàm pulchritudinis animi, vanitatis, quàm veritatis, superbiæ quàm humilitatis, luxuriæ quàm pudicitiæ, contra illud 1.Pet.3.quorum ornatus sit non externus, &c. qualis fuit, puellarum Hierosolymitanarum, Isa. 3. quæ partim se ornabant vt concupiscerentur à viris: partim ex superbia, vt pulchriores essent aliis, vel saltem non excederentur ab aliis, partim ex amore vanæ gloriæ & laudis, vt dicatur, quòd ipsæ sint pulchræ, &c.
units.tr: Thirdly, Moses mentions the beauty of the daughters of men. They therefore had greater regard for the beauty of face and form, which, as the poet says, is a fragile good, and, as Bion of Borysthenes says, a foreign good, than for the beauty of the soul; for vanity rather than truth, pride rather than humility, lust rather than chastity, contrary to 1 Pet. 3: "whose adornment should not be external," etc. Such was the adornment of the daughters of Jerusalem (Isa. 3), who partly adorned themselves that they might be desired by men; partly out of pride, that they might be fairer than others, or at least not be surpassed by others; partly out of love of vainglory and praise, so that it might be said that they themselves are beautiful, etc.

units.la: Sed quid pulchritudo & species mulierum aliud est, quàm oculorum dolor, vt Alexander de Perficis puellis (quas ob id in conspectum venire vetuit) dicebat: it em gladius igneus[?] testante Hieronymo. Diogenes formosa scorta similia dicebat, multo lætalibus venenis temperato, quòd afferrent quidem initio voluptatem, sed quàm perpetuus dolor consequeretur. Theocritus formam appellauit eburneum detrimentum, quòd grata quidem sit aspectui, sed multorum incommodorum causa. Propter speciem enim mulieris, inquit Scriptura Ecclesi. 9. multi perierunt, & ex hoc concupiscentia, quasi ignis exardescit. & nouissima illius, inquit Prouerb. 5. amara sunt quasi absynthium, & acuta quasi gladius biceps. Ipsam enim mulierem in qua est, lædit per superbiam: & ipsos aspicientes (quales esse solet plurimum ij, qui commorantur in vino, & student calicibus epotandis, Prouerbiorum vigesimo tertio.) per luxuriam. vel potest dici gladius biceps, quia corpori & animæ occasio est mortis æternæ. Cùm Dionysius Siciliæ tyrannus (vt Erasmus refert lib. 1. Apophth.) filiabus Archidami vestes splendidas multiquè precij dono misisset, recusauit accipere, dicens, Vereor ne hoc amictu puellæ mihi turpes videantur. Intellexit vir prudens virgines nullo cultu melius ornari, quàm simplici: porrò sericis, gemmis & auro dehonestari magis, quàm ornari: propterea quòd vestium luxus arguit animum parum sobrium, & intoentium animos ad libidinem solicitat citius, quàm ad honestam opinionem. Decet autem vt virgo tota & vndique virgo sit, nec vlla ex parte det corruptæ mentis fignificationem.
units.tr: But what is the beauty and appearance of women other than a pain to the eyes, as Alexander said of the Persian maidens (whom for that reason he forbade to come into his sight), since, as Jerome testifies, it is a fiery sword? Diogenes said that beautiful harlots were like poisons mixed with much honey, because they bring pleasure at the beginning, but what lasting pain follows. Theocritus called beauty an ivory loss, because it is indeed pleasing to the eye, but is the cause of many troubles. For "on account of the beauty of a woman, many have perished, and from this desire burns like a fire," says Scripture (Eccl. 9); "and her last end," says Proverbs 5, "is bitter as wormwood and sharp as a two-edged sword." For she wounds the woman herself in whom it is, through pride, and those who look upon her (such as are usually those who linger over wine and strive to empty the cups, Prov. 23) through lust. Or it can be said to be a two-edged sword, because it is an occasion of eternal death both for body and soul. When Dionysius, tyrant of Sicily, sent splendid garments of great price as a gift to the daughters of Archidamus, they refused to accept them, saying: "I fear lest in this dress my girls may seem disgraceful to me" (as Erasmus reports, Apophth. 1). The wise man understood that virgins are adorned better by no finery than by simplicity; and that they are disgraced rather than adorned by silks, gems and gold, because the luxury of clothing shows a mind not very sober and sooner incites the minds of onlookers to lust than to a good opinion. A maiden ought to be wholly and on every side a maiden, and show in no part any sign of a corrupted mind.

units.la: Quarto loquitur de impatietia correptionis spiritus in carnalibus hominibus prisci seculi. Ait enim, Non contendet spiritus meus cum homine in perpetuum: vel, vt Lutherus vertit: <bl>Die menschen wöllen sich meinen geist nicht mehr</bl> <bl>straffen lassen</bl>: eò quòd ipsi caro sunt, id est, quia carnalibus operibus seipsos totos dedunt, & animæ substantia abutuntur, & quasi sola carne circundati anima carerent, sic vitam suam absumunt: quemadmodum Chrysost. ait.
units.tr: Fourthly, he speaks of the impatience of the Spirit's correction in the carnal men of the old age. For he says: "My spirit shall not contend with man for ever"; or, as Luther translates it: "People will no longer let themselves be rebuked by my spirit," because they are flesh, that is, because they have given themselves wholly to carnal works and abuse the substance of the soul, and, as if surrounded by flesh alone, they live out their lives as though they lacked a soul; as Chrysostom says.

units.la: Alij autem hæc Dei verba sic exponunt: Spiritus meus. i. verbi mei arguens per ministros prophetas mundum de peccato, non amplius homines iudicabit aut corripiet. Est vero hæc grauissima pœna, subtractio vi del. verbi Dei, Amos. 8. Sunt prætere a qui interpretantur spiritum Dei, de vitali spiritu, quem homini Deus sit adempturus, adducto in terram diluvio: qui spiritus, Dei spiritus appelletur, vt a Deo Adamo inspiratus.
units.tr: Others, however, explain these words of God in this way: "My Spirit," that is, my Word, reproving the world of sin through the ministers and prophets, will no longer judge or correct men. This is indeed the most grievous punishment, the withdrawal of the Word of God (Amos 8). Moreover, there are some who interpret the Spirit of God as the vital spirit, which God was going to take away from man when the flood was brought upon the earth; this spirit is called the Spirit of God because it was breathed into Adam by God.

units.la: Postremò fit hoc loco mentio annorum 120. ad pœnitentiam assignatorum, quibus resipiscerent: qui locus de lenitate Dei est, pœni ad ignoscendum, de qua Luc.12. Rom. 2.1. Pet.3.& 2.Pet. 3. Diluvium enim subito non invehit, inaehit[?], sed totis centum annis arca construitur. Interim homines stolidi Noam voluntati diuinae obsequentem irridebant. Imo tametsi cerneret vniuersas belluas coire, quem admodum diuinus ille vir Ephraemus ait, elephantos ab India Persideque aduentare, leones ac pardalides inter eos atque capras promiscue accedere, reptiles bestias cum auibus eodem se persequente nemine confer re ac circum arcam commorari: nihilo tamen magis poenitentiae stimulos sentiebant. Quid igitur factum est? Ne hos quidem centum viginti annos vniuersos impij illi vixerunt, propter insignem videlicet improbitatem. Nam qui prius durante 100. annorum interuallo non resipuerant, intra 20. annos poenitentiam acturi non erant. Atq; hoc loco mihi obserua, Deum nonnunquam nobis non resipiscentibus eam vitam praecidere, quam prius pollicebatur, vt hic fieri videmus (de sententia Glycae par. 2. Annal.) nonnunquam minatum se perditurum, reapse minas non exequi, nobis resipiscentibus, id quod Niniuitis videmus vsuuenisle[?], Ion. 3. Ierem. 18.
units.tr: Finally, in this place mention is made of the 120 years assigned for repentance, in which they might come to their senses. This passage concerns the gentleness of God, who is ready to forgive, as in Luke 12, Romans 2, 1 Peter 3 and 2 Peter 3. For God does not bring the flood suddenly, but the ark is built over a full hundred years. Meanwhile foolish men mocked Noah, who obeyed the will of God. Indeed, even though they saw all the beasts coming together, as that divine man Ephraem says, elephants arriving from India and Persia, lions and leopards mingling with goats, reptiles and birds gathering around the ark with no one driving them, nevertheless they felt no more of the goads of repentance. What, then, happened? Those impious men did not even live out these whole hundred and twenty years, on account of their extraordinary wickedness. For those who had not come to their senses during the hundred years were not going to repent within the last twenty. And here observe for me that God sometimes cuts off the life that he had promised before, when we do not repent, as we see happen here (according to the opinion of Glycas, part 2 of the Annals); sometimes he threatens to destroy us, but in fact does not carry out the threats when we repent, as we see happened to the Ninevites (Jonah 3; Jeremiah 18).

units.la: 3 Quid nobis ex omnibus istis discendum est, vt diligentem curam geramus oculorum nostrorum. Hi enim saepe nos seducunt, vt cernere est ex Gen. 3. 12. 34[?]. 39. Iosu. 7. 2. Reg.11. Sira.9. 25. 42. Mat. 5. Decet enim (vt Sophocli poetae collegae suo in praetura, videnti casu praeterire formosum puerum: Pericles dicebat) non solum manus, sed etiam linguam,& (vt Cicero refert, 1.Off.) oculos abstinentes habere. Videntes autem aliquid pulchri, sic cogitemus primum: O quàm pulcher est ipse creator & autor omnis pulchritudinis: vtinam olim videre mihi liceat eum cum omnibus filijs suis. Deinde, si mulier illa tam pulchrè ornat suam carnem, quanto iustius est, vt tu & ipsa, & nos omnes ornemus nostras animas, ne sint nudæ, sed indutæ nuptiali veste? Tertiò, si homo peccator adhuc existens, tam formosus apparere potest in terris, quàm elegantes & splendidi erimus olim ab omnibus peccatis liberati, quando lucebimus vt sol in regno patris nostri?
units.tr: 3 What we must learn from all these things is that we take careful charge of our eyes, for they often lead us astray, as can be seen from Genesis 3, Joshua 7, 2 Kings 11, Sirach 9 and 25 and 42, and Matthew 5. For it is fitting (as Pericles said when he saw the handsome boy passing by by chance, to Sophocles the poet, his colleague in the praetorship) to keep not only the hands but also the tongue and, as Cicero reports (1 Off.), the eyes in check. When we see something beautiful, let us think first: O how beautiful is the Creator himself and the author of all beauty; would that one day I may be permitted to see him together with all his children. Then: if this woman adorns her flesh so finely, how much more right is it that you and she, and all of us, adorn our souls, so that they are not naked but clothed in the wedding garment? Thirdly: if a sinner, while still existing, can appear so comely on earth, how elegant and splendid shall we be one day, freed from all sins, when we shine like the sun in the kingdom of our Father?

units.la: Discamus etiam hic, ne in contrahendis coniugijs spectemus magis formâ, opes, &c. quàm imaginem Dei. Olympias Alexandri mater quum accepisset adolescente quendam aulicum duxisse vxorem elegante quidem forma, sed famæ parum fecundæ: Ille, inquit, non sapit, qui vxorem oculis, non etiam aurib.duxerit. Forma cernitur oculis, fama auribus deprehenditur. Quidam autem nec auribus nec oculis, sed digitis ducunt, solam spectantes dotem. Præterea obseruandum hoc loco ne cum infidelibus ducamus iugum, contra præceptum Domini, Deut.7.
units.tr: Let us also learn here that in contracting marriages we should look not so much at beauty, wealth, and so on, as at the image of God. When Olympias, the mother of Alexander, heard that a certain young courtier had married a wife of elegant form but of little reputation, she said: "He is not wise who has married a wife with his eyes but not also with his ears. Form is perceived by the eyes; reputation is discovered by the ears." Some, however, lead a wife neither with their ears nor with their eyes, but with their fingers, looking only at the dowry. Besides, in this place one must take care not to yoke ourselves with unbelievers, contrary to the command of the Lord (Deut. 7).

units.la: 2 Cor.6. Nam solent filiæ alienigenæ in domos maritorum falsam parentum religionem, prauosque mores quibus verum cultum & honestatem labefactant, importare. Exemplo est Salomon, cuius cor per mulieres alienigenas legitur a Deo aversum fuisse, 3. Regum undecimo.
units.tr: 2 Cor. 6. For foreign daughters are wont to bring into their husbands' houses the false religion of their parents and depraved morals, by which they undermine true worship and honesty. Solomon is an example, whose heart is read to have been turned away from God by foreign women (3 Kings 11).

units.la: Denique ne secundum carnem vinamus[?], ne spiritu vivificate privemur & moriamur in æternum: à qua morte fervet nos Dominus Iesus, Amen.
units.tr: Finally, let us not live according to the flesh, lest we be deprived of spiritual life and die eternally; from which death may the Lord Jesus preserve us. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO IIII.
units.tr: CONCIO IIII.

units.la: Genes. 9.
units.tr: Genes. 9.

units.la: Tbenedixit Deus Noah atq; filiis eius,et dixit ad eos:Fructum ferte & multiplicamini, atque implete terram.
units.tr: And God blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them: Bear fruit, and multiply, and fill the earth.

units.la: I Qui matrimonium commendare solent, commendant illud non solum, ab authoritate instituentis, qui ipse Deus est, non Augustin. non Benedictus, non alius quispiam vel homo, vel angelus: nec solum à loco, in quo institutum est, id est, paradiso, à statu, scil. innocentiæ, ab antiquitate, ab eo quod legimus de matre Domini, quæ hunc ordinem intrare voluit, inq; eo Christum peperit, ab eo, quòd Dominus voluit honorare nuptias sua præsentia, & primo miraculo, quod fecit coram discipulis suis: verum etiam ex eo, quòd nunc solum ordinem salvavit Deus tempore diluuij, quo finito, eundem denuò confirmauit. In arca enim tantum salvati sunt Noe & uxor eius, & tres filii eius & uxores eorum. Si qui erant concubinarii, si quę meretrices, omnes diluvio sunt submersi. Deniq; commendatur etiam coniugium ex fine, qui est propagatio sobolis, seu preciosus fructus, qui ex matrimonio sequitur. (quam benedictionem Deus veluti quoddam donum matrimonio obtulit, ut Theodoretus scribit in Epit. Diu. decr.) Generantur enim inde filii huius seculi, qui potest per adoptionem fiunt filii Dei. Si quis haberet vineam, quæ annuatim ferret mille modios vini, valde amaret eam. Quantum ergo amandum est matrimonium, unde pueri procreatur, cum puer unus prævaleat omni vino quod in mundo est? Ex matrimonio generantur virgines. Proinde si virginitas multum amanda est, & matrimonium multum amandum est. Unde Hieronymus: Laudo coniugium, quia virgines generat. Propagatione demum liberorum tres administrationes conseruantur, œconomica, civilis, & ecclesiastica. In domestica curatione, mariti in uxorem, & uxoris atque mariti in liberos, domini in servos rectio spectatur. In civili administratione eorum qui parent, moderatio. In ecclesiastica autem regni sacri spiritus per sceptrum Euangelii gubernatio locum habet. At nulla ex his moderatio sine procreatione liberorum consistit.
units.tr: 1 Those who commend marriage usually commend it not only on the authority of its institutor, who is God himself and not Augustine, not Benedict, not any other man or angel; nor only on the place where it was instituted, namely paradise; nor only on its state, that of innocence; nor on its antiquity, or on what we read about the mother of the Lord, who chose to enter this order and in it bore Christ; nor on the fact that the Lord chose to honour marriage with his presence and with the first miracle he performed before his disciples. They commend it also because God preserved this order alone at the time of the flood, and, when that was over, confirmed it again. For only Noah and his wife, and his three sons and their wives, were saved in the ark; all the fornicators and harlots, if there were any, were drowned in the flood. Lastly, marriage is commended also by its end, which is the propagation of offspring, or the precious fruit that follows from marriage. (God offered this blessing to marriage as a kind of gift, as Theodoret writes in his Epitome of the Divine Decrees.) For from it come the children of this world, who through adoption become children of God. If someone had a vineyard that yielded a thousand measures of wine each year, he would love it greatly. How much, then, must marriage be loved, from which children are born, since one child outweighs all the wine in the world? Virgins are born from marriage. Therefore, if virginity is to be greatly loved, marriage too is to be greatly loved. Hence Jerome: "I praise marriage, because it begets virgins." Finally, three administrations are preserved by the propagation of children: the domestic, the civil and the ecclesiastical. In domestic government we look to the rule of husband over wife, of wife and husband over children, and of masters over servants. In civil administration there is the moderation of those who rule over those who obey. In ecclesiastical administration there is the governance of the sacred kingdom of the Spirit by the sceptre of the Gospel. Yet none of these forms of moderation can exist without the procreation of children.

units.la: De hoc autem præcipuo fine coniugii Deus ipse hoc loco verba facit ad Noe & filios eius, postquam unà cum suis uxoribus exarca egressi sunt, inquiens: Crescite & multiplicamini & replete (scilicet, prole vestra) terram. Hoc de homine facto necessario iterare curauit (inquit Iunilius in Genes.) nequis honorabili connubio inesse peccatum, thorumque fœditati ac fornicationi putaret comparandum. Et, si benedictione Dei crescit & multiplicatur genus humanum, ecquanta sint maledictione digni, qui prohibęt nubere, & dispositionem cœlestis decreti quasi à diabolo comperta m condemnant? Non ergo damnandæ sunt nuptiæ: quas ad propagationem generis humani, terramque replendam, supernæ gratia benedictionis instituit, &c.
units.tr: Concerning this chief end of marriage, God himself speaks in this place to Noah and his sons, after they had come out of the ark with their wives, saying: "Increase and multiply, and fill (namely, with your offspring) the earth." Since man had been made, God took care to repeat this (says Junilius on Genesis), lest anyone suppose that sin dwells in honourable wedlock, or that the marriage bed is to be compared with filthiness and fornication. And if the human race grows and multiplies by the blessing of God, how great a curse do those deserve who forbid marriage and condemn the arrangement of the heavenly decree, as if it had been discovered by the devil? Marriage, then, is not to be condemned: God in his heavenly grace instituted it for the propagation of the human race and the filling of the earth, and so on.

units.la: 2 Has commendationes matrimonij scire & perpendere, eò facit, ut nuptiæ honorabiles habeantur inter omnes: neque ipsum matrimonium damnetur aut contemnatur, propter quosdam coniuges in hoc statu viræ peram agentes, turpiterque viventes: & ut doctrina Dei à dæmoniorum doctrinis discernatur. Sunt enim qui matrimonium prohibent, & interim scortationem approbant: quasi Deus non sit pacis & ordinis, sed confusionis Deus, Heb.13.1. Tim. 4.1.Cor.14.
units.tr: 2 To know and weigh these commendations of marriage serves to ensure that honourable marriage is held in esteem by all, that marriage itself is not condemned or despised because of certain spouses who live a shameful life in this state and conduct themselves disgracefully, and that the teaching of God is distinguished from the doctrines of demons. For there are those who forbid marriage and at the same time approve fornication, as if God were not the God of peace and order but of confusion (Heb. 13.1; 1 Tim. 4.1; 1 Cor. 14).

units.la: 3 Docent etiam hæc verba Dei generationem liberorum esse Dei benedictionem: &, qui hanc benedictionem consequatur, nempe Noe & filij eius, hoc est, iosti[?], illorumque posteri. Nam semen impiorum peribit: &, generatio rectorum benedicetur,Psal.37.112. Rectum autem ac iustum fuisse Noe, testantur Moses,Gen.6.Paul.Heb.11.Petrus 2.cap.
units.tr: 3 These words of God also teach that the begetting of children is God's blessing, and that those who obtain this blessing are Noah and his sons, that is, the righteous and their descendants. For the seed of the wicked will perish, but the generation of the upright will be blessed (Ps. 37.12). Moses, Paul (Heb. 11) and Peter (2 Pet. 2) bear witness that Noah was upright and just (Gen. 6).

units.la: 2. Porrò fœcunditatem atque uim gignendi liberos non esse naturæ aut sexus munus,sed Dei donum, probant etiam clausi per minas Dei, & aperti per promissionem uteri: item loci Scripturæ Gen.30.Deut.7.Psal.113.127. 118. Væ igitur illis, qui dicunt benedictionem maledictionem: aut herbis, radicibus, pharmacis, aut etiam ferro, hanc benedictionem evertere ac tollere nituntur, ut meretrices & infanticidæ,&c. facere solent.
units.tr: 2. Moreover, that fruitfulness and the power of bearing children are not the gift of nature or of sex, but the gift of God, is proved also by the wombs closed by God's threats and opened by his promise; likewise by the passages of Scripture in Genesis 30, Deuteronomy 7, and Psalms 113, 127 and 118. Woe, then, to those who say that a blessing is a curse, and who strive to overturn and remove this blessing with herbs, roots, drugs, or even iron, as harlots and infanticides commonly do.

units.la: Quòd si vero generatio liberorum in benedictionib. Domini recensetur, multo magis regeneratio: si item terræ impletio, multo magis impletio cœli. Hinc Paulus Rom. 9. Non est volentis,neque currentis, sed miserentis Dei.&. 1.Corinth.3.Neque qui plantat,est aliquid,neque qui rigat,sed qui dat incrementum Deus.
units.tr: But if the generation of children is counted among the blessings of the Lord, how much more is regeneration; and if the filling of the earth is a blessing, how much more the filling of heaven. Hence Paul (Rom. 9): "It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy"; and (1 Cor. 3): "Neither he who plants is anything, nor he who waters, but God who gives the increase."

units.la: 4 Quoniam autem lex spiritualis est,teste Paulo:quæritur quomodo iusti spiritualiter crescere,multiplicari & terram replere debeant? Respondet Apostolus 2.Pet.1.inquiens: Sed & in hoc ipsum omni adhibito studio, subministrate in fide vestra virtutem,in virtute vero scientiam, in scientia temperantiam, &c. item, 2. Petri 3. Crescite in gratia & cognitione Domini & servatoris Iesu Christi. Item ipse Christus Ioann. 15. Ego elegi vos,& constitui vos, ut eatis & fructum asseratis, & fructus vester maneat. Et Apoc.22. Qui iustus est, iustificetur adhuc, & sanctus sanctificetur amplius. Unde D. Basilius, Duplex est (inquit) incrementum, alterum corporis, alterum animae. Verum animae incrementum, est additamentum per disciplinas ad perfectionem (1.Pet.2.) corporis incrementum est a parua ad iustam mensuram progressus. Crescite itaque, brutis quidem animantibus iuxta corporis perfectionem, secundum naturae absolutionem dictum est. Nobis autem, crescite iuxta internum hominem, secundum profectum ad Deum. Qualis erat Paulus, ad ea quae ante ipsum erant intentus, eorum vero quae retro ipsum erant obliuiscens, Philip.3.[?] Hoc est incrementum speculationum, pietatis assumptae ampliatio ac extensio, appetere nos semper ultra praesentia, id quod prius factum est semper retro se dimittere, quod vero restat pietatis id ipsum pro viribus inquirere. Crescite igitur incremento, perfectionem videlicet secundum Deum, iuxta hominem internum. Multiplicamini. Ecclesiae est benedictio. Ne in uno circumscribatur Theologia, sed in omnem terram praedicetur Euangelii salutis. Multiplicamini. Quinam? qui secundum Euangelium generati estis. Replete terram. Carnem datam vobis in ministerium, replete bonis operibus (seu fructibus iustitiae, ut Paulus vocat, Philip.i.) Oculus plenus fit visu ac conspectu eorum quae decent. Manos plena sit bonorum operum. Pedes parati sint ad visitationem aegrotorum, ita vt eant ad ea quae decent. Omnis membrorum nostrorum constitutio plena sit operationibus iuxta praecepta: hoc est, replete terram, &c.
units.tr: 4 Since, however, the law is spiritual, as Paul testifies, the question arises how the righteous ought to grow, multiply and fill the earth spiritually. The Apostle answers in 2 Peter 1: "But for this very reason, applying all diligence, supply in your faith virtue, in virtue knowledge, in knowledge temperance," and so on. Likewise in 2 Peter 3: "Grow in grace and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ." Likewise Christ himself, John 15: "I chose you and appointed you, that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain." And Revelation 22: "He who is righteous, let him be justified still; and he who is holy, let him be sanctified more." Hence Basil the Great: "Growth is twofold," he says, "one of the body, the other of the soul. The growth of the soul is the addition, through disciplines, to perfection (1 Pet. 2); the growth of the body is the progress from small to full measure. Grow, then: for the brute animals it was said, 'grow' according to the perfection of the body, according to the completion of their nature; but to us it is said, 'grow' according to the inner man, according to advance toward God. Such was Paul, intent on what lay before him and forgetting what lay behind (Phil. 3). This is the growth of contemplation, the enlargement and extension of the piety we have taken up: to strive always beyond the present, always to leave behind what has already been done, and to seek with all our strength what remains of piety. Grow, therefore, by growth, that is, toward perfection according to God, according to the inner man. Multiply. This is the blessing of the Church: that theology should not be confined to one place, but that the Gospel of salvation be preached in every land. Multiply. Who? You who have been begotten according to the Gospel. Fill the earth. Fill the flesh given to you for ministry with good works (or with the fruits of righteousness, as Paul calls them, Phil. 1). The eye is full when it sees and looks upon what is fitting. The hand is full of good works. The feet are ready to visit the sick, so that they go to what is fitting. The whole constitution of our members is full of works according to the precepts: that is, fill the earth, and so on."

units.la: Origenes talem allegoriam horum verborum allegat Homil.1.in Genef.cap.1. Interior homo noster (inquit) ex spiritu & anima constat. Masculus spiritus dicitur, foemina anima potest nuncupari. Haec si concordiam[?] inter se habeant & consensum, conuenientia inter se ipsa crescunt & multiplicantur, generantque filios sensus bonos & intellectus vel cogitationes utiles, per quas repleant terram & dominentur in ea: hoc est, subiectum sibi sensum carnis ad meliora instituta convertunt, & dominantur eis, scilicet cum in nullo caro contra voluntatem spiritus insolescit. Iam vero si anima coniuncta spiritui, atque (vt ita dicam) coniugio copulata, declinet aliquando ad corporeas voluptates, sensumque suum in delectationibus carnalibus inclinet, & aliquando quidem obtemperare videatur salutaribus monitis spiritus, aliquando vero vitijs carnalibus cedat: talis anima velut adulterio corporis maculata, neque crescere, neque multiplicari legitimè dicitur, quoniam quidem filios adulterorum impersectos Scriptura designat. Talis enim anima, quae spiritus coniunctione deserta, sensui se carnis, & desiderijs corporalib. totam prosternit, velut auersa à Deo imprudenter, audiet, quia facies meretricis facta est tibi, sine pudore effecta es ad omnes. Veluti meretrix ergo punietur, & filij eius ad occisionem præparari videbuntur. Dominus Deus noster liberet atque seruet nos ab omni immundo & meretricio spiritu per Christum Iesum, Amen.
units.tr: Origen offers such an allegory of these words in his first homily on Genesis, chapter 1: "Our inner man," he says, "consists of spirit and soul. The spirit may be called masculine, the soul feminine. If these have agreement and harmony between them, they grow and multiply in mutual accord and beget good senses and useful understandings or thoughts, by which they fill the earth and rule over it: that is, they turn the sense of the flesh, made subject to them, toward better aims and rule over it, namely when the flesh never rebels against the will of the spirit. But if the soul, joined to the spirit and, as it were, united with it in marriage, sometimes turns aside to bodily pleasures and inclines its sense toward carnal delights, and sometimes seems to obey the wholesome admonitions of the spirit, and sometimes gives way to carnal vices, such a soul, stained as if by adultery of the body, is not rightly said to grow or multiply, since Scripture describes the children of adulterers as imperfect. For such a soul, deserted by the union with the spirit, which prostrates itself wholly to the sense of the flesh and to bodily desires, and is turned away from God unwisely, will hear: 'The face of a harlot has become yours; you have become shameless toward all.' Like a harlot, then, she will be punished, and her children will seem to be prepared for slaughter. May the Lord our God deliver and keep us from every unclean and harlot spirit, through Christ Jesus. Amen."

units.la: CONCIO V. Genes. 12.
units.tr: SERMON V. Genesis 12.

units.la: ERat autem fames in illa terra, & ob id descendit Abram in Aegyptum, ut peregrinaretur ibi: nam erat grauis fames in terra. Et factum est cum applicasset ut intraret in Aegyptum, dixit ad Sarai uxorem suam: En scio quod tu sis mulier pulchro aspectu. Erit itaque, quando viderint te Aegyptij, dicet: uxor illius est hæc, & interficient me, te vero in vita conseruabunt. Dic obsecro quod soror mea sis, ut scilicet bene sit mihi propter te, et viuat anima mea tui causa. Factum itaq; est, cum venisset Abram in Aegyptum, contemplati sunt Aegyptij mulierem: nam erat valde pulchra. Viderunt quoq; eam principes Pharaonis, & laudauerunt eam apud Pharaonem, sublataq; est mulier in domum Pharaonis. Et is quidem benefecit ipsi Abram propter illam: habuitq; oues & boues, & asinos, seruos & ancillas, asinas & camelos. Et percussit Dominus Pharaonem plagis magnis, & domum eius, propter Sarai uxorem Abram. Vocansq; Pharao Abram, dixit: Cur id fecisti mihi? quare non indicasti mihi, quod uxor tua esset? quare dixisti, soror mea est, & accepi eam mihi in uxorem? nunc igitur ecce uxor tua, tolle & vade. Et præcepit Pharao super eo viris, & emiserunt eum, atq; uxorem illius, & omnia quæ habuit.
units.tr: Now there was a famine in that land, and therefore Abram went down into Egypt to sojourn there, for the famine was grievous in the land. And when he was come near to enter into Egypt, he said to Sarai his wife: Behold, I know that thou art a woman of fair countenance. Therefore when the Egyptians shall see thee, they will say, This is his wife, and they will kill me, but they will save thee alive. Say, I pray thee, that thou art my sister, that it may be well with me for thy sake, and that my soul may live because of thee. So it came to pass, when Abram was come into Egypt, that the Egyptians beheld the woman, for she was very fair. The princes of Pharaoh also saw her and commended her before Pharaoh, and the woman was taken into Pharaoh's house. And he dealt well with Abram for her sake; and he had sheep, and oxen, and asses, menservants and maidservants, she asses and camels. And the Lord plagued Pharaoh with great plagues, and his house, because of Sarai, Abram's wife. And Pharaoh called Abram and said: What is this thou hast done to me? Why didst thou not tell me that she was thy wife? Why didst thou say, She is my sister, so that I took her to be my wife? Now therefore behold thy wife; take her and go. And Pharaoh gave his men charge concerning him, and they sent him away, and his wife, and all that he had.

units.la: 1 Ut omnia in nostram doctrinam præscripta sunt, teste Apostolo, Rom.15. sic & ista historia de sanctis coniugibus Abrahamo & Sara: ad quos nobis attendendum esse, monent Isaias cap.51.&Petrus in 1.Epist.cap.3. Verè enim inter illos erat coniugium: quoniam non solùm in prosperitate, sed & in periculis simul obambulabant. Idem quoque verissimum esse experti sunt, non semel, sed sæpius, quod D. Paulus de coniugibus scribit, 1.Corinth,7. in hunc modum: Attamen afflictionem in carne habituri sunt huiusmodi. Legimus enim hic primùm de descensu Abrami in Ægyptum (anno orb.2026.) propter famem: quæ etiam in aduentu & præsentia iusti erat valida:id quod audire debér, monente Chrysostomo, qui temerè & incircum spectè loquuntur & diuinant, dicentes, Quoniam quispiam aduenit, fames facta: & quoniam adfuit, hæc contigerunt. Deinde legimus de rapina Saræ à Pharaone facta, id est, rege Ægypti. Pharao enim commune nomen regum fuit apud Ægyptios. Non igitur satis erat, Abrahamum reliquisse patriâ, nisi etiam peregrinus in aliena terra fame afflictaretur, de periculo vitæ & vxoris pudicitiæ tentaretur. Hæc sunt strategemata sancti patris, omnibus credentibus in exemplum propositi. Hic quantum interfit inter mundi iudicium & fidei intelligitur. Mundus præsentia spectans, Dei fauorem à præsentibus opibus & bonorum affluentia metitur. Fides in præsentia nihil nisi exilia, rerum inopiam, insectationes hostium sæuas, mortem intuens, futura bona per patientiam spe præsumit, quæ spes nunquam pudefacit: quemadmodum & euentus huius tragœdiæ probat. Legimus enim hic etiam de indignatione Dei, quam in Pharaonem & domum eius, ob suam erga iustum curam immisit: nec nō de reditu patriarchæ ab Ægypto magna cum gloria. Et qua de causa, cùm rex peccet, omnes de domo eius pœnæ sunt participes? Non absque ratione hoc fit, sed ut per hoc regis insania compescatur. Graviori enim plaga indigebat, ita ut ipse exterreretur. Et ut[?] bi, inquis, hoc iustum, propter illum alios puniri? Non propter illum solum poenam sustinuerant, sed verisimile est eos cooperatos fuisse, ut aliquando committeretur iniquitas. Audiuisti enim supra Scripturam dicentem: Quia ut viderunt eam principes Pharaonis, laudauerunt, & introduxerunt eam in domum eius. Vidisti eos lenonis agere officium in regis gratiam, auferendo iusti uxorem? Quapropter non ipse solus, sed & omnes qui adhaerebant, poenae fuerunt participes: ut discant, quòd non in peregrinum simplicem furorem suum exercuerint, neque in hominem è medio vulgo: sed in virum; cuius tutor Deus, tanta illum cura dignans, & propter illum reges, ut in Psalmis est, corripiens. Et idcirco acerbissima poena concutiens eius mentem, discedere fecit ab nephario flagitio, coercuit ab irrationali impetu, cohibuit incontinentem mentem, alligauit incontinentiam indomitam.
units.tr: 1 As all things are written for our instruction, as the Apostle witnesses (Rom. 15), so also this history of the holy spouses Abraham and Sarah: to whom we are bidden to attend, as Isaiah (ch. 51) and Peter (1 Epist. ch. 3) admonish. For truly there was a real marriage between them, since they walked together not only in prosperity but also in dangers. They experienced the truth of what St. Paul writes of married persons (1 Cor. 7), not once but often: "Yet such shall have trouble in the flesh." For here we read first of Abram's descent into Egypt (in the year of the world 2026) because of the famine, which even in the coming and presence of the righteous man was severe. This is something we ought to hear, as Chrysostom warns, that those who speak and divine rashly and without circumspection say: "Since a certain man has come, a famine has arisen; and since he was present, these things have happened." Next we read of the seizure of Sarai by Pharaoh, that is, the king of Egypt, for Pharaoh was the common name of the kings among the Egyptians. It was not enough, then, that Abraham had left his homeland, unless he were also, as a stranger in a foreign land, afflicted by famine and tested over the danger to his life and his wife's chastity. These are the stratagems of the holy father, set forth as an example for all believers. Here one sees how great the difference is between the judgment of the world and that of faith. The world, looking at present things, measures God's favour by present wealth and abundance of goods. Faith, looking in the present at nothing but exile, want of goods, the cruel persecutions of enemies and death, hopes in advance for future good things through patience, and this hope never puts to shame, as the outcome of this tragedy also proves. For here we read also of God's wrath, which he sent upon Pharaoh and his house because of his care for the righteous man, and likewise of the patriarch's return from Egypt with great glory. And for what reason, when the king sins, do all of his household share in the punishment? This is not done without reason, but so that by this the king's madness may be restrained. For he needed a heavier blow, so that he himself might be terrified. "And how is it just, you say, that others should be punished on his account?" They had not suffered punishment merely on his account, but it is likely that they had cooperated, so that the wickedness might at some time be committed. For you have heard Scripture above saying: "When the princes of Pharaoh saw her, they praised her and brought her into his house." Do you see them performing the office of pimps to win the king's favour by taking away the righteous man's wife? Therefore not he alone, but all who adhered to him, shared in the punishment, so that they may learn that they had not exercised their madness against a simple stranger, nor against a man from the common crowd, but against a man whose protector is God, who honours him with such great care, and who, as the Psalm says, rebukes kings on his account. And so, shaking his mind with a most bitter punishment, he made him depart from the wicked crime, restrained him from irrational impulse, curbed his incontinent mind, and bound his unruly incontinence.

units.la: Caeterum qualis clades seu poena fuerit, qua Pharao (Saram in uxorem ductūrus: idque ad liberandos utrōsque) & eius domus affecta est, hic non explicatur.
units.tr: But what kind of calamity or punishment it was with which Pharaoh (who was about to take Sarai as his wife, and that for the liberation of both) and his house were afflicted, is not explained here.

units.la: Arbitrantur nonnulli talem fuisse, qualis Abimelechus Genes. 20. legitur, propter eandem Saram punitus.
units.tr: Some think that it was of the kind described in Genesis 20, where Abimelech was punished on account of the same Sarah.

units.la: Si quis hic miretur, cur tam graviter sit castigatus[?] Pharao ob Saram postulatam in matrimonium, quam ignorarit uxorem esse Abrahami, is sciat primo, non rectè factum à Pharaone, quod Saram, non consulto Abrahamo, vel eo inuito, voluerit ducere vxore. Deinde per ignorantiam delictum illud non fuisse purgatum, qui prius quàm Saram duceret vxorem, diligentius de statu illius inquirere debuerat. Deus igitur, qui cognitam teneret libidinem Pharaonis, iusto iudicio illum puniuit, ignorantia eius cum petulantia coniuncta non commotus.
units.tr: If anyone here wonders why Pharaoh was so severely chastised on account of Sarai, whom he sought in marriage, not knowing that she was Abraham's wife, let him know, first, that Pharaoh did not act rightly in wishing to take Sarai as wife without consulting Abraham, or against his will. Second, that this fault was not excused by ignorance, since before he took Sarai as wife he ought to have inquired more carefully into her condition. God, therefore, who knew Pharaoh's lust, punished him by a just judgment, not moved by his ignorance joined with wantonness.

units.la: Porrò plagis, quæ hîc leguntur, præluditur ijs, quibus sequentibus temporibus Æ-gyptij cum rege suo afficiendi erant. Nec nō quod toti posteritati ferendum erat, in patre credentium auspicari Deus voluit. Affligi oportuit vniuersam familiam Abrahami in Ægypto, priusquam Chananæam in hæreditatem reciperet. Cui præiens pater Abrahamus, non antè vel pedem latum partem in promissa terra adeptus est, quàm prior in Ægypto exilium expertus fuisset. Remoue velum mysticæ historiæ, quæ Ægyptus sanctis prius subeunda sit cum variis tentationibus, ipse & fide superandis, quàm superna[?] hæreditatem adeant, obscurum nō est. Quo pertinet, Descendit; verbum suprà memoratum: arcana videlicet significatione non carere in Ægyptum descendi, & in terram promissam ascendi. Nec [illegible, ~4 letters] vox à mysterio crucis abludit, in qua afflictio notatur & angustia.
units.tr: Moreover, the plagues read of here foreshadowed those with which the Egyptians and their king were to be afflicted in later times. And God willed that what was to be borne by the whole posterity should begin in the father of the believers. The whole family of Abraham had to be afflicted in Egypt before it received Canaan as an inheritance. Father Abraham, going before them, did not gain a single foot's breadth of the promised land before he had first experienced exile in Egypt. It is not obscure that, if one removes the veil of the mystical history, Egypt must first be undergone by the saints, who are to be overcome with various temptations by faith itself, before they reach the heavenly inheritance. To this pertains the word "descended" mentioned above: that the going down into Egypt and the going up into the promised land have, it is clear, a hidden meaning. Nor does [illegible] this word differ from the mystery of the cross, in which affliction and distress are signified.

units.la: {ɩ}Sunt adhuc multa hîc obseruanda circà personam Abræ & Saræ. Apparet enim Abramum futūre[?] prophetam. Sicut enim prædixit de pulchritudine (quam studium pietatis non imminuit) Saræ (quæ iam sexaginta annos excesserat, quæq; nobis ecclesiam adumbrat, Cant.i. Ephes.5.[?]) & de conversatione vitæ suæ: ita accidit. Idem quoque (vt nonnulli scribunt) in spiritu prophetiæ cognoscebat, quòd ex hoc, quòd vxor sua effet ablata, non sequeretur aliquid contra vxoris pudicitiam: sed potius laus Dei, & eius cognitio apud ipsos infideles reluceret. Cognoverunt enim Pharao & sui, quòd Dominus eos flagellabat maximis plagis propter Sarai vxorem Abrahæ, vt patet in litera: & sic diuinam prouidentiam & eius iustitiam aliqualiter fatebantur promptius & humilius quàm Philistæi, 1. Reg.6. Adde quòd Abram probabiliter æstimare poterat, fore vt vxor eius referretur regi propter sui pulchritudinem, sicut & factum est. Sciebat enim, quòd tempore illo reges non accedebant ad vxores suas de nouo acceptas, nisi post anni circulum, Hester 2. & infra tantum tempus sperabat de Dei adiutorio sibi, vxori & familiæ affuturo.
units.tr: {ɩ} Many things here are still to be observed concerning the persons of Abram and Sarai. For Abram appears to be a future prophet. For just as he foretold concerning the beauty of Sarai (which the zeal of piety did not diminish), who had already passed sixty years, and who figures for us the Church (Song 1; Eph. 5), and concerning the conduct of her life, so it came to pass. The same man (as some write) also knew by the spirit of prophecy that from the fact that his wife was taken away, nothing contrary to her chastity would follow, but rather the praise of God and the knowledge of him would shine forth among those very unbelievers. For Pharaoh and his people recognised that the Lord was scourging them with the greatest plagues on account of Sarai, Abram's wife, as appears in the text; and so they acknowledged, in some measure, the divine providence and its justice more readily and more humbly than the Philistines did (1 Sam. 6). Add that Abram could reasonably judge that his wife would be reported to the king on account of her beauty, as indeed came to pass. For he knew that in that time kings did not approach their newly taken wives until after a full year's cycle (Esther 2), and he hoped that within so short a time God's help would be at hand for himself, his wife and his household.

units.la: Quare autem Abrahamus timuit mortem? Quia nondum (inquit Chrysostomus) mortis erat soluta tyrannis, propterea in adulterium vxoris consentit iustus, & quasi seruit adulterio, in mulieris contumeliam, vt mortem effugiat. Erat adhuc terribilis facies mortis, nondum erant æreæ portæ conftractæ, nondum erat aculeus eius hebetatus.
units.tr: Why did Abraham fear death? Because, says Chrysostom, the tyranny of death had not yet been dissolved; therefore the righteous man consented to his wife's adultery, and as it were served the adultery, to the shame of the woman, so that he might escape death. The terrible face of death was still there; the brazen gates had not yet been broken, nor had its sting yet been blunted.

units.la: Enimuerò (inquit idem) sicut admirabile & rarum erat videre virum desideriorum (id est Danielem) stare in medio ferarum, & nihil pati: sed quasi oues eum circumire, ita il-læsum egredi é lacu. Et tres pueros in camino, quasi in prato & paradiso versari, & nihil ab igne læsi, sed egredi inde, ut virorum fortissimos. Ita admiratione dignum est & hoc facinus, quod iusti uxor nullam contumeliam experta à rege Aegyptio, tyranno, intemperante exiuit salua (ut vidua Iudith ab Holoferne, per angelum Domini custodita, Iudit.13.) Deus enim erat, qui faciebat omnia, & in inuiis viam dabat, & spem bonam semper in rebus deploratis afferre valet, Iesa.43. Et tunc, inquit: Ecce mulier tua coram te, accepta ea ocyus vade. Ne existimes, inquit, à nobis violatam illam, &c.
units.tr: Indeed, says the same writer, just as it was a wonderful and rare thing to see the man of desires (that is, Daniel) standing in the midst of lions and suffering nothing, but going round him like sheep, so he came out of the den unharmed; and the three boys walking in the furnace as if in a meadow and a paradise, and coming out from there unhurt by the fire, like the bravest of men: so this deed is also worthy of wonder, that the wife of the righteous man came out safe from the king of Egypt, a tyrant and a man of unrestrained lust, having suffered no insult (as the widow Judith was guarded from Holofernes by the angel of the Lord, Judith 13). For it was God who did all things, who makes a way in the pathless places and is able to bring good hope in desperate situations, Isa. 43. And then, he says: "Behold your wife before you; take her and go quickly." Do not suppose, he says, that she was violated by us, etc.

units.la: Cur dixerit Saram sororem suam esse, Genes. vigesimo habetur. Sed & in Græco Tobia cap.5. 7. 8. uxores Tobiæ senioris & iunioris, & Raguelis, eorundem sorores vocantur. Mulieres enim & viri de eadem cognatione propinqua, fratres & sorores nominabantur. Unde Genes.13. Abram vocavit Loth nepotem suum fratrem. Sciebat, inquit Lyranus, Abram, nephas esse apud Aegyptios adulterium, & mortis plectendum: & minus reputabant homicidium viri, quàm accedere ad uxorem alicuius ipso vivente. (quanquam homicidium per se grauius est quàm adulterium: ne enim homicidium fieret, permisit Moses dari libellum repudij, & ideo ad hoc periculum euitandum, dixit vxori suæ: Dic obsecro quòd soror mea sis, &c.
units.tr: Why he said that Sarah was his sister is set out in Genesis 20. But also in the Greek of Tobit, chapters 5, 7 and 8, the wives of the elder and younger Tobias and of Raguel are called their sisters. For women and men of the same near kindred were called brothers and sisters. Hence in Genesis 13 Abram called his nephew Lot his brother. Abram knew, says Lyra, that adultery was an abomination among the Egyptians and punishable by death, and they regarded the killing of a husband as less serious than approaching another man's wife while he was still alive (although homicide in itself is more grave than adultery; for to prevent homicide Moses permitted a bill of divorce to be given). And so, to avoid this danger, he said to his wife: "Say, I beg you, that you are my sister," etc.

units.la: Vide autem germanæ charitatis indicium in Sara, quæ vt vxor bona, qualis Eccles. 26. describitur, & Ephes. 5. marito obediuit, vt viuere posset. Non sic diadema in capite positum, regem præclarum ornat, atque obedientia illa, qua consilio iusti paruit, beatam & illustrem & claram demonstrauit. Quis non obstupesceret hanc parendi facilitatem? Quis non obstupesceret, si recte recogitet, quòd post tantam continentiam, & in tali ætate ad hoc vt iustum seruet, quantum in sua voluntate pendebat, etiam adulterio se exposuit, & barbarorum tulit congressum?
units.tr: Note, however, the sign of genuine affection in Sarah, who, as a good wife, such as is described in Ecclesiasticus 26 and Ephesians 5, obeyed her husband so that he might live. A diadem placed on the head does not adorn a distinguished king as that obedience, by which she yielded to the counsel of the righteous man, showed her to be blessed, illustrious and famous. Who would not be astonished at this readiness to obey? Who would not be astonished, if he considers rightly, that after such great continence, and at such an age, in order that the righteous man might be kept safe, so far as lay in her own will, she exposed herself even to adultery and endured the company of barbarians?

units.la: ʒ[?] Postremò in Ægyptijs, id est, maledicti Chami posteris obseruandum venit, quàm periculosum & scandalis plenum fit intendere oculos ad formam mulierum, Genes.6. Sirac.9. Matth.5. Item morem aulicorum esse fere vbique, colloqui & sermones conferre de rebus vanis & carnalibus.
units.tr: Lastly, what must be observed among the Egyptians, that is, among the posterity of the cursed Ham, is how dangerous and full of scandal it is to fix one's eyes on the beauty of women, Genesis 6, Sirach 9, Matthew 5. Likewise, it is almost everywhere the custom of courtiers to converse and exchange talk about vain and carnal things.

units.la: Et, dignos esse pœna non solùm eos, qui faciunt mala: sed etiam qui assentiuntur ijs, aut operam suâ præbent, qui faciunt, Rom.I.
units.tr: And that not only those who do evil deserve punishment, but also those who consent to those who do it, or lend their help to those who do it, Romans 1.

units.la: Et, Deum esse iudicem scortatorum & adulterorum, Heb.13. Deniq; ignorantiam cum petulantia coniunctam non excusare quenquam. Dominus Iesus det nobis omnibus castam, puram & sanctam mentem, ut olim videre possimus Deum Opt.Max.& pulcherrimum, atque eundem & amare & laudare in secula seculorum, Amen.
units.tr: And that God is the judge of fornicators and adulterers, Hebrews 13. Finally, that ignorance joined with wantonness excuses no one. May the Lord Jesus give us all a chaste, pure and holy mind, so that we may one day see God, the best and greatest, most beautiful, and love and praise Him for ever and ever, Amen.

units.la: CONCIO VI.
units.tr: SERMON VI.

units.la: Genef. 16.
units.tr: Genef. 16.

units.la: TAQ̄VE Sarai vxor Abrami non genuit illi: habuit autem ancillam Aegyptiam, nomine Hagar. Dixitque Sarai ad Abram: En prohibuit me dominus ne parerem, ingredere quaeso ad ancillam meam, si forte aedificer ex ea: & obediebat Abram voci Sarai. Tulitque Sarai uxor Abram, Hagar Aegyptiam ancillam suam, a fine decem annorum, quo habitauit Abram in terra Chanaan, et dedit eam Abra marito suo in uxorem. Qui cum ingressus esset ad Hagar, concepit illa: vidensque se gravidam, vilipensa est domina eius in oculis suis. Et dixit Sarai ad Abram: Iniuria mea super te est: ego dedi ancillam meam in sinum tuum, quæ videns quòd conceperit, vilipendor ego in oculis illius, iudicet Dominus inter me & te. Dixit autem Abram ad Sarai: Ecce ancilla tua in manu tua, fac illi quod bonum est in oculis tuis: & cùm affligeret eam Sarai, fugit illa à facie eius. Invenit autem eam angelus Domini iuxta fontem aquæ in solitudine, iuxta illum inquam fontem, qui est in via Sur. Dixitq;, Hagar ancilla Sarai, unde venisti, & quò vadis? dixit illa, à facie Sarai domina mea ego fugio. Dixitq; ad eam angelus Domini: Reuertere ad dominam tuam, & humilia te sub manibus eius. Rursumq; dixit ad eam angelus Domini: Multiplicando multiplicabo semen tuum, & non numerabitur præ multitudine. Dixitq; ad eam angelus Domini: Ecce tu prægnans es, et paries filium, vocabisq; nomen eius Ismael: audiuit enim Dominus afflictionem tuam.
units.tr: Now Sarai, Abram's wife, had borne him no children; but she had an Egyptian maidservant named Hagar. And Sarai said to Abram: Behold, the Lord has kept me from bearing; go in, I beg you, to my maidservant; perhaps I may be built up through her. And Abram obeyed the voice of Sarai. So Sarai, Abram's wife, took Hagar her Egyptian maidservant, after Abram had lived ten years in the land of Canaan, and gave her to her husband Abram as a wife. And when he had gone in to Hagar, she conceived; and seeing that she was with child, her mistress was despised in her eyes. And Sarai said to Abram: The wrong done to me is upon you; I gave my maidservant into your bosom, and now that she sees she has conceived, I am despised in her eyes; let the Lord judge between me and you. But Abram said to Sarai: Behold, your maidservant is in your hand; do to her what is good in your eyes. And when Sarai dealt harshly with her, she fled from her face. Now the angel of the Lord found her by a spring of water in the wilderness, by that spring, I mean, which is on the way to Shur. And he said: Hagar, maidservant of Sarai, where have you come from, and where are you going? She said: I am fleeing from the face of my mistress Sarai. And the angel of the Lord said to her: Return to your mistress, and humble yourself under her hands. And again the angel of the Lord said to her: I will greatly multiply your seed, so that it shall not be numbered for multitude. And the angel of the Lord said to her: Behold, you are with child, and you shall bear a son, and you shall call his name Ishmael, for the Lord has heard your affliction.

units.la: Quemadmodum nonnulla sunt in epistolis Pauli (teste Petro) difficilia intellectu, quæ indocti parumque firmi detorquent ad suam ipsorum perniciem: sic & in quinque libris Mosis.
units.tr: Just as some things in the epistles of Paul (as Peter testifies) are hard to understand, and the unlearned and unsteady twist them to their own destruction, so it is also with the five books of Moses.

units.la: Scribitur hoc loco de Abramo, quòd praeter vxorem suam Sarai,acceperit etiam in uxorem ancillam Hagar, & quòd ingressus fit ad eam: quo verbo pudicè concubitus defignatur. Posset igitur aliquis cogitare, Abramum vel in hoc peccasse: vel si non peccauit, nobis licere ipsius exemplum sequi.
units.tr: It is written here of Abram that, besides his wife Sarai, he also took Hagar as a wife, and that he went in to her; a word by which intercourse is modestly indicated. Someone might therefore think that Abram sinned in this too; or, if he did not sin, that we are allowed to follow his example.

units.la: Sed hic nobis sciendum est, facta sanctorum virorum non debere sine discrimine & iudicio in exempla referri, quæ quis imitetur. Si enim promiscuè deberent in exemplum & legem trahi facta eorum omnia, sequeretur, nobis quoque licere ea peccata facere, quæ aliquando fecerunt ipsi, imbecillitate carnis, ut homines, victi. Verum tantum abest ut hoc liceat, ut nec in iis omnibus debeamus imitari eos, quì ipsi sine discrimine atq; peccato fecère. Non enim frustra dominus Iesus increpauit discipulos suos, dicentes, Domine vis, ut ignis descendat de cœlo, & consumat illos, quemadmodum & Helias fecit? Luc. 9. Hinc apud multos usitatum est distum[?]: Actiones bonorum non facere legem vniuersalem. Neque enim exempla sunt rerum agendarum canones, sed Dei præcèpta, ut recte monet Andreas Hyperius lib.2. de Theologo,cap.21. obser.5. Et Chrysostomus in caput quintum Matthæi: Vides, inquit, quemadmodum eædem ipsæ res fecundum tempora, nunc bonæ, nunc vero contrarii esse generis appareant. Nam & vestem non indui paruulo quidem honestum est, viro autem pudendum. Vis ne etiam é[?] diuerso discere, quemadmodum puero apta non sint ea, quae viro sunt? Da puero veste virilem, & plurimus omnino risus sequitur, maiusque erit incedentis periculum, & sæpe[?] huc illucque nutantis. Da illi negocia curære ciuilia, & vel mercari, vel ferre, ac metere, & erit rursus grande ridiculum. Et quid ego ista commemoro, quando homicidium quoque ipsum, quod à diabolo inuentum esse manifestum est (Ioann. octauo) opportunè aliquando factum, eum, qui id operatus est, Phinees scilicet maximè fecit sacerdotij honore decorari. Abraham verò non homicida solum, verùm etiam parricida, quod certè est grauius effectu, magis Deo magisque complacuit. Sed & Petrus geminum fecit homicidium, fuit tamen opus spirituale, quod factum est. Non sola igitur respiciamus opera, sed tempus, & causam, & voluntatem, & personarum differentiam: & quantacunque alia ipsis operibus acciderint, diligentissimè requiramus: non enim possumus ad veritatem aliter peruenire. hæc ille.
units.tr: But here we must understand that the deeds of holy men ought not to be cited as examples to be imitated without discrimination and judgment. For if all their deeds were to be drawn indiscriminately into example and law, it would follow that we too may commit those sins which they at some time committed, overcome as men by the weakness of the flesh. But so far is this from being permitted that we ought not to imitate them even in all those things which they did without discrimination and without sin. For the Lord Jesus rightly rebuked his disciples who said: Lord, do you want us to command fire to come down from heaven and consume them, as Elijah did? Luke 9. Hence it is commonly said among many: The actions of good men do not make a universal law. For examples of things to be done are not rules, but God's precepts, as Andreas Hyperius rightly advises in book 2 of On the Theologian, chapter 21, observation 5. And Chrysostom on the fifth chapter of Matthew: You see, he says, how the very same things appear now good, now of the contrary kind, according to the times. For it is fitting for a small child to wear clothes, but shameful for a man. Do you wish to learn from the opposite how things suited to a boy are not suited to a man? Dress a boy in a man's clothes, and a great laughter follows, and he will be in greater danger of falling as he staggers this way and that. Give him civil business to manage, to trade, or to carry and reap, and again he will be a great laughing-stock. And why do I recall these things, when even homicide itself, which is clearly invented by the devil (John 8), was on some occasion done fittingly, and Phinehas, who did it, was honoured with the great dignity of the priesthood? Abraham, however, who was not only a murderer but also a parricide, which is certainly worse in effect, pleased God more and more. But Peter also committed a double homicide, yet the deed that was done was a spiritual one. Therefore let us not look only at the deeds, but diligently inquire into the time, the cause, the will, and the difference of persons, and whatever other circumstances attend the deeds themselves; for we cannot otherwise arrive at the truth. So far he.

units.la: Pertinet huc illud Nicolai de Lyra super istud: Cumque ille acquiesceret deprecanti, &c. Propter quod Abraham non vituperatur de bigamia, sicut Lamech? Quia non accepit secundam vxorem motus libidine, sed prolis amore: nec absque consensu primæ vxoris, immo ipsa supplicante: quod non fecit Lamech, scilicet libidine motus, & sine consensu alterius vxoris. His non dissimilia ferè scribit D.Augustinus lib.16. de Ciuitate Dei, capite 25. ait enim: Quod attinet ad rem gestam, nullo modo est inurendum de hac concubina crimen Abrahae. usus est ea quippe ad generandam prolem,non ad explendam libidinē:nec insultans,sed potius obediens coniugi, quae suae sterilitati credidit esse solatium, si secundum ancillae uterum, quod natura non poterat, voluntate faceret suum, & eo iure, quo dicit Apostolus (1. Corin. 7.) Similiter & vir non habet potestatem corporis sui, sed mulier, uteretur mulier ad pariendum ex altera, quod non poterat ex seipsa. Nulla est hic cupido lasciuiae, nulla nequitiae turpitudo. Ab uxore causa prolis ancilla marito traditur: à marito causa prolis accipitur: ab utroque non culpae luxus, sed naturae fructus exquiritur. Deniq; cùm ancilla grauida dominae sterili superbiret,& hoc Sara suspicione muliebri viro potius imputaret, etiam ibi demonstrauit Abraham se non amatorem seruum, sed liberum fuisse genitorem, & in Hagar Sarae coniugi pudicitiam custodisse: nec voluptatem suam, sed voluntatem illius impleuisse: accepisse ,nec petijsse:accessisse, non haesisse:feminasse,non amasse. Ait enim: Ecce ancilla tua in manibus tuis, utere ea, quomodo tibi placuerit. O virum viriliter utentem foeminis,coniuge temperanter,ancilla obtemperanter,nulla inteperanter. His adde, quòd antiquis iustis nō vitio vertitur, quod pluribus feminis usi sunt: nec contra naturam hoc fecerunt, cum non lasciuiendi causa, sed gignendi hoc facerent: nec contra morem, nec contra præceptum, quia nulla lege erat prohibitum: nec dum promulgata erat unius uxoris lex Euangelica. Habebat insuper Abram promissionem à Deo multiplicandi feminis sui, Genes. 15. sed nec dum sciebat, ex qua uxore: quia postea demum cap.17.dictum est ei de Sara: Ex illa dabo tibi filium, cui benedicturus sum, &c. Huc pertinet illud Malach.2. de Abrahamo, cuius exemplo & zelo inconsulto Iudæi tempore prophetæ abuti conabantur. Et quid unus ille (nempe Abrahamus fecit[?]) quærebat semen Dei, i. Messiam, verum & patri coæternum Dei filium, quem ex sua stirpe nasciturum esse, ex promissione didicerat. Et sensus est: Non immoderata & cæca libido Abrahamum impulit, ut Hagarem sibi desponsaret: sed inconsideratus salutis humanæ zelus, qui ex promissi feminis immodico desiderio enatus fuerat, primo ipsam Saram, deinde Abrahamum quoque mouit, ut tale quid facerent, cum ipsis iam senio multo cōtabescentibus feminis promissi spes interitura videretur. Vestra autem longe alia est ratio, qui ex libidine nefanda hoc facitis, & uxoribus vestris reclamantibus alias vobis adiungitis, &c. ubi rursum admonemur, in exemplis sanctorum non modo videndum esse quid factum sit, sed quis illis factorum suorum finis & fcopus fuerit, & num bene & recte fecerint omnia, quae de illis commemorantur. Quia.n. illi quoq; diuinis legibus tenentur, illorum quoque facta ad illarum regulam examinari debent. Prudenter ergo Paulus ait : Imitatores mei estote, sicut & ego Christi sum.
units.tr: Nicholas of Lyra's remark on that passage, "And when he acquiesced to her entreaty, etc.," bears on this: Why is Abraham not blamed for bigamy, as Lamech was? Because he did not take a second wife moved by lust, but by love of offspring; nor without the consent of the first wife, indeed at her own pleading; which Lamech did not do, namely, moved by lust and without the consent of his other wife. Augustine writes things not unlike these in book 16 of The City of God, chapter 25; for he says: As far as the deed itself goes, the crime cannot in any way be charged against Abraham concerning this concubine. He used her indeed for begetting offspring, not for satisfying lust; not insulting but rather obeying his wife, who believed it would be a solace for her barrenness if, through the womb of the maidservant, she made her own by will what nature could not do, and by that right of which the Apostle speaks (1 Cor. 7): Likewise the husband has no power over his own body, but the wife does; the wife would use another to bear what she could not bear herself. There is here no desire of wantonness, no shamefulness of wickedness. The maidservant is handed over by the wife to the husband for the sake of offspring; the husband takes her for the sake of offspring; from both is sought not the luxury of fault but the fruit of nature. Finally, when the pregnant maidservant grew proud toward her barren mistress, and Sarah in womanly suspicion imputed this to her husband rather, Abraham showed there too that he had been a father, not a lover, of a slave, but a free one, and that he preserved chastity toward Sarah his wife in Hagar: he fulfilled not his own pleasure but her will; he took, and did not seek; he approached, did not cling; he had to do with women, did not love them. For he says: Behold your maidservant is in your hands; use her as it shall please you. O man who uses women manfully, temperate toward his wife, obedient toward the maidservant, intemperate toward no one. Add to these that in the ancient righteous men it is not held against them that they had several women; nor did they do this against nature, since they did it not for the sake of wantonness but for begetting; nor against custom, nor against a command, since it was forbidden by no law, nor yet had the Gospel law of one wife been promulgated. Moreover Abram had God's promise of multiplying his seed, Gen. 15, but he did not yet know from which wife; for afterwards it was said to him at chapter 17 concerning Sarah: From her I will give you a son, whom I will bless, etc. To this pertains that passage of Malachi 2 about Abraham, by whose example and unadvised zeal the Jews of the prophet's time tried to justify themselves. And what did that one (namely Abraham) seek? "The seed of God," that is, the Messiah, the true Son of God coeternal with the Father, whom he had learned from the promise would be born of his stock. And the sense is: it was not an immoderate and blind lust that impelled Abraham to take Hagar to himself; rather an ill-considered zeal for human salvation, which had sprung from an immoderate desire for the promised seed, first moved Sarah herself, then Abraham too, to do such a thing, since with both of them already wasting away in great old age, the hope of the promise seemed about to perish. Your reason, however, is quite different, who do this from abominable lust, and take other wives to yourselves while your wives protest, etc. Here we are again warned that in the examples of saints one must look not only at what was done, but also at what end and aim they had in their deeds, and whether they did all things recorded of them well and rightly. For since they too are bound by divine laws, their deeds too must be examined by the rule of those laws. Wisely therefore Paul says: Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ.

units.la: 2[?] Etsi autem non omnia facta sanctorum veterum iuxta literam imitari debemus: tamen utilissimae sunt ipsorum historiae: praefertim si secundum spiritum intelligantur: sicut & praesens historia intelligenda est, monente Apostolo, Galat. 4. ubi de duplici statu liberorum Abrahami loquitur: quorum alter lege continetur, alter gratia: uterque verò suis mysticis lineis hoc loco adumbratur. Qui lege continentur, eos liberos habet, qui sui iuris non sunt, sed alieni: neque partem ullam in haereditate obtinent,sed cum Ismaele domo expulsi foràs bonis suis ornantur. Hoc ipsum est, natum esse ex Hagare ancilla ad ser-uitutem, quae in iure peccati & mortis in iugo externi cultus legis cernitur. Qui autem status in gratia & promissione cōsistit[?], is liberos educat natos ex Sara domina, verò liberos à potestate peccati & mortis, & à legis paedagogia. Alterum statum Apostolus testamentum à Sina monte generans ad seruitutem, alterum à Hierosolyma, quae libera est, & omnium credentium genitrix testamentum vocat.
units.tr: 2. Although we are not bound to imitate all the deeds of the holy men of old according to the letter, their histories are nonetheless most useful, especially if they are understood according to the spirit. So too this present history must be understood, as the Apostle reminds us in Galatians 4, where he speaks of the twofold state of the children of Abraham: one of them is bound by the law, the other by grace; and both are here foreshadowed in their mystical lines. Those who are bound by the law have children who are not their own masters but belong to another; they obtain no share of the inheritance, but, like Ishmael, are cast out of the house and go forth stripped of their goods. This is precisely to be born of Hagar the handmaid, to slavery, which is seen in the bondage of sin and death, under the yoke of external worship of the law. But the state that stands in grace and promise bears children born of Sarah the mistress, who are free from the power of sin and death and from the schoolmaster of the law. The Apostle calls the one covenant, which generates to slavery, the covenant from Mount Sinai, and the other, which is free and is the mother of all believers, the covenant from Jerusalem.

units.la: 3[?] Sunt autem plura adhuc in hac nobis hi storia obseruanda:in qua omnia geruntur ratione diuina, concubitus nimirum, conceptus, cōtemptus, afflictio, fuga in desertum, apparitio angeli, reditus. Poteit [?] enim hic locus, vt D. Chrysostomus scribit, docere & viros & mulieres, vt magna inter se concordia viuant, & coniugij vinculum indifruptum seruent: & neque vir insurgat aduersus mulierem, sed vt vasi infirmiori maiorem illi veniam tribuat: neque mulier viro se opponat, aut ab eo dissideat, sed vt vicisim alter alterius onera ferre certet, domesticamque pacem omnibus bonis praeferant. Quando enim concordia & pax & vinculum dilectionis cum muliere & viro fuerit, omnia simul affluunt bona, & nullis insidijs expositi sunt, magno & inexpugnabili quodā muro circumdati, sua iuxta Dei præceptum cōncordia. Hoc ferro fortiores eos reddet, hoc omnibus diuitijs & abundantia magis locupletabit, hoc supernam gloriam eis conferet, hoc & Dei benevolentiam eis vbertim conciliabit. Illae enim verae sunt diuitiae, illae maximae sunt facultates, si vir cum muliere non discordet, sed coniuncti sunt vt corpus vnum. Tales etsi in paupertate sint, etsi in vilitate, omnium sunt beatissimi, veram percipiunt voluptatem, & in continua consistunt tranquillitate. Sed rursum vbi non est mutuus amor coniugum (quemadmodum Philippus Melanchthon scribit) ibi discordia sauciat mentes, impedit inuocationem Dei, turbat totam domesticam confuetudinem, & parit multa peccata. Interdū & cùm voluntates distractæ sunt, sequuntur adulteria & pœnæ, in quibus multi ruunt in noua scelera & in tragicas calamitates.
units.tr: 3. Moreover, there are still many things in this history to be observed, in which everything is done by divine plan: the intercourse, the conception, the contempt, the affliction, the flight into the wilderness, the appearance of the angel, the return. For this passage, as Chrysostom writes, can teach both husbands and wives to live in great harmony with one another and to keep the bond of marriage unbroken: the husband should not rise up against his wife, but should show her greater indulgence as the weaker vessel; and the wife should not oppose her husband or quarrel with him, but each should strive to bear the other's burdens in turn and prefer domestic peace to all goods. For when there is concord, peace and the bond of love between wife and husband, all good things flow together at once, and they are exposed to no snares, being surrounded by a great and impregnable wall, namely their concord, which is in accordance with God's precept. This will make them stronger than any iron, this will enrich them more than all riches and abundance, this will confer on them heavenly glory, and this will abundantly win them the goodwill of God. For those are true riches and the greatest resources, if the husband does not disagree with his wife, but they are joined together as one body. Such people, even if they are in poverty, even if in lowly estate, are the most blessed of all: they receive true pleasure and live in continual tranquillity. But conversely, where there is no mutual love of spouses (as Philip Melanchthon writes), there discord wounds the minds, hinders the invocation of God, disturbs the whole domestic order, and gives birth to many sins. Sometimes, when wills are pulled apart, adulteries and punishments follow, in which many fall into new crimes and tragic calamities.

units.la: Vide etiam, quantum olim virtutis studium apud veteres exercebatur, quomodo & viri temperati erant, & magnam continentiam habebant rationem, & mulieres zelotypiæ carebant vitio. Dedita enim opera dicit Scriptura: Et vt tulit Sara Hagarem ancillam. Et iterum: Dedit eam in vxorem: vt dicas quomodo absque affectione negocii egerit, & quantum apud eos virtutis studium.
units.tr: See also how greatly the pursuit of virtue was practised among the ancients, how both the men were temperate and held great self-restraint, and the women were free of the vice of jealousy. For Scripture says deliberately: "And when Sarah took Hagar the handmaid," and again: "She gave her to him as a wife," so that you may see how she acted without any passion in the matter, and how great was the pursuit of virtue among them.

units.la: In Sarai laudandum est, quòd non dicit marito suo, Da mihi liberos, alioquin moriar, vt Rachel Iacobo, Genes. trigesimo: sed agnoscit penes Dominum positum claudendi & aperiendi vteri vim: & parere liberos, Dei opus & munus esse, non naturæ: iuxta illud Psal. 113. Qui habitare facit sterilem in domo, matrem filiorum lætantem. Et Genes. 30. Recordatus quoque Dominus Rachelis, exaudiuit eam, & aperuit vuluam eius, quæ concepit & peperit filium. Item Ruth 4.
