Hanc (sponsam) imitentur mulieres: hunc (sponsum) æmulentur viri: sic sponsas ducere curent.
units.tr: 4 "You have seen," says Saint Chrysostom, "how in former times they used to take wives for their sons! How they sought the nobility of the soul rather than an abundance of wealth! Nowhere were there written contracts, nowhere agreements and other foolish things, such as are now made among us, and those words that are contained in documents: 'If he dies without children,' and 'if this or that should happen.' But among them there was nothing of the kind; their chief and most serious concern was the maiden's character. Nowhere were there cymbals and dances." And again: "Consider, I beg you, how nowhere were those superfluous and useless things, nowhere the devilish pomp, nowhere cymbals, flutes and dances, and those satanic feasts and jests full of every obscenity; but all honesty, all wisdom, all gentleness. Let women imitate her (the bride); let men emulate him (the bridegroom); thus let them take care to take brides."

units.la: Quare enim, dic oro, statim ab initio fordibus impleri finis puellæ aures, tam turpibus cantilenis: tam intempestiua illa pompa,[?] nescis quomodo adolescentia per se in malum propensa? cur honesta nuptiarum mysteria inuulgas? oportebat omnia hæc depellere, & verecundiam principio docere puellam, & sacerdotes vocare, & precibus & benedictionibus concordiam coniugij constringere: ut amor sponsi augeatur, & puellæ continentia crescat, & omnia quæ fiunt, eo spectent, ut virtutis opera ingrediantur in domum illam, tollanturque é medio omnes diaboli insidiæ: & ipsi gratia Dei uniti, iucundè vitam perficiant: qua nobis omnibus frui detur gratia, & misericordia domini nostri Iesu Christi, cui cum patre & Spiritu sancto sit gloria in secula fecu!orum.
units.tr: "Why, tell me, I beg you, from the very beginning do you allow the girl's ears to be filled with filth, with such shameful songs and such untimely display? Do you not know how youth is of its own accord inclined to evil? Why do you make the honourable mysteries of marriage common? It was fitting to drive out all these things, to teach the girl modesty from the start, to call the priests, and by prayers and blessings to bind the harmony of the marriage, so that the husband's love may grow, the girl's self-restraint may increase, and everything that is done may aim at this: that the works of virtue may enter that house, and all the snares of the devil may be removed from the midst; and, united with the grace of God, they may live their life happily. May the grace and mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ be granted to us all, to whom with the Father and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever and ever."

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XI.
units.tr: CONCIO XI.

units.la: Genef. 26.
units.tr: Genef. 26.

units.la: Acta est autem fames in terra, praeter famem priorem, quae fuit in diebus Abrahā: et abijt Isahac ad Abimelech regem Palestinae in Gerar. Apparuitq; ei Dominus, & ait: Ne descendas in Aegyptum, sed habita in terra, quam dixero tibi. Peregrinare in terra ista, & ego ero tecum, benedicamq; tibi: nam tibi & semini tuo dabo omnes terras istas, & confirmabo iuramentum, quod iurau i Abraham patri tuo. Multiplicabo quoque semen tuum sicut stellas coeli, & dabo semini tuo omnes terras istas, benedicenturq; in semine tuo omnes gentes terrae. Eo quod audierit Abraham vocem meam, & custodierit observantiam meam, praecepta mea, statuta mea, & leges meas. Sedit itaq; Isahac in Gerar. Et interrogauerunt viri illius loci de uxore sua: ipse vero dixit, soror mea est: timens dicere, uxor mea est: ne forte occidant me viri loci huius propter Rebeccam, quae pulchra erat aspectu. Factum est autem tum ei in longum extenderentur dies in eo loco,vt aspiceret Abimelech,rex Paleftina per fenestram,et videret Ifaac ridetem cum Rebecca vxore sua. Et vocauit Abimelech Ifaac,dixitq;: vtique ipsa vxor tua est, & cur dixisti soror mea est? cui respondit Ifaac: quoniam dixi,ne forte moriar propter ipsam. Ait Abimelech: cur id fecisti nobis? parum abfuit, quin vnus e populo dormijfet cum vxore tua, & induxisses super nos delictum. Prxcepit itaque Abimelech omni populo,dicens: Qui tetigerit virum illum & vxorem eius, morte interficietur. Seminauit autem Ifaac in terra illa,& inuenit in illo anno centum modios, benedixitq; ei Dominus. Et creuit vir ille, & eundo profecit atque euectus est, quousq; supra modum magnificatus est. Habuit enim possessionem ouium, & possessionem boum atque multiplex famulitum,& ob id Palæstini ei inuidebant. Nam omnes puteos,quos foderunt serui patris eius in diebus Abraham, obturauerunt Palaftini,implentes eos puluere. Et dixit Abimelech ad Ifaac: recede à nobis,quoniam robustior factus es nobis vehementer. Abijt igitur inde Ifaac, & mansit in torrente Gerar, habitauitq; ibi.
units.tr: Now there was a famine in the land, besides the first famine that was in the days of Abraham. And Isaac went unto Abimelech king of the Philistines unto Gerar. And the LORD appeared unto him, and said, Go not down into Egypt; dwell in the land which I shall tell thee of: sojourn in this land, and I will be with thee, and will bless thee; for unto thee, and unto thy seed, I will give all these countries, and I will perform the oath which I sware unto Abraham thy father; and I will make thy seed to multiply as the stars of heaven, and will give unto thy seed all these countries; and in thy seed shall all the nations of the earth be blessed; because that Abraham obeyed my voice, and kept my charge, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws. And Isaac dwelt in Gerar. And the men of the place asked him of his wife; and he said, She is my sister: for he feared to say, She is my wife; lest, said he, the men of the place should kill me for Rebekah; because she was fair to look upon. And it came to pass, when he had been there a long time, that Abimelech king of the Philistines looked out at a window, and saw, and behold, Isaac was sporting with Rebekah his wife. And Abimelech called Isaac, and said, Behold, of a surety she is thy wife: and how saidst thou, She is my sister? And Isaac said unto him, Because I said, Lest I die for her. And Abimelech said, What is this thou hast done unto us? one of the people might lightly have lain with thy wife, and thou shouldest have brought guiltiness upon us. And Abimelech charged all his people, saying, He that toucheth this man or his wife shall surely be put to death. Then Isaac sowed in that land, and received in the same year an hundredfold: and the LORD blessed him. And the man waxed great, and went forward, and grew until he became very great. For he had possession of flocks, and possession of herds, and great store of servants: and the Philistines envied him. For all the wells which his father's servants had digged in the days of Abraham his father, the Philistines had stopped, and filled them with earth. And Abimelech said unto Isaac, Go from us; for thou art much mightier than we. And Isaac departed thence, and pitched his tent in the valley of Gerar, and dwelt there.

units.la: 1 Ex hac historia de Ifaaco & sua coniugę discimus primò, sanctorum vniuersam vitā nihil aliud, quàm perpetuam in varijs afflictionibus militiam esse, vt Iob ait cap.7. militiam inquam aduersus famem, pestes, bella, peccatum, mortem, & potestates peccati & mortis. Hic enim Ifaacus ob famem rerumq; penuriam, in regionem externam, nempe in Gerar, metropolim Palestinæ, proficisci cogitur cum Rebecca (quæ simul cum marito iugum tulit) & ibi non modo propter Rebeccæ formositatem in vitæ periculum venit, sed etiam varijs Philistinorum molestijs & iniurijs afficitur.
units.tr: 1 From this history of Isaac and his wife we learn first that the whole life of the saints is nothing other than a constant warfare amid various afflictions, as Job says in chapter 7: a warfare, I say, against famine, plagues, wars, sin, death, and the powers of sin and death. For Isaac, because of the famine and the lack of goods, is compelled to set out for a foreign region, namely Gerar, the chief city of Palestine, together with Rebekah, who bore the yoke along with her husband; and there he not only comes into danger of his life on account of Rebekah's beauty, but is also harassed by various troubles and injuries from the Philistines.

units.la: Cæterum Dominus Deus noster non patitur, vt sui electi auxilio diuino destituti suprimantur. Ipse enim ad confolandū & adiuuandum in tentatione famis apparuit Isaaco: & non solum mandatum ei dedit, ne descenderet in Aegyptum, exemplo patris, Genes.12. sed maneret in Geraris, in quo submonuit eum conditionis vitæ præsentis, quæ nihil nisi peregrinatio est: verūmetiam promisit ei præsentiam & benedictionem suam, inquiens: Ego ero tecum. q.d. cum suppeditatorem bonorum omnium habeas, ne sis solicitus, ne sis anxius: ego enim Dominus omnium ero tecum. Et præterea benedicam te, hoc est, gloriosum te faciam, & benedictio-nem [?]dem meam præbebo: idq; propter patris tui Abrahami fidem & obedientiam. Verum itaq; est, quod Exod.20.legitur: Et faciens beneficium in mille ætates ijs qui diligunt me, sed ita, si filij patrem referant innocentia, vt fecisse legitur Isaacus. Obediuit enim & ipse Deo, & mansit in Gerar: vt vitaret famem, ne Deum tentaret.
units.tr: Moreover, our Lord God does not allow his elect, when destitute of divine help, to be crushed. For he appeared to Isaac to comfort and help him in the temptation of famine; and he not only commanded him not to go down into Egypt, following the example of his father (Gen. 12), but to remain in Gerar, where he reminded him of the condition of the present life, which is nothing but a pilgrimage. He even promised him his presence and blessing, saying, "I will be with you." As if to say: since you have the provider of all good things, do not be anxious or troubled; for I, the Lord of all, will be with you. And besides, I will bless you, that is, I will make you glorious, and I will bestow my blessing upon you; and this for the sake of your father Abraham's faith and obedience. So it is true what is read in Exodus 20: "showing mercy unto thousands of them that love me," provided that the children follow their father in innocence, as Isaac is read to have done. For he too obeyed God, and remained in Gerar, so that he might avoid the famine and not tempt God.

units.la: Vide interim Dei sapientiam, quomodo erigit mentem iusti, & alacriorem reddit: & vt patris imitator fiat, efficit. Nam si ille, inquit, quia meæ obediuit voci, tanta pollicitatione dignus habitus est, & propter illius virtutem in te, qui ex eo natus es, sum impleturus: si & ipse illius imitator fueris, & eadem qua ille via incesseris, cogita quantam apud me beneuolentiam habiturus sis, & quanta mea cura te dignaturus sim. Nam si cui ob alterius virtutem bene futurum est, si & ipse virtute præditus fuerit, multo maiore dignus habebitur cura.
units.tr: Consider meanwhile the wisdom of God, how he raises up the mind of the righteous man and makes it more cheerful, and brings it about that he becomes an imitator of his father. For, he says, if that man, because he obeyed my voice, was thought worthy of so great a promise, and I am going to fulfil it for you who were born of him because of his virtue; if you also become his imitator and walk in the same way he walked, consider how great goodwill you will have with me, and how great my care will be to count you worthy. For if someone is to fare well because of another's virtue, and he himself too is endowed with virtue, he will be thought worthy of much greater care.

units.la: 2 Quòd autem Isaacus vxorem suam sororem vocauit (sicut Abrahamus suam Saram, Genef.20.) factum est fortasse non solum ob metum mortis, quæ nondum erat per Messiam victa: sed etiam propter familiam & cognationem, de qua Rebecca erat: nec non propter figuram Christi & ecclesiæ eius, quæ ipsius & vxor, Ephef.5. & soror, Matth.12. est, idque per fidem, quæ purificat cor eius, Act.15. vt pulchra appareat.
units.tr: 2 That Isaac called his wife his sister (as Abraham called his Sarah his sister, Gen. 20) happened perhaps not only from fear of death, which was not yet conquered by the Messiah, but also on account of the family and kinship from which Rebekah came; and also on account of the figure of Christ and of his Church, which is both his wife (Eph. 5) and his sister (Matt. 12), and this through faith, which purifies her heart (Acts 15), so that she may appear beautiful.

units.la: Quod ad lusum & iocum, seu risum Isaaci (cui Deus benedictum semen promiserat) cum vxore sua attinet, vide quid sit, Prouer. 5. & Eccles. 9. Vbi Salomon ait, Fruere tuae iuuentutis vxore, amabili cerua, &c. Fruere vita cum dilecta tibi coniuge, &c. Quid vero absurdum, si propheta carnale aliquid lusit, vt eum caperet affectus vxoris, cum verbum Dei caro factum fit, vt habitaret in nobis?
units.tr: As for the play and sport, or laughter, of Isaac (to whom God had promised a blessed seed) with his wife, see what it is in Proverbs 5 and Ecclesiastes 9, where Solomon says: "Rejoice with the wife of your youth, a lovely hind," etc.; "Enjoy life with the wife you love," etc. And what is absurd if the prophet played something carnal, so that the affection of his wife might take hold of him, since the Word of God was made flesh, that he might dwell among us?

units.la: Nemo autem iocetur cum aliena, sed quisque propriam vxorem habeat, 1. Corinth. 7. vt vitet fornicationem & adulterium: quod peccatum est grande etiam iudicio Abimelechi, id est, regis Palaestinorum (Abimelech enim regiae dignitatis commune nomen erat: vt apud Aegyptios Pharao, & apud Romanos Caesar) qui rex cognouit Rebeccam Isaaci vxorem esse ex eo, quod vidit eum cum illa iocantem. Nemo enim cum germana sorore congreditur nisi incestuosus. Idem rex quoque tanquam pater patriae prohibuit populo suo, peregrinis, & coniugibus honestis vim inferre. Sed & de Alexandro Magno legitur, quod animum habuerit alienum à constupranda aliena vxore. Quum.n.puella multa nocte ad eum efferet deducta, cum eo dormitura, rogauit rex vbi fuisset tamdiu: illa respondente, se expectasse donec maritus isset cubitum: ministros accitos acriter obiurgauit, Reducite, inquit, hac: parum enim abfuit, quia vestra culpa fuerim factus adulter.
units.tr: Let no one, however, joke with another man's wife, but let each have his own wife (1 Cor. 7), so that he may avoid fornication and adultery; which is a great sin even in the judgment of Abimelech, that is, king of the Philistines. (Abimelech was a common name for royal dignity, as Pharaoh among the Egyptians and Caesar among the Romans.) This king recognized that Rebekah was Isaac's wife from the fact that he saw him joking with her. For no one has intercourse with a true sister unless he is incestuous. The same king, too, as the father of his country, forbade his people to do violence to foreigners and to honourable wives. And of Alexander the Great it is read that he had a mind alien to debauching another man's wife. For when a girl was brought to him late at night, to sleep with him, the king asked where she had been so long; she replied that she had waited until her husband had gone to bed. Calling in the attendants, he rebuked them sharply: "Take her back," he said, "for I came very close to becoming an adulterer through your fault."

units.la: ¶ Porro consideranda nobis hic venit Dei bonitas & veritas. Stat enim promissis, benedicit Isaaco: qui quidem seuit & laborauit, sed à Domino benedictionem expectavit, atque accepit tantam, ut & Palæstinos ad inuidiam moueret, & regem illorum ad odium: id quod Isaacus patienter tulit. Omnes igitur sperent, non in principibus, sed in solo Deo: qui suos semper cruce probat, sed ab ea tandem liberat: cui debetur honor, gloria & potestas in secula seculorum, Amen.
units.tr: ¶ Furthermore, here we must consider the goodness and truth of God. For he stands by his promises and blesses Isaac, who indeed sowed and laboured, but expected and received the blessing from the Lord, and received so great a blessing that it stirred the Philistines to envy and their king to hatred; which Isaac bore patiently. Let all therefore hope, not in princes, but in God alone, who always tests his own by the cross, but at length delivers them from it; to whom be honour, glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XII
units.tr: CONCIO XII

units.la: Genef. 28.
units.tr: Genef. 28.

units.la: Vocauit itaque Isahac Iacob, & benedixit eum: præcepitq; ei, et dixit ad eum: non accipies uxorem de filiabus Chanaan. Surge, vade in Mesopotamiam, ad domũ Bethuel patris matris tuæ, & sume tibi inde uxorẽ de filiabus Laban fratris matris tuæ. Deus autem omnipotens benedicat tibi, & faciat te crescere, atque multiplicet te, ut sis in congregationem populorum. Det quoque tibi benedictionem Abraham, tibi & semini tuo tecum, ut in hæreditatem accipias terram peregrinationum tuarum, quam dedit Deus Abraham. Dimisit itaque Isahac Iacob, & ille abiit in Mesopotamiam ad Laban filium Bethuel Syri, fratrem Rebecca, matris Iacob & Esau. Et videns Esau quod benedixisset Isahac Iacob, & quod misisset eum in Mesopotamiam, unde sibi sumeret uxorem, atque praecepisset ei cum benediceret eum, dicens: non accipies uxorem de filiabus Chanaan. Et quod Iacob obediisset patri suo & matri suae, & abiisset in Mesopotamiam. Videns etiam Esau, quod malae essent filiae Chanaan in oculis Isahac patris sui. Abyit ipse Esau ad Ismaelem, & accepit Mahalath filiam Ismaelis filii Abraham, sororem Nebaioth, super uxores suas sibi in uxorem. Egressus itaque est Iacob de Beer Saba, ut veniret in Haran.
units.tr: So Isaac called Jacob, blessed him, charged him, and said to him: You shall not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan. Arise, go to Mesopotamia, to the house of Bethuel, your mother's father, and take a wife for yourself from there, from the daughters of Laban, your mother's brother. May God Almighty bless you, make you grow, and multiply you, that you may become a congregation of peoples. May he also give you the blessing of Abraham, to you and your seed with you, that you may receive as an inheritance the land of your wanderings, which God gave to Abraham. So Isaac sent Jacob away, and he went to Mesopotamia, to Laban the son of Bethuel the Syrian, brother of Rebekah, the mother of Jacob and Esau. And Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and had sent him to Mesopotamia to take a wife from there, and that when he blessed him he had charged him, saying: You shall not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan. And that Jacob had obeyed his father and his mother and had gone to Mesopotamia. Esau also saw that the daughters of Canaan were evil in the eyes of his father Isaac. So Esau went to Ishmael and took Mahalath, the daughter of Ishmael the son of Abraham, the sister of Nebaioth, as a wife in addition to his wives. Then Jacob went out from Beersheba to go to Haran.

units.la: 1 De duobus viris hic legimus, qui duxerunt uxores. unus est Iacobus, alter Esaus. Iacobum debemus imitari, si modo gratiae vasa esse maluerimus, quam irae. Dicit enim Dominus Deus Malach. 1. Iacob dilexi, Esau vero odio habui. Item Abd. 1. Et erit domus Iacob ignis, & domus Iosephflamma, & domus Esau stipula: & succendentur in eis, & devorabunt eos, & non erunt reliquiae domus Esau, quia Dominus loquutus est.
units.tr: 1 Here we read of two men who took wives: one is Jacob, the other Esau. We ought to imitate Jacob, if we would rather be vessels of grace than of wrath. For the Lord God says in Malachi 1: "Jacob I have loved, but Esau I have hated." Likewise in Obadiah 1: "The house of Jacob shall be a fire, and the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau stubble; they shall be kindled among them and devour them, and there shall be no remnant of the house of Esau, for the Lord has spoken."

units.la: Quid ergo fecit Iacobus parentibus suis morem gessit, eorumque voluntate matrimonium contraxit. Obedire autem patri & matri in bonis & licitis rebus, est principiū totius boni, Deoque summopere placet, Exod.20.Ierem.35.Ephes. 6.
units.tr: What then did Jacob do? He obeyed his parents and entered marriage by their will. To obey father and mother in good and lawful matters is the beginning of all good and is greatly pleasing to God: Exodus 20, Jeremiah 35, Ephesians 6.

units.la: Neque enim de genere Chanaan maledictio in Chamo (id est, mercatorum & negotiatorum confringendorum, qui ad nuptias filij regis venire nolunt, quiq; è templo Domini eijciuntur, Matth.21.22.) Iacobus vxorem duxit: sed profectus est, vt parens iusfit[?], in Mesopotamiam in medio fluminum fitam(de quo mysterio Origen.in fine Homil. 10.in Gen.)ad domum Bethuel (quod filiationem Dei significat) & accepit vxorem de filiabus Laban (quod sonat albus) Non est, igitur cum impijs coniungenda amicitia aut familiaritas,Deut.7. 2. Corin.6. neque delectus in contrahendis matrimonijs negligendus: quem cum filij Dei non haberent, Genef. 6. nubentes in familiam Cainam, diluvio puniti sunt.
units.tr: For Jacob did not take a wife from the race of Canaan, under the curse on Ham (that is, of the merchants and traders who refuse to come to the king's son's wedding and who are cast out of the temple of the Lord, Matthew 21 and 22). Instead he set out, as his parent commanded, into Mesopotamia, which lies between rivers (on this mystery see Origen at the end of Homily 10 on Genesis), to the house of Bethuel (which signifies the sonship of God), and he took a wife from the daughters of Laban (which means white). Therefore friendship and familiarity are not to be joined with the ungodly, Deuteronomy 7, 2 Corinthians 6, and the choice in contracting marriage must not be neglected. When the sons of God did not keep this, marrying into the family of Cain, they were punished by the flood, Genesis 6.

units.la: 2 Quid autem fecit Efau, cuius exemplum imitari nequaquam debemus?Hic quicquid parentib. suis displicere intellexit, operatus est, & contra voluntatem eorū vxores duxit. Sic enim legimus Gen.26.Factus vero est Efau filius quadraginta annorū, & accepit vxorem, nomine Iehudith, filiā Beeri Hitthęi, & Basmath filiā Elon Hitthæi. Et fuerunt amaritudo spiritus ipsi Isahac & Rebeccae. Itè[?] Gen.27. Et dixit Rebecca ad Isahac, tædet me vitę meæ propter filias Heth:si acceperit Iacob uxorem de filiabus Heth, ut sunt istæ, de filiabus inquam huius terræ, ut quid mihi vitæ q.d. Nolo vivere, si Iacob duxerit talem uxorem, quales sunt uxores Esau, quæ scilicet sunt Hetthæ & filiæ huius terræ. Hoc autem Capite legimus, quòd Esau videns malas esse in oculis Isaac patris sui, vel molestas .i. displicere patri suo filias Chananæorum, neque libenter eas aspicere, quasi corrigere volens erratū suum & placare patrem, ultra uxores quas habuit, duxit & filiam Ismael in uxorem. Sed etsi credebat, per hoc satisfacere patri & matri: tamen non fecit, quia malam super malas adduxit. Coniunxit autem Esaum & Ismaelem similitudo conditionis, vitæ studiorum inter se. Uterque enim venator erat, uterque gladio vitam in desertis exercebat, uterque iure primogenituræ privatus fratribus non perinde æquus erat.
units.tr: 2 But what did Esau do, whose example we must by no means imitate? Whatever he understood to displease his parents, he did, and he took wives against their will. For we read in Genesis 26: "When Esau was forty years old, he took a wife named Judith, the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath, the daughter of Elon the Hittite. And they were a bitterness of spirit to Isaac and Rebekah." Again, Genesis 27: "Rebekah said to Isaac: I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth. If Jacob takes a wife from the daughters of Heth, such as these, from the daughters, I say, of this land, what good is life to me?" That is, "I do not want to live if Jacob takes such a wife as Esau's wives, who are Hittites and daughters of this land." In this chapter we read that Esau, seeing that the daughters of Canaan were evil, or troublesome, that is, displeasing, in the eyes of his father Isaac, and that he did not willingly look at them, wished as it were to correct his error and appease his father, and so, besides the wives he already had, he took the daughter of Ishmael as a wife. But although he believed that by this he would satisfy his father and mother, he did not, because he brought evil upon evil. Esau and Ishmael were joined by the likeness of their condition and their way of life. For both were hunters, both lived by the sword in the wilderness, and both, deprived of the birthright, were not equal to their brothers.

units.la: Porrò omnes qui in ecclesia catholica terrena sapiunt, terram diligunt, terram concupiscunt, & omnem spem suam in terra constituunt, ad Esau pertinet, teste Augustino Sermon. 78. de Temp. Quicunque ideo Deo servire optat, ut honoribus crescat, & lucra terrena percipiat, & ipse ad Esau, id est, ad terrenam felicitatem pertinere cognoscitur. In Esau enim (ex quo sunt Idumæi) carnales intelliguntur: in Iacob vero (ex quo sunt Israelitæ) spirituales[?].
units.tr: Moreover, all who in the Catholic Church mind earthly things, love the earth, covet the earth, and place all their hope in the earth, belong to Esau, as Augustine witnesses in Sermon 78 on the Times. Whoever desires to serve God so that he may grow in honours and gain earthly profit is recognised as belonging to Esau, that is, to earthly happiness. For in Esau (from whom come the Edomites) are understood the carnal, but in Jacob (from whom come the Israelites) the spiritual.

units.la: ʒ[?] Discant etiam parentes hoc loco bené[?] consulere liberis suis : benedictionem illis ab omnipotent[?]e Deo optare, & non maledictionem (vt hodie passim fit) item non mirari, quando inobedientes habent filios, vt Ifaacus Efau, perinde quasi nouum aliquid ipsis obtingat: & prudentiam adhibere, qualem mater Iacobi habuit. Consuluit enim illa quidem filio suo, quæ Christus discipulis suis consulebat, videlicet, ne temere se periculis immiscerent, sed secessu insaniam malè affectorum demulcerent. Hoc etiam illa puero consuluit, primum mentem animans & firmans: cùm autem secessum ille non detrectaret, nec ægreferret, tunc & causam honeftam profectioni eius excogitat, ita vt non manifestè videatur propter fratris inuidiam cedere, neque pater sciat veram peregrinationis causam, Efau scilicet indignationem contra illum. Videtur & illud prudentiæ fuisse, quòd Ifaac, quia nolebat filium ducere vxorem de filiabus Chanaan, iussit illum relicta terra Chanaan proficisci in Padan.i.regionem Aram, vel Syriæ, hoc est, in Mefopotamiam. Obiecta enim mouent sensus. Contra vero, vt Germanicum habet prouerbium: <bl>Abaugen /abherz.</bl> <bl>Beywohnung aßer thut vil.</bl> Hæc cùm ita sint, orandus fuerit Dominus, vt nobis det suum spiritum, qui nos in viam rectam ducat, & gubernet omnia confilia nostra, omnes sensus, omnia membra corporis nostri, idque per Christum Iesum, Amen.
units.tr: Let parents also learn here to take good counsel for their children: to wish them blessing from almighty God and not cursing (as is done everywhere today), and not to marvel when they have disobedient sons, like Isaac with Esau, as if something new had happened to them; and to apply prudence, such as Jacob's mother had. For she gave her son the counsel that Christ gave his disciples, namely not to thrust themselves rashly into dangers, but to soothe the madness of the ill-disposed by withdrawing. She gave this counsel to the boy as well: first she encouraged and strengthened his mind; then, when he did not refuse withdrawal or take it badly, she devised an honourable reason for his departure, so that it would not clearly seem he was giving way out of his brother's envy, and so that his father would not know the true cause of the journey, namely Esau's anger against him. It also seems to have been prudent that Isaac, since he did not want his son to take a wife from the daughters of Canaan, ordered him to leave the land of Canaan and go to Padan, that is, the region of Aram, or of Syria, that is, to Mesopotamia. For forbidden things move the senses. On the contrary, as the German proverb has it: "Out of sight, out of heart. Living apart does much." Since these things are so, we must pray to the Lord that he give us his Spirit, who may lead us in the right way and govern all our counsels, all our senses, and all the members of our body, through Christ Jesus. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XIII.
units.tr: CONCIO XIII.

units.la: Genes. 29.
units.tr: Genes. 29.

units.la: Erant[?] autem ipsi Laban duae filiae: nomen maioris erat Leah, minoris vero nomen Rahel. Porro oculi Leah erant teneri, Rahel vero erat pulchra forma & decoro aspectu. Dilexitq; Iacob Rahelem & ait: seruiam[?] tibi septem annis pro Rahele filia tua minori. Respondit Laban: melius est ut ego dem eam tibi, quàm quòd eam tradam viro alteri: mane apud me. Seruiuit itaque Iacob pro Rahele septem annis, & fuerunt in oculis eius sicut dies pauci, eo quòd diligebat illam. Et ait Iacob ad Laban: da uxorem meam, quoniam impleti sunt dies mei, et ingrediar ad illam. Et congregauit Laban omnes homines illius loci, fecitq; conuiuium. Et factum est ad vesperam, et tulit Leam filiam suam, introduxitq; eam ad illum, et ingressus est ad eam. Dedit quoque Laban illi Zilpam ancillam suam, Leae in quam filiae suae in famulam. Factumq; est illucescente die, & ecce ea erat Lea: quapropter ait ad Laban: Cur hoc mihi fecisti? nonne pro Rahele seruiui tibi? & quare sefellisti me? Respondit Laban: non sic fit in loco nostro, ut tradatur iunior ante priorem. Imple septenarium istius, & dabitur quoque tibi ista pro seruitute, qua seruies mihi adhuc septem annis aliys. Fecit itaque Iacob sic, & impleuit septenarium illius, & tradidit sibi Rahelem filiam suam in uxorem. Dedit quoque Laban Raheli filiae suae Bilham ancillam suam, illi in famulam. Et ingressus est quoq; ad Rahelem, & dilexit Rahelem plus quàm Leam, seruiuitq; illi adhuc septem aliys annis.
units.tr: Now Laban had two daughters: the name of the elder was Leah, and the name of the younger was Rachel. Leah's eyes were weak, but Rachel was beautiful in form and lovely to look upon. Jacob loved Rachel and said, "I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel." Laban answered, "It is better that I give her to you than that I give her to another man; stay with me." So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him but a few days, because he loved her. Then Jacob said to Laban, "Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled, and I will go in to her." So Laban gathered all the men of that place and made a feast. In the evening he took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and he went in to her. Laban also gave his maidservant Zilpah to his daughter Leah as her maid. But when morning came, behold, it was Leah. So Jacob said to Laban, "What is this you have done to me? Did I not serve you for Rachel? Why have you deceived me?" Laban answered, "It is not our custom in this place to give the younger before the firstborn. Complete the week of this one, and we will give you the other also, in return for the service you will render me for another seven years." Jacob did so, and completed the week of Leah, and Laban gave him Rachel his daughter as wife. Laban also gave his maidservant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her maid. Jacob went in to Rachel too, and he loved Rachel more than Leah, and served Laban another seven years.

units.la: 1 Utile est historias veterum tenere, sed non satis, nisi inde aliquam doctrinam accipiamus, & spiritualem intellectum. Nam quæcunque præscripta sunt, in nostram doctrinam præscripta sunt, ut per patientiam & consolationem scripturarum spem habeamus, inquit Apostolus, Roman. 15. & 1. Corinth. 10. ait: Hæc autem omnia figuræ contigerunt illis. & Rom. 7. Scimus enim quòd lex spiritualis est.
units.tr: 1. It is useful to know the histories of the ancients, but it is not enough unless we draw from them some teaching and a spiritual understanding. For whatever has been written was written for our instruction, that through patience and the comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope, says the Apostle (Rom. 15). And in 1 Cor. 10 he says: "Now all these things happened to them as figures." And Rom. 7: "For we know that the law is spiritual."

units.la: 2 Discamus ergo ex hac historia patientiam, dicamusq; cum sancto Iobo: Si bona suscepimus de manu Domini, mala cur non sustineamus? Nam & Laban habuit non solùm filiam pulchram,sed etiam deformem. Et Jacob soceri placitis licet durioribus vifis, acquevit, cùm pro Rachel, quam longo meruerat officio, suppositam acciperet uxorem Leam.
units.tr: 2. Let us therefore learn patience from this history, and let us say with holy Job: "If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil?" For Laban had not only a beautiful daughter but also an ugly one. And Jacob, though his father-in-law's terms seemed rather harsh, consented, when instead of Rachel, whom he had earned by long service, he received Leah as his wife, who had been put in her place.

units.la: Discant filii obedientiam, neque uxores ducant contra voluntatem parentum. Jacob enim ambiuit non Chananæam, sed filiâ Labanis, ut præceperunt parentes, Gen. 27. 28.
units.tr: Let children learn obedience, and let them not take wives against their parents' will. For Jacob sought a wife not from the Canaanites but from the daughters of Laban, as his parents had commanded (Gen. 27, 28).

units.la: Discant patres tradere filias potius piis & prudentibus viris, juxta præceptum Siracidæ, capite septimo, quàm diuitibus ac impiis. Nam & Laban filio justi viri dare voluit filiam suam.
units.tr: Let fathers learn to give their daughters rather to pious and prudent men, according to the precept of Jesus the son of Sirach, chapter seven, than to rich and impious men. For Laban too wished to give his daughter to the son of a righteous man.

units.la: Discant Domini eligere probos seruos; propter quos non raró Deus benedicere folet Dominis: quia & Laban orauit Jacobum, ut maneret apud fe; imò propterea quia vidit Laban virtutem viri, & cogitauit, quòd non aliter eum vinceret & persuaderet, ut diutius apud fe maneret, ita ei imposuit, & dedit ei Leam cum Zilpa ancilla.
units.tr: Let masters learn to choose upright servants, for the sake of whom God often blesses their masters. For Laban also urged Jacob to stay with him; indeed, the reason was that Laban saw the man's virtue and thought that he could not otherwise overcome him and persuade him to stay longer with him. So he deceived him, and gave him Leah with her maid Zilpah.

units.la: Discant ferui præstare quod polliciti sunt. Quemadmodum enim Jacob promisit fe ferviturum septem annis: ita fecit.
units.tr: Let servants perform what they have promised. For just as Jacob promised to serve seven years, so he did.

units.la: Discant viri, uxores non accipere renuentibus puellarum parétibus, vel ante tempus: nuptias autem testimonio & præfentia fidedignorum testari, proprias coniuges amare,&c. Nam & Jacob (qui jam, ut supputát, octuaginta quatuor annos natus erat, cùm primo acciperet uxorem) ad Laban ait, Da mihi vxorem meam (pro qua seruiui septem annis) quia iam tempus est impletum ut ingrediar ad eam i. ut fruar illa, siue ut dem opera proli. Et Laban vocatis multis amicorum turbis ad conuiuium, fecit nuptias. Iacob vero Rahelem dilexit: ut Moses testatur.
units.tr: Let men learn not to take wives against the wishes of the girls' parents, or before the appointed time; and let them attest their marriage by the testimony and presence of trustworthy witnesses, and love their own spouses, and so on. For Jacob too (who, as they reckon, was eighty-four years old when he first took a wife) said to Laban, "Give me my wife, for whom I served seven years, because the time has come to fulfil the term, that I may go in to her," that is, that I may enjoy her or give her offspring. And Laban, having called together a great crowd of friends to the feast, made the wedding. But Jacob loved Rachel, as Moses bears witness.

units.la: Obseruandum hoc loco etiam est, quae temperantia desponsatorum & nubentium fuerit apud veteres, & cautio ante diem iustarū nuptiarum & legitimi conuentus, non congrediendi. Atque hanc temperantiam adhuc seruatam esse tempore noui testamenti probat Musculus in cap. 1. Matth. Si enim, inquit, aliquid ad causam facit, quam sibi Euangelista priore loco probandam sumpsit: nempe ideo Mariam a Iosepho sponso suo non esse grauidatam & impregnatam, quod ante quam conuenirent, inuenta sit in utero habens: oportebit omnino tum temporis eam fuisse castimoniam, & custodiam desponsatorum, ut piaculum fuerit illos ante diem legitimum nuptiarum congredi. Si.n.istud suisset liberum, non bene probasset institutum suum Euangelista. Nam mox potuisset obijci: Et quid est quod antequam conuenerint, inuenta est in utero habens? An non potuit a sponso suo ante diem nuptiarum cognosci & impregnari? Sed hoc nostro seculo quae inoleuerit impudentia, & quae intemperantia, magis deplorandum est quam recensendum. Atque ideo tam casta iam habemus passim coniugia. Introducatur exemplum iunioris Tobiæ. Ridiculum est, quod plerumque congressus non solum nuptias, sed & ipsam desponsationem præueniunt. Olim non habebantur rata talia matrimonia, sed plane adulterina. Maria cum effet desponsata, vt est Lucæ 1. quæ desponsatio facta est etiá ante salutationem angelicam, nō mox iungitur sponso suo, sed primum abit ad congnatam suam Elizabeth, & cum illa mansit tres menses, antequam domum reuerteretur[?]. Tanta videlicet fuit virginis castimonia[?] & temperantia, imò & Iosephi, qui eam non ad se coëgerit mox post desponsationē.
units.tr: It should also be observed here what moderation betrothed and marrying couples observed among the ancients, and what caution they took before the day of the lawful wedding and the lawful agreement, not to come together. And Musculus, on chapter 1 of Matthew, proves that this moderation is still kept in the time of the New Testament. For if, he says, anything bears on the matter which the Evangelist first set out to prove, namely that Mary was not made pregnant by Joseph her betrothed, because before they came together she was found to have a child in her womb, then it must certainly have been the case at that time that such chastity and guarding of betrothed couples prevailed, that it would have been a sin for them to come together before the lawful day of the wedding. For if that had been permitted, the Evangelist would not have proved his point well. For it could soon have been objected: "And what is it that, before they came together, she was found to have in her womb? Could she not have been known and made pregnant by her betrothed before the day of the wedding?" But what shamelessness and what intemperance has grown up in our own age is more to be lamented than recounted. And so we now have such chaste marriages everywhere. Let the example of the younger Tobias be brought forward. It is ridiculous that intercourse very often anticipates not only the wedding but even the betrothal itself. In former times such marriages were not regarded as valid, but were plainly adulterous. Mary, when she was betrothed, as is said in Luke 1, which betrothal took place even before the angelic greeting, was not at once joined to her husband, but first went away to her kinswoman Elizabeth, and stayed with her three months before she returned home. So great, evidently, was the virgin's chastity and self-control, and indeed Joseph's too, who did not take her to himself straight after the betrothal.

units.la: § Quæritur autem primùm, quur Iacob Rahelem dilexerit præ Lea, adeò vt ei septem anni seruitutis visi fuerint pauci dies præ amoris magnitudine, id est, ita vt amor magnus & laborem & temporis longitudinem succiderit, & breue videri fecerit? Responderetur, quia Rahel fuit & pulchra, & prouidentia diuina primò ad puteum tanquam sutura sponsa post promissam in itinere benedictionem oblata. Quod vtrunque amorem Rahelis in ipso Iacobo excitare potuit. Nam quod ad pulchritudinem attinet, quàm hæc natura sua animos nostros capiat, nisi cæci ea de re dubitarint, & quàm fœminas exornet, vt viros robur, vates Græcus docet:
units.tr: § The first question is why Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah, so much so that the seven years of service seemed to him only a few days because of the greatness of his love; that is, so that great love cut short both the toil and the length of time and made them seem brief. The answer is: because Rachel was both beautiful, and by divine providence she was first offered to him at the well as a future bride, after the blessing promised on his journey. Each of these could stir Rachel's love in Jacob himself. For as to beauty, how it captures our minds by its very nature, unless the blind have doubted it, and how it adorns women as strength adorns men, the Greek poet teaches:

units.la: Μορφὰ δ᾽ ἀλυτέ[?]ησι τέλει κα[?]λὸν ἀνδρὶ δ᾽ ἀλκά.
units.tr: Beauty is a fine adornment for a woman, and strength for a man. [Μορφὰ δὲ γυναικὶ τέλος καλὸν, ἀνδρὶ δ᾽ ἀλκά]

units.la: Et Theophrastus, qui formam silentem fraudem vocauit, eo quòd absque verbis persuadeat. Et Carneades, qui eandem ἀδόξευ-
units.tr: And Theophrastus, who called beauty a silent fraud, because it persuades without words. And Carneades, who called the same thing [ἀδόξευ-

units.la: φέρητορ βασιλέων [?] .i. regnum abfq; satellitio appellauit, quód formosi impetrent quicquid volunt, nulla adhibita vi. Cornelius Agrippa in lib. de Nobilitate & præstantia mulierum, probat, quód pulchritudo mulierum non solum apud homines laudabilis, grata & accepta sit, verum etiam apud Deum & angelos.
units.tr: φέρητορ βασιλέων] a kingdom without bodyguards, because handsome people obtain whatever they want without any force being applied. Cornelius Agrippa, in his book on the nobility and excellence of women, proves that the beauty of women is not only praiseworthy, pleasing and acceptable among men, but also before God and the angels.

units.la: Proinde rectè quidam cùm interrogaretur, cur quæ pulchra sunt amarentur? respondit τυφλὸς ἐρώτησιν [?], id est, cæci interrogationem esse. Erasmus adscribit Aristoteli. Quod vero ad curam diuinam attinet, qua primò oblata fuit Rahel, quantum hæc valeat in piorum animis, satis fides ipsa agnoscit & testatur.
units.tr: Accordingly, when someone was once asked why beautiful things are loved, he rightly answered that it was a blind man's question [τυφλὸς ἐρώτησιν]. Erasmus ascribes this to Aristotle. As for the divine care by which Rachel was first offered, how much this avails in the hearts of the pious, faith itself recognises and attests well enough.

units.la: Cæterùm si iustus ille (inquit Diuus Chrysostomus Hom.55. in Genes.) propter puellæ amorem septennium seruire, ferreque pastoralium laborum ærumnas decreuit, & non sentit vel labores, vel temporis longitudinem, sed omnia ei leuia & facilia videntur, expectationeque & spe fructus alitur, ita vt dies paucos longum illud tempus putet: quare nos habebimus excusationem, qui non pari studio erga Dominum nostrum & benefactorem & curatorem, & qui nobis fit omnia, afficimur? Sed quando proponitur lucrum temporale, omnia alacriter sustinere volumus, etiamsi laboriosum fit, & valde ærumnosum & sordidum, & poenam in præsenti & futuro seculo præbens: propter nostra autem salutem, & vt supernam nobis salutem conciliemus, remissi & supini, & dissoluti videmur? Et qualis nobis erit venia, qualisue excufatio sic negligentiæ deditis qui neq; quantum beatus ille: pro puella amorem desiderauit, tatam[?] in Deum charitatem habemus: idque cum tanta possumus numerare beneficia in nos collocata, & quæ quotidie collocantur?
units.tr: But if that righteous man (says Saint Chrysostom, Hom. 55 on Genesis), out of love for the girl, resolved to serve seven years and endure the hardships of shepherding, and did not feel the labours or the length of the time, but everything seemed light and easy to him, and he was sustained by expectation and hope of the reward, so that the long period seemed only a few days: will we have an excuse, we who are not moved with equal zeal toward our Lord, both our benefactor and our keeper, who is all things to us? When a temporal gain is set before us, we are willing to endure everything eagerly, even if it is laborious, very troublesome and squalid, and brings punishment in the present and future age; yet for our salvation, and to win for ourselves heavenly salvation, we appear slack, listless and careless? What pardon, what excuse will there be for us, given over to negligence like this, who do not have toward God the love that the blessed man had for the girl, although we can count so many benefits bestowed on us, and which are bestowed on us every day?

units.la: Meminerimus etiam hic illius Pfalm. 45. Audi filia & vide, & inclina aurem tuam, & obliuiscere populum tuum & domum patris tui, Et concupiscet rex decorem tuum, quoniam ipse est Dominus tuus, & adorabis eum. Ornemus igitur omnibus modis animæ generositatem, vt claritate pulchritudinis suæ conciliemus nobis vniuersorum Dominum. Nam vbi viderit animæ venustatem, statim assistet. Dicit enim: Super quem alium respiciam, quàm super mansuetum & quietum & trementem sermones meos? Vidisti quomodo nos docuit omnes colores, quibus animæ pulchritudo potest decorari? De tali interno ornatu scribit etiam Apostolus 1. Petri 3.
units.tr: Let us also remember here that passage of Psalm 45: "Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father's house. And the king will desire your beauty, since he is your Lord, and you shall worship him." Let us therefore adorn the nobility of the soul in every way, so that by the brightness of its beauty we may win for ourselves the Lord of all. For when he sees the loveliness of the soul, he will at once be present. For he says: "On whom else shall I look, but on the one who is gentle and quiet and trembles at my words?" Have you seen how he has taught us all the colours with which the beauty of the soul can be adorned? Of such inward adornment the Apostle also writes in 1 Peter 3.

units.la: Secundò quæritur, quare Iacob Leam no[?] sta[?] non cognouerit, cùm potuisset eam vel ex voce, vel ex tactu cognoscere? Hic, primum simplicitas Iacobi considerari debet, & quomodo ab omni malitia alienus, deceptus sit. Deinde in hoc ostenditur laus Iacobi, quia noste illa forsitan non tetigit Leam, sed tontinens ab ea oratioui vacauit, ut de Tobia exemplum extat. Præterea si tetigit eam carnaliter, nec tamen agnouit, signum est, ut quidam annotant, quòd non quæsiuerit in uxore sua blanditias meretricias in tactibus & verbis, sed magis ea usus est in castitate maritali. Legitur in Chronicis de quodam iuuene nobili, quòd rem habuerit cum Rosimunda uxore Alboini regis Longobardorum, nescien s illam esse, donec ipsamet sese prodidisset. putabat enim ille esse virginem, quam amabat in gynæcio.
units.tr: Secondly, it is asked why Jacob did not recognise Leah, since he could have known her by her voice or by her touch. Here, first, the simplicity of Jacob must be considered, and how, being free of all malice, he was deceived. Next, in this the praise of Jacob is shown: for that night perhaps he did not touch Leah, but abstained from her and kept himself free for prayer, as there is an example of this in Tobias. Moreover, if he did touch her carnally and yet did not know her, it is a sign, as some note, that he did not seek in his wife the harlot's caresses in touches and words, but rather used her in marital chastity. It is read in the Chronicles of a certain young nobleman that he had relations with Rosamund, the wife of Alboin, king of the Lombards, not knowing who she was until she herself revealed it; for he believed she was a maiden whom he loved in the women's quarters.

units.la: Tertio quæritur, cur Iacobus duas sorores duxerit, quod tamen, Leuitici decimo octauo capite prohibitum est? Primo is mos fuit eo tempore, quem seruare non putauit nefas esse Iacobus. Deinde non repugnauit instituto huiusmodi verbum Domini, qui hoc coniugium benedictione prolis commendarit. Demum arcana notatione, duplicis ecclesiæ status huiusmodi connubium haud caruit: Alter status in tetra crucis specie, quæ in Lea maiore natu debili oculis & deformi apparet: alter in gloria, quæ in Rachele minore & speciosa adumbratur, cernitur. De priore Salomon his verbis, Cant. 1 [?]. Nolite me considerare quòd fusca sum, quia decoloravit me sol. De altero idem, Tota pulchra es amica mea, & macula non est in te: ut quæ exprompta sit ex pulchro, de quo propheta, Speciosus forma præ filiis hominum. Hic est Iesus Christus, seruus Dei laborans pro ecclesia, & moriens præ amore, præfiguratus per Iacobum patriarcham.
units.tr: Thirdly, it is asked why Jacob married two sisters, which nevertheless is forbidden in Leviticus, chapter 18. First, that was the custom of that time, which Jacob did not think it wrong to keep. Next, the word of the Lord, who commended this marriage by the blessing of offspring, did not oppose such an arrangement. Finally, by a hidden signification, a marriage of this kind was not without meaning for the two states of the Church: the first state, in the form of the harsh cross, which appears in the elder Leah, weak in the eyes and unlovely; the second, in glory, which is shadowed forth and seen in the younger and beautiful Rachel. Of the former Solomon speaks in these words (Song 1): "Do not look at me because I am dark, because the sun has scorched me." Of the latter the same: "You are wholly beautiful, my love, and there is no blemish in you," as one drawn from the beautiful one of whom the prophet speaks: "Fairer in form than the sons of men." This is Jesus Christ, the servant of God labouring for the Church and dying out of love, foreshadowed by the patriarch Jacob.

units.la: Sed quaeras, num in administratione novi fœderis hoc Iacobi factum tanquam exemplum sequi conveniat? Respondetur, Nequaquam. Nam sanctorum patrum facta sine fide imitari non licet. Sine fide autem huiusmodi connubiorum imitatio fieret, ut quibus non solum consuetudo hodie, & verbum Dei non patrocinetur, sed etiam posterioribus temporibus de vitandis huius generis matrimonijs tradita à Mose lex aduersetur[?]. Certum est (ut Georgius Maior scribit) sanctos patres contra conscientiam non fuisse polygamos, sed hoc aut more gentis & consuetudine inueterata, cuius magna vis est, & sic ex ignorantia fecisse, quae ignorantiae peccata piis non imputantur. Aut propter promissionem factam Abrahæ: Faciam te in gentem magnam: Item, Multiplicabo semen tuum sicut stellas cæli, &c. Aut ut hoc modo semen promissum filius Dei liberator generis humani, tandem nasceretur. Mal. 2. Quare haec patrum facta, non sunt trahenda in exemplum, in quibus fieri potest, ut aliquid fuerit vitij, quod ipsis propter promissum semen, in quod crediderunt, condonatum est. Imitemur potius ipsorum fidem, constantiam, patientiam, atque alias excellentes virtutes. D. Augustinus inquit, Pro ingenti crimine obijciuntur Iacob quatuor uxores. Sed quoniam tunc mos erat, crimen non erat:nunc autem crime est, quia mos non est. Alia sunt peccata contra naturam, alia contra mores, alia contra præcepta. Sed Iacob non contra naturam hoc fecit, qui non lasciviendi, sed gignendi causa illis mulieribus utebatur: nec contra morem, quia illo tempore in illis terris hoc factitabatur: nec contra præceptum, quia nulla lege prohibebatur.
units.tr: But you may ask whether, in the administration of the New Covenant, it is fitting to follow Jacob's deed as an example. The answer is: by no means. For the deeds of the holy fathers may not be imitated without faith. Yet an imitation of marriages of this kind would be without faith, since they are supported neither by present custom nor by the word of God, and since the law given by Moses in later times forbids marriages of this kind. It is certain (as Georg Major writes) that the holy fathers were not polygamists against their conscience, but did so either by the custom of the people and an ingrained habit, which has great force, and so acted out of ignorance, and sins of ignorance are not imputed to the godly; or on account of the promise made to Abraham: "I will make you into a great nation," and likewise, "I will multiply your seed as the stars of heaven," etc.; or so that by this means the promised seed, the Son of God, the deliverer of the human race, might at last be born (Malachi 2). Therefore these deeds of the fathers are not to be drawn into example, since in them it may be that there was some fault, which was pardoned them on account of the promised seed in whom they believed. Let us rather imitate their faith, constancy, patience and their other excellent virtues. Saint Augustine says: "Four wives are cast up against Jacob as a great crime. But since at that time it was the custom, it was not a crime; but now it is a crime, because it is not the custom. Some sins are against nature, some against custom, some against precepts. But Jacob did not do this against nature, since he used those women not for lust but for begetting children; nor against custom, since at that time this was practised in those lands; nor against a precept, since it was forbidden by no law."

units.la: Nunc vero legibus & moribus hoc non licet. Quæ duo si quis contempserit, etiamsi tantummodo causa generandi utatur pluribus fœminis, peccat tamen, & humanam violat societatem, &c. Angelomus contra polygamiam ita scribit in cap.5.lib.Reg. Nunc reges si plures habeant uxores vel concubinas, in crimine reputatur: quia iam transierunt figuræ, pro quibus uxorum vel concubinarum venia concedebatur. At nunc quia figuræ transierunt, venia nulla datur. Huc facit quod & Lombar.ait lib.4.Dist.33[?].pro varietate temporum varia inuenitur dispensatio conditoris. veniente plenitudinis tempore, quo Christi gratia vbique est dilatata, reducta est lex nuptiarum ad priorem honestioremque institutionem, vt vnus vni in figura Christi & ecclesiæ coniungatur. Demum patrum fidem semper sequi conuenit, facta non item. Verbum enim Domini regula & norma est fidei sanctorum, non facta & res gestæ, quæ mutatur pro tempore, regula nomutata, vt legimus: Ego Dominus, & non mutor:cui fit honor & gloria in æternum, Ame[?].
units.tr: But now it is not permitted by laws and customs. If anyone should despise these two, even if he uses several women only for the purpose of begetting children, he nevertheless sins, and violates human society, etc. Angelomus writes against polygamy in this way, on chapter 5 of the book of Kings: "Now if kings have several wives or concubines, it is counted as a crime; because the figures, for which the pardon of wives or concubines was granted, have now passed away. But now, since the figures have passed away, no pardon is given." To this point also the Lombard says (book 4, distinction 33) that the Creator's dispensation is found to vary with the variety of times; when the fullness of time came, in which the grace of Christ has been spread everywhere, the law of marriage was brought back to its earlier and more honourable institution, so that one man is joined to one woman in the figure of Christ and the Church. Finally, it is fitting always to follow the faith of the fathers, but not their deeds. For the word of the Lord is the rule and norm of the faith of the saints, not the deeds and events, which change with the times; the rule is not changed, as we read: "I am the Lord, and I do not change"; to whom be honour and glory for ever. Amen.

units.tr: SERMON XIV.

units.la: EGRESSA est autem Dina filia Lea, quam peperit ipsi Iacob, ut videret filias illius terræ. Quam ut vidit Sichem, filius Hamor Hivai principis illius terræ, tulit eam & dormiens cum ea violauit illam. Adhæsitq; anima eius cum Dina filia Iacob, & dilexit puellam, loquutusq; est super cor puellæ. Et dixit Sichem ad Hamor patrem suum: accipe mihi puellam istam in vxorem. Audiuit itaque Iacob, quod ille polluisset Dinam filiam suam, existentibus filijs eius cum pecoribus suis in campo, & tacuit, donec illi venirent. Egressusq; est Hamor pater Sichem ad Iacob, vt loqueretur cum eo: & venientes filij Iacob de campo, atq; audientes, contristati sunt viri illi, et sic censuerunt apud se valde, quod ille rem absurdam fecisset in Israel, dormiendo cum filia Iacob, quod minime fieri conueniebat. Loquutus est autem Hamor cum eis dicens: Sichem filius meus ex animo suo diligit filiam vestram: date quaso eam il-li in li in uxorem. Facite nobiscum affinitatem, & date nobis filias vestras, & filias nostras accipite vobis. Habitabitisq; apud nos, & terra ipsa erit coram vobis: habitate & negotiamini in ea, & possidete in ea. Sichem vero dixit ad patrem illius, & ad fratres eius: Inveniam gratiam in oculis vestris, & quicquid dixeritis ad me, dabo. Augete etiam plurimum super me dotem & munus, & dabo iuxta quod dixeritis mihi, modo detis mihi puellam in uxorem, &c.
units.tr: DINAH the daughter of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob, went out to see the daughters of that land. When Shechem, the son of Hamor the Hivite, prince of that land, saw her, he took her and, lying with her, violated her. Yet his soul clung to Dinah the daughter of Jacob, and he loved the girl and spoke tenderly to her heart. And Shechem said to Hamor his father: Get me this girl as a wife. Now Jacob heard that he had defiled Dinah his daughter, but his sons were in the field with their cattle, so he held his peace until they came. Then Hamor the father of Shechem went out to Jacob to speak with him. The sons of Jacob came in from the field when they heard it, and those men were grieved and greatly angered, because he had done a shameful thing in Israel by lying with Jacob's daughter, which ought not to be done. Hamor spoke with them, saying: My son Shechem longs for your daughter with all his heart; please give her to him in marriage. Make marriages with us: give us your daughters and take our daughters for yourselves. You shall dwell among us, and the land shall be before you: dwell and trade in it, and possess it. And Shechem said to her father and her brothers: Let me find favour in your eyes, and whatever you say to me I will give. Raise the dowry and the gift as high as you like, and I will give what you ask, only give me the girl as a wife, etc.

units.la: 1 Ut facilius comprehendamus historiam in hoc capite contentam, distribuemus eam in tres partes: quarum prima fit de Dina filia Iacobi & Liæ. Hanc enim legimus egressam fuisse, nempe de tabernaculo seu domo patris sui, temerè & non consultis parentibus, ut videret mulieres regionis illius, & earum mores quales essent, perdisceret:item copressam esse à Sichem filio Emor:id quod nobis præscriptum est in doctrinam & admonitionem, 1. Corinth. 10. Rom. 15. Discant igitur puellæ occasiones peccatorum vitare, ac domi se potius continere, quàm extra paternas ædes (cum filio prodigo, Luc. 15.) hinc inde vagari: nam ut grauissimè Electra apud Euripidem inquit: [illegible, ~25 letters] <bl>Dann außgeben war nie so gut/ innen</bl> <bl>bleiben war besser,&c.</bl> non curiosæ esse,ficut & Eua fuit, quæ arborem vetitam quoque gustare voluit: &, oculos frenare, ne occasione ac duƈtu illorum incidant in tentationes: &, non iniquè ferre seueram super fe parentum custodiam, qua egent, Eccles. 26. & non facilè credere pollicitationibus hominum etiam blandè fe alloquentium. Cæterum si hominibus, vt Dina filio Emor, tantum credimus, quàm firmiter & promptè credere debemus promissionibus Dei, qui mentiri nescit ?
units.tr: 1 So that we may more easily grasp the history contained in this chapter, we shall divide it into three parts. The first concerns Dinah, the daughter of Jacob and Leah. We read that she went out, namely from the tent or house of her father, rashly and without consulting her parents, to see the women of that region and to learn what their customs were like. She was also violated by Shechem, the son of Hamor; this is set down for our teaching and admonition (1 Cor. 10; Rom. 15). Let young women therefore learn to avoid the occasions of sin, and to keep at home rather than wander here and there outside their father's house (like the prodigal son, Luke 15). For, as Electra says in Euripides, most gravely: [...] "To go out was never so good; to stay within was better," etc. They should not be curious, as Eve was, who wished to taste even the forbidden tree; they should restrain their eyes, lest through the occasion and enticement of such things they fall into temptation; they should not bear with ill grace the strict watch of their parents, which they need (Ecclus. 26); and they should not easily believe the promises of men who address them flatteringly. Moreover, if we trust men as Dinah trusted the son of Hamor, how firmly and readily ought we to trust the promises of God, who knows not how to lie?

units.la: 2 Altera pars sit de Emor & filio eius Sichem, amatore Dinæ: qui ipsam vidit, adamāuit, rapuit, vi oppressit: patrem suum, vt illam sibi daret in vxorem, rogauit: opes & corpus suum parui habuit, vt eam in vxorem habere posset: tandem sua concupiscentia & libidine patri & toti ciuitati perditionis author fuit. Vnde discamus, oculos eruere, quando nobis obstaculo esse volunt (Matth. 5. Eccles. 9.) vt feré solent, si metu Dei non custodiantur: sine parentum nutu matrimonium non contrahere, ne iudicemur à Siche, qui ad patrem suum dixit, Accipe mihi puellam hanc coniugem: secundum carnem non ambulare, ne & nos & nostri simul pereamus: Amorem potentem esse, vt mortem, eumque aquis (sed & diuitiæ aquæ sunt fluentes ab vno ad alium) extingui non posse.
units.tr: 2 The second part concerns Hamor and his son Shechem, the lover of Dinah. He saw her, loved her, seized her, and forced her; he asked his father to give her to him as a wife; he held his wealth and his own person cheap, so that he might have her as his wife; at last, through his lust and desire, he became the author of ruin for his father and the whole city. From this let us learn to pluck out our eyes when they become a stumbling block to us (Matt. 5; Eccles. 9), as they usually do if they are not guarded by the fear of God; not to contract marriage without the consent of parents, lest we be judged like Shechem, who said to his father: Get me this girl as my wife; not to walk according to the flesh, lest we and ours perish together; and to know that love is as strong as death, and that it cannot be quenched by waters (though riches too are waters that flow from one to another).

units.la: Cæterum si tatum amor in homines potest, quantum valere debet, & quàm magnus esse debet erga Deum, summum & pulcherrimū bonum? In Emor autem notandum, quod patrem puellæ de ea appellat. Potestas enim parentum in liberos naturæ etiam lege in profanis gentibus confirmata est.
units.tr: Moreover, if love for men has such power, how great should it be, and how much greater should it be towards God, the highest and most beautiful good? It should be noted, however, that Hamor calls the girl's father by her name. For the power of parents over their children is confirmed by the law of nature, even among the profane nations.

units.la: ʒ Tertia pars capitis huius est de Iacobo & eius filijs, qui non mercatores ad fraudem comparati, non sanguinarij milites, non ociosi & inertes homines, sed pastores dicuntur fuisse. Iacob autem sine dubio filiam suam honestè educauerat. Si ergo illius filiæ hoc accidit, nullus parens nimis confidere debet suis filiabus: verùm si diligens fuerit in erudiendis & custodiendis illis, & tale quid ei acciderit, cogitet hoc etiam sancto patriarchæ accidisse: qui pro sua mansuetudine nihil loquutus est, sed patienter vim filiæ factam tulit, non ignorans illud Prophetæ: In silentio & spe erit fortitudo vestra. Filij autem non item, in quibus tamen eorum tristitia ob peccatum commissum proposita nobis est ad imitandum, sed immodica eorū ira non item. Nam maledictus furor eorū, inquit Iacob Gen.49. quia pertinax & indignatio eorum, quia dura. Interim hoc in loco videmus, quanto Deus odio stupra atque scortationes sit persequutus, ut propter illa totam ciuitatem euerterit. Quemadmodum enim propter paucorum iustitiam multis nonnunquam bene fit, Gen.18. Actor.27. sic non raro ob unius peccatum plures puniuntur, Ios. 7. 2. Reg. 21. 2. Reg.24. Luc.15. Unde Hesiodus : [illegible, ~40 letters] Sicut enim accensa pyra, & qui propè habitant, periculi sunt participes, igne omnia depascente: eodem modo & hic adolescentis in temperantia, non solùm patrem, sed & omnes ciues perdit. Ita vnius Paridis adulterium toti Troiae exitio fuit. Non enim ij solùm digni sunt morte, qui iniusta faciunt: verùm etiá qui assentiuntur ijs, qui ea faciunt, Rom.2.
units.tr: 3 The third part of this chapter concerns Jacob and his sons, who are said to have been not merchants bent on fraud, not bloodthirsty soldiers, not idle and lazy men, but shepherds. Jacob, without doubt, had brought up his daughter honourably. If this happened to her, then no parent ought to trust too much in his daughters; yet if he has been diligent in teaching and guarding them, and something of this kind has befallen him, let him reflect that it also happened to the holy patriarch, who, for his gentleness, said nothing, but bore patiently the violence done to his daughter, not ignorant of the prophet's words: In quietness and in hope shall be your strength (Isa. 30). The sons, however, did not act likewise, although their sorrow over the sin committed is set before us as an example to imitate; but their immoderate anger was not to be imitated. For, as Jacob says in Gen. 49, "Cursed be their anger, for it was fierce, and their wrath, for it was cruel." Meanwhile, in this place we see how greatly God pursued fornication and adultery with hatred, so that for their sake He overthrew the whole city. For just as at times many are blessed for the righteousness of a few (Gen. 18; Acts 27), so often many are punished for the sin of one (Josh. 7; 2 Kings 21; 2 Kings 24; Luke 15). Hence Hesiod says: [...] For just as when a fire is kindled, those who live nearby share the danger, as the flames consume everything, so in the same way this young man, through his lack of self-control, destroyed not only his father but all the citizens. So the adultery of Paris was the ruin of all Troy. For not only those who do unjust things deserve death, but also those who consent to those who do them (Rom. 2).

units.la: Adde quòd Sichemitae (quorum passio iniusta fuit, etsi actio filiorum Iacob iniusta erat) non solùm propter vitium, quo familiam sanctam Iacobæam polluerunt, sed etiam propter hypocrisim, perditi sunt. Ausi sunt sacris sancti populi, suscepta circumcisione, cùm interim neque Dei Israelitarum gloriam, neque populi electi commoditates, sed suas spectarent. Ab eiusmodi horrenda simulatione, necnon ab omni fornicatione custodiat nos sancta veritas, Christus Iesus.
units.tr: Add that the Shechemites (whose suffering was unjust, although the action of Jacob's sons was also unjust) perished not only on account of the vice by which they polluted the holy family of Jacob, but also on account of their hypocrisy. They dared to take up the sacred things of the holy people by accepting circumcision, while in fact they looked to neither the glory of the God of Israel nor the advantages of the chosen people, but only to their own. May holy truth, Christ Jesus, keep us from such dreadful pretence, and from all fornication.

units.tr: Genesis 39.

units.la: Dimisit autem (Potiphar) omnia sua in manu Ioseph, nec cognoscebat cum eo quicquam nisi panem, quem ipse comedebat: & erat Ioseph eleganti forma atque pulchræ aspectu. Factumque est post hæc hac verba, ut leuaret uxor domini sui oculos suos in Ioseph, diceretq;: dormi mecum. Qui renuens ait ad uxorem domini sui: En herus meus non cognouit mecum quicquam in domo, cunctaq; quae habet, tradidit in manum meam. Non est maior quispiam in hac domo quam ego sim, nec quicquam mihi prohibuit nisi te, eo quod tu uxor illius sis: quomodo igitur faciam malum istud tam magnum, & peccabo in Deum? Et factum est, cum ipsa sic loqueretur ad Ioseph quotidie, ut ille non audiret eam, neque dormiret cum ea, aut esset cum ea. Accidit vero opportuna quadam die, ut veniret domum, faceretq; opus suum, nec esset vir ullus ex familia in domo. Et illa apprehendit eum cum veste eius, dicens: Concumbe me cum: qui deserens vestem suam in manu illius, fugit, atq; egressus est foras. Et factum est cum illa vidisset, quod reliquisset vestem suam in manu eius, fugisset q; foras, vocauit viros domus suae, dixitque ad eos: Ecce introduxit ad nos virum Hebraum, ut illuderet nobis. nam venit ad me, ut concumberet mecum, & ego cœpi clamare voce magna. Factumq; est cùm audiret, quòd ego eleuassem vocem meam & clamassem, dimisit vestem suam apud me, & fugiens egressus est foras. Dimisit itaque illa vestem eius apud se, donec veniret dominus eius domum. Et locuta est ad eum his verbis, dicens: Venit ad me seruus ille Hebraeus, quem adduxisti ad nos, vt illuderet mihi. Factumq; est cùm eleuassem vocem meam, & clamassem, dereliquit vestem suam apud me, & fugit foras. Audiens vero dominus eius verba uxoris suae, quae ad illum loquebatur, dicens: Secundum verba ista fecit mihi seruus tuus, commotus est furor eius. Tollensq; herus Ioseph, posuit eum in carcerem, in eum scilicet locum, vbi vincti regis conclusi tenebantur, fuitq; ibi in domo carceris. Sed erat Deus cum Ioseph, piè illi inclinatus, dedit q; illi gratiam in oculis principis carceris.
units.tr: Potiphar left all that he had in Joseph's hand, and he knew nothing he had, save the bread which he did eat. And Joseph was a goodly person, and well favoured. And it came to pass after these things, that his master's wife cast her eyes upon Joseph; and she said, Lie with me. But he refused, and said unto his master's wife, Behold, my master wotteth not what is with me in the house, and he hath committed all that he hath to my hand; there is none greater in this house than I; neither hath he kept back any thing from me but thee, because thou art his wife: how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God? And it came to pass, as she spake to Joseph day by day, that he hearkened not unto her, to lie by her, or to be with her. And it came to pass about this time, that he went into the house to do his business; and there was none of the men of the house there within. And she caught him by his garment, saying, Lie with me: and he left his garment in her hand, and fled, and got him out. And it came to pass, when she saw that he had left his garment in her hand, and was fled forth, that she called unto the men of her house, and spake unto them, saying: See, he hath brought in a Hebrew unto us to mock us; he came in unto me to lie with me, and I cried with a loud voice: and it came to pass, when he heard that I lifted up my voice and cried, that he left his garment with me, and fled, and got him out. And she laid up his garment by her, until his lord came home. And she spake unto him according to these words, saying, The Hebrew servant, which thou hast brought unto us, came in unto me to mock me: and it came to pass as I lifted up my voice and cried, that he left his garment with me, and fled out. And when his master heard the words of his wife, which she spake unto him, saying, After this manner did thy servant to me; his wrath was kindled. And Joseph's master took him, and put him into the prison, a place where the king's prisoners were bound: and he was there in the prison. But the LORD was with Joseph, and shewed him mercy, and gave him favour in the sight of the keeper of the prison.

units.la: 1 Duas graues tentationes Iosephum fusti [?] nuisse hic legimus: vnam in re carni corruptæ accepta: alteram in re carni aduersa & in grata. Fuit enim solicitatus ab hera sua ad concubitum (sicuti Miles quidam Decij à muliere impudica in libidinem concitatus est: de quo Hieronymus in vita Pauli eremitæ,& Cent.Ecclef.3.cap.12.)& coniectus à domino suo in carcerem. Prioris tentationis grauitas cognoscitur, si expenderimus illa, nempe adolescentiam Iosephi, formam, dominæ authoritatem, procacitatem & instantiam, occasionem, solitudinem, &c. Poste-[?] rioris, si Iosephi fidem & innocentiam. Quidam enim impatienter ferunt iniurias sibi illatas præter meritum, dicentes: Equidem libenter hanc pœnam ferrem, si commeruissem: sed quid mali feci? &c.
units.tr: 1 Here we read that Joseph endured two grievous temptations: one arising from the corrupt flesh, the other from circumstances that were adverse to the flesh and yet pleasing to it. For he was solicited to lust by his mistress (just as a certain soldier under Decius was stirred to lust by an immodest woman, as Jerome tells in the Life of Paul the Hermit, and as the Magdeburg Centuries record in Book 3, chapter 12), and was cast by his master into prison. The gravity of the first temptation becomes clear if we weigh his youth, his beauty, the authority of his mistress, her boldness and persistence, the opportunity, the solitude, and so on. The gravity of the second becomes clear if we weigh Joseph's faith and innocence. For some bear unjust injuries inflicted on them with impatience, saying: "Indeed I would gladly bear this punishment if I had deserved it, but what evil have I done?" and so on.

units.la: 2 Ecce autem malitiam & perfidiam mulieris, quæ Iosephum tentauit. Primum enim oculos suos in Iosephum coniecit: deinde illum sæpe de concubitu alloquuta est: postea illum est aggressa, & vestimentum illius apprehendit: tandem spe sua frustrata laruam castitatis assumpsit, & se castam esse gloriata est falsò, & castissimum Iosephum accusauit, quasi ipse voluisset eam stuprare: postremò in causa fuit, ut dominus Iosephi iratus coniecerit illum in carcerem, nimium credens pessimæ fœminæ accusanti, & signa (quæ sæpissimè fallunt) ostendenti: quemadmodum Fausta Constantini Magni vxor persuasit marito suo, ut proprium filium Crispum interficeret, ut habetur in Chronicis. Idem vxor Othonis 3. Imperatoris fecit, Maria de Aragonia, quæ accensa amore Comitis circa Mutinam, solicitauit cum de adulterio: cum vero honestissimus vir illi bestiæ nollet gratificari, accusauit eum coram Imperatore, quasi comes voluerit ipsi vim inferre, qua de delatione Imperator accensus, non facta diligentiori inquisitione, iussit eum decollari.
units.tr: 2 Consider now the malice and treachery of the woman who tempted Joseph. First she cast her eyes upon Joseph; then she often addressed him about lying with her; afterwards she assailed him and seized his garment; at last, her hope frustrated, she put on the mask of chastity, falsely boasted that she was chaste, and accused the most chaste Joseph, as though he had wished to violate her. Finally, she was the cause of his master's anger, so that he cast Joseph into prison, too readily believing a most wicked woman who accused him and displayed signs (which very often deceive). In the same way Fausta, wife of Constantine the Great, persuaded her husband to kill his own son Crispus, as is recorded in the Chronicles. The wife of the Emperor Otto III did the same, Maria of Aragon, who, inflamed with love for a count near Modena, solicited him to adultery; but when that most honourable man would not gratify that beast, she accused him before the Emperor, as though the count had wished to use force against her. The Emperor, roused by this accusation, without making a more careful inquiry, ordered him to be beheaded.

units.la: § Videamus nunc castitatem & fortitudinem Iosephi malentis mori, quam seruire voluptatibus, quemadmodum D. Chrysostomus loquitur in Serm. de Continentia. Quomodo igitur is tentationem vicit? quibus armis peccato luxuriae restitit? quomodo ab adulterio custoditus est? Principio credidit & cognouit, adulterium esse non simpliciter malum, sed grande malum, & magnum scelus, Iob. 31[?] ferens secum incommoda animae, corporis, famae, & rerum; sicuti testimonia & exempla literarum sacrarum & prophanarum, & quotidiana experientia docent.
units.tr: § Let us now look at the chastity and courage of Joseph, who preferred to die rather than to serve his lusts, as Chrysostom says in his sermon on Continence. How then did he overcome the temptation? With what weapons did he resist the sin of lust? How was he kept from adultery? First, he believed and recognised that adultery is not simply an evil but a great evil and a serious crime (Job 31), bringing with it harms to the soul, the body, reputation and property, as the testimonies and examples of sacred and profane letters, and everyday experience, teach.

units.la: Secundo cogitauit, si hoc malum committeret, quod iniquus, perfidus, & ingratus fieret in suum herum, qui fidei Iosephi omnia commisit, excepta uxore, quae non Iosephi, sed Potipharis erat. Qui autem aufert uxorem alteri, quae cum suo marito est una caro, perinde est ac si ei ipsummet auferret: quoniam uxor est corpus mariti, & maritus caput uxoris. Ad haec, qui furatur, qui occidit, qui diis alienis seruit, peccat quidem & ipse, verum peccat solus, nec quenquam peccato suo necessario inuoluit: sed hoc genus peccati, nempe adulterium & scortatio, sic comparatum est, ut duos simul homines coplectatur, & in perditionem abijciat: atq; ita diabolus simul binos & binos lucretur, idq; vilissimo vilisimo precio. Qui alias peccat,quoniam solus peccat, solus resipiscens restituitur, & in conscientia sua per gratiam Dei pacatur. Adulter vero vbi resipiscit, fi veré resipiscit, non poterit non plurimū in conscientia sua, eius quoque nomine turbari,cum qua peccauit,& cui peccandi fuit author, præsertim fi videat eam in peccato pergere & perire. Ergo adulterium valde iniuriosum est proximo,quod etiam per hoc ostendi potest,quod aufert ei non sua, sed seipsum, Prouerb. 6. & quod ille qui hoc vitio laborat, nulli fidem feruat. Dauid enim suum fidelem militem fecit occidi pro vxore eius,2.Reg.11.Hinc est quod Abraham & Ifaac petierunt ab vxoribus suis, vt fe sorores esse illorum diceren!, ne propter ipsas occiderentur,Gen.12.20.26.
units.tr: Second, he reflected that if he committed this evil he would become unjust, faithless and ungrateful to his master, who had entrusted everything to Joseph's good faith except his wife, who belonged not to Joseph but to Potiphar. For whoever takes another man's wife, who is one flesh with her husband, is just as if he took the husband himself, since the wife is the husband's body and the husband is the wife's head. Besides, whoever steals, whoever kills, whoever serves other gods, sins indeed, but he sins alone and does not necessarily involve anyone else in his sin. But this kind of sin, namely adultery and whoring, is so constituted that it entangles two people at once and casts them into destruction; and so the devil gains two for one, and at the cheapest price. Whoever sins otherwise, since he sins alone, when he repents he is restored alone, and through the grace of God is pacified in his conscience. But the adulterer, when he repents, if he truly repents, cannot help being greatly troubled in his conscience also on account of her with whom he sinned, and to whom he was the author of sinning, especially if he sees her persisting and perishing in sin. Therefore adultery is very injurious to one's neighbour, which can also be shown by this, that it takes from him not his own goods but himself (Prov. 6); and that the man who is afflicted with this vice keeps faith with no one. For David made his faithful soldier to be killed for the sake of his wife (2 Sam. 11).
