units.la: 1 Sicut prior Psalmus docuit Dei benedictione omnia simpliciter fortunari, non nostro labore aut cura: ita hic psalmus docet, vbi fit illa benedictio, nempe apud pios, qui timent Dominum. Timentis autem Deum beatitudo in laboribus manuum, in vxore & liberis, in spirituali æternaq; apud Deum gratia, hic describitur. Neque vero hic tantum ostenditur, quanta fit beatitas timentium ac reuerentium Deum, iuxtaq; normam eius viuentium, seu ambulantium in vijs eius, hoc est, interiores & exteriores cultus in agnitione mediatoris præstantium,
units.tr: 1 As the previous Psalm taught that all good things come simply by the blessing of God, not by our labour or care, so this psalm teaches where that blessing is found, namely among the godly, who fear the Lord. Here is described the happiness of one who fears God: happiness in the labour of his hands, in his wife and children, and in the spiritual and eternal grace he has with God. Nor does this psalm show only how great is the blessedness of those who fear and revere God and live according to his rule, that is, of those who walk in his ways, who render inward and outward worship in the knowledge of the Mediator,

units.la: sed etiam in permultis aliis Scripturæ locis: vt Tob. 4. ὅσα περ[?] ἔχεις σοι πολλά, ἐὰν φοβῇ τὸν θεόν, &c. Sirac. 1. τὸν φοβούμενον τὸν κύριον[?] ἐν ἰσχύι[?] ἐν ἰσχύϊ[?] τῶν. Psal. 31. Quàm magna bonitas tua, quàm abscondisti timentibus te, & exhibuisti eis qui sperant in te. Psal. 33. Ecce oculi Domini super metuentes eum, & super eos qui sperant in misericordia eius. Psal. 112. Beatus vir qui timet Dominum, qui mandatis eius delectatur valde, &c.
units.tr: but it does so also in very many other places of Scripture: as Tob. 4. "Whatever you have, give abundantly, if you fear God," etc. [ὅσα περ ἔχεις σοι πολλά, ἐὰν φοβῇ τὸν θεόν]. Sir. 1. "To him who fears the Lord ..." [τὸν φοβούμενον τὸν κύριον]. Ps. 31. "How great is your goodness, which you have laid up for those who fear you, and have shown to those who trust in you." Ps. 33. "Behold, the eyes of the Lord are upon those who fear him, and upon those who hope in his mercy." Ps. 112. "Blessed is the man who fears the Lord, who takes great delight in his commandments," etc.

units.la: 2 Quid est igitur timere Deum? ponere Deum in conspectu suo: quod qui fecerit, divertet à malo & faciet bonum, inquiret pacem & persequetur eam, Psal. 34. Hinc illa, Sirac. 2, οἱ φοβούμενοι κύριον, ἑτοιμάσουσι καρδίας αὐτῶν, καὶ ἐνώπιον αὐτῶν ταπεινώσουσι τὰς ψυχὰς αὐτῶν. & 15. ὁ φοβούμενος κύριον, ποιήσει ἀγαθόν. Prouerb. 8. Timor Domini odit malum. & 16. In timore Domini declinatur à malo. Iob. 28. Psalm. 111. Initium Sapientiæ timor Domini. Exod. 20. Vt enim probaret vos, venit Deus, & vt terror illius esset in vobis, & non peccaretis.
units.tr: 2 What, then, is it to fear God? It is to set God before your eyes. Whoever does this turns away from evil and does good; he seeks peace and pursues it (Ps. 34). Hence that saying in Sir. 2: "Those who fear the Lord will prepare their hearts, and humble their souls before him" [οἱ φοβούμενοι κύριον, ἑτοιμάσουσι καρδίας αὐτῶν, καὶ ἐνώπιον αὐτῶν ταπεινώσουσι τὰς ψυχὰς αὐτῶν], and in 15: "He who fears the Lord will do good" [ὁ φοβούμενος κύριον, ποιήσει ἀγαθόν]. Prov. 8: "The fear of the Lord hates evil." Prov. 16: "By the fear of the Lord one turns from evil." Job 28. Ps. 111: "The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord." Exod. 20: "For God has come to test you, and that his fear may be before you, so that you do not sin."

units.la: Vnde autem oriatur metus Domini, oftedit illud Psal. 119. Horruit à timore tui caro mea: à iudiciis enim tuis timui. Attamen ob feruandum est timorem Dei esse duplicem, vnum seruilem, qui timet poenas, nec per fidem accipit consolationem: alterum filialem, qui cum fide coniunctus est, de quo Rom. 8. Non enim accepistis spiritum seruitutis iterum ad timorem, sed accepistis spiritum adoptionis, per quem clamamus Ab-ba pater.
units.tr: Whence the fear of the Lord arises is shown by Ps. 119: "My flesh trembles for fear of you, and I am afraid of your judgements." Yet it must be observed that the fear of God is twofold: one kind is servile, which fears punishment and does not receive comfort through faith; the other is filial, which is joined with faith, of which Rom. 8 speaks: "For you have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you have received the spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, Abba, Father."

units.la: Quid est ambulare in viis Domini? Est credere Deo & amare proximum. Vniuersæ enim viæ Domini misericordia & veritas, Psalm.25. quem Dominum D.Apostolus lucem & charitatem vocat, 1.Ioan.1.4. Est ambulare in Christo, per quem solum itur ad patre, Ioan.14. & ambulare sic, vt ambulauit Christus, id est, in dilectione, 1.Ioan.2. Eph.5. Est introire per arctam[?] portam: hæc enim est quæ adducit in vitam, quæ Deus est & Christus eius, Matth.7. Deuter.30. Ioan.11. Est versari non in impiorum consilio, non improborum insistere viam, non in fede scurrarum sedere, sed delectari lege Domini, Psal.1. eundemq; cum Dauide orare, Psal.25. Vias tuas (.i. totam rationem qua nos ad te deducis) Domine demonstra mihi, & semitas tuas edoce me. & Psal.86. Doce me Domine viam tuam, & ingrediar in veritate tua, unias cor meum, vt timeat nomen tuum. & 119. Gressus meos dirige secundum eloquium tuum, & non dominetur mei omnis iniustitia. & 143. Notam fac mihi viam, in qua ambulem: Spiritus tuus bonus deducat me in viam rectâ. Monet insuper hic Psalmus, in timore Dei coniugium esse ineundum: id quod & angelus Tobia facere iussit, Tob.6. quod & fecit, Tob.8. nec ipse solum, sed etiã Sara: cuius verba hæc sunt: Tu scis Domine, quia nunquam concupiui virum, & mundã seruaui animam meam ab omni concupiscentia. Nunquam cum ludentibus miscui me:
units.tr: What is it to walk in the ways of the Lord? It is to believe God and to love one's neighbour. For all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth (Ps. 25). The Apostle calls this Lord light and love (1 John 1:4). It is to walk in Christ, through whom alone one comes to the Father (John 14), and to walk as Christ walked, that is, in love (1 John 2; Eph. 5). It is to enter through the narrow gate, for this is the gate that leads into life, which is God and his Christ (Matt. 7; Deut. 30; John 11). It is to dwell not in the counsel of the ungodly, not to stand in the way of sinners, not to sit in the seat of scoffers, but to delight in the law of the Lord (Ps. 1), and with David to pray (Ps. 25): "Show me your ways, O Lord (that is, the whole plan by which you lead us to yourself), and teach me your paths." And Ps. 86: "Teach me, O Lord, your way, and I will walk in your truth; unite my heart, that it may fear your name." And Ps. 119: "Direct my steps according to your word, and let no iniquity have dominion over me." And Ps. 143: "Make known to me the way in which I should walk; your good Spirit lead me into the right path." Moreover, this psalm warns that marriage is to be entered upon in the fear of God. The angel ordered this for Tobias (Tob. 6), and Tobias did it (Tob. 8), and so did Sarah, whose words are these: "You know, O Lord, that I have never desired a husband, and I have kept my soul pure from all lust. I have never mixed myself with those who play, nor have I made myself a partner with those who walk in levity. But I have accepted a husband with your fear, not with my lust," etc. (Tob. 3).

units.la: neque cum his qui in leuitate ambulant, participem me praebui. Virum autem cum timore tuo, non cum libidine mea, confessi suscipere, &c. Tob.3[?].
units.tr: Nor have I ever joined myself to those who walk in frivolity. But I accepted a husband in fear of you, not in my own lust, and I confessed it," etc. (Tob. 3).

units.la: ¶ Sed quid tandem boni euenient timenti Dominum, iuxta hunc Psalmum: Propheta hoc epithalamio seu carmine nuptiali & consolatur coniuges, & eis omnia felicia precatur & promittit a Deo. Labores, inquit, manuum tuarum manducabis, beatus es, & bene tibi erit: id est, laboribus & actionibus tuis Deus benedicet: Deus te alet: ipsoque adiicente, manducabis ex labore manuum, dum alij vel frustra laborant, vel certe cum magna animi molestia partis vtuntur. Manuum, inquam, tuarum, vt non de alieno, sed de tuo, idque non malis artibus, sed iustis laboribus acquisito, viuas & tuos alas. Quod si cui datur, felicitatis loco censendum est. Cum manducas (inquit Augustinus) labores fructuum tuorum, beatus (in praesenti), cum perueneris ad fructum laborum tuorum, bene tibi erit (in futuro.) Hic etiam videmus verum esse illud Prouerb.13. Substantia quae (parta est) vanitate, minuetur: quod autem quis congregat per manum, id augescit. Hoc est, Bona acquisita fraude & rapina, cito dilapidabuntur: quae autem acquiruntur labore manuum, his Deus dat incrementum: cui etiam soli debetur gratia. Si enim hoc Pytho confessus est faciendum esse, multo magis nos facere decet. Is enim Atheniensibus ob res feliciter gestas ipsum admirantibus ac prædicantibus quòd Coryn regem interemisset, Dijs, inquit, habenda est gratia, quibus autoribus hoc tacinus [?] praeclarè gestum est. Nam ipse nihil aliud quàm manum & operam meam commodaui. Euentus ergo rei in manu Dei est, & huic debetur gratia, si quid feliciter cesserit. Sed interim vult nostram operam accedere. Quoniam si quis non vult operari, nec manducet, inquit Apost. 2. Thes. 3.
units.tr: ¶ But what good will in the end come to one who fears the Lord, according to this psalm? The prophet, in this wedding song or nuptial poem, both comforts married couples and prays for and promises them all happiness from God. "You shall eat the labour of your hands; you are blessed, and it shall be well with you." That is: God will bless your labours and actions; God will feed you, and with his help you shall eat from the labour of your hands, while others either labour in vain or at least enjoy what they have with great anxiety of mind. Of your hands, I say, so that you may live and feed your own on what is yours, not on what belongs to another, and gained not by wicked arts but by honest labour. If this is granted to anyone, it must be counted as happiness. "When you eat the labour of your fruits (says Augustine), you are blessed (in the present); when you come to the fruit of your labours, it shall be well with you (in the future)." Here we also see that the saying in Prov. 13 is true: "Wealth gained by vanity will be diminished, but what one gathers by hand will increase." That is: goods acquired by fraud and robbery will quickly be squandered, but those acquired by the labour of the hands God gives increase, and to him alone thanks are due. For if Pythius confessed that this ought to be done, how much more fitting is it for us to do so! When the Athenians admired and praised him for his successful deeds, because he had killed King Coryn, he said: "Thanks must be given to the gods, under whose guidance this deed was nobly done. For I myself contributed nothing but my hand and effort." Therefore the outcome of a matter is in God's hand, and to him thanks are owed if anything turns out well. Yet meanwhile he wants our effort to be added. For "if anyone is unwilling to work, neither let him eat," says the Apostle (2 Thess. 3).

units.la: Vxor tua sicut vitis fructifera in lateribus domus tuæ, &c.) Licet debile & defpectum lignum sit vitis, quæ seipsam nequit sustentare, dulcem tamen profert fructum: sic vxor imbecille est organum, quæ absque viri præsidio vix viuere potest, parit tamen dulces liberos, qui plantulis oliuarum comparantur, quòd sanctorum filij more oliuarum semper optima floreant fama. Admonetur autem vxor hoc simili à vite sumpto sui officij: ne videlicet sit in star rhamni aut dumi spiniferi [?] & scuti, sed tanquam vitis fructifera & [illegible, ~7 letters] materque familias.
units.tr: "Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine in the sides of your house," etc. Although the vine is a weak and despised wood, which cannot support itself, it nevertheless bears sweet fruit. So the wife is a feeble vessel, who can scarcely live without the protection of her husband, yet she bears sweet children, who are compared to olive plants, because the children of the saints always flourish, like olives, with the best reputation. The wife is admonished by this image taken from the vine concerning her duty: that she should not be like a thorn-bush or a prickly briar and shield, but like a fruitful vine, [illegible] and a mother of the household.

units.la: Ecce sic benedicetur homo qui timet Dominum.) Deus ei benedicet, si habuerit vxorem, si filios: si vero non habet, non tamen sine benedictione aut prouidentia Dei erit, & quicquid habet, ꝓ [?] diuitijs computat. Semper enim gratus est Deo, & contentus sua sorte.
units.tr: "Behold, thus shall the man who fears the Lord be blessed." God will bless him if he has a wife and sons; but if he does not have them, he will not be without God's blessing or providence, and whatever he has he counts as riches. For he is always pleasing to God and content with his lot.

units.la: Benedicat tibi Dominus ex Zion) id est, benedictione forti ac æterna. vel, multiplicet te in bonis & spiritus & corporis Dominus,qui habitat in Zion, id est,in loco sancto suo. Alludit enim ad id, quod tunc Deus in Zion colebatur, & præsens secundum promissionem credebatur, quæ nunc est Ecclesia sanctorum, ut & tunc verè erat. vel, benedicat tibi Dominus ex Zion .i. faciat te Dominus participem earum benedictionum, quib. Zioni civitati ac populo suo benefacit.
units.tr: May the Lord bless you out of Zion: that is, with a strong and eternal blessing. Or: may the Lord, who dwells in Zion, that is, in his holy place, multiply you in goods both of spirit and of body. For it alludes to the fact that God was then worshipped in Zion and was believed to be present there according to his promise, which is now the Church of the saints, just as it truly was then. Or: "May the Lord bless you out of Zion," that is, may the Lord make you a sharer in those blessings with which he favours Zion, his city and his people.

units.la: Ut videas bona Ierusalem omnibus diebus vitæ tuæ) ut videas profectum civium Ierusalem, id est, gratiam populi Dei semper, quæ augescit fide verbi Dei, & omnibus aduersarijs superior evadit. Et quia felicitas privata non satis firma stat sine publica, rectè rogat, ut Deus benefaciat toti civitati, ut in ea tutè[?] vivere possint colentes Deum.
units.tr: That you may see the good of Jerusalem all the days of your life: that is, that you may see the prosperity of the citizens of Jerusalem, that is, the grace of the people of God, which always grows by faith in the Word of God and comes out superior to all adversaries. And because private happiness does not stand firm enough without public happiness, he rightly prays that God would do good to the whole city, so that those who worship God may live securely in it.

units.la: Et videas filios filiorum tuorum) qui sunt corona & gaudium senum, Proverb. 17. Ecclef. 25. id est, ut sis longaevus: & gaudeas avus de nepotibus æquè ac tu, timentibus Deum, nempe à te institutis.
units.tr: And that you may see your children's children: they are the crown and joy of the elderly (Prov. 17; Ecclus. 25), that is, that you may be long-lived and rejoice as a grandfather over grandchildren, no less than you, who fear God, have raised them to do so.

units.la: Pacem super Israel) id est, gratiam & misericordiam super populum Dei, unde pax conscientijs est æterna: quæ præ omnibus corporalibus beneficijs optanda est. Hanc etiam nobis largiatur Dominus noster Iesus Christus,
units.tr: Peace upon Israel: that is, grace and mercy upon the people of God, from which comes eternal peace of conscience, which is to be desired above all bodily benefits. May our Lord Jesus Christ also grant this to us.

units.la: Amen,
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XXIII
units.tr: SERMON XXIII

units.la: Proverb. 6.
units.tr: Proverbs 6.

units.la: Custodi fili mi praeceptum patris tui, & ne deseras legem matris tuae. Liga ea super cor tuum iugiter, & adnecte ea gutturi tuo. Cum ambulaveris ducet te, & cum dormieris custodiet te, & cum evigilaveris ipsa loquetur tecum. Quia lucerna est praeceptum, & lex est lumen: atq; via vitae, correptio & castigatio. Ut custodiat te a muliere mala, & a blanditiis linguae extraneae. Non concupiscas pulchritudinem eius in corde tuo, ne capiat te palpebris suis. Quoniam propter mulierem meretricem (peruenit fornicator) usque ad massam panis, & mulier venatur preciosam animam viri. Numquid fouebit aliquis ignem in sinu suo, ut vestimenta sua non comburantur? Aut si gradietur quis supra carbones ut pedes eius non aduruntur? Sic qui ingreditur ad uxorem proximi sui, non innoxius erit, quisquis accesserit ad eam. Non contemptui habent furem, quando furatur ut adimpleat animam suam, esuriens enim facit. Et deprehensus reddit septuplum , & totam substantiam domus suæ rependit. Qui autem adulterium committit cum muliere, is deficit corde:et qui vult perdere animam suam, agit in hunc modum. Plagam & ignominiam inueniet, atq; opprobrium eius non delebitur. Zelus enim est furor viri: & non parcit in die vltionis. Non accipit faciem vllius placationis, nec acquiescet, etiā si multiplicaueris munera,
units.tr: My son, keep your father's commandment, and do not forsake your mother's law. Bind them continually upon your heart, and tie them about your throat. When you walk, they will lead you; when you sleep, they will keep you; and when you awake, they will talk with you. For the commandment is a lamp, and the law is a light, and the way of life is correction and chastisement: that they may keep you from the evil woman, and from the flattering tongue of a stranger. Do not lust after her beauty in your heart, nor let her take you with her eyelids. For because of a harlot a man is brought down to a piece of bread, and the adulteress hunts for the precious soul of a man. Can a man carry fire in his bosom and his garments not be burned? Or can one walk upon coals and his feet not be scorched? So he who goes in to his neighbour's wife shall not be innocent, whoever touches her. Men do not despise a thief when he steals to satisfy his soul, being hungry; yet when he is caught he restores sevenfold, and gives up all the substance of his house. But he who commits adultery with a woman lacks understanding; he who does so destroys his own soul. He shall find wounds and dishonour, and his reproach shall not be wiped away. For jealousy is the fury of a man, and he will not spare in the day of vengeance. He will not accept the face of any ransom, nor will he consent, though you multiply gifts.

units.la: 1 Quoniam fidem coniugalem frangere & mœchari turpe est, & malum: sicut contrà here matrimonium ac fidem seruare honestum & bonum (siquidem sit in Domino) quemadmodum Apostolus dicit, Heb.13. Honorabile est inter omnes coniugium, & cubile impollutum: scortatores autem & adulteros iudicabit Deus: & quoniam nunc sunt extrema tempora, quæ sunt, ut Christus prædixit, sicut tempora Nohæ & Lothi: idcirco diligenter monendi sumus, ut fugiamus omnem immunditiam, scortationem, & adulterium: ne cum mundo pereamus.
units.tr: 1 Since breaking the marriage faith and committing adultery is shameful and evil, while on the contrary keeping marriage and faith is honourable and good (provided it be in the Lord), as the Apostle says, Heb. 13: "Marriage is honourable among all, and the bed undefiled; but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge." And since now are the last times, which are, as Christ foretold, like the times of Noah and Lot, we are therefore to be diligently warned to flee every uncleanness, fornication and adultery, lest we perish with the world.

units.la: Ut autem cauere queamus à mala fœminina, obseruemus primo, quod Salomon hic dicit: Retine fili mi (alloquitur autem Deus in Salomone omnem hominem) patris tui præceptum (honorandi enim sunt parentes) neue omitte aut deferas legem matris tuæ (per quam etiam Ecclesia Christi intelligi potest, ut per patrem Deus loquens in Ecclesia. Non autem alia commendat mater filio servanda, quàm quæ patri placuisse cognoscit.) liga ea super cor tuum, (firmiter retinendo, ne diffluant verba in corde tuo ut literæ in mala papyro) & annecte ea gutturi tuo (vel collo, ut solent res preciosæ, catenæ aureæ, &c.) cum ambulaveris ducant te (& sequere tu illa, non mundi illecebras) & cùm dormieris custodiant te, & cùm evigilaveris (maximè enim foris ambulantibus, aut in lecto existentibus tentationes ad libidinem incidere solent) loquere cum eis (& meditare illa, vel resume meditationem de ipsis.) Quia lucerna est præceptum (ut & Psalm. 119. dicitur:) & lex lux (ostendit enim quid agere, quidve omittere debeamus. Et nota epitheta verbi Dei, quòd gladius spiritus est, quo fugatur Malus cum suis ignitis telis.) & vitæ via correptio & disciplina. Non enim ad mortem ducit, sed ad vitam & salutem hominis confert castigatio disciplinæ, etsi à principio amara videatur. Hebræor. 12. Neque solùm custodit verbum Dei externum actum obscœnum, sed etiam cor, ne concupiscat, & gestus ne sint immodesti.
units.tr: So that we may be able to guard against the evil woman, let us first observe what Solomon says here: "Hold fast, my son" (for God speaks to every man in Solomon), "your father's commandment" (for parents are to be honoured), "and do not omit or forsake your mother's law" (by which the Church of Christ may also be understood, just as God speaks through the Father in the Church; the mother commends to her son nothing to be kept except what she knows has pleased the father). "Bind them upon your heart" (holding them firmly, lest the words flow out of your heart like letters written on worthless papyrus), "and tie them about your throat" (or neck, as precious things are worn, golden chains, etc.). "When you walk, they will lead you" (and follow them yourself, not the allurements of the world), "and when you sleep, they will keep you, and when you awake" (for temptations to lust are wont to arise especially in those walking abroad or lying in bed), "talk with them" (and meditate on those things, or take up meditation on them again). "For the commandment is a lamp" (as also Psalm 119 says), "and the law a light" (for it shows what we ought to do and what we ought to leave undone; and note the epithets of God's Word: it is a sword of the Spirit, by which the Evil One is put to flight with his fiery darts), "and the way of life is correction and discipline." For correction does not lead to death, but though at first it may seem bitter, the chastisement of discipline serves man's life and salvation (Heb. 12). Nor does the Word of God only guard against the outward obscene act, but also the heart, that it not lust, and that gestures not be immodest.

units.la: 2 Secundo sciamus, etiam occasiones scortandi vitandas esse, veluti ocium, de quo in principio huius capitis: item ebrietatem, de qua Proverb. 23. imò ipsos oculos, si obstaculo sint, eruendos, Matth. 5. Eccles. 9. Prouerb. 5. & pedes amputandos, ne adurantur igne gehennae.
units.tr: 2 Secondly, let us know that the occasions of fornication are also to be avoided: such as idleness, of which at the beginning of this chapter; likewise drunkenness, of which Prov. 23; indeed, if the eyes themselves are a stumbling block, they are to be plucked out, Matt. 5; Eccles. 9; Prov. 5; and feet are to be cut off, lest they be burned with the fire of Gehenna.

units.la: ȝ[?] Praeterea grauitas adulterij, & mala quae inde oriuntur expendamus. Periculosius est & detrimentosius atque peius est adulte-rare, quàm furari (quod hodie pauci credunt, id quod ex supplicijs furum & adulterorum intelligitur) adhaec scortatio, mala animae, corporis, famae & fortunae importat. vt ex Luc. 15. etiam cognoscere licet, nec non ex Germanico illo prouerbio: <bl>Spiel/ Hu-rey / vnd sauffen / macht</bl> <bl>daß ich muß haben vnd gut verkauffen : oder / von hauß vnnd hoff lauffen.</bl>
units.tr: 3 Furthermore, let us weigh the gravity of adultery and the evils that arise from it. Adultery is more perilous, more damaging and worse than theft (which few believe today, as is understood from the punishments of thieves and adulterers). Besides, fornication brings evils to soul, body, reputation and fortune, as may also be known from Luke 15, and from that German proverb: <bl>Gambling, whoring and drinking make a man have to sell his goods and run out of house and farm.</bl>

units.la: Attenuatur[?] autem hic peccatum furti non simpliciter, pro quo grauis poena infligitur secundum legem, sed temporalis & citra mortem, vt scilicet reddat septuplum, id est, plura quàm abstulit indeterminatè, boues quinque pro vno, oues quatuor pro vna, Exod.22. vel totum quod habet: sed comparatione adulterij longè grauioris, Is enim adulter remedium vxoris habet & matrimonij, vel habere debet, qua incontinentiae medeatur. Fur vero necessitate compulsus, nempe famis iniuriam euadere cupiens, deprehensus vero satisfacit, minori confusioni obnoxius postea, quàm illi, qui necessitatem patienti non succurrerunt, in ius traxerunt, spoliaverunt bonis pauperem, qui non vt ditesceret, sed vt esurientem stomachum placaret & impleret, furatus est. Adulter vero excaecatur carnali libidine, fit insanus & stultus, vt non sentiat pericula famae, vitae, & rerum, sed vt ebrius & mente captus, perpetua ignominia sese comaculat, & inexpiabili infamia aspergitur, iustamque secundum Dei legem vitae amissionem promeretur. Qui scorto se afsociat [?], in tantam veniet egestatem, vt cogatur mendicare frustum panis: & ne dum exterioribus priuatur bonis, verum & preciosam animam venalem diabolo exponit. Et et si scortum foedum haberi potest frusto panis: tamen talis mulier viri nobilem animam illaqueat. Quam stultus autem & insanus est, qui ob momentum voluptatis carnalis amittit vitam aeternam, & seipsum praecipitat in iram & furorem Dei, qui fortis zelotes est, & iustus iudex omnis carnis. Huic fit honor & potestas in secula seculorum, Amen.
units.tr: Here, however, the sin of theft is not treated simply, for which a heavy penalty is laid down by the law, but a temporal one short of death, namely that he restore sevenfold, that is, more than he took, without fixed amount: five oxen for one, four sheep for one, Exod. 22; or everything he has. But this is in comparison with adultery, which is far more grave. For the adulterer has, or ought to have, the remedy of a wife and marriage, by which to cure incontinence. The thief, however, is driven by necessity, wishing to escape the injury of hunger, and when caught he makes satisfaction, and is afterwards liable to less shame than those who did not succour the needy man who suffers want, who dragged him into court, and who stripped of goods the poor man who stole not to grow rich, but to appease and fill a hungry stomach. The adulterer, however, is blinded by carnal lust; he becomes mad and foolish, so that he does not feel the dangers to reputation, life and property; drunk and out of his mind, he defiles himself with perpetual disgrace, is smeared with infamy that cannot be expiated, and deserves the loss of life, which is just according to God's law. He who joins himself to a harlot comes to such poverty that he is forced to beg a crumb of bread; and not only is he deprived of outward goods, but he also exposes his precious soul to be sold to the devil. And although a foul harlot may be had for a crumb of bread, yet such a woman ensnares a man's noble soul. How foolish and insane is he who, for the sake of a moment of carnal pleasure, loses eternal life and hurls himself into the wrath and fury of God, who is a strong avenger and a just judge of all flesh. To him be honour and power for ever and ever, Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XXIIII
units.tr: SERMON 24

units.la: Prouerb. II.
units.tr: Proverbs 2.

units.la: Monile aureum in naribus porci est mulier formosa, quae destituitur iudicio rationis.
units.tr: A golden ring in a pig's snout is a beautiful woman who lacks the judgment of reason.

units.la: 1 Quid dedeceat non solum vxores, sed etiam virgines & viduas, Salomon hoc loci, veluti in speculo ostendit. Dicit enim, quemadmodum alij hoc prouerbium interpretantur: Circulus aureus in naribus suis: mulier pulchra & fatua: vel insulsa, quæ carot prudentia, vel cotumax sermone, vel, die vn⁠züchtige geßärden hat. Ein schön Weib ohn zucht/ist wie ein sau mit einem güldnen harband. ὥσπερ ἐν [illegible, ~10 letters] χρυσ[?] ἐν [illegible, ~8 letters], οὕτως γυναικὶ [illegible, ~12 letters] Vt enim sus monile foedat in luto, ita quoque stulta mulier abutitur pulchritudine sua, vt verè plumbeus gladius fit in aurea vagina, sicut in prouerbio dicitur: vel in eburnea vagina, quemadmodum Diogenes loquitur. Audiens enim adolescentem honesta specie, verbis parum honestis vtentem, Non te pudet, inquit, qui ex eburnea vagina plumbeum educas gladium? Ebur enim olim in summo erat precio. Dedecet ergo mulierem stultitia, imprudentia, impudentia, immodestia, socordia. Neque refert illam quidem esse pulchram & formosam, carere autem sapientia, destitui iudicio rationis, abuti pulchritudine, nec reputare qua ratione, & ad quem vsum naturale hoc donum à Deo susceperit. Fallax enim est gratia, & vana est pulchritudo: mulier timens Dominum, ipsa laudabitur, Prou. vlt. Forma bonum fragile est: & ob id non valde appetendum, neque in eo gloriandum. Qui pulchritudinem corporis diligit (D. Bernardo teste Serm. 64. de modo bene viuendi ad foro⁠ rem) semetipsum decipit. Quare? quia pulchritudo corporis fallax est, vana est, terra & cinis est, deceptio est hominis. Antisthenes Atheniensis, cuidam adolescenti, qui curarat
units.tr: 1 What unbecomes not only wives but also virgins and widows, Solomon here shows, as in a mirror. For he says, as others interpret this proverb: a golden ring in its snout is a woman who is beautiful but foolish or insipid, who lacks prudence, or who is stubborn in speech, or who has no modest bearing. A beautiful woman without decency is like a sow with a golden headband. As a sow in mud defiles a golden ring, so a woman without discretion [Greek illegible in the scan]. For as a sow defiles a ring in the mud, so a foolish woman abuses her beauty, so that it is truly a leaden sword in a golden sheath, as the proverb says, or in an ivory sheath, as Diogenes puts it. For when he heard a young man of respectable appearance using rather indecent words, Diogenes said: "Are you not ashamed to draw a leaden sword out of an ivory sheath?" Ivory was once of the highest price. Folly, imprudence, shamelessness, immodesty and carelessness therefore disgrace a woman. It makes no difference that she is beautiful and comely, if she lacks wisdom, is without the judgment of reason, abuses her beauty, and does not consider for what purpose and to what use she has received this natural gift from God. For grace is deceitful and beauty is vain: a woman who fears the Lord, she shall be praised (Prov. last chapter). Beauty of form is a fragile good, and so it is not to be greatly desired, nor to be boasted of. He who loves the beauty of the body (as St Bernard testifies, Sermon 64 on how to live well, addressed to the people) deceives himself. Why? Because bodily beauty is deceptive, vain, earth and ash, the deception of man. Antisthenes of Athens said to a certain young man who had had himself cast in bronze and was shaping himself to that image: "If the bronze could utter a voice, in what would it most glory?" "In its beauty," said the young man. "Then are you not ashamed," he said, "to boast of something lifeless?" meaning that one ought to boast more of the goods of the mind than of the form, which the statue also shared. The same man, if he saw a woman splendidly adorned, would go to her house and bid her husband bring out arms and a horse; if these pleased him, he allowed the woman to indulge in her pleasures, since there was someone to defend her; but if not, he advised her to lay aside that finery lest she become the prey of others. From this it is understood that beauty, especially when it is joined with adornment, is also dangerous.

units.la: sese ex aere sculpendu, & ad eam imaginem sese conformabat, dixit, Si aes posset vocem aedere, qua de re potissimum gloriaretur? De pulchritudine, inquit adolescens. Non igitur, inquit, erubescis, qui cum inanimo gloriaris? significans magis gloriandum de bonis animi quàm de forma, quam haberet tum statua communem. Idem si quam uidiffet[?] mulierem egregiè cultam, adibat aedes illius, iubebatque virum proferre arma & equum, quae si placuissent, patiebatur mulierem indulgere delicijs, quòd esset qui defenderet: sin minus, suadebat vt eum ornatum deponeret, ne praeda fieret aliis. Ex quo intelligitur pulchritudinem, praesertim si accesserit ornatus, etiam periculosam esse.
units.tr: Yet it should be noted that foolish and impious men are often compared in the Scriptures to beasts, such as swine, etc. So too the woman who has beauty of face, or the ornaments of earrings, necklaces and garments, but defiles her beauty and loses her grace by polluting herself with the mire of lust and adultery. Likewise she who, like a swine, tramples pearls under her feet, that is, does not chew over, consider or value the holy word, but despises it (Matt. 7); who more gladly handles the sins of others with her mouth than the virtues; who with her mouth speaks evil, speaks or sings base things. What is this other than eating husks, indeed dung with swine? For the songs of fornication (says St John Chrysostom, Hom. 38 on Matthew) are far more abominable than dung, and just as filth and mud are wont to stop up the ears of the body, so the songs of harlots, the fables of this age, are wont to stop up the ears of the mind and make them unclean; for such conversations are like pouring dung into the ears. Hiero fined the comic poet Epicharmus, because in the presence of his wife he had said something indecent. Epicharmus was a Sicilian, and by the nature of his region he was very full of jokes. But the king judged that such respect was owed to marriage that he counted it a crime to jest more wantonly while the wife was listening. And the courtesan Gnathaena, rebuked by the philosopher Stilpo for corrupting young men, said: "You and I, Stilpo, are caught in the same crime: you teach the young men who associate with you useless and amorous sophisms, so it makes no difference whether they consort with a philosopher or with a courtesan."

units.la: Notandum autem, stultos & impios homines saepe comparari in Scripturis bestiis, veluti porcis, &c. vt hic mulier, quae quidem pulchritudinem vultus habet, vel ornamenta inaurium, monilium & vestimentorum: sordidat autem pulchritudinem suam, & amittit decorem, coinquinando se coeno libidinis & adulterio. Item, quae, instar porci, margaritas conculcat pedibus suis, id est, sanctum verbum non ruminat, nec meditatur, nec in precio habet, sed contemnit, Matth. 7. quae aliorum peccata libentius ore tractat, quàm virtutes: quae ore suo maledicit, turpia loquitur aut canit: quod quid aliud est, quàm comedere siliquas, imo stercus cum porcis. Nam fornicatorij cæntus ( inquit D. Chryfoftomus Hom.38 in Matth.) multo mag s quàm stercora sunt abominabiles, Ac queminadmodum sordes & limus aures corporis obstruere solent: sic meretricij cantus, huius seculi fabulæ, aures mentis solent obstruere atque immundas facere: quasi enim stercus auribus immittunt huiusmodi colloquia. Hieron Epicharmo comico poetæ, quod præsente ipsius vxore dixisset quiddam inhonestum, multam dixit. Epicharmus Siculus erat, iuxta regionis naturam plurimi ioci. At rex tantum iudicauit esse tribuendum reuerentiæ coniugio, vt crimen existimaret, audiente vxore iocari lasciuius. Et Gnathæna meretrix reprehensa à Stilpone Philosopho, quod adolescentes corrumperet, Tu, inquit, egoque Stilpon in eodem hæremus crimine, qui adolescentes tecum versantes inutilia quædam & amatoria sophisimata doces, vt nihil referat cum Philosopho versentur an cum meretrice.
units.tr: 2 From the opposite side it is now understood what befits a woman and adorns her: not so much bodily comeliness as honesty of mind, wisdom, the fear of the Lord, discipline of morals, obedience, docility, chastity, the inner beauty which belongs to the soul and pleases God the Best and Greatest (1 Pet. 3), and which is worth something even without outward beauty. For we do not praise other things by their form or colour, but by their service and proper function. Thus we call a servant handsome who serves us well, not one who is good-looking and soft; and we call teeth the best not those which are finely formed and set in a straight line, but those which can easily chew and cut food. Socrates (and not badly) used to bid men often look at themselves in a mirror: if they were ugly, so that they might make up for the deformity of the body by the beauty of the mind; if handsome, so that they might commit nothing unworthy of their outstanding form.

units.la: 2 Ex contrario iam intelligitur, quid conueniat mulieri, eamque ornet, nempe non tam formositas corporis, quàm honestas mentis, sapientia, timor Domini, disciplina morum, obedientia, tractabilitas, pudicitia, interna pulchritudo, quæ animi est, & Deo Opt.Max.placet, 1.Pet.3. & valet etiam externa absente. Non enim ex forma, aut ex colore etiam cæteras res prædicamus, sed ex ministerio, atque ex officio proprio. Ita enim seruum vocamus pulchrum, qui nobis aptè ministrat,non qui speciosus atque mollis est: & dentes optimos, non eos, qui pulchrè atque ad lineam compositi sunt,sed qui mandere & concidere cibum facile possunt. Socrates iubebat (nec male) homines saepe fe in speculo contemplari: vt fi effent deformes, eam corporis deformitatem pulchritudine animi compensarent:fi formosi, vt nihil indignum egregia forma committerent.
units.tr: 2 From the opposite side, it is also clear what befits a woman and adorns her: not so much bodily beauty as the honesty of her mind, her wisdom, the fear of the Lord, good discipline of manners, obedience, tractability, chastity, and the inner beauty that belongs to the soul, which pleases God the best and greatest, 1 Pet. 3. This inner beauty is worth more even when outward beauty is absent. For we do not praise other things by their shape or colour, but by their service and their proper function. Thus we call a servant handsome not if he is graceful and delicate, but if he serves us well; and we call teeth the best not if they are set in a neat and regular row, but if they can easily chew and cut food. Socrates rightly advised people to look often into a mirror, so that if they were ugly they would make up for their bodily ugliness with beauty of soul, and if they were handsome they would do nothing unworthy of their fine appearance.

units.la: 3 Quomodo spiritualiter intelligendum est hoc prouerbium? Quicunque sacras[?] literas intentè meditatur,& iugiter perfcrutatur diuina eloquia,accipit ornamenta fcientiae. Quòd si male viuendo corrumpit,quod bene intelligit, circulum aureum habet in naribus, sed more porci terram fodit, coinquinat,& luto immergit;quia ornamentum, quod per notitiam scripturarum immunda actione fordidauit, talis anima mulier pulchra & fatua:pulchra,quae per scientiam,sed dedita carnalibus deleftationibus, fatua est per actionem. Tales porci sunt omnes, qui vngulas quidem diuidunt,scripturasque intelligunt, ac voluntatem Dei ex verbo eius nouerunt,sed non ruminant, sermones Domini non faciunt, voluntatem eius non exequuntur,habentes formam pietatis,sed vim eius abnegantes,2.Tim.4.[?] Deum profitentes fe scire,caeterum factis negantes,cùm sint abominabiles, & dicto non audientes, & ad omne opus bonum reprobi, Tit. 1. Virgines fatuæ, Matth. 25. apostatæ, 2. Pet. 2. Hinc Chrysostomus Hom. 17. in Matth. Porcos, inquit, intelligendos puto Christianos carnalibus & immundis voluptatibus deditos, quoniam propter fidem quidem suam mundi sunt, propter actus autem suos sordidos habentur immundi. Dominus noster Iesus Christus ita nobis adaugeat fidem, ut eam ostendere possimus ex factis nostris, propter nomen suum sanctum & salutare, Amen.
units.tr: 3 How should this proverb be understood spiritually? Whoever diligently meditates on the sacred Scriptures and constantly searches the divine words receives the ornaments of knowledge. But if he corrupts by a wicked life what he understands well, he has a golden ring in his nose, yet like a pig he digs in the earth, befouls himself and wallows in the mud. For the ornament which he has dirtied by an unclean life, through his knowledge of the Scriptures, makes such a soul a beautiful and foolish woman: beautiful because of her knowledge, but foolish in her conduct because she is given over to carnal pleasures. All who divide the hoof and understand the Scriptures, and know the will of God from his word, but do not chew the cud, do not do the words of the Lord, do not carry out his will, are such pigs. They have the form of godliness but deny its power, 2 Tim. 4. They profess that they know God, but deny him by their deeds, since they are abominable and disobedient, and reprobate for every good work, Tit. 1. They are the foolish virgins, Matt. 25, the apostates, 2 Pet. 2. Hence Chrysostom, Homily 17 on Matthew: "I think," he says, "that the pigs should be understood as Christians given over to carnal and unclean pleasures, since on account of their faith they are indeed clean, but on account of their filthy deeds they are held unclean." May our Lord Jesus Christ so increase our faith that we may show it by our deeds, for the sake of his holy and saving name. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XXV.
units.tr: CONCIO XXV.

units.la: Proverb. 12.
units.tr: Proverbs 12.

units.la: Mulier sedula corona est mariti sui: sed quasi putredo in ossibus eius est (mulier) confusione digna.
units.tr: A diligent wife is a crown to her husband: but she is like rottenness in his bones, a woman worthy of shame.

units.la: 1 Hoc unum est ex dictis Salomonis, quæ parabolæ & proverbia nuncupantur. Parabolæ quidem sive similitudines, quia occulta sunt, & secreta mysteria significat: Proverbia autem, quia talia sunt, quæ sæpius in ore fidelium versari, ac memoriæ commendari, ac retineri debent. Simus igitur & illius dicti memores, & sciamus id non solum juxta literam esse intelligendum, sed aliter quoque ac spiritualiter.
units.tr: 1 This is the one saying of Solomon's which are called parables and proverbs. They are called parables, or similitudes, because they are obscure and signify secret mysteries; they are called proverbs because they are of the sort that ought to be often on the lips of the faithful, and commended to memory and retained. Let us therefore keep this saying in mind too, and understand that it is to be taken not only according to the letter but also otherwise, that is, spiritually.

units.la: 2 Quæ est ergo sententia simplex huius loci? Mulierem magnum bonum, item magnum malum esse, quemadmodum etiam Chrysostomus testatur in epistola ad Hebr. Vbi mentionem facit vxoris Iobi. Bonum quidem est, fi fit sedula, diligens, strenua, ἀν-ἀρετῇ[?] virtutibus ornata, muliebri mollitie nō dissoluta: fi diligat & honoret maritum fuū, qui hīc בעלי[?] vocatur, id est, magister, vel dominus: fi amet liberos, fi fit sobria, pura, casta, domus custos, bona, suo viro lubdita & obediens, deniq; אישי[?] vt hic vocatur, & Prouer.vlt.describitur. Est enim magnopere in vxore commendandum, vbi ea cum honestate rem auxerit: quanquam in nobilium domibus late nunc regnat ocium & mollities. Nam quæ illustris habere vult, ea præter suam generisque dignitatem se fecisse iudicet, si quid operis in mariti domo fecerit, à quo quidem omnino, semperq; cessare ocio, marcentis est fœminę, libidinemq; fouentis: contrà vero probæ & frugi (qualis fuit Hanna vxor Tobiæ, Tob. 2.) nullum pati tempus frustra elabi, quædamque in ipso propatulo facere: quædam etsi minimè deceant ante ostium, eadem tamen si intra cubiculum exercentur, vel maximè deceant. Malum autem quid mulier est, si sit pudenda, gerens res confusione dignas, negligens & ignaua in e-xequendis domus ministerijs, κακότροπος[?], socors, imperiosa, impia, maledica. Nam ficut bona mulier est corona, gloria, honos, gaudium, & ornamentum viri sui, de qua gloriari potest, & per quam domus honorificè subsistit: ita mala est quasi quoddam pus in eius membris, & putredo in eius ossibus, quasi vermis in ligno: <bl>Sin heimlichs</bl> <bl>leyden</bl>[?], quod palàm conqueri non audet, vel potest, animo autem semper sentit, & ferre cogitur, sicuti nec calcei pressura cernitur, quantumlibet elegantis & prementis.
units.tr: 2 What, then, is the plain sense of this passage? That a woman is a great good and likewise a great evil, as Chrysostom also testifies in his letter to the Hebrews, where he speaks of the wife of Job. She is a good thing if she is diligent, careful, vigorous, adorned with virtues and not dissolved by feminine softness; if she loves and honours her husband, who here is called baal, that is, master or lord; if she loves her children; if she is sober, pure, chaste, a keeper of the house, good, subject and obedient to her husband; and finally, as here she is called ishshah, and as is described at the end of Proverbs. For a wife is greatly to be commended when, with honesty, she has increased the household property. Indeed, in the houses of nobles idleness and softness now reign widely. For a woman who wishes to be thought distinguished should judge that, apart from her own dignity and her family's rank, she has achieved something if she has done some work in her husband's house; to be altogether idle, always, is the mark of a languid woman who nourishes lust. On the contrary, a woman who is upright and thrifty (such as Hannah, the wife of Tobias, Tob. 2.) allows no time to slip away uselessly, and does certain things in full view; certain things, though they would scarcely be fitting before the door, are most fitting if they are done within the bedchamber. But a woman is bad if she is shameful, doing things worthy of shame, negligent and lazy in carrying out the duties of the household, ill-natured, slothful, domineering, impious, slanderous. For just as a good woman is a crown, a glory, an honour, a joy and an ornament to her husband, of whom he can boast, and through whom the household stands honourably, so a bad woman is like a kind of pus in his limbs and rottenness in his bones, like a worm in wood. She suffers in secret what she dares not or cannot complain of openly, yet always feels in her mind and is forced to endure, just as the pressure of a shoe is not seen, however elegant and pinching it is.

units.la: Interim tamen vt membrum corporis, nō ideó abijcitur, quia pus habet, sed potius sanatur: sic & vxor non repudianda propter quaedam vitia, sed potius modestè corrigenda, vel patienter ferenda.
units.tr: Yet, just as a limb of the body is not therefore cast off because it has pus, but rather is healed, so a wife is not to be repudiated on account of certain faults, but rather is to be corrected with moderation or patiently endured.

units.la: 3 Quomodo spiritualiter illud dictum est intelligendum? Si per mulierem ecclesiam, & per virum Christum Dominum & magistrum & caput nostrum intelligas, Eph. 5. Debet enim ecclesia operam dare, vt corde, ore, & corpore, hoc est, fide, confessione, & operibus bonis, caput suum ornet atque glorificet, Rom. 4. Psal. 34. Matth. 5. eiusque nomen non blasphemet, Rom. 2. Nam quicunque honorificauerit me (inquit Dominus 1. Reg. 2.) glorificabo eum: qui autem contemnunt me, erunt ignobiles. Ille idem Dominus suam largia: ur nobis gratiam, vt in illis nostris diebus ita credamus, loquamur & viuamus, vt in die Domini resurgere possimus non ad ignominiam & opprobrium, sed ad vitam & gloriam sempiternam, Amen.
units.tr: 3 How is that saying to be understood spiritually? If by the woman you understand the Church, and by the husband Christ the Lord, our Teacher and Head, as in Eph. 5. For the Church ought to take care to adorn and glorify its Head with heart, mouth and body, that is, with faith, confession and good works, as in Rom. 4, Ps. 34, Matt. 5; and not to blaspheme his name, Rom. 2. For, says the Lord in 1 Sam. 2, whoever honours me I will glorify, but those who despise me will be made of no account. May that same Lord grant us his grace, so that in these our days we may so believe, speak and live that on the day of the Lord we may rise not to shame and disgrace, but to life and eternal glory. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XXVI.
units.tr: CONCIO XXVI.

units.la: Proverb. 14.
units.tr: Proverbs 14.

units.la: Mulieres sapientes instaurant domum suam, stulta autem manibus suis evertet eam.
units.tr: The wise women build up their house, but the foolish pulls it down with her own hands.

units.la: Qui ambulat in rectitudine sua, timet Dominum: qui autem se avertit a viis eius, despicit eum.
units.tr: He who walks in his uprightness fears the Lord, but he who turns aside from his ways despises him.

units.la: In ore stulti est virga superbia : labia autem sapientum conservant eos.
units.tr: In the mouth of the fool is a rod of pride, but the lips of the wise preserve them.

units.la: Ubi boves non sunt, ibi praesepe vacuum est: & ubi multa sunt fruges (hapro veniunt) viribus bovis [?].
units.tr: Where there are no oxen, the manger is empty, but much produce comes from the strength of the ox.

units.la: 1 Quomodo pia & felix instituenda sit οἰκονομία[?], docet hîc Salomon. Est autem eligenda vxor non insipiens, etiamsi diues aut nobilis, aut pulchra sit, sed sapiens, iuxta illud Siracidæ cap. 7. μὴ ἀσχ[illegible, ~40 letters]. Nam, uti-dem inquit, cap. 36. qui bonam vxorem nactus est, principium habet facultatum, adiutorem sibi accommodatum, & columnam in qua conquiescat. Hoc non perpendunt, qui vel pecuniæ cupiditate, vel ambitione capti præcipitantur in nuptias: nescientes nobilitatis & amplæ dotis duo pessima mala socia esse, vxoris superbiam, & viri seruitutem. Itaque non iniuria apud Plautum veretur ille magnatem, dotatamque matronam ducere,ne sibi dicendum esset, Argentum accepi, dote imperium vendidi.
units.tr: 1 Here Solomon teaches how a wife is to be chosen, and how a household is to be managed piously and happily. One should choose a wife who is not foolish, even if she is rich, noble or beautiful, but who is wise, in accordance with the saying of Ecclesiasticus, chapter 7: [illegible in the scan]. For, as he says in chapter 36, whoever has found a good wife has the beginning of his possessions, a helper suited to him, and a pillar on which to rest. Those who rush into marriage, carried away by greed for money or by ambition, do not consider this. They do not realise that nobility and a large dowry are two very bad companions, a wife's pride and a husband's servitude. So it is not without reason that Plautus has his character fear taking a great lady with a dowry as his wife, lest he have to say: "I took silver; with the dowry I sold my authority."

units.la: Rursus mulier det operam, ut sit, aut si non est, ut fiat sapiens, & fugiat stultitiam, si modo domum suam ædificare, instruere, & instaurare velit, imo saluare & illustrare, sicut Abigail domum suam salvavit refrenando iram Dauidis, 1. Reg. 25. & non manibus suis, id est, operibus malis, destruere, evertere, disperdere, & omni bono familiam destituere, prole scilicet, honestate, fama, substantia, honore & gratia, sicut Iezabel inducens virum suum Achab & prolem suam ad idolatriam, propter quod tota domus illa per Iehu fuit destructa, 4. Reg. 9.
units.tr: Again, a woman should take care to be wise, or, if she is not, to become so, and to flee foolishness, if indeed she wishes to build up, equip and restore her house, or rather to save and adorn it, as Abigail saved her house by restraining David's anger (1 Sam. 25). Otherwise she will destroy, overturn and ruin it with her own hands, that is, by evil deeds, and deprive the family of every good: of offspring, honour, reputation, property, esteem and grace. Jezebel did this when she led her husband Ahab and her children into idolatry, on account of which that whole house was destroyed by Jehu (2 Kings 9).

units.la: <bl>Der mann muß verderben/der ein vnfeißlich[?] weib hat/</bl>dicit Lutherus. Vulgo autem fertur: [illegible, ~22 letters]. Litteraria testatur, in veteribus esse sapientiam, Iob.12. in corde aut pueri stultitiam, Prou.22. ergo iuxta consilium & admonitionem D. Iacobi cap. 1. Cui deest sapientia, postulet ab eo qui dat, nempe Deo.
units.tr: "A man must come to ruin who has an unwise wife," says Luther. It is commonly said: [illegible in the scan]. Scripture bears witness that wisdom is found among the aged (Job 12), but foolishness in the heart of a boy (Prov. 22). Therefore, following the counsel and admonition of St James in chapter 1: if anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask it of him who gives, namely God.

units.la: 2 Quod vero sit initium sapientiae, docet alter versiculus, nempe timor Domini, cuius sive signum, sive effectus est, ambulare in rectitudine sua. i. recte, vel recto itinere, in rectitudine mandatorum Dei, nec ad dextra declinare, nec ad sinistram per viam virtutis, rectamque viam Dei, quae est fidere Deo & amare proximum: conuersari sine offensa Dei & proximi: probè se gerere & innocenter: ut contrà contemptus Dei est, ab institutis eius recedere, à vijs eius se auertere, nihilque reste agere, id quod stulti faciunt atque impij, qui non sapiunt, neque curant diuinas res & animae salutares.
units.tr: 2 That the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom is taught by the second little verse. Walking in one's uprightness is either the sign or the effect of this fear: walking uprightly, or by a straight course, in the rectitude of God's commandments, turning neither to the right nor to the left, but walking the path of virtue and the straight way of God, which is to trust in God and love one's neighbour, to live without offence to God and neighbour, and to conduct oneself honestly and innocently. On the other hand, to despise God is to depart from his ordinances and turn away from his ways, and to do nothing right. This is what fools and the ungodly do, who have no understanding and do not care for divine things and the salvation of the soul.

units.la: 3 Cæterum vbi timo: Domini occupauit cor hominis, necesse est vt ibi quoq; sint recti, non praui sermones, & iusta, non mala opera: id quod sequentia duo prouerbia indicant. Dicit enim primum: In ore stulti est virga superbiæ.i. lingua percutiens & faucians proximum. <bl>Dann Narren reden tyran-</bl> <bl>nisch</bl>/ sæuiunt contra proximū: sibi placent, omnes præter se iudicant, reprehendunt, damnant. Hinc Sira.3.Maledictio matris eradicat fundamenta domus. Et latro in cruce dicit ad alterum, Ne times quidem tu (blasphemans) Deum. Vel, in ore stulti baculus est superbiæ, hoc est, stultus superbiloquentia efficit vt vapulet. Labia aut sapientum conseruant eos.i. bene loquuntur proximo, tantum abest, vt illi sint nocumento: vel, sapientes loquuntur sancta, honesta, & in tempore, ad vtilitatē: vel, sapientes suis seruantur labijs, vel, custodiunt os suum. Nā Iacob inquit cap.1. Si quis videtur religiosus esse inter vos, qui non frenat linguam suā, sed aberrare finit cor suū, huius vana est religio. Deinde dicit, Vbi nō sunt boues, præsepe mundum .i. vacuum est: & in boum viribus sita est proventus copia. Hoc exponitur duplicitēr: vno modo de bobus ad literam, quibus solum antiquitus {ut}ebantur[?] homines ad agriculturam, & adhuc in plurimis terris. Et ideo ubi erat defectus boum, ibi erat etiam defectus agricultura & segetum: & per oppositum abundantia segetum, ubi erat abundantia boum. Qui ergo laborat, ille habet unde manducet: & qui otium sectatur, ille egestatem habet.
units.tr: 3 Moreover, where the fear of the Lord has taken hold of a man's heart, it is necessary that there be right words and not wicked ones, and just deeds and not evil ones. The two following proverbs indicate this. The first says: "In the mouth of the fool is a rod of pride," that is, a tongue that strikes and wounds the neighbour. "For fools speak tyrannically": they rage against their neighbour, they please themselves, they judge all others besides themselves, they rebuke and condemn. Hence Ecclesiasticus 3: "A mother's curse uproots the foundations of a house." And the thief on the cross says to the other, "Do you not even fear God, you who blaspheme?" Or: "In the mouth of the fool is a staff of pride," that is, the fool, by his boastful talk, brings it about that he is beaten. "But the lips of the wise preserve them," that is, they speak well to their neighbour, so far are they from doing him harm. Or: the wise speak holy and honest things, and at the right time, for profit; or: the wise are preserved by their lips, or they guard their mouths. For James says in chapter 1: "If anyone among you seems to be religious, and does not bridle his tongue but deceives his own heart, his religion is vain." Then he says: "Where there are no oxen, the manger is clean," that is, empty; and the abundance of produce lies in the strength of the oxen. This is explained in two ways. In one way it is taken literally of oxen, with which in ancient times men alone ploughed the fields, and which still do so in very many lands. Where there was a lack of oxen there was also a lack of tillage and crops, and conversely, abundance of crops where there was abundance of oxen. So he who labours has something to eat, and he who pursues idleness has want.

units.la: <bl>Dann faulehänd[?]/verarmend.</bl>
units.tr: For idle hands make for poverty.

units.la: Alio modo exponitur, ut per boues intelligantur homines idonei ad res gerendas. Ubi non sunt boni doctores, perturbatur ecclesia, ut Salomon inquit Pro. 29. Cum cessauerit prophetia, dissipabitur populus. Item, Ubi non sunt gubernatores idonei (ut scribit Melanchthon) pereunt Respub. iuxta illud Ecclesiastis cap.10. Vae terræ cuius rex puer est. Potest quoque dici: Ubi non est labor studij in lege, ibi non est cibus animae: multus autem prouentus sacræ eruditionis & salutis, ubi est assiduum studium verbi Dei. Item, ubi est defectus doctorum, ibi est paucitas fidelium, qui per segetes designantur: & ubi est pluralitas fidelium, ibi apparet manifeste labor doctorum & prædicatorum. Ut ager nostræ ecclesiæ fructificet, sexit[?] ipse Dominus caput suæ ecclesiæ, & det docentibus os & sapientiam: audientibus vero aures ad audiendum, ut cum sponso ad nuptias, quemadmodum de prudentibus virginibus legitur, intrare possint,
units.tr: It is explained in another way, so that by the oxen are understood men fit for carrying out affairs. Where there are no good teachers, the Church is thrown into disorder, as Solomon says in Proverbs 29: "When prophecy ceases, the people will be scattered." Likewise, where there are no fit governors (as Melanchthon writes), the commonwealth perishes, according to the saying of Ecclesiastes 10: "Woe to the land whose king is a child." It can also be said: where there is no labour of study in the law, there is no food for the soul; but there is a great harvest of sacred learning and salvation where there is constant study of the Word of God. Likewise, where there is a lack of teachers, there is a paucity of believers, who are signified by the crops; and where there are many believers, the labour of teachers and preachers clearly appears. So that the field of our Church may bear fruit, may the Lord himself, who has set the head over his Church, give the teachers mouth and wisdom, and the hearers ears to hear, so that they may enter with the bridegroom to the wedding, as is read of the wise virgins.

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XXVII.
units.tr: SERMON XXVII.

units.la: Prouerb. 17.
units.tr: Proverbs 17.

units.la: Melior est bucella sicca, vbi est tranquillitas, quàm domus plena victimis, vbi est contentio.
units.tr: Better is a dry morsel where there is tranquillity than a house full of sacrifices where there is contention.

units.la: Viuentes in matrimonio, ut recte beateque agant, necesse est, ut ante omnia dilectionem ad se inuicem habeant quemadmodum Apostolus praecipit illis, Ephes.5. Tit.2. quae dilectio excedat omnem dilectionem mundi, sitque perpetua, & proficiscatur ex corde: id quod nonnulli etiam annulo significari dicunt, quem sponsus sponsae tradit. Hic enim plerunque aureus est, & rotundus, & in quarto digito positus. Sic autem vir diligit uxorem suam, ut suum ipsius corpus: ut Christus suam ecclesiam: ut non sit amarus erga illam, ut cohabitet secundum scientiam: Ephes.5. Coloss.3.1. Pet.3.
units.tr: Those living in marriage, if they are to live rightly and happily, must above all have love for one another, as the Apostle commands them (Eph. 5; Titus 2). This love should surpass all the love of the world, be lasting, and proceed from the heart. Some say this is also signified by the ring that the bridegroom gives to the bride, for it is usually golden and round and placed on the fourth finger. The husband should love his wife as his own body, as Christ loves his church: he should not be bitter towards her, but live with her according to knowledge (Eph. 5; Col. 3; 1 Pet. 3).

units.la: Uxor autem charitatem erga maritum suum ostendat, in hoc, ut honoret illum, exemplo Mariae, quae prius nominauit Iosephi, quàm seipsam[?], Lucae 2. & non contemnat eum propter senectutem, infirmitatem, paupertatem, &c. item in hoc ut obediat illi in omnibus.
units.tr: The wife should show her love for her husband by honouring him, following the example of Mary, who named Joseph before herself (Luke 2), and by not despising him on account of old age, infirmity, poverty, etc. Likewise, she should obey him in all things.

units.la: Deinde habere debent coniuges inter se pacem, siquidem voluerint Deum pacis habere secum, Sirac.25.2. Corinth.13. Matth.18. Qui enim iracundi sunt & litigiosi, miserrimam vitam ducunt, etiamsi domum plenam diuitiis habeant. κρείσσων, inquit, ψωμὸς μετ' εἰ- ρήνης ἐν ἀγάπῃ, ἢ οἶκος πλήρης [?] ἀγαθῶν, [?] ἀδίκων θυμάτων μετὰ μάχης. Et iterum Prouerbiorum 15. κρείσσων ἔστιν ἄριστον λαχάνων μετὰ φιλίας ἢ σιτίον μόσχων μετὰ ἐχθρᾶς. lucundius igitur & expetibilius est, homine vesci sicca buccella panis cum pace & gaudio, vel cibo parato ex oleribus, cum consensu & charitate conuiuiū, quàm potiri lautitijs mensarum, vel prandio lauto ex optimis carnibus (quales in sacrificijs salutaribus haberi solebant) cum rixa & odio. Adde quòd ira, odium, contentio, rixa, manifesta sunt opera carnis, Galat. 5. à quibus Christiani longissimè abesse debent.
units.tr: Next, spouses ought to keep peace between themselves, if they wish to have the God of peace with them (Sir. 25; 2 Cor. 13; Matt. 18). Those who are quick to anger and quarrelsome lead a most wretched life, even if they have a house full of riches. "Better," it says, "is a morsel with peace in love than a house full of good things with unjust sacrifices in strife" [κρείσσων, inquit, ψωμὸς μετ' εἰρήνης ἐν ἀγάπῃ, ἢ οἶκος πλήρης ἀγαθῶν, ἀδίκων θυμάτων μετὰ μάχης]. And again, in Proverbs 15: "Better is a dinner of herbs with love than a fattened ox with hatred" [κρείσσων ἔστιν ἄριστον λαχάνων μετὰ φιλίας ἢ σιτίον μόσχων μετὰ ἐχθρᾶς]. It is therefore more pleasant and more desirable for a man to eat a dry morsel of bread in peace and joy, or a meal of vegetables shared in agreement and charity, than to enjoy the delicacies of tables or a sumptuous dinner of the choicest meats (such as were customarily had in the peace offerings) amid quarrel and hatred. Add to this that anger, hatred, contention and strife are manifest works of the flesh (Gal. 5), from which Christians ought to keep far away.

units.la: Tertiò requiritur fides, ne frangant promissum committendo adulterium. Deus enim adulteros iudicabit. Heb.13.
units.tr: Thirdly, faithfulness is required, so that they do not break their promise by committing adultery. For God will judge adulterers (Heb. 13).

units.la: Quartò patientia in laboribus, vt se inuicem iuuent, & verè sint Συζυγοί[?].
units.tr: Fourthly, patience in labours, so that they help one another and are truly yoke-fellows [Συζυγοί].

units.la: Quintò temperantia in actu coniugali, vt is fiat non tempore illicito, aut ob finem nō verum, Eccles. 3. 1. Cor. 7.
units.tr: Fifthly, temperance in the conjugal act, so that it is performed not at an unlawful time or for an untrue end (Eccles. 3; 1 Cor. 7).

units.la: Sextò, diligentia in educatione liberorum, vt eos ad virtutes instruant, &c.
units.tr: Sixthly, diligence in the upbringing of children, so that they instruct them in the virtues, etc.

units.la: Septimò, fidelitas in rebus temporalibus, ne vxor furetur marito: neque maritus profundat bona.
units.tr: Seventhly, faithfulness in temporal matters: the wife should not steal from her husband, nor the husband squander the goods.

units.la: 2 Porrò Iudæi à nostris edocti dicunt: Melius est homini pauca scire clarè, & distinctè, quàm multa superficie tenùs & obscurè. Aliter dicunt: Melius est scire simplicia, communia ac vera, quàm subtilia & falsa, vel cum opinione. Item dicunt: Melius est modicum didicisse de rebus diuinis, quàm multa de creaturis. Nos possumus & illud addere: Melius esse Christum Dominum (qui est panis viuus qui de coelo descendit) in ecclesia discere & gustare, quàm omnes artes & disciplinas, quae in scholis & academijs docentur, scire, omnesque libros de philosophia, humanis legibus, historijs gentium devorare. In Christo enim sunt omnes thesauri sapientiae (quae pacifica est) ac scientiae reconditi, Colos. 2. Iacob. 3. Qui ad hunc venit, nō esuriet: & qui credit in eum, non sitiet vnquam, Ioan. 6. Ipsi sit honor & gloria in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: 2 Furthermore, the Jews, taught by us, say: it is better for a man to know a few things clearly and distinctly than many things superficially and obscurely. They also say otherwise: it is better to know simple, common and true things than subtle and false ones, or those held merely by opinion. They also say: it is better to have learned a little about divine things than much about creatures. We may add this as well: it is better to learn and to taste Christ the Lord (who is the living bread that came down from heaven) in the Church than to know all the arts and disciplines taught in schools and academies, and to devour all books on philosophy, human laws and the histories of the nations. For in Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom (which is peaceable) and knowledge (Col. 2; James 3). "Whoever comes to him will not hunger, and whoever believes in him will never thirst" (John 6). To him be honour and glory for ever. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XXVIII.
units.tr: SERMON XXVIII.

units.la: Prouerb. 21.
units.tr: Proverbs 21.

units.la: Melius[?] est manere in terra deserta, quàm cum muliere contentiosa & morosa. Thesaurus desiderabilis & oleum est in habitaculo sapientis: stultus autem homo devorat illum.
units.tr: It is better to dwell in a desert land than with a contentious and fretful woman. A desirable treasure and oil is in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man devours it.

units.la: 1 Adeò res mala est mulier rixosa & irritabilis, ut satius sit degere in terra deserta, & ut Siracid. inquit cap. 25. cum leone & dracone, quàm cum illa:atque praestet,vt Salomon & hoc cap. & 25.dicit,in angulo tecti(.i. solitariè: vbi potest homo bona facere & cogitare) versari ac habitare, quàm contentiosam vel rixosam(quae impedit hominis bona)habere vxorem:& domum communem. Rixosa enim vxor, stillicidium perfluens est,Prouerb.19.27. Neque ira super iram mulieris: καὶ μικρὰ πᾶσα κακία πρὸς κακίαν γυναικὸς [?] Eccle.25. Caueat ergo sibi quisque ab istiusmodi muliere, hoc est, sit timens Domini: oret illum, vt se custodiat à tali:sit circumspectus,ac prius exploret,aut explorare sinat, qualis quaeque sit. Mulier bona,inquit Siracid. cap.26. sors bona est, quae Dominum metuentibus sorte datur. Kursum inquit Concionator, cap.7. inueni amariorem morte mulierem, quae laqueus venatorum est, & sagena cor eius: vincula sunt manus illius, qui placet Deo,effugiet illam : qui autem peccator est, capietur ab illa.
units.tr: 1 So bad a thing is a quarrelsome and irritable woman that it is better to live in a desert land, as Ecclesiasticus says in chapter 25, "with a lion and a dragon," than with her. And it is better, as Solomon says in this chapter and in chapter 25, to dwell and live "in a corner of the roof" (that is, alone, where a man can do good things and think them), than to have a contentious or quarrelsome wife, who hinders a man's good works, and a shared house. For a quarrelsome wife is a dripping water, Proverbs 19:27. Nor is anger upon anger in a woman; "and all wickedness is small compared with the wickedness of a woman" [καὶ μικρὰ πᾶσα κακία πρὸς κακίαν γυναικὸς] Ecclesiasticus 25. Let each man therefore beware of such a woman; that is, let him be one who fears the Lord, pray to him that he may keep him from such a woman, be watchful, and first examine, or allow himself to examine, what sort of woman each is. "A good wife," says Ecclesiasticus 26, "is a good portion, given by lot to those who fear the Lord." Again the Preacher says in chapter 7: "I have found a woman more bitter than death, who is the hunter's snare, and whose heart is a net; her hands are bonds. He who pleases God will escape her, but the sinner will be taken by her."

units.la: Si ergo tantum malum est vxor contentiosa & iracunda: quantū malum est ipsa contentio & ira? D. Paulus Gal. 5. recenset hæc mala inter opera carnis. vide Matt. 5. Iacob.1.
units.tr: If, then, a contentious and angry wife is so great an evil, how great an evil are contention and anger themselves? St Paul, Galatians 5, lists these evils among the works of the flesh. See Matthew 5 and James 1.

units.la: Caueant igitur & abstineát ab his vitijs & vxor & maritus. Quod enim vni dicitur, alteri quoque dicitur. Nam sunt vna caro. Discant autem à Christo pacem & mansuetudinem exercere,Matt.5.11.Mulier enim typum gerit ecclesiæ,cuius est dominum suum {1}equi. Cæterum si cui morosa ac litigiosa cotigerit uxor, pro Deo fereda est, à quo datur & in bono vincenda, exercitii causa sustinenda, dum interim Dei prouidentia supportatur à malis grauioribus. Antonium Panormitam, cum ab eo quaereretur, quibus maximè opus e[illegible, ~12 letters] ad conubij tranquillitatem: respondentem audiuit inquit Louianus Pont. lib.3[?] de Obed. cap.2.) Nullas nec quietas nec felices satis nuptias esse posse, praeterquam si vir surdus esset, uxor vero caeca. Idem dixisse Alphonsum Aragonum regem, refert Erasmus lib.8. Apophtheg.
units.tr: Let wife and husband therefore beware of these vices and abstain from them. For what is said to one is said to the other too, for they are one flesh. Let them learn from Christ to practise peace and gentleness, Matthew 5:11. For the woman bears the type of the Church, whose part is to revere her own lord as is fitting. But if anyone should happen to have a fretful and quarrelsome wife, she is to be borne for God's sake, who gives her, and to be overcome by good conduct, to be endured for the sake of discipline, while in the meantime, under God's providence, he is spared from worse evils. When Antonius Panormita was asked by someone which things were most needed for the tranquillity of marriage, he heard him reply (as Louianus reports in his book on obedience, chapter 2) that there could be no marriage that was quiet or happy enough, unless the husband were deaf and the wife blind. Erasmus, in book 8 of the Apophthegms, reports that King Alfonso of Aragon said the same.

units.la: 2 Sequens prouerbium, siue parabola ostendit primo rem bonam ac utilem esse sapientiam. Nā in habitatione sapientis (inquit) thesaurus desiderabilis & oleū, vel elegantes opes & unguenta sunt: id est, in domo sapientis bonorum abundantia est, & copia rerum utilium artificialium & naturaliū. Dominus enim illi benedicit in omnibus: non est enim ociosus, non feruit ventri, non profundit substantiam suam ad vitae lasciuiā. Quis autem sit sapiens, intelligitur ex contrario. Contrarius est insipiens, de cuius ingenio, vita & moribus Psa.14.
units.tr: 2 The following proverb, or parable, shows first that wisdom is a good and useful thing. For in the dwelling of the wise, it says, there is a desirable treasure and oil, that is, choice riches and perfumes: in the house of the wise there is an abundance of goods and a supply of useful things, both artificial and natural. For the Lord blesses him in all things; he is not idle, he does not serve his belly, he does not squander his substance on a life of wantonness. What sort of man the wise man is, however, is understood from the contrary. The contrary is the fool, whose nature, life and manners are described in Psalm 14.

units.la: Spiritualiter intelligi potest etiam hic locus. Nam thesaurus ille coelestis, id est, Christus: & oleum illud laetitiae, id est, spiritus sanctus, est in corde sapientum, Matth. 25. Ephes. 1. 1. Ioan. 2. in domo sapientiae, id est, in ecclesia Christi: in credentibus, diligentibus & timentibus Dominum. Denique in domo patris & ciuitate Dei sunt summae diuitiæ & delitiæ. 4. Efd.[?] 7. Vbi enim sunt gaudia? (canit ecclesia) <bl>nirgend mehr dann da/</bl> <bl>da die engel singen</bl> noua cantica: <bl>vnd die schellen</bl> <bl>Klingen</bl> in regis curia: <bl>Ia[?] wern wir da/ &c.</bl>
units.tr: This passage can also be understood spiritually. For that heavenly treasure is Christ, and that oil of gladness is the Holy Spirit, which is in the hearts of the wise, Matthew 25; Ephesians 1; 1 John 2; in the house of wisdom, that is, in the Church of Christ, in those who believe, love and fear the Lord. Finally, in the house of the Father and the city of God there are the greatest riches and delights (4 Ezra 7). For where are joys? (the Church sings) "nowhere more than there, where the angels sing new songs, and the bells ring in the king's court; yes, we would be there too, etc."

units.la: Secundò ostendit hoc prouerbium, re detrimentosam esse stultitiam. Nam vesanus homo, inquit, abligurit, seu deuorat illum. i. thesaurum à maioribus haereditate relictû, hoc est, vt sapiens diuitias parit, sic stultus eas decoquit. Hinc supra Prouer. 14. Sapiens mulier domum suam instruit: stulta suis manibus euertit. Deus sapientiæ liberet nos à stultitia, & det nobis spiritum sapientiæ, vt possimus cum filio eius & sponso pulcherrimo intrare ad nuptias illas cœlestes, Amen.
units.tr: Secondly, this proverb shows that folly is harmful to one's goods. For the senseless man, it says, devours, or consumes, that treasure, that is, the wealth left as an inheritance by his forebears. Just as a wise woman builds up riches, so a fool squanders them. Hence above, Proverbs 14: "A wise woman builds up her house; a foolish one tears it down with her own hands." May the God of wisdom deliver us from folly, and give us the spirit of wisdom, so that we may enter with his Son and most beautiful bridegroom into those heavenly nuptials, Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XXIX.
units.tr: CONCIO XXIX.

units.la: Hoseæ 4.
units.tr: Hosea 4.

units.la: Ornicatio & vinum atq; mustum auferunt cor. Populus meus lignum suum consultat, & baculus eius nunciat ei. Quia spiritus fornicationum fecit(eum) errare, & fortati sunt à Deo suo.
units.tr: Whoredom and wine and new wine take away the heart. My people ask counsel at their stock, and their staff declares unto them. For the spirit of whoredoms has caused them to err, and they have gone astray from under their God.

units.la: 1 Duo sunt mala potissimum, quæ clade afficiunt matrimonium, fornicatio & ebrietas: quia vinculum matrimonij frangunt, & egestatem coniugibus inferunt, Matt. 5. Eccles. 19. Ideo toties scripturæ sanctæ ab his vitijs nos dehortantur, ac simul indicant damna quæ oriuntur ex illis.
units.tr: (1) There are two evils above all that strike at marriage, fornication and drunkenness, because they break the bond of marriage and bring want upon spouses (Matt. 5; Eccl. 19). For this reason the Holy Scriptures so often warn us away from these vices, and at the same time point out the losses that arise from them.

units.la: Auferunt autem Venus & vinum .i. abusus vini, homini cor, hoc eit, fortitudinem fidei, vel intellectum seu mentem, ac ipsam fedem sapientiæ, & præstantissimam hominis partem, ex qua rationis vsus, vita & salus uniuersa dependet, & qua sola à brutis disseri mus. Qui enim occupatur & iugiter versatur in fornicationibus & ebrietatibus, ille onem amittit intellectum, ut fine ullo timore Dei ambulet, & facile ab eius cultu recedat: id quod Israelitis contigisse multi scribūt prophetæ: quippe qui carnalibus illis vitijs immersi, gloriâ Dei cōmutarunt in gloriam ligni .i. idoli. Fornicationem igitur carnis (propter quā vitandam suā quisq; vxorem habeat, & suū quæq; viru, 1.Cor.7.[?]) sequitur fornicatio mentis, Num.25. ȝ[?], Reg.11. & hanc perditio, Psal.73. Unde Salom.Prou.6. inquit: Qui adulterium committit cum muliere, is deficit corde: & qui vult perdere animam suā, agit in hunc modum. & Prou.23. Si quidem fouea profunda est meretrix, & puteus angustus alie-na (i.vt ex profunda fouea nemo facile ascendere potest, ita citra difficultate nullus liberari poterit, quæ scortorum nexus semel ligauerint) Ipsa enim in modum raptoris infidias struit, & adijcit (sibi) homines facinorosos: vel, conficit homines persides: vel, homines prævaricatores, ut quidam interpretantur. Vetus interpres vertit incautos. Verum enimuero nemo est qui libenter ferat se criminari stultum: cur ergo Venerei & ebriosi se stultos & amentes faciunt? Adde quod adhuc plura mala, testantibus literis sacris, nascuntur ex illis peccatis, scortatione & ebrietate, nempe damnum corporis & vitæ, Prou, 23. 1. Reg. 13. facultatum & opum, Luc.15 honoris & famæ, Eccl.8. item animæ, atq; amissio æternæ vitæ. 1. Cor.6. Gal.5.
units.tr: Now "whoredom and wine," that is, the abuse of wine, take away the heart of man, that is, the strength of faith, or the understanding or mind, and the very seat of wisdom, the most excellent part of man, on which the use of reason, life and all well-being depend, and by which alone we differ from the brutes. For whoever is occupied with and constantly engaged in fornication and drunkenness loses his understanding, so that he walks without any fear of God and easily falls away from his worship. Many prophets write that this happened to the Israelites, who, immersed in these carnal vices, exchanged the glory of God for the glory of a tree, that is, an idol. Therefore fornication of the flesh (for the sake of avoiding which each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband, 1 Cor. 7) is followed by fornication of the mind (Num. 25; 1 Kings 11), and this by destruction (Ps. 73). Hence Solomon says in Proverbs 6: "He who commits adultery with a woman lacks heart; he who wishes to destroy his own soul acts in this way." And Proverbs 23: "Indeed, a harlot is a deep pit, and a narrow well is a stranger" (that is, just as no one can easily climb out of a deep pit, so no one who has been bound by the snares of harlots once will be freed without difficulty). For she lays snares like a robber and gathers to herself wicked men, or makes men faithless, or men who transgress, as some interpret. The Old Interpreter translated "the unwary." Yet truly no one gladly bears being called a fool; why then do lechers and drunkards make themselves foolish and senseless?
