Add that, as the sacred letters testify, many more evils arise from these sins of whoredom and drunkenness: loss of body and life (Prov. 23; 1 Kings 13), of goods and wealth (Luke 15), of honor and reputation (Eccl. 8), likewise of the soul, and the loss of eternal life (1 Cor. 6; Gal. 5).

units.la: Solet de his mundus leuiter admodū iudicare, & vix eos patitur, qui illa cauenda, aut etiam extirpanda esse sentiunt. Sed longe aliter nos iudicare docet Deus hoc loco, quando ista cor hominis auferre (instar pes[?]imorum furum) dicit. At quis non nocentissimam modisque omnibus fugiendam pestem esse dicat, quae cor aufert? At hoc auferri, adeo ut nullus ipsius[?] nobis usus sit, ipsa experientia abundè docet. Nam si quos scortationis æstrum exagitat, ij fœdissima suorum scortorum vitia non obseruant: adhæc omni pudore posito obscœna quæque dicunt & faciunt: opes suas totumq; patrimonii turpiter profundunt, uxoris legitimæ & dulcissimorum liberorum curam abijciunt, & breuissimæ voluptatis causa corpus & vitam periculis grauissimis scientes & volentes exponunt, nec ullis minis, legibus aut exemplis sese coerceri patiuntur. Taceo quod corpus suum scorti membrum faciunt, quod ut spiritus sancti templum esset, suo sanguine Christus consecravit: id quod multo maioris insaniæ ac stulti-tiæ tiæ signum est, quàm si quis ex pulcherrimo cubiculo vel cœnaculo faceret hará, vel stabulum equorum. Quis ergo tales sana mente vti dicat? Eadè est ebrietatis ratio. Vt primùm enim vinum immodicè haustu fuerit, mox rationis lumine obscurato, lingua sibi ad conuitia, blasphemias, obscœna dicta & promissa incauta habenas laxat, oculi circa formas alienas vagantur, manus ad arma promptæ sunt, & brutis animalibus vel impudetia, vel ferocitate, vel stultitia similis redditur, qui illis præstare & ad Dei exempla viuere debe[ illegible, ~4 letters], Dan. 5. Attamen lusus iocosque hæc omnia dixeris, si eos spestes, quibus ebrietas incestuum, cædium & proprię etiam necis causa fuit. Quo nomine veteres olim illam voluntariam insaniam dixerēre: nec temerè Christus Luc. 21. de nouissimorum temporum periculis differens monet ne corda nostra ebrietate & crapula aggrauari patiamur. Nū ergo vinum corda auferre negabimus? Certè nostro seculo, proh dolor, ebrietatis vitio omnis loci & ordinis homines ita dementatos esse videmus, vt nec quotidiana damna agnoscant, nec de illis vitandis & declinandis serió cogitent. Cùm tamen non impossibile sit ab istis vitijs abstinere. Si enim Rechabitæ, si Saraceni possunt abstinere profusà vino, cur Christianus non posset ab ebrietate? Beatus qui pœnitentiam egerit, & in Christi Iesu nomine peccatorum remissio nem petierit, & ab his peccatis destiterit.
units.tr: The world is accustomed to judge these things rather lightly, and hardly tolerates those who feel that such things must be guarded against or even rooted out. But God teaches us to judge far otherwise in this place, when he says that these things take away the heart, like the worst of thieves. Yet who would not say that what takes away the heart is the most harmful pest and to be fled by every means? That this is taken away, so that a man has no use of it, experience itself abundantly teaches. For if the goad of lust drives anyone, such men do not notice the most foul vices of their harlots; moreover, with all shame set aside, they say and do every obscene thing; they shamefully squander their resources and the whole of their patrimony, they cast off the care of a lawful wife and most dear children, and for the sake of the briefest pleasure they knowingly and willingly expose body and life to the gravest dangers, and they allow themselves to be restrained by no threats, laws or examples. I say nothing of the fact that they make their own body a member of a harlot, which Christ consecrated with his own blood to be a temple of the Holy Spirit; this is a sign of far greater madness and folly than if someone should turn a most beautiful bedroom or upper room into a brothel or a horse stable. Who, then, would say that such men use a sound mind? The same is the case with drunkenness. For as soon as someone has drunk wine immoderately, the light of reason is at once darkened, the tongue lets loose its reins for insults, blasphemies, obscene speech and rash promises, the eyes wander after the forms of others, the hands are ready for weapons, and he is made like brute animals, either in shamelessness, or ferocity, or stupidity, though he ought to excel them and live according to the examples of God (Dan. 5). Yet you would call all these things mere sport and jest, if you looked at those cases in which drunkenness was the cause of incest, of slaughter, and even of one's own death. For this reason the ancients once called that voluntary madness; and not without cause Christ, speaking of the dangers of the last times (Luke 21), warns that we should not allow our hearts to be weighed down by drunkenness and surfeiting. Shall we then deny that wine takes away the heart? Certainly in our age, alas, we see men of every place and rank so stupefied by the vice of drunkenness that they do not recognize the daily losses, nor seriously think about avoiding and shunning them, although it is not impossible to abstain from these vices. For if the Rechabites, if the Saracens, can abstain from wine in abundance, why could not a Christian abstain from drunkenness? Blessed is he who has repented and sought the forgiveness of sins in the name of Jesus Christ, and has ceased from these sins.

units.la: ʒ Neautem quis se mundum à peccatis esse gloriētur, & alios contemnat (vt Pharisaeus fecit, Luc. 18.) cum nec scortationi nec ebrietati fit deditus, ostendit propheta longe deteriorem esse idolatrarum & hypocritarum, qui se aliis sanctiores esse arbitrantur, conditione, nec habere quo glorientur. Qua si dicat: Fateor sane magnas esse scortationis & ebrietatis vires, & pudendum est, homine ad imaginē Dei conditum his ita immergi, vt amentis & insani instar omnia absq; pudore & ratione agat. At multo grauior est vestra culpa, qui cum meus populus dici & censeri velitis, non tamen me vno estis contenti: sed ligna vestra .i. imagines à vobis ex ligno factas, interrogatis, & à baculo vestro respondere petitis. Quid magis stultum expectari potest, quam à mutis idolis consilium aut opem petere, & coram ijs prosterni, quae vel tuis manibus, vel impensis facta sunt? Quid item magis absurdum, quam ab incerto auium volatu pendere eos, quos per verbum suum Deus plenissimē de omnibus instruxit, quae ad nostrae salutis cognitionem faciunt? Atqui haec (inquit propheta) facit populus meus, quem fornicationis spiritus seduxit, vt scies volens, relicto Deo suo ad muta idola & vani-ssimas vaticinandi artes deflexerit. Quis ergo non in ipsis quoq; scortatione & ebrietatem agnoscat longē nocentiorem, quam quae corporaliter exercetur, cum omnem rationis vsum simul & pudorem exuerint? Deus omnipotens & misericors custodiat nos ab omnis generis scortatione per Christum Iesum, Amen.
units.tr: Yet that someone should boast that he is clean of sins and despise others (as the Pharisee did, Luke 18), because he is not given to whoredom or drunkenness, the prophet shows to be far worse in the case of idolaters and hypocrites, who think themselves holier than others, and yet have nothing in which to glory. As if he were to say: "I confess indeed that the powers of whoredom and drunkenness are great, and it is shameful that a man, created in the image of God, should be so immersed in them that he acts like a madman or a lunatic, without shame and reason. But your guilt is much graver, you who, though you wish to be called and counted my people, are nonetheless not content with me alone; you ask your trees, that is, the images made by you from wood, and seek answers from your staff. What can be more foolish than to seek counsel or help from mute idols, and to prostrate yourselves before things made either by your own hands or at your expense? What is likewise more absurd than to depend on the uncertain flight of birds, when God has most fully instructed you through his Word in all things that pertain to the knowledge of our salvation? And yet, says the prophet, this is what my people do, whom the spirit of whoredom has led astray; knowingly, having abandoned their God, they have turned to dumb idols and the most empty arts of divination. Who, then, does not recognize that in these very things, whoredom and drunkenness, the harm is far greater than what is practised bodily, since they have cast off at once all use of reason and all shame? May almighty and merciful God keep us from every kind of whoredom through Jesus Christ, Amen."

units.la: CONCIO XXX.
units.tr: SERMON XXX.

units.la: Tobiae I.
units.tr: Tobit 1.

units.la: C[?]um vero factus fuisset vir, accepit uxorem Hannam, de tribu sua, genuitque ex ea filium, nomen suum imponens ei, quem ab infantia timere Deum docuit, & abstinere ab omni peccato. Igitur dum per captiuitatē deuenisset cum uxore sua & filio, in ciuitatem Niniuen cū omni tribu sua, & cum omnes ederent ex cibis gentilium, iste[?] custodiuit animam suam, & nunquam contaminatus est in escis eorum. Et quoniam memor fuit Domini in toto corde suo, dedit illi Deus gratiam in conspectu Salmanasar regis, & dedit illi potestatem quocunq; vellet ire, habens libertatem quacunq; facere voluisset. Pergebat ergo per omnes qui erant in captiuitate, et monita salutis dabat eis.
units.tr: When he had become a man, he took a wife, Hannah, of his own tribe, and by her he had a son, whom he named after himself. From infancy he taught him to fear God and to abstain from every sin. Then, when he and his wife and son had been carried into captivity to the city of Nineveh, with all his tribe, and while all the others ate the food of the Gentiles, he kept his soul pure and was never defiled by their meats. And because he remembered the Lord with his whole heart, God gave him grace in the sight of King Shalmaneser, and gave him the freedom to go wherever he wished and to do whatever he pleased. So he went about among all who were in captivity, giving them wholesome counsel.

units.la: I Vt caeterae scripturae sanctae in doctrinam & consolationem nostram praescriptae sunt[?] sic etiam ille locus scripturæ: in quo coniugibus, & futuris coniugibus egregia imago proponitur, docens, quo pacto se in reconiugali gerere debeant, vt benedictionem Domini & gratiam consequantur. Non enim debent contrahere matrimonium ante tempus & iustam ætatem. Tobias enim vt adoleuit, & factus est vir. i. potens generare, & sciens regere domum suam, iam consummata natura & integra ætate, uxore duxit, exemplo patriarcharum veterum & sanctorum, qui rarò ante trigesimum annum uxores ducebant, ideo fortunatiores, & naturæ solidioris filios generabant. Rursum Iudas patriarcha noluit filium suum dare Thamari, donec creuisset, Gen.38. Et Noemi ad nurus suas dicebat: Etiamsi possem hac nocte concipere, & parere filios, si eos expectare velitis donec crescant, & annos pubertatis impleant, ante eritis vetulæ, quàm nubatis, Ruth.1. Quomodo enim quæso pueros educabunt, qui ipsi pueri sunt: Lycurgus is qui Lacedæmonijs leges condidit, quum certum tempus præscripsisset quo puellæ nubere, iuuenes ducere deberet: interrogatus cur id statuendum putarit, Vt, inquit, soboles ex adultis perfectæq; ætatis parentibus nata, valida sit & vegeta. Excoitu præpropero non solum læduntur corpora gignentium, verum etiam proles nascitur imbecilla. Tum qui ante tempus dant operam liberis, carent apud illos autoritate, quam ætas conciliat: rursus qui vergente iam ætate, nec fruuntur liberis suis, nec eos possunt ad perfectâ institutionem perducere, morte senioq; praeuêti. Olympiodorus in ʒ.cap.Eccl. inquit: Opportuno quis tempore suae commiscetur uxori,cum appetit filios procreare: praeter tempus vero, voluptatis & concupiscentiae causa hoc facit. Ut vero adolescentuli tempus honesti matrimonij patientius expectare possint,non sunt illi quidè sine disciplina castitatis sinendi, sed in primaeua aetate instituendi ad utiles disciplinas artium, ad occupationes fructuosas, vel terrae colendae, vel mechanicis honestis artibus adaptandi,ad negotiationes iustas,ad patriae & familiae decorem & usum: liberalibus quoq; ue disciplinis instituendi, & ad frugalitatis amorem edocendi,cum temperantia rerum in omni victu & amictu, absque ocio & libidinis' studio. Quod si fiat,facilius continere poterunt, & tardius Veneris importunas libidines sentier[?], plurib.honestis studijs occupati.
units.tr: I. As the other holy Scriptures have been written down for our teaching and comfort, so also this passage of Scripture sets before married people, and those who are about to marry, an outstanding picture, teaching them how they ought to conduct themselves in wedlock, so that they may obtain the blessing and grace of the Lord. For they ought not to contract marriage before the proper time and the right age. Tobias, when he grew up and became a man, that is, one able to beget children and skilled in governing his household, and when his nature was fully developed and his age complete, took a wife, following the example of the ancient patriarchs and saints, who seldom took wives before their thirtieth year, and so had children who were more fortunate and of sturdier nature. Again, the patriarch Judah was unwilling to give his son to Tamar until he had grown up (Gen. 38.). And Naomi said to her daughters-in-law: "Even if I could conceive and bear sons tonight, would you wait for them until they grew up and reached the years of youth? Would you then remain unmarried until you were old women?" (Ruth 1.) For how, I ask, will boys bring up children when they are boys themselves? Lycurgus, who gave laws to the Lacedaemonians, when he had fixed a set time at which girls should marry and young men should take wives, was asked why he thought this should be decided; he answered: so that offspring born of parents who are grown and in full maturity may be strong and vigorous. Not only are the bodies of those who beget harmed by a premature union, but the children born are also feeble. Those who have children before the right time lack the authority that maturity brings among them; and those who, when their age is already advancing, neither enjoy their children nor can bring them to full training, are forestalled by death and old age. Olympiodorus, on Ecclesiastes 3, says: "A man has intercourse with his wife at the opportune time when he desires to beget children; but outside that time he does it for the sake of pleasure and lust." But so that young men may more patiently wait for the proper time of honourable marriage, they are not to be left without the discipline of chastity; they are to be trained in early life in useful disciplines and arts, fitted for fruitful occupations, either for tilling the soil or for honest mechanical crafts, for lawful trade, for the honour and use of their country and family; they are also to be instructed in the liberal disciplines and taught the love of frugality, with moderation in all food and clothing, free from idleness and the pursuit of lust. If this is done, they will be able to restrain themselves more easily, and the troublesome lusts of Venus will press upon them more slowly, since they are occupied with many honest studies.

units.la: 2 Quo autem respexit Tobias uxorem dusturus[?] procul dubio non ad diuitias,aut voluptates,sed ad Dei verbum & timorem:nec non ad debitum finem coniugij. Nam duxit uxore de tribu sua atq; cognatione, nempe Naphtali,quç una erat ex populo Dei,hoc est, Israelitico, Annam nomine,gratiosam & amabilem, qualis & mater Samuelis fuerat, & vidua octoginta annorum Euangelica: & genuit ex ea filium (dixit enim Deus Gen.1. & 9. Crescite & multiplicamini & replete[?] terram)nomen suum imponens ei(nam cùm piuit etiam illum esse virum bonum. Interpretatur enim טוב [?] bonus Deus, vel Domini bonitas, qua fit, ut ex pijs parentib. sancto matrimonio ad id instituto nascantur pij filij. Domini bonitatem agnoscêtes in omnibus, à quo omne bonum desuper allábitur timentibus Deum. Hunc fructum matrimonij, i. hunc filium docuit (quemadmodum fiéri debet, Deut.6 Ephe.6.) ab infantia [illegible, ~6 letters] ut Sirac. monet faciendum, cap.7.) timere Deum (quo nihil melius, Ecc.25.) & abstinere ab omni peccato, Tob.4. Non.n.sufficit generare liberos, nisi eosdem etiam instruamus in timore Domini, ut non solum nostri, sed & Dei filij sint. Cæterum quòd Tobias uxorem duxit de sua tribu & cognatione, hoc non solus fecit. Idem enim Isaacum, Iacobũ, patrem Mosis, &c. fecisse legimus, Gen. 24. 2&[?]. Exod.2. idque secundum præceptum Domini, Num.36. Deuter.7. ut hæreditas iuxta Dei legem in familijs permaneret, & fortes non confunderentur.
units.tr: 2. Tobias, when about to take a wife, certainly looked not to riches or pleasures but to the Word and fear of God, and to the proper end of marriage. For he took a wife from his own tribe and kindred, namely Naphtali, who was one of the people of God, that is, of Israel. Her name was Hannah, gracious and lovable, just as the mother of Samuel had been, and like the widow of eighty years in the Gospel. He begot a son from her, for God said (Gen. 1 and 9): "Increase and multiply and fill the earth." He named him after himself, for he also perceived that this son would be a good man. The name means "good" [טוב], that is, God is good, or the goodness of the Lord, by which it comes about that godly children are born of godly parents in holy marriage, which was instituted for this purpose; they acknowledge the Lord's goodness in all things, from whom every good descends upon those who fear God. This fruit of marriage, that is, this son, he taught (as ought to be done, Deut. 6 and Eph. 6) from infancy (as Sirach advises it should be done, ch. 7) to fear God (than which nothing is better, Ecclus. 25) and to abstain from every sin (Tob. 4). For it is not enough to beget children unless we also instruct them in the fear of the Lord, so that they are not only ours but also sons of God. Moreover, that Tobias took a wife from his own tribe and kindred was not something he alone did. For we read that Isaac, Jacob, the father of Moses, and others did the same (Gen. 24; Exod. 2), and this was done according to the command of the Lord (Num. 36; Deut. 7), so that the inheritance might remain in families according to God's law, and the tribes not be confused.

units.la: 3 Docuit autem Tobias suum filium non verbis tantùm, verùm etiam factis ac suo exemplo. Fuit enim vir iustus & pius, & constans in veritate: memor Dei & eius verbi omni tempore, etiam in captiuitate. Non enim contaminauit se ex escis gentilium, in lege prohibitis, Leuit.11. sed animam suam custodiuit, i. sibi ipsi temperauit, appetitui imperauit, ne quod alioqui delectat, libeat degustasst. preciosior in conscientia sua erat sacra Dei lex & sanctio, quàm ut pauperie vel gentiliùm fauore induceretur ad illicita obeunda; sicut & Daniel cum socijs in Babylone, Joseph in Ægypto, Judith in castris Holofernis, Gen.43.Judith 12. Omnia quidem munda sunt mundis. Verùm legis Mosaicæ ritus usque ad Christum Judæis omnibus observandus erat, & idolatriæ occasio summa diligentia evitanda. Polluebantur igitur Israelitæ ferè omnes, i.e. plurimi contra legem agendo, quam Tobias summopere semper observare satagebat, ne peccaret in Deum, & contra conscientiam illicita sumeret, cum licita per Dei gratiam non deessent. Atque huius sanctitatis præmium Tobias etiam in hoc mundo accepit. Donatus est enim a rege Salmanasar libertate, ut illi licuerit pergere & operari, ut voluit. Sed ipse hac sua libertate, ex gratia Dei (cuius opera & ferræ, & tyranni mansuefieri, velint nolint, coguntur) accepta, non abusus est: sed ititans ad omnes captiuos, eos salutariter monuit atque consolatus est. Porrò quæ salutis monita fuerint, quæ illis dedit Tobias, videris in commentarijs Pellicani. Exhortatus enim est concaptiuos ad tolerantiam exilij, ad obedientiam regi præstândam, etiamsi immo destior & discolus iam eis contigisset, quado id Domino placuisse viderent ex facto, pœnam esse codignam criminibus non possent ignorare: forti animo omne solum patriam esse, gloriam Dei hoc pacto spargendam in gentes multas, pro qua praedicanda idoneos se possent praedicatores praestare, experti bonitatem Dei in beneficiis & praemonitionibus prophetarum, nunc vero iustitiam in contemptores legum suarum, &c. Talem charitatem tum erga Deum, tum erga proximum, largiatur nobis omnibus & singulis Dominus noster & seruator Iesus Christus.
units.tr: 3. Tobias taught his son not only by words but also by deeds and his own example. For he was a just and godly man, constant in the truth, mindful of God and of his Word at all times, even in captivity. He did not defile himself with the food of the Gentiles, which the law forbade (Lev. 11), but kept his soul, that is, governed himself and restrained his appetite, so that he would not taste what otherwise would have pleased him. The holy law and command of God were more precious to him in his conscience than that he should be drawn by poverty or the favour of the Gentiles into doing unlawful things. So also Daniel with his companions in Babylon, Joseph in Egypt, and Judith in the camp of Holofernes (Gen. 43; Judith 12). "To the pure all things are pure," it is true; but the ritual of the Mosaic law was to be observed by all Jews until Christ, and the occasion of idolatry was to be avoided with the greatest care. Thus almost all the Israelites were defiled, that is, most of them acted against the law, which Tobias always strove most diligently to observe, so that he would not sin against God or take unlawful things against his conscience, since lawful things were not lacking through God's grace. And Tobias received the reward of this holiness even in this world. For he was granted liberty by King Shalmaneser, so that he was allowed to go about and work as he wished. But he did not abuse this liberty, which he had received from the grace of God (by whose work even the fierce and tyrants are made gentle, whether they wish it or not), but went among all the captives and warned and comforted them for their salvation. What the wholesome counsels were that Tobias gave them, you may see in the commentaries of Pellicanus. For he exhorted his fellow captives to endure exile patiently, and to render obedience to the king, even if harsher and more unruly treatment had befallen them; since they saw from the event that this was pleasing to the Lord, they could not be ignorant that the punishment was worthy of their crimes. With a brave heart they should consider every land their homeland, and the glory of God should be spread among many nations in this way, and they could present themselves as fit preachers to proclaim it, having experienced God's goodness in benefits and in the forewarnings of the prophets, and now his justice against the despisers of his laws, and so on. May our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ grant such love, both toward God and toward neighbour, to all of us, each and every one.

units.la: CONCIO XXXI.
units.tr: SERMON XXXI.

units.la: Tob. 10.
units.tr: Tob. 10.

units.la: T vero Raguel dicebat ad generum suum: Mane hic, & ego mittam nuncium salutis de te ad Tobiam patrem tuum.
units.tr: And Raguel said to his son-in-law: Stay here, and I will send a messenger of good news about you to Tobias your father.

units.la: Cui Tobias ait: Ego noui, quia pater meus & mater mea modo dies computant, et cruciatur spiritus eorum in ipsis. Cum que verbis multis rogaret Raguel Tobiam, & ille eum nulla ratione vellet audire, tradidit ei Saram, & dimidiam partem omnis substantiae suae, in pueris, in puellis, in pecudibus, in camelis, & in vaccis, & pecunia multa, & saluum atq; gaudentem dimisit eum a se, dicens: Angelus Domini sanctus sit in itinere vestro, perducatq; ducatq; vos incolumes, & inueniatis omnia recte circa parentes vestros, & videant oculi mei filios vestros priusquam moriar. Et apprehendentes parentes filiam suam, osculati sunt eam, & dimiserunt ire, monentes eam honorare soceros, diligere maritum, regere familiam, gubernare domum, & seipsam irreprehensibilem exhibere.
units.tr: Tobias replied: I know that my father and mother are now counting the days, and their spirit is tormented within them. When Raguel urged Tobias with many words, and he would not agree to stay on any account, Raguel gave him Sara, and half of all his substance, in menservants and maidservants, in sheep, camels and cattle, and a great sum of money. He sent him away safe and rejoicing, saying: May the holy angel of the Lord be with you on your journey, bring you there and back in safety, and may you find all things well with your parents, and may my eyes see your sons before I die. Then the parents took hold of their daughter, kissed her, and let her go, admonishing her to honour her parents-in-law, love her husband, rule the household, govern the house, and show herself blameless.

units.la: 1 In hac narratione est primum quod facere & imitari debent soceri, deinde liberi, tertio coniuges.
units.tr: 1 In this narrative there is first what parents-in-law ought to do and imitate, then what children do, and third what spouses do.

units.la: Socer enim Tobiae Raguel generum suum ita dilexit, ut hospitalitatem erga eum exercuerit quatuordecim dies, & id facere voluerit. Audito autem quod parentes generi ob moram filij soliciti essent, tradidit ei filiam, & dimidiam partem omnis substantiae suae: & cum fausto omine dimisit eos, pro catusq; est illis, non cacodaemonem aut mille diabolos, sed comitantem angelum Dei bonum: non morbos corporis, vt pestem, Gallicum morbum, &c. sed incolumitatem: non vt omnia perdita, sed salua inueniant apud parentes: non sterilitatem, sed quod in primis in matrimonio est intendendum, prolis vbertatem & felicitatem, quando nihil in hoc mundo parentibus poterit suauius contingere, quàm filij & nepotes, in quibus etiā in hoc mundo sese norunt post mortem superesse[?] & viuere, & bis esse felices, si tamen in timore Dei nutrierint quos genuerunt filios & nepotes. Sic loquuntur honesti homines, utilia nempe & grauia ad rem pertinentia, non ludicra vel obscoena, non rixas vel odia, nō peierationes vel maledictiones. Discenda esset hoc loco vel loquendi formula inter pios: solent enim seculo & prauis moribus initiati homines, siue sese inueniat vel dimittant, siue edant, siue bibant, sedentes vel commigrantes, non nisi prophana, otiosa, turpia, pernitiosa[?] vel imprudentia loqui, friuolos ac inutiles prorsus miscere fermones, leuitatibus delectari & risibus, si non etiam mendacijs ad minus ociosis: & si quis sensatior sensatiora loquatur, ludibrio habetur, & inhumanior, si non etiam stultior. Hoc in libello, ex quo hic noster textus praelectus est sumptus, ubique rationabilia, pia, honesta, grauia, utilia, sancta & gratiosa dicuntur, ut legis per totum, ut discas sanctimoniam veterum, & simul nostri seculi vanitatem inspicias insignem, & vix tolerabilem pijs, quin & impijs non fructuosam.
units.tr: Raguel, Tobias's father-in-law, loved his son-in-law so much that he kept him as a guest for fourteen days and wished to do so. When he heard that the young man's parents were anxious because of his delay, he gave him his daughter and half of all his substance, and sent them off with a good omen. He prayed for them that they might have not an evil spirit or a thousand devils, but the good angel of God as their companion; not bodily sicknesses such as plague or the French pox; not that they should find everything lost, but everything safe with their parents; not barrenness, but what must above all be aimed at in marriage, a rich and happy offspring. For nothing in this world can be sweeter to parents than sons and grandsons, in whom, even in this world, they know they will survive and live after death, and be doubly happy if they bring up the sons and grandsons they have begotten in the fear of God. Honest people speak in this way: useful and weighty things pertinent to the matter, not frivolous or obscene talk, not quarrels or hatreds, not perjuries or curses. Here one should learn a form of speech among the godly. For men initiated into the age and its bad customs, whether they find themselves or dismiss, eat or drink, sit or move about, are wont to speak only profane, idle, shameful, pernicious or imprudent things, to mix in utterly trivial and useless chatter, and to take delight in levities and laughter, if not even in lies, at least idle ones. If someone more sensible speaks more sensibly, he is held up to ridicule, and if he is less humane, he is considered at least foolish. In this little book, from which the text we have just read is taken, things are called reasonable, pious, honest, weighty, useful, holy and gracious throughout. Read it through, so that you may learn the holiness of the ancients and at the same time see the remarkable vanity of our age, which is barely tolerable to the godly and not fruitful even to the ungodly.

units.la: 2[?] Filius autem Tobæi Tobias parentes suos, etiam ducta uxore, ita honoravit, ut propter convivia moram facere noluerit apud socerum, ne patrem & matrem suam tristitia afficeret: quorum φιλοστοργία[?] Tobiæ per experientiam satis perspecta erat. Non sunt igitur negligendi affectus pij parentum, non sunt extra extremam necessitatem aliquatehus[?] perturbandi à filijs probis, sed colendi proximè post cultum Dei: sic enim Dominus & natura præcipiunt.
units.tr: 2 Tobias, son of Tobit, honoured his parents so much, even after he had married, that he was unwilling to stay long at his father-in-law's for the feasts, so that he would not grieve his father and mother; Tobias's affection for them had been sufficiently proved by experience. Therefore the devoted affections of parents must not be neglected, nor should they be disturbed by good sons except under the most extreme necessity; they must be cherished next after the worship of God. For this is what the Lord and nature both command.

units.la: 3 Raguel denique cum uxore sua utilissima præcepta dedit filiæ suæ, quo pacto nimirum debeat se gerere erga soceros, maritum, familiam, & seipsam. Aiunt enim primum: Tuum socerum & socrum, qui nunc tui parentes sunt, magno in honore habeto (ut Ruth socrum suam Noemi) Nam vir & uxor sunt quasi una persona: & ideo sicut vir tenetur honorare parentes proprios, ita & eius uxor, ut sese filium syncerè amare ostendat. Liquido enim proditur fictus & insuauis amor consortis, si eiusdem parentes amare nō potest, vel reverentia non dignatur.
units.tr: 3 Finally, Raguel gave his daughter, together with her mother, very useful precepts on how she ought to conduct herself towards her parents-in-law, her husband, the household and herself. For they say first: Honour your father-in-law and mother-in-law, who are now your parents, with great respect (as Ruth did her mother-in-law Naomi). For husband and wife are as it were one person, and therefore, just as the husband is bound to honour his own parents, so too his wife should do, to show that she sincerely loves her husband. For a feigned and unpleasant love of a spouse is plainly revealed if she cannot love his parents or does not deserve their respect.

units.la: Secundo, maritum diligito, tanquam unam personam. Oportet enim uxores esse φιλάνδρες[?], Tit. 2. Cùm enim sine amore alicuius rei subsistere non possit iuvencula, conflat, neglecto sponsi amore, aliud quippiam vel alium impensè amare: cum Dominus conciliauerit sic naturas, ut inhumanum omnino sit, inter sponsum & sponsam desiderari amorem, sine quo fides necessaria non invenitur, quæ grata esse possit.
units.tr: Second, love your husband as one person. For wives ought to be [φιλάνδρες] affectionate to their husbands (Titus 2). For since a young woman cannot exist without love for something, it is clear that, neglecting her husband's love, she will love something else or someone else eagerly. The Lord has so joined natures that it is utterly inhuman for love to be lacking between husband and wife, and without it the necessary faith, which can be pleasing, is not found.

units.la: Tertiò, familiam regito: idque ex instituto ordinationeque mariti: alioqui patrisfamilias est, totam gubernare domum: uxoris autem est commonefacere, ne quid negligatur, quod præcepit maritus, cuius adiutorium est & esse debet. Quarto, domum gubernato, id est, legitimè dispensato, quæ maritus importat & sua acquirit industria, ut nihil perdatur, dissipetur, pereat, nec nimis, nec minus fiat, quàm ratio rei familiaris admonet & exigit, ut prospiciatur necessarijs domus in tempore, ne quid intempestiue procuretur. Sed & Paulus vult mulieres esse οἰκουργούς[?], Tit. 2. Nam in domo aliqua sunt agenda, quæ magis decent fieri per mulieres, quàm per viros. Adde quod viri circa exteriores occupationes sunt magis intenti, ut circa mercaturas, agriculturas & huiusmodi. Denique uxorem iuuare debere œconomiæ administrationem, monent etiam illa dicta: Mulier sedula corona est viri, at illaudata mulier tabefaciet ossa, Proverb.12. Mulier sapiens ædificat domum suam, stulta verò evertit eam, Proverb.14. Probam mulierem quis inveniet? Ea præstat gemmis, confidit ea cor mariti, & res familiaris non deficiet, reddat ei bonum & nō malum perpetuò. Tractat lanam & linum, & voluptati ei est officium suum facere. Perinde est atque nauis mercatoris, ex longinquo afferens panem suum. Noctu surgit, &c. Proverb.31[?]. Qui habet diligentem matrem familias, constabilit rem familiarem, & sociaam habet fidam, & columnam qua consolari posit. ubi non est sepes, vastatur prædium: & ubi non est materfamilias, ibi maritus miser est, quasi errabundus vagetur, Ecclesiastici trigesimo septimo. Quinto, te ipsam inculpatam praestato. Hoc fit, quando mulier in fide manet, ac dilectione, & sanctificatione cum castitate, 1.Timoth.2.quando sobria est, pura, bona, ornata virtutibus, ne sermo Dei male audiat, Tit. 2.quando denique verbis, factis, incessu, ornatu, vestibus, domi & foris, honestatis semper habet & seruat rationem diligentissimè, ut ab omni inhonesto verbo abhorreat, sensus corporis ad verecundiam regat, speculu[?] se[?] praebeat in moribus & verbis, ancillis & seruulis, filijs & filiabus, &c.
units.tr: Third, rule the household, and do so according to the arrangement and ordinance of the husband. Otherwise, it is the head of the family's task to govern the whole house, and it is the wife's to remind [the household] that nothing is neglected that the husband has commanded, for she is and ought to be his helper. Fourth, manage the house, that is, dispense lawfully what the husband brings in and acquires by his industry, so that nothing is lost, squandered or wasted, and nothing is done too much or too little, as the reckoning of household affairs advises and requires; so that the needs of the house are provided for in good time, and nothing is done at an inopportune moment. Paul also wants women to be [οἰκουργούς] keepers of the house (Titus 2). For there are things to be done in a house that are more fittingly done by women than by men. Add to this that husbands are more occupied with outside affairs, such as trade, farming and things of that kind. Finally, those sayings also advise that a wife ought to help in the administration of the household: A diligent woman is a crown to her husband, but a shameful woman rots his bones (Prov. 12). A wise woman builds her house, but a foolish one tears it down with her own hands (Prov. 14). Who will find a virtuous woman? She is more precious than jewels; the heart of her husband trusts in her, and the household will not lack; she will render him good and not evil all the days of her life. She works with wool and flax, and it is her delight to do her work. She is like a merchant's ship, bringing her bread from afar. She rises by night, etc. (Prov. 31). He who has a diligent mother of the family establishes his household, and has a faithful companion and a pillar on which he can lean. Where there is no hedge, the estate is laid waste; and where there is no mistress of the house, the husband is wretched and wanders about as one lost (Ecclus. 37). Fifth, present yourself blameless. This happens when a woman remains in faith and love, and in holiness with chastity (1 Tim. 2); when she is sober, pure, good, adorned with virtues, so that the word of God is not spoken ill of (Titus 2); and when, finally, in words, deeds, bearing, dress and clothing, at home and abroad, she always keeps the rule of honesty and observes it most diligently, so that she shrinks from every dishonourable word, governs the senses of her body to modesty, and shows herself as a mirror in her manners and words to her maids and servants, sons and daughters, and so on.

units.la: Hæc erat salutaris admonitio, quam parentes Sarę filię suæ jam abeunti cum marito suo insinuabant, ut verba quę recedens ab eis audiret,in corde ipsius arctius impressa remanerent.
units.tr: This was the wholesome admonition that Sara's parents gave their daughter as she was now leaving with her husband, so that the words she heard from them as she departed would remain more firmly impressed upon her heart.

units.la: 4 Ex ista autem doctrina & admonitione facile colligere potest etiam vir, quid ipsum facere deceat, nempe multò magis hęc omnia facere, id est, honorare maiores, diligere propriam uxorem, patrem familias agere, sua non dissipare, irreprehensibilem seipsum exhibere. Sic enim Raguel etiam Tobiam allocutus est, quemadmodum inquisibusdam[?] exemplaribus extat: Fili mi, Dominus Deus cœlorum conducat te in pace, ut faciat me videre ex te & ex Sara filia mea filios bonos ante Dominum, antequam moriar. Et ecce Sara filia mea in manu tua est, tu ne affligas eam cunctis diebus tuis, sed ite in pace: benedicensque & osculans eos, dimisit eos. Christus Iesus doceat tum maritos, tum uxores omnes facere quod iustum est coram Deo, Amen.
units.tr: 4 From this teaching and admonition a husband too can easily gather what is fitting for himself to do: namely, to do all these things much more, that is, to honour his elders, love his own wife, be the head of the household, not squander what is his, and show himself blameless. For Raguel also spoke to Tobias in this way, as it stands in some copies: My son, may the Lord God of heaven lead you in peace, and grant that I may see good sons from you and from my daughter Sara before the Lord, before I die. And behold, my daughter Sara is in your hand; do not afflict her all your days, but go in peace. And blessing and kissing them, he let them go. May Christ Jesus teach all husbands and wives to do what is just before God. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XXXIII
units.tr: SERMON XXXIII

units.la: Eccles. 4.
units.tr: Eccles. 4.

units.la: Ne[?] te domi tuæ geras in modum leonis, nec in domesticos tuos insane sævitas (aut opprimas tibi subiectos.) Ne manum habeas porrectam ad accipiendum, ad reddendum autem contractam.
units.tr: Do not behave in your house like a lion, nor savagely rage against your household (or oppress those subject to you). Do not keep your hand stretched out to receive, but drawn in when you give.

units.la: 1 Hæc admonitio non solùm pertinet ad reges, principes, gubernatores ciuitatum, & episcopos ecclesiarum, sed etiam ad patres & matres familiâs. Omnes enim illi mansueti & prudentes esse debent, non crudeles in subditos, vel inexorabiles, aut saftuosi, omnia perturbantes ex ira vel impatientia; domesticos præcipuè, quos præstat piè tractare, & ædificare, non opprimere vel vastare. Crudele & superbum animal leo est, atque tyrannicum, qualem non decet Præla tum esse, sed mansuetum & modestum, ad benefaciendum propensiorem, quàm ad nocendum, ducere potius volentem in suam sententiam, quàm trahere violenter. Suscipite infirmos, Paulus dicit Thessalonicensibus, patientes estote ad omnes. Iesaias quoque:
units.tr: (1) This admonition applies not only to kings, princes, governors of cities and bishops of churches, but also to fathers and mothers of families. All of them ought to be gentle and prudent, not cruel towards their subjects, nor unyielding, savage, or upsetting everything through anger or impatience. This is especially true of household members, whom it is better to treat dutifully and build up than to oppress or lay waste. The lion is a cruel, proud and tyrannical animal, and that is not fitting for a prelate to be. He should be gentle and moderate, more inclined to do good than harm, preferring to lead people into his own opinion rather than drag them by force. "Support the weak," Paul says to the Thessalonians, "be patient with everyone." Isaiah too:

units.la: Væ qui condunt leges iniquas, & scribentes iniustitias, ut opprimant in iudicio pauperes, & cætera ibidem in hanc sententiam multa. Non mirandum est autem, quòd Sapiens dicit homini, Nefis quasi quidam leo in domo tua. Est enim nonnunquam homo deterior leone, alijsq; bestijs, quemadmodũ sapientes apud gentes & Iudæos testantur. Sic enim Aristot. lib.7. Ethic. cap 7. scribit: μυρία γὰρ ἂν κακὰ ποιήσειεν ἀνθρώπῳ κακὸς ὢν θηρίων [?] hoc est: Homo enim si prauus sit, plura infinitis partibus detrimenta & incommoda, quàm fera inferre potest. Et Bias: Pernities homini (inquit) quæ maxima? solus homo alter. Idem interrogatus (vt Erasmus refert lib.7 Apoph.) quod esset animal omnium maximè noxium? Si de feris, inquit, percontaris, tyrannus: si de mitibus, adulator. Sed & Diogenes interrogatus, quæ bestia morsum haberet nocentissimum? Si de feris, inquit, interrogas, obtrectator: si de cicuribus, adulator. Nam obtrectator præ se fert odium, adulator sub amici persona multò etiam lædit grauius. Et Salomon Proverbiorum 17. Præstat occurrere virum urso orbato, quàm fatuo (obstinato) in stultitia sua. & 21. Melius est habitare in terra deserta (vbi ferę versari solent, Marci primo) quàm cum mulere rixosa & iracunda. Et Iosua filius Syrachi cap 2 ς. Συνοικήσω λέοντι καὶ δράκοντι ἐνδοκήσω, ἢ συνοικήσω μετὰ γυναικὸς πονηρᾶς: id est, Cum leone malim & dracone [?] habitare, quàm cum muliere nequam. degere, quàm cum mala muliere habitare. Vnde etiam illud prouerbium: ἄνθρωπος ἀνθρώπῳ λύκος[?], id est, Homo homini lupus. Iudæi idem conqueruntur de Herode, quod plura mala passi sint ab eo, quàm ab vlla bestia fieri posset, sicut Iosephus scribit lib. Antiquit. 17. cap. 17. Sed & Dauid Goliathum Philistæum illum incircumcisum, qui contumelijs affecit acies Dei viuentis, non meliorem reputauit, quàm vel leonem, vel vrsum, vt est 1.Reg. 17. Demosthenes inter infaustissimas[?] bestias quibus Pailas delectetur, populum recenset, qui pessimam gratiam referre solet optimè de se meritis.
units.tr: "Woe to those who make unjust laws and write injustice, to oppress the poor in judgement," and much more to the same effect in the same place. It is not surprising, however, that the Wise Man says to a man, "Be not like a lion in your house." For a man is sometimes worse than a lion or other beasts, as wise men among the Gentiles and the Jews attest. Thus Aristotle, Ethics book 7, chapter 7, writes: [μυρία γὰρ ἂν κακὰ ποιήσειεν ἀνθρώπῳ κακὸς ὢν θηρίων]. That is: a wicked man can inflict on a man countless evils, in more ways than a wild beast can. And Bias: "What is the greatest destruction to a man?" he said, "another man." The same man, asked (as Erasmus reports, Apophthegms book 7) what animal was the most harmful of all, answered: "If you ask about wild beasts, a tyrant; if about tame ones, a flatterer." Diogenes too, asked which beast has the most harmful bite, answered: "If you ask about wild ones, a slanderer; if about tame ones, a flatterer. For the slanderer displays his hatred openly, but the flatterer, under the guise of a friend, wounds much more grievously." Solomon, Proverbs 17: "It is better to meet a bear robbed of its cubs than a fool obstinate in his folly." And Proverbs 21: "It is better to dwell in a desert land (where wild beasts are wont to roam, Mark 1) than with a quarrelsome and angry woman." And Jesus son of Sirach, ch. 25: "I would rather dwell with a lion and a dragon than dwell with a wicked woman" [Συνοικήσω λέοντι καὶ δράκοντι ἐνδοκήσω, ἢ συνοικήσω μετὰ γυναικὸς πονηρᾶς]. Hence also the proverb [ἄνθρωπος ἀνθρώπῳ λύκος], that is, man is a wolf to man. The Jews complain of Herod the same way, that they suffered more evils from him than any beast could inflict, as Josephus writes, Antiquities book 17, chapter 17. David too did not think Goliath the uncircumcised Philistine, who insulted the armies of the living God, any better than a lion or a bear, as 1 Kings 17 tells. Demosthenes, listing the most wretched creatures in which Pallas takes delight, counts the people who usually repay their best benefactors with the worst return.

units.la: Cùm autem alibi leonum similes laudentur, vt iustus, Prouerb. 28. Iudas Machabæus, 1. Mac. 3. vt Christus rex Iudæorum, Apoc. 5. & populus eius, Mich. 5. & omnis qui memor est accepti beneficij, quemadmodum de leone quodam narratur (ex Apione Græ. vt Erasmus refert lib. 7. Eccles.) qui pastori pepercit, qui ante aliquot tempus ei spinam è pede extraxerat: quæritur cur hic Ecclesiasticus moneat, dicens: Noli esse sicut leo? Respondemus: quemadmodum in serpentibus aliisque bestijs quædam insunt, quæ Dominus nos imitari iubet, Matth. 10. sic in leonibus cæterisque animantibus quædam insunt, quæ nos vitare ac fugere decet. In quibus leoni homo similis esse non debeat, Sapiens ipse videtur ostendere, quum addit: Neue cerebrosus domesticos contunde, aut subditos opprime. <bl>Bist nicht ein wütrich/oder der ein wütender</bl> <bl>polderer</bl> (φαυλασιοχοπτῶν)[?] <bl>in vnd gegen deinem haußgesind</bl>, id est, ne familiae offeras speciem terroris, inquirendo omnia terribiliter, & saeuiendo in ipsos. Vnde etiam Ecclef ;3.[?] ἐ ἵστι σεὶ οἰκέτης, ὡς αὐτὸν ὡς τέκνον[?]. Et Agapetus cap.23. Talem te praesta tuos erga famulos, qualem optas erga te Dominum esse. Item Paulus Colof.4. Viri diligite vxores, & ne fitis amarulenti aduersus illas. Et Petrus 1. Pet. 3. Viri similiter cohabitent secundum scientiam, velut infirmiori vasi muliebri impartientes honorem, &c.
units.tr: Yet elsewhere lions are praised as likenesses of the righteous (Prov. 28), of Judas Maccabeus (1 Macc. 3), of Christ as King of the Jews (Rev. 5), and of his people (Mic. 5), and of everyone who remembers a kindness received. It is told of a certain lion (from Apion the Greek, as Erasmus reports, book 7 of Ecclesiastes?) that he spared a shepherd who had earlier drawn a thorn from his foot. So the question is asked why this Ecclesiasticus warns, saying "Be not like a lion." We answer: just as there are some qualities in serpents and other beasts which the Lord bids us imitate (Matt. 10), so there are some qualities in lions and other animals which it is fitting for us to avoid and flee. The Wise Man himself seems to show in what respects a man should not be like a lion, when he adds: "Do not, like a raging brawler, strike your household, nor oppress your subjects." [Bist nicht ein Wütrich, oder der ein wütender Poltrer in und gegen deinem Hausgesind], that is, do not present your family with the appearance of terror, by investigating everything terribly and raging against them. Hence also Ecclesiasticus [ἐάν σοι ἔστιν οἰκέτης, ὡς αὐτὸν ὡς τέκνον]: if you have a servant, treat him as a child. And Agapetus, ch. 23: "Show yourself towards your servants such as you wish the Lord to be towards you." Likewise Paul, Col. 4: "Husbands, love your wives, and do not be bitter towards them." And Peter, 1 Pet. 3: "Husbands likewise live with their wives according to knowledge, showing honour to the woman as the weaker vessel," etc.

units.la: Non solum autem leonum similes esse nō debemus, quo ad crudelitatem & saeuitiam, verum etiam quo ad cupiditatem & auaritiam, seu rapacitatem, quae leonibus quoque in Scripturis attribuitur: Naum 2.Psal.104. Dicit enim Sapiens: Ne manum habeto ad accipiendum porrectam, ad reddendum contractam: qualem habere solent auari & sordidi heri, qui suae familiae multum quidem laboris & oneris imponunt, parum vero mercedis & cibi apponunt: sponte accipiunt, & grauatim largiuntur. Ne igitur rapiamus aliena, sed potius largiamur nostra. Beatius enim est dare, quam accipere: Actor.20.
units.tr: Yet we ought not to be like lions only in cruelty and savagery, but also in greed and avarice, or rapacity, which is attributed to lions in Scripture too (Nah. 2; Ps. 104). For the Wise Man says: "Do not keep your hand stretched out to receive, but drawn in to give." This is the habit of stingy and miserly masters, who lay much toil and burden on their household, yet offer little wages and food; they receive readily and give grudgingly. Let us therefore not seize what belongs to others, but rather give away what is ours. For it is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20).

units.la: Praeterea leonum est rugire, & vorare, Amos 3. Psal. 22. Ezech. 19. 1. Pet. 5. Instar leonum rugiunt, qui vociferantur, clamant, maledicunt, blasphemant, murmurant. Recte igitur Paulus 1.Tim.3. vxores sint [illegible, ~8 letters] & Eph. 4. Omnis amarulentia, & tumor, & ira, & vociferat o, & maledicentia tollatur à vobis cum omni malitia, &c. Instar leonum vorat, qui corda sua crapula & ebrietate grauant, Luc. 21. ebriosi operarij, Eccles. 19.
units.tr: Moreover it is the nature of lions to roar and to devour (Amos 3; Ps. 22; Ezek. 19; 1 Pet. 5). Those who shout, cry out, curse, blaspheme and mutter roar like lions. Rightly, therefore, Paul says (1 Tim. 3) that wives should be [illegible] and (Eph. 4): "Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking be put away from you, with all malice," etc. Those who weigh down their hearts with gluttony and drunkenness devour like lions (Luke 21); so do drunken workers (Ecclus 19).

units.la: ʒ Cæterum quid faciendum est illi, qui vel leoninam naturam habet, vel coniugem, aut principem leoni similem, cuiusmodi fuit Nabal, Herodes, Cambyses, Nero, &c. Orandus Dominus (qui Dauidem, Danielem, Paulum de manu & ore leonum eripuit, 1. Reg. 17. Dan. 6. 2. Tim. 4.) pro spiritu (quo Samson leonem vicit & dilaceravit, Iudic. 14.) idque fide (qua occludi possunt ora leonum, Hebr. 11.) & humili animo. <bl>Dann Des grausamen Löwen zorn vnd</bl> <bl>vbermut / vberwinde[?] das hündlin mit demut.</bl> Pater noster cœlestis liberet nos à pessimo illo[?] leone, qui diabolus est, per Christum Iesum, Amen.
units.tr: But what must be done by one who has either a lion's nature, or a wife, or a prince who is like a lion, such as Nabal, Herod, Cambyses, Nero, and others? The Lord must be prayed to, who snatched David, Daniel and Paul from the hand and mouth of lions (1 Sam. 17; Dan. 6; 2 Tim. 4). We pray for the spirit by which Samson conquered and tore apart the lion (Judg. 14), and for faith, by which the mouths of lions can be shut (Heb. 11), and for a humble mind. [Dann des grausamen Löwen Zorn und Übermut überwinde das Hündlin mit Demut.] May our heavenly Father deliver us from that most wicked lion, which is the devil, through Christ Jesus. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XXXIIII.
units.tr: SERMON XXXIV.

units.la: Eccles. 7.
units.tr: Ecclesiastes 7.

units.la: Vxore sapiente bonaq; caue ne excidas (si quam secundum religione Domini nactus es:) nam venustas eius praestantiar[?] auro est. Ne male tractes famulum operantem fideliter, nec mercenarium sese totum impendentem. Famulum cordatum charum habeas animo, nec defraudes eum libertate. Pecudes si tibi fuerint, fac cures eas: & si tibi sunt utiles, apud te permaneant. Si liberi tibi fuerint, erudias eos, & ceruicem eorum domes à iuuentute. Si filiae tibi sint, asserues corpus earum, nec vultum tuum offendas iis hilarem. Eloca filiam, & magnum opus peregeris. Caterum fac eam viro cordato colloces. Vxorem ex sententia natus ne repudies, nec te permittas odiosa.
units.tr: A wise and good wife, take care not to lose her (if you have gained one who is religious before the Lord), for her charm is worth more than gold. Do not treat a servant badly when he works faithfully, nor a hireling who gives himself wholly to his task. Hold a prudent servant dear in your heart, and do not cheat him of his freedom. If you have cattle, see that you look after them; and if they are useful to you, let them remain with you. If you have children, instruct them and bend their necks from their youth. If you have daughters, guard their bodies, and do not show them a cheerful face to offend you. Give your daughter in marriage, and you will have done a great work. But take care to join her to a sensible man. Do not reject a wife who suits your own mind, and do not let yourself be made hateful.

units.la: I Discimus ex verbis illis, qualem uxorem sibi quisque eligere & accipere, & vero etiam retinere debeat, nempe sapientem & bonam. Inquit enim, μὴ ἀπόχι[?]ς γαυκὸς σοφῆς & ἀγαθῆς. <bl>So wirstu es wol</bl> <bl>treffen/und nit fallen.</bl> dicerisque [illegible, ~5 letters]. Sapiens est, quae timet Dominum (unde Latinus interpres addit, quam sortitus es in timore Domini .i. quam Domini metuentem natus es) & sapientiam .i. Christum, eiusque spiritum in se habet manentem per fidem. Haec vero sapientia inuenitur in Scripturis sanctis, ac discitur ex Dei verbo, & comparatur precibus fidei à Deo, 2. Tim. 3. Psalm. 119. Iacob 1. Bona vel proba mulier est, quae à Deo bona reddita, ex bono thesauro cordis sui depromit bona, virtuosa, honesta, ἀγαθὴ καὶ ἀλ[?]α- ἀγαθοποιοῦσα, edens fructum spiritus, ἀγαθωσύνην, non rixosa, iracunda, mala. Quae talis est & eiusmodi virtutibus ornata, nobilior existit, & gratior est viro omni auro: quod nullo modo sic est expetendum, ut spiritus sapientiae, ut spiritus placidus & quietus. Duo ergo commendat in uxore, prudentiam & bonitatem: quae efficiunt ut ea & sciat, & velit cum marito, liberis totaque familia rectè viuere. Bonitas vel probitas ad voluntatem ac fidem pertinet: sapientia vero ad ingenium & industriam.
units.tr: I. From those words we learn what sort of wife each man ought to choose, accept, and indeed keep: namely a wise and good one. For he says: do not cast away a wife who is wise and good [μὴ ἀπόχι[?]ς γαυκὸς σοφῆς & ἀγαθῆς]. "So you will hit it right and not fall," as the German has it. And you will be called [illegible]. She is wise who fears the Lord (whence the Latin translator adds: whom you have obtained in the fear of the Lord, that is, whom you were born to, one who fears the Lord), and who has in herself wisdom, that is Christ, and his Spirit remaining in her through faith. This wisdom is found in the holy Scriptures, is learned from the Word of God, and is obtained from God by the prayers of faith (2 Tim. 3; Ps. 119; James 1). She is a good or upright wife, who, having been made good by God, brings forth good things from the good treasure of her heart: virtuous, honest, good and doing good [ἀγαθὴ καὶ ἀλ[?]α- ἀγαθοποιοῦσα], bearing the fruit of the Spirit, goodness [ἀγαθωσύνην], not quarrelsome, angry or spiteful. A woman who is such, and adorned with such virtues, is nobler and more pleasing than all the gold in the world; and she is not to be sought in the way that the spirit of wisdom is sought, the peaceful and quiet spirit. Therefore he commends two things in a wife, prudence and goodness, which make her both know and will to live rightly with her husband, her children and the whole household. Goodness or uprightness pertains to the will and to faith; but wisdom pertains to the mind and to diligence.

units.la: 2 Discimus etiam qualiter paterfamilias se gerere debeat erga suam domum .i. ea quae habet in domo, seu familia sua. Si enim habet seruum bonum, in veritate operante, aut mercenarium fidelem, dantem animam suam (propter quos seruos Dominus saepe benedicit patresfamilias, ut propter Iacob, Ioseph, &c.) aequitatem illi exhibeat, Col. 4. non male tractet illum, neque affligat conuitijs, verberibus, mercedis fraudatione aut dilatione: neque illum in suo obsequio inuitum detineat ultra tempus à lege praefixum, Exod. 21. Deut. 15. sed libertate donet, necsine munere dimittat.
units.tr: 2. We also learn how the head of the household ought to conduct himself towards his own house, that is, towards those whom he has in his home or family. For if he has a good servant, who works in truth, or a faithful hireling who gives his life, (for whose sake the Lord often blesses the heads of households, as for the sake of Jacob, Joseph, etc.), he should show them fairness (Col. 4), not treat them badly, nor afflict them with insults, blows, or cheating them of wages or delaying them; nor should he keep them against their will in his service beyond the time fixed by law (Exod. 21; Deut. 15), but should give them their freedom and not let them go empty-handed.

units.la: Si habet pecora, curet & inspiciat ea, Proverb. 12. & 27. Exod. 20. Deut. 25. non maledicat illis, ut nunc vulgò fit: & attendat illis, quid ipsi facto opus sit de illis, vendenda ne sint, an seruanda. Et si senserit ea sibi utilia esse carne, pelle, fimo, lacte & prole, apud ipsum perseuerent. Talis enim olim patriarcharum prouentus erat, atque iusta substantia, & utilis vehementer ad familiæ sustentationem amplissimæ. Intelligi quidem moraliter potest de præla-tis & pastoribus ecclesiasticis commodè: sed hæc literalis instructio minimè est aspernanda. Non enim honestior est victus, quàm ex animalibus & agricultura, quibus se maiores honestè & felicius nutrierūt & quietius. Vult autem dominum pecuarium eam curam ac diligentiam adhibere, ut pecus suum sæpe inspiciat. Nam oculus domini equum impinguat.
units.tr: If he has livestock, let him care for them and look after them (Prov. 12 and 27; Exod. 20; Deut. 25); let him not curse them, as is now commonly done; and let him attend to what needs to be done with them, whether they are to be sold or kept. And if he judges them useful to himself for meat, hide, dung, milk and offspring, let them remain with him. For such was once the increase of the patriarchs, and a just wealth, and very useful for the support of a most ample household. It may indeed be understood morally, and fitly applied to the prelates and ecclesiastical ministers; but this literal instruction is by no means to be despised. For no livelihood is more honourable than that from animals and agriculture, by which our forefathers were fed honestly, more happily and more quietly. Moreover, he wishes the master of the herds to bring such care and diligence that he often inspects his flock; for the eye of the master fattens the horse.

units.la: Si habet natos, Dei beneficio acceptos, erudiat illos in literatura ac moribus, idque vel per seipsum, vel per alios: iuxta Apostolum, Ephes. 6. Patres educate filios vestros in disciplina & timore Domini. Obligantur enim parentes proli alimentum, doctrinam, & disciplinam, siue castigationem: de qua sequitur: Curua seu flecte collum eorum, id est, reprime illorum affectus & passiones à pueritia illorum, cùm adhuc sunt ductiles, teneri, & dociles: sicut ramus tener facilè curuatur, non autem postquam induratur & fortificatur. Unde Salomon: Noli subtrahere à puero disciplinam, tu virga percutis eum, & animam eius de inferno liberabis. & alibi: Stulitia colligata est in corde pueri, & virga disciplinæ fugabit eam.
units.tr: If he has children, received by God's kindness, let him instruct them in learning and morals, either himself or through others, according to the Apostle (Eph. 6): Fathers, bring up your children in the discipline and fear of the Lord. For parents are bound to provide food, teaching, and discipline or correction for their offspring. Of this it follows: bend or turn their neck, that is, restrain their desires and passions from their childhood, while they are still pliable, tender and teachable; as a young branch is easily bent, but not after it has hardened and grown strong. Hence Solomon: Do not withhold discipline from the boy; if you strike him with the rod, you will deliver his soul from hell. And elsewhere: Folly is bound up in the heart of a boy, and the rod of discipline will drive it away.

units.la: Si vxorem ex animi sententia vel secundum animam .i. voluntatem habet, non eijciat, non expellat, non repudiet illam[?] (loquitur veteri & Iudaico more: nam ex legę Hebræis durisimæ ceruicis hominibus permittebatur libellus repudij, Deut.24. Matt. 19. ) nec facile credat de illa male loquentibus, ne animo suo auertatur ab ea, vel proijciat eam: sed potius diligat, iuxta Apostolum dicentem, Viri diligite vxores vestras, sicut & Christus ecclesiam, &c. vel, Odibili non credas, tradas, aut committas te in toto corde. h.e. Mulieri instabili, peruersæ, astutæ, & blandæ, quam aliquando perfidam sensisti, non vnquam sic confidas, vt ei reueles occulta tua, quod ægrè communiter secreta feruet pro loquacitate sua, ne tibi quod Samsoni contingat ex Dalila. item Fuluio ex Martia, cuius Erasmus meminit in lib. de Lingua. Et Michæas inquit: Ab ea quæ dormit in sinu tuo, custodi claustra oris tui. Sed & sapiens Proverb. 31. dicit, Quæso te fili veteri mei, fili exoptatissime, ne da mulieribus opes tuas, & vias tuas: perdunt enim reges. Cato feni-orum [illegible, ~15 letters] vitam accidisse dixit, quo-rum [illegible, ~10 letters]: primum, si quid arcani fœminæ credidisset: secundum, si quopiam naufragio vectus esset, quo pedestri itinere peruenire licuisset: tertium, si quis dies ipsi per negligentiam absque fructu effluxisset.
units.tr: If he has a wife according to his own mind, or according to his soul, that is, his will, let him not cast her out, drive her away, or repudiate her (he speaks in the old Jewish manner: for by the law a bill of divorce was permitted to the Hebrews, men of hard necks, Deut. 24; Matt. 19), nor let him readily believe those who speak ill of her, lest his mind be turned away from her or he cast her off; but rather let him love her, according to the Apostle who says: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the Church, etc. Or: do not trust, hand over, or commit yourself with your whole heart to one who is hateful, that is, to an unstable, perverse, crafty and flattering woman whom you have at some time found faithless; never trust her so far as to reveal your secrets to her, which she commonly cannot keep hidden because of her talkativeness; lest what happened to Samson through Delilah should happen to you, and likewise to Fulvius through Martia, whom Erasmus mentions in his book On the Tongue. And Micah says: From her who sleeps in your bosom, guard the doors of your mouth. But the wise man too, in Prov. 31, says: I beg you, my son, my dearly desired son, do not give your wealth and your ways to women, for they destroy kings. Cato said that three things brought about the unhappy life of old men: first, if he had entrusted some secret to a woman; second, if he had been carried by some shipwreck from which he could have reached land on foot; third, if some day had slipped away for him through negligence without profit.

units.la: 5 Cæterum de filiabus singulare dat præceptum: quoniam ille sexus est leuior atque lasciuior. Inquit igitur: Si tibi filiæ sunt, obseruato earum corpus, nec eis hilarem vultum præbeto, de quo plura Sapiens cap. 26.
units.tr: 5. Moreover, he gives a particular precept concerning daughters, since that sex is lighter and more wanton. He says therefore: If you have daughters, guard their bodies, and do not show them a cheerful face; on which the Wise Man says more in chapter 26.

units.la: ȝ6.42.Non enim est permittenda filiab. euagationis licentia, ne ex pudicitia periclitentur, ad exemplum Dinę, quam Dei prouidentia idcirco fœdari permisit, vt cunctis fidelium filiabus duraret in exemplum. Seruandum summa diligentia corpus filiæ est, ne publicis permittatur spectaculis, multò diligentius ne priuatis couenticulis illudatur. Lubrica est enim fama pudoris. Maturitate, feueritate ac grauitate aut opus est parentum in filias, maximè verò patris. Ideo dicitur: Non ostendas faciem hilarem ad illas, ne fiduciam peccandi, vel audaciam corripiant, ne assueficant ad viros affici, ne fine parentum scitu digrediantur domo, semper sint in timore & solicitudine, omnia etiam tuta vereantur, timeant semper patrem, & diffamiæ omnis notas abhorreant semper: sunt tamen moderato rigore tractandæ, nec non suo tempore elocandæ. Ait enim: [illegible, ~5 letters] [illegible, ~6 letters]. Trade filiam (nam enim decet filiam nubere præter parentum voluntatem) & grande opus feceris (& bonum, 1. Cor. 7. vnde spes sit procreandæ prolis religiosæ & honestæ: est ergo hoc opus non leuiter & sine deliberatione agendum) & homini (non cuilibet, sed) sensato, seu viro prudenti, Συνέτῳ, da illam: ([illegible, ~8 letters] .i. muneri dato eam). est enim puella optimis præditæ moribus præstantissimum donum, quod viro alicui offerri possit) prudenti inquam, qui nimirum prudenter & strenuè rei familiari incubere noueris, etiamsi diuitiæ absint, iuxta illud Themistòclis, de quo Cicero. 2. Off. Malo filiæ meæ virum, absq; pecunia, vel qui egeat pecunia, quàm pecuniam quæ egeat viro. Ad mores & prudentiam in his respiciendum est maxima ad opes, vel genus, vt Marcus Antonius Imperator, non qui longam generis seriem præferrent, aut qui opes nimias ostentarent: sed qui morum probitate atque modestia, vitæque innocentia præcellerent, eos sibi generos deligendos putauit. vnde & Salamon Prouerb. 11. ait: Mulier gratæ (conuersationis) retinet gloriam: improbi autem apprehendunt diuitias. Hoc est, mulier quæ gratia prædita est, vel propter probitatem vitæ omnibus grata est, reliquit post se nomen gloriosum: & qui in ducenda vxore magis spectant ad diuitias, quàm ad probitatem vitæ, nebulones sunt. Id enim significat [illegible, ~3 letters]. Et Prouer. 16. Possidere sapientiam, melius est, quàm habere aurum: & possidere intelligentiam, magis est eligendum, quàm (habere) argentum. Quanquam expediat connubia fieri inter personas non multum dispares, iuxta illud Pitaci Mitylenæi: Aequalem ducito. Quantis ebuccinarent verbis, qui cœlibatum tantopere euehunt, si de turpi eorum munditia tale præceptum haberet ex Scripturis, quale hic de matrimonio legunt, iteratum post verbum Dei, à constituto mundo prolatum. Nostrum autem est, qui scimus statum matrimonij à Deo iustitutum, qui & corporum & animarum nostrarum est conditor, ut eundem in Deo & secundum Deum teneamus, & in eo collocati, pie, iuste & sobrie viuamus, ut Dominus Deus hic & in futuro seculo benedictionem suam nobis largiatur per Christum Iesum: cui sit honor & gloria in sempiternum, Amen.
units.tr: 36.42. For there is no permission to be given to daughters for gadding about, lest they be endangered in their chastity, after the example of Dinah, whom God's providence allowed to be defiled for this reason, that it might be an example to all the daughters of the faithful. The body of a daughter must be guarded with the greatest diligence, lest she be allowed at public spectacles, and much more diligently lest she be mocked at private gatherings; for the reputation of chastity is slippery. The parents, and especially the father, must show maturity, sternness and seriousness towards their daughters. Hence it is said: Do not show a cheerful face to them, lest they take up confidence in sinning or boldness, lest they become accustomed to being attracted to men, lest they leave the house without their parents' knowledge; let them always be in fear and anxiety, let them fear all things as unsafe, let them always fear their father, and always shun every mark of disgrace. Yet they are to be handled with moderate strictness, and given in marriage in their proper time. For he says: [illegible] [illegible]. Give your daughter in marriage (for it is fitting that a daughter marry, not against her parents' will), and you will have done a great work (and a good one, 1 Cor. 7, whence there is hope of begetting religious and honest offspring; this work is therefore not to be undertaken lightly and without deliberation), and give her to a man (not to just anyone, but) sensible, or a prudent man, to a prudent man [Συνέτῳ]: give her [illegible]; that is, give her as a gift. For a girl endowed with the best morals is the most excellent gift that can be offered to any man. Prudent, I say, that is, one who knows how to apply himself prudently and vigorously to domestic affairs, even if riches are lacking; according to that saying of Themistocles, of whom Cicero speaks (De Officiis 2): I would rather my daughter had a husband without money, or one who needs money, than money that needs a husband. In these matters one must look above all to character and prudence, not to wealth or birth; as the Emperor Marcus Antonius thought that those should be chosen as sons-in-law who excelled not in showing off a long line of ancestors or excessive riches, but in the uprightness of their morals, their modesty and the innocence of their lives. Hence Solomon also says in Prov. 11: A woman of pleasing conversation retains glory; but the wicked seize riches. That is, a woman who is endowed with grace, or who is pleasing to all because of the uprightness of her life, leaves behind her a glorious name; and those who in taking a wife look more to riches than to uprightness of life are scoundrels. For this is what [illegible] signifies. And Prov. 16: To possess wisdom is better than to have gold; and to possess understanding is more to be chosen than (to have) silver. Although it is expedient that marriages be made between persons not greatly unequal, according to the saying of Pittacus of Mytilene: take an equal. How loudly would they cry out, who so greatly extol celibacy, if the Scriptures had such a precept about their filthy chastity as this which they read here concerning marriage, repeated after the Word of God, uttered from the founding of the world! But it is our part, who know that the state of marriage was instituted by God, who is the creator both of our bodies and of our souls, to keep it in God and according to God, and, placed in it, to live piously, justly and soberly; so that the Lord God may here and in the future age bestow his blessing upon us through Jesus Christ, to whom be honour and glory for ever, Amen.

units.tr: SERMON XXXIV.

units.la: Eccles. 9.
units.tr: Eccles. 9.

units.la: Uxorem quam complecteris, ne prosequaris zelotypia, nec eā malam in te arte doceas. Nec permittas animum tuum mulieri adeò, ut pessundet potestatem tuam, (tuq; dedecus incurras) Mulieri meretrici ne te des obuiam, ne forte in laqueos eius incidas. Cantatricem mulierem ne frequentes (nec audias) ne forte conatibus eius capiaris. Ne contempleris virginem, ut ne noxam ex precioso ipsius cultu contrahas. Ne appellas animum tuum ad meretrices, ne perdas (te simul &) tuam possessionem. In vicis urbis ne circumspectes, nec in secretis eius locis oberres. A muliere formosa auertas oculos, nec contempleris pulchritudinem alienam. Nam multiforma mulierum seduli sunt, & amor ex ea in modum ignis exardescit. Apud mulierem maritatam ne sedeas omnino, nec inter ulnas eius recumbas, neue committas cum ea compotandi gratia symbolum, ut ne forte ad eam inclinet animus tuus, & affectu tuo prolabaris in pernitiem:
units.tr: Be not jealous of the wife you embrace, lest you teach her an evil art against yourself. Do not give your mind so entirely to a woman that she overthrows your authority and you incur disgrace. Do not expose yourself to a harlot, lest you fall into her snares. Do not frequent a singing woman, nor listen to her, lest you be caught by her wiles. Do not gaze at a virgin, lest you draw harm from her precious adornment. Do not turn your mind to courtesans, lest you lose yourself and your possessions together. Do not wander about the streets of the city, nor loiter in its lonely places. Turn your eyes away from a beautiful woman, and do not gaze at another's beauty. For many women are crafty, and love kindles from them like fire. Do not sit at all beside a married woman, nor lie down between her arms, nor drink with her in company, lest your mind inclines towards her and your feelings carry you into ruin.

units.la: 1 Docet Iesus Syracides his sententijs primum, quomodo vir se gerere debeat erga uxorem: dein quomodo erga alias mulieres, siue sint meretrices, siue virgines, siue maritatæ. Estque hæc doctrina nostris temporibus valde utilis & necessaria. Prædixit enim Christus, Luc.17. quod sic erit in diebus filij hominis (.i. postremis, qui nunc sunt) sicut accidit in diebus Noe: nam edebant, bibebant, uxores ducebant, &c. Item videntes filij Dei (ut Moses testatur Genesis 6.) filias hominum, quod essent pulchræ, acceperunt sibi uxores ex omnibus quas elegerant.
units.tr: 1 Jesus the son of Sirach teaches in these sentences, first, how a husband ought to conduct himself towards his wife, and then how towards other women, whether they be harlots, virgins or married women. And this teaching is very useful and necessary in our own times. For Christ foretold (Luke 17) that it would be in the days of the Son of Man (that is, in the last days, which are now) as it happened in the days of Noah: for they ate, drank, and took wives, etc. Likewise, as Moses testifies (Genesis 6), the sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were fair, and took wives for themselves from all whom they chose.

units.la: 2 Dicit autem Sapiens: Ne zeles mulierem sinus tui) i.amor uxoris non sit nimius: in sinu tuo quiescentem non ames amore zelotypo, ut [?]uiter timeas ab ipsa te minus amari, amati[?] autem & ab alijs, propter quod & eam amar[?] etius quàm par fit, folicitè custodias: non sis nimium suspiciosus de castitate uxoris propriæ. Ratio: ne ostendat super te malitiam doctrinæ nequam :) vel vt Lutherus vertit: <bl>Dann solch hart aufffehen bringt</bl> <bl>nichts guts</bl>, h.e. ne malis artibus tibi insidiari incipiat, & nouissima illius experiaris amara quasi absynthium: ne exerceat contra te artificium muliebre nequam, edocta ab improbis. Etenim si proba est, nimium arceri non debet: si improba, custodiri non poterit, proficiet potius de malo in peius, dicente Hieronymo: Quid prodest diligens custodia, quum vxor seruari impudica non possit, pudica non debeat? Infida enim custos castitatis est necessitas: & illa verè pudica dicenda est, cui licuit peccare, sed noluit. Huc & illud Germanorum pertinet: <bl>Oder es hilfft nicht/</bl> <bl>oder es darff sich nicht.</bl> Adde quòd zelus, sicut iracundia & tristitia minuunt dies, & ante tempus senectam adducit cura, Eccles. 20. Vulgus quoque non improprie hunc assectum gelosiam vocat, quod animum assiduo metu territet adeo, vt continua suspicionum recurfatione gelu quodam sanguis ipse concrescat (teste Iouiano lib. 3. de Obed. 6.) quæ solicitudo quanquam multarum in se habeat discordiarum semina, raroque gratia in illa esse domo potest, in qua radices altiores egerit: origo tamen eius ab amore est, qui metu ac suspicione victus, diffidensque ac pauitans, & nunc dolore, nunc ira percitus, mentem adeo perturbat, & animum concutit, vt eius ferri vix possit impotentia. Quocirca fugiendus est is animi morbus, & solicitudinis plena perturbatio:quæ vbi vehementior est,quàm proximè accedit ad insaniâ,&c.
units.tr: 2 The Wise Man says: "Do not be jealous of the wife of your bosom": let your love for your wife not be excessive. Do not love with a jealous love her who rests in your bosom, so that you fear that she loves you less, and that she is loved by others, and for that reason guard her with more anxious care than is right. Do not be overly suspicious about the chastity of your own wife. The reason: lest she show against you the malice of wicked teaching; or, as Luther translates it: "Such harsh watchfulness brings <bl>nothing good</bl>", that is, lest she begin to lay snares for you by evil arts, and you experience her last deeds as bitter as wormwood, lest she practise against you the wicked feminine craft she has learned from the wicked. For if she is chaste, she ought not to be guarded too strictly; if she is unchaste, she cannot be guarded, and you will merely progress from bad to worse. As Jerome says: "What good is a careful watch, when a wife cannot be kept unchaste but ought not to be chaste? For necessity is a faithless guardian of chastity; and she is truly chaste who was free to sin but chose not to." To this belongs also the German saying: <bl>either it helps not, or it is not permitted</bl>. Add that jealousy, like anger and sorrow, shortens the days, and care brings old age before its time (Ecclesiasticus 20). The common people also not inappropriately call this affection "gelosia", because it terrifies the mind with constant fear, so that by the continual recurrence of suspicions the blood itself congeals as with a kind of ice (as Jovianus testifies, book 3 On Obedience, ch. 6). Although this anxiety contains within itself the seeds of many discords, and rarely can grace be in that household where it has struck deeper roots, its origin nevertheless lies in love, which, overcome by fear and suspicion, distrustful and fearful, and now stirred by grief, now by anger, so disturbs the mind and shakes the spirit that its violence can scarcely be borne. Wherefore this disease of the mind, and this disturbance full of anxiety, must be fled; and when it becomes more vehement, it comes very near to madness, etc.

units.la: Fertur Nicolaitarum hæresis,à quodâ Nicolao Antiocheno proselyto, qui fuit vnus ex septem diaconis,quorum Acto[?].6. mentio fit,initium sumpsisse, idque praua quadam æmulatione. Qua de re Clemens Stratoni. lib.3. sic scribit: Cum formosam haberet vxorem, & post Seruatoris assumptionem ei fuisset ab Apostolis exprobrata zelotypia,in medium adducta muliere,permisit cui vellet nubere. Aiunt.n. hanc actionem illi voci consentaneam: quæ dicit, quòd carne uti oporteat: eiusque factum & dictum absolutè & inconsideratè sequentes,qui eius hæresim persequuntur, impudenter effuseque fornicantur,&c. Quáta mala ex zelotypia oriatur, duo ista exempla probant quoque,quæ Hieronymus Vuellerus recenset in libello de officio Ecclesiastico,polit.& œcon. vbi agit de officio coniugis.
units.tr: It is said that the heresy of the Nicolaitans began from a certain Nicolaus of Antioch, a proselyte, who was one of the seven deacons whose mention is made in Acts 6, and that it arose from a certain perverse jealousy. Concerning this matter Clement, in book 3 of the Stromata, writes thus: "When he had a beautiful wife, and after the Saviour's ascension the Apostles reproached him for jealousy, he brought the woman into the midst and allowed her to marry whomever she wished." For they say that this action agrees with that saying which declares that one ought to use the flesh [carne uti oporteat]; and those who pursue his heresy, following his deed and saying absolutely and without consideration, commit fornication shamelessly and licentiously, etc. How many evils arise from jealousy, these two examples also prove, which Hieronymus Wuellerus recounts in his little book on the ecclesiastical office, in the Politics and Economics, where he treats of the duty of a spouse.

units.la: Vt autem vxor propria non est nimis arctanda,ita nec nimis laxanda, ideo subditur: Non des mulieri potestatem animæ tuæ) .i. non sinas mulierem in te dominari,vel auctoritatem vsurpare, vt Paulus loquitur, 1. Timot.2. Vir enim caput est mulieris. Sub viri,Dominus inquit Gen.3[?]. potestate eris, & ipse dominabitur tui.
units.tr: But just as a wife should not be restrained too tightly, so neither should she be loosed too much; therefore it is added: "Do not give your power over your soul to a woman", that is, do not allow a woman to dominate you or usurp authority, as Paul speaks in 1 Timothy 2: "For the man is the head of the woman."
