The Lord says to the woman in Genesis 3: "You shall be under the man's power, and he shall rule over you."

units.la: Ne ingrediatur in virtute tua) vel, ne ipsa supra vires ascendat tuas, id est,ne virtutem tuam blanditijs suis emolliat,ne virtutem in te suam vsurpet,ne tecum conuersetur vt domina,vsurpans sibi quod est mariti. Præcipit hæc sententia moderationem ac temperantiam in amanda coniuge: nam fi amor viri in vxorem est vehementior, ita inuertit ordinem naturæ, vt mulier quæ ὑποτάσσεσθαι[?] hoc est subiecta viro, esse debebat, eum sibi subjiciat, atq; inde existat γυναικοκρατία[?] imperium muliebre contra ordinationem Dei occupatum. Quare beneuolentia debita quam præcipit Paulus 1.Cor.7. vxori tribuenda est, nō ea amoris vehementia atq; impotentia, qua vir in potestatem eius redigatur.
units.tr: "Lest she enter into your strength", or, lest she rise above your powers, that is, lest she soften your strength with her flatteries, lest she usurp your power over you, lest she live with you as mistress, appropriating to herself what belongs to the husband. This sentence prescribes moderation and temperance in loving a wife: for if a husband's love for his wife is too vehement, the order of nature is so inverted that the woman, who ought to be subject to her husband [ὑποτάσσεσθαι, that is, subject to the husband], subjects him to herself, and from this arises female rule [γυναικοκρατία], a dominion of women seized contrary to God's ordinance. Therefore the kindness that Paul enjoins in 1 Corinthians 7 is to be shown to a wife, not that vehemence and impotence of love by which a husband is reduced to her power.

units.la: Vnde & confundaris) vt effeminatus, exemplo Samfonis: de quo Ambrosius, Samson validus & fortis leonem suffocauit, sed amorem suum suffocare non potuit: vincula rupit hostium, sed suarum non soluit nexus cupiditatum: messes incendit alienas, sed vnius ipse mulieris accensus igniculo messem suæ virtutis amisit.
units.tr: "Lest you also be confounded", that is, be made effeminate, as in the example of Samson, of whom Ambrose says: "Samson, strong and brave, choked a lion, but he could not choke his own love; he broke the bonds of enemies, but did not loosen the knots of his own desires; he set fire to others' harvests, but himself, kindled by the little spark of one woman, lost the harvest of his own virtue."

units.la: Cæterum ex his etiam vxor intelligere poteft, quomodo fe erga maritum gerere debeat, nempe etiam abstinere à zelo seu obtrectatione: item subdita esse, & non αὐθεντεῖν[?] ἀνδρός.
units.tr: Moreover, from these things a wife may also understand how she ought to conduct herself towards her husband: namely, that she also abstain from jealousy or detraction; likewise that she be subject, and not domineer [αὐθεντεῖν] over her husband.

units.la: 3 Sequentes sententiæ monent vitandas esse occasiones libidinum, & fugiendam esse fcortationem. Non enim ideo licet impune scortari, quia non licet zelare. Inquit igitur,
units.tr: 3 The following sentences warn that occasions of lust are to be avoided, and that fornication is to be fled. For it is not lawful to fornicate with impunity merely because it is not lawful to be jealous. He therefore says:

units.la: Ne respicias mulierem multiuolam )quæ nunc hunc cupit, nunc aliū:vel, ne occurrito mulieri meretricanti, qualem describit Sapiens
units.tr: "Do not regard a woman who is many-minded", who now desires this man, now another; or, do not meet a woman who plays the harlot, such as the Wise Man describes.

units.la: Prou.7. Ne forté incidas in laqueos illius) id est, fraudibus & concupiscentijs capiaris, per figna lasciuiae tibi ostensa. Inuenit enim Ecclesiastes mulierem amariorem morte, & quod laqueus est venatoris, & sagena cor eius, & vincula sunt manus eius. vnde & Diogenes, animaduertens Olympionicem quendam oculos defigere in scortum, adeo vt praeteritum capite reflexo intueretur: Ecce vt, inquit, aries Martius à puella publica, obtorto collo vinctus abducitur. Ridiculum existimabat, certare cum electis viris, & à vili puella veluti captiuum trahi sine funibus. Rec-tius igitur Alexander Magnus, quum inuitaretur vt Darij filias quas habebat captiuas inuiseret: praedicabantur .n. puellae admirabili esse forma, noluit ire, dicens, sibi non committendum, vt quum viros vicisset, à mulieribus vinceretur.
units.tr: Proverbs 7. "Lest perhaps you fall into her snares", that is, lest you be caught by deceits and lusts, through signs of wantonness shown to you. For Ecclesiastes found a woman more bitter than death, and that she is a hunter's snare, and her heart a net, and her hands are bonds. Hence also Diogenes, noticing a certain Olympic victor fixing his eyes on a prostitute so that he looked at her with his head turned back, said: "Look, the Martian ram is led away by a public girl, bound with its neck twisted." He thought it ridiculous to contend with chosen men, and to be dragged like a captive, without ropes, by a vile girl. Rather more rightly Alexander the Great, when he was invited to visit the daughters of Darius whom he held captive (for they were reported to be of admirable beauty), refused to go, saying that it was not for him to allow himself, having conquered men, to be conquered by women.

units.la: Cum assiduus fis: nec audias illam, ne forté pereas in efficacia illius) vel, vt Græcus habet: μὴ ψαλλούσης μὴ ἐνδελχίζῃς, μὴ τρο-τὶ ἄλλως ἐν τοῖς ἐπιχειρήμασιν ἀνῆς.[?] Saltatricem vocat (inquit Pellicanus) cum lasciuia & petulanter studioseque choreis assuetam, huiusmodi vitandam ac fugiendam docet: gestu enim, aspectu & tactu, alloquio & cantu prouocat ad libidinem. Tali Herodiadis filia captus est improbus alioqui rex Herodes, vt Baptistam Ioannem decollari praeceperit. Sara autem Tobiae iunioris vxor: Tu, inquit, scis Domine, quod nunquam concuui virum, & mundam seruaui animam ab omni concupiscentia: nunquam cum ludentibus miscui me, nec cum his qui in leuitate ambulant, participem me præbui.
units.tr: "While you are constantly with her, do not listen to her, lest perhaps you perish through her enticement": or, as the Greek has it: "Do not let her sing, do not wind yourself about her, do not be led on in any way in her undertakings" [μὴ ψαλλούσης μὴ ἐνδελχίζῃς, μὴ τρο-τὶ ἄλλως ἐν τοῖς ἐπιχειρήμασιν ἀνῆς]. He calls her a dancer (says Pellicanus), one accustomed to dances with wantonness and petulance and eagerness, and teaches that such a woman is to be avoided and fled: for she provokes to lust by gesture, looks, touch, speech and song. By such a woman, the daughter of Herodias, the otherwise wicked King Herod was captured, so that he ordered John the Baptist to be beheaded. But Sarah, the wife of the younger Tobias, said: "You know, Lord, that I have never lain with a man, and have kept my soul pure from all lust; I never mingled myself with those who play, nor did I make myself a partner with those who walk in levity."

units.la: Nec audias illam, procaciter & inuerecunde cantillantem, vel inhonestè alloquetem, vocis modulatione efficaci ludentem ad perdendum animas. Aspectu enim & apparatu blando alliciunt, & insipientium corda fœdis concupiscentis vulnerant ac subuertut. Significat omnes voluptatum illecebras(etiam aurium) quibus homines ad aliquod fagitium deduci possunt, fugiendas esse.
units.tr: Do not listen to her when she sings shamelessly and immodestly, or speaks indecently, playing with an effective modulation of the voice to ruin souls. For with a winning look and attractive attire they entice, and they wound and overthrow the hearts of the foolish with foul desire. This signifies that all the allurements of pleasure, including those of the ears, by which people can be led into some shameful act, are to be avoided.

units.la: Virginem ne conspicias, ne forte scandalizeris in decore illius).i.non solùm meretricem fugere debes, sed nec adolescentulam incautè ac morose aspicere ad concupiscendum eam, ne ex formæ pulchritudine illicito accendaris amore, exemplo Dauidis: sed magis sancti Iobi pudicitiam æmulare, dicentis cap. 31[?]. Pepigi fœdus cum oculis meis, ne cogitarem quidem de virgine. Etiamsi matrimonium ambiat sacrum vir quisquam, non ex decore metietur virginem deligendam, sed ex pudicitia & verecundia. Vide supra Concionem I I I.
units.tr: Do not look at a virgin, lest perhaps you be scandalized by her beauty. That is, you must not only flee the harlot, but you must not look at a young girl carelessly or foolishly with a view to desiring her, lest you be set on fire by an unlawful love from the beauty of her form, as David was. Rather, imitate the chastity of holy Job, who says in chapter 31: "I made a covenant with my eyes, that I should not even think about a virgin." Even if a man seeks a holy marriage, he should not choose a virgin by her beauty, but by her chastity and modesty. See above, Sermon III.

units.la: Ne des fornicarijs animam tuam in ullo, ne perdas te & hæreditatem tuam).i. Non consentias aliquatenus libidinosis fœminis alteris, vel meretricibus in amore Venereo. Nam ut in Prou. est cap. 5. Mulier huiumodi preciosam viri animam rapit: Ne simul multa incidas incommoda. primùm peccando in corpus: secundò animam necando: tertiò, opes annihilando. Qui n. nutrit scortum, perdet substantiam, exemplo prodigi filij. Luc. 15. qui dissipauit substantiam suam cum meretricibus viuendo luxuriosè.
units.tr: Do not give your soul to harlots in any way, lest you destroy yourself and your inheritance. That is, do not consent in any measure to other lustful women or prostitutes in Venereal love. For as it is in Proverbs, chapter 5: "Such a woman hunts down the precious soul of a man." Do not fall into many misfortunes at once: first, by sinning against the body; second, by destroying the soul; third, by annihilating your wealth. For he who keeps a harlot will lose his substance, as in the example of the prodigal son, Luke 15, who squandered his substance by living riotously with harlots.

units.la: Noli circumspicere in vicis ciuitatis, ne oberraueris in plateis illius) vel ne per eius infrequentia loca vagare. Effugere peccata non potest, qui peccandi occasionem non fugit, quas oculus incautior abundè suppeditat, secundum Augustinum: Impudicus oculus impudici cordis est nuncius. Plateas urbium peruagare qui diligit, facilè per inordinatos appetitus aberrabit. Si Dina mansisset domi, non fuisset vitiata à Sichem, Genef. 34. Præstat disciplinam & verecundiam seruare in visu. Sunt enim secundum Senecam oculi irritamenta vitiorum, duces scelerum: huic ministrant oculi adulterium, huic domum, quam concupiscat. Nam ἐκ τῆς ὄψεως[?] γίνεται τὸ [illegible, ~8 letters]. Unde & vetus ille Hebræus: Aspectus (inquit) oculi, initium est praevaricationis. Oculus enim videt, & cor concupiscit: atque instrumenta operis (intellige cordis membra) perficiunt. Hinc Democritus sibi ipsi oculos eruisse scribitur. Hinc ipse quoque Homerus humanioris literaturæ parens, cæcus est. Itaque averte potius oculos, ne videant vanitatem: quemadmodum sequitur:
units.tr: Do not look around in the streets of the city, lest you wander in its squares, or roam through its deserted places. He cannot escape sin who does not flee the occasion of sinning, which a less cautious eye supplies in abundance, according to Augustine: "The impudent eye is the messenger of an impudent heart." Whoever loves to roam the squares of cities will easily wander away through disordered desires. If Dinah had stayed at home, she would not have been violated by Shechem, Genesis 34. It is better to keep discipline and modesty in what you see. For according to Seneca the eyes are the incitements of vices and the leaders of crimes: the eyes serve adultery, they point out the house which one may desire. For [Greek: ἐκ τῆς ὄψεως γίνεται τὸ] comes from sight. Hence also that ancient Hebrew said: "The look of the eye is the beginning of transgression." For the eye sees, and the heart desires, and the members of the body (understand the limbs of the heart) carry out the work. Hence it is written that Democritus blinded himself. Hence Homer too, the father of more humane literature, was blind. Therefore, turn your eyes away rather, lest they see vanity, as follows:

units.la: Averte faciem tuam à muliere compta, & ne circumspicias speciem alienam ).i. curiosé ornatam fœminam non inspicias, ne assectu inhonesto alliciaris: limosi.n. sunt oculi, cito adhæret eis species mulieris. A minimis peccatis prudenter abstinere iubet, ne paulatim incidamus in maiora, Eccles. 19. Psal.127. Ideo etiam Christus monet Matt.5. (ubi præceptum de adulterio exponit) & dicit: Quod si oculus tuus dexter obstaculo tibi fuerit, erue illum, &c. At quod de scortatione & adulterio dicitur, in aliis quoq; peccatis locum habet: neque alius sensus est ad mouendos affectus efficacior, quàm visus, si ei vel modicum indulgeas. ut enim lupus visa oue in rabiem accenditur, sic auarum peI cuniæ & opum conspectus, invidum alienæ felicitatis splendor, iratundum hostis visus commouet, ut abrupto rationis fræno in sceJlus ruant. Et Plato hanc vim oculorum ad amandum significauit, quum sapientiam dixit, si oculis cerneretur, mirabiles sui amores excitaturam.
units.tr: Turn your face away from a woman adorned, and do not look at the strange beauty, that is, do not gaze at a woman elaborately dressed, lest you be drawn by an immodest affection. For the eyes are slippery, and the image of a woman quickly clings to them. He bids us prudently abstain from the smallest sins, lest we gradually fall into greater ones, Ecclesiasticus 19; Psalm 127. For this reason Christ also warns in Matthew 5, where he expounds the command about adultery, and says: "If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out," etc. What is said about fornication and adultery holds also for other sins. Nor is there any sense more effective for stirring the passions than sight, if you indulge it even a little. For as a wolf is inflamed to fury at the sight of a sheep, so the sight of greedy wealth and riches, the splendour that envies another's happiness, and the sight of an enemy stir up the angry, so that, the bridle of reason broken, they rush into crime. Plato also signified this power of the eyes for loving, when he said that if wisdom could be seen with the eyes, it would arouse wonderful loves for itself.

units.la: Propter speciem mulieris multi periérut, & ex hoc concupiscentia quasi ignis exardescit) Sola naturali pulchritudine, & humani corporis corrupta libidine satis provocat mulier viri appetitum, ut Sara, Genes.12. Susanna, Dan.13. Bethsaba, 2. Reg. 11. ideo decori ingenito superaddere fucum, vestiumque ornatum, prorsus iniquum & insolens est. Ideo Petrus præcipit 1. Pet.3. Quarum ornatus sit non externus, qui situs est in plicatura capillorum,& additione auri,aut in palliorū amictu. Perijt ob mulieris speciem Amnon, Salomon,Dauid,Sichem,Olofernes.Ex hoc ergo mulieris malo concupiscentia quasi ignis exardescit. Vt enim ignis lignorum struc excrescit,subtractioneque decrescit:sic luxuria per compturas & sensuum inordinatos motus: quib. subtractis, paulatim decrescit.
units.tr: Because of a woman's beauty many have perished, and from this desire blazes up like a fire. By natural beauty alone, and by the corrupt lust of the human body, a woman provokes a man's appetite enough, as Sarah did (Genesis 12), Susanna (Daniel 13), Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11). Therefore to add paint to innate beauty and to decorate one's clothing is altogether unfair and improper. For this reason Peter commands in 1 Peter 3 that their adornment should not be external, which consists in the plaiting of the hair, the addition of gold, or the wearing of fine cloaks. Amnon perished because of a woman's beauty, and Solomon, David, Shechem, Holofernes. From this evil of women, then, desire blazes up like a fire. For just as fire grows with a heap of wood and dies down when it is taken away, so lust grows through adornments and disordered movements of the senses, and when these are removed it gradually dies down.

units.la: De hoc igne dicitur Iob 31.Ignis est vsque ad consumptionem deuorans. Et Tractat.2.Cypriani de habitu virginum: Omnia licet, sed non omnia expediunt,non omnia edificant.
units.tr: Of this fire it is said in Job 31: "It is a fire that devours to destruction." And in Cyprian's second treatise, On the Dress of Virgins: "All things are lawful, but not all things are expedient; not all things build up."

units.la: Caeterum si tu te fumptuosius comas, & per publicum notabiliter incedas, oculos in te iuuentutis illicias,suspiria adolescetum potes te trahas, concupiscendi libidinem nutrias, peccandi fomenta succendas: ut etsi ipsa non pereas,alios tamen perdas, & velut gladium & venenum videntib. praebeas,excusari non potes,quasi mente casta sis & pudica. Redat guit te cultus improbus & impudicus ornatus, nec computari iam potes inter puellas & virgines Christi, quae sic viuis, ut possis adamari.
units.tr: Otherwise, if you adorn your hair too lavishly and walk conspicuously through the public place, drawing the eyes of young men upon you, and you can draw the sighs of young men, and nourish the lust of desire, and kindle the fuel of sin, then even if you yourself do not perish, you will still destroy others and offer a sword and poison to those who see you. You cannot be excused, as if you were chaste and modest in mind. An improper and immodest dress has betrayed you, and you can no longer be counted among the girls and virgins of Christ, since you live in such a way that you can be loved.

units.la: Pambus (ut refert lib.7.Eccles. Histor. Tripar.cap.1.) Athanasio episcopo praecante, ab eremo descendit in Alexandriam.
units.tr: Pambo (as the Tripartite Ecclesiastical History, book 7, chapter 1, reports), at the prayer of Athanasius the bishop, came down from the desert to Alexandria.

units.la: Cumque vidisset ibi mulierem Theatralem, fleuit: & a praesentibus rogatus quare ploraret? Duae,inquit,me res mouerunt,vna quae est illius perditio:altera vero, quod ego non tantum studeo placere Deo, quantum haec vt turpibus placere possit hominibus.
units.tr: And when he had seen there a theatrical woman, he wept; and when those present asked him why he was weeping, he said: "Two things have moved me: one is her destruction; the other is that I do not study to please God as much as she studies to please foul men with her beauty."

units.la: Cum aliena muliere non sedeas omnino, nec accumbas cum ea super cubitum, & non alterceris cum illa in vino, ne forte declinet cor tuum in illam, & sanguine tuo labaris in perditionem) Praefentius remedium(vt Pelicanus ait) contra libidines, stupra & impurum coelibatum excogitari & praestari non potuit, quàm quod naturae humanae creator & instaurator praecepit & instituit, matrimonij [?] sacramentum, quo solo carnis incentiua reformantur, ordinantur & sanctificantur, 1. Cor.nth. 7. ut cum aliena muliere ledere nec liceat, nec libeat, hoc est, cupiditatum occasiones perquirere vel sectari. Sic ut apud ethnicos probatiores, non licuerit viros paritercum mulieribus coenam sumere. Quod intelligi videtur per id quod hic subiungitur: Nec accumbas cum ea super cubitum, id est, non comedas pariter maiorum more discumbens. Non praesumas ad aequales potus vinum bibere cum muliere, vel amicitiae hilaritatisque gratia unà bibere vinum.
units.tr: Do not sit at all with another man's wife, nor recline with her on a couch, nor drink wine with her in dispute, lest perhaps your heart turn aside to her and you be ruined by your blood. Pellican says that no more effective remedy against lusts, debauchery and impure celibacy could be devised or provided than what the Creator and Restorer of human nature ordained and instituted: the sacrament of marriage, by which alone the incitements of the flesh are reformed, ordered and sanctified (1 Corinthians 7). So it is neither lawful nor pleasing to play with another's wife, that is, to seek out or pursue occasions of desire. Thus among the more upright of the heathen it was not permitted for men to take a meal together with women. This seems to be meant by what follows here: "Do not recline with her on a couch," that is, do not eat side by side with her, reclining in the manner of the great. Do not presume to drink wine with a woman as an equal, or to drink wine together for the sake of friendship and merriment.

units.la: Patriarcharum uxores feorsim cum ancillis & filijs in proprijs habitabant tabernaculis, ut patet in Genesi. Ne forte duplici fomento libidinis tentatus, vino & familiaritate, cum vicinitate loci cor tuum praeter decorum in illam declinet, ne vel consensu turpi animus maculetur, quem opportunitas protrudat in actum, unde prodeat effusio sanguinis, vitae pernicies & occasus.
units.tr: The wives of the patriarchs lived apart with their maids and sons in their own tents, as is clear from Genesis. Lest, tempted by a double incitement of lust, by wine and familiarity, and with the nearness of place, your heart inclines to her beyond what is fitting, lest the soul be stained even by a shameful consent, which opportunity thrusts into action, from which comes the shedding of blood, the ruin and downfall of life.

units.la: Legitur de Zenone Cittieo, quòd ipse simul & Cleanthes assedederint Chæremonidæ. At ille quum sentiret affectum amoris, furrexit. Hoc admirante Cleanthe, etiam à bonis, inquit, medicis audio, aduerius inflationes optimum esse remedium quietem. Subduxit se vir integerrimus imminenti periculo. Filius castissimæ virginis, autorque vitæ ac optimus medicus Iesus Christus sanctificet corda nostra, & auertat oculos nostros, ne videant vanitatem, & illuminet mentes nostras, vt cernant veritatem, quæ nos verè liberos reddat, & in nobis regem, vinum, & mulieres vincat, Amen.
units.tr: It is recorded of Zeno of Citium that he and Cleanthes both sat down beside Chaeremon. But when he felt the stirring of love, he rose up. Cleanthes marvelled at this, and he said: "I hear also from good physicians that quiet is the best remedy against swellings." The most upright man withdrew himself from the impending danger. May the Son of the most chaste Virgin, and the author of life and the best physician, Jesus Christ, sanctify our hearts, turn away our eyes lest they see vanity, and enlighten our minds so that they may discern the truth, which truly sets us free and in us conquers the king, wine, and women. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XXXV.
units.tr: CONCIO XXXV.

units.la: Eccles. 19.
units.tr: Eccles. 19.

units.la: Perarius ebriosus non ditescet, & paulatim sublabetur, qui spernit exigua. Vinum & mulieres etiam cordatos auferunt (sugillantq; sapientes:) & qui consuevit meretricibus, euadit confidentior. Caries & vermes occupabunt eum, & anima confidens auferetur (grauiq; supplicio contabescet.)
units.tr: The drunkard who loves to feast will not grow rich, and he who despises small things will fall little by little. Wine and women lead even the wise astray and confound the prudent, and he who keeps company with harlots becomes more brazen. Rottenness and worms will take hold of him, and a bold soul will be taken away, and it will waste away under heavy punishment.

units.la: 1 Duo grauissimi morbi iam passim grassantur, quos sanare vult Sapiens his verbis. Alter vocatur Ebrietas, alter Fornicatio. Quando enim recenset mala & calamitates, quæ oriuntur ex his vitijs, animique morbis, quid aliud facit, quàm quòd ab ijs nos deterrere cupit? Esse autem hos morbos sanabiles, plurimorum exemplis probari potest, quorum memorabile est illud Isaei sophistæ Assyrij. Is etenim quum primam ætatem dicasset voluptatibus, simul vt ad virilem peruenit, velut alius subito factus miram induit morum seueritatem. Itaque percontanti cuidam, num illa, fœminam ostendens, videretur formosa? σχηματίζεται, inquit, ὀφθαλμῶν id est, desij laborare ab oculis. Ab altero quopiam interrogatus, quis piscis, aut quæ auis esset ad vescendum suauissima? [illegible, ~8 letters], inquit, ταῦτα [?] id est, ista curare desij. Et adiecit, συννῆκα γὰρ τῆς Ταντάλου κήπου τρυγᾶν [?], id est, sensi enim me à Tantali hortis fructus colligere. Subindicans omnes eiusmodi voluptates, quibus iuuentus capitur, nihil aliud esse quàm vmbras ac somnia, qualia de Tantalo fabulantur Poetæ.
units.tr: 1 Two very serious diseases are now spreading everywhere, and the Wise Man in these words wishes to heal them. One is called drunkenness, the other fornication. For when he recounts the evils and calamities that arise from these vices and diseases of the soul, what else is he doing but wishing to turn us away from them? That these diseases can be cured is proved by many examples, of which the memorable one is that of Isaeus the Assyrian sophist. When he had given the first part of his life to pleasures, as soon as he reached manhood he suddenly, as if he were another man, put on a remarkable seriousness of conduct. So when someone asked him whether that woman, pointing to a female, seemed beautiful, he replied: "I have ceased to suffer from the eyes" [σχηματίζεται ὀφθαλμῶν], that is, I have stopped being troubled by my eyes. When another asked him which fish or which bird was most delightful to eat, he answered: "[illegible], these things" [ταῦτα], that is, I have stopped caring about such things. And he added: "For I have understood that I was gathering the fruits of Tantalus' garden" [συννῆκα γὰρ τῆς Ταντάλου κήπου τρυγᾶν], that is, I have realised I was gathering fruit from Tantalus' garden. By this he hinted that all such pleasures, by which youth is captured, are nothing but shadows and dreams, like those the poets tell of Tantalus.

units.la: 2 Ab ebrietate igitur cur abstinendum? Quia, inquit, operarius ebriosus non locupletabitur. i. ebrietas non solum nocet corpori, famæ, animæ, idque hic & in futuro seculo: sed etiam bonis fortunæ, etiamsi hoc vitio deditus iuxta multum laboret ac operetur. Etenim per ebrietatem lucrum consumit: & vero etiam dum ebrietati indulget, ab opere & labore impeditur necessario. Multo autem grauius periclitatur, qui non est operarius,sed ociofus & vino indulget. Sic & Salomon Prouerb.21. Qui inquit,diligit epulas,in egestate erit: qui amat vinum & pinguia,non ditabitur. & Prouerb.23. Noli esse in conuiuijs potatorum, nec in commeffationibus eorum qui carnes ad vescendum conferunt:quia vacantes potibus, & commeffatores consumentur: & vestietur pannis dormitatio. Exemplo est acolaftus, Lucæ capite decimoquinto. Idem tamen ad frugem bonam euasit.
units.tr: 2 Why, then, must we abstain from drunkenness? Because, he says, a drunken labourer will not grow rich; that is, drunkenness not only harms the body, reputation and soul, here and in the life to come, but also harms the goods of fortune, even if the man given to this vice works hard and labours much. For through drunkenness he consumes his gain, and indeed, while he indulges in drunkenness, he is necessarily hindered from work and toil. Much more dangerously is he placed who is not a labourer but idle and indulges in wine. So Solomon also says in Proverbs 21: "He who loves feasts will be in want; he who loves wine and rich food will not grow rich." And in Proverbs 23: "Do not be among drinkers of wine, nor among those who gorge themselves on meat, for drunkards and gluttons will come to poverty, and drowsiness will clothe them in rags." An example is the prodigal son, in Luke chapter 15. Yet he afterwards turned out to be a good man.

units.la: Deinde addit: Qui spernit modica,paulatim cadit. Et hoc dupliciter intelligi potest: primum sic, vt fit di&um contra prodigos, qui modica non æque diligenter curant & colligunt, atque magna,quique non tollunt fragmenta iuxta illud Christi,Ioann.6. συναγάγετε[?] τὰ περισσεύσαντα[?] κλάσματα[?], ἵνα μή τι ἀπόληται[?]. Dein vt fit di&um aduersus contemptores exiguorum seu leuium peccatorum, quæ fi nollemus propter fe ipsa fugere,tamen fugere debe remus propter ea,quę ex his nafcuntur, vt ex ebrietate nascitur ἀσωτία, Ephef. 5. Iufus, 1.Corinth. 10. incestus, Genef. 19. cædes,&c. Gregorius dicit: Si curare parua negligimus infenfibiliter seduc'ti, audacter maiora perpetramus. Qui autem soluerit, ait Christus Dominus Matth. 5. vnum de mandatis istis minimis, & docuerit sic homines, minimus vocabitur in regno cœlorum. Rectè igitur Locrenfis Zancleus (vt & Pittacus Mitylenæus) ebrios, fi ob delicta & maleficia in ius vocabantur, & ebrietatem excusabant, excusationem non recipiebat: sed duplici poena eos dignos iudicabat, tum quod ebrietatem intemperatia sibi contraxissent, tum quod per ebrietatem deliquissent. Hæc sententia in Olynthiacis à Demosthene est illustrata similitudine rerum domesticarum & humanorum corporum, in quibus parua incommoda initio accepta & neglecta, maximam postea calamitatem afferunt. In ædificijs parua domus vitia neglecta magnam sæpe ruinam trahunt, in corporibus exiguæ morborum offensiones aut occultæ aut neglectæ, maxima vi tandem erumpunt, ipsumque hominem opprimunt. Idem accidit in re familiari, in qua parua damna detrimentaq; in principio neglecta dissipationem patrimonij attulerunt.
units.tr: Then he adds: "He who despises small things falls little by little." This can be understood in two ways. First, as said against spendthrifts, who do not care for and gather small things as diligently as great ones, and who do not pick up the fragments, in keeping with Christ's words in John 6: "Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost" [συναγάγετε τὰ περισσεύσαντα κλάσματα, ἵνα μή τι ἀπόληται]. Second, as said against those who scorn small or light sins; even if we would not flee them for their own sake, we ought nonetheless to flee them on account of what arises from them, as from drunkenness arises dissolute living [ἀσωτία], Ephesians 5; incest, 1 Corinthians 10; murder, Genesis 19, and so on. Gregory says: "If we neglect to heal small wounds, we are led on without feeling it, and then we boldly commit greater ones." And Christ the Lord says in Matthew 5 that whoever breaks one of the least of these commandments and teaches men so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. Rightly, therefore, the Locrian Zaleucus (and Pittacus of Mytilene too) ruled that if drunkards were brought to court for crimes and misdeeds and pleaded drunkenness as an excuse, the excuse was not accepted; instead they judged them worthy of a double penalty, both because they had brought drunkenness on themselves through intemperance and because they had offended through drunkenness. Demosthene illustrates this judgement in his Olynthiacs with the comparison of household matters and human bodies, in which small troubles, received at first and neglected, afterwards bring the greatest calamity. In buildings, small faults in a house neglected often bring about a great collapse; in bodies, slight illnesses, either hidden or neglected, at last break out with great force and overwhelm the man himself. The same happens in domestic affairs, in which small losses and damages, neglected at the beginning, have brought about the dissipation of an inheritance.

units.la: Tertiò ab immoderato usu vini abstinendum, quia vinum apostatare facit, siue deprauat sapientes, [illegible, ~8 letters] / [illegible, ~8 letters] <bl>oder</bl> [illegible, ~7 letters] / & arguit, id est, arguendos facit sensatos. Aufert enim cor, ut Hoseas 4. ait cap. & grauat cor (quod sedes sapientiæ dicitur) quemadmodum Christus Iesus testatur, Luc. 21. Proinde gentiles, ut turpitudinem ebrietatis quodammodo demonstrarent, Bacchum, ab incondita ebriorum voce isto nomine denotarunt. Fingunt enim nudum, propter impudentiam: nam ebriosos deserit pudor: vel propter paupertatem, quod ebrietatis studiosi ad inopiam redigantur. Affingunt illi cornua, propter ferociam & in faniam ebriorum. Comites eius recensent Satyros, Silenos, Salios, Priapos, Senidas, Phallos, &c. Pythagoras quoque, sicut & Anacharsis, interrogatus, quomodo quis fugere ac euitare posset ebrietatem? respondit: Si frequenter tecum in animo volueris & reuolueris, quae ebrius facis, vel inspexeris ea, quae alij ebrij faciunt. Plato temulentiae dicitis suadebat, ut poti ad speculum sese contemplarentur, ita fore, ut ab eo vitio recederent, conspecta foeditate. Perpendat quisquis etiam illa verba, quae manus adpinxit parieti in conuiuio Balthafaris, Dan. 5. & congnoscet, ebrietatem nos priuare omnibus virtutibus: quas si Deus velit numerare, nullas reperiet in ebrio. <bl>Wenn wein eingeht/ so geht</bl> <bl>witz aus.</bl> Si velit ebrium probare impositum librae, nullam inueniet grauitatem, quae vel minimum faciat momentum Christiano dignum, <bl>fonder wirtals</bl> <bl>ein Bößwicht erfunden.</bl> Regnum coeleste ab illo seiungitur, & sobrietatis candidatis attribuitur. Deniq; magnae sunt vires vini, ut est 3. Efd. 3. imo ignea vis vini, teste Basilio, quam primum corpore humano fuerit immoderatius recepta, incendit ignita diaboli iacula. Nam vinum rationem & mentem demergit: at cupiditates & voluptates non secus ac oleum flammam, in flammat. Vnde non raro in scripturis haec duo peccata coniunguntur, videl. ebrietas & fcortatio: ut Hof. 4. Prouerb. 23. Rom. 13. Gal.5.& hoc loco. Dicit enim Siracides: Vinuum & mulieres deprauant prudentes, confutantque cordatos. Indicauit & Anacharsis vinū adimere homini rectum iudicium. Quidam enim (vt refert Athenæus lib. 9.) in conuiuio videns vxorem illius, vxorem, inquit, deformem duxisti Anacharsi. Hic Anacharsis, Prorsus ita mihi videtur, inquit, sed heus puer infunde mihi meracius, vt eam reddam formosam.
units.tr: Thirdly, we must abstain from immoderate use of wine, because wine makes men fall away from the faith, or corrupts the wise, (illegible) and convicts, that is, makes the sensible ones fit to be convicted. For it takes away the heart, as Hosea says in chapter 4, and weighs down the heart (which is called the seat of wisdom), as Christ Jesus testifies in Luke 21. Accordingly the Gentiles, to show in some way the shamefulness of drunkenness, named Bacchus by this name from the disorderly speech of drunkards. For they represent him naked, on account of shamelessness, for shame deserts drunkards; or on account of poverty, because those devoted to drink are reduced to want. They attach horns to him, on account of the ferocity and madness of drunkards. His companions they list as Satyrs, Silenuses, Salii, Priapuses, Senides, Phalli, and so on. Pythagoras too, as also Anacharsis, when asked how someone might flee and avoid drunkenness, answered: "If you often call to mind and recall in your own mind what drunkards do, or observe what other drunkards do." Plato advised those who suffered from drunkenness to look at themselves in a mirror when they had drunk, so that, seeing their own foulness, they would withdraw from the vice. Let whoever considers also those words which a hand painted on the wall at Belshazzar's feast, Daniel 5, and he will recognise that drunkenness deprives us of all virtues; if God wished to count them, he would find none in a drunkard. "When wine goes in, wit goes out." If one wished to weigh a drunkard in the balance, one would find no gravity that would carry the least weight worthy of a Christian; he is found to be a scoundrel in the tavern. The kingdom of heaven is cut off from him and assigned to the candidates of sobriety. Finally, the powers of wine are great, as in 3 Esdras 3; indeed, according to Basil, the fiery force of wine, once it has been taken into the human body immoderately, kindles the burning darts of the devil. For wine drowns reason and mind, but it sets desires and pleasures alight, just as oil does to a flame. Hence in Scripture these two sins are often joined together, namely drunkenness and fornication, as in Hosea 4, Proverbs 23, Romans 13, Galatians 5, and in this place. For Ecclesiasticus says: "Wine and women corrupt the prudent and confound the wise." Anacharsis also showed that wine takes from a man right judgement. For someone (as Athenaeus reports in book 9), seeing his wife at a banquet, said: "You have married an ugly wife, Anacharsis." Anacharsis replied: "That is indeed how she seems to me. But, boy, pour me something stronger, so that I may make her beautiful."

units.la: ʒ Primum ergo eadem de causa cauendum à scortatione & seruitute mulierum, qua ab ipsa ebrietate. Quemadmodum enim vini, sic etiam mulierum immoderatus vsus & amor, ipsos quoque qui fuerant sapientes, decipit, & à Deo auertit. Scimus quid per mulieres acciderit Adamo, Lotho, Samsoni, Dauidi, Iobo, Petro, &c. De Salomone legitur ʒ. Reg.11. Et auerterunt mulieres cor eius. Cumque effet senex, deprauatum est cor eius per mulieres, vt sequeretur deos alienos. Si hoc Salomoni accidit, regi tanta sapientia à Deo (qui secundò ei apparuit) ornato, vt vniuersa terra desiderarit vultum eius, vt audiret sapientiam eius: quid putamus alijs hominibus non tam sapientibus, tum accidisse, tum accidere posse? Non enim temerè dixit Zorobabel, ʒ. Esdr. 4. Multi propter mulieres mente alienati sunt, multi serui facti, multi perierunt, multi propter fœminas lapsi peccauerunt. Crates Thebanus dicebat, mœchos tragicos præmia referre exilia ac cædes: comicos scortatores ex luxu &[?] temulentia lucri facere insaniam.
units.tr: 3 First, therefore, we must guard against fornication and slavery to women for the same reason as against drunkenness itself. For just as with wine, so the immoderate use and love of women deceives even those who had been wise, and turns them away from God. We know what happened through women to Adam, Lot, Samson, David, Job, Peter, and so on. Of Solomon we read in 3 Kings 11: "And his wives turned away his heart." And when he was old, his heart was corrupted by women so that he followed strange gods. If this happened to Solomon, a king adorned by God with such great wisdom (who appeared to him a second time), so that the whole earth desired to see his face, to hear his wisdom, what do we think has happened, and what can happen, to other men who are not so wise? For Zerubbabel did not speak carelessly in 3 Esdras 4: "Many have lost their minds because of women, many have become slaves, many have perished, many have sinned and fallen because of women." Crates of Thebes used to say that adulterers in tragedies bring rewards of exile and slaughter, and that whoremongers in comedies make madness a source of profit through luxury and drunkenness.

units.la: Secundo igitur loco Sapiens dicit: Qui meretricibus hæret, seu fornicarijs se iungit, erit nequam: vel, est nequior. Nam per fornicationem trahitur ad alia nequiora: sicut Salomon fuit tractus per mulieres ad sequenda idola.i. tandem peruenit ad spiritualem fcortationem: quemadmodum & Israelitæ, Num. 25. Ita Dauid de adulterio descendit ad homicidium. Alij pro πονηρότεροι[?] legunt τολμηρότεροι[?]: temerarior erit: Germani vertunt: <bl>wirdt frech vnd wild[?].</bl> Discet lasciuiam, procacitatem, & omnem inhonestatem ab illis, scil. πόρνοις[?], qui se illis sociat (Haec perpendant, qui lupanaria defendunt) Ideo Paulus monet: Non commiscemini fornicarijs: & nolite iugum ducere cum infidelibus.
units.tr: In the second place, then, the Wise Man says: Whoever clings to harlots, or joins himself to whoremongers, will be worthless, or rather, will be worse. For through fornication a man is drawn on to other, worse things, just as Solomon was led through women to follow idols, that is, he finally came to spiritual fornication, as the Israelites did in Num. 25. So David descended from adultery to murder. Others read [πονηρότεροι] as [τολμηρότεροι]: he will be more reckless. The Germans render it, "becomes bold and wild." He will learn wantonness, impudence and every kind of dishonour from those [πόρνοις], namely the harlots, with whom he associates himself. (Let those who defend brothels weigh this.) For this reason Paul warns: Keep no company with fornicators, and do not be yoked together with unbelievers.

units.la: 1. Corinth. 5. 2. Corin. 6.
units.tr: 1. Corinth. 5. 2. Corin. 6.

units.la: Tertio addit, Putredo & vermes hæreditabunt, vel obtinebunt illum .i. loco mercedis accipiet atq; sibi acquiret morbum Gallicum, pediculos & cæteros morbos mendicorum, vt Luther.exponit. Atque sic abbreviabit suam vitam: varie .n. periclitabitur ebrietate & sodalitio criminosorum, vt ante tempus & præmatura morte intercipiendus & infeliciter occidendus, futurus proximè putredo & vermis: sed & gehennæ fœtores, & conscientiæ perpetuum vermem, qui nunquam moritur, experietur (nisi resipuerit) qui nunc dum viuit fœtore & corruptione luxuriae delectatur. Non .n. frustrà scriptum est Pro.10. Anni impiorum breuiabuntur. & Eccles.7. Humilia valde animam tuam, memento iram non tardaturam : quoniam vindicta impij, ignis & vermis. Et Heb.13. Scortatores & adulteros iudicabit Deus. Item hoc loco: Homo temerarius tolletur, graviqué supplicio contabescet: idque alijs in exemplum, ad terrendum non solum minores, sed etiam maiores. Sic.n.vetus interpres legit: Et extolletur in exemplum maius, & tolletur de numero anima eius. Extolletur) .i. extra consortium bonorum tolletur. Graecus habet, ἐξαιρεθήσεται[?]. Quo verbo etiam Apostolus usus est 1.Cor.5. inquiens: ἐξάρατε τὸ πονηρόν, ἐξ ὑμῶν αὐτῶν[?]. Et tolletur de numero) selectorum. Anima eius) rapta à daemonibus. Sic Lyranus explicat. Porro maius exemplum nominat (inquit Pellican,) publicum supplicium à magistratu indictum. Publicè .n. talis ad aliorum terrorem punietur, ut tollatur de medio vita fidelium praevaricatoris, ut pestilente flagellato stultus aliquà do sapientior fiat. Deus faxit, ut vel videntes, vel audientes iudicia eius, quae in peccatores exercet, vitam nostram emendemus, ac ita nos geramus, quemadmodum Christus filius Dei, Luc.13. & Apostolus eius, 1.Corin. 10. nos monent, ne in eadem iudicia & supplicia incidamus,
units.tr: Thirdly he adds: rottenness and worms will inherit him, or will obtain him; that is, he will receive as his wages, and acquire for himself, the French pox, lice and the other diseases of beggars, as Luther explains. And so he will shorten his life. For he will be variously endangered by drunkenness and the company of criminals, so that he will be cut off before his time, by premature death and unhappily destroyed, soon to become rottenness and worm. He will also experience the stench of hell and the perpetual worm of conscience, which never dies (unless he repents), he who now, while he lives, delights in the stench and corruption of lust. For it is not without reason written in Prov. 10: The years of the wicked will be shortened; and in Eccles. 7: Humble your soul greatly, remember that vengeance will not be delayed, for the vengeance of the wicked is fire and worm; and in Heb. 13: God will judge fornicators and adulterers. Likewise in this place: The reckless man will be taken away and will waste away under heavier punishment, and that as an example to others, to terrify not only the lesser but also the greater. For so the Old Translator reads: "He shall be lifted up as a greater example, and his soul shall be taken from the number." Shall be lifted up: that is, he shall be taken out of the fellowship of the good. The Greek has [ἐξαιρεθήσεται], a word the Apostle also used in 1 Cor. 5, saying: "Put away the evil from among yourselves" [ἐξάρατε τὸ πονηρόν, ἐξ ὑμῶν αὐτῶν]. And shall be taken from the number: of the chosen. His soul: snatched away by demons, so Lyra explains. Moreover, he names a greater example (says Pellican): public punishment inflicted by the magistrate. For such a man will be punished publicly for the terror of others, so that the evil of the transgressor is removed from the midst of the life of the faithful, and so that the fool, scourged like a plague, may become somewhat wiser. May God grant that we, whether seeing or hearing his judgments which he executes on sinners, amend our lives and conduct ourselves as Christ the Son of God (Luke 13) and his Apostle (1 Cor. 10) warn us, so that we do not fall into the same judgments and punishments.

units.la: Amen.
units.tr: Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XXXVI.
units.tr: SERMON XXXVI.

units.la: Eccles. 25.
units.tr: Eccles. 25.

units.la: Tria[?] me exhilarant, & coram Domino simul & hominibus condecorant. Nempe concordia fratrum, amicitia proximorum, & vir ac vxor inter se bene consentientes.
units.tr: Three things delight me, and make me honourable before the Lord and before men: namely, the concord of brothers, the friendship of neighbours, and a husband and wife agreeing well with one another.

units.la: 1 Æquum atque adeo iustissimum est, vt diligentissimè studeamus placere Deo & illius sapientiae i[?] filio eius Christo Iesu domino nostro, in omnibus, & quibuscunque rebus possumus: quoniam non solum creauit nos, cum nondum essemus, sed etiam liberauit nos & saluos fecit, non secundum opera nostra, sed secundum misericordiam & gratiam suam, per Iesum Christum filium suum dilectum, cui non pepercit: sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit illum, cum adhuc inimici & peccatores essemus.
units.tr: 1. It is fair, and indeed most just, that we should most diligently strive to please God and his wisdom, that is, his Son Christ Jesus our Lord, in all things and in whatever we can. For God not only created us when we did not yet exist, but also freed and saved us, not according to our works but according to his mercy and grace, through Jesus Christ his beloved Son, whom he did not spare, but delivered up for us all while we were still enemies and sinners.

units.la: Quia vero non illud Deo placitum est & acceptum, quod nobis rectum videtur, qui corrupto iudicio fumus, & quorum viae ac cogitationes longissimè à cogitationibus & viis Dei distant, ideo ex verbo Dei, in quo suam mentem & voluntatem expressit Deus, discendum fuerit, quid velit & à nobis exigat.
units.tr: Yet since what seems right to us is not what pleases and is acceptable to God, for we are corrupt in judgement, and our ways and thoughts are far removed from the thoughts and ways of God, we must therefore learn from the Word of God, in which God has expressed his mind and will, what he wills and requires of us.

units.la: Audiamus igitur spiritu veritatis loquentem per Sirachi filium, qui ostendit nobis quæ non solum Deo, verumetiam hominibus probantur ac placent, seu quibus Sapientia se exornari, & apud Dominum & apud homines venustam effici dicit, nempe illa tria, concordia fratrum, amicitia propinquorum seu vicinorum, & unitas viri & uxoris. Cum enim Deus sit charitas, quid melius illi placere potest, quàm cum homines se mutuo charitatis officijs prosequantur? Siquidem ubi charitas est, ibi omne odium & rixa, & contentio, & cætera mala longissimè[?] absunt. Unde & Paulus inquit Rom.14. Si propter cibum frater tuus contristatur, non iam secundum charitatem ambulas. Ne cibo tuo illum perdas, pro quo Christus mortuus[?] est. Ne vestrum igitur bonum, hominum maledicentiæ sit obnoxium. Non est enim regnum Dei cibus ac potus, sed iustitia & pax & gaudium in spiritu sancto. Etenim qui per hæc seruit Christo, acceptus est, & probatus hominibus. Itaque quæ pacis sunt sectemur, & quæ ædificationis, alius erga alium.
units.tr: Let us then listen to the Spirit of truth speaking through the son of Sirach, who shows us what is approved and pleasing not only to God but also to men. He says that wisdom is adorned by these things and made lovely before the Lord and before men, namely those three: the concord of brothers, the friendship of kinsmen or neighbours, and the union of husband and wife. For since God is love, what can please him better than men showing one another the duties of love? Where love is, there all hatred, strife, contention and other evils are far absent. Hence Paul also says, Romans 14: "If your brother is grieved because of food, you no longer walk according to love. Do not destroy with your food the one for whom Christ died. Therefore let not your good be exposed to the slander of men. For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit. For whoever serves Christ in these things is acceptable and approved by men. So let us pursue the things of peace and the things by which we build up one another."

units.la: 2 Si autem unquam opus fuit exhortari homines ad amplexandam colendamq; pacem, charitatem & concordiam: certè hodierno die quam maximè opus est. Quandoquidem reuera nùc illud tempus existit, de quo Christus Matth. 24. Consurget gens contra gentem, & regnum contra regnum. Et quoniam abundabit iniquitas, refrigescet charitas multorum. Item Apostolus Paul. 2. Timot. 3. Erunt enim homines φιλαύτοι, ἀτοξοι,[?]
units.tr: 2. If ever there was need to exhort men to embrace and cultivate peace, charity and concord, then surely there is the greatest need of it today. For indeed that time is now at hand of which Christ speaks, Matthew 24: "Nation will rise against nation and kingdom against kingdom. And because iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold." Likewise the Apostle, 2 Timothy 3: "For men will be lovers of themselves, covetous, boastful, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, unholy, without love..."

units.la: [illegible, ~8 letters] [?] Nonne enim omnes Christiani dici volunt? Quotusquisque autem est, in quo appareat signum Christiani hominis ac fratris, de quo Christus Ioan. 13. In hoc cognoscent omnes, quod discipuli mei estis, si charitate habueritis inter vos mutuam? Caeterum nos, qui vere Christiani non solum dici, sed & esse volumus, debemus, ut semper & in omnibus placere Deo & doctrinam servatoris nostri ornare, iuxta Apostoli admonitionem, 2 Cor. 5. Tit. 2. sic etiam in illis tribus rebus, de quibus hoc loco Sapiens: qui ternarium format, cum plura componere possit. Quod genus antiquae doctrinae est, & hanc commoditatem habet, ut quae sic traduntur & numeris comprehenduntur, memoria facilius comprehendi possint.
units.tr: [illegible] Do not all Christians wish to be called so? But how few are there in whom the sign of a Christian and a brother appears, of which Christ speaks in John 13: "By this shall all men know that you are my disciples, if you have love one for another"? We, however, who wish to be truly Christians, not only called but also actually so, ought always and in all things to please God and to adorn the doctrine of our Saviour, according to the Apostle's admonition (2 Cor. 5; Titus 2). So also in those three things of which the Wise Man speaks in this place, who forms a triad though he could have put together more. This is the kind of ancient teaching it is, and it has this advantage: what is handed down in this way and comprehended in numbers can be grasped more easily by the memory.

units.la: § In tribus, inquit, placitum est spiritui meo, quae sunt probata coram Deo & hominibus (ita legit vulgatus interpres) primum est, ὁμόνοια ἀδελφῶν[?]. i. concordia fratrum, vel amicorum eiusdem parentelae, vel consanguineorum, qui etiam dicuntur fratres in scriptura. Sic. n. dicit Abraham ad Loth, nepotem suum: Ne quaeso sit iurgium inter me & te, & inter pastores meos & pastores tuos. Fratres. n. sumus. De hac φιλαδελφίας[?] habemus etiam Gen. 37. Psal. 133. 1. Cor. 1. 2. Pet. 1. 1. Ioa.
units.tr: "In three things," he says, "my spirit is pleased, which are approved before God and men" (so the Vulgate translator reads). The first is the concord of brothers [ὁμόνοια ἀδελφῶν], that is, harmony of brothers, or of friends of the same kinship, or of blood relations, who are also called brothers in Scripture. For so Abraham says to Lot, his nephew: "Let there be no strife, I pray you, between me and you, and between my herdsmen and your herdsmen; for we are brethren" (Gen. 13). We have also examples of this brotherly love [φιλαδελφίας] in Gen. 37, Ps. 133, 1 Cor. 1, 2 Pet. 1, 1 John

units.la: 3. Sic. n. Iudas fratribus suis dixit de Iosepho: Quid nobis prodest, si occiderimus fratrem nostrum[?], & celaverimus sanguinem ipsius? melius est vt vendatur Hismaelitis,& manus nostræ non polluantur: frater.n. & caro nostra est. Ita Dauid,Ecce quàm bonū & quàm iucundū,habitare fratres in vnū. Sicut oleū preciosum super caput, quod descēdit in barbam Aaron, quod descendit in oræ vestimenti eius. Sicut ros Hermon qui descendit in montem Sion: Quoniam illic promisit Dominus benedictionē, & vitam vsq; in seculū. Ita Paulus, Obsecro vos fratres, per nomen [?] Domini nostri Iesu Christi,vt idē loquamini omnes,& non sint inter vos dissidia,sed sitis integrum corpus, eadē mente & eadem sententia. Sic Petrus: In pietate aut [?] subministrate [?] fraternam charitatem. Et Ioannes,Nos scimus quòd translati sumus de morte ad vitā, quia diligimus fratres. Qui nō diligit fratre, manet in morte. Omnis qui odit fratrem suum, homicida est. Et scitis quòd omnis homicida non habet vitam æternam in se manentem. Per hoc cognouimus charitatem,quoniam ille animam suam pro nobis posuit, & nos debemus pro fratribus animas ponere. Hæc etsi de omnibus Christianis & spiritualibus fratribus dicta sunt: tamen etiam ad naturales fratres referri possunt ac debent. Est autem fratrū inter se concordia (vt Antisthenes dixit) quouis muro firmius munimentum.
units.tr: 3. So Judah said to his brothers about Joseph: "What profit is it to us if we slay our brother and conceal his blood? It is better that he be sold to the Ishmaelites, and that our hands not be defiled; for he is our brother and our flesh" (Gen. 37). So David: "Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity! It is like the precious ointment upon the head, that ran down upon the beard, even Aaron's beard, that went down to the skirts of his garments; it is like the dew of Hermon, that falls upon the mountains of Zion; for there the Lord commanded the blessing, even life for evermore" (Ps. 133). So Paul: "I beseech you, brethren, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all speak the same thing, and that there be no divisions among you, but that you be perfectly joined together in the same mind and the same judgement" (1 Cor. 1). So Peter: "In godliness... minister brotherly kindness" (2 Pet. 1). And John: "We know that we have passed from death unto life, because we love the brethren. He that loveth not his brother abideth in death. Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer; and ye know that no murderer hath eternal life abiding in him. Hereby perceive we the love of God, because he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren" (1 John 3). Although these things are said of all Christians and spiritual brothers, they can and ought also to be applied to natural brothers. Indeed, the concord of brothers, as Antisthenes said, is a defence firmer than any wall.

units.la: Secundum, quod pulchrum est, & Deo ac hominibus placet, est φιλία πλησίων [?], i. amor proximorum, dum ciues & vicini mutuum sibi diligunt: erunt enim ciuitas firma. melior est vicinus iuxta, quàm frater procul, Prou. 27. Non aurum splendidum (vt Plato ex veteri poemate citat) neque adamas ita fulgurat in oculis, sicut bonorum virorum mentes consentientes. Ideo mandauit dominus Leuit. 19. ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου ὡς ἑαυτόν. Ecclef. 6. οἱ ἀγωνιῶντές σοι ἔγραψαν πόλει[?]. Ieremiæ 29. Quærite pacem ciuitatis ad quam transmigrare vos feci, & orate pro ea ad Dominum, quia in pace illius erit pax vobis. Et Romanor. 12. Si fieri potest, quantum in vobis est, cum omnibus hominibus in pace viuentes.
units.tr: The second, which is fair and pleasing to God and men, is friendship of neighbours [φιλία πλησίων], that is, love of neighbours, when citizens and neighbours love one another mutually; for the city will be strong. "Better is a neighbour that is near than a brother far off" (Prov. 27). Not gold, as Plato cites from an old poem, nor the diamond flashes so brightly in the eyes as the agreeing minds of good men. Therefore the Lord commanded in Lev. 19: "You shall love your neighbour as yourself" [ἀγαπήσεις τὸν πλησίον σου ὡς ἑαυτόν]. Ecclus. 6: "Those who are anxious for you have written to the city" [οἱ ἀγωνιῶντές σοι ἔγραψαν πόλει]. Jeremiah 29: "Seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the Lord for it; for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace." And Rom. 12: "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men."

units.la: Tertium est, ἡ γυνὴ ἀνδρὶ ἑαυτῆς συμπεφιλωμένοι[?] .i. vxor atque vir inter se consentientes, siue concorditer coniuncteq; viuentes: scil. in bona domus dispensatione, & vero etiam in cæteris rebus, ne discordiæ interserantur, neque preces interrumpantur, 1. Pet. 3. Amicus enim (inquit Ecclef. 40.) & socius commodè conueniunt, sed vtrunque antecellit vxor iuncta viro .i. <bl>ein weib / das mit ihrem</bl> <bl>mann eins ist.</bl> Sed contrà βοοζύγιον[?] Καλλύμενον γυνὴ πονηρά[?]. Ecclef. 26. Si ergo vxorem habes ex animi tui sententia, ne eam repudiaueris, Ecclef. 7. Relinquet enim homo patrem suum & matrem & adhærebit vxori suæ, & erunt in carnem vnam, Gen 2. Quod ergo Deus copulauit[?], homo ne separet, Matth. 19. Vt vero possfit[?] bene conuenire inter coniuges, nihil eon[?] fulius[?] faerit, quàm vt singuli suum officium diligenter considerent & faciant. Vxor subdita sit viro proprio, veluti domino, in omnibus, tum paruis, tum magnis rebus, ijsq; honestis & iustis. Vir diligat vxorem suam, sicut & Christus dilexit ecclesiam. Vxor reuereatur virum. Et vir non sit amarulentius aduersus vxorem, Ephes.5. Col.1[?]. Praecipuum (vt scribit Chrysostomus in cap.2.ep. ad Titum) illud est domesticae pacis, ac bonorum omnium fundamentum, si vxor viro per omnia consentiens sit. Nam vbi hoc fit, nihil triste contingere poterit. Quo pacto enim, cum caput corpori connexum, coniunctumque sit, vlla ibi seditio, vlla dissensio possit exoriri? Necessario profecto reliqua omnia in pace sunt. Principibus namque pacatis, quis iam pacem diuidere possit, atque discindere? &c.
units.tr: The third is the wife and husband being of one mind with each other [ἡ γυνὴ ἀνδρὶ ἑαυτῆς συμπεφιλωμένοι], that is, a wife and husband agreeing with each other, or living together harmoniously: namely in the good management of the household, and indeed in all other matters, so that discords do not creep in and prayers are not hindered (1 Peter 3). For "a friend and a companion meet well together," says Ecclesiasticus 40, "but a wife joined to a husband surpasses both": a wife who is one with her husband. But on the contrary, a wicked wife is a yoke that burdens [βοοζύγιον]. Ecclesiasticus 26. If then you have a wife after your own mind, do not put her away (Ecclus. 7). "For a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and they shall be one flesh" (Gen. 2). "What God has joined together, let not man put asunder" (Matt. 19). But so that husband and wife may agree well, nothing is more useful than that each diligently consider and perform his own duty. Let the wife be subject to her own husband, as to a lord, in all things, both small and great, and in honest and just matters. Let the husband love his wife, as Christ also loved the Church. Let the wife revere her husband. And let the husband not be bitter against his wife (Eph. 5; Col. 3). Chrysostom, in his commentary on the Epistle to Titus, chapter 2, writes that the chief thing for domestic peace, and the foundation of all good things, is if the wife agrees with her husband in all things. For where this is so, nothing sad can happen. For how can any sedition or dissension arise there, when the head is joined and connected to the body? Surely all the rest must then be in peace. For when the princes are at peace, who can then divide or tear apart the peace? And so on.

units.la: 4 Porrò hæc tria sicuti sunt probata coram Deo & hominibus: sic contraria sunt re probata. Ac fieri non potest, vt vitam miserabilem non ducant fratres, vicini, & coniuges, inter quos discordia, odium & dissensio exsistit. Deus, qui est author non confusionis, sed pacis, sit cum omnibus nobis in Christo Iesu, Amen.
units.tr: 4 Moreover, just as these three things have been shown to be approved before God and men, so their opposites have been shown by experience. Nor can it be that brothers, neighbours and spouses among whom discord, hatred and dissension exist do not lead a wretched life. May God, who is the author not of confusion but of peace, be with all of us in Christ Jesus. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XXXVII
units.tr: SERMON XXXVII

units.la: Eccles. 26.
units.tr: Eccles. 26.

units.la: Beatus est vir probæ mulieris: nam numerus dierum ipsius duplicabitur. Mulier strenua virum suum exhilarat, facitq; ut annos vitæ suæ exigat per tranquillitatem. Vxor bona, portio est bona, propræmio obtinget Dominum reverentibus. Tam divitis cor quàm pauperis lætificat, ut omni tempore vultu sint hilari.
units.tr: Blessed is the man who has a good wife, for the number of his days shall be doubled. A capable wife gladdens her husband and makes him spend the years of his life in tranquillity. A good wife is a good portion; she shall obtain a reward among those who fear the Lord. She gladdens the heart of rich and poor alike, so that at all times their faces are cheerful.

units.la: 1 Hæc verba non solùm ostendunt, qui in fausto matrimonio sint constituti: sed etiam simul docent, quid in mulieribus spectare, & quales ipsimet esse debeant, qui fauste ac bene in coniugio vivere cupiunt. Dicit enim Sapiens: Bonæ fæminæ vir beatus est, & duplicem vivit ætatem. Nam & hæc vita suam beatitudinem, etsi imperfectam habet. Mulier bona unde cognosci queat, ex verbis Christi loquentis de homine bono, à Deo scilicet hoc habente, ut sit bonus, liquet, Matt. 12. Si enim spiritum habet placidum & quietum, 1. Pet. 3. si linguæ eius inest pietas, comitas, & sanitas, non est vir eius humanæ conditionis .i. ita felix est, ut Deus esse videatur. Eccles. 36[?]. Unde Salomon Proverb. 18. Qui invenit mulierem bonam, invenit bonum, & hauriet iucunditatem à Domino: & ut hîc legimus, Numerus dierum illius duplex est. Eorum enim vita pro iucunditate & fide diutius perseverat. Animus enim, gaudens floridam facit ætatem.
units.tr: These words do not only show who are placed in a happy marriage; they also teach at the same time what to look for in women, and what kind of women themselves ought to be, if they wish to live happily and well in wedlock. For the Wise Man says: the man who has a good wife is blessed, and he lives a double life, for this life also has its happiness, though an imperfect one. How a good wife may be recognised is clear from the words of Christ speaking of a good man, that is, one to whom God has given this, that he be good, Matt. 12. For if he has a calm and quiet spirit, 1 Pet. 3, and if piety, courtesy and soundness are present in his speech, he is not of ordinary human condition, that is, he is so happy that he seems to be God. Eccles. 36[?]. Hence Solomon in Prov. 18: Whoever finds a good wife finds a good thing, and shall draw delight from the Lord. And, as we read here, the number of his days is doubled, for their life persists longer in delight and faith. For a joyful mind makes for a flourishing old age.

units.la: Zelus autem & iracundia minuent dies, & ante tempus senectam cogitatus molestus adducet, Eccles. 30. Melior quoque mors quàm vita amara: quin & melius est modico tempore vivere cum iucunditate, quàm diutius cum cordis amaritudine. Ideo pergit Sapiens & dicit, (praecedentem versum clarius exponens) Mulier fortis oblectat virum suum, & annos vitæ illius in pace implebit. Fortis mulier intelligitur fidelis, solida, virtuosa & constans in bono, [?]ἀνδρεία, etiam si corpore fragilior fit & mollior, quæ scilicet strenuè instat familiæ & domui gubernandæ, ist heuslich / mannlich / fœmineum ingenium masculo animo excitans, 2. Mach. 7. omnia agens virili animo, [?]חיל Prou. 31. & 12. minimè otiosa, dissoluta aut vana. Huiusmodi oblectat virum suum, in conversatione iucunda, pacifica, honesta, cū qua diutius vivit, quia tranquillè usq; ad finem vitæ: non enim senem exhorrescet, sed in primo amore perseverabit semper: non enim tantùm carnalis est amor ut tabescat cum tempore, sed virtuosus, qui cū virtute & canicie semper maturescit. Posse aut & mulierem fortem & dici & esse testatur etiā Socrates, qui dicebat muliebrem sexum non minus esse docilem & ad disciplinas, & ad omnem virtutem, etiam fortitudinem, quae tanquam viris propria, Graecis a viro dicitur ἀνδρεία, si diligenter instituatur. Id collegit ex puella saltatricula, quae induta in conuiuium mira arte trochos duodecim in altum proiectos excipiebat, ita temperato altitudinis spacio, numerisque pedum, ut nunquam falleret: eadem inter acutissimos gladios, non sine horrore spectantium, impauida saltaret. Praeterea inquit, Mulier bona pars vel fors bona est. i. praecipuum Dei donum. Item: Tam diu vites quam pauperes, si bonae mentis sunt, ij semper in Domino vultum habentes hilarem exultant. vel, vt Lutheri versio habet: Es sey reich oder arm/ so ists im ein trost/ vnnd macht jhn allzeit frölich. Hinc Theocritus, Κυρ' ἀγαθῆς γλυκύτερον ἀνδρὶ γυναικός. Hoc est, nihil Cyrne, dulcius viro bona coniuge. Et alius Poeta inquit, [illegible, ~20 letters] ἰτὶν ἀχοίλις. Id est, viro tristi solatio est uxor.
units.tr: Zeal and anger, however, shorten the days, and a troubled thought brings on old age before its time, Eccles. 30. Death too is better than a bitter life; indeed it is better to live for a short time with delight than longer with bitterness of heart. Therefore the Wise Man goes on and says, explaining the preceding verse more clearly: a strong wife delights her husband, and will fill the years of his life in peace. A strong wife is understood to be faithful, steadfast, virtuous and constant in goodness, courage [ἀνδρεία], even if she is more fragile and softer in body; she who vigorously sets about governing the household and the home, strength [חיל], Prov. 31 and 12, arousing a womanly nature with a manly spirit, 2 Macc. 7, doing all things with a manly spirit, and by no means idle, dissolute or vain. Such a wife delights her husband in pleasant, peaceable and honourable company, and he lives with her longer, because she remains calm until the end of life. For she will not shrink from him when he is old, but will always persevere in the first love; for love is not merely carnal, to waste away with time, but virtuous, which always matures together with virtue and grey hair. That a woman can be called and be strong is also attested by Socrates, who said that the female sex is no less teachable in the disciplines, and for every virtue, even courage, which is called by the Greeks andreia from anēr, a man, as if proper to men, if it is diligently taught. He drew this conclusion from a young dancing girl who, brought into a banquet, caught twelve hoops thrown high with remarkable skill, so measuring the height and the number of steps that she never failed; and the same girl danced among the sharpest swords, to the horror of the spectators, without fear. Moreover, he says, a good wife is a part or a good chance, that is, a special gift of God. Likewise: as long as rich and poor, if they are of a good mind, always rejoice with a cheerful countenance in the Lord. Or, as Luther's version has it: whether rich or poor, it is a comfort to him and always makes him cheerful. Hence Theocritus: "Nothing, Cyrne, is sweeter to a man than a good wife" [Κυρ' ἀγαθῆς γλυκύτερον ἀνδρὶ γυναικός]. And another poet says: a wife is a consolation to a sad husband [ἰτὶν ἀχοίλις]; that is, a wife is a solace to a gloomy husband.

units.la: 2 Haec cum ita sint, non solum mulieres operam dare debent atque studere, ut sint bonae & fortes, <bl>nicht trauch[?] vnd saul</bl> (siquidem non vituperari, sed laudari velint, Pro. ult.) sed etiam viri in contrahendo matrimonio spectare debent, non diuitias mundanas, gloriam terrenam, formam corporis, sed potius bonitatem & fortitudinem: si modo felix habere coniugium desiderent. Ante omnia autem tam viri quam mulieres Dominum timeant. Quemadmodum enim Salomon in fine Prouerbiorum dicit de muliere: Mulier quæ timet Dominum, illa laude est digna : Date ei de fructu manuum eius, & laudent eam in portis opera eius: sic scribit de viro hoc loco Siracid. ἐν [?]μερίδι φοβουμένων κύριον δοθήσεται.i. Dominum metuentibus forte datur. vel vt vulgatꝰ interpres habet: in parte bona timentium Deum (id est, pro bona parte mulier bona est inter timentes Deum) dabitur viro(scilicet à Deo. Domus enim & diuitiæ dantur à parentibus: à Domino autem proprie vxor prudens, Prouerb. 19.) pro factis bonis (seu ob recte facta : unde dicitur communiter, vxorem bonam esse speciale Dei donum : item: <bl>(Ein from weib ist des mans-</bl> <bl>ö[?]-der herzens heil/ man findt sie aber selten feil.)</bl> Huc facit etiam Psalmus Dauidis 128. qui sic incipit: Beatus quicunq; timet Dominum, qui ambulat in viis eius,&c.
units.tr: Since this is so, not only should women take care and strive to be good and strong, (since they wish to be praised and not blamed, Prov. last chapter), but men too, when contracting marriage, ought to look not to worldly riches, earthly glory or bodily form, but rather to goodness and strength, if indeed they desire to have a happy marriage. Above all, both men and women should fear the Lord. For just as Solomon says at the end of the Proverbs about the woman: "A woman who fears the Lord is worthy of praise: give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her in the gates," so Ben Sira writes here about the man: en merida phoboumenōn kyrion dothēsetai [ἐν μερίδι φοβουμένων κύριον δοθήσεται], that is, perhaps it is given to those who fear the Lord. Or as the Vulgate translator has it: in the good portion of those who fear God (that is, a good wife is, for a good portion, among those who fear God) it will be given to the man (namely by God. For house and riches are given by parents, but a prudent wife is given properly by the Lord, Prov. 19), for good deeds (or on account of righteous acts; whence it is commonly said that a good wife is a special gift of God). Likewise: a pious wife is a man's health of heart, but one seldom finds her for sale. Psalm 128 of David also bears on this, which begins thus: Blessed is everyone who fears the Lord, who walks in his ways, etc.

units.la: 3 Porrò si beatus est vir, qui habet vxorem bonam & strenuam, quàm beati sunt & vir & mulier, quorum sponsus & maritus est optimus ille & maximus, clementissimus & potentissimus rex, idem & speciosissimus inter filios hominum Iesus Christus, Dei & Mariæ filius: de quo Paulus 2. Corinth. 11. Adiunxi vos vni viro, &c. qui & agnus Dei, & leo de tribu Iuda recte dicitur, propter suam mansuetudinem & fortitudinem, Ioan.1. Apoc. 5. Hic est illa sapientia, de qua Sap.8 Hanc amaui & exquisiui à iuuentute mea,&c quaesiui sponsam ducere mihi, & amator fastus sum pulchritudinis illius, &c.
units.tr: Furthermore, if the man is blessed who has a good and strong wife, how blessed are both man and woman whose bridegroom and husband is that best and greatest, most merciful and most powerful King, the same most beautiful among the sons of men, Jesus Christ, the son of God and of Mary; of whom Paul says in 2 Cor. 11: I have joined you to one husband, etc. He is rightly called both the Lamb of God and the Lion of the tribe of Judah, because of his gentleness and his strength, John 1, Rev. 5. He is that wisdom of which Wisdom 8 speaks: I have loved her and sought her from my youth, etc. I sought to take her as my bride, and I became a lover of her beauty, etc.

units.la: 4 Postremo si felix est vir mulieris bonae & strenuae, utique miser est ille, qui malam, seu iracundam, atq; morosam, & socordem, siue pigram habet. Unde Aristoteles in Rhet. Quibus coniugium infelix contingit, hi fere plus quàm dimidia parte beatitudinis suae priuati sunt. Et Euripides: [illegible, ~25 letters] [illegible, ~25 letters] ὡς γυνὴ κακή. Hoc est, Inopia acerba, acerba alia quàm plurima, Sed nil ita acerbum & noxium, ut mulier mala. Et Ecclesiasticus cap.25.inquit: Nullum caput serpentis capite nocentius est: nulla ira, mulieris iram superat. Cum leone malum & dracone degere, quàm cum mala muliere habitare. Mulieris nequitia eius aspectum immutat, & vultum tanquam faccū infuscat. Ea efficit, ut vir eius cogatur inter alios sedere, & acerbè gemere. Parua est quae uis prauitas præ mulieris prauitate, in quam precor improbi forte cadant. Quod scrupulofus ascensus est pedibus senis, id est linguax mulier quieto viro. In fœminæ pulchritudinem ne offendito, neue mulierem voluptatis causa concupiscito. Ingens poena, & impudentia, & turpitudo est mulier, si suo viro imperat. Afflicta mens, & moesta facies, & animi vulnus est, & remissae manus, resolutaque genua, ubi mulier mala est, quae virum suum nequaquam beat. Et Salomon Prouerb.12[?]. Strenua mulier (ait) mariti sui ornamentum est: at pudenda, est quasi quod dampnus in eius membris. Et Prouerb. 21. & 25. Praestat in angulo tecti degere, quàm vxorem habere rixosam, & domum communem. vel, quam cum muliere rixosa in domo ampla. i. Melius est habitare incommodissimè sine rixis, quàm commodissimè cum rixosa coniuge. Et cap. 30. Si morosa nupserit, perturbat terram. Deus & pater Domini nostri Iesu Christi, à quo descendit omnis datio bona, & omne donum perfectum, det omni petenti bonam & fortem vxorem, & omni habenti vxorem malam & dissolutam, Iobi sapientiam & patientiam. Amen.
units.tr: Lastly, if the man of a good and strong wife is happy, then surely he is wretched who has a bad wife, or an angry, peevish and slothful or lazy one. Hence Aristotle in the Rhetoric: those to whom an unhappy marriage falls are deprived of nearly more than half of their happiness. And Euripides: [illegible]... as a bad wife [ὡς γυνὴ κακή]. That is: bitter poverty, and many other bitter things, but nothing so bitter and harmful as a bad wife. And Ecclesiasticus chapter 25 says: No head is more hurtful than the head of a serpent; no wrath surpasses the wrath of a wife. To dwell with a lion and a dragon is better than to live with a bad wife. A wife's wickedness changes her husband's face and darkens his countenance like sackcloth. It makes her husband forced to sit among others and groan bitterly. Little is the evil that equals the wickedness of a woman, upon whom I pray that the wicked may perhaps fall. A talkative wife is a steep ascent for a quiet husband, like a climb on old feet. Do not stumble at a woman's beauty, nor desire a woman for the sake of pleasure. A wife who commands her own husband is a great punishment, and shamelessness and disgrace. When a wife is bad and does not make her husband happy at all, the mind is afflicted, the face sad, and there is a wound of the spirit, hands go limp and knees give way. And Solomon in Prov. 12: a strong wife, he says, is the crown of her husband, but a shameful one is like rot in his bones. And Prov. 21 and 25: it is better to dwell in a corner of the roof than to have a quarrelsome wife and a shared house; or, than with a quarrelsome wife in a spacious house; that is, it is better to live most uncomfortably without quarrels than most comfortably with a quarrelsome spouse. And ch. 30: If a peevish woman marries, she disturbs the land. May God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom comes down every good gift and every perfect gift, give to everyone who asks a good and strong wife, and to everyone who has a bad and dissolute wife, the wisdom and patience of Job. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XXXVIII
units.tr: SERMON XXXVIII

units.la: Eccles. 26.
units.tr: Eccles. 26.

units.la: OMITAS vxoris delectat virum suum, & ossa ipsius pinguefacit eiusdem peritia. vxor taciturna & cordata donum Dei est, nec est quo pretio permutes eruditam animam. Gratia alia super aliam est vxor pudens & fidelis, nec tanti ponatur est vllum, vt eo rependas animi ipsius modestiam. Quod est in supremis Domini Sol oriens, hoc in ornatu domus sua pulchritudo bona mulieris.
units.tr: The graciousness of a wife delights her husband, and her skill makes his bones grow fat. A silent and sensible wife is a gift of God, and no price can be set on a learned soul. A modest and faithful wife is grace upon grace, and nothing is so precious that it can repay the moderation of her spirit. As the sun rising is to the heights of the Lord, so is the beauty of a good woman to the adornment of her house.

units.la: Lucerna splendens in sancto candelabro, venustas faciei in ætate constanti est. Instar columnarum aurearum super basi argentea sunt crura formosa cum pectore stabili.
units.tr: A lamp shining on a holy candlestick is the loveliness of a face in a settled age. Beautiful legs with a steady breast are like pillars of gold set on silver bases.

units.la: 1 Quinque potissimum margaritas atque virtutes ostendit Sapiens in his verbis, quas mulieres habere debent, ijsque ornare sese. Prima est gratia, sive comitas, sive mansuetudo, sive amor, cuius contrarium est ira, inhumanitas, invidia, odium. Dicit enim, Gratia mulieris (Latinus addit, sedulæ .i. diligentis erga domum, & devotæ circa Deum, Germanus vertit, ein freundlich weib .i. ein rechtegnaden frau: Prouerb. 11. [illegible, ~3 letters]) delectabit virum eius: virique impinguabit artus, eius scientia .i. cor mariti reficitur, si sapienter tractetur ab uxore, qua sapientia erudita mulier comiter versatur cum viro, sicut Rebecca cum Isaaco, cui cibos parabat, sicut eum velle nouerat, Gen.27[?]. Coniungit hic Sapiens comitatem suavitatemque morum in muliere cum prudentia atque intelligentia: quarum altera iucunda est, altera etiam utilis, & ad gubernandam rem familiarem opportuna. Cæterum si mulier sit nequam & iracunda, tristitia afficitur vir eius, iuxta illud Eccles.25. Cor humile, & facies tristis, & plaga mortis, mulier nequam. Sicut autem hilaris mens corpus totum refrigerat, bonaque valetudine facit: sic spiritus tristis exiccat offa, Prouerb 17.12. Altera virtus est taciturnitas, seu ἡσυχία[?] quam & Apostoli requirunt in muliere, 1. Corinth. 14. 1. Tim. 2.
units.tr: 1 Above all, the wise man in these words shows five pearls and virtues which women ought to have and with which they should adorn themselves. The first is grace, whether courtesy, gentleness or love, whose opposites are anger, inhumanity, envy and hatred. For he says, "The grace of a woman (the Latin adds: careful, that is, diligent towards the household, and devoted towards God; the German renders it 'a friendly wife, that is, a woman of true grace': Prov. 11. [illegible, ~3 letters]) will delight her husband, and will make the limbs of her husband fat, that is, her knowledge: the heart of the husband is refreshed if he is wisely treated by his wife." A woman educated in wisdom lives courteously with her husband, as Rebekah did with Isaac, preparing food for him as she knew he wished, Gen. 27[?]. Here the wise man joins courtesy and sweetness of manners in a woman with prudence and understanding: the one is pleasant, the other also useful and suited to managing household affairs. But if a woman is wicked and quarrelsome, her husband is afflicted with sadness, according to that saying in Ecclus. 25: "A humble heart and a sad face and a wound of death is a wicked woman." Just as a cheerful mind refreshes the whole body and makes it healthy, so a sad spirit dries up the bones, Prov. 17:22. The second virtue is taciturnity, or quietness [ἡσυχία], which the Apostles also require of a woman, 1 Cor. 14, 1 Tim. 2.

units.la: 1. Pet. 3. Ait enim: Domini donum est mulier sensata (scilicet animo, vel cordata:) & taciturna (scilicet ore, [illegible, ~8 letters] 1. Tim. 3. Tit. 2.) neque quicquam est quod doctum animum aequiparet. Nam secundum animum est & lingua, siquidem ex abundantia cordis os loquitur, Matth. 12.
