Recte coniunxit[?] Siracides haec duo, taciturna & cordata coniunx. Qui enim moderatur sermones suos, doctus & prudens est, & preciosi spiritus. Stultus quoque, si tacuerit, sapiens reputabitur: & si compresserit labia sua, intelligens, Prou. 17. Iob 13. Caeterum linguax mulier & garrula, molesta est sibi ipsi, ut saepe verbis excedens mendacij arguatur: grauior autem est aliis, quos ducit, & qui eam optarent correctam: sed grauissima est homini amanti quietem. Sicut n. ascensus arenosus in pedibus veterani: sic mulier liguata homini quieto, Ec. 25. Impedit n. illum in honestis & necessarijs studiis suis: tristitia afficit eius cor, &c. Ita nimium loquax fuit Eua, cum haberet colloquium cum serpente, Genes. 3. nimium loquax Potiphar uxor, accusans Iosephum coram marito suo, Genes. 39[?]. Nimium loquax Rachel dicens Iacobo, Da mihi liberos, alioquin moriar, Genes. 30. Nimium Maria, loquens contra Mosen, propter uxorem eius Æthiopissam[?], Num. 12. Nimium uxor Samsonis, nimium Dalila, Iud.14. 16. Nimium Anna vxxor Tobiæ, Tob.2. Nimium vxor Iobi, Iob.2. Nimium Michol filia Saul, 2.Reg. 6. Nimium Iezabel vxor Achabi, 3.Reg.21. Nimium vxor imperatoris Valentis, quæ sua blandiloquentia maritum ad Arianas partes traxit, vt habetur lib.7. Eccles.hist.cap.12.
units.tr: 1 Pet. 3. For he says: a sensible woman is the gift of the Lord (that is, in mind, or sensible in heart), and a silent woman (that is, in mouth, [illegible, ~8 letters] 1 Tim. 3, Tit. 2), and nothing is worth as much as a learned mind. For speech goes with the mind, since out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks, Matt. 12. Ecclesiasticus rightly joined these two, a silent and a sensible wife. For he who governs his words is learned and prudent, and a man of precious spirit. Even a fool, if he keeps silent, will be counted wise, and if he shuts his lips, intelligent, Prov. 17, Job 13. But a talkative and chattering woman is a trouble to herself, so that she is often convicted of lying by her own words; she is also more burdensome to others whom she leads, and to those who would wish her corrected; but she is most burdensome to a man who loves quiet. For just as a sandy ascent is hard on the feet of an old soldier, so is a talkative woman to a quiet man, Ecclus. 25. For she hinders him in his honourable and necessary studies; she afflicts his heart with sadness, etc. Thus Eve was too talkative when she held conversation with the serpent, Gen. 3; Potiphar's wife was too talkative, accusing Joseph before her husband, Gen. 39[?]; Rachel was too talkative, saying to Jacob, "Give me children, or otherwise I shall die," Gen. 30; Miriam was too talkative, speaking against Moses on account of his Ethiopian wife, Num. 12; the wife of Samson was too talkative, and Delilah too much, Judg. 14, 16; Anna, the wife of Tobit, was too talkative, Tob. 2; Job's wife was too talkative, Job 2; Michal the daughter of Saul was too talkative, 2 Sam. 6; Jezebel the wife of Ahab was too talkative, 1 Kings 21; the wife of the emperor Valens was too talkative, who by her flattering speech drew her husband to the Arian party, as is related in book 7 of the Ecclesiastical History, chapter 12.

units.la: Aliter autem se gesserunt, & multo laudabilius Anna vxor Elcanæ, 1 Reg.1. Abigail vxor Nabalis, 1.Reg.25. Maria mater Domini, Matth.1.Luc.2.Ioan. 2.
units.tr: But others have behaved otherwise, and much more praiseworthily: Hannah, the wife of Elkanah, 1 Sam. 1; Abigail, the wife of Nabal, 1 Sam. 25; Mary the mother of the Lord, Matt. 1, Luke 2, John 2.

units.la: Tertia virtus, quæ ornat mulierem magis quàm smaragdus aut purpura, teste etiam Cratete Thebano, est pudicitia, seu verecundia, qua ornata fuit Susanna, Dan.13. Nam multiplex gratia, vel, gratia super gratiam, in quit noster Sapiens, est mulier pudica & fidelis .i. quum summus mulieris pudor (quo cauet omnem in dictis & factis turpitudinê, ex eaque hominum, in primisque mariti offensionem) cum fidelitate (quę in rebus commissis creditisq; versatur) coniungitur, nec vlla re digne potest rependi eius animi continentia: qua nimirum se continet non tantùm à Venere, sed etiam à vino & multiloquio, discursu, auaritia. Continentia enim genus est ad quamplurimas suas species. Vt autem pudicitia, quæ ex continenti animo proficiscitur, decet mulierem: sic mores, fermones & gestus obscoeni atq; turpes illam dedecent.
units.tr: The third virtue, which adorns a woman more than emerald or purple, as Crates of Thebes also testifies, is chastity or modesty, with which Susanna was adorned, Dan. 13. For, says our wise man, the manifold grace, or grace upon grace, is a chaste and faithful woman: that is, when the highest modesty of a woman (by which she guards against all indecency in words and deeds, and against offence to people, and above all to her husband) is joined with faithfulness (which concerns things entrusted and committed to her), and the self-restraint of her spirit cannot be worthily repaid with anything. By this she restrains herself not only from Venus, but also from wine, much talking, gadding about and avarice. For continence is a genus with very many species. As chastity, which arises from a continent mind, becomes a woman, so obscene and base manners, speech and gestures disgrace her.

units.la: Quarta est, honestas seu bonitas. Dicit enim: Quod est in sublimi sol oriens Domini, hoc est bonę fœminę pulchritudo in eius domus ornamento. Sicut enim sol in meridie dū ab exortu iam peruenit ad altissima, hoc est, ad lineam meridianam, vel circulum, per polos & cenith capitis transeuntem, mundū illuminat: sic virtuosa mulier illuminat domum suam: & eius honestissima species, habitudo & praesentia, domum & domesticos suos perornat, clarificat & gubernat. Sicut turpis & improba confundit totam suam pgeniem.
units.tr: The fourth is honesty or goodness. For he says: "What the rising sun is to the height of the Lord, that is the beauty of a good woman in the adornment of her house." For just as the sun at midday, when it has risen from the east and reached the highest point, that is, the meridian line, or circle passing through the poles and the zenith of the head, illuminates the world, so a virtuous woman illuminates her house; and her most honourable appearance, bearing and presence adorn, brighten and govern the house and its members. Just as a base and wicked woman confounds her whole family.

units.la: Quæ vero sit honesta & bona mulier, videntur Apostoli exponere, 1. Tim. 2.1. Pet. 3. nempe quæ in amictu modesto cum verecundia & castitate ornat semetipsam, non tortis crinibus, aut auro, aut margaritis, aut vestitu sumptuoso, sed quod decet mulieres profitentem pietatem per bona opera. Quæ enim bona est, benefacit, bonumque operatur, tum erga omnes, tum vero maxime erga familiares, & domesticos fidei, Galat. 6.1. Timot. 5. sicuti decet filias Sarae.
units.tr: What kind of woman is honourable and good, the Apostles seem to set out, 1 Tim. 2, 1 Pet. 3: namely, one who adorns herself in modest clothing with shame and chastity, not with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly apparel, but with what becomes women professing godliness through good works. For she who is good does good, and works good both towards all and above all towards those of her household and the domestic members of the faith, Gal. 6, 1 Tim. 5, as befits the daughters of Sarah.

units.la: Quinta est constantia & perseuerantia in bonitate & virtutibus praedictis: vt non terreatur mulier vllo timore, sed occultus, qui est in corde homo, careat omni corruptela, quemadmodum Petrus docet. Sic enim hic legimus: Lucerna splendens in sacro candelabro, est formae venustas in aetate constanti.i. formosa mulier quae proba manet. Aureæ columnæ in basibus argenteis, sunt formosi pedes cū pectore stabili .i. mulier constanti, & in verbo Dei bene fundato animo prædita. Contrà inquit Salomon Prou. ii. Circulus aureus in narib. porei, mulier pulchra & fatua .i. quæ pulchra est,sed non pulchrè facit:quæque de Sodoma egreditur,sed egressa post se respicit,vt vxor Loth.Gen.19. Porrò hęc omnia dicuntur in hunc finem,vt mulieres studio harum virtutum incendantur:viri vxores ducturi,eiusmodi virtutibus ornatas quærant: tales nasti, Deo gratias agant:non habentes istiusmodi mulieres. Deum precentur, vt eas ita formet: denique vt ijdem quoque his virtutibus studeant. Quandoquidem de illis etiam scriptum est, ne sint instar leonum, neque amarulenti aduersus vxores, sed vt illas diligant, Eccles. 4. Col. 3. neque multum loquantur, sed tardi sint ad loquendum, Iac. 1. neque erubescant de reb. honestis,sed turpibus,Eccle. 41 neque male, sed benefaciant, vt glorificetur per illos Deus,Matth.5.1 Cor.10. vtque stent in fide,viriliter agant,sint fortes, 1. Corinth. 16.
units.tr: The fifth is constancy and perseverance in goodness and the aforesaid virtues, so that a woman is not frightened by any fear, but the hidden man of the heart is free from all corruption, as Peter teaches. For so we read here: "A lamp shining on a holy candlestick is the loveliness of a face in a settled age," that is, a beautiful woman who remains upright. "Golden pillars on silver bases are beautiful feet with a steady breast," that is, a woman who is steadfast and endowed with a mind well grounded in the word of God. On the contrary, Solomon says in Prov. 11: "A gold ring in the nose of a swine is a beautiful woman who is foolish," that is, one who is beautiful but does not act beautifully, and who goes out of Sodom but, having gone out, looks back after herself, like Lot's wife, Gen. 19. Moreover, all these things are said to this end: that women should be inflamed with zeal for these virtues; that husbands about to take wives should seek those adorned with such virtues, and give thanks to God when they have such wives, and pray to God that he may form them so; and finally that they themselves also should strive after these virtues. For it is also written of husbands: "Be not like lions, nor bitter against your wives, but love them," Col. 3; "Do not speak much, but be slow to speak," James 1; "Do not blush at honourable things, but at base things," Ecclus. 41; "Do not do evil, but do good, that God may be glorified through them," Matt. 5, 1 Cor. 10; "stand in the faith, act manfully, be strong," 1 Cor. 16.

units.la: ¶ Quin hæc omnia pertinent ad vniuersos,& vniusquemq; eorum,qui volunt Christi esse sponsa atq; coniunx, eumq; delectare & honorare. Dicit n. Matt.11. Discite à me, quòd mitis sim & humilis corde,&12. Dico vobis, quòd de quocunque verbo otioso, quod loquuti fuerint homines,reddituri sint rationem in die iudicij. Ezec.36. Confundimini & erubescite super vijs vestris domus Israel. 1. Corin. 8. procurantes honesta, non tantum coram Domino, sed etiam coram hominibus. Luc. 9. Matth. 10. Nemo qui manum suam a Jmota[?] aratro respexerit à tergo, aptus est regno Dei: verùm qui sustinuerit usque ad finem, hic saluus fiet. Ut hanc salutem & hoc regnum omnes consequamur, impleat oleo lætitiæ lampades nostras Christus Iesus rex noster, & pontifex: cui sit honor, laus, benedictio & gloria in sempiternam, Amen.
units.tr: ¶ Indeed all these things pertain to all and to each one of those who wish to be the bride and wife of Christ, and to delight and honour him. For he says in Matt. 11: "Learn of me, for I am meek and lowly in heart." And in Matt. 12: "I tell you that for every idle word that men speak they shall give account on the day of judgement." Ezek. 36: "Be confounded and ashamed for your ways, house of Israel." 1 Cor. 8: "providing honest things not only before the Lord but also before men." Luke 9, Matt. 10: "No one who has put his hand to the plough and looked back is fit for the kingdom of God; but he who endures to the end, he shall be saved." That we may all obtain this salvation and this kingdom, may Christ Jesus our king and high priest fill our lamps with the oil of gladness, to whom be honour, praise, blessing and glory for ever. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XXXIX.
units.tr: CONCIO XXXIX.

units.la: Eccles. 40.
units.tr: Ecclus. 40.

units.la: Ut amicus commodè congruat cum amico, vir tamen & uxor concor- des utriquè præferendi sunt.
units.tr: That a friend fittingly agrees with a friend, but husband and wife, agreeing with each other, are to be preferred to both.

units.la: 1 Varijs verbis hæc sententia ab interpretibus redditur. Græci habent: φίλος δὲ ἑταῖρος ὡς καιρὸν ἀπαλλάσσοντες, ὑπὲρ ἀμφότερα γυνὴ μετ' ἀνδρός.[?] Latini vertunt sic: Amicus & Iodalis ad tempus occurrentes (vel in tempore conuenientes) & super utraque (vel utrosque) mulier cum viro. i. Amicus & socius commodè conueniunt, sed utrumque antecellit uxoriunta viro. Germani sic: Ein freund vnd ein gsell die einander eren fleissig begegnend: vber die beide ist ein weib/ das mit jrem mann eins ist. Item: Ein freund kompt zum anderen in der not[?], aber man vnd weib viel mehr. Sed hæ interpretationes omnes incidunt ferè in unum & eundem sensum, qui eiusmodi est: Tametsi laudabilis & jucunda inter omnes sit amicitia, pax, charitas, mutuumque ossicium, Pf. 133. tamen maximè inter coniuges: neque ulla est amicitia aut sodalitas quæ cum coniugio honesto, fideli, concordiaque fit coparanda. Ut enim rerum malarum gradus & discrimina sunt, & aliud malum alio maius est, atque adeò minus malum potius, quàm maius eligendum, sicut Aristoteles dicit lib.5.Eth. cap.3. & Dauid fecit, 2.Reg. 24. sic etiam in rebus bonis & jucundis alia præstat alteri. Probata sunt coram Deo & hominibus concordia fratrum, amicitia propinquorum: omnium maximè verò vir & uxor inter se bene convenientes, Eccles. 25. Et quemadmodum frater, qui adiuuatur à fratre, quasi ciuitas firma: melior tamen est vicinus juxta, quàm frater procul, teste Salomone, Proverb. 18. & 27. ita tempore necessitatis uxor viro plus beneficij & auxilij exhibere solet ac potest (siquidem sit non contra virum, sed cum viro & pro viro, ut Michol pro Dauide, quem demittebat per fenestrà, cùm Saul illum quaereret interfectum, 1.Reg.19.} quàm vel socius vel frater. Nihil in hoc mundo dulcius hominibus, quàm grata & jucunda sodalitas, quam etiam bruta sectantur & diligunt. Applaudit enim simile simili. Homo autem præ cunctis sociale animal, multò minus solitarié vivere potest, ob multas necefsitates naturæ, ob quas unus necessariò indiget auxilio aliorum, ex ipsa natiuitatis origine,ut non fit imbecellius animal in orbe, quatenus tanto amabilior coalesceret charitas & amicitia hominum ex mutuis beneficijs. Iucunda est ergo amici cum sodali suo conuentio in tempore,dum sibi pulchrè concordat, & afficiuntur ex animo. Sed super omnia est amicitia mariti & vxoris,dum concordant votis & pacificè conuiuantur. Sunt enim à Domino ordinati, ut sint vna caro, & sibi se mutuum communicent, animam, vires,officia,& solicitudines,ad prolè legitimè educandam. Hierocles in lib. de Nuptijs ait:
units.tr: The interpreters render this sentence in various words. The Greek reads: [φίλος δὲ ἑταῖρος ὡς καιρὸν ἀπαλλάσσοντες, ὑπὲρ ἀμφότερα γυνὴ μετ' ἀνδρός]. The Latin translators put it thus: "A friend and a companion meeting at the right time, and a woman with her husband above both." That is, friend and companion agree fittingly, but a wife with her husband surpasses both. The Germans render it: "A friend and a companion who diligently meet one another in honour; above both is a wife who is one with her husband." Likewise: "A friend comes to another in need, but a husband and wife far more." All these interpretations fall more or less into one and the same sense, which is this: although friendship, peace, charity and mutual service are praiseworthy and pleasant among all people (Ps. 133), yet they are most so between spouses. No friendship or fellowship can be compared with an honest, faithful and harmonious marriage. For there are degrees and differences among evils, and one evil is greater than another, so that the lesser evil should rather be chosen than the greater, as Aristotle says (Eth. 5, ch. 3) and David did (2 Sam. 24). So too in good and pleasant things, one excels another. Concord between brothers and friendship between kinsmen are approved before God and men, but most of all that of a husband and wife living well together (Ecclus. 25). And just as a brother helped by a brother is like a strong city, yet a neighbour nearby is better than a brother far away, as Solomon testifies (Prov. 18 and 27), so in time of need a wife is accustomed and able to give her husband more help and support (provided she is not against her husband, but with him and for him, as Michal was for David, whom she let down through a window when Saul sought to kill him, 1 Sam. 19) than either a companion or a brother. Nothing in this world is sweeter to men than a pleasant and agreeable fellowship, which even the brute beasts seek out and love. For like delights in like. Man, however, above all other creatures a social animal, can much less live alone, because of the many needs of his nature, for which one necessarily requires the help of others from the very origin of his birth. Indeed no animal in the world is so helpless, so that the love and friendship of men might grow the more lovable through mutual kindnesses. Pleasant, then, is the meeting of a friend with his companion at the proper time, when they agree well and are affectionately disposed to each other. But above all is the friendship of husband and wife, when they agree in their wishes and live together peacefully. For they have been ordained by the Lord to be one flesh and to share with each other soul, strength, duties and cares, for the lawful upbringing of their offspring. Hierocles, in his book On Marriage, says:

units.la: • μὴ πείθῃ[?] ἐχθρὸς[?] γαμέτης γυναικὸς καὶ τῶν τέκνων, ἀ-[?] ἐστὶ τῆς ἀληθινωτάτης καὶ γνησίας εὐνοίας. Item: ἀρ-[illegible, ~30 letters] συμφυέστερον, ἑκάτερον ὁ γάμος.
units.tr: [Μὴ πείθῃ ἐχθρὸς γαμέτης γυναικὸς καὶ τῶν τέκνων, ἅ ἐστὶ τῆς ἀληθινωτάτης καὶ γνησίας εὐνοίας]. Likewise: [...] marriage joins each more closely.

units.la: De excellentia & vi amoris coniugalis videtur etiam illud dictū Ecclef.36. Pulchritudo mulieris vultum exhilarat, omnemque humanam iucunditatem excellit. Si linguae eius inest comitas, lenitas & salubritas, maritus eius non est filijs hominum comparandus. Item illud Dauidis, 2.Reg.1. Moeror est mihi propter te frater mi Ionathan: gratisimus enim mihi fuisti: mirabilis(id est, praestans & singularis) factus est mihi tui amor super amorem mulierum. Est autem, inquit Rabi Leui, mulieris amor tam fortis, ut si maritus eam iam percusserit, & illi maledixerit, non possit vel in modico minui amorem eius, imo plerunque arctius diligit. Caeterum amor mulierum hoc loco nō similiter ab omnibus intelligitur. Alij enim accipiunt de amore, quo viri impotentius mulieres amant, qui quantus sit, declarat Zorobabel ȝ[?]. Esd. 4. Hanc sententiam sequitur Paraphrastes, qui de amore, quo Dauid duas suas vxores amplexus est, interpretatur. Alij de amore intelligunt, quo mulieres in viros exardescunt, qui quantus sit, declarat illud Latini vatis:
units.tr: The excellence and power of conjugal love is also shown by the saying in Ecclus. 36: "The beauty of a woman cheers the face and surpasses all human pleasantness. If there is courtesy, gentleness and kindness in her tongue, her husband is not to be compared with the sons of men." Likewise David's words, 2 Sam. 1: "I grieve for you, my brother Jonathan; you were very dear to me; your love for me was wonderful (that is, outstanding and singular), beyond the love of women." Rabbi Levi says that a woman's love is so strong that even if her husband has struck her and cursed her, her love cannot be lessened in the least; indeed it often holds on even more tightly. However, the phrase "the love of women" is not understood in the same way by all. Some take it of the love with which men love women more intemperately, and how great this is Zerubbabel declares (1 Esd. 4). The Paraphrast follows this view, interpreting it of the love with which David embraced his two wives. Others understand the love with which women burn for men, and how great this is is declared by that line of the Latin poet:

units.la: Improbe amor, quid non mortalia pectora cogis?
units.tr: Wicked love, what do you not compel mortal hearts to do?

units.la: vel de amore, quo suos liberos profequuntur: cuius vim apud vatem Iesaiam cap. 49. diuinus Spiritus his verbis explicat: Numquid obliuisci potest mulier infantem suum, ut non misereatur filij uteri sui?
units.tr: or the love with which they cherish their children, whose force the divine Spirit explains through the prophet Isaiah, ch. 49, in these words: "Can a woman forget her infant, so as not to have compassion on the son of her womb?"

units.la: Sed tamen excipitur (inquit Pellicanus) amor fidelium animarum cum creatore suo, Christi & ecclesiæ[?], qui non tantum per omnem vitam durare potest mortalem, ut amor coniugalis: sed sic in præsenti vita coalescere debet & roborari, ut perseueret in seculo animarum fine fine. De magnitudine & vi illius amoris & adhæsionis, siue coiunctionis sunt illa, Luc.14. Si quis venit ad me, nec odit patrem suum ac matrem, & vxorem, non potest meus esse discipulus. Ergo nullum locum habebit excusatio illa, vxorem duxi, & ideo non possum venire. Ephef. 5. Christus dilexit ecclesiam suam, & semetipsum exposuit pro ea, ut illam sanctificaret, &c. Rom.8. Quis nos separabit à dilectione Dei? num afflictio? num angustia? num persecutio? num fames? num nuditas? num periculum? num gladius? &c. Ioan.6. Domine ad quem ibimus? verba vitæ æternæ habes. 1.Cor.6. Qui adglutinatur Domino, vnꝰ spiritus est. Psal.7[?]4. Quem in cœlo & in terra præter te desiderarem? &c.
units.tr: But, says Pellicanus, the love of faithful souls for their Creator, Christ and the Church, is excepted. This love can last not only through the whole of mortal life, as conjugal love does, but ought to grow and be strengthened in the present life so that it persists into the endless ages of souls. Of the greatness and power of that love and attachment, or union, are those words of Luke 14: "If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father and mother and wife, he cannot be my disciple." Therefore the excuse "I have married a wife, and so I cannot come" will have no place. Eph. 5: "Christ loved his Church and gave himself up for her, to sanctify her," etc. Rom. 8: "Who shall separate us from the love of God? Shall affliction? Or distress? Or persecution? Or famine? Or nakedness? Or danger? Or the sword?" etc. John 6: "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life." 1 Cor. 6: "He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit." Ps. 73: "Whom have I desired in heaven or on earth but you?" etc.

units.la: 2 Quanquam nihilominus coniuges tenentur le[?] inuicem quoque diligere. Sunt enim multæ causæ, propter quas excellens esse debet inter illos dilectio, pax, & concordia, idq; in Domino, non contra Dominum eiusue gloriam.
units.tr: 2 Nevertheless, spouses are also bound to love one another. There are many reasons why love, peace and concord between them should be outstanding, and this in the Lord, not against the Lord or his glory.

units.la: Ac primùm quidem hoc fieri decet atque debet, propter præceptum coniugibus singulariter datum, Eph.5. Col.3. Tob.10. Tit.2. Diserte enim iubet Spiritus sanctus per Apostolum viros diligere vxores: & rursum vxores esse φιλάνδρυς.
units.tr: First, this ought and must be done on account of the command given specially to spouses (Eph. 5; Col. 3; Tob. 10; Titus 2). For the Holy Spirit clearly bids, through the Apostle, that husbands love their wives, and again that wives be lovers of their husbands [φιλάνδρους].

units.la: Deinde propter exemplum Christi & ecclesiæ. Hæc enim diligit illum, quoniam ipse prior dilexit eam, Eph.5.1.Ioan.4.
units.tr: Second, on account of the example of Christ and the Church. For she loves him because he first loved her (Eph. 5; 1 John 4).

units.la: Tertiò, propter promissionem in pace agentibus factam. Scriptum est enim 2.Corinth.13. Vnanimes estis, in pace agite, & Deus charitatis ac pacis erit vobiscum.
units.tr: Third, on account of the promise made to those who live in peace. For it is written (2 Cor. 13): "Be of one mind, live in peace, and the God of love and peace will be with you."

units.la: Quartò, propter bene placitum Domini. Amor enim & concordia mariti & vxoris tū Deo (qui pacis Deus est, & nos in pace vocauit, 1.Cor 14.7.) tum hominibus multum placet, Eccl. 25.
units.tr: Fourth, on account of the good pleasure of the Lord. For the love and concord of husband and wife greatly please both God (who is the God of peace, and has called us in peace, 1 Cor. 7:15) and men (Ecclus. 25).

units.la: Quintò, propter summam & singularem communitatem & coniunctione viri & mulieris inter sese. Corpus enim mulieris est ipsius viri, & contrà, 1. Cor. 7. Ac vir est caput mulieris, & haec illius corpus. Eph.5.Vir denique qui adglutinatur uxori, unum corpus est. Redigentur enim, inquit, duo in carnem unam. Itaque jam non sunt duo, sed una caro, Math.19. & velut una arbor, quę profert fructus preciosissimos, id est, filios hominum, qui per adoptionem fiunt filij Dei altissimi, quorum unus praevalet omnibus fructibus terrae. Sicut enim planta & ramus, qui plantae inseritur, unam arborem efficiunt, & neuter illorum sufficiens est ad serendos fructus: sic nec vir absque muliere, neque mulier sine viro sufficiens est ad generandam prolem, 1.Cor. 11. Jam vero cùm ametur arbor propter bonos & copiosos fructus, quos profert: cur non ametur coniunx propter egregios fructus ventris? Unde & Socrates Alcibiadi, demiranti, quòd Xantippen supra modum rixosam domi perpeteretur, dixit, At tu nonne domi tuae toleras gallinarum glottientiū[?] strepitū? Tolero, inquit Alcibiades, sed gallinae mihi pariunt ova pullosq;. Et mihi, ait Socrates, mea Xantippe parit liberos.
units.tr: Fifth, on account of the supreme and singular communion and union of man and woman with one another. For the woman's body belongs to the husband, and conversely (1 Cor. 7). The husband is the head of the woman, and she is his body (Eph. 5). Finally, the man who is joined to his wife is one body. For, it says, the two shall be made one flesh. So they are no longer two, but one flesh (Matt. 19). They are like one tree which bears most precious fruits, that is, the sons of men, who through adoption become sons of the Most High God, one of whom outweighs all the fruits of the earth. For just as a plant and a branch grafted into it make one tree, and neither is sufficient by itself to bear fruit, so neither a man without a woman nor a woman without a man is sufficient to beget offspring (1 Cor. 11). Now since a tree is loved for the good and abundant fruit it bears, why should a spouse not be loved for the excellent fruit of the womb? Hence also Socrates, when Alcibiades marvelled that he put up with Xanthippe, who was excessively quarrelsome at home, said: "But do you not put up at home with the noise of your cackling hens?" "I put up with it," said Alcibiades, "but my hens lay me eggs and chicks." "And my Xanthippe," said Socrates, "bears me children."

units.la: Sextò propter formam creationis mulieris, quae nō procul à corde viri desumpta, sed de viri costa formata est. Unde Apostolus, Eph.5. Sic debent viri diligere suas uxores ut sua ipsorum corpora. Qui diligit suam uxorem, seipsum diligit. Nullus enim unquam suá ipsius carnem odio habuit,imò enutrit ac fouet eam,sicut & Dominus ecclesiam. Quoniam membra sumus corporis eiusde, ex carne eius & ex ossibus eius. Interim tamen observatione dignū, quòd mulier non de pede viri sumpta est, ne à viro conteneretur, 1.Pet.3. neq; de capite, ne viro dominaretur, 1.Tim.2. Si enim maritus vincatur, & uxor dominetur, (dicit Augustinus in Psal.143.) pax perversa est. Si autem uxor marito dominanti subijciatur, pax recta. Io. Iouianus scribit cap.3. de Obed. lib.3. Quænam pax in illa esse domo potest, in qua mulieris dominetur appetitus? Neq;.n.aut induere omnes Scratè possunt, aut ducendæ uxoris finis is est viro, ut patientia assuescat, toleràdisq; clamorib.
units.tr: Sixthly, on account of the manner of the creation of woman: she was taken not from near the heart of man, but formed from the rib of man. Hence the Apostle, Eph. 5: "So ought men to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but rather nourishes and cherishes it, as the Lord does the Church, since we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones." Yet it is worth observing that woman was not taken from the foot of man, lest she be trampled by him (1 Pet. 3), nor from the head, lest she dominate the man (1 Tim. 2). For if the husband is overcome and the wife rules, (as Augustine says on Psalm 143) the peace is perverted; but if the wife is subject to a husband who rules, the peace is right. Johannes Jovianus writes, chapter 3 of On Obedience, book 3: What peace can there be in that house in which a woman's appetite rules? For men cannot all be Socrates, and the purpose of taking a wife is that a man may grow accustomed to patience and to bearing shouting.

units.la: Septimó propter unam & eandem spem vocationis, qua & vir & mulier, abs-q; perfonarum acceptione vocati sunt ad hæreditatem gratiæ vitæ.Ephes.4.1.Pet.3.Si ergo sperant coniuges se simul victuros[?] in summa pace & tranquillitate post hanc vitam in regno Dei; cur non etiam hic ad momentum saltem student pacificè viuere? At patientia illis est opus, ut ubi voluntatem Dei peregerint, reportent promissionem, Hebr. 10. Neque enim seruari unquam concordia, nisi per solam patientiam valet, sicut Gregorius testatu lib. Moral. 5. Crebrò namque in humana actione nascitur, unde mentes hominum vicissim à suavitate & dilectione separentur. Et nisi ad adversa toleranda in animo[?] se præparent, cùm aduersitatis aliquid acciderit, quod animus ferre non valet, fraternā concordiam relinquent. Sed qui alienam imperfectionem ferre non valens deserit: ipse sibi testis est, quòd perfectè nec dum prosicit.
units.tr: Seventhly, on account of the one and the same hope of calling, by which both husband and wife, without respect of persons, have been called to the inheritance of the grace of life (Eph. 4; 1 Pet. 3). If therefore spouses hope that they will live together after this life in the kingdom of God, in the greatest peace and tranquillity, why do they not strive to live peaceably here, at least for a moment? But they need patience, so that when they have done the will of God they may receive the promise (Heb. 10). For concord can never be preserved except by patience alone, as Gregory testifies in Moralia, book 5. For often in human affairs there arises something by which the minds of men are separated from one another in sweetness and love; and unless they prepare themselves in spirit to bear adversities, when some adversity befalls that the spirit cannot bear, they will abandon brotherly concord. But whoever, unable to bear another's imperfection, deserts him, is himself a witness that he has not yet advanced to perfection.

units.la: Vnde iterum Iouianus ait: Recte familiaris meus compater Neapolitanus, cum ab amicis graviter accusaretur, quòd iam grandis natu, & diuitijs satis bonis tam ab re abhorreret vxoria, deesse sibi patientiā (quam quidam robur Socraticum vocat) caulatus [?] est, qua vna vel maximè opus esse duceret, vxorem enim cum dote simul clamores ac supercilium in domum illaturam, at sibi patientiam nullam esse.
units.tr: Hence Jovianus again says: My friend and co-father, the Neapolitan, rightly answered when, being severely accused by his friends, because although already advanced in years and rich enough in means he shrank so much from marriage, that he lacked patience (which some call the Socratic strength), and thought this the chief thing needed, since a wife brings with her dowry, shouting and haughtiness into the house, while he himself had no patience at all.

units.la: Octauò, quia mulier adiutorium & solatiūm est viri à Deo datum, Genes. 2. 24. Eccles. 4. 9. & 16. atque adeò omnium prima societas humana, est coniunctio mariti & fœminæ: quam deinde secutæ sunt reliquæ societates & amicitiæ, vt fratrum, vicinorum, sociorum, amicorum, &c.
units.tr: Eighthly, because woman is a help and comfort given to man by God (Gen. 2:24; Eccles. 4:9 and 16), and thus the conjunction of husband and wife is the first of all human societies, which was afterwards followed by the other societies and friendships: of brothers, neighbours, companions, friends, and so on.

units.la: Nonò, quia etiam consanguinei coniugū propter coniugium eorum se mutuò amant. Si ergo alij propter ipsos se inuicem diligūt, cur ipsi se non mutuò diligerent?
units.tr: Ninthly, because even the blood relatives of spouses love each other mutually on account of their marriage. If therefore others love one another for the sake of them, why should they not love each other mutually?

units.la: Decimò, quia vterque coniugum proprios parentes relinquit, vt sibi inuicem adhæreant, Genes. 2.
units.tr: Tenthly, because each of the spouses leaves their own parents, so that they may cling to one another (Gen. 2).

units.la: Taceo osculum, quod olim sibi in nonnullis ecclesijs coniuges mutuò dabant, in signū pacis. Prætereo anulum capientem vnum digitum, & eum plerunque, in quo est vena, quæ vsque ad cor protenditur: quia coniuges, ut & cæteri homines ex corde, eòque puro [?] inuicem amare debent, 1.Pet. 1.
units.tr: I pass over the kiss which spouses once gave each other in some churches as a sign of peace. I pass over the ring placed on the one finger, and that usually the one in which there is a vein that extends to the heart, because spouses, like other men, ought to love one another from the heart, and that pure (1 Pet. 1).

units.la: ʒ Hæc cùm ita sint, à discordia summopere cauere debent omnes homines, præsertim coniuges ac contra seruare & colere pacem atque concordiam. Refert Plutarchus in præceptis politicis de Leone Byzantio Sophista, quòd venerit Athenas populo disidijs tumultuani concordiam suasurus. Vbi verò prodisset in suggestum, corpore admodum pusillo, omnium risus obortus est. Ille fortuitam occasionem vertens in proœmium, Quid, inquit, ô viri Athenienses, si conspiceretis uxorem meam, quæ tam pusilla est, ut vix pertingat ad genua mea. Ad hanc vocem quum maior etiam populi risus sublatus esset, subiecit, At nos tam pusillos, si quando disidemus, vix civitas Byzantium capere potest. Sed hoc Philostratus in Sophistis multò aliter narrat, idque & probabilius, & festiuius. Nempe quum prodisset ad populum dicturus de concordia, ipsa statim specie risum mouit populo, quod obesus esset ac ventre prægrandi. At ille nihil turbatus risu multitudinis, Quid, inquit, ridetis viri Athenienses? uxor mihi est multò obesior & tamen concordes unus capit lectulus, discordes ne tota quidem domus. Porrò nulla civitas, aut domus tam stabilis est, quæ non odijs & dissidijs euerti possit, vt Cicero testatur. Imo Christus ipse dicit, Matt. 12. Omne regnum diuisum aduersus sese desolatur, & omnis ciuitas aut domus diuisa aduersus seipsam, non stabit. Vnde Salomon Prou. 27. Tecta perstillantia in die frigoris, & litigiosa mulier comparantur. Ne sint ergo mulieres litigiosae, sed mansuetae: neque sint viri aduersus illas amarulenti, sed lenes & patientes: & Deus pacis omnisque consolationis aderit illis in Christo Iesu, Amen.
units.tr: These things being so, all men, and especially spouses, ought to beware above all of discord, and on the contrary to keep and cultivate peace and concord. Plutarch relates in the Political Precepts about Leo of Byzantium the sophist, that he came to Athens to persuade the people, who were in tumult from quarrels, to concord. But when he had mounted the platform, being of a very small body, laughter arose from all. He, turning the chance occasion into his prologue, said: "What, men of Athens, if you were to see my wife, who is so small that she scarcely reaches my knees?" At this word, when a still greater laughter of the people had arisen, he added: "But we, so small, when we quarrel, the city of Byzantium can scarcely hold us." But Philostratus in the Lives of the Sophists tells this much differently, and more probably and more wittily. Namely, when he had come forward to speak to the people about concord, his very appearance at once moved the people to laughter, because he was fat and had a very great belly. But he, not at all disturbed by the laughter of the crowd, said: "What are you laughing at, men of Athens? My wife is much fatter than I am, and yet when we agree one couch holds us; when we disagree, not even the whole house is enough." Moreover, no city or house is so stable that it cannot be overturned by hatreds and dissensions, as Cicero testifies. Indeed Christ himself says (Matt. 12): "Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation, and every city or house divided against itself will not stand." Hence Solomon (Prov. 27) compares a leaking roof on a day of cold to a quarrelsome woman. Let women therefore not be quarrelsome, but gentle; nor let husbands be bitter against them, but mild and patient; and the God of peace and of all consolation will be with them in Christ Jesus. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XL.
units.tr: SERMON XL.

units.la: Eccles. 42.
units.tr: Eccles. 42.

units.la: Filia[?] patri occultam affert vigiliam, & somnum abigit solicitudo eius, ne maturitas aetatis eius exolescat, neue odium nupta mereatur: ne stupro polluatur in sua virginitate, neue in domo paterna fiat grauida: ne quando viro iuncta faciat flagitium, aut ne in matrimonium data sterilescat. Filia inuerecunda custodiam adhibe, ne te ridiculum faciat inimicis, ciuitatiq; fabulam, ne famosum in populo, neue in vulgus reddat ignominiosum. Ne contempleris quenquam hominem gratia pulchritudinis, nec inter mulieres desideas: nam ut tinea uta[?] nascitur e vestimentis, ita a muliere nequitia muliebris. Melior est nequitia viri, quam mulier benignam se prastans, mulier quae eadem author est probrosae turpitudinis.
units.tr: A father's daughter keeps a hidden vigil, and his anxiety drives away sleep: lest the ripeness of her age wither, or she earn hatred as a bride; lest she be defiled by shame in her virginity, or become pregnant in her father's house; lest, joined to a husband, she commit a disgrace, or, given in marriage, she grow barren. Keep a watch over an shameless daughter, lest she make you a laughingstock to your enemies, a byword in the city, a scandal among the people, and bring you dishonour before the crowd. Do not look upon any man for the sake of his beauty, and do not linger among women; for as the moth comes from garments, so wickedness comes from a woman. Better is the wickedness of a man than a woman who shows herself kind, a woman who is the author of shameful disgrace.

units.la: Principium horum verborum admonitio quaedam videtur communis dicti: proles minor paruam exigit solicitudinem, maiores maximam. <bl>Kleine Kind/Kleine Sorg: groß Kind/groß Sorg[?].</bl> Id vero in primis de filiabus sentitur, quae cum nubiles euaserint, non sine graui & molesta solicitudine asseruatur, quas etiamsi pater domi abscônderit, non tamen solicitudine exonerabitur. Possunt enim & domi, si ambiant, comprimi: aut flore aetatis excedere, vt metuendum sit, si manent innuptae vltra annos florentis aetatis, forma earum deflorescat exolescatque vna cum aetate, atque ob hanc causam maritos non facile reperiant. Vnde & parentibus adducit noctes insomnes pro cura filiae & impendentibus periculis. Timere enim coguntur, ne infolenter viuens filia, familiae & parenti diffamiam inferat, si copulata marito fidelis non perstiterit, sed non contenta eo marito, fiat odibilis propter lasciuiam. Alius quoq; parentum timor incumbit, ne forte stupretur adhuc existens in parentum domo, vnde in maximam ignominiam patris, eam iuxta legem lapidari contingat. Sed & non modica olim patribus cura erat, ne forte qualibet ratione sterilis filia fieret, & maledictionis illius rea iudicaretur, quae habebatur de sterili, Deuter. 7. Unde & Bensyræ sententia fuit: Qui non habet filios, non est ædificatus, sed quasi dissipatus. Scriptura liberorum procreationem, ædificationem nominat: quòd, sicut ædificium aliquod extruendo curam, studium & diligentiam requirit, similiter & in conservando: ita & liberorum educatio. Hinc בֵּן[?] filius à בָּנָה[?] ædificauit, quemadmodum etiam בַּת filia dicuntur apud Hebraeos. Longè autem probrosius, si iam marito cohabitans, ex educatione mala insolentior adultera deprehendatur & lapidanda.
units.tr: The opening of these words seems to be a general saying of admonition: a small child brings little care, a grown one great care. This is felt especially about daughters, who, once they have become marriageable, are guarded not without heavy and troublesome anxiety; even if the father keeps them shut up at home, he will not be relieved of his anxiety. For even at home they can be corrupted, if they are inclined to it, or they may pass out of the bloom of youth, so that, if they remain unmarried beyond the years of flowering age, their beauty fades and withers along with their age, and for this reason they do not easily find husbands. Hence the parents also have sleepless nights over the care of their daughter and the dangers that hang over her. For they are compelled to fear that a daughter living wantonly will bring infamy upon the family and her parents, if, once joined to a husband, she does not remain faithful but, not content with her husband, becomes hateful through lewdness. Another fear also weighs on parents: lest she be defiled while still in her parents' house, whence, to the great disgrace of her father, she is to be stoned according to the law. But also in former times the fathers had no small care lest a daughter somehow become barren and be judged liable to that curse which was held to rest on the barren, Deut. 7. Hence also came the saying of Ben Sira: He who has no sons is not built up, but is as though scattered. Scripture calls the procreation of children "building up," because just as the construction of a building demands care, zeal and diligence, so also does its preservation; so too is the upbringing of children. Hence the word for son, בֵּן [ben], is derived from בָּנָה [banah], "he built"; in the same way daughters are also called בַּת [bat] among the Hebrews. But it is far more shameful if, already living with her husband, a woman is caught as an adulteress, and deserving of stoning, because of a bad upbringing that made her too wanton.

units.la: 2 Monet ergo Sapiens parentes, ut summa cura asseruent filias quae multa sollicitudine ab infantia instituendae sunt, ut discant castimoniam, pudicitiam, horrorem virorum, donec tradendae sint nuptui. Si ex signis, inquit, quæ multa sunt, deprehenderis filiam tuam propensam ad luxuriam, diligenter talem custodias domi & foris, feverissimam[?] ei adhibeas custodiam, ut etiam cap 26. hortatur: adverteas illius mores & studia, ne quando occasione oblata stupretur, & tu incurras ignominiam & confusionem, non tantùm in tua conscientia & familia, sed etiam derisui pateas inimicorum tuorum, insultantium, & tibi imputantium turpitudinem filiæ tuæ, & de angustia tua lætentur, ut sis duplo miser, dum de tua miseria hostes sibi gratulantur: sed & conciuium tuorum iudicium iustum incides, ex ruina eius, quam imprudentiæ tuæ adscribent & negligentiæ: unde & abiectio plebis in multitudine populi eris, & abominatio ex confusione filiæ, quam nimis blandè nutrieris & sine solicitudine necessaria. Consueuit enim totum vulgus obloqui parentibus, & non indignè, qui filiam meretricem lortiuntur [?] & petulantem. Solebant olim Græci ac Iudæi, & adhuc solent Itali, ut & Venetiis fit, occultare summo studio suas virgines, putates aliquid de earum castitate ac pudore decerpi, si ab aliis conspiciantur: sic & Phocylides præcipit iuuentutem utriusque sexus occultari. Atque à tali sollicita virginitatis custodia ac occultatione vocatur ab Hebræis virgo עַלְמָה[?] Almah.
units.tr: 2. The Wise Man therefore warns parents to guard their daughters with the greatest care. They must be instructed from infancy with much diligence, so that they learn chastity, modesty, and a dread of men, until they are to be given in marriage. If, he says, you find from the many signs that your daughter is inclined to lust, watch her carefully at home and abroad, and keep a very strict watch over her, as he also urges in chapter 26: observe her manners and pursuits, lest, when an opportunity is offered, she be defiled and you incur shame and confusion, not only in your own conscience and household, but also expose yourself to the mockery of your enemies, who, exulting, will impute the shame of your daughter to you and rejoice in your distress, so that you are doubly wretched while your foes congratulate themselves on your misery. You will also incur the just judgment of your fellow citizens, who will ascribe her ruin to your folly and negligence; and so you will become a thing cast out among the mass of the people, and an abomination because of the disgrace of a daughter whom you have nursed too indulgently and without necessary care. For the whole common people is wont to complain against parents, and not without reason, when they bring up a daughter who is a harlot and wanton. The Greeks and Jews used to, and the Italians still do, as is also done at Venice, keep their virgins hidden with the utmost care, thinking that something of their chastity and modesty is lost if they are seen by others. So too Phocylides commands that the youth of both sexes be kept hidden. And from this careful guarding and concealing of virginity, the Hebrews call a virgin עַלְמָה [almah], Almah.

units.la: Cæterum optima institutio & eruditio liberorum esse videtur, ut quidam scribit, quando parentes non solùm vigilant, sed etiam orant pro liberis suis, ac eosdem quoque orare docent.
units.tr: Moreover, the best training and instruction of children seems to be, as a certain writer says, when parents not only keep watch but also pray for their children, and teach them to pray as well.

units.la: ¶ Præterea docet hîc Sapiens, non esse incautè & curiosius inspiciendum, quod non est desiderandum: ideoque nec mulier viru[?], nec vir mulierem ex specie admiretur, & cum voluptate aspiciat, ne sensualiter & ad peccatum afficiatur, unde anima polluatur, & insurgat tentatio, & mors per fenestras transeat[?]. Multo minus iuuenis vel vir quicunque tutum sibi putet cohabitare extraneis mulieribus, unde periculum inciditur castitatis. Species enim mulierum, eloquium; gestus, & ornatus, & quicquid in eis est, flamma est, ideoque speciem mulieris alienæ multi admirati, reprobi facti sunt. Colloquium enim illius quasi ignis exardescit. Nihil autem tutius & sanctius, quàm matrimonium colere. Sicut autem de vestimento generatur tinea ad eius corruptionem: sic ex muliere iniquitas mulieris: sic enim quidam legunt: vel ex muliere extranea viro accidit, sicut licet affectuum malitia & carnis iniquitas, dum aspectu, affatu, tactu, & cohabitatione viri ad libidinem excitantur, & mulieris nutibus capiuntur. Mulier enim viri preciosam animam capit, & iniquitatis ream constituit, vel sola aspectu. Nunquid enim homo potest abscondere ignem in sinu suo, ut vestimenta illius non ardeant? Unde recte <bl>Germani, Das strow vom fewz/so brens</bl> <bl>nit. Weit[?] Darnon/ ist gut fürs gesch[?].</bl> Igitur Alexander Magnus, quum Darij filias haberet captiuas, demissis oculis eas salutabat, idque raro, sibi metuens ab illarum insigni forma. Idem quum apud Antipatridem cœnaret, isque ad cœnam formosam psaltriam induxisset, aspectu motus in illam exarsit; mox rogavit Antipatridem, nunquid ipse mulieris amore teneretur, illo confitente, o scefte, inquit, non tu protinus abduces è conuiuio mulierem? Ita Cyrus abstinebat à conspectu Pantheæ[?]: & Arafpo dicenti, mulierem esse insigni forma, dignam regis ocu-lis lis, Ob istuc ipsum, inquit, magis est ab illa abstinendum.
units.tr: ¶ Furthermore, the Wise Man teaches here that one should not look carelessly and too curiously at what is not to be desired. Therefore neither should a woman admire a man, nor a man a woman, for his or her appearance, and look upon them with pleasure, lest they be stirred up sensually and to sin, whereby the soul is polluted, temptation arises, and death passes in through the windows. Much less should a young man, or any man, think it safe to live together with strange women, for thereby the danger to chastity is incurred. For the beauty of women, their speech, gesture and dress, and whatever is in them, is a flame; and therefore many who have admired the appearance of another's wife have become reprobate. For their conversation kindles like a fire. Nothing, however, is safer and holier than to cultivate marriage. But just as the moth is generated from a garment to its corruption, so iniquity comes from a woman, that is, from a woman's wickedness; for so some read it, or it comes to a man from a strange woman, as the malice of the affections and the iniquity of the flesh, while by sight, speech, touch and living together a man is stirred to lust and is caught by a woman's nods. For a woman captures the precious soul of a man and makes him guilty of iniquity, even by her look alone. Can a man hide fire in his bosom and his clothes not burn? Hence the German saying rightly goes: Keep the straw away from the fire, and it will not burn; it is good to keep far from it. Therefore Alexander the Great, when he had the daughters of Darius as captives, greeted them with lowered eyes, and that rarely, fearing for himself because of their remarkable beauty. The same man, when he was dining at the house of Antipater, and Antipater had brought in a beautiful harpist for the dinner, was moved by her looks and flared up with desire for her; soon he asked Antipater whether he himself was held by love for the woman. When he confessed it, Alexander said: "You villain, will you not at once take the woman out of the banquet?" So Cyrus abstained from looking at Panthea; and when Araspes said that the woman was of remarkable beauty and worthy of the king's eyes, he said: "For that very reason one must abstain from her all the more."

units.la: 4 Additur alia ratio, propter quam Sapiens consuluit & praecepit, ne ullum homi-nem aspiciamus in pulchritudine, neque commoremur in medio mulierum. Ait enim: [illegible, ~45 letters] Quae verba multis non solum obscura, sed etiam haud digna fide videntur, praesertim mulieribus & earum praedicatori Cornelio Agrippae. Unde factum, ut alij aliter interpretati sint. Dauid Chytraeus sequutus Lutherum vertit sic: Tutius est cōuersari viro duro & terrico, quàm mulieri blandulæ, quæ contumeliæ eum exponit & ludibrio. Castalio in hoc modum: Satius est cum improbo viro contrahere, quàm cum muliere proba quidem, sed quæ causa sit turpis infamiæ.
units.tr: 4. Another reason is added, on account of which the Wise Man counselled and commanded that we should not look upon any man for his beauty, nor linger in the midst of women. For he says: [illegible] These words seem to many not only obscure but also hardly worthy of belief, especially to women and to their advocate Cornelius Agrippa. Hence it has come about that others have interpreted them differently. David Chytraeus, following Luther, translates thus: It is safer to associate with a harsh and frightening man than with a flattering woman, who exposes him to insults and mockery. Castalio, in this manner: It is better to contract with a wicked man than with a woman who is indeed upright, but who is the cause of shameful infamy.

units.la: Videtur malitia etiam apud Germanos capi pro ira. Dicimus enim de irato: <bl>Er ist bös.</bl> Apud Hebraeos sumitur etiam malitia pro tristitia, Nehem. 2. <bl>Wenn einer nicht guter Ding ist:</bl> nec non pro afflictione quae parit tristitiam. Matth. 6. Vatablus sic interpretatur: Melior est, id est, minus mala, nequitia viri quàm mulier benignam se præstans, mulier quæ eadem autor est probrosæ turpitudinis. Q. d. Ad turpes amores plus est periculi à benignitate & comitate mulierum, quàm ab aperta virorum nequitia. Quid si melior est deformitas viri, quàm pulchra mulier, &c. propter æquiuocationem vocum Hebraicarum רע[?] quæ malum & deformem, & טוב quæ bonum & pulchrum significat. Hinc nos de deformi dicimus: <bl>Er hat ein böse färb.</bl>
units.tr: The word malice is also taken among the Germans for anger; for we say of an angry man: He is bad-tempered. Among the Hebrews malice is also taken for sadness, Neh. 2., "If someone is not in good spirits"; and likewise for affliction, which brings forth sadness, Matt. 6. Vatablus interprets thus: Better is, that is, less evil, the wickedness of a man than a woman who shows herself kind, a woman who is the author of shameful disgrace. That is to say: there is more danger in kindness and courtesy of women for base loves than in the open wickedness of men. What if the ugliness of a man is better than a beautiful woman, etc.? This is on account of the ambiguity of the Hebrew words רע [ra], which means both evil and ugly, and טוב [tob], which means both good and beautiful. Hence we say of an ugly man: He has a bad complexion.

units.la: Pellicani expositio talis est: Securius est homini habitare & commorari cum viro alio quo malo & infensato, quàm cum muliere bona & speciosa longo scil. tempore: parit enim societas familiaritatem, familiaritas afsectus conciliat, qui vt vehementes sunt inter amantes, & maximè in fœmina, tandem & fragiles deprehenduntur. Quin & honestas, verecundia, probitas & facetiæ, omnia promouent in viro amorem, qui licet ab initio syncerus appareat, degenerat tamen in carnem. Omnibus enim istis rationibus fœminæ placent, & ad libidinem etiam nolentes trahunt, vnde peruenitur tandem ad confusionem & opprobrium.
units.tr: Pellicanus's explanation is this: it is safer for a man to live and remain with another man, even one who is bad and hostile, than with a good and beautiful wife over a long time. For companionship produces familiarity, and familiarity wins affection, which, being intense between lovers, and especially in a woman, is in the end found to be fragile. Indeed, her honesty, modesty, uprightness and charm all foster love in the man, and although at first it appears pure, it degenerates into the flesh. For women please men in all these ways, and draw them, even unwilling, toward lust, whence at last one comes to disgrace and shame.

units.la: Videntur huc etiam accommodari posse illæ sententiæ, de quibus idem Autor supra cap. 25. vbi dicit: Non est ira super iram mulieris: & Parua omnis malitia ad malitiam mulieris. Possunt nonnunquam mulieres melius, ac maius damnum inferre, quàm viri. Nouerunt enim tegere suam malitiam sub specie boni. Vt autem stultitia Dei (id est, quod stultitiæ speciem habet) sapientior est, quàm homines, 1. Corin. 1. sic malitia viri melior est quàm benefacies mulier. Adde quod etiam plus nocent mulieres dum benefaciunt, & non aliter sentiunt, quàm quod benefaciant: quemadmodum Zares, quum suadebat suo marito Aman, vt Mardochæo crucé pararet, quo ipse cum rege Ahasuero lætus ad conuiuium iret, Helter [?] 5. & sicut vxor Saturi, de qua Victor libro primo de persecutione Vandalorum, quum dicebat ad maritum: Miserere mei dulcissime simul & tui, miserere communibus liberis, quos conspicis ipse: & sicut Iezabel, quum dicebat regi Achab tristi & decumbenti: Surge & comede panem, & æquo animo esto. Ego dabo tibi vineam Naboth Iezraelitæ, 3.Reg.21. Melior erat malitia, id est, obiurgatio viri Eliæ, de qua cap.eodem, quàm ista mulier benefaciens. Salomon Prouerb.27. dicit: Meliora sunt vulnera diligentis, quàm fraudulenta oscula [?] odientis.
units.tr: Those sayings also seem applicable here, about which the same author says above, in chapter 25, where he states: "No wrath is above the wrath of a woman," and "All malice is small compared with the malice of a woman." Women can sometimes inflict greater and worse harm than men, for they know how to hide their malice under the appearance of good. And just as the foolishness of God (that is, what has the appearance of foolishness) is wiser than men (1 Cor. 1), so the malice of a man is better than a woman who does good. Add that women also do more harm when they do good, and think of nothing but doing good: as Zeresh, when she urged her husband Haman to prepare a cross for Mordecai, so that he might go happily with King Ahasuerus to the banquet (Esther 5); and as the wife of Saturus, of whom Victor writes in the first book of his history of the persecution of the Vandals, when she said to her husband: "Have mercy on me, most sweet one, and on yourself, have mercy on our common children whom you see"; and as Jezebel, when she said to King Ahab, sad and lying down: "Get up and eat bread, and be of good cheer. I will give you the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite" (1 Kings 21). The rebuke of Elijah, the man, mentioned in the same chapter, was better than that woman's doing good. Solomon says in Proverbs 27: "The wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses of one who hates."

units.la: Præterea cum malitia etiam significet peccatum & iniquitatem, videtur vir qui peccauit quidem, sed propter peccatum dolet ac resipiscit, melior, quàm mulier superba, quæ benefacit quidem, sed de suis benefactis gloriatur, vt Pharisæus, Lucæ 18. aut quæ officia exprobrat. Deus omnipotens, cuius imbecillitas robustior est, quàm homines, feruet nouos illos coniuges, qui iam præsentes sunt, atque nos omnes, à peccato immunes, & statuat in conspectu gloriæ suæ incontaminatos, cum exultatione, per Christum Iesum Dominum nostrum, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, since malice also signifies sin and iniquity, a man who has indeed sinned, but grieves over his sin and repents, seems better than a proud woman who does good indeed but boasts of her good deeds, like the Pharisee in Luke 18, or who reproaches others for their services. May almighty God, whose weakness is stronger than men, bless those new spouses who are now present, and all of us, free from sin, and set us unstained before the sight of his glory with exultation, through Christ Jesus our Lord, Amen.

units.la: Finis quadraginta Concionum ex vetere desumptarum instrumento.
units.tr: The end of the forty sermons taken from the Old Testament.

units.la: CONCIO XLI.
units.tr: SERMON XLI.

units.la: Matt. 5.
units.tr: Matt. 5.

units.la: Audistis[?] quod dictum fuerit antiquis, Non committes adulterium. At ego dico vobis, quod quicunque aspexerit uxorem alterius ad concupiscendum eam, iam adulterium cum ea commisit in corde suo. Quod si oculus tuus dexter offendiculo tibi fuerit, erue illum, & abijce abs te. Expedit enim tibi ut pereat unum membrorum tuorum, ac non totum corpus tuum conijciatur in gehennam. Et si dextera tua manus offenderit tibi, amputa eam, & proijce abs te. Expedit enim, ut pereat unum membrorum tuorum, ac non totum corpus tuum conijciatur in gehennam.
units.tr: You have heard that it was said to the ancients, "You shall not commit adultery." But I say to you that whoever looks at another man's wife in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. If your right eye is an occasion of stumbling to you, pluck it out and throw it away from you. For it is profitable for you that one of your members perish, and that your whole body not be cast into hell. And if your right hand offends you, cut it off and throw it away from you. For it is profitable that one of your members perish, and that your whole body not be cast into hell.

units.la: I Scopus horum verborum est, Christum Dominum usque adeo non tollere legem Dei suam doctrina, ut illam magis adimpleat, perfectioremque a suis iustitiam exigat, quam fuerit Scribarum & Pharisaeorum: idque declarat iam exemplo de adulterando, ut prius de occidendo. Asserit enim non solum impurum esse, & adulterij reum, eum qui opere alienam attingit: sed & eum, qui vel concupiscit, vel oculis impudicis intuetur, proximi vxorem : atque multò magis eum, qui non tantùm concupiscentiam videndi curiositate colligit, & ad hoc aspicit, vt oblectet suum aspectum, verùm etiá verbis pudicitiam alterius sollicitat: (Genef. 39.) & ita non suæ tantùm, sed & alienæ perditionis autor efficitur. Concupiscentiam & lex ipsa damnat, dicens: Ne concupiscas vxorem proximi tui. Sciebant hoc Iudæi, verùm adulterij loco haberi coram Deo cordis concupiscentiam, non animaduertebant. Opus igitur erat, vt hoc declararetur. Nam ob eam causam data est lex, vt cordis malitiam detegeret & accusaret.
units.tr: 1 The aim of these words is to show that Christ the Lord does not abolish God's law by his teaching but rather fulfils it more fully, and demands from his people a greater and more perfect righteousness than that of the scribes and Pharisees. He demonstrates this first by the example of adultery, as he did before with murder. For he declares that not only the one who actually touches another's wife is impure and guilty of adultery, but also the one who lusts after her or looks at her with an immodest eye, and much more the one who does not merely gather desire by curiously gazing, looking only to delight in the sight, but even solicits another's chastity with words (Gen. 39). In this way he becomes the author not only of his own ruin but of another's too. The law itself condemns covetousness, saying, "You shall not covet your neighbour's wife." The Jews knew this, yet they did not notice that before God the lust of the heart counts as adultery. It was therefore necessary that this be made plain. For the law was given for this very reason, that it might uncover and accuse the wickedness of the heart.

units.la: 2 Sunt autem duo visus genera hic consideranda : vnum, quod concupiscentiam praecedit: alterum, quod sequitur. Primum per se quidem peccatum non est, carni tamen timore Dei non refrenatæ causam adfert concupiscendi, hoc est, concupiscentiæ malum in corde latens excitat. Alterum, quo concepto concupiscentiæ stimulo oculi sallaces in mulierem cupidius injiciuntur, notam habet libidinis, & hæc Christi sententia condenatur. De hoc est locus Petri 2. Pet. 2. Oculos, inquit, habentes plenos adulterio. Neque enim apertius testimonium est libidinis in corde gliscentis. Vnde & duo iniqui seniores iusserunt, vt Susanna discooperiretur, vt vel sic fallarentur[?] decore eius, Dan. 3.[?] Et Isa. 3.[?] impudicitia filiarum Israel notatur his verbis[?]: Et nutibus oculorum ibant. Malu concupiscentiæ huius peruersæ, in corde quidem est, unde adulterium, teste Christo Matt. 15. egreditur: verum illam externa obiecta, etiamsi non inferunt, tamen excitant & inflammant, haud aliter atque scintillam flatus. Obiecta vero, quibus concupiscentia excitatur, per sensus capiuntur, & virus illud malum in intimis visceribus haerens irritant: vt sunt auditus, tactus & visus. Sensus autem omnium velocissimus, ac pestilentissimus est visus, vt recte ille dixerit, Eccles. 1ȝ[?]. Nequius oculo quid creatum est? Per hunc obiecta species corde penitus insculpitur, & concupiscentia libidini ampletenda traditur. Hinc Græci dicunt: Ἐκ τῆς ὄψεως γίνεται τὸ ἔρως[?]. Ex visu amor. Et vulgò Germani dicunt: <bl>Auß Den augen</bl> <bl>/ auß dem finn.</bl> Diogenes animaduertens Olympionicem quendam oculos defigere in scortum, adeo vt præteritum capite reflexo intueretur: Ecce vt, inquit, aries Martius à puella publica, obtorto collo vinctus abducitur. Ridiculum existimabat, certare cum electis viris, & à vili puella veluti captiuum trahi fine funibus. Proinde magno timore Dei, & diligenti cautione custodienda est oculorum procacitas ac temeritas, ne laqueis illorum irretiti, concupiscentiæ tyrannidi subijciamur. Quàm enim periculosum sit oculis cautionis adimere frenum, & liberum permittere re excursum, præter quotidianam nostri seculi experientiam, etiam aliquot scripturæ exemplis declaratur. Gen. 6. Viderunt filij potentum filias hominu, quod essent pulchrae, & acceperunt sibi ex illis, quascunque lubebat. Gen.34. Dina egreditur incautius ad videndum mulieres regionis illius, videtur concupiscitur, rapitur, opprimitur. Gene.39. vxor Putiphar is oculos in Iosephum coniicit, & concupiscentia erga adolescentem accenditur. Et ne quis causetur horum impietatem: Dauid propheta & vir Dei, cum videret lauantem Beerfaba, videndo concupiscit, & concupiscendo in opus adulterij abripitur, 2. Reg. 11. Hæc non ideo dicuntur, quod vel oculis, vel formæ muliebri peruersi quicquam naturaliter infit. Absit. utraque bonæ Dei creaturæ sunt, in quibus sapientia ac prouidentia creatoris etiam cum fructu considerari queant. Vicium non est in obiectis, neque in videndi organis, sed in cordibus nostris: quæ si infirmata concupiscentia defecatisque carnis affectibus spiritus imperio subessent, possemus utique absque periculo, imo non absque periculo tantum, sed & ad laudem creatoris quasuis comtemplari vel mulierum, vel aliarum rerum formas, sicuti de Abbate Pambone traditur.
units.tr: 2 Two kinds of looking must be considered here: one that goes before lust, and another that follows it. The first is not in itself a sin, but it gives the flesh, which is not restrained by the fear of God, an occasion to desire; that is, it stirs up the evil of concupiscence lying hidden in the heart. The second is the kind in which, once the sting of desire has been conceived, deceitful eyes are cast upon a woman more eagerly; this bears the mark of lust, and it is this that Christ's saying condemns. Peter's passage on this is 2 Pet. 2: "Having eyes full of adultery," he says. Nor is there any plainer testimony of lust blazing up in the heart. Hence also the two wicked elders ordered Susanna to be uncovered, so that they might be deceived by her beauty (Dan. 13). And the immodesty of the daughters of Israel is noted in Isaiah 3 in these words: "And they went with the winking of their eyes." The evil of this perverse desire is indeed in the heart, from which adultery comes forth, as Christ testifies in Matt. 15. Yet external objects, even if they do not bring it in, nevertheless arouse and inflame it, just as a breath kindles a spark. The objects by which concupiscence is aroused are taken in through the senses and stir up that evil poison which clings to the innermost parts: these are hearing, touch and sight. Of all the senses, however, sight is the swiftest and the most destructive, as the author rightly said: "What created thing is more wicked than the eye?" (Eccles. 13 [i.e. 14 in some editions]). Through it the object's image is carved deeply into the heart, and desire is handed over to be embraced by lust. Hence the Greeks say: "From seeing comes loving" [Ἐκ τῆς ὄψεως γίνεται τὸ ἔρως]. And the Germans commonly say: "From the eyes, from the mind." Diogenes, noticing a certain Olympic victor fixing his eyes on a prostitute so that he kept looking at her even after she had passed, with his head turned back, said: "Look, the Martian ram is being led away by a public girl, dragged along by the neck." He thought it ridiculous to compete with chosen men, and to be led off like a captive by a cheap girl without any ropes. Therefore the boldness and rashness of the eyes must be guarded with great fear of God and careful caution, lest, caught in their snares, we be subjected to the tyranny of desire. How dangerous it is to strip the eyes of the bridle of caution and let them run free, apart from the daily experience of our age, is also shown by several examples from Scripture. Gen. 6: "The sons of the mighty saw the daughters of men, that they were fair, and they took for themselves whichever ones they pleased." Gen. 34: Dinah went out too carelessly to see the women of that land; she was seen, desired, seized and violated. Gen. 39: the wife of Potiphar cast her eyes upon Joseph, and desire for the young man was kindled. And lest anyone excuse their impiety: David the prophet and man of God, when he saw Bathsheba bathing, desired her by looking, and by desiring he was swept into the deed of adultery (2 Sam. 11). These things are not said because there is anything perverse by nature either in the eyes or in the form of a woman. Far from it! Both are creatures of the good God, in which the wisdom and providence of the Creator can even be considered with profit. The fault lies not in the objects, nor in the organs of sight, but in our hearts. If concupiscence were weakened and the affections of the flesh purged, and the spirit ruled, we could certainly contemplate the forms of women or of other things without danger, indeed not only without danger but even to the praise of the Creator, just as is told of Abbot Pambo.

units.la: Cæterum, quemadmodum nos, cum gladium teneri videmus a puero (teste Chrysostomo) etiamsi nondum eum vulneratum in de esse cernamus, verberamus tamen, ac sæpe minantes denunciamus, ne quandoque illum rursus attingat: ita etiam Deus inuerecundum coercet affectum, ne quandoque in ipsam quoque incidat actionem. Etsi autem cordis concupiscentiæ adulterij coram Deo damnetur: multum tamen non in humano tantùm statu & conuictu, sed & coram Deo, inter concupiscentiam, & opus peccati, discriminis esse ostenditur. Multò enim grauius peccat, qui opere quoque vxorem proximi stuprat(id quod & speciali præcepto prohibitum est) quàm qui illam duntaxat concupiscit.
units.tr: Moreover, just as when we see a boy holding a sword (as Chrysostom testifies), even though we do not yet see him wounded by it, we nevertheless scold him and often warn him, threatening, lest at some time he touch it again, so too God restrains the shameless affection, lest at some time it also fall into the act itself. Although the lust of the heart is condemned before God as adultery, it is nevertheless shown that there is a great difference, not only in human status and intercourse but also before God, between concupiscence and the deed of sin. For the one who also violates his neighbour's wife in deed sins far more gravely (which is also forbidden by a special commandment) than the one who merely desires her.

units.la: 3 Discimus porrò ex ista expositione legis de adulterando, non modò peccata nostra cognoscere, quod sanè necessarium est, si ab illis absolui voluerimus, Ioan.9.& 1.Ioa.1. sed etiam quomodo Christus venerit hanc legem adimplere: nimirum non solum imputando nobis suam iustitiam & sanctimoniam, remissis peccatis & immundicijs nostris, per fidem: verùm etiam præscribendo nobis rationem, & tribuendo facultatem spiritus sui istud præceptum faciendi. Ait enim: Quòd si oculus tuus dexter obstaculo tibi fuerit, erue illū, & abijce abs te, id est, pactionem fac cum oculo tuo nequaquam aspicere virgines, vt Iobus fecit, Iob.31. & auerte oculos à muliere formosa, nec alienam contemplare pulchritudinem, vt Siracides monet, Eccles.9. & 42. ac spiritu facta corporis mortifica, membra tua terrestria neca, carne cum[?] affectibus & concupiscentijs crucifige, ne regnet peccatum in corpore tuo mortali, vt obedias illi per cupiditates eius, quemadmodum Paulus docet, Rom. 8. & 6, Col. 3. Gal. 5. Denique quicquid te ad peccandum pellicit aut impellit, vita & abijce, etiamsi sit oculo charius. Habet enim hæc particula adhortationem de vitanda peccati occasione, ex præmissa de cordis adulterio sententia natam. Quia crebrò homines per occasiones non euitatas incidunt in adulteria aut scortationes. Imitatur autem hoc loco Christus studium boni medici, qui non solum morbi causas & grauitatem ægroto aperit, vt sciat quàm perniciosè decumbat, sed simul quid faciendum sit præcipit, & vt infirmitatis suæ rationem habeat admonet, quatenus etsi nequeat in vniuersum excutere morbum, vires illi tamé, & occasionem inualescendi amputet. Atque hac ratione iubet quæcunque morbo vires addunt studiosè vitare, nisi velit de ipsa vita periclitari.
units.tr: 3 Furthermore, from this exposition of the law concerning adultery we learn not only to recognise our sins, which is certainly necessary if we wish to be absolved from them (John 9; 1 John 1), but also how Christ came to fulfil this law: namely, not only by imputing to us, through faith, his own righteousness and holiness, our sins and uncleanness being forgiven, but also by prescribing to us the way and by granting us, through his Spirit, the ability to do this command. For he says: "If your right eye is an obstacle to you, pluck it out and throw it away from you," that is, make a covenant with your eye never to look upon virgins, as Job did (Job 31), and turn your eyes away from a beautiful woman, nor gaze upon another's beauty, as Sirach advises (Eccles. 9 and 42). And by the Spirit, mortify the deeds of the body, put to death your earthly members, crucify the flesh with its affections and desires, so that sin does not reign in your mortal body and you do not obey it in its lusts, as Paul teaches (Rom. 8 and 6; Col. 3; Gal. 5). In short, whatever entices or impels you to sin, cast it away from you, even if it is dearer than your eye. For this phrase contains an exhortation to avoid the occasion of sin, arising from the preceding saying about adultery of the heart. For people often fall into adultery or fornication through occasions they have not avoided. Here Christ imitates the care of a good physician, who not only reveals to the sick man the causes and seriousness of his disease, so that he may know how dangerously he lies ill, but at the same time prescribes what must be done and advises him to take account of his weakness, so that even if he cannot entirely drive out the disease, he may at least cut off its strength and the occasion for it to grow. In this way he orders that whatever adds strength to the disease be carefully avoided, unless one wishes to be imperilled as to life itself.

units.la: Planè ad hunc modum verus ille animarum nostrarum medicus de vitanda peccati occasione adhortationem subijcit: præcedenti diuinæ legis expositione morbum corruptæ nostræ naturæ in imis visceribus latentem aperuit, & quanti sit periculi exposuit. Iam consequenter considerato morbi huius, id est, concupiscentiæ corruptæ, ac peruersæ ingenio, quàm necessarium sit, vt omnem illi occasionem sese exerendi, & inualescendi amputemus, diligenter admonet.
units.tr: Plainly in this manner that true physician of our souls also adds an exhortation to avoid the occasion of sin. Having already set out the exposition of the divine law, he has revealed the disease of our corrupt nature lying hidden in the innermost viscera, and has laid out how great the danger is. Now, consequently, having considered the nature and perverse character of this disease, that is, corrupt concupiscence, he diligently warns how necessary it is that we cut off from it every occasion of showing itself and gaining strength.

units.la: Tantundem itaque est quod hîc dicit (vt Musculus exponit) Quoniam ita comparati est-is, ut peruersa fitis concupiscentia corrupti, & malum illud cordis vestri opinione citius per obiecta externa, fi illa oculos vestros incurrant, excitetur, & fe e exerat: deinde quoniam ea est diuinae iustitiae ἀχρειωσία[?], ut adulterij condemnetur, quisquis alienam vxorem ad concupiscendum intuitus fuerit: etiam atque etiam videndum vobis est, nisi perire volueritis, ut infirmitatis vestrae ratione habentes, omnem occasionem offendiculi, aut incitamenti ftudiofisimè declinetis: nec quicquam vsque adeo charum vobis esse sinatis, cuius gratia, fi cedat ad ruinam, fempiterno vos permittatis obnoxios fieri exitio.
units.tr: Therefore what he says here amounts to the same thing (as Musculus expounds it): Since you are so constituted that the perverse lust of a corrupt desire is aroused, and that evil of the heart, by your own opinion, more quickly through external objects if they fall under your eyes, and breaks forth; and then since it is the divine justice's [ἀχρειωσία?] that whoever looks upon another's wife to desire her is condemned for adultery, you must look to it again and again, unless you wish to perish, that, bearing your infirmity in mind, you most diligently avoid every occasion of stumbling or incitement; and do not allow anything to be so dear to you that, for its sake, if it leads to your ruin, you permit yourselves to be exposed to everlasting destruction.

units.la: Nihil tam est vobis affine, nihil adeo coniunctum, nihil etiam agnatum, & ita intimum, quod non fit amputandum, fi ruinae occasionem adferat: hoc est, fi causam præstet contra Deum delinquendi, etiamsi membrum aliquod corporis vestri fit, imo præcipuum & necessarium membrum, qualia sunt, oculus dexter, & manus dextera. Nam etiamsi carendum fit his membris, satius tamen est abfque illis seruari, quàm cum eis abijci in gehenam: à qua nos custodiat ille, qui potest in nobis corda munda creare, à peccato immunes feruare, & statuere in conspectu gloriae suae, incontaminatos, cum exultatione, hoc est, solus sapiens Deus seruator noster, cui gloria & magnificentia, & imperium, & potestas, nunc & in omnia secula, Amen.
units.tr: Nothing is so akin to you, nothing so joined to you, nothing even so related and so intimate, that it should not be cut off if it brings the occasion of ruin; that is, if it furnishes a cause for offending against God, even if it is some member of your body, indeed a principal and necessary member, such as the right eye and the right hand. For even if one must go without these members, it is nonetheless better to be preserved without them than, with them, to be cast into Gehenna; from which may that One guard us, who is able to create pure hearts in us, to keep us free from sin, and to set us without blemish before the presence of his glory with exultation: that is, the only wise God our Saviour, to whom be glory and majesty, dominion and power, now and for ever. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XLII.
units.tr: CONCIO XLII. (SERMON 42)

units.la: Matth. 9.
units.tr: Matt. 9.

units.la: T[?]unc adeunt eum discipuli Ioannis dicentes: Quam ob causam nos & Pharisæi ieiunamus plerunque, discipuli vero tui non ieiunant? Et dixit illis Iesus: Num possunt filij sponsi lugere, quandiu cum illis est sponsus? Venient autem dies, quum tolletur ab eis sponsus, & tunc ieiunabunt. Nullus immittit assumentum panni rudis in vestem veteri: aufert enim supplementum illius a vestimento, & peior ruptura fit. Neque mittunt vinum nouum in vtres veteres, alioqui rumpuntur vtres, & vinum effunditur, & vtres perëunt. Sed mittunt vinum nouum in vtres nouos, & vtraque simul seruantur.
units.tr: Then came the disciples of John to him, saying: Why do we and the Pharisees fast often, but your disciples do not fast? And Jesus said to them: Can the children of the bridegroom mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then they will fast. No one puts a piece of new cloth on an old garment; for the patch pulls away from the garment, and the tear becomes worse. Nor do they put new wine into old wineskins, otherwise the skins burst, the wine is poured out, and the skins perish. But they put new wine into new skins, and both are preserved together.

units.la: ı Quæstio hic proponitur Christo (qui cum peccatoribus comederat) de ieiunio, quæ duo habet. vnum, quam ob causam discipuli Ioannis & Pharisæi crebrò ieiunent: alterum, cur discipuli sui (quos tamen ipse conetur docere viam meliorem & perfectiorem ad vitam æternam) non ieiunent, sed vt Lucas habet cap. 5. edant & bibant? In qua expostulatione multa notanda sunt. Primò: Non mirū esse, si nemo ex nobis tam alto māne surgere potest ut omnibus placeat, cum & Christus nunquam tam benefacere ac docere potuerit, quin fuerint, qui id reprehenderint.
