units.tr: 1 Here Christ, who had been eating with sinners, is asked a question about fasting, which has two parts: first, why the disciples of John and the Pharisees fast so often; second, why his own disciples (whom he nevertheless tries to teach the better and more perfect way to eternal life) do not fast, but, as Luke has it in chapter 5, eat and drink. Many things are to be noted in this complaint. First, it is no wonder if none of us can rise so early in the morning as to please everyone, since Christ himself could never do good or teach so well that there were not those who found fault with it.

units.la: Deinde, quomodo ilico externa religionis opera supercilium adducant, & ad judicandum alios permoveant eos, qui solida justitia prædit i non sunt: cum tamen externa illa, non solum nil sint sine fide & charitate, sed & abominatio in conspectu Dei, Jesa.1.
units.tr: Second, how quickly outward works of religion raise the eyebrows of those who are not sound in true righteousness, and move them to judge others; yet those outward works are not only nothing without faith and charity, but are an abomination in the sight of God, Isaiah 1.

units.la: Tertiò, Quàm morosum fit ingenium hypocritarum, quod nullũ genus vitæ probat, nisi quod ad ipsorum exemplar instituru est, nihilq; putat sanctum, nisi quod à communi vitæ statu abhorret.
units.tr: Third, how fastidious is the temper of hypocrites, who approve no way of life except the one they have prescribed as their own pattern, and think nothing holy except what shrinks from the common state of life.

units.la: Quarto, Quàm appositus sit animalis homo, animalis auditor, ad hæresis ingenium.
units.tr: Fourth, how readily an animal man, an animal listener, is inclined to the spirit of heresy.

units.la: Discipuli enim Joannis (non illi, qui verâ fidem à Joanne didicerant, & mox Christum sectati sunt, sed qui hypocrisim tantũ è Joanne collegerunt) contra Christum & suos cum Pharisæis conspirant, cùm tamen Christo & Joanni optimè convenerint. Joannes etenim nihil aliud quæsivit, quàm gloriam Christi. Nihilominus tamen contra Christum invidiæ zelo pro Joanne suo ducuntur discipuli Joannis,Joann.3. Ad eum modum & Corinthii faciebant,1. Corinth.1.
units.tr: For the disciples of John (not those who had learned the true faith from John and soon followed Christ, but those who had gathered only the hypocrisy from John) conspire with the Pharisees against Christ and his followers, although they agreed very well with Christ and John. For John sought nothing but the glory of Christ. Nevertheless the disciples of John, out of zeal of envy, are led against Christ on behalf of their John, John 3. The Corinthians did the same, 1 Corinthians 1.

units.la: Quinto, quę veritatis sit fors.contra illam enim in unum conspirant, etiam qui intra se aliàs dissident: ut Joannis discipuli, & Pharisæi, qui Joannem non receperunt, Matth.11.
units.tr: Fifth, consider what kind of company truth has: against it even those who otherwise disagree among themselves unite in one conspiracy, as the disciples of John and the Pharisees, who did not receive John, Matt. 11.
21. Luke 7.

units.la: Sextò, non rarum esse, nec absurdum alios ab aliis etiam bene concordibus aliter atque aliter instituì. Oportet omnino observare commoditatem subiectorum. Hinc illud Augustini, Epist.86. Sit vna fides vniuersæ, quæ vbiq; dilatatur ecclesiæ, tanquam intus in membris, etiamsi ipsa fidei vnitas quibusdam diuersis observationib. celebratur, quibus nullo modo quod in fide verum est, impeditur. Hæc ille. Cauendum ergo est, ne ob ritus externos scindatur fidei consensus, & rumpatur charitatis vinculum.
units.tr: Sixth, it is not rare, nor absurd, that some are instituted differently from others even when they agree well together. One must certainly observe the convenience of those who are under instruction. Hence that saying of Augustine, Epistle 86: There is one faith of the whole Church, which is spread everywhere, as if inwardly in its members, even though the unity of the faith is celebrated by various observances, by which in no way is what is true in the faith hindered. So he. We must therefore take care that the agreement of faith is not torn apart over external rites, and the bond of charity broken.

units.la: 2 Porrò quemadmodum quæstio calumniosa, de qua diximus, duo obiecit: ita & responsio Christi duo habet. Primùm autem respondet ad posterius, dicens: Num possunt filij sponsi, seu thalami nuptialis, i.e. amici & sodales ad nuptias inuitati, lugere, quàm diu cum illis est sponsus, &c. Quibus verbis, nec negat discipulos suos non ieiunare, nec ieiunia calumniatur (quæ olim in publicis afflictionibus observabantur à mane vsque ad vesperam, vt homines aptiores essent ad orandum, Iud. 20. Ioann. 3.) sed tantum ostendit illis nondum esse ieiunij tempus, propter præsentiam sponsi, qui ipsemet erat, Ioan. 3. fore autem aliquando, vt & ipsi luctum acturi & ieiunaturi sint, Actor.13.14. Vt enim totum tempus desponsationis vsque ad nuptias curis vacat, vbi vero sponsus iam factus est maritus, & sponsa vxor, curæ mox incipiunt, & augetur subinde in finem usque : sic res habuit omnino cum Christo & discipulis. Interim enim diu apud eos fuit, quibus nam molestijs presi fuit ? profecto nullis. Unde & Dominus audet rogare, Luc.22. Quum mihi vos sine sacculo & pera, & calciamentis, numquid defuit vobis ? Sed postquam est ablatus ab eis, tunc impletum est quod praedixerat, Ioan. 16. In mundo afflictionem habetis. Tunc & ieiunarunt & precati sunt, quo possent perfistere in tentationibus tribulationibusque.
units.tr: 2 Furthermore, just as the captious question we have mentioned raised two points, so Christ's answer also has two parts. He first answers the second point, saying: Can the children of the bridegroom, that is, the bridegroom's attendants, the friends and companions invited to the wedding, mourn as long as the bridegroom is with them? By these words he neither denies that his disciples do not fast, nor finds fault with fasting (which was once observed in public afflictions from morning until evening, so that men might be better fitted for prayer, Judges 20; John 3), but only shows them that it is not yet the time for fasting, because of the presence of the bridegroom, who was himself the one, John 3; but that the time will come when they too will mourn and fast, Acts 13 and 14. For just as the whole time of betrothal until the wedding is free from cares, but once the bridegroom has become husband and the bride wife, cares soon begin and increase continually to the end, so it was altogether with Christ and his disciples. For while he was with them for a long time, by what troubles were they pressed? Surely by none. Hence the Lord even dares to ask, Luke 22: When I sent you without purse, bag, and sandals, did you lack anything? But after he was taken from them, then what he had foretold was fulfilled, John 16: In the world you have affliction. Then they fasted and prayed, so that they might persevere in temptations and tribulations.

units.la: Caeterum cum Christus se sponsum hoc loco dicat, necesse est, ut sponsam habeat : & quoniam non legimus illum mundano more nupsisse, opus erit, ut nuptiæ ipsius cœlestes sint & spirituales. Hinc quasi manu ducimur ad sublime illud humanæ reconciliationis ac redemptionis mysterium, ab æterno quidem prædestinatum divinitus, nouissimis vero tandem temporibus præstitum, & per euangelium mundo revelatum, quod omnium pulcherrimè per nuptialis fœderis ac pacti similitudinem, considerandum nobis hoc & aliis locis proponitur, ut videamus reconciliationem humani generis esse iucundissimam, utilissimam & omnium firmissimam, ne quo pacto illi diffidamus. Quemadmodum .n. apud magnates ac principes huius seculi, quando qui antea graviter à se invicem discrepaverant, reconciliantur, quatenus fausta & firma fit reconciliatio, imo maior amicitia, quam fuerat ante discordiam, contrahatur & corroboretur, nuptiæ instituntur: ita ad certificandam & corroborandæ reconciliationis fiduciæ instituta sunt à Deo nuptiæ, sumptis ex utroque latere, qui connubiali vinculo coadunati, quasi quædam reconciliationis pignora essent & obsignatio: nempe ex parte Dei demissus est, non angelus aliquis, sed ipse Dei filius unigenitus, qui sponsus esset, & ex terris in uno homine assumpta est in sponsam ipsa humani generis natura, atque ita hoc nuptiali fœdere in unum coiere cœlestia & terrestria, Col.1.corroborataque est in perpetuum ista reconciliatio, qua genus humanum cum creatore suo Deo reconciliatum est. Desponsatio ista facta est per incarnationem Verbi, qua in unam personam[?] coadunatæ sunt divinitas & humanitas, quaque factum est, ut filius Dei iam sit caro de carne nostra, & nos spiritus de spiritu ipsius. De hoc mysterio vide ad Eph.5. Ex virtute itaque huius desponsationis non solum corroborata nobis est reconciliatio cum Deo, sed ipsa humana natura omnino divinam gloriam & potentiam in Christo adepta est, ita ut iam nostra sint omnia, quæ Christi sunt: & vicissim quæ nostra erat miseria, Christi facta fit. Hinc est, quod Paulus dicit: Omnia vestra sunt, vos autem Christi, Christus vero Dei. Prorsus ineffabile est desponsationis huius gloria & maiestas. Quis enarret benevolentiam Dei, qua filium suum in has seces mortalium demissum perditissimo hu[?] mano generi etiam connubialiter coniungi voluit? Cogitent hæc secum, qui nuptijs interfunt. Sit etiam vel ob hoc mysterium, inter omnes coniugium honorabile, videantque hinc coniuges, quàm sanctè statum tam sanctum colere debeant. Statuat omnis sponsus sibi ob oculos exemplum Christi, qui sponsus factus est: & omnis sponsa exemplum ecclesiæ, quæ sponsa est.
units.tr: Moreover, since Christ here calls himself the bridegroom, he must of necessity have a bride; and since we do not read that he married in the worldly manner, it must be that his marriage is heavenly and spiritual. Hence we are led, as if by the hand, to that sublime mystery of human reconciliation and redemption, decreed by God from eternity but accomplished in the last times, and revealed to the world through the gospel; this is set before us, here and in other places, most beautifully under the likeness of a nuptial covenant and pact, so that we may see that the reconciliation of the human race is most joyful, most useful, and the most firm of all, so that we may in no way distrust it. For just as among the great men and princes of this age, when those who had previously been seriously at odds are reconciled, weddings are arranged so that the reconciliation may be happy and firm, and even a greater friendship than before the discord may be formed and strengthened: so God instituted a marriage to certify and strengthen the confidence of reconciliation, taking persons from each side, who, joined by the bond of marriage, would be as pledges and seal of the reconciliation. On God's side, indeed, was sent not some angel but the only-begotten Son of God himself, who was to be the bridegroom; and from the earth, in one man, human nature itself was taken as the bride; and so in this nuptial covenant heaven and earth came together into one, Colossians 1, and that reconciliation by which the human race has been reconciled with its Creator God was confirmed forever. This betrothal was made through the incarnation of the Word, by which divinity and humanity were joined into one person, and by which it came about that the Son of God is now flesh of our flesh, and we are spirit of his Spirit. On this mystery see Ephesians 5. By the power of this betrothal, therefore, not only has our reconciliation with God been strengthened, but human nature itself has wholly obtained the divine glory and power in Christ, so that now all things that are Christ's are ours, and conversely what was our misery has become Christ's. Hence Paul says: All things are yours, and you are Christ's, and Christ is God's. Truly ineffable is the glory and majesty of this betrothal. Who can declare the goodwill of God, by which he wished that his Son, sent down into these depths of mortals, should be joined in marriage even to the most lost human race? Let those who attend weddings think on these things. Let marriage be honourable among all for this mystery alone, and let spouses see from this how holily they ought to keep so holy a state. Let every bridegroom set before his eyes the example of Christ, who became a bridegroom; and every bride the example of the Church, which is the bride.

units.la: Discamus insuper ex hac parte responsi Christi, neminem sibi sine vocatione crucem debere imponere: sed quando in nuptiis est, i. præsentibus beneficijs Dei, non reiunare, non abijcere beneficia Dei, sed his cum gratiarum actione uti: post nuptias autem, i. ablato sponso, & præsentibus afflictionibus, ieiunare patienter, & Dominum invocare. Verum enim ieiunium, id est, crucis & ossicij difficultates patienter toleratas, Christus longissimè præfert cæremoniario ac electitio.
units.tr: Let us further learn from this part of Christ's answer that no one should lay a cross on himself without a calling. While the wedding lasts, that is, while God's blessings are present, we should not fast or reject God's gifts, but use them with thanksgiving. After the wedding, that is, once the bridegroom has been taken away and afflictions are present, we should fast patiently and call upon the Lord. For the true fasting, that is, the difficulties of the cross and of one's duty patiently endured, Christ far prefers to the ceremonial and the chosen observances.

units.la: 3 Postremò Dominus ad primum, quod attinet ad crebra Pharisæorum & discipulorum Joannis ieiunia, sic respondet: Nullus immittit assumentum panni rudis in veste veteri, &c. Quæ verba variè exponuntur: Alij enim his duabus similitudinibus idem doceri aiunt, quod antè docuerat Jesus de nuptias agentibus. Quidam ita exponunt, ut per vestimentum vetus, & utres veteres intelligant discipulos Christi, propter illorum infirmitatem, & per pannum rudem & vinum nouum,traditionem ieiuniorum, tarft[?] quam seriorem, quàm quæ teneritudini discipulorum Christi conuenire potuerit. Ex quo inferunt, rudibus in fide non continuò esse imponenda omnia. Sed verisimilius est,per vtres veteres & vestimentũ vetus intelligi debere Ioannis discipulos, & per vinum nouum, Christianæ fidei & libertatis doctrinam. Q. d. Christus: Non est mirum, quòd vobis doctrina mea non arridet. Quomodo enim illam amplecteremini, qui adeò insenuistis maiorum traditionibus, vt & vitam vos in illis habere putetis: vnde fit, vt libertatem filiorum Dei, & regni Dei iustitiam non agnoscentes, offendamini in hoc, quòd discipulos meos ad ieiuniorum crebram obseruantiam non instituam. Ex eo quod doctrinam suam Christus comparat vino nouo, & immissuræ panni noui, documentum accipimus, non semper malum esse, quod nouum est. Quanquam Euangelion Christi, quod pollicetur remissionem peccatorum gratis per fidem propter Christum, non ideò nouo pánno[?] confertur, quòd fit religio recens excogitata ( est enim in paradiso prædicatum, & subinde magis magisque illustratum:) sed quòd Pharisæis & discipulis eorum inauditum, infoslitum & incognitum erat, & videbatur ipsis noua religio. Vtinam nec nos, qui Euangelici vocamur,immittamus vinum nouum in vtres veteres .i. ne misceamus actuveteris hominis & novi, sed exuto vetere homine cum actibus suis, induamus novum, in Christo Iesu Domino nostro, Amen.
units.tr: 3 Last of all, the Lord answers the first point, concerning the frequent fasts of the Pharisees and the disciples of John, in this way: "No one puts a piece of unshrunk cloth on an old garment," and so on. These words are explained in various ways. Some hold that these two similitudes teach the same thing that Jesus had taught before about those who celebrate weddings. Some explain it so that by the old garment and old wineskins they understand Christ's disciples, because of their weakness, and by the unshrunk cloth and the new wine the tradition of fasts, which is too severe to suit the tenderness of Christ's disciples. From this they infer that not everything should be imposed at once on those who are untaught in the faith. But it is more probable that by the old wineskins and the old garment we should understand John's disciples, and by the new wine the Christian faith and the doctrine of liberty. That is, Christ says: It is no wonder that my teaching does not please you. For how would you embrace it, you who have grown so old in the traditions of your forefathers that you think life is to be found in them? Hence it happens that, not recognising the liberty of the sons of God and the righteousness of the kingdom of God, you take offence that I do not appoint my disciples to the frequent observance of fasts. From the fact that Christ compares his teaching to new wine and to a piece of new cloth, we learn that what is new is not always bad. Yet the gospel of Christ, which promises the forgiveness of sins freely through faith on account of Christ, is not compared to a new cloth because it is a religion recently devised (for it was preached in paradise and has been made clearer and clearer from time to time), but because it was unheard of, unusual and unknown to the Pharisees and their disciples, and seemed to them a new religion. May we, who are called evangelical, never pour new wine into old wineskins, that is, may we not mix the works of the old man with those of the new, but, putting off the old man with his deeds, put on the new in Christ Jesus our Lord. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XLIII.
units.tr: SERMON XLIII.

units.la: Matth. 16.
units.tr: Matth. 16.

units.la: Tunc Iesu dixit discipulis suis: Si quis vult post[?] me venire, abneget semetipsum, & tollat crucem suam, ac sequatur me.
units.tr: Then Jesus said to his disciples: If anyone wants to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.

units.la: 1 Nullum genus personarum est, quod per se impediat hominem, quo minus post Christum venire possit, hoc est Christi discipulus seu Christianus, & salvus fieri, & ibi esse, ubi Christus est, eiusdemque maiestatis particeps reddi. Dicit enim filius Dei Iesus ad omne[?], teste Luca cap. 9. quum convocasset t[?]urbam[?] una cum discipulis suis, ut Marcus scribit, cap 8. Si quis vult: q.d. Nemini cogo, neminem crinibus attraho, voluntarium & spontaneum peto: sed neminem etiam excludo, si quis sive vir sive mulier, sive maritus, sive caelebs, sive magistratus, sive privatus, &c. voluerit post me venire, & evangelio nomen dare, hunc recipiam. Nullus ergo in matrimonio constitutus dicat, Uxorem duxi, & ideo non possum venire, Luc. 14. Haec enim excusatio calua non accipitur. Nemo etiam attendat spiritibus impostoribus, ac doctrinis daemoniorum per simulationem falsiloquorum, cauterio notatam habentium conscientiam, prohibentium contrahere matrimonium, 1. Tim. 4. abhorrentium à coniugio, & tàquam rem prophanam damnantium: quales fuerūt Encratitæ, de quibus Eusebius lib.4.Eccles.hist.cap.28. & Irenæus de Continentibus cap.30. lib.1. Tatiani, Cathari cum sua secta, Manichæi, Hierax, nec non Syricius Papa, qui dicit, coniugium esse in carne viuere, & Deo placere non posse: Dist.82.[?] Can.2.
units.tr: 1 There is no class of people which of itself hinders a person from being able to come after Christ, that is, to become a disciple or Christian of Christ, to be saved, to be where Christ is, and to be made a partaker of his majesty. For the Son of God Jesus speaks to everyone, as Luke tells in chapter 9, when he had called the crowd together with his disciples, as Mark writes in chapter 8. "If anyone wants": that is, I compel no one, I do not drag anyone by the hair; I ask for a willing and spontaneous following. Yet I exclude no one, whether man or woman, married or single, magistrate or private person, etc., who wants to come after me and give his name to the gospel: I will receive him. Therefore no one who is married should say, "I have taken a wife, and so I cannot come" (Luke 14). For that excuse is not accepted. Nor should anyone heed deceiving spirits and doctrines of demons, spoken through the hypocrisy of liars whose conscience is branded (1 Tim. 4), who forbid marriage and abhor the married state, condemning it as something profane. Such were the Encratites, of whom Eusebius writes in Ecclesiastical History book 4, chapter 28, and Irenaeus in On the Continent, chapter 30, book 1; the Tatians, the Cathari with their sect, the Manichaeans, Hierax, and also Pope Siricius, who says that marriage is living in the flesh and cannot please God (Dist. 82, can. 2).

units.la: 2 Quoniam autem omnes capiunt Christi esse & post eum venire, in quocunque tandem statu sint: operæ precium est, indicare modum, quo id effici queat. Multi enim hoc volunt, seu potius velle dicunt, sed interim viam quæ huc ducit non curant, neque ambulare volunt: cùm tamen nullus ordo sit vel fuerit in Papatu, siue Augustinianorum, siue Franciscanorum, siue aliorum, qui non cognouerit & diligenter seruauerit sui Ordinis regulam. Itaque & nos Christiani seruemus nostram: de qua hoc loco ipse Christus: Etenim si quis, inquit, vult meus esse, abnegato seipso, & cruce sublata, me sequatur, vel ad exemplum meum se conformet.
units.tr: 2 Since, however, all people who in whatever state they may be are able to belong to Christ and to come after him, it is worth the effort to show the way by which this can be accomplished. For many want this, or rather say they want it, but meanwhile they do not heed the path that leads there, nor are they willing to walk it. Yet among the Papists there is, or has been, no order, whether of the Augustinians, the Franciscans, or others, which has not known and carefully kept the rule of its own order. So let us Christians too keep ours, of which Christ himself speaks in this place: "For if anyone," he says, "wants to be mine, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me," or conform himself to my example.

units.la: Ergo Christi discipulus censeri debet, qui verus eius imitator existit, ac in eodem currere stadio paratus est. Nam discipulorum est, ut præceptores suos sequantur.
units.tr: Therefore he ought to be counted a disciple of Christ who is his true imitator and is ready to run in the same race. For it is the mark of disciples to follow their teachers.

units.la: 3 Breuem autem imitationis regulam præscribit, ut sciamus qua præcipuè in re v[?] lit sibi nos esse similes: ea vero duobus modis constat, abnegatione nostri, & voluntaria crucis tolerantia. Abnegatio haec late patet, ut scil. renunciantes proprio ingenio, & omnibus carnis affectibus valere iussis, parati sumus in nihilum redigi, modo in nobis viuat ac regnet Deus. Nam abnegare semetipsum est voluntatem suam, affectusque proprios exuere, & alterius voluntati ac potestati se tradere, eique viuere, cuius voluntati nos addixerimus. Non quaero, ait Christus (qui seipsum exinaniuit, Philip. 2.) voluntatem meam, sed voluntatem eius qui misit me, Ioan. 5. & Luc. 22. Pater non mea voluntas, sed tua fiat. Denique abnegare seipsum est animae suae bona (constituimur enim ex corpore & anima, & habet unaquaeque pars sua bona, quibus accedunt & ea, quae vocantur fortunae bona) ita fastidire, ut etiamsi auferantur, & iudicemur aut stulti, aut indocti, aut iniusti, aut alio animi vitio obnoxij, non tamen derelinquamus Christum & vocationem eius: est bona corporis sui ita contemnere, ut etsi auferantur, non tamen reddamus malum pro malo, (1. Pet. 3.) nec abnegemus Christum, sed in Christi confessione & vocatione eius persistamus: est bona fortunae suae ita negligere, ut etiamsi auferantur, non tamen discedas à confessione Christi: est animum à suis bonis ita liberum habere, ut non moveris ad perpetrandam iniquitatem[?], etiamsi auferantur. De cruce tollenda ideo Christus concionatur, quia etsi communibus miseriis promiscuè iubiecta est omnium vita (adeoq; & coniugam, de quibus 1. Cor. 7. Apostolus inquit: Attamen afflictionem in carne habituri sunt huiusmodi) quia tamen peculiariter Deus suos exercet, ut conformes reddat imagini filii sui, hanc illis legem proprie dici non mirum est. Crucis dictio hic metaphoricè sumitur pro quavis afflictione, maximè extrema. Nam ad imitationem suae crucis, quam gravissimam laturus erat, omnemque afflictionum tolerantiam absoluturus, hac voce crucis utitur Christus, ostendens non solum leves quasdam afflictiones, sed & planè extremas discipulis suis ferendas esse: quia non dicit, Tollat paupertatem, ignominiam, famem, &c. sed crucem, in quo admonemur, quantum exigat Christiana prosessio fidei robur, & non solum bonorum huius mundi, sed & propriae vitae abnegationem.
units.tr: 3 Moreover, he prescribes a brief rule of imitation, so that we may know in what chief matter he wills us to be like himself. This rule consists of two things: the denial of ourselves and the willing bearing of the cross. This denial extends widely, namely that, renouncing our own natural disposition and bidding farewell to all the affections of the flesh, we are ready to be reduced to nothing, provided that God lives and reigns in us. For to deny oneself is to lay aside one's own will and private affections, and to surrender oneself to another's will and power, and to live for him to whose will we have bound ourselves. "I do not seek," says Christ (who emptied himself, Phil. 2), "my own will, but the will of him who sent me" (John 5). And Luke 22: "Father, not my will, but yours be done." Finally, to deny oneself is to hold the goods of one's soul in such contempt (for we consist of body and soul, and each part has its own goods, to which are added the so-called goods of fortune) that even if they are taken away, and we are judged foolish, unlearned, unjust, or subject to some other fault of mind, we do not forsake Christ and his calling. It is to hold the goods of one's body in such contempt that even if they are taken away, we do not render evil for evil (1 Pet. 3), nor deny Christ, but persist in the confession of Christ and in his calling. It is to neglect the goods of one's fortune in such a way that, even if they are taken away, you do not depart from the confession of Christ. It is to have the mind so free from its goods that you are not moved to commit iniquity, even if they are taken away. Christ preaches about taking up the cross because, although the life of all people is subject without distinction to common miseries (and so too that of married people, of whom the Apostle says in 1 Cor. 7: "Yet such people will have affliction in the flesh"), nevertheless, since God exercises his own people in a particular way, so as to make them conformed to the image of his Son, it is no wonder that this law is said to belong to them in a special sense. The word "cross" is here taken metaphorically for any affliction, especially the most extreme. For in order to imitate his own cross, which he was about to bear as the heaviest, and to complete all endurance of afflictions, Christ uses this word "cross," showing that not only some light afflictions but also the most extreme ones are to be borne by his disciples. For he does not say "let him take up poverty, disgrace, hunger," etc., but "the cross," by which we are reminded how much strength the Christian profession of faith requires, and that it demands the renunciation not only of the goods of this world but also of one's own life.

units.la: Quòd dicit, crucem suam, eo admonemur homini Christiano non esse tollendam, quavis crucem, sed suam. Quae illa est? crux Christianorum duplex est. Una est omnibus communis, de qua Galat. 5. Qui Christi sunt, carnem crucifixerunt cum affectibus & concupiscentijs. Crux est, ut faciamus obedienter ea bona opera, quae ipse Deus verbo suo facienda praecepit. Haec enim, etsi iucunda sunt spiritui, tamen carni sunt crux gr nifsima. Si quis exempli gratia, laesus fuerit a proximo, tunc caro excitatur ad iram & cupiditatem vindictae. Hic verbum Dei iubet ab ira & vindicta abstinere. Qua iussione imponitur carni grauissimum onus. Altera crux est, quam Dominus cuique specialiter imponit, ut feramus patienter omnia adversa, quae nobis vel propter iniustitiam, vel propter iustitiam accidunt, & quae non possumus legitime ac in vocatione Dei perseverantes effugere. Sicut autem grauis crux est carni, cedere voluntati Dei in faciendis bonis operibus, quae Deus praecepit: ita intolerabile ei onus videtur, cedere voluntati Dei in perferendis patienter malis, quae nobis accidere solent.
units.tr: In saying "his own cross," we are reminded that a Christian person is not to take up just any cross, but his own. What is that? The cross of Christians is twofold. One is common to all, of which Galatians 5 speaks: "Those who are Christ's have crucified the flesh with its affections and lusts." It is the cross to do obediently those good works which God himself has commanded by his word to be done. For these, although they are pleasant to the spirit, are nevertheless a most grievous cross to the flesh. For example, if someone has been wronged by a neighbour, then the flesh is stirred up to anger and the desire for revenge. Here the word of God commands abstaining from anger and vengeance. By this command the heaviest burden is laid on the flesh. The other cross is that which the Lord lays upon each person in particular, so that we bear patiently all the adversities that befall us, whether on account of injustice or on account of righteousness, and which we cannot lawfully escape while persevering in the calling of God. Just as the cross is heavy for the flesh, so it is to yield to the will of God in doing the good works which God has commanded; so it seems an intolerable burden to it to yield to the will of God in patiently enduring the evils that are wont to befall us.

units.la: Crucem ergo suam (quid enim ad te, quantam aliu[?] portet crucem, le-viorem ne tua aut graviorem, Ioan. 21.) tollere, non est sibi ipsi crucem eligere, quam vult, ut fecerunt sacerdotes Baal, Circumcelliones, &c. sed eam quam Dominus immittit.
units.tr: Therefore to take up one's own cross (for what is it to you how great a cross another carries, whether lighter or heavier than yours? John 21) is not to choose for oneself the cross one wants, as the priests of Baal did, or the Circumcellions, etc., but the one the Lord sends.

units.la: Quod non dicit, ferat, vel portet, sed tollat crucem suam: eo exigitur, non solum ut feramus quaevis adversa pro Christo, sed & cum gaudio & alacri mente feramus, crucisque oneri humeros libenter subijciamus, Iac.14[?] Actor. 5. Heb.10.
units.tr: That he does not say "let him bear" or "carry," but "let him take up" his cross, this requires not only that we bear whatever adversities for Christ's sake, but also that we bear them with joy and a ready mind, and willingly place our shoulders under the burden of the cross (James 1; Acts 5; Heb. 10).

units.la: Apud Lucam additur particula Quotidie: cui subest magnum pondus. Significat enim Christus nullum militiae nostrae finem, donec e mundo exeamus: ne quis exiitimet[?] se defunctum hac cruce ferenda, si unam tantum perpessus fuerit: sed persistendum est vsque ad finem, donec cursum consummauerimus. Sit igitur hæc assidua piorum meditatio, vbi pluribus ærumnis perfuncti fuerint, ad nouas ferendas se parare, nec vnquam fatigentur, etiamsi quotidiana fitcrux illorum. Et hoc est, quod Dominus Iesus dixit, Matth. 10. Qui perseuerauerit vsq; in finem, hic saluus erit. Graue quidem, quotidie premi cruce: graue quoque habere vxorem rixosam, quæ instar perfluentis stillicidij est: sed si cogites etiam Christū Dominū tulisse crucem suam, & quotidie multa ferre à sponsa sua: item si vitæ sequentis æternitatem, & istius breuitatem & fugacitatem consideres, leue erit quod in se graue putatur: idque per Iesum Christum Dominum nostrum, cui sit gloria & imperium in omne ævum, Amen.
units.tr: In Luke the particle "daily" is added, and it carries great weight. For Christ signifies that there is no end to our warfare until we depart from the world; lest anyone think himself released from bearing this cross if he has suffered only one. Rather, we must persevere until the end, until we have finished the course. Let this, then, be the constant meditation of the godly: when they have gone through many hardships, to prepare themselves to bear new ones, and never grow weary, even if their cross is daily. This is what the Lord Jesus said in Matthew 10: "He who perseveres to the end, the same shall be saved." It is indeed a grievous thing to be daily pressed by a cross; it is also grievous to have a quarrelsome wife, who is like a constantly dripping rain. But if you consider also that Christ the Lord bore his cross, and daily endured much from his bride; likewise, if you consider the eternity of the life to come and the brevity and fleetingness of this present life, what is thought heavy in itself will be light. This is so through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XLIIII
units.tr: CONCIO XLIIII

units.la: Matth. 19.
units.tr: Matth. 19.

units.la: Tacceserunt ad eum Pharisæi, tentantes eum, & dicentes ei: Licet ne homini diuortium facere cum vxore sua qualibet ex causa? Qui respondens ait eis: An non legistis, quod qui fecit ab initio masculum & fœminam fecit eos?
units.tr: The Pharisees came to him, testing him, and said to him: Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any cause? He answered and said to them: Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female?

units.la: Et dixit, Propterea deseret homo patrem et matrem, et adglutinabitur uxori suæ, & erunt duo in carnem unam. Itaque iam non sunt duo, sed una caro. Quod ergo Deus copulauit, homo ne separet.
units.tr: And he said: For this cause a man shall leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife, and they shall be two in one flesh. So they are no longer two, but one flesh. What therefore God has joined together, let not man put asunder.

units.la: 1 Ista verba nouis coniugibus apud nos quando benedicuntur in ecclesia (pertinent autem benedictiones nouorum coniugum ad præcepta de oratione, 1.Tim.2.&1.Tim.4. Paulus iubet cibis & matrimonio uti cum gratiarum actione) præleguntur, idque duas ob causas, sicuti ibidē legitur. Primùm ut intelligant ie in hoc statu posse Deo placere.
units.tr: 1 These words are read to new spouses among us when they are blessed in the church. (The blessings of new spouses pertain to the precepts on prayer, 1 Tim. 2 and 1 Tim. 4, where Paul bids us use food and marriage with thanksgiving.) They are read for two reasons, as is also read there. First, that they may understand that in this state they can please God.

units.la: Deinde, ut iugum coniugij (habebunt enim, ut ait Paulus, afflictionem in carne, qui in coniugio sunt) patientius ferant. Hanc enim consolationem, & illam doctrinam accipere possumus ex iis verbis. Quanquam & alia hinc discere licet, perpensis sin-gulis verbis.
units.tr: Second, that they may bear the yoke of marriage more patiently, for, as Paul says, those who are in marriage will have affliction in the flesh. For we can take this consolation and this teaching from these words. Other lessons may also be drawn from them, if each single word is weighed.

units.la: 2 Proponunt autem Pharisæi Christo hanc quæstionem, liceat ne homini diuortium facere cum uxore sua qualibet de causa? Sed hoc quærunt non discendi, sed tentandi causa, id est, occasionem captant, qua ipsum vel populo inuisum reddant, vel quæstionibus irretitum in vitæ periculum adducant. Dominus omnibus benefaciebat, atque ideo spargebatur longè lateque fama illius gloriæ; at hostes veritatis inuident Domino gloriam, dolentque quòd plebs defertis sacerdotibus & scribis Domino adhæreret. Adiunt ergo confertim Pharisæi. Et quamquam insidias Christo tendunt, & dolosè eum adoriuntur ut circumueniant. utiliter tamen nobis cessit eorum malitia[?]: sicuti Dominus mirificè in tuorum utilitatem convertere novit, quæcunque ad veræ doctrinæ subversionem machinantur impii. Nam hac occasione soluta fuit quæstio, quam pariebat repudii libertas, & de sacro ac infolubili[?] coniugii nexu certa lex tradita. Inde autem arrepta est captionis ansa, quia in utranque partem secundum ipsos non nisi odiosa esse poterat responsio. Nam quæstio admodum insidiosa est, ut si neget Christus atque damnet divortium, objiciant ei Mosem, clamentque, impiè ab ipso legem abrogari, Deut.24. quæ permittit quavis de causa dare repudii libellū, ac dimittere: sin permittat simpliciter, dicant esse magistrum licentiæ & corruptelæ morum, imo lenonem potius quàm Dei prophetam, qui sic virorum libidini indulgeat: aut secum pugnare, quum prius docuerit, non licere repudium,{*} Matth.5. Hoc quidem animis conceperant.
units.tr: 2 The Pharisees put this question to Christ: Is it lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any cause? But they ask it not to learn but to test him; that is, they seek an occasion by which they may make him hated by the people, or, entangling him in questions, bring him into danger of his life. The Lord did good to all, and so the fame of his glory spread far and wide. But the enemies of the truth envied the Lord his glory and grieved that the people, deserting the priests and scribes, clung to the Lord. So the Pharisees come together in a crowd. And although they lay snares for Christ and attack him deceitfully so as to ensnare him, their malice nonetheless turned out usefully for us, just as the Lord knows how wonderfully to turn to the good of his own whatever the impious plot to subvert true doctrine. For by this occasion the question was settled, which the freedom of divorce had raised, and a sure law was given concerning the sacred and indissoluble bond of marriage. They then seized on an opening for their trap, since, as they thought, the answer could only be hateful on either side. For the question is very insidious. If Christ denies and condemns divorce, they will object Moses and cry that he impiously abrogates the law of Deut. 24, which permits giving a bill of divorce for any cause and dismissing a wife. But if he simply permits it, they will say he is a teacher of licence and corruption of morals, a pimp rather than a prophet of God, who thus indulges the lust of men; or they will say he contradicts himself, since he had earlier taught that divorce is not lawful, Matt. 5. This is indeed what they had conceived in their minds.

units.la: Sed filius Dei (qui novit sapientes in astutia sua deprehendere) eos frustratus est illicitis repudiis severè resistens: & simul tamen demonstrans nihil se nisi legi consentaneum proferre.
units.tr: But the Son of God, who knows how to catch the wise in their own craftiness, frustrated them, sternly resisting unlawful divorces, and at the same time showing that he proposes nothing except what agrees with the law.

units.la: Nam duobus capitibus totam rem concludit: ordinem creationis debere esse instar legis, vt vir coniugalem fidem tota vita colat: diuortia autem esse permissa, non quod licita sint, sed quia cum praefracto & indocili populo negotium erat.
units.tr: For he settles the whole matter under two heads: first, that the order of creation ought to stand as a law, so that a husband keeps faith with his wife all his life; second, that divorces were permitted, not because they are lawful, but because the business was with a stubborn and unteachable people.

units.la: 3 [?] Verba responsionis Christi sic se habet; Annon legistis) Quia mouebatur quaestio à Pharisaeis, qui apud populum de Scripturae scientia[?] gloriabantur, ita loquitur Dominus, q.d. Quid me interrogatis hypocritae? Scripturam habetis, quam & legitis, atque ideo ignorantia excusari non potestis.
units.tr: 3 [?] The words of Christ's answer are these: Have you not read? Since the question was raised by the Pharisees, who boasted among the people of their knowledge of Scripture, the Lord speaks as if to say: Why do you question me, hypocrites? You have Scripture, which you also read, and therefore you cannot be excused by ignorance.

units.la: Quod is qui fecit) subaudi hominem. i.opifex deus. ab initio) creationis, vt Marcus addit, cap.10. masculum & foeminam fecit eos?) vel Deus sic homines condidit, vt sint masculus & foemina, i. simul viuant: vel sic instituit primum coniugium, vt vnus vni indissolubili copula iungeretur. Non dicit, Masculum & foeminas, vt vni masculo liceat plures foeminas possidere. Non.n. duas aut tres costas detulit de latere viri, & duas aut tres fecit mulieres. Quanquam olim concessae sunt maioribus Hebraeorum plures vxores, partim ad augendam sobolem, quae stellas caeli numero aequaret, partim propter mysticam rationem, de qua aliâs. Vide si placet Magistrum sententiarum lib. 4. Dist. 8[?]. Neque etiam dicit, Masculos & foeminam, vt vni foeminae liceat plures viros accipere. Neque,scortatorem & meretricem. Diabolus enim tales facit. Sed dicit, Masculum & foeminam creauit eos, Gen.1. Nam in numero duo[?] suo duali insistit. Sicuti & Malachias cap. 2. qu m aduersus polygamiam inuehitur, eandem rationem adducit, quod Deus in quo abundantior erat Spiritus, ut in eius arbitrio esset plures creare, unum tamen fecerit hominem, nempe qualis hic describitur à Christo. Ergo ex ordine creationis, siue vetustate ordinis, hoc est, ex prima institutione Dei, & creatione (ad quam omnia semper conformanda sunt, & ex ea abusus corrigendus) probatur matrimonij firmitas, id est, indiuidua viri cum una vxore societas, & quomodo singuli viri singulas habeant vxores.
units.tr: That he who made (understand "man": God the maker) from the beginning, that is, from the beginning of creation, as Mark adds in ch. 10, made them male and female: either God so constituted human beings that they are male and female, that is, that they live together; or he so instituted the first marriage that one man should be joined to one woman by an indissoluble bond. He does not say "males and females", so that one male may lawfully possess several females. For he did not take two or three ribs from the side of the man and make two or three women. Although in former times several wives were allowed to the greater men of the Hebrews, partly to increase offspring so that it might equal the stars of heaven in number, partly for a mystical reason, which I will treat elsewhere (see, if you like, the Master of the Sentences, book 4, dist. 8 [?]). Nor does he say "a male and females", so that one female may take several husbands. Nor "a fornicator and a harlot"; for the devil makes such. But he says: He created them male and female, Gen. 1. For he insists on the number two, its dual form. Just so Malachi, ch. 2, when he rails against polygamy, gives the same reason: God, in whom the Spirit was more abundant, so that it was in his power to create many, nevertheless made one man, namely such as is described here by Christ. Therefore from the order of creation, or the antiquity of the order, that is, from God's first institution and creation (to which all things must always be conformed, and by which abuse is to be corrected), the firmness of marriage is proved: that is, the indivisible partnership of one man with one wife, and that each husband should have a single wife.

units.la: Si quis obiiciat, hoc modo non fore licitum, mortua priore inducere alteram: facilis est responsio, non modo vinculum morte solui, sed vxorem secundam à Deo subrogari in locum prioris, quasi una & eadem esset.
units.tr: If someone objects that in this way it would not be lawful, once the first wife is dead, to bring in another, the answer is easy: not only is the bond dissolved by death, but God substitutes a second wife in place of the first, as if she were one and the same.

units.la: Et dixit) scilicet non Moses, sed conditor Deus per Adamum, seu prophetam, Gen.2.
units.tr: And he said: that is, not Moses, but the Creator God, through Adam, or through the prophet, Gen. 2.

units.la: Propterea).i.huius mutuae charitatis gratia deferet homo patrem & matrem, & agglutinabitur vxori suae.) Alterum argumentum ab excellentia coniugalis copulae sumptum.
units.tr: Therefore: that is, for the sake of this mutual love, a man shall leave father and mother and shall cleave to his wife. This is the second argument, taken from the excellence of the conjugal union.

units.la: Si à parentibus non licet temerè discedere, multò minus à coniuge, cui arctius adstricti sumus, vtpote qui ob hanc ab illis recesserimus, & qui cum hac una caro facti sumus, quod vinculum non fuit cum parentibus.
units.tr: If it is not permitted to depart lightly from parents, much less from a spouse, to whom we are bound more closely, inasmuch as we have left those parents for her sake and have been made one flesh with her, a bond that did not exist with our parents.

units.la: Sancta quidem est naturalis illa patris & matris cum filijs coniunctio: verum mariti & vxoris sanctior. Deferenda est ergo potius patris societas, si res ita exigat, quàm uxoris. Hinc sequitur, diuinum vinculum abrumpi, si vir ab uxore diuortium faciat. Relinquet inquit, i. non deferet prorsus, abrupta omni subiectione, amore & officijs (nam præceptum, Honora parentes, solui non potest: quia secum ipse pugnaret Deus, si coniugio aboleret, quam filijs erga parentes pietatem mandat) ied discedet, propriam familiam & domum constituendo. Chaldæus habet, Relinquet cubile parentum. Quare istud discedere aliqui exponunt de vitando incestu. Obseruetur hic etiam metaphora [illegible, ~8 letters] glutinationis, quæ etiam in Hebræo est. Quæ enim conglutinantur, arctissimè conjunguntur, & plane vnum corpus fieri censentur. Porrò de mysterio horum verborum videris Paulum ad Eph.5.
units.tr: That natural union of father and mother with their children is indeed holy, but the union of husband and wife is holier. The fellowship of the father is therefore to be left, if the matter requires it, rather than that of the wife. Hence it follows that the divine bond is broken if a husband divorces his wife. "He shall leave", he says, that is, he shall not altogether leave, with all subjection, love and duties abandoned (for the precept, "Honour your parents", cannot be dissolved, since God would contradict himself if by marriage he abolished the piety that he commands children to show their parents); but he shall depart, establishing his own family and house. The Chaldee paraphrast has: "He shall leave his parents' bed." Wherefore some explain this departing as avoiding incest. Observe here also the metaphor of gluing together [illegible word], which is also in the Hebrew. For things that are glued together are joined most tightly, and are judged to become one body. Moreover, for the mystery of these words, see Paul, Eph. 5.

units.la: Et erunt duo in carnem vnam ) Tertium argumentum à modo coniunctionis. Vt enim qui spiritualiter se diligunt, multorum animæ quasi vna anima esse dicuntur, Actor. 4. sic etiam vir & uxor, qui carnaliter se diligunt, vna caro dicuntur, vnusque homo, vel vna persona. Sic Anshelmus exponit: Et erunt duo in carne vna, non tres, id est, in carnali copula. Itaque quia vnum facit carnalis coniunctio, iam non sunt duo, sed vna caro, quod facit coniunctio carnalis. Hinc Paulus virum caput uxoris esse dicit, & uxorem corpus viri.
units.tr: And they shall be two in one flesh: this is the third argument, taken from the manner of the joining. For as those who love one another spiritually are said to be one soul in many souls (Acts 4), so also husband and wife, who love one another carnally, are said to be one flesh, and one man, or one person. So Anselm explains: "And they shall be two in one flesh, not three", that is, in carnal union. Therefore, since carnal union makes them one, they are no longer two, but one flesh, which is what carnal union makes. Hence Paul says that the husband is the head of the wife, and the wife the body of the husband.

units.la: Vt igitur sceleus est, in duo diuidere vnam carnem[?]: sic & mulierem à viro suo diripere iniquissimum est. Addit enim Christus: Itaque jam) siue posthac, nempe post initum coniugium. non sunt duo, sed una caro) i. non amplius sunt duo diuersi homines, sed vnus homo: quem denuò discerpere in duos, nefas est. Creati fuerant duo, non vnus, nimirum masculus & fœmina: rursus copula matrimonij è duobus reddidit vnum. Igitur tam præter naturam fuerit, vxorem à viro diuellere, quàm membrum à corpore rescindere. At qui vxorem repudiat, quasi dimidiam sui partem à seipso auellit. Hoc autem minimè patitur natura, vt corpus suum quispiam discerpat.
units.tr: Just as it is a crime to divide one flesh into two, so it is most unjust to tear a wife away from her husband. For Christ adds: "So they are no longer two, but one flesh" (that is, from now on, namely after marriage has been entered into), i.e. they are no longer two separate persons, but one man, and it is wrong to tear this one man apart again into two. They were created as two, not as one, namely male and female; but the union of marriage has again made one out of two. Therefore it would be as much against nature to tear a wife from her husband as to cut a limb from the body. Whoever puts away his wife, as it were, cuts off half of himself from himself. Yet nature does not at all allow anyone to tear apart his own body.

units.la: Cæterùm in Genesi cap.2[?]. vnde locus iste sumptus est, non legitur Duo: sed tantùm, Et erunt in carnem vnam. Sed Matthæus addit Duo, explicandi gratia: vt addidit & Paulus, 1. Corinth. 6. aut vterque sequutus est septuaginta Interpretes.
units.tr: Moreover, in Genesis chapter 2, from which this place is taken, the words "Two" are not read, but only "and they shall be one flesh." But Matthew adds "two" for the sake of explanation, as Paul also added it in 1 Corinthians 6; or both followed the Seventy translators.

units.la: Quòd porrò dicit illos duos jam unum esse, intellige primùm de tot mutuis iuribus, quibus sunt sibi inuicem obligatissimi, vt perinde alter alterum, vt suam propriam carnem fouere teneatur: deinde de mutuo amore ac sympathia, quòd perinde sese mutuò ament, ac membra inuicem, postremò de tot mutuis necessitatibus, adeò vt alter sine alterius ope, sicut membra unius corporis viuere nequeant: quam unitate hominis Deus etiam eo ipso indicauit, quòd mulieré ex ipso corpore viri desúpsit[?]. Quare iam nec vir fine muliere, nec contrà, in Domino, teste Paulo, 1.Cor. ii.
units.tr: As for what he says next, that those two are now one, understand it first of the many mutual rights by which they are most closely bound to one another, so that each is obliged to cherish the other just as his or her own flesh; then of the mutual love and sympathy, by which they love one another just as the members do one another; and lastly of the many mutual needs, so that the one cannot live without the help of the other, just as the members of one body cannot. God indicated this unity of man even by the very fact that he formed the woman from the body of the man. Therefore neither the man is without the woman nor the woman without the man in the Lord, as Paul witnesses, 1 Corinthians 11.

units.la: Quod ergo Deus copulauit, homo ne separet) Graecus habet: [illegible, ~10 letters], id est, coniugauit, & eodem iunxit iugo. Hinc coniuges vocantur, quòd in laetis pariter ac tristibus communicantes, velut idem ducunt iugum, vt Aquila & Priscilla, Act. 18. Translatum est enim à bubus simul ducentes idem iugû: Bonum coniugium, inquit Basilius lib.3. de virgin. sed tamen à iugo tractum. Idem in Hexamero coniugium vocat iugum naturae. Hoc est quartum argumentum ab authoritate conditoris sumptû: & illustratum emphatica simul & eleganti antithesi Dei & hominis, coniunctionis & defiunctionis. Coniungit autem Deus per parentum & ipsorum coniugum consensum, & per ministrum ecclesiae. Hac sententia frenat Christus virorum libidinem, ne vxores repudiando, sacrum nodum abrumpant. Quemadmodum autem in viri arbitrio esse negat coiugium dissoluere: ita & aliis omnibus legem edicit, ne sua authoritate illicita repudia confirment. Deus Opt. Max. det nobis omnibus & singulis spiritum suum sanctum, qui est spiritus sapientiae, intelligentiae, iudicij, ne vnquam coniungamus separanda, separemusue coniungenda, per Christum Iesum Dominuim nostrum, A-men.
units.tr: "What therefore God has joined together, let not man put asunder." The Greek has [συνέζευξεν], that is, has yoked together, and joined under the same yoke. Hence spouses are called "conjuges" (yoke-fellows), because, sharing alike in joys and sorrows, they draw the same yoke, as Aquila and Priscilla do, Acts 18. The term is transferred from oxen drawing the same yoke together; Basil, book 3 on virginity, says "marriage is a good thing, yet drawn from the yoke." In the Hexaemeron he likewise calls marriage the yoke of nature. This is the fourth argument, taken from the authority of the Creator, and it is illustrated at once by an emphatic and elegant antithesis of God and man, of joining and separating. God joins through the consent of the parents and of the spouses themselves, and through the minister of the Church. By this sentence Christ restrains the lust of men, lest by putting away their wives they break the sacred knot. Just as he denies that the dissolution of marriage lies in the man's power, so he also lays down a law for all others, that they not confirm unlawful divorces by their own authority. May God, the best and greatest, give us all and each one his Holy Spirit, who is the spirit of wisdom, understanding and judgement, so that we never join what must be separated, or separate what must be joined, through Christ Jesus our Lord. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XLV.
units.tr: SERMON XLV.

units.la: Matth. 19.
units.tr: Matth. 19.

units.la: Dicunt illi: Cur ergo Moses iusfit dare libellum repudij, ac dimittere eam? Ait illis: Moses ad duritiam cordis vestri permisit vobis repudiare uxores vestras, ceterum ab initio non fuit sic. Dico autem vobis, quod quicunque repudiauerit uxorem suam, nisi ob stuprum, & aliam duxerit, is committit adulterium. Et qui repudiatam duxerit, is adulterium committit.
units.tr: They say to him: Why then did Moses command us to give a bill of divorce and to dismiss her? He says to them: Moses, because of the hardness of your hearts, permitted you to divorce your wives, but from the beginning it was not so. I say to you that whoever divorces his wife, except for fornication, and marries another, commits adultery. And whoever marries one who is divorced commits adultery.

units.la: 1 Obijciunt aduersarij, vt antea meditati fuerant, Christo Mosen, Deut. 24. tanquam contrarium, illum certè instituisse repudiū[?]. Si, inquiunt, haec est matrimonij insolubilis firmitas: vt tu pronunciasti: quare ergo Moses legem de repudij dando libello, & vxoribus, si non acceptae sint, dimittendis, dedit? An Moses iussit quod illicitum est? Tu dicis esse illicitum: Moses vero fieri iussit, nosq; seduxit. Ergo vis tibi plus habendum esse fidei, quàm Mosi. Moses vero hanc legem, vt caeteras, à Deo accepit. Ergo tu repugnas diuinae doctrinae. Ad patrocinium viri sanctissimi Mosis confugiunt: sicut solent homines facere malam causam habentes, confugiunt ad potentes viros, vt si per infcitiam non possunt, vincant per personam.
units.tr: 1 The opponents, as they had prepared beforehand, object to Christ Moses, Deut. 24, as if he were contrary to him, since Moses certainly instituted divorce. "If," they say, "this is the unbreakable firmness of marriage, as you have declared, why then did Moses give a law about giving a bill of divorce and dismissing wives who were not pleasing? Did Moses command what is unlawful? You say it is unlawful, but Moses commanded it to be done, and so led us astray. So you want us to give more credit to yourself than to Moses. Moses, however, received this law from God, as he received the others. So you are contradicting divine teaching." They take refuge in the protection of the most holy Moses, as men usually do when they have a bad cause: they flee to powerful men, so that if they cannot win by knowledge, they may win by authority of the person.

units.la: 2 Sed quid respondet Christus? Negat Moses mandasse: sed permisisse tantum, idque ob singularem duritiem cordis eorum, vitandi nempe maioris mali causa, ne forte interficerent uxores, vt Hieronymus exponit, aut in coniugio scortarentur: sed Deum creatorem a principio non sic ordinasse, cuius ordinatio perpetuo valere debeat. Moses, inquit, πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν (quam Moses ipse, Israeli non semel exprobrauit, nominatim vero Deuter. 9. & 31.) permisit (non praecepit, quasi Deo probaretur, aut natura rectum esset: neque enim is probat diuortium, qui hoc maluit admitti, quam homicidium) vobis repudiare uxores vestras: caeterum ab initio non fuit sic: quum scilicet nondum increuisset hominum malitia: neque nunc relaxabitur idem ius, postea quam euangelica doctrina renouat ac perficit naturae synceritatem. Sequitur enim in responsione Christi, Dico autem vobis, quod quicunque repudiauerit uxorem suam, nisi ob stuprum (mulier enim scortando se quasi putridum membrum a viro resecindens, eum liberat, vñ bricht die ehe,) & aliam duxerit, is committit adulterium. Et qui repudiatam duxerit, is adulterium committit. Quanquam haec verba (quibus Christus indicat, quatenus liceat dimittere, aut non) Marcus cap. 10. seorsum discipulis suis fuisse dicta refert, quum domum venissent. sent. Matthæus autem omissa hac circumstantia sermonem contexit, ut sæpe Euangelistæ medium aliquid relinquunt, quia satis habent rerum summas colligere. Nihil ergo discriminis est, nisi quod alter altero distinctius rem exponit.
units.tr: 2 But what does Christ answer? He denies that Moses commanded it, but says only that he permitted it, and that because of the singular hardness of their hearts, namely to avoid a greater evil, lest perhaps they should kill their wives, as Jerome explains, or play the harlot within marriage. But God the Creator had not ordained it so from the beginning, and his ordinance ought to hold good forever. Moses, he says, [πρὸς τὴν σκληροκαρδίαν ὑμῶν] (which Moses himself reproached Israel for more than once, and especially at Deut. 9 and 31) permitted (did not command, as if it were approved by God or right by nature; for he does not approve divorce who preferred to allow it rather than murder) you to divorce your wives. But from the beginning it was not so, namely when the wickedness of men had not yet increased. Nor will this same right now be relaxed, since the evangelical teaching renews and perfects the purity of nature. For in Christ's reply there follows: "I say to you that whoever divorces his wife, except for fornication" (for a woman who, by playing the harlot, cuts herself off from her husband like a rotten limb, frees him; thus she breaks the marriage) "and marries another, commits adultery. And whoever marries one who is divorced commits adultery." Although Mark, chapter 10, reports that these words, by which Christ indicates how far it is lawful to dismiss a wife or not, were spoken apart to his disciples when they had come home, Matthew, leaving out this circumstance, has put the saying together as evangelists often leave out something in the middle, being content to collect the main points. There is therefore no difference, except that one sets out the matter more distinctly than the other.

units.la: Discendum quoq; existis Christi verbis, virorum esse diligere uxores suas, & non temerè priuata authoritate, Iudæorum more illas repudiare, ob quamuis leuiculam occasionem, aut etiam propter corporis, vel animi vitium: quod potius corrigendum, aut ferendum Christiano homini, seu discipulo Iesu Christi: qui & ipse multa vitia atq; peccata suæ ecclesiæ eiusque membrorum tulit, ac etiamnum fert, Ief. 53 [?]. Matt. 8.17. Rom. 9.
units.tr: We ought also to learn from the words of Christ that it is the duty of husbands to love their wives, and not to divorce them rashly on their own authority, after the manner of the Jews, for any trivial occasion, or even because of a bodily or mental defect. Such a defect should rather be corrected or borne by a Christian man, that is, a disciple of Jesus Christ, who himself also bore, and still bears, the many faults and sins of his Church and its members. Isa. 53; Matt. 8:17; Rom. 9.

units.la: Item, deliberandum diu, quod statuendū est semel: non enim licet amplius ductam uxorem, quam quis legitimè coniunctam habet, quæ & uxorem præstat, dimittere, nisi intercedat adulterium (quod grande peccatum esse scimus ex Genesi 39. Leuit. 20. Iud. 19.20. Eccles. 25. 1. Corinth. 6. Heb. 13. & aliis innumeris scripturæ locis) vel infidelis coniunx discedat. Hanc enim adhuc causam repudium, Paulus concedit, 1. Corinth. 7. quæ videlicet ex religionis dissidio oritur. Si vir infidelis (vt scribit Theophyl. in eum locum Pauli) uxori fideli iniungat vt secum sentiat, & particeps suæ infidelitatis fiat, dirimat potius matrimonium mulier, & à viro abscedat. Satius enim est connubium ipsum dissoluere, quam pietatem in Dei cultum dimittere. Huius causæ repudij Anfelmus hanc rationem reddit: Cum propter infidelitatem, inquit, coniunx dimitti possit, & iuxta Domini sententiam dimitti nequeat, nisi causa fornicationis: manifestum est, & in fidelitatem esse fornicationem. Quia scilicet idololatria, quâ sequuntur infideles, & quælibet noxia superstitio, fornicatio est. Vide Lombar. lib. 4. Dist. 39. Quidam alias causas excogitant propter quas possit altera partium repudiari: sed cauendum ne supra magistrum cœlestem sapere velimus, dum præter eius verbû aliquid fingere audemus. Minimè vero approbådum istorum facinus, qui ob monachismum vxores deferunt. Nā si Paulus iubet (vt Erasmus lib. 3. de Rat. concio argumentatur) vxorem Christianam manere in contubernio & obsequio mariti increduli & idololatræ, si modo ille nō quærat diuortium, quanto minus conuenit, vt ob factitiam religionem fpofus sponsam deferat?
units.tr: Likewise, what must be decided once should be considered at length: for it is not lawful to dismiss a wife once taken, whom one has lawfully joined in marriage and who fulfils her duty, unless adultery intervenes (which we know to be a great sin from Genesis 39, Leviticus 20, Judges 19 and 20, Ecclesiasticus 25, 1 Cor. 6, Heb. 13, and countless other passages of Scripture), or unless the unbelieving spouse departs. For Paul concedes this one further cause of divorce, 1 Cor. 7, which clearly arises from a difference in religion. If an unbelieving husband (as Theophylact writes on that passage of Paul) requires his believing wife to think as he does and to share in his unbelief, the woman should rather dissolve the marriage and leave her husband. For it is better to dissolve the marriage itself than to give up devotion to the worship of God. Anselm gives this reason for this cause of divorce: "Since a spouse may be dismissed on account of unbelief, and yet according to the Lord's judgment may not be dismissed except for the cause of fornication, it is clear that unbelief is also fornication." Namely, because idolatry, which unbelievers follow, and every harmful superstition, is fornication. See Lombard, book 4, distinction 39. Some devise other causes for which either party may be divorced; but we must take care lest we wish to be wiser than the heavenly Teacher, while we dare to invent something beyond his word. Yet the wicked deed of those who put away their wives for the sake of monasticism is by no means to be approved. For if Paul bids a Christian wife to remain in the company and obedience of an unbelieving and idolatrous husband, provided he does not seek a divorce (as Erasmus argues in book 3 of his De ratione concionandi), how much less fitting is it that a betrothed husband should abandon his betrothed for the sake of a made-up religion?

units.la: 3 Porrò quærunt aliqui: Num Mosi licuerit tale quid concedere, quod cum prima cóiugij institutione pugnare, & proinde Deo minus probari posse sciebat? Et illud Apostoli obiiciunt, Roman. 3. qui impiorum vocem esse ait: Faciamus mala, vt veniant bona. Vbi respondemus cum Gualthero scribente in Marcum, Borrhao in Deuteronômi m, Musculo in Matthæum, Mosem quidem nic nominari, sed eundem vt Dei seruû considerandum esse, qui nihil in Dei legibus vel mutare, vel saltem aliqua ex parte abfq; singulari spiritus sancti suggestione illis contrarium permittere voluerit. Nam fidelem seruum fuisse in tota Dei domo, ipsius Dei testimonio abunde constat, Numer.ii[?].Heb.3. Quare ad ipsum Deum ista concesio referri debet, cui de suo facere licet quodcunque ipsi libuerit. Ergone, inquis, sibi ipsi contradicit Deus, & temeraria quadam leuitate leges figit atque refigit? Nequaquam. Imo si probe rem excutiamus, nulla hic contradictio subesse apparebit, quando non eodem re fpectu dicuntur, quae olim per Mosem tradita, & hic per Christum plenius ac luculentius expolita sunt. Non idem vterque, sed diuersa in docendo spectauit: alter nimirum Hebræ gentis legi subiectae duritiem, & puerilis aetatis, quam populus ille vixit, infirmitatem: alter lenitatem & perfectionem adultioris aetatis, quam degunt ij qui feruntur spiritu adoptionis: alter item quid per se fas fit fieri, alter, quae ad declinanda maiora mala imbecillis & imperfectis ad tempus permittuntur, considerauit. Mosi cum populo durae ceruicis res fuit, cum quo variae rationes ineundae erant, vt peccata, quae in totum impediri non poterant, saltem aliquo modo coercerentur. At Christus ijs loquitur, quos ex femine verbi Dei renatos, spiritu adoptionis duci, & ad Christianam perfectionem indies contendere oportet, i.Pet.1. Rom.8. Deinde Moses uxorem repudiare non simpliciter iussit, sed si id ipsi vellent facere, qua ratione id fieri debeat, docuit.
units.tr: 3 Moreover, some ask: Was Moses allowed to concede something of this kind, which he knew conflicted with the first institution of marriage and therefore could less easily be approved by God? They also object that saying of the Apostle, Rom. 3, who says it is the voice of the ungodly: "Let us do evil that good may come." To this we answer with Walther, writing on Mark; with Borrhaus, on Deuteronomy; and with Musculus, on Matthew: Moses is indeed named here, but he must be considered as a servant of God, who wished to change nothing in God's laws, or at least to permit anything contrary to them in any respect, without a singular prompting of the Holy Spirit. For that he was a faithful servant in the whole house of God is abundantly established by God's own testimony, Numbers 12; Heb. 3. Therefore this concession must be referred to God himself, to whom it is lawful to do whatever pleases him. "Then," you say, "does God contradict himself, and by a certain rash levity fix and refix his laws?" By no means. Indeed, if we examine the matter carefully, no contradiction will appear to lie here, since the things handed down of old through Moses and set forth here more fully and clearly by Christ are not spoken with the same respect. The two did not look at the same thing in their teaching: the one considered the hardness of the people of Israel, who were subject to the law, and the weakness of the childish age in which that people lived; the other considered the gentleness and perfection of the more mature age, which those lead who are moved by the Spirit of adoption. Again, the one considered what is in itself permissible, the other what is permitted for a time to the weak and imperfect in order to avoid greater evils. Moses had to deal with a people of stiff neck, with whom various measures had to be taken, so that sins which could not be wholly prevented might at least be restrained in some way. But Christ speaks to those who have been born again of the seed of the word of God, who ought to be led by the Spirit of adoption and to strive daily toward Christian perfection: 1 Pet. 1; Rom. 8. Moreover, Moses did not simply command the divorce, but if they themselves wished to do it, he taught how it ought to be done.

units.la: Ad hæc non quamuis ob causam diuortium fieri voluit, sed tum demum illud coceffit[?], si quis in uxore rem fœdam deprehendisset, & sibi intolerabilem, etsi non eiusmodi effet, quæ publicis legibus plecteretur.
units.tr: Besides, he did not want divorce for just any cause, but he allowed it only when someone had discovered in his wife a shameful thing that was intolerable to him, even if it were not of such a kind as to be punished by public laws.

units.la: Præterea modum & rationem talem præscripsit, quæ ad prohibendum diuortium, & pacem inter coniuges dissidentes conciliandam plurimum seruiebat. Nam (vt apud Augustin. legimus lib. 19. contra Fau. Manich. cap. 26.) moram interposuit, vt in difsidium animus præceps, libelli conscriptione refractus abstineret, & quid mali effet uxorem dimittere cogitaret, &c.
units.tr: Furthermore, he prescribed a manner and method which greatly served to prevent divorce and to bring about peace between quarrelling spouses. For (as we read in Augustine, book 19 against Faustus the Manichaean, chapter 26) he interposed a delay, so that a hasty mind, checked by the writing of the bill, might refrain from rash estrangement and think about how great an evil it is to dismiss a wife.

units.la: Postremò ista repudiorum ratione non vitæ modò, verumetiam famæ uxorum consulebatur, ne ob adulterium, aut aliud quodpiam scelus capitale repudiatæ esse, aut ipsæ maritos turpiter deseruisse viderentur. Nam etiam hunc libellorum repudii usum fuisse ex Iesaia cap. 50. patet: apud quem Deus Iudæorum synagogam accusans, quòd priusquam eijceretur, ipsa sponte defecerit, vt amores suos idololatricos sequi posset, inter alia ait: Vbi est libellus repudii matris vestræ, quo eam dimiserim? Q.d. Si de mea morofitate[?] quiritamini, quasi iniquius vos reiecerim, agedum proferte libellu repudii ab me vobis datum. At non potestis quicquam tale proferre. In vobis ergo omnis culpa hæret, nec repudiatis vxoribus, sed turpissimæ adulteræ similes estis, quæ marito relicto amatores suos sectatur, &c. Quoad ergo consilium siue priuilegium per Mosem datum, ista repudiorum ratio mala non erat: merito autem reprehendi debebant Iudæi, qui hanc in effrenem suæ libidinis licentiam conuerterant: quæ causa est, quod illos Dominus nunc arctioribus terminis constringit.
units.tr: Finally, by this system of repudiation, care was taken not only for the life of wives but also for their reputation, so that they would not appear to have been repudiated on account of adultery or some other capital crime, or to have been shamefully deserted by their husbands themselves. That this practice of bills of repudiation existed is also clear from Isaiah 50, where God, accusing the synagogue of the Jews because, before she was cast out, she herself had willingly fallen away so that she could pursue her idolatrous lovers, says among other things: "Where is the bill of divorce of your mother, by which I put her away?" That is to say: if you complain about my harshness, as though I had cast you off more unjustly, then come on, produce the bill of repudiation given to you by me. But you cannot produce anything of the kind. The whole fault therefore clings to you, and you are not repudiated wives but resemble the most shameful adulteresses, who, having left their husbands, pursue their lovers, and so on. So as far as the counsel or privilege given through Moses is concerned, this system of repudiation was not bad; but the Jews deserved to be rebuked, since they had turned it into an unbridled licence for their lust. This is why the Lord now constrains them within narrower limits.

units.la: Habemus in his exemplum memorabile, quæ optima sit in legibus ciuilibus dispensandi ratio, & quando illa admitti, quando item legum authoritas seuerius vrgeri ac retineri debeat. Christus Iesus Dominus & seruator noster det nobis intellectum in omnibus, Amen.
units.tr: In these things we have a memorable example of what is the best practice in dispensing civil laws, and when such a law may be admitted, and when, likewise, the authority of the laws ought to be enforced and maintained more strictly. May Christ Jesus, our Lord and Saviour, give us understanding in all things. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XLVI
units.tr: SERMON XLVI

units.la: Matth. 19. -
units.tr: Matt. 19. -

units.la: DICVNT ei discipuli eius: Si ad ipsum modum habet causa hominis cum uxore[?], non expedit contrahere matrimonium. Qui dixit illis: Non omnes capaces sunt huius dicti, sed quibus datum est. Sunt enim eunuchi, qui de matris utero sic nati sunt: & sunt eunuchi, qui facti sunt eunuchi ab hominibus: & sunt eunuchi, qui seipsos castrauerunt propter regnum coelorum. Qui potest capere, capiat.
units.tr: His disciples said to him: If the case of a man with his wife is so, it is not expedient to marry. He said to them: Not all can receive this saying, but only those to whom it is given. For there are eunuchs who were so born from their mother's womb, and there are eunuchs who were made eunuchs by men, and there are eunuchs who castrated themselves for the kingdom of heaven. Let him who can receive it, receive it.

units.la: 1 Duram esse conditionem matrimonii discipuli colligunt ex eo, quod non licet dimittere uxorem, nisi fornicationis causa, sed necesse est illam retinere qualemcunque, vel certe adulterium incurrere, vel illi causam dare.
units.tr: 1 The disciples infer that the condition of marriage is hard, because it is not lawful to dismiss a wife except for the cause of fornication, but one must keep her, whatever she is like, or else fall into adultery or give her cause to do so.

units.la: Quam quidem collectionem Dominus non videtur omnino improbare. Habet enim matrimonium multas molestas: iuxta illud Apostoli: Afflictionem autem in carne tales habebunt: aperientes sibi ipsis per nuptias dolorum officinam, vt scribit Basilius lib.[?] de Virginitate. Eum enim, vt idem scribit ad Gregorium Theologum, Epist. 1. qui coniugio occupatus est, alius curarum tumultus excipit, si liberis careat, liberorum concupiscentia: si liberos acquirat, de educandis solicitudo, vxoris custodia, domus cura, seruorum ac familiae gubernatio, commerciorum detrimenta, contentiones cum vicinis, litium in foro iudiciali conflictus, negotiationis pericula, agriculturae labores, &c.
units.tr: The Lord does not seem to reject this inference altogether. For marriage has many troubles, according to that saying of the Apostle: "Such will have affliction in the flesh" (1 Cor. 7.28), "opening for themselves through marriage a workshop of pains," as Basil writes in his book On Virginity. For, as he writes to Gregory the Theologian (Epist. 1), the man who is occupied with marriage is seized by another tumult of cares: if he lacks children, the desire for children; if he has children, anxiety over bringing them up, the guarding of his wife, the care of the household, the management of servants and family, losses in trade, quarrels with neighbours, conflicts in the courts of law, the dangers of business, the labours of farming, and so on.

units.la: Cumprimis autem dura videtur esse seruitus, domi habere ac ferre morosam, rixosam, temulentam, aut simili vitio molestam mulierem, &, vt Chrysostomus scribit, tam atroces beluam in penetralibus domus saeuientem fouere, Prouerb.21.25. Ecclef.25. Vsi erant[?] Iudaei magna licentia repudiandarum uxorum:qua adempta, ut illicita, cogitabant etiam Apostoli satius esse, et expedire (non quidem ad salutem aeternam, sed ad commoditatem vitae praesentis) nullam prorsus uxorem ducere.
units.tr: Especially hard seems the servitude of keeping at home a peevish, quarrelsome, drunken woman, or one troubled by some similar vice, and, as Chrysostom writes, of nursing such a fierce beast raging in the innermost parts of the house (Prov. 21.25; Ecclus 25). The Jews had used great licence in divorcing their wives; when this was taken away as unlawful, the Apostles too thought it better and expedient (not indeed for eternal salvation, but for the convenience of this present life) to take no wife at all.

units.la: 2 Sed Dominus dicit, Non omnes capiunt hoc dictum seu verbum .i. non omnes praestare possunt hanc rem, seu hoc genus vitae: neque omnes hac molestia nubendi possunt esse liberi, nisi quibus datum est, scilicet divinitus. Quibus verbis Dominus primum clare demonstrat, non omnibus datum esse continentiae donum, sed id esse speciale, et perpaucorum, propterea quod hic affectus corporis sic omnium est communis, ut non alius fit violentior, aut invincibilior. Hinc D. Paulus inquit, 1. Corinth. 7. Nam velim omnes homines esse, ut et ipse sum. Sed unusquisque proprium donum habet ex Deo, alius quidem sic, alius autem sic.
units.tr: 2 But the Lord says: Not all receive this saying or word, that is, not all are able to perform this thing or this way of life; nor can all be free from this burden of marrying, except those to whom it is given, namely by God. By these words the Lord first clearly shows that the gift of continence is not given to all, but is a special gift of very few, because this bodily desire is so common to all that none is more violent or invincible. Hence St Paul says (1 Cor. 7.7): "For I would that all men were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that."

units.la: Deinde ostendit hanc commoditatem nō esse humani arbitrij, sed diuini muneris, id est, continentiam esse Dei donum, non naturae virtutem, iuxta illud Sapien. 8. Et ut sciui quoniam aliter non poterem esse continens, nisi Deus det (et hoc ipsum erat summa sapientia, scire cuius esset hoc donum) adijdo[?] minum, et deprecatus sum illum, &c. Unde conuincitur eorum superbia, qui sibi arrogare non dubitant, quod tam clare Christus admisit. Qui enim continentiae dono praediti non sunt, scire debent se ad coniugium creatos esse,ac se coniugio uti debere,non modò ut suo malo subueniant,sed potius ut Dei ordinationi obsequantur. Ita enim Paulus scribit[?],1.Corinth 7. Dico autem inconiugatis & viduis,bonum est eis,si manserint, ut & ego: quod si se non continent, contrahant matrimonium. Nam satius est matrimonium contrahere,quàm uri, seu ardere, scilicet, libidine. Tolle de Ecclesia (inquit Bernhard. Ser.66. super Cant.) honorabile coniugium, & thorum immaculatum, nonne reples eam concubinarijs,incæstuosis,feminisfluis[?],molibus[?], masculorum concubitoribus & omni denique genere immundorum?
units.tr: Then he shows that this freedom is not a matter of human choice but a divine gift; that is, continence is God's gift, not a power of nature, according to Wisdom 8: "And as I knew that I could not otherwise be continent unless God gave it (and this itself was great wisdom, to know whose gift it was), I approached the Lord and besought him," and so on. Hence the pride of those is refuted who do not hesitate to claim for themselves what Christ so clearly admitted. For those who are not endowed with the gift of continence should know that they were created for marriage, and that they ought to use marriage not only to remedy their own ill but rather to obey God's ordinance. For Paul writes thus (1 Cor. 7.8–9): "I say to the unmarried and to widows: it is good for them if they remain as I do; but if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn," namely with lust. "Take away from the Church," says Bernard (Sermon 66 on the Song of Songs), "honourable marriage and the undefiled bed: do you not fill it with concubinaries, incestuous persons, women with issue, effeminate men, sodomites, and finally every kind of unclean person?"

units.la: ʒ Quibus autem hoc datum est,& qui nam possunt coelibes viuere? Christus tria genera eunuchorum recenset. Alij enim eunuchi sunt naturales,alij artificiales, alij diuini.
