units.tr: 3 But to whom is this given, and who can live unmarried? Christ enumerates three kinds of eunuchs. For some eunuchs are natural, some artificial, and some made so by God.

units.la: Primum igitur genus eorum est, qui natura sunt spadones,nec possunt, aut non appetút congredi cum muliere.i. qui sic nascuntur, qui naturæ defectu laborant, & ad matrimonium sunt inepti, qui vitio naturæ frigidioris abhorrent à re uxoria, aut alio quopiam occulto naturæ affectu. Unde Augustinus in libro Meditationum: Tribus,inquit,modis à peccato me memini conseruatum, scilicet occasionis subtractione, resistendi data virtute, affectionis sanitate. Multa enim in peccata cecidissem, si data esset occasio: sed Dei miseratione non me talis opportunitas apprehendit. In multa quoque paulò minus cecicecidissem grauiter impulsus violentia tentationis: sed virtutem dedisti mihi Domine, vt sub me esset appetitus meus, & ei quam sentiebam concupiscentiæ minimè consentirem. Sed à quibusdam peccatis tam longè me fecit tua miseratio domine, vt penitus abominarer ea, & ne vlla me quidem eorum tentatio molestaret.
units.tr: The first kind of these are those who are eunuchs by nature, who cannot, or do not desire, to have intercourse with a woman. That is, those who are born so, who suffer from a defect of nature and are unfit for marriage, who through a colder natural constitution shrink from the marital act, or from some other hidden disposition of nature. Hence Augustine in his Book of Meditations: "I remember that I was kept from sin in three ways," he says: by the withdrawal of occasion, by the virtue given to resist, and by the health of my affections. "For I would have fallen into many sins had the occasion been given; but by your mercy, Lord, such an opportunity did not seize me. I would also have fallen into many others, a little less gravely, pushed by the violence of temptation; but you gave me virtue, Lord, so that my appetite was under my control, and I did not in the least consent to the lust I felt. But from certain sins your mercy, Lord, kept me so far away that I utterly abhorred them, and not even a temptation to them troubled me."

units.la: Alterum genus eunuchorum est, quos execuerunt homines. Qui autem ab hominibus castrati sunt, eos à coniugio arcet defectus, quia viri non sunt. Hoc genus eunuchorum Origenes Tractatu 7. in Matthæum sic descr[?]b[?]t: Quidam continentes sunt propter verba hominum: quorum concupiscentiam virilem præcidit non verbum diuinum, sed verba humana: vt puta qui philosophati sunt apud antiquos in gentibus, aut apud eos, qui prohibent nubere, apud hæreses (de quibus etiam, 1. Timoth. 4.) Basilius autem in hunc modum: Et sunt eunuchi, qui eunuchi facti sunt ab hominibus, per doctrinam & obseruationem virginitatem exercere persuasi: quemadmodum sanè & virgo quæ à patre seruatur, de quo dictum est: Qui vero decreuit in corde suo, vt seruet virginem suam, benefacit.
units.tr: The second kind of eunuchs are those whom men have castrated. Those who have been castrated by men are kept from marriage by their defect, because they are not men. Origen, in Tractate 7 on Matthew, describes this kind of eunuch thus: "Some are continent on account of the words of men. The divine Word does not cut off their male desire, but human words do; for example, those who have philosophised among the ancients in the Gentile world, or among those who forbid marriage, or among the heretics (of whom also 1 Tim. 4)." Basil, however, puts it this way: "And there are eunuchs who have been made eunuchs by men, persuaded through teaching and observance to practise virginity; just as indeed a virgin who is kept by her father, of whom it is said: 'But he who has decided in his heart to keep his virgin does well.'"

units.la: Cæterùm istorum castitas, qui nimirum inepti ad coniugium vel nati, vel postea facti sunt, nullam meretur laudem, quòd à necessitate proficiscatur, non à studio virtutis, teste Erafino[?] in Paraphras.
units.tr: But the chastity of those who are unfit for marriage, whether born so or made so later, deserves no praise, because it proceeds from necessity and not from zeal for virtue, as Erasmus testifies in his Paraphrase.

units.la: Tertium vero genus eorum est, qui ipsi se ipsos castrarunt propter regnum cœlorum: non amputato corporis membro (id quod Origenem fecisse scribit Eusb. Cæsa. Ecclesiast. Hist. lib. 5. cap. 6) sed ob amorem evangelij, deuicto affectu rei uxoriæ: vel, qui non plus rei habent cum fœminis, quàm si castrati essent, & qui quum mariti esse possunt, vltro cœlibatum sibi delegerunt, vt soli gloriæ Dei propagandæ inserviant: vel, qui cœleste illud indepti donum volentes se continent, propter regnum cœlorum, non promerendum, sed propagandum & promovendum verbo & opere, id est, vt vel, expeditius minis-trent prædicationi euangelicæ, vel vt magis indivulsè hæreant domino, eique per omnia se approbantes, sancti corpore & spiritu: denique vt omnino specimen quoddam futuræ vitæ & cœlestis exhibeant, nullum generantes malum, sed bonum, Iesa. 16. His demum bonum est absq; coniuge viuere: quia id datum est eis, & propter regnum cœlorum ita vivunt. (Nec enim alioqui laudem habet, quamuis castus cælibatus, nisi fuerit susceptus studio pietatis euangelicæ.) Talem se Paulus fuisse testatur, 1. Corinth. 7. & ad similem ibi felicitatem alios quoque hortatur, *quo minore sollicitudine eorum quæ in mundo sunt, Domino possint adhærere, & mundo verè vti tanquam non vterentur, quolibet momento parati hinc ad Christum concedere. Verùm & illud addit: Hoc autem ad id quod vobis conducibile est dico, non uti laqueum vobis injiciam.
units.tr: The third kind of these are those who have castrated themselves for the kingdom of heaven: not by cutting off a bodily member (which Origen is said to have done, as Eusebius of Caesarea writes in Ecclesiastical History book 5, chapter 6), but through love of the gospel, having overcome the desire for the married state. Or they are those who have no more to do with women than if they were castrated, and who, though they could marry, have of their own accord chosen celibacy, so that they may serve only the glory of God's propagation. Or they are those who, desiring to contain themselves by that heavenly gift for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, which is not to be earned but to be spread and advanced by word and deed, do so either so that they may minister more readily to the evangelical preaching, or so that they may cling more undividedly to the Lord and approve themselves to him in all things, holy in body and spirit; and finally so that they may altogether display a certain specimen of the future and heavenly life, bringing forth no evil but only good (Isa. 16). To these at last it is good to live without a spouse, because it is given to them, and they live thus for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. (For otherwise even chaste celibacy has no praise, unless it was undertaken from zeal for evangelical piety.) Paul testifies that he was such a man (1 Cor. 7), and there he urges others too to a similar happiness, so that with less anxiety about the things of the world they may cling to the Lord, and use the world truly as if they did not use it, ready at any moment to depart hence to Christ. But he also adds: "I say this for your advantage, not to cast a snare upon you."

units.la: Pertinent huc & illi, qui propter instantem necessitatem persecutionis abstinent à[?] matrimonio.
units.tr: These also belong here, those who on account of the pressing necessity of persecution abstain from marriage.

units.la: Porrò sicut tria genera sunt eunuchorum: sic etiam abstemiorum. Quidam enim natura sunt abstemii: quidam propter praeceptum hominum, ut Rechabitae, Ierem. 35. quidam studio continentiae, ut Timotheus,1. Tim.5.
units.tr: Moreover, just as there are three kinds of eunuchs, so too there are three kinds of those who abstain from marriage. For some are abstainers by nature; some on account of the precept of men, like the Rechabites, Jer. 35; some from zeal for continence, like Timothy, 1 Tim. 5.

units.la: 4 Sequitur finalis Christi sententia, nemini praecipiens caelibatum, sed omnibus pro gratia divinitus data liberum permittes. Ait enim: Qui potest capere, capiat.) Quibus verbis magis animat ad eligendam continentiam, quia arduum esse ostendit, quod discipuli parvum ac facile esse dicebant, & quia inaestimabili misericordia sua noluit ré[?] in necessitatem legis concludere. Ut ergo nemo ad matrimonium cogedus est, ita nec ad caelibatum. Bonum sanè homini, teste Apostolo, uxorem non attingere: attamen propter stupra vitanda, suam quisque uxorem habeat: & suum quaeque virum habeat. Primus gradus castitatis est, inquit Chrysostomus, Hom. 20. in Matth. syncera virginitas: secundus autem, fidele coniugium. Et Theophylactus ait in Ep. 1. ad Tim. cap. 4. Haud quaquam nos matrimonium prohibemus, caeterum eas quae nubere nolunt, ad virginitatem adhortamur: honoratior enim est ipsa. Atqui nuptiae & matrimonium propterea non sunt ingloria in celebriaue: quemadmodum neque quia aurum preciosius est, argentum gloria precioque vacat. Quod vero pretiosius est, pretiosio[?] pretiosius est: & quod melius est, bono melius est, non malo. Qui ergo potest, virginitatis aurum retineat: si vero non possit ituc[?], matrimonij argentum recipiat. Non ergo male facit vxorem ducens, in Domino: melius autem non ducens, quod ad commoditatem praesentis vitae attinet. Contra hanc libertatem pugnat tyrannis Romani pontificis, sacerdotibus adimens ius contrahendi matrimonium. Aqua tyrannide cum nos liberauerit Dominus Deus, sit illi honor & gloria in aeternum, Amen.
units.tr: 4 There follows the final sentence of Christ, which commands celibacy to no one but leaves it free to all, to whom grace has been given by God. For he says: "He who can receive it, let him receive it." By these words he encourages us more to choose continence, because he shows that it is difficult, whereas the disciples had said it was small and easy; and because with his immeasurable mercy he did not want to bind people by the necessity of a law. Therefore, just as no one is to be compelled to marriage, so no one is to be compelled to celibacy. Indeed, as the Apostle testifies, it is good for a man not to touch a woman; yet, in order to avoid fornication, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband. "The first degree of chastity," says Chrysostom, Hom. 20 on Matthew, "is pure virginity; the second is faithful wedlock." And Theophylact says on 1 Tim. chapter 4: "By no means do we forbid marriage; but those who are unwilling to marry we exhort to virginity, for it is more honourable." Yet marriage and wedlock are not without glory in their celebration, just as gold, because it is more precious, does not lack glory and value for silver. What is more precious is more precious; and what is better is better by a good thing, not by an evil one. Whoever can, then, let him keep the gold of virginity; but if he cannot, let him receive the silver of matrimony. Therefore he does not do wrong who takes a wife in the Lord, but he does better who does not take one, as far as the convenience of the present life is concerned. Against this liberty fights the tyranny of the Roman pontiff, who takes from priests the right of contracting marriage. May the Lord God, who has freed us from that watery tyranny, have honour and glory to him for ever. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XLVII.
units.tr: SERMON XLVII.

units.la: Lucæ 1[?].
units.tr: Luke 1.

units.la: Erat in diebus Herodis regis Iudææ, sacerdos quidam nomine Zacharias, de vice Abia, & uxor illius de filiabus Aaron, & nomen eius Elizabeth. Erant autem iusti ambo coram Deo, versantes in omnibus praeceptis & iustificationibus Domini irreprehensibiles: nec erat illis proles, eo quod esset Elizabeth sterilis, rilis ,& ambo proiecta iam essent aetatis.
units.tr: In the days of Herod, king of Judea, there was a certain priest named Zacharias, of the course of Abijah, and his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, and her name was Elizabeth. And they were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord blamelessly. But they had no child, because Elizabeth was barren, and both were now advanced in years.

units.la: Factum est autem, quum is sacerdotio fungeretur in ordine vicis sua coram Deo, secundum consuetudinem functionis sacerdotalis, sors illi obuenit, vt odores incenderet, ingressus in templum Domini, & omnis multitudo populi precabatur foris tempore thymiamatis. Apparuit autem illi angelus Domini stans a dextris altaris, in quo thymiamata solent adoleri. Et Zacharias turbatus est eo-visu[?], ac timor irruit super eum. Dixit[?] autem ad illum angelus: Ne timeas Zacharia, quoniam exaudita est deprecatio tua, uxorq; tua Elizabeth pariet tibi filium, & vocabis nomen eius Ioannem.
units.tr: Now it happened that, while he was serving as priest in the order of his course before God, according to the custom of the priestly office, it fell to him by lot to burn incense, entering the temple of the Lord; and the whole multitude of the people was praying outside at the hour of incense. And an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing at the right side of the altar on which incense is wont to be burned. And Zacharias was troubled at the sight, and fear fell upon him. But the angel said to him: Do not be afraid, Zacharias, for your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son, and you shall call his name John.

units.la: In hac historia de Zacharia & Elizabetha primùm quaedam de ipso coniugio notanda veniunt: deinde quaedam de iis, qui in coniugio viuunt: praeterea quaedam de fructu coniugij.
units.tr: In this story of Zacharias and Elizabeth, there are first some things to note about marriage itself; then some things about those who live in marriage; and finally some things about the fruit of marriage.

units.la: 1 Quod coniugium ipsum attinet, probat exemplum Zachariae & vxoris eius, honorabile esse coniugium inter omnes, etiam inter sacerdotes, ex quorum numero Zacharias suit, Hebræor. 13.
units.tr: 1. As for marriage itself, the example of Zacharias and his wife proves that marriage is honourable among all people, even among priests, from whose number Zacharias was (Hebrews 13).

units.la: Et, coniugium esse instituedum[?] iuxta bonas & æquas leges. Id enim Zacharias, qui ex genere sacerdotali fuit, & quidem exposteris Eleazar, qui patri in summum sacerdotium successerat, fecit. Quod enim Lucas dicit uxorem eius fuisse de filiabus Aaron, ideo fecisse videtur, ut ostenderet Zachariam non accepisse uxorem ex alia tribu, ut illi qui promiscue ex aliis tribubus assumebant, idque contra legem Dei: de qua lege Moses Numer 36. Omnes, inquit, viri ducent uxores de tribu & cognatione sua, & cunctae foeminae de eadem tribu maritos accipient: ut haereditas permaneat in familiis, nec sibi misceantur tribus, sed ita maneant, ut a Domino separatae sunt. Huius legis observator fuit etiam iunior Tobias, Tob.1.
units.tr: And that marriage ought to be contracted according to good and fair laws. Zacharias, who was of priestly stock, and indeed descended from Eleazar, who had succeeded his father in the high priesthood, did this. For when Luke says that his wife was of the daughters of Aaron, he seems to have done so to show that Zacharias had not taken a wife from another tribe, as those did who promiscuously took wives from other tribes, and that against the law of God. Moses speaks of this law in Numbers 36: "Every man," he says, "shall take wives from his own tribe and kindred, and all the women shall take husbands from the same tribe, so that the inheritance may remain in the families, and the tribes may not be mixed together, but may remain as the Lord has separated them." The younger Tobias also kept this law (Tobit 1).

units.la: Item, coniugium per se non esse impedimentum in eo existentibus, quo minus iustitiam exercere possint: id quod nonnulli praetexunt suae contumaciae, Lucae 14. Nónne enim Zacharias uxorem duxit & habuit, & tamen functione & vitę sanctimonia celeberrimus fuit? Huc pertinet illud Chrysostomi, quod & Glycas Par. 2. Annal. citat: Coniugium illis, qui grati & accepti esse Deo volunt, nihil impedimenti adfert. Nam ea de causa semel atque iterum indicant literae sacrae, Enochum Deo fuisse gratum, postquam Mathusalam genuisset, ideoque sublatum e medio fuisse, Genes.5. Porro nomen uxoris Zachariae fuit Elizabeth אֱלִישֶׁבַע[?], id est, Dei mei quies. Haec significatio huic mulieri haud male quadrauit, ut ex qua natus fuit, qui sempiternam demùm & beatâ quietem per Christum futuram praedicauit. Si per y scribatur in fine, Dei mei iuramentum: si per υ Dei mei virgam significat. Zacharias verò memorem Dei sonat.
units.tr: Likewise, marriage is not in itself an impediment to those who are in it, so that they cannot practise righteousness; a point which some put forward as a pretext for their stubbornness (Luke 14). For did not Zacharias take and have a wife, and yet was he not most renowned for his office and for the holiness of his life? To this belongs that saying of Chrysostom, which Glycas also cites in the second part of his Annals: "Marriage brings no hindrance to those who wish to be pleasing and acceptable to God." For the sacred writings indicate, more than once, for this reason, that Enoch was pleasing to God after he had begotten Methuselah, and therefore was taken out of the way (Genesis 5). Moreover, the name of Zacharias's wife was Elizabeth [אֱלִישֶׁבַע], that is, "rest of my God." This meaning fitted this woman not badly, since from her was born the one who preached that eternal and blessed rest would at last come through Christ. If it is written with a y at the end, it means "oath of my God"; if with a u, it signifies "rod of my God." Zacharias, however, sounds like "mindful of the Lord."

units.la: 2 Quòd verò ipsos coniuges attinet, habent illi quidem praeclarum exemplum in Zacharia & eius vxore, quo docentur, quales esse, & quomodo viuere debeant, vt Deo placere possint. Erant enim illi iusti, non coram hominibus tantùm, sed etiam coram Deo, (scrutante renes & corda) & ambulantes in omnibus praeceptis & iustificationibus Domini sine querela: indubiè sicut Paulus requirit Episcopum irreprehensibilem, 1.Tim.3. Hoc est, ita vixerunt vt iure à nemine reprehendi possent: nimirum non solum à malo, sed etiam ab omni specie mali abstinentes.
units.tr: 2. As for the spouses themselves, they indeed have a notable example in Zacharias and his wife, by which they are taught what they ought to be and how they ought to live, so that they may be able to please God. For they were righteous, not only before men but also before God (who searches the reins and hearts), and walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without complaint. Undoubtedly this is what Paul requires of a bishop, that he be blameless (1 Timothy 3). That is, they lived in such a way that no one could rightly reprove them: abstaining not only from evil but also from every appearance of evil.

units.la: Inter praecepta & iustificationes hoc inter est, quòd posteriùs nomen proprie ad pietatis & diuini cultus exercitia refertur: prius autem magis generale est, tamq; ad Dei cultum, quàm ad charitatis officia pertinet.
units.tr: Among "commandments" and "ordinances" this difference holds: the latter term is properly applied to the exercises of piety and divine worship, whereas the former is more general and pertains to the worship of God as much as to the duties of charity.

units.la: Caeterùm cùm Zacharias & Elizabeth nō modò sanctè & inculpatè versati sint inter homines, sed coram Deo etiam iustè, idque ante aduentum Christi, ante apparitionem gratiae, ante praedicationem euangelij: quam quaeso excusationem habebimus nos, qui sub Christo & salutifera eius gratia (de qua Tit.2.) & euangelio sumus, & non modò nō superamus illos pietate & iustitia, sed etiam ne similes quidem ac pares illis fumus?
units.tr: Moreover, since Zacharias and Elizabeth lived not only holily and blamelessly among men, but also righteously before God, and that before the coming of Christ, before the appearance of grace, before the preaching of the gospel: what excuse, I ask, shall we have, who are under Christ and his saving grace (of which Titus 2) and the gospel, and who not only do not surpass them in piety and righteousness, but are not even like or equal to them?

units.la: Haec autem non ideo dicuntur, quod homo suis viribus iustè vivere queat, & persectionem iustitiæ in hoc seculo assequi: sed ut in iustitia nostra non deficiamus, sed prosiciamus atque crescamus, hoc est, ambulemus.
units.tr: These things are said not because a man can live righteously by his own strength and attain perfection of righteousness in this age, but so that we may not fail in our righteousness, but may advance and grow, that is, may walk.

units.la: Etsi autem in hunc finem laudantur Zacharias & Elizabeth, ut sciamus, lucernam quæ præluxit Filio Dei, non ex obscura domo, sed ex illustri quodam sacrario sumptâ esse: sub eorum tamen exemplo nobis interim monstratur piè iusteque vivendi regula. Hoc ergo in vita rectè instituenda primum est, ut studeamus nos probare Deo. Scimus autem cor sincerum, & puram conscientiam ab eo maximè requiri. Itaque perversus erit ordo, si quis posthabita cordis integritate externam modo vitam in obsequium legis componat. Tenendum enim memoria est, Deum, ad quem respicere iubemur, non externam operum laruam, sed cor præcipuè intueri. Secundo deinde loco accedat obedientia, hoc est, ne sibi quisquam novam iustitiæ formam, quæ adlibuerit, sine Dei verbo fabricet: sed nos Dei imperio sinamus regi. Neque enim hæc definitio negligenda est, iustos esse, qui vitam suam formát ad legis præcepta. quo innuitur nihili apud Deum esse fictitios omnes cultus, & vagum esse ac erroneum humanæ vitæ cursum, simur ac discedit ab eius lege. Iustos igitur vocat Lucas Zachariam & Elizabeth, quod am b ilarentin[?] praeceptis Domini, quodque tales reputati sint coram Deo, propter ipsorum propositum, quod erat servire Domino. Neq; enim ideo iusti dicuntur, quod omnia legis praecepta, quae vocat iustificationes, observaverint (ut neq; Iob dictus est iustus, quod tota lege perfecerit) sed quod recepti in gratiam Dei, tum placuerint ei etiam cum suis operibus, aestimaveritq; opera illorum paterna indulgentia, non summo rigore. Etenim si etiam omnia fecerimus, quae praecepta sunt nō bis, sumus tamen servi inutiles, Luc.17.
units.tr: Although Zacharias and Elizabeth are praised for this purpose, so that we may know that the lamp which went before the Son of God was taken not from an obscure house but from a certain illustrious sanctuary, nevertheless under their example the rule of living piously and righteously is shown to us for the present. Therefore, in rightly ordering life, this comes first: that we strive to please God. We know that God chiefly requires a sincere heart and a pure conscience. Thus the order would be perverse if anyone, setting aside integrity of heart, should arrange merely his outward life in obedience to the law. For it must be kept in memory that God, to whom we are bidden to look, regards not the external mask of works but chiefly the heart. In the second place, obedience should follow: that is, let no one fashion for himself a new form of righteousness, such as he pleases, without the word of God; but let us allow ourselves to be ruled by the command of God. For this definition is not to be neglected: those are righteous who shape their life according to the precepts of the law. By this it is implied that all self-devised worship is worth nothing before God, and that the course of human life is wandering and erroneous as soon as it departs from his law. Luke therefore calls Zacharias and Elizabeth righteous because they walked in the precepts of the Lord, and because they were reckoned such before God, on account of their purpose, which was to serve the Lord. For they are not called righteous because they kept all the precepts of the law, which he calls ordinances (just as Job was not called righteous because he had fulfilled the whole law), but because, received into the grace of God, they pleased him even with their works, and he regarded their works with a fatherly indulgence, not with extreme rigour. Indeed, even if we have done all the things that are commanded, we are still unprofitable servants (Luke 17).

units.la: Quod insuper dicit Lucas, Erant autem iusti ambo: docemur similitudinem animorum, unitatemque in religione & iustitia, quàm maximè decere coniuges. Non.n.frustra dixit Dominus ad Israelitas de impijs gentibus, Non sociabis cum eis coniugia. Filiam tuam non dabis filio eius, nec filiam illius accipies filio tuo, quia seducet filiū tuū ne sequatur me, &c. Deu.7.3.Reg.11.1.Esd.9.
units.tr: Furthermore, when Luke says, "they were both righteous," we are taught that likeness of minds and unity in religion and righteousness befit spouses above all. For the Lord did not speak in vain to the Israelites about the impious nations: "You shall not make marriages with them. You shall not give your daughter to his son, nor take his daughter for your son, for she will turn your son away from following me," and so on (Deuteronomy 7:3; 1 Kings 11:1; Ezra 9).

units.la: ʒ Quò ad tertium, discimus ex præsenti historia, beneficium Dei esse habere liberos, præsertim pios & sanctos. Alioquin utilius est mori sine filijs, quàm relinquere filios impios, Eccles.16. Sap.4.
units.tr: 3. As to the third point, we learn from the present story that it is a blessing of God to have children, especially pious and holy ones. Otherwise it is better to die without sons than to leave ungodly sons (Ecclesiasticus 16; Wisdom 4).

units.la: Et, liberos pios evenire plerunq; iustis, eosq; impetrari precibus. Dicit enim angelus ad Zachariam: Quoniam exaudita est deprecatio tua, uxorq; tua Elizabeth pariet tibi filium. Ex quib.verbis colligi potest, Zachariam praecipua orandi parte defunctum, fe[?] cundo loco de se priuatim cogitauisse, proq[?] impetranda sobole, orasse. Quanquam vix probabile est, Zachariam tunc pro filio impetrando orasse, de quo desperauerat ob prouectam vxoris ætatem. Nec sane ex verbis angeli elicitur certum aliquod temporis momentum. Quare simpliciter intelligimus, exauditum tandem fuisse votum, quod iam à multo tempore coram Deo effuderat. Ergo sancti citra offensam Dei & pro suscipienda prole, atque aliis externis bonis, rectisimè Deum orare possunt, si præmittant animo hæc, Sanctificetur nomen tuum: Adueniat regnum tuum: Fiat voluntas tua. Quod autem patres tam vehementer prolem expeterent, in causa fuit Christus nondum mundo exhibitus, quem quisque exoptabat descendere ex suo semine. Quanquam vna etiam nobis cum illis causa communis est, quòd benedictionem Dei esse reputamus procreationem liberorum. Testimonium igitur quum sint diuinæ benedictionis liberi, sequitur nos posse expetere ea conditione, quæ dicta est. Gratia itaque & gloria ei, qui potest cumulatè facere vltra omnia quæ petimus in secula, Amen.
units.tr: And that pious children are commonly born to righteous parents, and are obtained by prayers. For the angel says to Zacharias: "Because your prayer has been heard, and your wife Elizabeth will bear you a son." From these words it can be gathered that Zacharias, having performed the chief part of prayer, secondly thought of himself privately and prayed for obtaining offspring. Yet it is hardly probable that Zacharias then prayed for obtaining a son, for whom he had despaired because of his wife's advanced age. Nor indeed is any definite moment of time drawn from the words of the angel. Therefore we understand simply that the vow, which he had poured out before God for a long time, was at last heard. So the saints, without offence to God, may very rightly pray for the gaining of offspring and other external goods, provided they first place these things in their minds: "Hallowed be your name; your kingdom come; your will be done." Moreover, the reason the fathers so eagerly desired offspring was that Christ had not yet been revealed to the world, and each one longed for him to descend from his own seed. Yet we too share a common cause with them, in that we reckon the procreation of children to be a blessing of God. Therefore, since children are a testimony of divine blessing, it follows that we may ask for them on the condition that has been stated. Thanks and glory therefore be to him who is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask, for ever and ever, Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XLVIII.
units.tr: CONCIO XLVIII.

units.la: Ioan. 3.
units.tr: John 3.

units.la: Ipsi vos testes estis, quod dixerim, Non sum ego Christus, sed missus sum ante illum. Qui habet sponsam, sponsus est: amicus autem sponsi, qui stat & audit eum, gaudio gaudet propter vocem sponsi. Hoc ergo gaudium meum impletum est. Illum oportet crescere, me vero minui.
units.tr: You yourselves are witnesses that I said, I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him. He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. This my joy therefore is fulfilled. He must increase, but I must decrease.

units.la: 1 Ioannes Baptista negat se esse Christum, quia non erat: dicit autem se missum esse ante illum, ut viam illi pararet, sicuti apparitores regibus solent: adeoque esse Christi ministrum, praeterea & amicum, neque aegre ferre Christi opera, sed maiorem in modum laetari. Ait enim, Amicus sponsi, qui stat & audit eum, gaudio gaudet propter vocem sponsi. Debet ergo amicus Christi stare .i. permanere in gratia quam accepit, constás esse, & non cadere, adeoque humilis esse, ut Ioannes: item audire vocem sponsi Christi, ut omnes oves ex Deo natae faciunt, Ioan.8. 10. praeterea gaudere, non mundi more in rebus mundanis, 1. Io. 2. sed propter vocem sponsi, in Domino, in spiritu sancto, Psal.119. Phil.4. Rom.14. Mimmonam[?] odisse, Matt.6. facere quod Christus praecepit, Ioan.15.
units.tr: John the Baptist denies that he is the Christ, because he was not; he says instead that he has been sent before him, to prepare his way, as attendants usually go before kings; and so he is a minister of Christ, and moreover a friend, who does not take Christ's works badly but rejoices greatly in them. For he says, The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly at the bridegroom's voice. The friend of Christ ought therefore to stand, that is, to remain in the grace he has received, and not to fall; and so to be humble, as John was; likewise to hear the voice of Christ the bridegroom, as all sheep born of God do (John 8.10); moreover to rejoice, not in the manner of the world in worldly things (1 John 2), but in the Lord and in the Holy Spirit at the bridegroom's voice (Ps. 119; Phil. 4; Rom. 14); to hate mammon (Matt. 6); and to do what Christ has commanded (John 15).

units.la: Utinam vero id, quod Ioannes dicit se gaudere, non ob sponsae, sed sponsi vocem, probè notarent, qui contra ipsissimum Christi verbum ecclesiae authoritatem obicere non verentur: quasi vero Christus, unicus & verus ecclesiae sponsus, imperfectam & mutabilem doctrinam fidelibus reliquerit. Ait enim Ioan.15. Jam non dicam vos seruos, quia ser [uus?] nescit quid faciat Dominus eius:vos autem dixi amicos, quia omnia quæ audiui à patre meo,nota feci vobis. Ergo omnis authoritas sponso datur, non sponsæ. Sponso datur vox loquendi & imperandi, sponsæ verò aures audiendi:iuxta illud:Audi filia & vide,& incl na aurem tuam, Psalm. 45. Affirmat igitur Baptista, se votorum omnium summam adeptum esse,nec jam esse quod desideret,vbi videt regnare Christum, propriaque voce docere, & illi audientiam, quam merentur dari. Q. d. Sicuti is qui sponsus non est, sed sponsi amicus & auspex, siue paranymphus, sponso nec invidet eam felicitatem, nec præripit sponsam: imò gratulatur potius sponso & sponsæ de nuptijs contractis, & astans istis tacitè & in sinu gaudet non vulgariter, quòd audit laborem illum suum nuptijs conciliandis insumptum cesssisse feliciter, & sponsam sponso adductam iucundissimo suavissimoque frui & colloquio & consortio: ita ego quum Christi sim præambulo, & quasi paranymphus, non sponsus, sed sponsi amicus, omnino cupiens illius nuptijs,fœderi & amicitiæ populum Dei inferere & copulare, nec invideo illi gloriam tantam, nec populum illi præripere volo, sed etiam atq; etiam gaudeo illum me in diem vixisse, quo oculis meis cerno feliciter, non inanem fuisse prædicationem meà, sed omnes celerrimo pede ad Christū accelerare, ad quem eos hactenus invitaui. hoc (inquâ) ingès gaudium meum impletû est. Porrò quod dicit de voce sponsi (cuius & Apoc.18. mentio fit) forte alludit (iuxta sententiam Flacij) ad aliquem veterem morem nuptiarum, vbi sponsus cecinit.
units.tr: Would that those who do not hesitate to set the authority of the Church against the very word of Christ would carefully note what John says he rejoices in: not the bride's voice but the bridegroom's! As if Christ, the only and true bridegroom of the Church, had left the faithful an imperfect and changeable doctrine! For he says in John 15: Now I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his lord is doing; but I have called you friends, because I have made known to you all things that I have heard from my Father. Therefore all authority is given to the bridegroom, not to the bride. To the bridegroom is given the voice of speaking and commanding; to the bride, the ears for hearing; according to that saying: Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear (Ps. 45). The Baptist therefore affirms that he has attained the sum of all his wishes, and that he has nothing more to desire, when he sees Christ reigning and teaching with his own voice, and his hearers being given the hearing they deserve. The sense is this: just as one who is not the bridegroom but the bridegroom's friend and go-between, or paranymph, does not envy the bridegroom that happiness nor snatch away the bride, but rather congratulates both bridegroom and bride on the marriage contracted, and standing by them quietly, rejoices inwardly, and not in an ordinary way, that the labour he spent in arranging the marriage has turned out happily, and that the bride, brought to the bridegroom, enjoys the most pleasant and sweet conversation and companionship: so I too, since I am the forerunner of Christ and, as it were, his paranymph, not the bridegroom but the bridegroom's friend, earnestly desiring his marriage, to join and bind the people of God in covenant and friendship with him, neither envy him so great a glory nor wish to snatch the people from him; but I rejoice again and again that I have lived to this day, when I see with my own eyes that my preaching was not in vain, and that all are hastening with the swiftest foot to Christ, to whom I have hitherto invited them. This, I say, my great joy is fulfilled. Moreover, what he says about the bridegroom's voice (which is also mentioned in Rev. 18) perhaps alludes (according to the opinion of Flacius) to some ancient custom of weddings, where the bridegroom sang.

units.la: 2 Omni autem sponso vtile est obseruare & saepe cogitare, quòd & Christus Iesus appellatur sponsus, non solùm hoc loco, sed etiam alibi, vt Psalm. 19. Hof. 2. Matth. 9. 25. idque propter ardentem amorem erga sponsam, id est, ecclesiam suam (quam redemit sanguine suo, & cui pignus dedit spiritum sanctū, vt Augustinus ait Tract. 8 in Ioan.) & copulationem arctissimam. Hoc etenim & doctrinae & consolationi eius seruit: propterea quòd hinc discit, quid ipse Christo debeat, tanquam sponso suo, cui pater humanum genus per incarnationis dispensationem, insolubili desponsationis vinculo coniunxit: & quid debeat vxori suae, tanquam sponsus. Neque hoc solum, sed etiam inde consolationem & magnum gaudium concipit. Si enim Christum sponsum suum habet, simul etiam particeps fit omnium bonorum Christi, quae ipse communicat suae sponsae, vt solet maritus vxori. Et si cogitat sponsum Christum ad multos næuos sponsae suae conniuere, tanto patientius feret etiam mores vxoris suae.
units.tr: 2 It is useful for every bridegroom to observe and often to consider that Christ Jesus too is called the bridegroom, not only in this place but also elsewhere, as in Ps. 19, Hos. 2, Matt. 9:15, 25; and this on account of his burning love for the bride, that is, his Church (which he redeemed with his own blood, and to which he gave the Holy Spirit as a pledge, as Augustine says, Tract. 8 on John), and the closest union. For this serves both his teaching and his comfort: from it he learns what he himself owes Christ as his bridegroom, to whom the Father joined the human race by the dispensation of the incarnation in the indissoluble bond of betrothal; and what he owes his wife as her bridegroom. And not only this, but from it he also conceives consolation and great joy. For if he has Christ as his bridegroom, he at the same time becomes a partaker of all the good things of Christ, which he communicates to his bride, as a husband usually does to his wife. And if he reflects that the bridegroom Christ winks at the many blemishes of his bride, he will bear with all the more patience even the ways of his own wife.

units.la: Quid autem sponsus seu vir debeat vxori suae, docet exemplum sponsi Christi, de quo Apostolus, Eph. 5. Viri diligite vxores vestras, sicut & Christus dilexit ecclesiam, & semetipsum exposuit pro ea, vt illam fanctificaret, mundatam lauacro aquę per verbum, vt adhiberet eam sibi gloriosam ecclesiá non habentem maculam aut rugam, aut quicquá eiusmodi, sed vt essct sancta & irreprehensibilis. Sic debent viri diligere suas vxores, vt sua ipsorum corpora. Qui diligit suam vxorem, seipsum diligit. Nullus enim vnquam suam ipsius carnem odio habuit, imò enutrit ac fouet eam, sicut & Dominus ecclesiam. Quoniam membra sumus corporis eiusdé, ex carne eius & ex ossibus eius. Huius rei gratia relinquet homo patrem ac matrem, & adiungetur vxori suæ, atque è duobus fiet vna caro. Mysterium hoc magnum est, verùm ego loquor de Christo & de Ecclesia. Quanquam & vos singulatim hoc præstate, vt suam quisque vxorem diligat, tanquam seipsum, &c.
units.tr: What a bridegroom or husband ought to owe his wife, the example of Christ the bridegroom teaches, of whom the Apostle speaks in Eph. 5: Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, cleansing her with the washing of water by the word, that he might present her to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she should be holy and blameless. So ought husbands to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but rather nourishes and cherishes it, as the Lord does the Church. For we are members of his body, of his flesh and of his bones. For this cause a man shall leave father and mother, and shall be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh. This mystery is great, but I speak of Christ and of the Church. Nevertheless, let each one of you also do this, that each love his own wife as himself, etc.

units.la: Quid verò quisque debeat Christo sponso suo, docet lex naturæ vnà cum lege Mosis & Prophetis, de qua ipse Dominus Matth.7, Omnia igitur quæcunque (inquiens) volueritis, vt faciant vobis homines, sic & vos facite illis. Omnis autem maritus seu sponsus cupit habere sponsam siue vxorem morigeram & obedientè: ergo quiuis etiam se Christo sponso suo obedientem præbere debet in omnibus. Sic enim rursus scribit Paulus ad Eph. Vxores proprijs viris subditæ sitis, veluti Domino, quoniam vir est caput vxoris, quemadmodum & Christus caput ecclesiæ: & idem est, qui salutem dat corpori. Itaque quemadmodum ecclesia subdita est Christo, sic & uxores suis viris subditae sint in omnibus, intellige, quae non sunt contra Dominū Deum nostrum: alioquin oportet Deo magis obedire quàm hominibus. Et iterum: Uxor autem reuereatur virum.
units.tr: What each one ought to owe to Christ his bridegroom, the law of nature teaches together with the law of Moses and the Prophets, of which the Lord himself speaks in Matt. 7: Therefore all things whatsoever you would that men should do to you, do so also to them. Every husband or bridegroom desires to have a bride or wife who is compliant and obedient; therefore everyone too ought to show himself obedient to Christ his bridegroom in all things. For so Paul also writes again in Eph.: Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as to the Lord, since the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ also is the head of the Church; and he is the one who gives salvation to the body. Therefore as the Church is subject to Christ, so also let wives be subject to their husbands in everything, that is, in those things which are not against the Lord our God; otherwise we must obey God rather than men. And again: Let the wife reverence her husband.

units.la: Cæterùm si uxor tam obediens esse debet viro suo, quanto magis quilibet Christianus Christo domino & sponso suo debet: esse obsequens: imò tantò magis, quanto maior est maiestas Christi, quàm authoritas cuiuslibet viri. Quanta verò sit maiestas sponsi Christi, docet etiam hîc Ioannes Baptista, quando de eo dicit: Illum oportet crescere, me verò minui. Hoc & diebus, quibus nati sunt, & mortibus, quibus passi sunt, figuratū esse scribit Augustinus. Nascitur namque Ioannes, ex quo dies incipiunt minui: nascitur Dominus, ex quo dies incipiunt crescere. Capite ille minuitur, dum occiditur: hic verò attollitur in cruce. Sit igitur huic optimo & maximo domino nostro Iesu Christo, qui seipsum tradidit pro sua sponsa, honor, & gloria, & laus in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, if a wife ought to be so obedient to her husband, how much more ought every Christian to be obedient to Christ the Lord and his bridegroom; indeed, by so much more as the majesty of Christ is greater than the authority of any husband. How great the majesty of the bridegroom Christ is, John the Baptist also teaches here, when he says of him: He must increase, but I must decrease. Augustine writes that this was foreshadowed both in the days on which they were born and in the deaths by which they suffered. For John is born from the time when the days begin to decrease; the Lord is born from the time when the days begin to increase. John is diminished by being beheaded; but he is lifted up on the cross. To this best and greatest of lords, our Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself up for his bride, therefore be honour, and glory, and praise for ever. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO XLIX.
units.tr: CONCIO XLIX.

units.la: 1. Corinth. 7.
units.tr: 1. Corinth. 7.

units.la: CAEterum de quibus scripsistis mihi: Bonum est homini, uxorem non attingere. Attamen propter supra ditanda, suam quisque uxorem habeat, & suum quaque virum habeat. Uxori vir debitam benevolentiam reddat: similiter autem & uxor viro. Uxor proprij corporis ius non habet, sed maritus. Similiter & maritus proprij corporis ius non habet, sed uxor. Ne fraudetis vos invicem, nisi si quid ex consensu, pro tempore, ut vacetis ieiunio & precationi: & rursum in unum conveniatis, ne tentet vos Satanas propter intemperantiam vestram. Hoc autem dico iuxta indulgentiam, non iuxta praeceptum, &c.
units.tr: Now concerning the things whereof ye wrote unto me: It is good for a man not to touch a woman. Nevertheless, to avoid fornication, let every man have his own wife, and let every woman have her own husband. Let the husband render unto the wife due benevolence: and likewise also the wife unto the husband. The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband: and likewise also the husband hath not power of his own body, but the wife. Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency. But I speak this by permission, and not of commandment, etc.

units.la: 1 Ad tria potissimum Apostolus Paulus, à Corinthijs, tanquam doctor ab ecclesia, rogatus, in principio huius capitis respondet. Primum, an sit contrahendum matrimonium: deinde, quibus de causis: praeterea, quomodo coniuges in matrimonio se gerere debeant erga se invicem, potissimè verò quod ad opus carnale, sive actum naturalem attinet.
units.tr: 1 The Apostle Paul, when asked by the Corinthians, as a teacher is asked by the Church, answers at the beginning of this chapter on three main points. First, whether marriage is to be contracted; then, for what reasons; and further, how spouses ought to conduct themselves in marriage towards one another, especially as regards the carnal act, or natural union.

units.la: Nam in eo, quod dicit, Bonum esse homini, uxorem non attingere, ostendit quòd nō solum ἀδιάφορον[?] & liberum sit uxorem ducere, aut non ducere (adeoque neminem ad coniugium cogendum) verumetiam melius, id est uti[illegible, ~4 letters] ac vitae huic corporali commodius, vel quietius, pu[illegible, ~2 letters]hrius & iucundi-us, us,nullam ducere (fi modò carere possit,casteque viuat) quàm ducere (præsertim malam.) Nam qui cœlebs est, inquit, curat eā quæ sunt Domini, quomodo placiturus sit Domino. At qui duxit vxorem,sollicitus est de his, quæ sunt mundi, quomodo placiturus sit vxori. Hinc etiam Christus ait, Qui potest capere capiat. Veruntamen non peccauit,qui duxit vxorem:neque virgo,aut vidua si nupserit (modò in Domino) peccauit. Quemadmodum enim si quis diceret, bonum esse homini non edere, nec bibere, nec dormire: is neque esum, neque potionem, neque somnum vituperaret, tanquam res vitiosas:sed quia tantum spiritui decedit, quantum his rebus datur, intelligeret nos beatiores fore si ab his auocamentis liberi,tati[?] possemus incumbere in rerum cœlestium meditationem. Sic Paulus hac ratione bonum esse dicit non illigari coniugio, quoniam in hoc multæ sunt tricæ, quæ hominem impeditum teneant: multæ molestiæ,solicitudines,tædia,quæ coniugatos manent. Nā & propter venturam tempestatem bellicam[?] Ieremiæ dicebatur capite decimo sexto:Noli vxorem ducere: non quòd peccatum, sed incommodum tum esset vxorem ducere.Est itaque hæc indefinita propositio contrahenda: quum nequaquàm vera esse possit in omnibus hominum generibus: quod planum est, quum Adamo, primo inquam homini, minimè conuenire potuerit. Neque valet aptari ijs qui matrimonio iam sunt coniuncti[?]: quorum neuter corporis sui potestatem habet. Nec item quadrat ijs, qui vel scortantur, vel adaruntur: quibus Apostolus mandat, ut nubant. Ideo Apostolus hanc propositionem postea corrigit, ne quis de matrimonio male suspicaretur. Non igitur pugnant hæc Pauli verba cum verbis Domini, ubi pronunciat, viro non esse bonum carere uxore, Genef. 2. Facilè enim hæc duo dicta conciliabuntur, si inter puram Dei ordinationem, & pœnas peccati, quæ deinde sequutæ sunt, distinguere meminerimus. Iuxta Matthiam Flacium Illyricū Deus illud (Non est bonum hominem esse solum) loquitur in genere de hominibus, quod plerique ita sunt geniti, taliquæ[?] natura præditi, ut non possint extra coniugium caste viuere. Hic vero Paulus loquitur de illis, qui excepti sunt ex regula, vel per naturæ imbecillitatem, vel per donum castitatis. Denique sicut melius esset prorsus abstinere ab omni cibo: nam careremus multis molestijs, ad quas cogimur cibi gratia. Verùm quum id fieri nequeat, melius est edere & bibere quàm fame periclitari: sic melius quidem est continere quàm nubere. Vbi vero deest continentia, melius est nubere, quàm vri, scilicet incendio concupiscentiæ, quod Chryfost. tyrannidem concupiscentiæ vocat. Taceo nunc de supplicio ignis, & incendio gehennæ, de quibus Gen. 38. Leu. 21. & Apoc. 21. Cæterum si ijs qui libidinis vstionem sentiunt, iinò incontinentibus antequam vrantur, nubendum est, ne vrantur, ne scortentur, ne, vt Chryf. habet, continendi laboribus & sudoribus subuertantur, quid iubendum est illis, qui iam pleno impetu scortantur?
units.tr: For in what he says, that it is good for a man not to touch a woman, he shows that taking a wife, or not taking one, is indifferent [ἀδιάφορον] and left free (so that no one is to be compelled to marriage); and moreover that it is better, that is more convenient and more quiet, and more pleasant for this bodily life, to take no wife (provided one can do without and live chastely) than to take one (especially a bad one). For, he says, he who is unmarried cares for the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord. But he who has taken a wife is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife. Hence also Christ says, "He who can receive it, let him receive it." Yet he does not sin who takes a wife; nor does a virgin or a widow sin if she marries (only in the Lord). For just as if someone were to say that it is good for a man not to eat, nor drink, nor sleep, he would not be condemning food, drink or sleep as vicious things; rather he would understand that we shall be happier if, free from these distractions, we can devote ourselves to meditation on heavenly things, since as much is taken from the spirit as is given to these things. So Paul, on this ground, says that it is good not to be bound to marriage, since in it there are many troubles which keep a man entangled: many annoyances, anxieties and weariness which await the married. For also, on account of the coming warlike storm, it was said to Jeremiah in the sixteenth chapter: "Do not take a wife"; not because marriage was a sin, but because at that time it would be an inconvenience. This proposition, therefore, "it is good for a man not to touch a woman," must be understood as indefinite; for it can by no means be true of all kinds of men, as is plain, since it could not fit Adam, the first man. Nor does it apply to those who are already joined in marriage, neither of whom has power over his own body. Nor does it suit those who either commit fornication or burn with lust, to whom the Apostle commands that they marry. Therefore the Apostle afterwards corrects this proposition, lest anyone should think badly of marriage. These words of Paul, then, do not clash with the words of the Lord, where he declares that it is not good for a man to be without a wife, Genesis 2. For these two sayings will easily be reconciled if we remember to distinguish between God's pure ordinance and the punishments of sin which followed afterwards. According to Matthias Flacius Illyricus, God spoke that saying ("It is not good for man to be alone") in general of men, because most are born and endowed with such a nature that they cannot live chastely outside marriage. But here Paul speaks of those who are excepted from the rule, either through the weakness of nature or through the gift of chastity. Finally, just as it would be better to abstain altogether from all food (for we would be free from many troubles to which we are driven for the sake of food), yet since this cannot be done, it is better to eat and drink than to be endangered by hunger; so it is indeed better to be continent than to marry. But where continence is lacking, it is better to marry than to burn, namely with the fire of concupiscence, which Chrysostom calls the tyranny of concupiscence. I say nothing now of the punishment of fire and the burning of hell, of which we read in Genesis 38, Leviticus 21 and Revelation 21. But if we must marry those who feel the burning of lust, nay, the incontinent before they burn, so that they do not burn, do not commit fornication, and (as Chrysostom has it) are not overthrown by the labours and sweats of striving for continence, what must be enjoined on those who already fornicate with full force?

units.la: 2 Oportet autem vt ob quatuor (etsi Lombardus plures recenset cùm honestas, tum minus honestas, lib.4. Dist.10.) harum causarum ad minimum vnam suscipiatur coniugium: vel propter augendam sobolem: dixit enim Deus Gen. 1. & 9. Crescite & multiplicamini, &c. Item Paulus, 1. Tim. 5. volo iuniores nubere, filios gignere, vel propter educandam atque instituendam sobolem ad cultum Dei: fecit enim Dominus vxorem in adiutorium viri, Gen. 2. Nec frustra dixit, Honora patrem & matrem, vult ergo vt pater & mater liberos educent: vel propter operam & studia, quae vxor marito praestare debet, tanquam corpus capiti, 1. Corinth. 11. vel propter vitanda stupra. Satius enim est teste Apostolo, contrahere matrimonium, quàm ardere. Is in hac corrupta natura vnus[?] ex primariis coniugii finibus aut usibus est. Remedium enim hoc licitum Deus huic infirmae naturae monstrauit: de quo Apostolus hoc in loco, vbi ait: Sed propter scortationes suam quisque vxorem habeat. Quibus verbis iubet, vt qui incontinentiae vitio sunt obnoxii, sive sint iuniores & fecundi, sive natu grandiores ac steriles, sive viri, sive mulieres,ad remedium confugiant:seu refrigerium, quo incendium in continentiae sopitur: cuius rei sibi quisque testis esse potest. Quicquid ergo difficultatis inconiugio certimus, quicunque carnis suae punctionibus resistere nequeunt, hoc sibi praeceptum a Domino impositum nouerint. Tametsi enim multa commoda habeat coelibatus,habet tamen simul cum his multum periculi,ne,quâ do id quod nô prohibet lex, vitare quis vult, aliquid contra legem admittat: id quod multis euenit volentibus euitare coniugium , vt incidant in alias foedas libidines. Solent enim qui compendium quaerunt, plerunque errare. Sed & Socrates rogatus ab adolescente quodam,vtrum melius censeret, vxore ducere, annon ducere? Vtruncunque,inquit,feceris,poenitebit: indicans & coelibatu & coniugium habere suas molestias,ad quas perferendas esset praeparandus animus. Caelibatum comitatur folitu lo,orbitas,generis interitus,haeres alienus : matrimonium perpetua folicitudo,iuges querelae, lotis exprobratio, affinium graue superciliuum , garrula socrus lingua,subsequi alieni matrimonij,in certus liberorum euentus, aliaque innumera incommoda. Proinde non hic est electio, qualis est inter bonum & malum, sed qualis inter leuiora & graviora in commoda.
units.tr: 2 It is necessary, however, that marriage be undertaken for at least one of four reasons (although Lombard enumerates more, both honourable and less honourable, Book 4, Distinction 10): first, for the increase of offspring, for God said in Genesis 1 and 9: "Increase and multiply," etc. Likewise Paul, 1 Timothy 5: "I will that the younger women marry, bear children"; second, for the bringing up and instruction of offspring in the worship of God, for the Lord made the wife as a helper for the man, Genesis 2. Nor is it in vain that he said, "Honour your father and mother"; he wills, therefore, that fathers and mothers bring up their children; third, on account of the labour and care which the wife ought to render to her husband, as the body to the head, 1 Corinthians 11; fourth, to avoid fornication. For, as the Apostle witnesses, it is better to contract marriage than to burn. In this corrupt nature this is one of the primary ends or uses of marriage. For God showed this lawful remedy to this weak nature; and of this the Apostle speaks in this place, where he says: "But because of fornications, let each man have his own wife." By these words he commands that those who are subject to the vice of incontinence, whether they are young and fertile or older and barren, whether men or women, should flee to the remedy, or cooling, by which the fire of incontinence is quenched; of which everyone can be his own witness. Therefore whatever difficulty we find in celibacy, whoever cannot resist the stings of his flesh, let him know that this command has been laid upon him by the Lord. For although celibacy has many advantages, it also has with them much danger, lest, while one wishes to avoid what the law does not forbid, one should admit something against the law; which happens to many who, wishing to avoid marriage, fall into other foul lusts. For those who seek a shortcut usually go astray. Socrates too, when asked by a certain young man whether he thought it better to take a wife or not to take one, answered: "Whichever you do, you will regret it," indicating that both celibacy and marriage have their troubles, for which the mind must be prepared to endure. Celibacy is accompanied by loneliness, childlessness, the extinction of the family, and an heir from outside; marriage by perpetual anxiety, constant complaints, reproach for the washing, the grave frowns of in-laws, a chattering mother-in-law's tongue, the following-on of another's marriage, the uncertain outcome of children, and countless other inconveniences. Therefore the choice here is not like that between good and evil, but like that between lesser and greater inconveniences.

units.la: Faciunt quoque haec Apostoli verba adversus bigamos & polygamos:iuxta primaeuam coniugij institutionem, Erunt duo in carne una, Genes. 2. quam Christus restituit, Matt. 19. Vult enim ut mulier unaquaeque proprium maritum habeat, afferens mutuam esse obligationem. Qui ergo fidem uxori semel astrinxit, diuidere se ab ea non debet: quod fieri constat per secundum nexū.
units.tr: These words of the Apostle also tell against bigamists and polygamists, in accordance with the original institution of marriage: "They shall be two in one flesh," Genesis 2, which Christ restored, Matthew 19. For he wills that each woman have her own husband, asserting that the obligation is mutual. Therefore he who has once pledged his faith to a wife must not separate himself from her; which is plainly done by a second bond.

units.la: Faciunt item haec verba contra concubinatum. Nam etiam inter scortatores reperias, qui mulierem penes se habeat, concubinam, qua fit contentus, & thori fide seruet, & qua etiam liberos suscipiat, id quod de se scribit Augustin.in Confess. lib. 4. cap. 2. qui & filium habuit ex concubina à Deo datum, Confess. lib. 6. cap. 15. Talis tamen copula illegitima est, quod & Augustinus fatetur. Coniugiū vero docetur ab Apostolo, cum dicit, Vnusquisque suam habeat, & vnaquaeque suum.
units.tr: These words also tell against concubinage. For among fornicators you may find one who keeps a woman beside him as a concubine, with whom he is content, and whom he keeps faithful to his bed, and by whom he even has children; which Augustine writes of himself in the Confessions, Book 4, chapter 2, who also had a son by a concubine given him by God, Confessions, Book 6, chapter 15. Yet such a union is illegitimate, as Augustine himself admits. But marriage is taught by the Apostle, when he says: "Let each man have his own, and each woman her own."

units.la: Quae extra connubium legitimum virum habet, non suum dicitur habere, sed alienum, Ioan. 4. Liquet itaq; concubinatum istum, quem pontificij sacerdotes liberè sectantur, nihil esse aliud quàm scortationem, cum nō sit coniugium legitimum, ad quod vitandae scortationis gratia quosuis adigit hic Apostolus iubens, vt quisque suam, & quaeque suum habeat.
units.tr: He who has a woman outside lawful wedlock is said not to have her as his own, but another's, John 4. It is clear, therefore, that the concubinage which the Papist priests freely pursue is nothing else than fornication, since it is not lawful marriage; and it is to avoid fornication that this Apostle, bidding each to have his own and each her own, compels anyone to marriage. ## [2]

units.la: §[?] Officium coniugum est, debitam benevolentiam sibi mutuo reddere. Debita enim reddi solent. Coniugale autem debitum, iuxta Hugonem de S. Victore, duobus modis consideratur, vt scilicet vterque alteri se & conferuet, & non neget. Complectitur autem sub nomine beneuolentiæ mutua ossicia coniugij omni studio præstanda, idque propterea, quòd vult ista ex animo præstari.
units.tr: §[?] The duty of spouses is to render to each other the mutual goodwill that is owed. For debts are customarily paid. The conjugal debt, according to Hugh of St. Victor, is considered in two ways: namely, that each should give himself to the other and not refuse. Under the name of mutual goodwill, moreover, are comprehended the offices of marriage to be performed with all zeal, and this because they are meant to be performed from the heart.

units.la: Et quia omnis vera beneficentia propriè ex beneuolentia charitateque proficiscitur, coplectitur simul etiam ipsum actum naturale, seu commistionem coniugalem: quemadmodum dum ex mox sequentibus liquet. Addit enim Paulus: Uxor sui corporis domina non est, sed vir: itemq; vir sui corporis dominus non est, sed uxor. Nolite alter alterum defraudare, &c. Itaque neuter coniunx habet ius sui corporis liberum, ut antea: sed alterius corpus est alteri obligatum.
units.tr: And because all true beneficence proceeds properly from goodwill and love, it also embraces the natural act itself, or conjugal intercourse, as is clear from what follows. For Paul adds: The wife has no authority over her own body, but the husband; and likewise the husband has no authority over his own body, but the wife. Do not defraud one another, etc. Therefore neither spouse has a free right over his own body, as before; but each body is bound to the other.

units.la: Debet ergo vnus alteri petenti reddere debitum, imò nonnunquam exigere opus illud ab ea coniuge, quæ præ verecundia non audet petere: ne scilicet in peccatum cadat, stuprumque vitetur. Nam morosi coniuges, qui ex superstitione negant debitum, sæpe dant alteri occasionem adulterandi. Rectè igitur sanctus ille vir Paphnutius, quum patres in concilio Niceno canonem statuissent, quo clericis cum proprijs coniugibus prohibebatur concubitus, restitit graui sua authoritate, afferens honorabiles nuptias, & castitatem esse dicens, concubitum cum propria coniuge: synodumque laudasse sententiam eius, nihilque hac parte statuisse: scribit Sozomenus Hist. Trip. libro secundo, capite decimo quarto. Tametsi inter eius cocilij canones recitatur vnus, quo clericis coiugium interdicitur: unde videri potest, vel à malevolis, vel à posteris suppositus. De Gregorio, eius nominis primo pontifice Romano, scriptum quidam reliquerunt (teste Andrea Hyperio lib. 4. de Theologo, cap. 2. Obser. 12.) quod caussam de cælibatu ministrorum ecclesiæ, magno ardore, in Italia maxime & Sicilia promouerit. Cæterum ubi post aliquantum tempus exspiscinis suis vidisset educi aliquot mille capita infantium, & quidem ab Ecclesiasticis, vetitum suum concubitum celare cupientibus, clàm, ut crede{*} batur, interfectorum, cæptis destitit. Et quidem istud rectè ac merito. Honorabile enim connubiũ, & thorus immaculatus in omnibus: fornicatores autem & adulteros iudicabit Deus, Hebr.13. Nam adulterans (ut ille ait) polluit pallium Diuæ Mariæ, quo occultauit cœlestem conceptum, Matth.1. Dicat ergo uxor scortatori sollicitanti, corpus non esse suum, sed sui mariti: & rursus maritus scorto tentanti dicat, corpus non esse suum, sed uxoris. Non enim minus vir adulter est, si scortetur, quàm uxor: quandoquidem perinde eius corpus est uxori obligatum, & uxoris caro, ut uxoris ipsi. Unde Lombar. lib. 4. Dist. 35. ait, Hoc etiam notandum est, quod cum Dominus concedat uxorem dimitti caussa fornicationis viro, eadem licentia non tollitur fœminis. Verùm hoc de mutua [?] obligatione corporis non tantùm ad congressum maritalem seu procreationem, sed etiam ad alia officia, aut usus corporis pertinet: ut exempli causa, Si vir se vellet dedere in servitutem, aut monasterium, aut sine necessitate abire in militiam, aut aliqua simili ratione obligare, aut lædere corpus suum.
units.tr: One ought therefore to render the debt to the other when asked, and indeed sometimes to demand that act from the spouse who, out of modesty, does not dare to ask, lest she fall into sin and fornication be avoided. For spouses who are sullen and from superstition refuse the debt often give the other occasion to commit adultery. Rightly, therefore, that holy man Paphnutius, when the fathers at the Council of Nicaea had enacted a canon by which intercourse of clerics with their own wives was forbidden, opposed it with his weighty authority, asserting that marriage is honourable and that intercourse with one's own wife is chastity; and the synod, he says, praised his opinion and enacted nothing on this point: Sozomen writes in the Tripartite History, book 2, chapter 14. Although one canon of that council is recited in which marriage is forbidden to clerics, whence it may be seen that it was either put in by malevolent men or inserted later. Some have left it on record concerning Gregory, the first Roman pontiff of that name (on the testimony of Andreas Hyperius, On the Theologian, book 4, chapter 2, observation 12), that he promoted with great zeal the cause of celibacy for ministers of the Church, chiefly in Italy and Sicily. Moreover, when after some time he saw from his fishponds some thousands of infants' heads brought out, and indeed of those whose ecclesiastical superiors wished to conceal their forbidden intercourse, secretly killed, as was believed, he desisted from his undertaking. And this indeed was right and deserved. For marriage is honourable and the bed undefiled in all things; but fornicators and adulterers God will judge, Heb. 13. For the adulterer (as that man says) defiles the mantle of the divine Mary, with which he concealed the heavenly conception, Matt. 1. Let the wife therefore say to a fornicator who solicits her that her body is not her own but her husband's; and again let the husband say to a whore who tempts him that his body is not his own but his wife's. For a husband is no less an adulterer if he fornicates than a wife is, since equally his body is bound to the wife, and his flesh is hers, just as hers is his. Whence Lombard, book 4, distinction 35, says: This also is to be noted, that although the Lord permits a wife to be dismissed for fornication, the same licence is not taken away from women. Yet this mutual obligation of the body pertains not only to marital intercourse or procreation, but also to other duties or uses of the body: for example, if a husband were to give himself into servitude, or into a monastery, or without necessity go off to war, or in some similar way bind or injure his body.

units.la: Porrò quum Paulus dicit, Ne fraudetis vos invicem (est autem fraus, quando quod debetur commenticio aliquo praetextu auferatur[?]) nisi forte ex mutuo consensu ad tempus, ut jejunio & precibus vacetis: ostendit conjugibus interdum licere, ut abstineant à congressu. Potest enim accidere tempus, cum aliquando jejunii aut precationis ardentioris causa intermittatur: non quod lædat conscientiam, sed quod olim certis temporibus penitus sese tali quasi ritui cuidam jugentes dedebant, ut Judæi, eorumq; imitatores: cujus rei quasi vestigium quoddam, li[?]cet multa superstitione contaminatum, in papistica[?] quadragesima videmus. Alioqui pios semper oportere precari, nemo ignorat: sed & universam eorum vitam jejunium esse oportet. Debent enim perpetuo parce ac frugaliter vivere, quod genus jejunii esse nemo ambigit, vide Luc, 18.21. & 1. Thessa-lonic. 5.
units.tr: Furthermore, when Paul says, Do not defraud one another (and fraud is when what is owed is taken away under some pretext of invention), unless perhaps by mutual consent for a time, that you may devote yourselves to fasting and prayer: he shows that spouses may at times be permitted to abstain from intercourse. For a time may come when it is suspended for the sake of a more ardent fast or prayer; not because it harms the conscience, but because formerly, at fixed seasons, men gave themselves wholly to a kind of rite of this sort, as the Jews and their imitators did; a certain trace of which, though contaminated by much superstition, we see in the Papist Lent. Otherwise, no one is ignorant that the godly ought always to pray, but their whole life ought also to be a fast. For they ought to live perpetually sparingly and frugally, which kind of fast no one doubts is, see Luke 18.21 and 1 Thess. 5.

units.la: Paulus igitur hic non loquitur de quolibet jejunio, nec de qualibet oratione: sed de jejuniis & precibus publicè ac solenniter suscipientis, ut quum ingruit aliqua calamitas, & appareat indicium iræ Dei, vel quum aliquo difficili negocio impedimur, vel quum aliquid agendum est magni momenti, qualis est institutio pastorum, vel necessitas ecclesiæ alia, aut conjugis, aut prolis, aut amicorum, &c. Tob. 6. 8. Zach. 12. Ioel. 2. Et 2. Sam. 11. de Vria legitur, quod nefas duxerit a ad uxorem suam ingredi, cum Israel bello gravi & periculoso esset implicitus.
units.tr: Paul therefore here does not speak of any fast, nor of any prayer, but of fasts and prayers undertaken publicly and solemnly: as when some calamity is upon us and a sign of God's wrath appears, or when we are hindered by some difficult business, or when something of great moment is to be done, such as the appointment of ministers, or some other need of the Church, or of a spouse, or of children, or of friends, etc. Tob. 6.8; Zech. 12; Joel 2. And in 2 Sam. 11 it is read of Uriah that he thought it wrong to go in to his wife while Israel was engaged in a heavy and dangerous war.

units.la: Obserua autem cautionem Apostoli, qui non solùm duas addit conditiones, quarum prima est, ut ex consensu fiat, nempe intermissio debiti conjugalis: altera, ut nō perpetuō, vel diu, sed ad tempus: verumetiá jubet eos maturè, expletis jejunii diebus, denuò convenire, ne Satanæ (qui autor est adulterii & mirus suasor mali) dent occasionem tentandi (nedum superandi ac perdendi: ut dum placet à concessa venere abstinere, ad inconcessam fœdius prolabantur. Nisi periculum esset etiam jejunantibus & precantibus à tentationibus satanæ, nihil hujus admonuisset. Imò hic potissimum timendæ sunt satanæ insidiæ, ubi à licitis seceditur, idq; immoderatè, ut ad illicita fiat lapsus. Rem hanc ipsa luce clariorem reddidit experientia. Igitur securiores sunt, ne per Satanam tententur, qui licitis utuntur remediis.
units.tr: Observe, moreover, the caution of the Apostle, who adds not only two conditions, of which the first is that it be done by consent, namely the suspension of the conjugal debt, and the second that it be not perpetual or long, but for a time; and indeed he bids them to come together again promptly when the days of fasting are completed, lest they give Satan (who is the author of adultery and a wonderful persuader to evil) an occasion of tempting them, not to mention overcoming and destroying them: so that, while they are pleased to abstain from lawful pleasure, they may not slip more shamefully into what is unlawful. Unless there were danger even to those who fast and pray from the temptations of Satan, he would not have admonished them of this at all. Indeed, the snares of Satan are most to be feared here, where men withdraw from what is lawful, and that immoderately, so that a fall into what is unlawful follows. Experience has made this clearer than the light itself. Therefore those are safer from being tempted by Satan who use the lawful remedies.

units.la: Cæterùm ne putent Corinthii suspensionem debiti ad tempus, esse juris divini: aut consuetudinè conjugium per se esse bonum opus: aut, ne quis posset obijcere, Quid? an times ne parùm ad libidinem sponte proclives sint viri & mulieres, quòd eos solicitas? reddit rationem suae doctrinae, ac testatur se non ideo commendasse thori societatem coniugibus, ut eos ad voluptatem alliciat, aut quia libenter id praecipiat, aut quod hoc praeceptum simpliciter ac per se fit mandatum: sed respexisse quod postulet infirmitas eorum quos alloquitur: quibus hoc concedit vitandae scortationis & tentationis causa. Fideli nostro Deo, qui non finit nos tentari supra id quod possumus: & filio eius Christo Iesu, qui arundinem comminutam non confringere solet: & benigno Spiritui sancto, qui auxiliatur infirmitatibus nostris, sit benedictio, honor, & gloria in æternum, Amen.
units.tr: Moreover, lest the Corinthians think that a suspension of the debt for a time is of divine right, or that marriage is in itself a good work by custom, or lest anyone could object, What? Are you afraid that men and women are too readily inclined to lust of their own accord, since you solicit them? he gives an account of his teaching and testifies that he has not therefore commended the fellowship of the bed to spouses in order to entice them to pleasure, or because he willingly prescribes it, or because this precept is simply and in itself a command; but that he has had regard to what the infirmity of those he addresses requires: to whom he concedes this for the sake of avoiding fornication and temptation. To our faithful God, who does not suffer us to be tempted beyond what we are able, and to his Son Christ Jesus, who is wont not to break the bruised reed, and to the gracious Holy Spirit, who helps our infirmities, be blessing, honour and glory for ever. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO L.
units.tr: SERMON L.

units.la: 1. Corinth. 7.
units.tr: 1. Corinth. 7.

units.la: De virginibus autem praeceptum Domini non habeo, consilium tamen do, tanquam misericordia consequutus a Domino, ut sim fidelis. Arbitror igitur hoc bonum esse propter praesentem necessitatem. Nam bonum est hominem sic esse. Alligatus es uxori[?]ne quaere diuortium. Solutus es ab uxore[?]ne quaeras uxorem. Quod si duxeris uxorem, non peccasti. Et si nupserit virgo, non peccauit. Attamen afflictionem in carne habituri sunt huiusmodi. Ego vero vobis parco. Caeterum illud dico fratres, tempus contractum est: superest, ut qui habent uxores, sint tanquam non habeant: & qui plorant, tanquam non ploret: & qui gaudent, tanquam non gaudeant: & qui emunt, tanquam non possideant: & qui utuntur mundo hoc, tanquam non utantur. Praeterit enim habitus huius mundi.
units.tr: Now concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give my counsel, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful. I think therefore that this is good because of the present necessity. For it is good for a man to remain as he is. Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek a divorce. Are you loosed from a wife? Do not seek a wife. But if you do marry, you have not sinned. And if a virgin marries, she has not sinned. Yet those who marry will have affliction in the flesh, and I would spare you that. But this I say, brethren: the time is short. It remains that those who have wives be as though they had none; and those who weep, as though they did not weep; and those who rejoice, as though they did not rejoice; and those who buy, as though they did not possess; and those who use this world, as though they did not use it. For the fashion of this world is passing away.

units.la: I An melius fit in matrimonio, aut in caelibatu viuere, ostedit Apostolus in his verbis. Nam verisimile est Corinthios ab illo quæssiuisse[?], an Christiani filias virgines elocare debeant, an veluti Christo sacras in perpetua virginitate tenere domi, quo liberius illi seruiant. Paulum ergo hisce nunc respondisse videmus, qui suam sententiam proponit, atque dicit, videri sibi bonum esse, virginem permanere: atque adeo beatiorem esse statum caelibatus seu virginitatis, quam coniugij. Duo autem in summa dat virginitati. Primum, esse liberam & nemini praeceptam. Deinde, esse utilem, tranquillam & commodam, certa de causa. Contra quam sententiam quidam obiciunt illud: Paulum tantum modo consilium suum dare, quidq; ipse sententiam ostendere, nec esse hoc praeceptum Domini, id quod verum est: sed tamen hoc confilium fidele ac bonum non est aspernandū. Quoniam Paulus spiritum Dei habuit (qui veritatis spiritus est, neque seducere potest) & divina misericordia confequutus est, ut dicat super ea re, quod videtur optimum: loqui enim se non ut hominem, sed ut fidum ecclesiae[?] doctorem & Christi apostolum asserit. Atque si quis propius animadvertat, videbit Paulum nihil hic proferre, quod non complexus sit Christus suis verbis, Matt. 19. sed per occupationem fatetur se non habere certum Domini præceptum in lege, quod definiat, quinam coniugium suscipere, aut non attingere debeant. Nam neque legem de virginitate ipse tulit Dominus, neque Apostolo quicquam potestatis dedit, illam pręcipiendi. Adde quod seipsum exponens docet, quale bonum sit manere in cælibatu, nempe tale, ut contrarium facere, nequaquam sit peccatum, id est, tantum utile bonum, non honestum. Quia liberum facit virgini, vel nubere, vel manere in cælibatu. Dicit enim: 'Quòd si duxisti, non peccasti: & si nupsit virgo, non peccavit. quasi dicat: Nihil es deterior coram Deo, nihil officit tibi matrimonium ad salutem, nihil es minus gratus Deo: coram quo perinde valet virginem vel cōiugem esse, sicut perinde valet circumcisum, vel incircumcisum esse, seruum sive liberum, modò[?] fides & cætera sint paria. Quia non huc est respectus oculorum Dei, sed ad animorum synceritatem, qualis qualis sit vitæ huius status, modò non illicitus. Rectè igitur Cæsarius dixit, ut Beda refert in Sentillis suis, de collatione coniugij & virginitatis: Melior est humilis coniugatus[?] quàm superba virginitas. Rationem huius dicti videtur reddere Bernhardus Hom. 1. de laude B. Mariæ, vbi inquit: Laudabilis[?] virginitas, sed magis necessaria humilitas. Illa consulitur, ista præcipitur: ad illam invitaris, ad istam cogeris. De illa dicitur, Qui potest capere, capiat: de ista dicitur, Nisi quis efficiatur sicut parvulus iste, non intrabit regnum cœlorum. Illa ergo remuneratur, ista exigitur. Potes denique sine virginitate salvari, sine humilitate non potes. In summa laudat Apostolus cælibatum, ut feliciorem: probat matrimonium, ut tutius. Volo (inquit Chrysostom. in Sermone de Evangelio: Nuptiæ factæ sunt, &c. contra Iudæos, gentiles & hæreticos) declarare vobis, quòd neq; divitiæ impediunt, neque inopia, neque militia, neque negotiatio, neque nuptiæ, neque pueri, neque seruitus, neque opificium, neq; aliquid tale. Vocatus est ille[?] ad nuptias. Venit, vel non venit? Certum quod venit. Quòd si venit, quomodo ergo nuptiæ malæ? non potes excusare. Ego autem non dico, quòd tantùm venerit. Sed quod & dona secum attulerit. Aquam in vinum mutavit. Ne excuses te propter nuptias, Dominus tuus nuptijs interfuit. & nuptias
units.tr: Here the Apostle shows whether it is better to live in marriage or in celibacy. For it is likely that the Corinthians asked him whether Christians ought to give their virgin daughters in marriage, or rather keep them at home as virgins dedicated in perpetual virginity to Christ, so that they might serve him more freely. We see that Paul now answers these questions, setting out his own opinion, and says that it seems good to him for a virgin to remain so; and thus the state of celibacy or virginity is happier than that of marriage. In sum, he gives two advantages to virginity. First, that it is free and commanded by no one. Second, that it is useful, calm and convenient, for a certain reason. Against this opinion some object that Paul gives only his counsel and his own judgment, and that this is not a command of the Lord, which is true; yet this counsel is not to be despised as faithful and good. For Paul had the Spirit of God (who is the Spirit of truth and cannot deceive), and obtained divine mercy so that he might say what seems best in this matter; for he asserts that he speaks not as a man but as a faithful teacher of the Church and an apostle of Christ. And if anyone looks more closely, he will see that Paul here brings forward nothing that Christ has not included in his own words, Matt. 19. But by a circumlocution he confesses that he has no certain command of the Lord in the law defining who ought to take up marriage or abstain from it. For the Lord himself did not enact a law about virginity, nor did he give the Apostle any power to command it.
