Add that, in setting out his meaning, he teaches what kind of good it is to remain in celibacy: namely, such that doing the opposite is by no means sin; that is, it is only a useful good, not a necessary one. For it leaves the virgin free either to marry or to remain unmarried. For he says: 'But if you have married, you have not sinned; and if a virgin has married, she has not sinned.' As if he were saying: you are no worse before God, marriage does not hinder your salvation, you are not less pleasing to God; before whom it is equally fine to be a virgin or a married woman, just as it is equally fine to be circumcised or uncircumcised, slave or free, provided that faith and the rest are equal. For God's eyes look not to outward circumstances but to the sincerity of minds, whatever the state of life, provided it is not unlawful. Rightly therefore Caesarius said, as Bede reports in his Sentences, on the comparison of marriage and virginity: 'A humble married person is better than a proud virgin.' Bernard seems to give the reason for this saying in his first homily on the praise of the Blessed Mary, where he says: Virginity is praiseworthy, but humility is more necessary. The one is counselled, the other is commanded; you are invited to the one, you are compelled to the other. Of the one it is said, 'He who can receive it, let him receive it'; of the other it is said, 'Unless you become like this little child, you shall not enter the kingdom of heaven.' The one is rewarded, the other is required. Finally, you can be saved without virginity, but you cannot be saved without humility. In short, the Apostle praises celibacy as the happier state and commends marriage as the safer. 'I want' (says Chrysostom in his sermon on the Gospel, 'The wedding was made', &c., against Jews, Gentiles and heretics) 'to make clear to you that neither riches hinder, nor poverty, nor military service, nor trade, nor marriage, nor children, nor servitude, nor a craft, nor anything of the kind. He was invited to the wedding. Did he come, or not? Certainly he came. But if he came, how then is marriage evil? You cannot make an excuse. I do not say that he merely came, but that he also brought gifts with him. He changed water into wine. Do not excuse yourself on account of the wedding: your Lord was present at the wedding and honoured the wedding; and do you accuse the wedding and say that marriage is an obstacle to piety? For there is no obstacle to piety. Do you want to know that having a wife and children harms nothing? Was not Moses married and did he not have children? Was not Elijah a virgin? Did not Moses bring down manna from heaven? Did not Elijah bring down fire from heaven? Did not Moses cause quails to fly in? Did not Elijah shut up heaven by a word? Did not God speak to Moses? Did he not also dwell with Elijah? Did not Moses divide the sea and lead the people across? Was Elijah not taken up into heaven in a fiery chariot? Did virginity harm the one, or were the wife and children a hindrance to the other? You have seen Elijah as a charioteer in the air, you have seen Moses as a traveller through the sea. Look also at Peter, the pillar of the Church, who also had a wife.' 'But it is not written,' you say, 'that Peter had a wife.' Look then, is it clear that he had one? I say it is. Jesus went into the house of Peter's mother-in-law, and she was ill, and he touched her, and the fever left her, and she rose and served them. You see that Peter too had a wife. For where there is a mother-in-law, there is plainly also a wife. You see that Peter had a wife (as Clement in book 3 of the Stromata and Ignatius in his letter to the Philadelphians also testify); do not keep harping on marriage. I say this so that no one may pretend, as an excuse, a wife or children, military service or trade, a craft or servitude, riches or poverty. This excuse, this pretext, are the snares of the devil, &c.' So he.

units.la: Note: the underlined passages in the text (Melior est humilis coniugatus quàm superba virginitas; Laudabilis virginitas, sed magis necessaria humilitas; Potes denique sine virginitate salvari, sine humilitate non potes) are emphasis lines in the printed text; the underlining itself is not transcribed. honestauit: & tu nuptias arguis, & dicis nuptias obstaculum esse ad pietatem? Nullum enim ad pietate est obstaculum. Vis cognoscere quod nihil nocet habere uxorem & pueros? Moses, nonne uxorem habuit & liberos? Helias, nonne virgo erat? Nonne Moses Mana e coelo deduxit? Nonne Helias igne e coelo deduxit? Nonne Moses coturnices aduolare fecit? Nonne Helias verbo coelum clausit? Nonne Mosi Deus locutus est? Nonne & cum Helia versatus est? Nonne Moses mare diuisit, & transduxit populum? Nonne Helias curru igneo in coelum sublatus est? An nocuit huic virginitas, an impedimento fuerunt illi uxor & liberi? Vidisti Heliam aurigam in aere, vidisti Mosen in mari viatorem: Vide & Petrum ecclesiae columnam, quod & ipse habuit uxorem. At non est scriptum, inquit, quod Petrus habuit uxorem: Vide ergo liquet, quod uxorem habuit? Ego dico. Ingressus est Iesus ad socrum Petri, & erat illa infirma, & tetigit eam: & reliquit eam febris, & stetit & ministrauit. Vides quod & Petrus uxorem habuit. Ubi enim socrus, manifestum quod ibi & mulier. Vides quod & Petrus uxorem habuit, (quod & Clemens lib. 3. Strom. & Ignatius in Epist.ad Philadelp. testantur) ne incules nuptias. Hæc dico, ut ne quis prætexat vel uxorem, vel liberos, vel militiam, vel negociationem, vel opificium, vel seruitutem, vel diuitias, vel paupertatem. Hæc excusatio, hic prætextus, diaboli insidiæ sunt, &c. Hæc ille.
units.tr: honoured it: and do you find fault with marriage, saying that marriage is a hindrance to godliness? For there is no hindrance to godliness in it. Do you want to know that having a wife and children harms nothing? Did not Moses have a wife and children? Was not Elijah a virgin? Did not Moses bring down manna from heaven? Did not Elijah bring down fire from heaven? Did not Moses cause quails to fly in? Did not Elijah shut up the heavens by his word? Did not God speak to Moses? Did he not also converse with Elijah? Did not Moses divide the sea and lead the people across? Was not Elijah taken up into heaven in a chariot of fire? Did virginity harm the one, or did a wife and children hinder the other? You have seen Elijah the charioteer in the air; you have seen Moses the traveller through the sea. Look also at Peter, the pillar of the Church, who likewise had a wife. But, you say, it is not written that Peter had a wife. Is it clear then that he had one? I say it is. Jesus entered the house of Peter's mother-in-law, and she was sick with a fever, and he touched her, and the fever left her, and she rose and served them. You see that Peter too had a wife, for where there is a mother-in-law, there is plainly a wife as well. You see that Peter had a wife (as Clement in the third book of the Stromata and Ignatius in his Epistle to the Philadelphians also bear witness). Do not, then, condemn marriage. I say this so that no one may plead as an excuse a wife, children, military service, trade, craft, slavery, riches or poverty. Such an excuse and such a pretext are the snares of the devil, etc. So he writes.

units.la: 2 Sed diças, quur igitur Apostolus Paulus dicit bonum esse homini sic esse, id est, manere in caelibatu, & abstinere à coniugio? Causam ipsemet adjicit, cur in suis hortationibus in caelibatum inclinet, ne videatur alterum statum alteri per se anteponere, & non propter consequentiam: dicitque multas molestias coniugio annexas esse: ideo se cupere omnes à coniugio esse liberos, qui immunes à molestiis esse velint: atque se cupere eos quàm maximè leuare cruce, & optare eos calamitatum esse expertes. Dicit ergo bonum (hoc est, commodum) esse in caelibatu manere, non propter status excellentiam, seu dignitatem aliquam virginitatis, aut propter ingens meritum (ut frustra iactant monachi, quod solæ virgines sint sponsæ Christi, quibus specialis aureola in cœlo debeatur) sed propter præsentem vel instantem necessitatem, & afflictionem in carne. Neque de suturo seculo hoc dicit bonum esse (in quo nō est ista necesitas) sed de præsenti. Porrò sunt qui necessitatem referant ad Apostoli seculum, quod certè pijs turbulentissimum fuit. Alij ad coniugij onera, partus, mœrores, educationes liberorum, curas & molestias, item & orbitates, &c. Sed videtur designare potius voluisse, inquietudinem, qua sancti perpetuò in præsenti vita iactantur, atque ita ad omnia secula extenditur: ut sensus sit, sanctos susque deq; versari sæpius in terra, & multis varijsque procellis esse obnoxiis os:ut minimè ad coniugium apposita esse vi deatur eorum conditio. Nam in urgentibus difficultatibus crucis cælebs expeditior est, quàm coniugatus. Per tribulationem vero seu afflictionem intelligit Apostolus matrimonij onera (de quibus etiam nonnulla Magnus Basilius scripsit in epistola ad S. Gregorium Theologum:) & nomine carnis externum hominem, & humanæ vitæ rationem. Faciunt autem hæ molestiæ coniugij ad nostram superbiam frangendam, & sunt pœnæ peccati admissi per Adamum, & aliorum peccatorum: non tamen sunt pœnæ matrimonij. Nam si puniretur, citra controversiam peccatum esset: quod tamen scriptura ut bonum & venerandum prædicat. Matrimonium ergo si molestias habet, id non suo, sed nostro vitio accidit. Si quis tamen cupit ut tristis aqua suarum molestiarum & necessitatum, vertatur in optimum exhilarans vinum admirandæ benedictionis Dei, hic ad nuptias suas invitet Christum. i. in fide & invocatione Dei contrahat matrimonium, parentum & amicorum consilio: defectum vini & omnes necessitates, Christo indicet: faciat quod iusserit in sua vocatione: & horam suæ benedictionis & auxilij patienter expectet, Ioan. z.
units.tr: 2 But you may ask: why then does the Apostle Paul say that it is good for a man to remain as he is, that is, to remain unmarried and to abstain from marriage? He himself adds the reason why in his exhortations he inclines toward the single state: lest it seem that he sets one state above the other for its own sake, and not on account of the consequences. He says that marriage brings many troubles, and therefore he wishes that all who want to be free from troubles were free from marriage; and he wishes to relieve them as much as possible of the cross, and desires that they be free of calamities. He therefore says that it is good (that is, advantageous) to remain unmarried, not because of any excellence of the state or any dignity of virginity, nor on account of great merit (as the monks vainly boast, that only virgins are the brides of Christ, to whom a special crown in heaven is owed), but on account of the present or imminent necessity and affliction in the flesh. Nor does he say this is good with regard to the future age (in which there is no such necessity), but with regard to the present. Moreover, there are those who refer the necessity to the age of the Apostle, which was certainly most turbulent for the godly. Others refer it to the burdens of marriage: childbirth, sorrows, the upbringing of children, cares and troubles, and likewise bereavements, etc. But it seems he meant rather to point to the restlessness by which the saints are constantly tossed about in the present life, and which thus extends to all ages; so that the sense is that the saints often live in a stormy way on earth and are exposed to many and various tempests, so that their condition does not seem to be suited to marriage. For under the pressing difficulties of the cross, the unmarried man is freer than the married. By tribulation or affliction, however, the Apostle understands the burdens of marriage (of which Basil the Great also wrote some things in his letter to Gregory the Theologian), and by the term flesh he means the outward man and the manner of human life. These troubles of marriage serve to break our pride, and they are punishments for the sin committed through Adam and for other sins; yet they are not punishments of marriage itself. For if marriage were punished, it would beyond doubt be a sin, which Scripture nevertheless proclaims as good and honourable. If marriage therefore has troubles, this comes about not through its own fault but through ours. Yet if anyone wishes that the bitter water of his troubles and needs be turned into the best wine, which gladdens with the wonderful blessing of God, let him invite Christ to his wedding, that is, let him contract marriage in faith and in the invocation of God, with the counsel of parents and friends; let him make known to Christ the lack of wine and all his needs; let him do what he commands in his calling; and let him patiently await the hour of his blessing and help. John 2.

units.la: ʒ[?] Quomodo autem coniuges se gerere debeant, neque hi solum, sed & cæteri, qui res humanas in hoc sæculo tractant, docet Paulus partim his verbis: Deuinctus es uxore, ne quære solutionem: Quod enim Deus conjunxit (dicit Christus Matt.19.) homo non separet: part m, quum inquit: Fratres, Tempus angustum est, seu contractum, a simile tempori vespertino, quo dies ad noctem vergit: restat, ut & qui uxores habent, perinde sint, ac si non habeant, &c. Breuiter enim hic nos monere vult, ne mundum sic diligamus, neque ijs quæ in mundo sunt ita adhæreamus, ut nobis impedimento sint, quo minus ad cœnam magnā, de qua Luc.14 veniamus, regnumque Dei quæramus. Fluxa enim & umbræ similes sunt omnia, & indigna quibus nimium hæreatur: nihil est in hoc mundo firmi aut solidi. Est nanque facies tantum, σχῆμα[?], vel externa apparentia, ut loquuntur, vel quædam species, non res ipsa, non solida veritas. Et ea ipsa species instabilis ac cito periens est. <bl>Es ist alles[?]</bl> <bl>nur ein vbergang in der Welt.</bl> Præterit enim (vel seducit, ut Stapulensis hic μεταγ[?] vertit) figura & habitus huius mundi: in quo ea quæ vel bona videtur vel mala, nec verè bona vel mala, nec diuturna sunt, sed umbratilia & trânsitoria. Laudatur Philippus rex Macedonum quod non insolenter gestierit ob rerum successum, sed fortunæ indulgentiam suspectam habuerit. Cum n[?] illi nuncium effet allatum, uno die multas res feliciter ac prosperè gestas esse: nam eodem tempore Tethrippo vicerat in Olympijs, & Parmenio[?] Dardanenses prælio fuderat, & Olympias ipsi masculum fœtum erat enixa: porrectis in cælum manibus. bus exclamauit: Et ô fortuna,inquit,pro tot[?] tantisq; bonis leui quopiam malo me affice. Nolimus ergo rebus fluxis & caducis hærere, sed quæramus cœlestia & æterna. Præclarè inquit Augustin. Tra. 40. in Ioan. Vtere mundo,non te capiat mundus. Quod intras-ti, iter agis: exiturus venisti, non remansurus. Iter agis, stabulum (vel diuersorium) est hæc vita. Vtere numimo[?] (vel mundo) quomodo viator in diuersorio vtitur, mensa,calice,vrceo,lectulo,dimissurus, non permansurus.
units.tr: Paul teaches how spouses ought to conduct themselves, and not only they but all who deal with worldly affairs in this age, partly in these words: "Are you bound to a wife? Do not seek a release" (1 Cor. 7). For, as Christ says (Matt. 19), "What God has joined together, let not man put asunder." Partly, when he says: "Brothers, the time is short, or shortened, like the evening hour when the day draws toward night; it remains that those who have wives be as though they had none," and so on. For here he briefly wants to warn us not to love the world so much, nor to cling to the things that are in the world in such a way that they hinder us from coming to the great supper, of which we read in Luke 14, and from seeking the kingdom of God. For all things are fleeting and like shadows, and unworthy to be clung to too much: there is nothing firm or solid in this world. There is only the appearance, the outward show, as they say, or a certain semblance, not the thing itself, not solid truth. And that very semblance is unstable and quickly perishes. <bl>Everything is</bl> <bl>only a passing in the world.</bl> For the form and fashion of this world passes away (or, as Stapulensis here translates the Greek, "leads astray"), in which those things that seem either good or bad, are neither truly good nor bad, nor lasting, but shadowy and transitory. King Philip of Macedon is praised because, when the success of his affairs was reported, he did not exult immoderately but regarded the indulgence of fortune with suspicion. For on one day, he was told, many things had gone well and prosperously for him: on the same day his racehorse had won at the Olympic games, and Parmenio had routed the Dardanians in battle, and Olympias had given birth to a son. Lifting his hands to heaven, he exclaimed: "O Fortune, for so many and such great blessings, afflict me with some small misfortune." Let us therefore not cling to fleeting and perishing things, but seek heavenly and eternal ones. Augustine rightly says in Tractate 40 on John: "Use the world, do not let the world hold you. You have entered, you are on a journey; you came to leave, not to remain. You are on a journey; this life is an inn (or lodging). Use the world as a traveler uses an inn: the table, the cup, the pitcher, the couch, intending to leave, not to stay."

units.la: Sed quæras, qui habentes vxores, sint tanquam non habentes? Iuxta Augustinum sunt illi, qui habentes vxores, reddunt & nō exigunt debitum: qui propter infirmitatem proprias ducunt vxores, plangentes potius, quòd sine vxoribus esse non possunt, quàm gaudentes quòd duxerint: qui pari consensu continentiam seruant. Iuxta Theophylactum, qui non omne studium circa nuptias & vxores consumunt. Secundum Ambrosium, qui ad generandum non sunt soliciti, neque ad visum ipsum vxoris deditì.i.plus æquo propensi. Iuxta Erasmum in 3. lib. de Rat. concion. illi, qui non sic sunt vxorij, vt studium pietatis voluptatis gratia negligât. Secundum Flacium Illyric. moderatè & castè ac in timore Dei vtentes, non toti in eas voluptates immersi aut effusi. contrarium est quod dicit Christus·Ement,nubent,vendent,&c. id est, toti addicti erunt illis rebus. Secundum alios illi, qui vxores neglectim habet, perinde quasi eas statim essent amissuri vel, qui non ponunt in re vxoria summam felicitatem, adeo vt Dei obliuiscantur, & abiiciant curam æternæ salutis: sed sciunt hæc quoque rem, vt alias, non esse perpetuam, sed temporaneam, & vna cum habitu mundi præterire.
units.tr: But you may ask, who are those who have wives and yet are as though they had none? According to Augustine, they are those who, having wives, render the debt and do not demand it; those who, because of weakness, take wives, lamenting rather that they cannot be without wives than rejoicing that they have married; those who by mutual consent keep continence. According to Theophylact, those who do not spend all their zeal on marriage and wives. According to Ambrose, those who are not anxious about begetting children, nor given over to the mere sight of the wife, that is, inclined more than is fitting. According to Erasmus, in the third book of his Ratio concionandi, those who are not so fond of their wives that they neglect the pursuit of piety for the sake of pleasure. According to Flacius Illyricus, those who use them moderately and chastely and in the fear of God, not wholly immersed or poured out into those pleasures. The opposite is what Christ says: "They marry, they give in marriage, they buy, they sell," etc., that is, they will be wholly devoted to those things. According to others, those who hold their wives carelessly, as though they were about to lose them at once, or who do not place the highest happiness in matrimony, so that they forget God and cast aside care for eternal salvation: but they know that this thing too, like others, is not perpetual but temporary, and passes away together with the fashion of the world.

units.la: Deniq; illi qui vxorores suas non amant supra Christum, neque sinunt se ab illis in profesione euangelij impediri, propter quod etiam parati sunt illas, iuxta Christi regulá, odisse, ac relinquere, si opus sit. Vt vero & nos velimus ac valeamus Christi causa & euangelij, relinquere non solum vxores & liberos, sed etiam parentes, fratres, sorores, domos, aut agros & omnia, quo tandem etiam vitæ æternæ cum Apostolis electis ac sanctis (Matthæi 19. ) sortiamur hæreditatem, largiatur nobis Deus pater spiritum sanctum per Christum Iesum Dominum nostrum, Amen.
units.tr: Finally, those who do not love their wives above Christ, and do not allow themselves to be hindered from professing the gospel by them, for which reason they are also prepared, according to the rule of Christ, to hate and leave them if need be. And that we too may wish and be able, for the sake of Christ and the gospel, to leave not only wives and children, but also parents, brothers, sisters, houses, fields and all things, so that at last we may obtain with the chosen and holy Apostles (Matt. 19) the inheritance of eternal life, may God the Father grant us the Holy Spirit through Christ Jesus our Lord, Amen.

units.la: CONCIO LI.
units.tr: SERMON LI.

units.la: 1. Corinth. 7.
units.tr: 1 Corinthians 7.

units.la: XOR alligata est matrimonio, quamdiu viuit maritus eius: quòd si dormierit maritus illius, libera est ad cui velit nubere, modò in Domino. Attamen beatior est, si sic maneat, iuxta meam sententiam. Opinor autem quod & ipse spiritum Dei habeam.
units.tr: A wife is bound to marriage for as long as her husband lives; but if her husband has died, she is free to marry whomever she wishes, only in the Lord. Yet she is happier if she remains so, in my judgement. And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.

units.la: 1 De conditione mulieris in matrimonio constitutae primum hic loquitur Apostolus: & licet[?] talem non esse liberam, sed alligatam legi, hoc est, contineri lege de adulterio, cauenti ne adultera fiat, si alteri viro copulatur viuente marito, Rom.7. Iam enim desiit sui[?] iuris esse, sed marito sese astrinxit foedere coniugij, donec ille vixerit. Sola mors dirimit hanc necessitudinem. Quisquis enim init matrimonium, hoc init animo, vt sit indiuulsa copula. Hinc non dicit, Vxor alligata est legi, scilicet viri, hoc est, matrimonio, quamdiu tempore fanus vel iuuenis est, vel domi versatur: sed, quanto tempore viuit maritus eius. Debet ergo coniugij vinculum durare vsque ad mortem alterius partis.
units.tr: Here the Apostle first speaks of the condition of a woman who has been placed in marriage. Although she is not free but bound, that is, held by the law against adultery, which forbids her to become an adulteress by joining herself to another man while her husband is alive (Rom. 7). For she has ceased to be her own mistress, and has bound herself to her husband by the covenant of marriage, for as long as he lives. Only death dissolves this bond. Whoever enters marriage does so intending that the union be unbroken. Hence he does not say, "A wife is bound by the law," that is, by the law of her husband, that is, by marriage, for as long as he is healthy or young or at home; but "for as long as her husband lives." The bond of marriage ought therefore to last until the death of one of the partners.

units.la: Alligata potest etiam dici vxor, quia sub potestate viri est, I.Cor. II. Satius autem est honesto coniugij vinculo stringi, quàm implicari non solùm scortatorum, sed & satanæ laqueis.
units.tr: A wife may also be called "bound" because she is under the power of her husband (1 Cor. 11). It is better, however, to be bound by the honourable bond of marriage than to be entangled not only in the snares of whoremongers but also in those of Satan.

units.la: Porrò si mulier lege obstricta est, quamdiu viuit eius vir: non debet illa quærere diuortium, nec à viro separari[?], vt nec vir ab vxore. Esset enim hoc, dirumpere vinculum, quo colligari & coniungi sunt: id quod tum postissimè fit, quando mulier viuente viro, se alteri innigit. Hoc facere volu t vxor Potipharis.Gen.39. Quam nullo modo debent imitari Christianæ sœminæ, sed potius castam Sufannam, Dan. 13. Sed & viri ab adulterio necesse habent abstinere[?], nisi velint iudicari à Domino, Hebr. 13. & à cœlorum regno excludi, 1. Corinth. 6. Galat. 5. & manifesti fieri cum pudore, Eccles. 23. Si enim Dauidis adulterium est patefactum (nihil enim est tectum, quod non sit retegendum[?]: & nihil occultum, quin futurum sit vt sciatur[?], Matt. 10.) quid nisi etiam aliorū stupra & adulteria manifesta fierent?
units.tr: Furthermore, if a woman is bound by law as long as her husband lives, she ought not to seek a divorce, nor to separate herself from her husband, and neither should a husband separate from his wife. For that would be to break the bond by which they were joined and united; and this happens above all when a woman, while her husband lives, gives herself to another. This is what Potiphar's wife wished to do (Gen. 39). Christian women must in no way imitate her, but rather the chaste Susanna (Dan. 13). Husbands too must necessarily abstain from adultery, unless they wish to be judged by the Lord (Heb. 13), to be excluded from the kingdom of heaven (1 Cor. 6; Gal. 5), and to be made manifest with shame (Ecclus 23). For if David's adultery was made known (for nothing is hidden that will not be uncovered, and nothing secret that will not be known, Matt. 10), what else would the fornications and adulteries of others also be made manifest?

units.la: Quum vero dicit mulierem astrictam viro quandiu vixerit, exceptio est addenda, quam Christus habet, nisi adulterium intervenerit, Matth. 5. nec non ea, quam ipse Paulus indicauit: Si coniux infidelis manere noluerit, 1. Corinth. 7. Meminit autem dissolutionis tantummodo, quae per mortem accidit: quia illa generalior est.
units.tr: When he says that a woman is bound to her husband as long as he lives, an exception must be added, which Christ gives: unless adultery has intervened (Matt. 5); and also the one Paul himself pointed out: if the unbelieving spouse is unwilling to remain (1 Cor. 7). He mentions only dissolution that comes about through death, because that is the more general case.

units.la: 2 Secundò loquitur apostolus de vidua, inquiens: Sin obdormierit vir eius, id est, mortuus fuerit (quemadmodum Rom. 7. aperte dicit, sæpe enim dormire, mori significat: tunc autem non ad animam, sed corpus refertur, Ioan. 11. 1. Corinth. 11. 15.) liberum est ei cui velit nubere, id est quæ sibi aptum putaverit: nulla habita ratione stultæ quæstionis Sadducæorum de vxore & septem fratribus qui omnes habuerunt eam. Matth. 22. Nota bene de qua libertate loquatur. Sunt enim qui verbum Dei peruertunt atque irrident. Libera est, inquit. Sed ad quid? Ad scortandum ne? Minimè gentium. Ad quid igitur? Ad nubendum (ait) cui velit, dummodò in Domino. Argumentum ducit à contrarijs. Nam si ad vitam mariti alligata est mulier, morte ergo soluitur: postquam soluta est, nubat cui velit. Hoc (cui velit) quadrat de viduis, de virginibus non item: Nam illæ sunt adhuc in potestate maiorum. Ambrosius eò refert, ut intelligamus coactas damnari nuptias. Quia (inquit) inuitæ nuptiæ solent malos proventus habere. His ergo verbis apertissimè fecundas nuptias approbat Apostolus aduersus eorum tyrannidem, qui vetuerunt illis interesse clericos. Idem[?] etiam facit, I.Tim. 5. cum inquit, Volo viduas iuniores nubere, &c. Vetus testamentum fecundas nuptias legitimas, altero coniuge mortuo, etiam non damnat, sed approbat. Nam Abrahamus aliam duxit uxorem, nomine Cethuram, Gen.25. & Abigail, Nabal mortuo, nupsit Dauidi, I.Reg.25. De nuptijs non solum fecundis, sed etiam tertijs & pluribus, idem sentiunt Ambrosius in cap.
units.tr: (2) Secondly, the Apostle speaks of a widow, saying: "But if her husband has fallen asleep," that is, has died (as Rom. 7 says plainly; for to sleep often means to die; and this refers to the body, not the soul, John 11; 1 Cor. 11, 15), "she is free to marry whom she wishes," that is, whomever she thinks suitable; with no regard for the foolish question of the Sadducees about the wife and the seven brothers who all had her (Matt. 22). Note well what kind of freedom he means. For there are those who pervert and mock the Word of God. "She is free," he says. But free for what? For whoring? By no means. For what then? "To marry," he says, "whomever she wishes, provided it is in the Lord." He argues from the opposite. For if a woman is bound during her husband's life, then she is released by his death; once released, let her marry whom she wishes. The phrase "whom she wishes" fits widows, but not virgins, for these are still under the authority of their elders. Ambrose refers this to show that marriages which are forced are to be condemned, because (he says) unwilling marriages tend to have bad outcomes. Therefore by these words the Apostle most clearly approves second marriages, against the tyranny of those who forbade clergy to attend them. He does the same in 1 Tim. 5, when he says, "I want younger widows to marry," etc. The Old Testament does not condemn second lawful marriages after the death of one spouse, but approves them. For Abraham took another wife, named Keturah (Gen. 25), and Abigail, after Nabal died, married David (1 Sam. 25). The same view, concerning marriages not only second but also third and more, is held by Ambrose on 1 Tim. 3; Epiphanius, book 2, vol. 1, heresy 59; Jerome in his letter to Marcellinus, and in the books against Jovinian; and Lombard, book 4, distinction 42.

units.la: 3. Epist. ad Tim. Epiphanius lib. 2. Tom. 1. Hæresi 59. Hieronymus in Epist. ad Marcellinum: & pro libris aduersus Iouianū. Lombardus lib. 4 Dist. 42. Sed quid est, quod addit, Modò in Domino? Hoc quidam intelligunt de coniugio pari, ubi fit utrinque religio eadem, hoc est, ut maritus incredula uxore liberatus, fidelem ducat, & uxor fidelis, ex experta prius, quifit[?] impio nexam esse, abhorreat ab impijs: pio vero nubat viro: q.d. Paulus: Modo fit Christianum coniugium, hoc est, ne turpitudinis gratia affectatum, & cū ejusdem religionis viro contractum. Quæ enim pars fideli cum infideli[?] 2. Corinth. 6.
units.tr: But what does he mean by adding "only in the Lord"? Some understand this of a marriage between equals, where both have the same religion; that is, that a husband who has been freed from an unbelieving wife should take a believing one, and a believing wife, having previously learned by experience that she was bound to an impious husband, should shrink from the impious and marry a pious man. As if Paul were saying: let Christian marriage now be made, that is, not sought for the sake of lust, and contracted with a man of the same religion. For "what fellowship has a believer with an unbeliever?" (2 Cor. 6).

units.la: Nonnulli tamen latius patere judicant, nempe ut religiosè & cum timore Domini id faciant, & secundum ejus præscriptum in nomine Domini Iesu, Colos. 3. in gloriam Dei, 1. Corinth. 10. non extra Dominum aut contra Dominum, sed consulto Domino & invocato nomine ejus. Sic enim auspicato matrimonia contrahuntur. Non igitur moveantur ut equus & mulus effrænata libidine, sed adsit verecundia & modestia Christianis digna. Nam qui Deum à se & à sua mente excludunt, super eos dæmon habet potestatem, Tob. 6. Et quoniam matrimonium est non solùm legitima, seu licita ex ordine & instituto Dei, sed etiam perpetua ac insolubilis, duorum maris scilicet & fœminæ, studio gignendæ sobolis, & vitandæ fornicationis, conjunctio seu copulatio in carnem unam: non temerè & absque consilio ac deliberatione ineundum est. Quoniam, ut habet Mimus Publianus: Deliberandum est diu, quod statuendum est semel:
units.tr: Some, however, judge that the phrase extends more widely, namely that they should do this religiously and with the fear of the Lord, and according to his command in the name of the Lord Jesus (Col. 3), to the glory of God (1 Cor. 10), not outside the Lord or against the Lord, but with the Lord consulted and his name invoked. For marriages are entered upon thus under good auspices. They should therefore not be moved like a horse or mule by unbridled lust, but Christian modesty and decency should be present. For those who exclude God from themselves and from their minds, the demon has power over them (Tob. 6). And since marriage is not only a lawful union, licit by the order and institution of God, but also perpetual and indissoluble, the conjunction or coupling of a male and a female into one flesh, for the purpose of begetting offspring and avoiding fornication, it must not be entered upon rashly and without counsel and deliberation. As the mime-writer Publilius has it: what is to be decided once must be deliberated on for a long time.

units.la: <bl>Dann vorgethan/und erst darnach betracht/ Hat manchen in groß leiden gebracht.</bl>
units.tr: Who acts first and thinks afterward has brought many into great suffering.

units.la: ȝ[?] Tertiò ostendit Paulus, utrum melius & commodius sit in viduitate permanere, vel iterum matrimonium contrahere. Felicior est, inquit, (non coram Deo, sed in hac vita, id est, non sanctior erit, sed commodius habebit)fi sic manserit (& donū castitatis hābuerit:de hujusmodi enim intelligendū est) mea quidem sententia. i. juxta meum judicium: quantum ego intelligere possum: Hoc dicit, ne rem istam necessitatem arbitreris, sed consilium: divinum tamen. Quia addit: videor autem ego quoque mihi habere Dei spiritum. Magnæ id humiliationis argumentum est. Non dixit: Habeo,sed δοκῶ[?],id est,puto, seu arbitror sive existimo. Iuxta quosdam non videtur ironia carere, quod dicit: Existimo,seu opinor. Nam quum Pseudoapostoli spiritu Domini inflatis buccis identidem jactarent, ad authoritatem sibi arrogandam, & interea Paulo detrahere studerent, dicit se quoque sibi videri compotem Spiritus non minus quàm ipsos. q. d. Non minus de spiritu Dei, & forsan aliquanto verius gloriari possum, quàm isti, quos tantopere suspicitis.
units.tr: (3) Thirdly, Paul shows whether it is better and more advantageous for a widow to remain as she is or to contract marriage again. "She is happier," he says (not before God, but in this life; that is, she will not be holier, but will have it more conveniently), "if she remains so" (and has the gift of chastity; for it is of such a person that this must be understood), "in my opinion," that is, according to my judgement, as far as I can understand. He says this so that you will not think the matter a necessity, but a counsel, yet a divine one. For he adds: "I think that I too have the Spirit of God." This is a sign of great humility. He did not say "I have," but dokō, that is, I think, or suppose, or judge. Some hold that the phrase "I suppose, or think" is not without irony. For when the false apostles were boasting, with puffed-up cheeks, of the Spirit of the Lord, in order to claim authority for themselves while trying at the same time to disparage Paul, he says that he too seems to himself to possess the Spirit no less than they do. As if he were saying: I can boast no less, and perhaps somewhat more truly, of the Spirit of God than those whom you so greatly admire.

units.la: Permittit igitur Apostolus fecundas nuptias, contra spiritus impostores (qui concilio quodam mandarunt sacerdotibus, ut nec benedicant secundas nuptias, hæc ad prædia illarum vocari se sinant, ut citat Musculus) testaturque eas non tantùm licitas esse, sed etiam fieri in Domino, inque ejus timore, favore, ac etiam comprobatione & benedictione. Veruntamen beatiorem eam judicat, quæ in viduo statu permanet, & studio vacandi Christo tuetur redditam libertate: non quia viduitas per se fit virtus: sed quia pauciores habet molestias in cælibatu, quàm in conjugio. Etenim quæ nupserit, & subdita est viro, multis curis domesticis implicatur. Quemadmodū ergo primis nuptiis ob hac causam præfertur virginitas, sic secundis primæ sunt potiores, quod extra matrimonium minus curarum & afflictionum fit devorandum, quàm in eo.
units.tr: The Apostle therefore permits second marriages, against the deceitful spirits (who, by a certain council, ordered priests neither to bless second marriages nor to allow themselves to be summoned to the estates of such women, as Musculus cites), and he testifies that such marriages are not only lawful but also take place in the Lord, in his fear, with his favour, and even with his approval and blessing. Yet he judges her happier who remains in the state of widowhood and, freed by that liberty, keeps herself devoted to the Lord's service; not because widowhood is in itself a virtue, but because it has fewer troubles in celibacy than in marriage. For she who marries and is subject to her husband is entangled in many domestic cares. Just as, therefore, virginity is preferred to first marriage for this reason, so the first state is preferable to second marriages, because outside matrimony less care and affliction must be endured than within it.

units.la: Hinc & Apostoli dicunt Christo: Si ad istum modum habet causa hominis cum uxore, non expedit contrahere matrimonium: & hic illis, Qui potest (inquit) capere capiat. Est enim & hoc magnum commodum cælibatus præconjugio (quemadmodum ipse Apostolus versu 32[?]. huius capitis exponit:) quod cælibes possunt liberius vacare cultui ac religioni divinæ (præsertim si sint in aliquo publico ministerio) quàm conjuges, qui domesticis curis ac occupationibus distrahuntur.
units.tr: Hence the Apostles also said to Christ: "If the case of a man with his wife is like this, it is not expedient to marry." And he answered them: "He who can receive it, let him receive it." For remaining single before marriage has this great advantage (as the Apostle himself explains in verse 32[?] of this chapter), that the unmarried can more freely devote themselves to the worship and service of God (especially if they hold some public ministry) than married people, who are pulled apart by domestic cares and occupations.

units.la: Taceo nunc quod manere in viduitate & maioris castitatis indicium, & maioris amoris signum ad primum virum sit. Unde Bernardus ait: Pudeat ad negocium honestum rationem non posse in homine, quod natura potest in volucre, nimirum in turture. Et Portia Minor, quum laudaretur apud eam mulier quædam ut bene morata, quæ tamen iterarat matrimonium: Felix, inquit, ac pudica matrona non nubit nisi semel.
units.tr: I say nothing now of the fact that remaining in widowhood is a sign of greater chastity and a sign of greater love toward the first husband. Hence Bernard says: "Shame on a man, that in an honourable matter reason cannot do in him what nature can do in a bird, namely in the turtle-dove." And Porcia the Younger, when a certain woman was praised in her presence as well-behaved, though she had married a second time, said: "A happy and chaste matron marries only once."

units.la: Non passa est illam inter bene moratas numerari, quæ citra necessitatem ascisceret alterum virum. Nam multas huc cogit egestas Porrò coitus gratia nubere, non est verè pudicarum. Eoque dixit Felix, excusans necessitatem. Rursum Hieronymus refert, quòd cùm Valeria vidua rogaretur secundum virum accipere, respondit se hoc non posse facere: quia vir suus adhuc viveret: quibus admirantibus dixit: Quandiu vixero, vir meus (Servius) per amorem semper vivet in corde meo. Sed & Annia, propinquis admonentibus ut alteri nuberet: esse enim illi & ætatem integram, & faciem bonam, quorum alterum spem faceret prolis, alterum promitteret amorem mutuum: Nequaquam, inquit, hoc faciam. Si enim bonum virum nactus fuero, nolo timere ne perdam: sin malum, quid necesse est, post optimum perpeti pessimum. Item Martia Catonis filia minor, rogata quur à morte mariti nollet iterum nubere: Quoniam, inquit, non invenio virū, qui me magis velit, quàm mea. Non probavit conjugium, quod non conciliaret amor mutuus. Quæ ducitur dotis causa, conductum habet concubinum verius quàm conjugem.
units.tr: She did not allow that woman to be counted among the well-behaved, who without necessity took on another husband. For want compels many to this; but to marry for the sake of intercourse is not characteristic of truly chaste women. So Felix said it, excusing necessity. Again, Jerome reports that when the widow Valeria was asked to take a second husband, she replied that she could not do this, because her husband was still alive. When people marvelled, she said: "As long as I live, my husband (Servius) will always live in my heart through love." But also Annia, when her relatives urged her to marry another (for she had both full youth and a good face, the one of which would hold out hope of offspring, the other promise mutual love), said: "Certainly not, I will not do this. For if I find a good husband, I do not want to fear losing him; but if a bad one, why is it necessary to suffer the worst after the best?" Likewise Martia, the younger daughter of Cato, when asked why she did not want to marry again after her husband's death, said: "Because I do not find a man who would love me more than mine did." She did not approve of a marriage that was not built on mutual love. She who is led into marriage for the sake of a dowry has a hired concubine rather than a wife.

units.la: Eadem quum diutius lugeret maritum, rogata, quem esset habitura diem luctus[?] ultimum: respondit: Quem & vitæ.
units.tr: The same woman, when she mourned her husband for a long time, was asked which day she would have as the last day of her mourning. She answered: "The one that is also the last day of my life."

units.la: Sic illa ethnica, magno sanè cum dedecore plurimarum Christianarum, quæ viro non dum elato jam nupserunt. Sed unusquisque proprium donum habet ex Deo, alius quidem sic, alius autem sic. Idem Deus unicuique det sua dona ad id quod expediat, per Christum Iesum Dominum nostrum, Amen.
units.tr: Thus that heathen woman, to the great disgrace of many Christian women, who have married again before their husband was even carried out. But "each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that" (1 Cor. 7.). "May the same God give to each his gifts as is fitting, through Christ Jesus our Lord, Amen."

units.la: CONCIO LII.
units.tr: SERMON LII.

units.la: Ephes. 5.
units.tr: Ephes. 5.

units.la: Uxores propriis viris subditae sint, veluti Domino, quoniam vir est caput uxoris, quemadmodum & Christus est caput Ecclesiae: & idem est, qui salutem dat corpori. Itaque quemadmodum Ecclesia subdita est Christo, sic uxores suis viris subditae sint in omnibus. Viri diligite uxores vestras, sicut & Christus dilexit Ecclesiam, & semetipsum exposuit pro ea, ut illam sanctificaret, mundatam lavacro aquae per verbum, ut adhiberet eam sibi ipsi gloriosam Ecclesiam, non habentem maculam, aut rugam, aut quicquam eiusmodi, sed ut esset sancta & irreprehensibilis. Sic debent viri diligere suas uxores, ut sua ipsorum corpora. Qui diligit suam uxorem, seipsum diligit. Nullus enim unquam suam ipsius carnem odio habuit, imo enutrit ac fovet eam, sicut & Dominus Ecclesiam. Quoniam membra sumus corporis ejusdem,
units.tr: Wives, submit yourselves to your own husbands, as to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife, as Christ is the head of the Church, and he is the Saviour of the body. Therefore, just as the Church is subject to Christ, so let wives be subject to their husbands in everything. Husbands, love your wives, as Christ also loved the Church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water with the word, so that he might present the Church to himself in glory, without spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she might be holy and blameless. In the same way husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. For no one has ever hated his own flesh, but rather he nourishes and cherishes it, just as the Lord does the Church. For we are members of his body,

units.la: ex carne ejus & ex ossibus ejus. Hujus rei gratia, relinquet homo patrem ac matrem & adjungetur uxori sua, atq; e duo bus fiet una caro . Mysterium hoc magnum est, verum ego loquor de Christo & de ecclesia. Quanquam & vos singulatim hoc praestate, ut suam quisq; uxorem diligat tanquam seipsum: uxor autem ut revereatur virum.
units.tr: of his flesh and of his bones. For this cause a man shall leave father and mother and shall be joined to his wife, and the two shall become one flesh. This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and the Church. Nevertheless, let each one of you also love his own wife as himself, and let the wife see that she respects her husband.

units.la: I Paulus instituturus varia officia Christianorum, atq; post praecepta in genere ad omnes & erga omnes pertinentia, traditurus œconomica praecepta domesticarum personarum, erga se mutuò: haud temerè primum instituit Christianum matrimonium. Rectius enim atque melius habebunt etiam reliqua officia, si rectè institutum sit conjugium. Iuventus enim Reipubl. seges est.
units.tr: Paul, about to set out the various duties of Christians, and after giving general precepts applying to all people and toward all people, and about to deliver the household rules for the members of a household toward one another, rightly begins first with Christian marriage. For the remaining duties will also turn out better and more rightly ordered if marriage is rightly instituted. The youth of the commonwealth is the seed-crop of the state.

units.la: At si grando aut alia quaedam calamitas segetem corrumpat, mesis nulla fuerit spes reliqua. Et si recte instituantur adolescentuli & pueri, rectius per omnes aetatum austus[?] habebunt. Sed quid saperent aut discerent liberi in male instituto conjugio? Malè institutū conjugium est, in quo rixis & verberibus certatur de imperio, in quo nulla partium suum facit officium, in quo deest timor Dei, nullaq; certa ratio rerum gerendarū habetur. Ita enim animo & corpore perçeunt miseri, perdunt & liberos. Sequitur inopia malesuada, fraus, mendacium, & omnis iniquitas: deniq; & extremum supplicium desperatio.
units.tr: But if hail or some other calamity destroys the crop, there is no hope of a harvest left. And if young men and boys are rightly brought up, they will turn out better through every stage of life. But what could children learn or become in a badly ordered marriage? A marriage is badly ordered when there is quarrelling and beating over who rules, when neither party performs its duty, when the fear of God is absent, and when no sound plan for managing affairs is kept. For in such a case the wretched people are ruined in mind and body, and they lose their children too. There follows wretched poverty, fraud, lying, and every kind of wickedness, and finally the last punishment, despair.

units.la: Proinde ut tanta mala e domo propelleret Christiana Paulus, diligenter instituit matrimonium. Non autem melius hoc institui potuit, quàm si coformetur conjunctioni Christi & ejus Ecclesiae, hoc est, mirando illi foedeři, quo Deus sibi Ecclesiam copulavit, & summo ac inenarrabili amori divino erga sponsam Ecclesiam:cujus foederis imago & commonefactio est maris & foeminae corporalis conjunctio in hac vita.
units.tr: Therefore, so that Paul might drive such great evils out of the Christian household, he set out marriage with care. Yet it could not have been set out better than by conforming it to the union of Christ and his Church, that is, to that wonderful covenant by which God joined the Church to himself, and to the supreme and inexpressible divine love toward the bride, the Church. The bodily union of male and female in this life is an image and reminder of this covenant.

units.la: Quemadmodum namque maritus indiffolubili vinculo amoris uxori astringitur, adeo ut & fecunda & adversa omnia communia habeant: sic & Christus Ecclesiae suae copulatus est, dum illius poenam pro peccatis meritam in sua carne dependit, & dum ipse unicus & naturalis haeres Patris sui nos aeterni gaudii cohaeredes facit. Unde hoc! o Paulus: τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν, ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω [?]εἰς Χριστὸν καὶ εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν[?]. Quae exclamatio innuit non posse verbis explicari, quàm magna & admirabilis sit spiritualis Christi & ecclesiae conjunctio. Notandum vero obiter hic errore veteris versionis deceptos sophistas, quae vocem mysterium (qua Apostolus & alibi usus est, ut Ephes.5. 2.Thessal.2. 1.Tim. 3.) vertit sacramentum, statuisse matrimonium esse unum ex septem sacramentis.
units.tr: For just as a husband is bound to his wife by the indissoluble bond of love, so that they share all things, both prosperous and adverse, so also Christ is joined to his Church, while he bears in his own flesh the punishment she deserved for her sins, and while he, as the only and natural heir of his Father, makes us co-heirs of eternal joy. Whence this exclamation, O Paul: "This mystery is great, but I speak concerning Christ and the Church" [τὸ μυστήριον τοῦτο μέγα ἐστίν, ἐγὼ δὲ λέγω εἰς Χριστὸν καὶ εἰς τὴν ἐκκλησίαν]. This exclamation implies that it cannot be explained in words how great and admirable is the spiritual union of Christ and the Church. It should be noted in passing that the sophists, deceived by the error of the old version, which rendered the word mystery (which the Apostle also uses elsewhere, as in Eph. 5, 2 Thess. 2, 1 Tim. 3) as sacrament, have held that marriage is one of the seven sacraments.

units.la: Tot enim enumerant, quum duo Christus duntaxat instituerit. Sed contrà nec vetust{1}[?] patres, ut Hieronymus, Augustinus, aut etiam Dionysius, sic conjugium vocant: nec usquam legitur in novo Testamento, matrimonium esse sacramentum. Vide, si placet, Erafmi verba in Annot. & Augustinum in Tract. 9. super Ioannem. Deinde non convenit ei definitio aut proprium sacramenti, quod per id nobis remissio peccatorum, aut reconciliatio cum Deo repraesentetur ac offeratur. Est quoque matrimonium commune & Iudaeis & Gentibus, inde à condito mundo, ut & ipsorum sacramentum esset. Praeterea non vident isti caeci duces (decepti vel ambigua significatione nominis, vel potius ignorantia linguae Graecae) se sibimet contradicere, cùm matrimonium habeant pro re carnali & profana. Quin etiam eorum Syricius Papa dicit, matrimonium esse in carne vivere, & neminem in eo Deo placere posse. Vide Distinct. 82. Cùm sit ergo res tam profana & impura, quomodo potest esse sacrosanctum Dei sacramentum, ac solenne gratiae Dei symbolum? Postremò etiam disertè Paulus testatur, se in hoc dicto non de corporali hominum matrimonio, sed de conjunctione Christi & Ecclesiae loqui, sicut & Oecumenius hunc locum exponit. Inquit enim: Ego autem loquor de Christo & ecclesia. Hoc mysterium, seu arcanum, magnum est. Quomodo magnum? Quia quum Christo in propria gloria manere licuisset, seseipsum assumpta humanitate demisit, ut adhæreret ac adjungeretur Ecclesiæ, factiq; sunt duo unus spiritus. Nam qui adglutinatur sive adhæret Domino, unus spiritus est, 1.Corinth.6. Hoc verè magnum mysterium est: quia & magni momenti, & valde a judicio rationis absconditum est. Nam ita conjunctio Christi & Ecclesiæ non est res ficta, nec carnale aliquid, sed spiritualis, & à communi hominum more captuque remotissima conjunctio, & denique magis fide credenda, quàm intellectu percipienda, & nihilominus vera, solida, & planè admiranda.
units.tr: For they count up seven, whereas Christ instituted only two. But on the contrary, the ancient Fathers, such as Jerome, Augustine, and even Dionysius, do not call marriage a sacrament, nor is it anywhere read in the New Testament that marriage is a sacrament. See, if you please, the words of Erasmus in his Annotations, and Augustine in Tractate 9 on John. Furthermore, the definition and the proper character of a sacrament do not fit marriage, since through a sacrament the forgiveness of sins or reconciliation with God is represented and offered to us. Marriage is also common to Jews and Gentiles from the creation of the world, so it would have to be a sacrament of theirs too. Besides, those blind leaders do not see (deceived either by the ambiguous meaning of the word, or rather by ignorance of the Greek language) that they contradict themselves, since they hold marriage to be a carnal and profane matter. Indeed, their own Pope Siricius says that marriage is living in the flesh, and that no one can please God in it. See Distinction 82. Since, then, it is a thing so profane and impure, how can it be the most holy sacrament of God and the solemn symbol of the grace of God? Lastly, Paul himself clearly testifies that in this saying he is not speaking of the bodily marriage of men but of the union of Christ and the Church, as Oecumenius also explains this passage. For he says: "But I speak concerning Christ and the Church." This mystery, or secret, is great. How is it great? Because, although Christ might have remained in his own glory, he humbled himself by taking on humanity, so that he might cling to and be joined to the Church, and the two became one spirit. For he who is joined to the Lord is one spirit, 1 Cor. 6. This is truly a great mystery, because it is of great importance and is very much hidden from the judgment of reason. For the union of Christ and the Church is not a fictitious thing, nor anything carnal, but a spiritual union, most remote from the common custom and understanding of men, and finally something to be believed by faith rather than grasped by the intellect, and nevertheless true, solid, and plainly admirable.

units.la: 2 Quæ sunt igitur officia, quæ Paulus uxoribus præscribit? Iubet subditas esse propriis maritis,juxta Domini præceptum, Gen.3. Sub viri potestate eris, & ipse dominabitur tui. Et hoc generale officium mulierum erga suos maritos omnia alia complectitur . Nam mulieris partes sunt, maritum suum φοβᾶσθαι[?], id est, non servorum more timere, vel ut hostem & carnificem: sed ut uxorem decet, sanctè revereri, non tantùm ut virum, sed etiam ut patrem, præ oculis habere, honorareque illum tanquam caput & principem & patronum suum, ac solicitam esse, ne illum offendat: vel, ut Chrysostomus hunc timorem declarat, ut non contradicat, ut non insurgat contra virum, nec superiorem dignitatem appetat: sed (quemadmodū Musculus exponit) se non primo, sed secundo loco constitutam, propterque illum, nou illum propter se conditam esse agnoscat: deniq; ita revereatur virum suum, quemadmodum lunam videmus revereri solem, in cujus præsentia splendorem suum plurimum contrahit. In absentia viri potestas domus sit penes uxoré, sic tamen ut nihil contra voluntatem illius tentet: in præsentia vero abstineat ab imperio, claudat os, & aperiat aures ad audiendum mariti sui vocem: hujus imperium agnoscat, obediat, & sponte quidem: imò & amet eundem candidè, verè & sinceriter. Arduum enim id est, quod sanctissimum Christi & Ecclesiæ exemplum proponitur, quo non sanctius aliud invenias. Necesse ergo est sanctum quoque sit matrimonium, & amor ejus eximius.
units.tr: 2 What, then, are the duties that Paul prescribes to wives? He bids them be subject to their own husbands, according to the Lord's precept, Gen. 3. "You shall be under your husband's power, and he shall rule over you." This general duty of wives toward their husbands includes all the others. For it is the wife's part to fear [φοβᾶσθαι] her husband, that is, not to fear him in the manner of slaves, or as an enemy and executioner, but to revere him with holy respect, as a wife ought, to keep before her eyes not only him as husband but also as father, to honour him as her head, prince, and protector, and to be careful not to offend him. Or, as Chrysostom explains this fear, she should not contradict him, should not rise up against her husband, nor seek a higher dignity; but (as Musculus expounds it) she should acknowledge that she has been placed not in the first but in the second place, and that she was made on account of him and not he on account of her. Finally, she should revere her husband as we see the moon revere the sun, whose light she greatly lessens in his presence. In his absence, the authority in the house is to rest with the wife, yet in such a way that she attempts nothing against his will; but in his presence she should refrain from command, shut her mouth, and open her ears to hear her husband's voice. She should acknowledge his authority, obey it, and do so willingly. Indeed, she should also love him frankly, truly, and sincerely. For this is a demanding thing, since the most holy example of Christ and the Church is set before her, and you cannot find a more holy one. It is necessary, therefore, that marriage also be holy and its love extraordinary.

units.la: Omnia autem eloquitur Apostolus propriissimis verbis. Uxores, inquit, τοῖς ἰδίοις viris subditæ sitis. Propriis, inquit, significanter. Per hoc enim illud obsequium excludit, quod scortū scortatori, & adultera adultero præstat. Samaritana illa mulier, de qua Joan. 4. quinque viros habuit, sed non suos, i. proprios. Notatur ergo his verbis fides matrimonii, & excluditur scortationis vanitas atque perfidia. Deinde addit, Veluti Domino: non quia sit æqualis authoritas, sed quia mulieres Christo obedire neque unt[?], nisi se obsequentes viris præbendo: &, ne qua arrogantius obijceret: Egon' subderer illi viro? Ideo, Subditæ sitis, ait scientes, quòd serviatis Deo: hoc est, si non propter virum: inprimis, propter Dominum tamen. Nam si exteriori adeoq; mundi potestati resistens, Domini potestati resistit, quanto magis quę marito suo reluctatur? Itaq; è contrario, quę marito obedit, Domino obedit, cultumq; præstat Deo. Illius enim voluntas est, ut viris vestris subditę sitis. In hac ergo appendice tum magnitudo, sinceritasq; subjectionis indicatur, tum etiam probatio aut causa, cur id faciendum sit continetur: quia Dominus ipse mulieri viro subjectam esse præceperit, primùm quidem in creatione mitiore quadam subjectione, postea in pœna peccati duriore. Col. 3. inquit, non multò aliter, Vxores subditæ sint propriis viris, ut convenit in Domino. Potest nihilominus ibi sensus esse, salva ante omnia pietate.
units.tr: The Apostle, moreover, expresses all these things in the most fitting words. "Wives," he says, "be subject to your own [τοῖς ἰδίοις] husbands." He says "own" deliberately. For through this word he excludes the obedience that a prostitute gives to her pimp, and an adulteress to her lover. That Samaritan woman of whom we read in John 4 had five husbands, but they were not her own, that is, not her proper ones. So by these words the faithfulness of marriage is marked, and the vanity and treachery of fornication are excluded. Then he adds, "as to the Lord": not because the authority is equal, but because wives cannot obey Christ unless they show obedience by submitting to their husbands; and so that no woman might object arrogantly, "Should I be subject to that man?", he says, "be subject," knowing that you serve God; that is, if not for the sake of the husband, then at least for the sake of the Lord. For if someone who resists an outward and worldly power also resists the power of the Lord, how much more does she who struggles against her own husband? On the contrary, therefore, she who obeys her husband obeys the Lord and renders worship to God. For it is his will that you be subject to your husbands. In this clause, then, both the greatness and sincerity of the subjection are indicated, and also the proof or reason why it must be done is contained: because the Lord himself commanded that the woman be subject to the man, first indeed in the gentler subjection of creation, afterwards in the harsher punishment of sin. In Col. 3 he says in nearly the same way, "Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as is fitting in the Lord." Nevertheless, there can be a sense there too, provided that piety comes first in every case.

units.la: Observemus hinc, mulieres contumaces, rixosas, perfidas, & non subijcientes sese viris suis, satanæ, non Christo servire: ut habet Glossa Matthiæ Flacii.
units.tr: We may observe from this that women who are contumacious, quarrelsome and faithless, and who do not subject themselves to their husbands, serve Satan and not Christ, as the Gloss of Matthias Flacius has it.

units.la: Sequitur in Pauli verbis secunda & tertia ratio, cur mulier marito subjecta esse debeat: quia vir est caput uxoris, quod declarat collatione Christi & ecclesiæ. Est autem vir caput uxoris, jure, præstantia & utili regimine ipsius, 1.Corin.ii. Præterea quia talis subjectio est utilis mulieri, & toti domui, quia perinde fervet dominium patris totum corpus familiæ, sicut Christi regimen servat ecclesiam. Quanquâ hoc dictû, Salutem dat, &c. rectius refertur ad Christû, quàm ad virum: nihilominus tamen verum est, quòd paterfamilias fervet domum, alendo, regendo, & tuendo: sicut mox declarat Apostolus viri esse, fovere uxorem suam, tanquam propriam carnem. Itaque merito debet dominari. Proinde sicuti Christus ecclesiæ suæ præest in ejus salutem: ita nihil est mulieri utilius, nec magis salubre, quàm ut marito subsit. Perireigitur affectant, quæ renuunt subjectionem, sub qua salvæ esse poterant.
units.tr: In Paul's words there follows a second and third reason why a wife ought to be subject to her husband: because the husband is the head of the wife, which he shows by comparing Christ and the church. The husband is head of the wife by right, by pre-eminence and by the useful governance of her. (1 Cor. 11.) Moreover, such subjection is useful both to the wife and to the whole household, since the father's government preserves the whole body of the family just as Christ's rule preserves the church. Although the saying "He gives salvation" etc. refers more fittingly to Christ than to the husband, it is nevertheless true that the head of the household preserves it by feeding, governing and protecting it. As the Apostle soon declares, it is the husband's part to cherish his wife as his own flesh; therefore he rightly ought to rule. Accordingly, just as Christ presides over his church for its salvation, so nothing is more useful or more healthful for a wife than to be subject to her husband. Those women therefore pursue their own ruin who refuse the subjection under which they could have been safe.

units.la: Quomodo porrò & in quibus uxor marito subdita esse debeat, Apostolus quoque ostendit, cum inquit, Ac quemadmodum Ecclesia Christo paret, sic uxores suis viris parere debent in omnibus. Apertius docet, quod supra dixit, Obtemperate propriis maritis, tanquam Domino. q. d. Quemadmodum ecclesia (nimirum vera, quæ est electorum & unica: vel ut Oecumenius exponit, tota multitudo: nam inter singulos is etiam continetur, qui inobediens est) Christum sponsum, caput & principium suum veneratur, suspicit, illi unicè adhæret, fidit, & tota ab illo pendet: talis quoque reverentia, amor, & fides uxorem decet erga maritum suum. Ecclesia uni Christo adhæret, alios viros nescit, solum audit, hunc ineffabili amore amat, huic servire & immori gaudet, hunc cogitat, huc somniat, hunc unicè complectitur, & quocunque ierit sequitur. Ad eundem ergo modum subdita fit marito suo uxor Christiana: idq; in omnibus, salva tamen pietate & honeftate: vel per omnia, sancta (inquam,) & honesta, & utilia, & possibilia, qualia à marito tanquâ capite ac servatore uxori ipsius recte praecipi possunt. Si enim his diversa & contraria maritus praeceperit (quod tamen fidelis nunquam sciens faciet: de infidelibus autem Paulo nunc non est sermo) illud Petri Actor.5.ab uxore obijci potest: Obedire oportet Deo magis quàm hominibus. Sed & ubi ufuvenit, ut voluntas viri abludat à voluntate Dei, conveniat autem illi voluntas uxoris, ibi vir potius uxoris suae, quàm uxor viri vocem audire, sequeque debet: sicuti videre est in historia Abrahae & Sarae, Genef.21. ubi jubetur Abraham divino oraculo, ut quod dixerat Sara, audiat & faciat, propterea quòd verbum Sarae secundum voluntatem Dei: voluntas vero illius admodum ab illa diversa erat. Ad eundem modum & Isaac praedicatur, quòd in ablegando filio Iacob, uxori suae Rebeccae paruerit. Sed quum nihil jubet maritus, quod divinae legi fit adversum: uxor in omnibus obsequi debet. Exemplum habent uxores ejusmodi obedientiae in eadem Sara, Genef.12.18. 1.Petri 3. & in Sunamitide, quae petit à marito veniam eundi ad Elisaeum, cum ejus filius esset mortuus, 4. Reg.4. Hic ergo corruunt illa mulierum dicta, Quod si maritus meus talis aut talis esset, iubens illi obedirem, &c.
units.tr: In what manner and in what things a wife ought to be subject to her husband, the Apostle also shows when he says: "As the church obeys Christ, so let wives obey their husbands in all things." He teaches more plainly what he said above, "Obey your husbands as the Lord." That is to say: as the church (namely the true church, which is that of the elect and is one; or, as Oecumenius explains, the whole multitude, for even the disobedient person is included among the individuals) venerates Christ, its bridegroom, head and beginning, looks up to him, clings to him alone, trusts him, and depends wholly on him, so also such reverence, love and faith befit a wife toward her husband. The church cleaves to Christ alone, knows no other man, hears him only, loves him with an unspeakable love, rejoices to serve him and to die for him, thinks of him, dreams of him, embraces him alone, and follows him wherever he goes. In the same way the Christian wife becomes subject to her husband, and this in all things, yet saving piety and honesty; that is, in all things holy (I say), honest, useful and possible, such as may rightly be commanded by a husband as head and saviour to his wife. For if the husband should command things different and contrary to these (which, however, a faithful man will never knowingly do; for Paul is not now speaking of unbelievers), the saying of Peter in Acts 5 may be opposed by the wife: "We ought to obey God rather than men." Moreover, where it happens that the will of the husband departs from the will of God, while the will of the wife agrees with it, there the husband ought rather to hear and follow the voice of his wife, as can be seen in the story of Abraham and Sarah (Gen. 21), where Abraham is bidden by divine oracle to hear and do whatever Sarah has said, because Sarah's word accorded with the will of God, whereas his own will was quite different from hers. In the same way Isaac is praised for having obeyed his wife Rebekah in sending away Jacob his son. But when the husband commands nothing contrary to the divine law, the wife ought to obey him in all things. Wives of this kind of obedience have examples in the same Sarah (Gen. 12, 18; 1 Pet. 3) and in the Shunammite, who asks her husband's leave to go to Elisha when her son had died (2 Kings 4). Here therefore those sayings of women collapse: "If my husband were such and such, commanding me, I would obey him," and so on.

units.la: Quaecunque enim uxor est, quacunque sit natalium ac fortunae dignitate praestans, feruare ac præstare debet officium uxoris, subdita suo marito, tanquam Domino. Quem{*} admodum rursus, quisquis maritus est, sive episcopus sit, sive balneator: sive rex, sive subulcus: sive dives, sive pauper, officium mariti præstare debet.
units.tr: For whatever wife she is, however eminent she may be in the dignity of her birth and fortune, she ought to keep and perform the duty of a wife, subject to her husband as to a lord. Again, whatever husband he is, whether he be a bishop or a bath-keeper, a king or a swineherd, rich or poor, he ought to perform the duty of a husband.

units.la: § Quod autem officium mariti sit, & quo{*} modo hic se erga subditam sibi uxorem gerere debeat, Apostolus copiosè docet. Quoniam enim vir liberioris videtur esse potestatis & arbitrii, utpote quasi quidam in sua domo αὐτοκράτως, pluribus illum instruit, ossicium-que illius aliquanto majore cum diligentia explicat, ne dignitate ac potestate sua erga infirmam ac subjectam sibi uxorculam tyrannicè ac contemptim abutatur, atque ita statum à Deo ordinatum corrumpat.
units.tr: What the duty of a husband is, and how he ought to conduct himself toward his wife who is subject to him, the Apostle teaches at length. For since the husband seems to have freer power and choice, as it were a kind of autocrat in his own house, he instructs him in many things and explains his duty with somewhat greater care, lest he abuse his dignity and power tyrannically and contemptuously against his weak little wife who is subject to him, and so corrupt the state ordained by God.

units.la: Dicit ergo, Viri diligite uxores vestras. Quare non dicit, Dominamini, & imperate uxoribus vestris: estis enim illarum magistri ac domini, quare subijcite eas, & cogite, ut jussis vestris obediant? Quorsum attinet de dilectione præcipere, ubi agitur de subditis, cum subjectio & dominium magis, quàm subjectio & dilectio sibi invicem correspondeant? An non hoc juris habet vir in uxorem, ut illi dominetur? idque secundum sententiam Dei, de qua ad Evam dixit: Sub viri potestate eris, & ipse dominibitur tibi: Respondemus cum Vvol. Musculo: Respectus Apostoli hoc loco non est, quid juris habeat maritus in uxore suam, sed quid illi dedebeat. Loquitur utrobique de debito. Subjectionem debet uxor viro. Postquam de hac admonuit uxores, jam vicissim admonet viros, quid illi uxoribus suis debeant. De jure potestatis ac dominii satis meminit, dum præcipit uxoribus, ut viris suis sint subditæ. Convenientius de illo admonuit uxores, quàm si viris dixisset: Viri dominamini uxoribus vestris. Et Deus ipse non dixit Adæ, Potestatem exerce in uxorem, ac dominare illi: sed Evę, Sub potestate viri, inquit, eris, & ipse dominabitur tibi. Aliàs abunde notum est viris, quid juris habeant in uxores suas, ut de illo nulla sint necessitate admonendi, quemadmodū & uxoribus necesse non est, ut de jure quod habent in viros suos instruantur. Utriq; plus æquo propensi ad hoc sunt, ut jus suum persequantur: omnium autem de eo rarissimè cogitant, quid alter alteri debeat. Quare omnium confultissimè factum est ab Apostolo, quòd quemadmodùm uxores admonuit, quid viris suis debeant, subjectionem videlicet: ita mox & viros admonet, quo sint debito uxoribus suis vicissim obstricti, dicens: Viri diligite uxores vestras. Unde rectè Theophylactus: Quid verò, inquit, si non metuat mulier? tu tamen dilige, tuoque officio fungere. Similiter & mulier: etiamsi enim non diligatur, metuat tamen. Vis autem uxorem tibi subditam esse veluti Domino? dilige eam (inquit Oecumenius) sicut Christus ecclesiam, &c.
units.tr: He therefore says: "Husbands, love your wives." Why does he not say: "Lord it over your wives, and command them"? For you are their masters and lords; why not subject them and compel them to obey your orders? What is the point of prescribing love where the subject is concerned, when rule and dominion correspond to subjection more than subjection corresponds to love? Does not a husband have the right to rule over his wife, in accordance with the sentence of God, of which he spoke to Eve: "You shall be under your husband's power, and he shall rule over you"? We reply with Wolfgang Musculus: the Apostle's concern in this place is not what right a husband has over his wife, but what he owes her. He speaks in both cases of duty. The wife owes subjection to her husband. Having admonished the wives about this, he now in turn admonishes the husbands what they owe their wives. He has said enough about the right of power and dominion when he commands wives to be subject to their husbands. It is more fitting that he admonished the wives about this than if he had said to the husbands: "Husbands, rule over your wives." Nor did God himself say to Adam, "Exercise power over your wife and rule over her," but to Eve: "You shall be under the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you." Otherwise it is well enough known to husbands what right they have over their wives, so that there is no need to admonish them about it, just as wives need not be instructed about the right they have over their husbands. Each side is too inclined to pursue its own right, but very rarely do they think about what the one owes the other. Therefore it was most wisely done by the Apostle that, just as he admonished wives what they owe their husbands, namely subjection, so he at once admonishes husbands by what duty they are bound in return to their wives, saying: "Husbands, love your wives." Hence Theophylact rightly says: "But what, he says, if the wife does not fear? Nevertheless you love her and perform your duty. Likewise the wife too: for even if she is not loved, she should still fear. Do you want your wife to be subject to you as to the Lord? Love her," says Oecumenius, "as Christ loved the church," etc.

units.la: Rursus dixerit quisquâ: Quid attinet monere viros, ut uxores suas diligant, cùm sit ipsis naturaliter insitum, ut diligant mulieres? Respondemus: Non dicit, Viri diligite mulieres: sed, Viri, diligite uxores vestras. Aliud est diligere mulierem ut mulierem, aliud diligere eam ut uxorem. Prius quidem inest viris ut viris naturaliter: posterius vero non ita. Quia natura nostra corrupta nō accommodat se constitutioni divinæ, quę legitimam uxoris dilectionē requirit, quemadmodum neq; mulieres naturali sunt ductu viris suis subditæ. Aliud enim est simpliciter subdi mulierem viro ut masculo: aliud vero subdi eam, ut uxorem suo marito, capiti ac servatori subjectione legitima, qualem constitutio divina poscit. Est itaque non nisi piorum ac timentium Dei virorum diligere uxores suas, propterea quòd sunt ipsorum uxores, à Deo ipsis conjunctæ. Qui sic animati sunt, non respiciunt in uxoribus suis subjectionem, & jus potestatis, quod in illas habent: sed ordinationem divinam, & indissolubilem conjugalis vitæ societatem. Dum ita consideramus, facilè intelligimus, quàm non fit præter rationem, quòd viris præcipit Apostolus, ut uxores suas diligant. Corrupta nostra caro, in vetitum semper connitens, & negata concupiscens, propensior ad hoc est, ut alienas diligat uxores.
units.tr: Someone may again object: what is the point of admonishing husbands to love their wives, since it is naturally implanted in men to love women? We reply: he does not say, "Husbands, love women," but, "Husbands, love your wives." It is one thing to love a woman as a woman, and another to love her as a wife. The former is naturally present in men as men; the latter is not so. For our corrupt nature does not accommodate itself to the divine ordinance, which requires the lawful love of a wife, just as women are not by natural inclination subject to their husbands. For it is one thing for a woman simply to be subject to a man as a male, and another to be subject to her husband as her head and saviour by the lawful subjection which the divine ordinance demands. It is therefore only the pious men who fear God who love their wives, because they are their wives, joined to them by God. Those so animated do not look in their wives for subjection and the right of power they have over them, but the divine ordinance and the indissoluble partnership of married life. When we consider this, we easily understand how not beside reason it is that the Apostle commands husbands to love their wives. Our corrupt flesh, always striving toward what is forbidden and coveting what is denied, is more inclined to love other men's wives.

units.la: Quemadmodum autem Ecclesiam uxoribus, ita Christum viris imitandum exem-pli pli vice proponit. Præscribit enim illis ardentem dilectionem erga uxores, quam ornat, illustrat ac confirmat collatione officii ac beneficiorū Christi erga Ecclesiam: quam similitudinem tum ideo adhibet, ut tantò magis excitet conjuges ad mutuum officiū, tum etiam, ut hac occasione declaret mysterium Christi & ecclesiæ. Ait ergo Christum adeò dilexisse Ecclesiam, ut semetipsum pro ea tradiderit, quæ est ingens amplificatio, aut declaratio dilectionis Christi erga suam ecclesiam. Majorem enim dilectionem nemo habere potest, teste Christo apud Ioannem, quàm ut animam suam pro dilecto ponat. In hac ergo collatione primū posset videri causa præcepti in verbis: Sicut dilexit: deinde modus aut quantitas delectionis in verbis, Seipsum tradidit. Vnde & de Davide legitur, qui typus Christi fuit, quòd duas uxores suas ab Amalechitis captas cum periculo vitæ liberarit, atque eruerit, 1. Reg.30. Cupidè autem solet Apostolus per occasionem, ab inferioribus doctrinis ad nobiliores & præstantiores digredi: sicut hic à conjugio ad conjunctionem Christi & Ecclesiæ. Occasione igitur dilectionis officiorumque mariti erga uxorem, transit ad dilectionem & beneficia Christi erga ecclesiam, cujus gratiæ gradus aptissimè hic distribuuntur tribus versibus: primum enim dilexit ecclesiam: deinde ex dilectione tradidit seipsum pro ea, sicque eam ex servitute diaboli & peccati, sibi in propriam sponsam redemit: tertio, sanctificat sibi ecclesiam, remissione peccatorum & regeneratione, inhabitatione spiritus, adoptioneque & insitione in corpus suum: quartò modus & instrumenta hujus sanctificationis indicantur, nempe per verbum & sacramenta, quibus fides, ut correlativum, respondet: illa enim sunt larga patris cœlestis manus, omnia bona sua nobis largientis: hæc vero, nostra manus mendica, omnia bona ab ipso precario accipiens: quinto, indicantur duo fines, ut planè esset munda & inculpata, & esset sponsa ipsius: postremo addit, quod etiam simus membra corporis Christi. In quo alludere videtur ad creationem hominis, ubi mulier dicitur caro de carne viri, Genef.2. Etsi autem hic tantum ipsum simile urget: tamen vult inde intelligi etiam ipsam rem similitudine declaratam, de qua institutus est sermo. Quandoquidem enim multi mariti suæ inhumanitati erga uxores præteexere solent earum aliquas infirmitates: ideo jubet ipsos expendere, quàm immundam sponsam Christus primū acceperit, & dilexerit (Rom.5.) & quàm nō abhorruerit ab ejus sordibus, adeò ut eas in se transtulerit, ipsamque suo sanguine abluerit, & abluere quotidie pergat, donec eam penitus purificet: in qua sponsa vult etiam, ut nos ipsi nostras originales simul & quotidianas sordes, & Christi lotiones diligenter consideremus, gratoque animo celebremus. Hanc verò totam similitudinem videtur Apostolus ex Ezechiele cap.16. huc transf tulisse.
units.tr: Just as he sets the Church before wives as a model to imitate, so he sets Christ before husbands as an example to follow. For he prescribes for them an ardent love towards their wives, and he adorns, illustrates and confirms it by comparing it with the office and benefits of Christ towards the Church. He uses this comparison partly so that he may stir up spouses all the more to mutual duty, and partly so that on this occasion he may set forth the mystery of Christ and the Church. So he says that Christ loved the Church so much that he gave himself up for her, which is a great enlargement, or a clear statement, of Christ's love towards his Church. For no one can have greater love, as Christ says in John, than to lay down his life for his friend. In this comparison, the reason for the command may first be seen in the words "as Christ loved", and then the manner or measure of the love in the words "gave himself up". Hence also it is read of David, who was a type of Christ, that he rescued and delivered his two wives from the Amalekites at the risk of his life (1 Reg. 30.). The Apostle is also in the habit of eagerly moving, on the occasion of a subject, from lower teachings to higher and more excellent ones, as here he passes from marriage to the union of Christ and the Church. So, on the occasion of the love and duties of a husband towards his wife, he passes to the love and benefits of Christ towards the Church, whose degrees of grace are most aptly set out here in three verses. First he loved the Church; then, out of that love, he gave himself up for her, and so redeemed her from the slavery of the devil and of sin to be his own bride.
