Third, he sanctifies the Church to himself by the forgiveness of sins and regeneration, by the indwelling of the Spirit, and by adoption and ingrafting into his body. Fourth, the means and instruments of this sanctification are indicated, namely the Word and the sacraments, to which faith corresponds as its correlative; for these are the generous hand of the heavenly Father, bestowing on us all his good things, while faith is our beggar's hand, receiving all good things from him as a gift. Fifth, two ends are indicated: that she should be altogether clean and blameless, and that she should be his bride. Lastly, he adds that we are also members of the body of Christ. In this he seems to allude to the creation of man, where the woman is called flesh of the flesh of the man (Genef.2.). Although here he presses only the comparison itself, yet he wishes the very thing illustrated by the comparison, which is the subject of his discourse, to be understood from it as well. For since many husbands are wont to cover up their own inhumanity towards their wives with some of the wives' weaknesses, he therefore bids them consider how unclean a bride Christ first took and loved (Rom. 5.), and how he did not shrink from her filth, so much so that he took those defilements upon himself, washed her with his own blood, and continues to wash her daily until he has made her wholly pure. In this bride he also wishes us to consider carefully our own original and daily defilements, and Christ's washings, and to celebrate them with a grateful heart. The Apostle seems to have transferred this whole comparison here from Ezekiel, chapter 16.

units.la: Cæterum dilectionis Christi excellentia hactenus est proposita viro, ut sicubi uxorem naetus fuerit, cujus præcedens vita non admodum fuerit munda & casta, & morigerata, hoc illam nomine non fastidiat: sed nihilominus ex animo tanquam uxorem diligat, & si qua ratione poterit, à pristinis sordibus repurget. Exempli enim hujus imitatio nihil poscit eorum, quæ præstari à marito non possunt, sed peculiaria sunt Christo: qualia sunt, quòd dilexit nos priusquam essemus, & existentes quoq; priusquam sponsa ipsius per fidem fieremus, & quòd semetipsum pro peccatis nostris Deo victima expiationis qua redimeremur, obtulit, & quæ alia sunt ejusmodi. Satis ad exemplū Christi diligit uxorem suam, qui quam habet, & cū qua vivit, sic diligit, ut ampliore eam dilec-tione prosequi non possit.
units.tr: Moreover, the excellence of Christ's love has so far been set before the husband in such a way that, if he has taken a wife whose earlier life was not very clean, chaste and obedient, he should not therefore despise her, but should nonetheless love her sincerely as his wife, and, as far as he can, cleanse her of her former filth. For the imitation of this example demands nothing of those things that cannot be done by a husband, but which are peculiar to Christ: such as that he loved us before we were, and when we were still existing, before we became his bride through faith, and that he offered himself as a victim of atonement to God for our sins, by which we were redeemed, and other things of this kind. It is enough for the example of Christ that a man loves his wife, whom he has and with whom he lives, in such a way that he cannot love her with greater love.

units.la: Primum ergo ac potissimū conjugalis hujus dilectionis exemplum est in dilectione Christi, qua ecclesiam suam ad mortem usq; dilexit. Alterum est in ea, qua nostra ipsorum corpora diligimus. Dicit enim: Sic debet viri diligere suas uxores, ut sua ipsorum corpora. Quae particula bifariam accipi potest. Primò sic, ut sit αἰτιολογία, & causam dilectionis exprimat in hunc sensum: Viri debent uxores suas diligere, tanquam sua ipsorum corpora. i. eò quòd sunt ipsorum corpora. Huic sensui concordant, quæ sequuntur. Corpus sanè uxoris, ut de viro est sumptum, ita est & viri corpus. Quare haud frustrà requiritur à viris, ut uxores suas vel hoc nomine diligant, quòd sunt ipsorum corpora. Deinde ut sit alterum exemplum, ad quod se viri uxores suas diligendo conformare debeant, & expressio magnitudinis dilectionis illius, hoc sensu: Sic debent viri diligere suas uxores, quemadmodum diligunt sua ipsorum corpora, hoc est, seipsos. Sic etiam in conclusione materiæ hujus dicit: Quanquam & vos singulatim (nemine dempto) hoc præstare, ut suam quisque uxorem diligat tanquam seipsum: id quod etiam bifariam exponi potest, vel ut sit, Sicut seipsum. i. quemadmodum seipsum diligit, ita diligat & uxorem suam. quo sensu dictum est & illud, Diliges proximum tuum sicut teipsum. Vel ut sit, Tanquam teipsum, sicut Erasmus vertit: quod nihil est aliud, quàm tanquam suum ipsius corpus, tanquam suam ipsius carnem, tanquà eam, quę est alter ipse, tanquam eam in qua seipsum diligat. Unde etiam ait: Qui diligit suam uxorem, seipsum diligit. q. d. Quemadmodum qui corpus suum diligit, seipsum diligit: ita & qui uxorem suam diligit, seipsum diligit: quia uxor est corpus viri & alter ipse. Nullus autem unquam suam ipsius carnem odio habuit, sed enutrit ac fovet eam: videlicet, ne qua cibi ac vestitus penuria auria [?] laboret.Hoc argumento,ex communi ac naturali mortalium omnium affectu, ductu ac studio sumpto, demonstrant eos, qui uxores oderunt, propriam carnem instar suriosorum [?] hominum odisse, & cum natura ipsa pugnare: quia sicut quisque proprium corpus diligit, ita etiam teneatur,& naturaliter soleat uxorem, existente corpus suum, diligere & fovere. Consecutionem primùm probat, collatione mysticæ conjunctionis Ecclesiæ ac Christi eam implentis instaurantisque, denuò rediens ad illam nobiliorem doctrinam:deinde de testimonio Dei, qui & ordinet ac pronunciet, duos conjuges adeò esse conjunctos, ut sint instar unius individui, constituantque (ut vulgò loquuntur) unam personam, ut jam non sint duo, sed unus homo, una caro, unum corpus. Ut sic unum sint atque esse possint singuli conjuges, sicut Deus vult ac præcipit, faxit ille qui dixit Marthæ, Luc. 10. Unum est necessarium: & Patri cœlesti, Ioan.17.Non pro eis autem rogo tantum, sed & pro his, qui credituri sunt per sermonem eorum in me, ut omnes unum sint, sicut tu Pater in me,& ego in te, ut & ipsi in nobis unum sint,ut credat mundus quòd tu me miseris,& ego gloriam, quam dedisti mihi, dedi eis: ut sint unum, sicut & nos unum sumus: Ego in eis, & tu in me, ut sint consummati in unum,& ut cognoscat mundus quòd me misisti, & dilexisti eos,sicut & me dilexisti Pater,quos dedisti mihi, volo ut ubi sum ego, & illi sint mecum, ut videant gloriam meam, quam dedisti mihi. O qualis gloria! Gloria videlicet filiorum Dei, gloria sponsæ Christi, gloria regis regū, & Domini dominantium, gloria immortalitatis, gloria clarificationis ac cœlestis splendoris: cujus glorię utinâ & nos omnes, quotquot adsumus, unà cum reliquis membris Ecclesiæ, quam sibi Christus ἔνδοξον[?], i. gloriosam sistet & adjunget, ut secum sit in sempiternum, μέτοχοι[?] & κοινωνοί[?], i. participes ac consortes fiamus, inq; ea cum ipso Christo, vita nostra cùm apparuerit, appareamus, Amen.
units.tr: The first and chief example of this conjugal love, then, is in the love of Christ, by which he loved his Church even unto death. The second is in that love by which we love our own bodies. For he says: "So ought husbands to love their wives as their own bodies." This particle can be taken in two ways. First, so that it is an <hi>aetiology [αἰτιολογία]</hi>, expressing the cause of the love, in this sense: husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies, that is, because they are their own bodies. What follows agrees with this sense. Indeed the wife's body, since she was taken from the husband, is also the husband's body. Therefore it is not without reason that husbands are required to love their wives, if only for this reason, that they are their own bodies. Second, so that it is another example to which husbands, in loving their wives, ought to conform themselves, and an expression of the greatness of that love, in this sense: husbands ought to love their wives just as they love their own bodies, that is, themselves. So also in the conclusion of this subject he says: "Let each one of you too (none excepted) do this, that he love his own wife as himself." This too can be explained in two ways: either as "as himself", that is, just as he loves himself, so let him love his wife too (in which sense it was also said, "You shall love your neighbour as yourself"); or as "as yourself", as Erasmus translates it, which is nothing other than "as his own body, as his own flesh", as her who is another self, as one in whom he loves himself. Hence he also says: "He who loves his own wife loves himself," that is, just as he who loves his own body loves himself, so he who loves his wife loves himself, because the wife is the body of the husband and another self. But no one has ever hated his own flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, namely so that it may not suffer from any lack of food or clothing. By this argument, drawn from the common and natural affection of all mortals, they show that those who hate their wives hate their own flesh like madmen, and fight against nature itself, since, just as each one loves his own body, so he is bound, and naturally accustomed, to love and cherish his wife, since she is his own body. He first proves the consequence by comparing the mystical union of the Church and Christ, which fills and restores it, returning again to that nobler teaching; then by the testimony of God, who ordains and declares that two spouses are so joined together that they are like one individual, and constitute (as people commonly say) one person, so that they are no longer two but one man, one flesh, one body. May he who said to Martha (Luc. 10.), "One thing is needful," and who prayed to the heavenly Father (Ioan. 17.), "Not for these only do I pray, but for those also who shall believe in me through their word, that they all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you, that they also may be one in us, that the world may believe that you have sent me; and the glory which you gave me I have given them, that they may be one, as we are one: I in them and you in me, that they may be made perfect in one, and that the world may know that you have sent me and have loved them as you have loved me. Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my glory, which you have given me," grant that each of the spouses may be one in this way, as God wills and commands. O what a glory! The glory, that is, of the sons of God, the glory of the bride of Christ, the glory of the King of kings and Lord of lords, the glory of immortality, the glory of clarification and heavenly splendour, of which glory may we all, as many as are present, together with the other members of the Church, which Christ will present and join to himself as <hi>glorious [ἔνδοξον]</hi>, that is, glorious, so that she may be with him for ever; and may we become <hi>partakers [μέτοχοι]</hi> and <hi>fellow-partakers [κοινωνοί]</hi>, that is, sharers and companions, and in her may we appear with Christ himself when our life shall appear. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO LIII.
units.tr: SERMON LIII.

units.la: Colos. 3.
units.tr: Colos. 3.

units.la: Tquicquid egeritis sermone aut facto, omnia in nomine Domini Iesu Christi facite, gratias agentes Deo & patri per illum. Vxores, subdita estote proprijs viris, sicut convenit in Domino. Viri diligite uxores, & ne sitis amarulenti adversus illas.
units.tr: Whatever you do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, giving thanks to God the Father through him. Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as is fitting in the Lord. Husbands, love your wives, and do not be bitter towards them.

units.la: I Quis hæc verba loquatur, sciendū est: ut quando intelligemus loquentem ac præcipientē magnum esse, libentius ac diligentius audiamus. Est autem ea loquutus ille, qui de se Gal. 1. scribit: Neq; enim ego ab homine accepi illud (nempe Evangelium) neq; didici, sed per revelationem Iesu Christi: h.e. Apostolus seu legatus Iesu Christi domini nostri, à quo ille accepit, quod tradidit nobis.r[?], Corinth. ii. imò Dominus Iesus ipse, spiritusq; Patris per Apostolum illum Paulum, 2. Corint. 13[?]. Matth. io[?].
units.tr: I First, we must know who is speaking these words, so that when we understand that the speaker is great and that he gives commands, we may listen more willingly and more attentively. The one who speaks is he who writes of himself in Galatians 1: "For I did not receive that gospel from man, nor was I taught it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ." That is, he is the apostle, or envoy, of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom he received what he handed on to us. (See 1 Cor. 2.) Indeed, the Lord Jesus himself, and the Spirit of the Father, speak through the apostle Paul (2 Cor. 13; Matt. 10).

units.la: Verùm ne putemus ea, quae hîc præscribit atq; docet, ad nos nihil spectare, videndum fuerit etiam qui sint illi, quibus hæc præscribit ac loquitur. Primò autem in genere alloquitur omnes Christianos omnis status & conditionis: deinde hoc specialiter & partialiter facit, & singularum conditionū singulas personas admonet, quid quenque in sua conditione deceat. Et quia præeminentissima vitæ conditio est conjugium, ab eo exorditur, & primùm instruit uxores (quoniam mulier prior peccavit) deinde viros: nec solùm illos, qui jam nunc matrimonium contrahunt, sed etiam eos, qui olim contraxerunt, ut si hactenus officio suo non sint functi[?]; nunc corrigant, & pro venia delictorum rogent: & insuper quoque illos, qui cogitant de matrimonio conjungendo, ut discat in tempore ea, quibus opus est in conjugio, ut sit felix & faustum.
units.tr: But lest we think that what he prescribes and teaches here has nothing to do with us, we must also consider who those are to whom he prescribes and speaks these things. First, he addresses in general all Christians of every rank and condition. Then he does this more specifically and in part, and admonishes each individual person of each condition about what befits them in their own state. And since marriage is the most eminent condition of life, he begins with it, and first instructs wives (since the woman sinned first), and then husbands. He addresses not only those who are now entering marriage, but also those who entered it long ago, so that if they have not yet fulfilled their duty, they may now correct themselves and ask pardon for their faults. Moreover, he also addresses those who are thinking of joining themselves in marriage, so that they may learn in good time what is needed in marriage, so that it may be happy and prosperous.

units.la: 2 Quid igitur omnibus in universum Christianis hominibus præcipit doctor ille gentium: Generale illis regulâ[?] omnium actionum praescribit. Quia enim fidem & spiritum sanctum habent, non possunt non aliquid agere. Nam & loquuntur & operantur, Psalm. 116. Tit. 3. & sicut arbores bonae bonos fructus faciunt. Quoniam autem & bona non bene fieri possunt (Matth. 6. 1. Corinth. 13.) docet, quomodo omnia, quaecunque agimus sermone aut facto (seu quae dicenda faciendaque nobis sunt, tanquam hominibus Christianis, non tanquam malis & carnalibus) facere debeamus. Quicquid, inquit, vel verbis vel re facitis, id in Domini Iesu nomine facitote, Deo patriq; per eum gratias agentes. Per eum, inquit, per quem scilicet nihil nō vertit nobis in bonum, qui‑ que est mediator noster inter nos & Deum patrem. Est autem justum, ut per quem pater omnia bona largitur, per eundem illi gratiae agantur, Hebr. 13.1. Petr. 2. idq; semper & pro omnibus, Ephes. 5. 1. Thessal. 5. Psalm. 34. Sive laeta sint, sive tristia quae accidunt, agendae sunt Deo gratiae, qui non laetis modo, sed & tristibus salutis nostrae rationem habet: & dum nos castigat, cavet ne hoc cum mundo damnemur: τὶ γὰρ ἄλλο ἔργον Θεοῦ, ἢ τοῦτο, τὸ εὐχαριστεῖν τῷ [?] ἀν [?] ... ἀλλ' ἀπὸ [?] ... γίνεσθαι, ὁ [?] ... καλὸν εἶναι [?] ... ἀλλ' ἀναι [?] ..., inquit Chrysost. Sed quomodo omnia in nomine Domini Iesu (in cujus peculium per gratiam Dei assumpti sumus) facienda sunt? aut quid est facere aliquid in nomine Domini? Est ex illius jussu & mandato, secundum illius praescriptum aliquid facere. Vult enim Dominus ut fervemus quaecunque ipse praecepit nobis, Matth.28. vel est sic aliquid agere, ut ad illius gloriam pertineat ac fiat, 1.Corinth. 10. vel ita facere, ut dirigatur ad Dominum, tanquam vitae nostrae scopum. Hunc enim cogitare debemus in omnibus viis nostris, Proverb. 3. & jugiter propositum habere ob oculos. Psal. 16. vel, facere aliquid quod non sit contra salutem nostram. Nomen enim Domini est Iesus, id est, salvator, Matth.1. vel facere omnia tanquam ex virtute, quam suppeditat Deus & Dominus, sine quo nihil facere possumus, nec tanquam ex viribus nostris, 1. Petr. 4. vel est, fiducia nominis Christi aliquid facere, illumque nominare & invocare, non angelos ipsos inducere: actum demum opera aggredi, ubi primum preces ad D. Iesum fuderis. Ergo etiam oratione ad conjugium accedendum est, quemadmodum angelus monet, Tob. 5. & exemplum Tobię & Saræ, Tob. 8. Est & alius modus faciendi aliquid in nomine Domini Iesu, quo videlicet in persona, loco & authoritate Domini aliquid facimus: id quod proprié est ministrorum Domini. Omnium vero Christianorum est sic instituere vitam, ut quiequid dicunt aut faciunt, hoc totum regatur auspiciis Christi, & in ejus gloriam tanquam in scopum respiciat. Commodè enim utrumque hoc verbo comprehendemus, nempe ut exordium ab invocatione Christi habeant studia nostra omnia, & ejus gloriæ serviant. Usus porrò adhortationis hujus est, ut religione nominis Christi à malis tam verbis quàm operibus avocemur, ut quæ à nobis nec authoritate, nec fiducia illius fieri possunt. Omnium namque impiissimum esset, si mali quicquam vel dicturi, vel facturi, nomen Domini nostri Iesu Christi, prætexeremus, quasi ille vel author, vel auxiliator possit esse malorum.
units.tr: 2 What, then, does that teacher of the Gentiles prescribe to all Christians in general? He sets out a general rule for all actions. For since they have faith and the Holy Spirit, they cannot but do something. For they both speak and work (Ps. 116; Titus 3), and "as good trees bring forth good fruit." Since, however, good things cannot be done well without (Matt. 6; 1 Cor. 13), he teaches how we ought to do all that we do in word or deed (that is, whatever must be said and done by us as Christian men, not as wicked and carnal men). "Whatever you do," he says, "whether in word or in deed, do it in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him." Through him, he says, through whom indeed nothing turns out to our harm, and who is our mediator between us and God the Father. It is right that thanks be given to the Father through the same one through whom the Father bestows all good things (Heb. 13; 1 Pet. 2), and that always and for all things (Eph. 5; 1 Thess. 5; Ps. 34). Whether the things that happen are joyful or sad, thanks must be rendered to God, who cares for our salvation not only in joyful things but also in sad ones; and while he chastises us, he takes care that we are not condemned along with the world. [τί γὰρ ἄλλο ἔργον Θεοῦ, ἢ τοῦτο, τὸ εὐχαριστεῖν] For what other work of God is there than this, to give thanks, says Chrysostom; but the rest of the Greek passage is too corrupt to render. But how must all things be done in the name of the Lord Jesus (into whose possession we have been taken by the grace of God)? Or what does it mean to do something in the name of the Lord? It means to do something by his command and order, according to his prescription. For the Lord wants us to observe whatever he has commanded us (Matt. 28). Or it means to act in such a way that it pertains to his glory and is done for it (1 Cor. 10). Or to do it so that it is directed to the Lord as the goal of our life. For we ought to think of him in all our ways (Prov. 3), and constantly keep him before our eyes (Ps. 16). Or it means to do something that is not contrary to our salvation. For the name of the Lord is Jesus, that is, Savior (Matt. 1). Or it means to do all things as from the strength that God and the Lord supplies, without which we can do nothing, and not as from our own strength (1 Pet. 4). Or it is to undertake something in confidence in the name of Christ, calling upon him and invoking him, not bringing in angels themselves; finally, to set about the work once you have poured out your prayers to the Lord Jesus. Therefore one must also approach marriage with prayer, as the angel advises (Tob. 5), and as the example of Tobias and Sara shows (Tob. 8). There is also another way of doing something in the name of the Lord Jesus, namely when we act in the person, place and authority of the Lord; this properly belongs to the ministers of the Lord. But it is the duty of all Christians so to order their lives that whatever they say or do may be governed wholly by the auspices of Christ and look to his glory as its goal. For we may conveniently comprehend both senses in this phrase: that all our pursuits should begin with the invocation of Christ and serve his glory. The use of this exhortation, moreover, is that by reverence for the name of Christ we be kept back from evil words as well as evil deeds, since such things cannot be done by us either with his authority or with confidence in him. For it would be most impious of all, if we were to pretend the name of our Lord Jesus Christ while about to say or do something evil, as if he could be the author or helper of evil things.

units.la: ¶ Quid Apostolus singulariter uxoribus Christianis præscribit hoc loco? Idem planè, quod & in epistola ad Ephes. cap. 5. Ait enim: Uxores subditæ estote propriis viris, sicuti convenit in Domino. Cur autem non in omnibus epistolis, sed in hac, & ad Ephes. & in epistolis ad Timoth. ac Titum hæc præcipit? vel quia verisimile est (testante Theophylacto) quòd in his urbibus tales diffensiones fuerint: vel quia firma erat hic Ecclesia, ac reliqua apud eos bene habebant, rectèque transigebantur, quod supererat de hisce loquitur. Porrò aliis in altioribus dogmatibus deliquium patientibus magis erat necessarium de iis etiam scribere, ac hujusmodi adhortationes prætermittere. Christianæ uxori duplicis generis *** propositum est. Unum, quod statum conjugii in se apud omnes gentes concernit, in quo hoc est legitimum & laudabile, ut uxor subsit & obediat suo marito. sic enim est ordinatum à Deo. Alterum, quod respicit ad fidem ac religionem Christi. Hujus admonet Apostolus hîc, cùm dicit: Sicuti convenit ac decet in Domino.i. sicut Dominicis dignum est: vel, sicut convenit uxori, quæ est in Domino i.est Christiana. Hanc decet omnem præstare obedientiam viro debitam, ne quo pacto nomen ac fidem Christi infamet, si se gerat secus quàm convenit. Deinde, ne ultra limites honesti conjugii in iis quoque quæ religionem concernunt, viro contra Dominum obediat: proponitur illi respectus Domini, ut subdita sit sicut convenit ei quæ est in Domino. Si maritus jubeat abnegare Christum, & adhærere Ethnicismo, non est hic Christiana mulier obstricta ad obediendum: quia id non convenit ei quæ est in Domino. Hoc sensu servit præsens particula conjugibus illis, quæ maritos habent infideles, cùm ipsæ sint Christianæ. Hodie illam sic recte formabis: Uxores subditæ estote propriis viris, sicuti convenit in Evangelio, propter imparia conjugia, in quibus passim alter conjugum evangelio, alter Papismo adhæret, ubi uxor evangelica non tenetur contra evangelium obedire suo marito, papisticis abominationibus dedito.
units.tr: ¶ What does the Apostle prescribe in particular to Christian wives in this place? Plainly the same thing that he says in the epistle to the Ephesians, chapter 5. For he says: "Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as is fitting in the Lord." But why does he give these precepts not in all his epistles, but in this one, and in the one to the Ephesians, and in the epistles to Timothy and Titus? Either because it is likely (as Theophylact testifies) that such dissensions had arisen in those cities; or because the Church there was sound, and the rest of their affairs were going well and being carried on rightly, so that he speaks only of what remained. Moreover, for others who were suffering a lapse in more important doctrines, it was more necessary to write to them also about these matters, and to omit exhortations of this kind. For a Christian wife, the admonition has two aspects. The first concerns the state of marriage itself among all nations, in which it is lawful and praiseworthy that the wife be subject to and obey her husband; for this is so ordained by God. The second concerns faith and the religion of Christ. The apostle reminds her of this here when he says: "as is fitting in the Lord," that is, as is worthy of those who belong to the Lord; or, as is fitting for a wife who is in the Lord, that is, a Christian. She ought to render all the obedience due to her husband, lest in any way she bring disgrace upon the name and faith of Christ by behaving otherwise than becomes her. Then again, so that she may not, within the limits of an honorable marriage, obey her husband against the Lord even in matters that concern religion, the regard for the Lord is set before her, so that she is subject as is fitting for one who is in the Lord. If a husband commands her to deny Christ and cleave to heathenism, a Christian wife is not bound to obey, because that does not befit one who is in the Lord. In this sense the present particle serves those spouses who have unbelieving husbands while they themselves are Christians. Today you will rightly frame it thus: "Wives, be subject to your own husbands, as is fitting in the gospel," on account of mismatched marriages, in which often one spouse clings to the gospel and the other to Papism; where an evangelical wife is not bound to obey her husband, who is given over to papistical abominations, against the gospel.

units.la: Quidam sic contexunt verba illa: Subjectæ estote in Domino, quemadmodum decet. Sed alii rectius: Sicut in Domino decet, h.e. secundum Domini institutionem: ut mulierum subjectionem Dei authoritate confirmet, qui ita ab initio voluit, ut viro mulier subijceretur. Unde Theophylactus, Quid autem (inquit) est, In Domino pro eo quod est, propter Dominum obedite: non enim tantum à natura obedientiam, quam eis debetis, à vobis exigo. Hoc enim indicat per hoc quod ait, Quemadmodum oportet, sive decet: h.e. ut conveniens est & decorum: sed potissimum etiam eam, quæ est propter Dominum.
units.tr: Some join those words thus: "Be subject in the Lord, as is fitting." But others more correctly read: "As it is fitting in the Lord," that is, according to the Lord's institution, so that he confirms the subjection of women by the authority of God, who from the beginning willed that the woman be subject to the man. Hence Theophylact says: "What does 'in the Lord' mean, in place of 'obey on account of the Lord'? For I do not require from you only the obedience that is owed by nature. He indicates this by what he says, 'as it is fitting,' that is, as is suitable and proper; but above all he also means the obedience that is for the Lord's sake."

units.la: Porrò quemadmodum & reliqua præcepta Dei (quæ sunt præcepta medici) duo in se habent: primum quod morbum produnt & impugnant: alterum quod ad sanitatem promovent: ita & hoc præceptum uxoribus traditum duorum istorum rationem habere necesse est. Primò nanque docet mulieres quales sint, quàmque corruptæ. Quæ enim naturam habent incorruptam, his certè nihil est opus præcipere ut faciant, quod alios qui naturæ ductu faciunt. Quod ergo præcipitur mulieribus[?], ut suis viris subditæ sint, indicat eas ita corruptas esse, ut viris propriis non sint subditæ ac obedientes, sed malint ipsæmet potius magistræ esse ac viris suis dominari, quàm illis subiici. ut Vasthi uxor regis Ahasueri, Esther 1. Deinde docet hoc præceptum, uxores quales esse debeant, ut verè Christianæ sint atque felices. Idem & de præcepto viris dato sentiendum est.
units.tr: Moreover, just as the remaining precepts of God (which are the precepts of a physician) have two aspects: first, that they expose and attack the disease; second, that they promote health, so this precept given to wives must also have regard to both. For first it teaches what women are like and how corrupt they have become. Those who keep an uncorrupted nature need no precept to make them do what others do by the guidance of nature. What is commanded to women, that they be subject to their husbands, therefore shows that they are so corrupt that they are not subject and obedient to their own husbands, but would rather be mistresses themselves and lord it over their husbands than be made subject to them, like Vashti, the wife of King Ahasuerus (Esther 1). Second, this precept teaches what wives ought to be, so that they may truly be Christian and happy. The same is to be understood of the precept given to husbands.

units.la: 4 Quid ergo his Apostolus præcipit: Viri (inquit) diligite uxores, & ne sitis amarulenti adversus illas. Quo mandato docemur, quàm & nos viri simus depravati, diligentes non proximum, sed nos ipsos: non proprias uxores, sed alienas. Alioqui quid opus erat praecipere, ut uxores nostras diligamus? Ad Ephesios enim capite 5. Apostolus addit ἑαυτὰς[?]: Viri, inquiens, diligite uxores vestras. Est autem diligere vel amare (ut Aristoteles definit lib. 2. Rhetor.) velle alicui quæ putes bona, non tui ipsius gratia, & ꝓ[?] viribus etiā ea quæ volueris illi præstare. Diligendi ergo vocabulo omnia comprehenduntur, quę suis uxoribus mariti debet.
units.tr: 4 What, then, does the Apostle command them? "Husbands," he says, "love your wives, and do not be bitter toward them." By this command we are taught how depraved we husbands are, loving not our neighbour but ourselves, not our own wives but other men's. Otherwise, why would it have been necessary to command us to love our wives? For in Ephesians chapter 5 the Apostle adds [ἑαυτάς]: "Husbands," he says, "love your own wives." To love, or to be fond of (as Aristotle defines it in book 2 of the Rhetoric), is to wish someone what you think good, not for your own sake, and, as far as your powers allow, to provide them with what you wish. Therefore all that a husband owes his wife is comprehended in the word "love."

units.la: Animadverte autem (inquit Theophylast.) quomodo ejus quod cuique generi competit commonefaciat, uxores quidem ut obediant, maritos verò ut diligant: ab illis requirit subjectionem, ab his in uxores benevolentiam. Neque enim adeò subditorum requitur[?] in principes amor, ut principum in subditos charitas poscitur. Mulier nanque cùm adamatur, & ipsa reciprocam refert amoris vicissitudinem: obsequio vir mansuescit, & benignum se præbet. Quia vero fieri potest, ut quisquam diligat, & interim tamen sit amarulentus exasperatusque: maximè enim erga amatas personas hæ contingunt amarulentiæ: propterea inquit, Ne exasperemini, néve in eas sævite, more leonum, Eccles. 4. neque nimis exquirite & observate materiam objurgandi, neque exactè semper punite, neque pro levibus rebus tragœdiam excitate. Revera enim ex multa hoc fit amarulétia, quod quisquam dissideat adversus membrum suum. Ut ergo mutua & Christiana pax domi fervetur, omnem amarulentiam & nimiam morositatem procul abesse oportet. Unde hoc loco D.Paulus in descriptione officii maritorum addit: Et ne sitis amarulenti, hoc est, duri, severi, difficiles, acerbi adversus illas. Etenim amarulentiae opponitur mansuetudo, placabilitas, affabilitas, &c. Ac videtur quidem prima fronte haud necessario hoc esse adjectu.
units.tr: "Notice, however" (says Theophylact) "how he admonishes each kind of person about what belongs to it: wives indeed to obey, but husbands to love. From the former he requires subjection, from the latter goodwill toward their wives. For the love of subjects toward their rulers is not required in the same way as the charity of rulers toward their subjects is demanded. A wife, when she is loved, returns the love in turn; by her compliance the husband is softened and shows himself kind. But since it can happen that someone loves and yet is at the same time bitter and harsh (for such bitternesses arise especially toward persons who are loved), therefore he says, 'do not be exasperated, nor be savage toward them, like lions' (Eccles. 4), and do not look too closely for material for rebuke, nor punish always with exactness, nor stir up a tragedy over trifles." For in truth much of this bitterness arises from one's being at odds with one's own member. So if mutual and Christian peace is to be kept at home, all bitterness and excessive moroseness must be kept far away. Hence here Saint Paul, in describing the duty of husbands, adds: "and do not be bitter," that is, harsh, severe, difficult, sour toward them. For gentleness, placability, affability, and the like are opposed to bitterness. At first sight this addition seems hardly necessary.

units.la: Qui enim uxorem suam diligit, amarulentus erga illam esse non poterit, ut Musculus annotavit. Verum si consideremus, quam frequenter accidat, ut amor laesus in acerbissimam mutetur amarulentiam, <bl>daß man ein andern erleydet/ vnd die</bl> <bl>erste liebe erlöschet oder verbitteret wirt</bl>, id quod carnali amori evenire solet: puto manifestum fieri haud esse particulam hanc frustra adjectam ab Apostolo, ne hoc in Christianorum conjugiis fiat, cavendum esse censuit. In seculo crebra est haec mutatio, ut viri uxores suas, quas initio impense juxta carnem adamarunt, acerbo odio levi de causa prosequantur. In huiusmodi [illegible, ~9 letters] non poterunt legitimi conjugii jura servari[?]. Quare & lex divortii permittebat, ubi uxor gratiam in oculis mariti sui reperire non poterat. Deuteron. 24. Hortatur itaque Apostolus Christianos viros, ut uxores suas no uno duntaxat mense, sed constanter diligant, & caveant, ne seculariuim [?] hominum exempla secuti, conjugalem dilectionem in odium, & quæ ex odio nascitur, amarulentiam degenerare sinant. Pugnat enim amarulentia hæc ex diametro contra voluntatem Dei, qui marem & fœminam in unam carnem conjunxit, & admodum Christianorum conjugia infamat.
units.tr: For he who loves his wife cannot be bitter toward her, as Musculus has noted. But if we consider how often it happens that love that has been wounded turns into the most bitter bitterness, [that one suffers another, and the first love is extinguished or made bitter], which is wont to happen to carnal love, I think it becomes clear that this particle was not added by the Apostle in vain: he judged that care must be taken that this should not happen in the marriages of Christians. In the world this change is frequent: husbands pursue with bitter hatred, for slight cause, the wives whom at first they loved intensely according to the flesh. In such [illegible] the rights of lawful marriage cannot be kept. Therefore even the law permitted divorce where a wife could not find favour in the eyes of her husband (Deut. 24). The Apostle therefore urges Christian husbands to love their wives not for a single month only, but constantly, and to take care that, following the examples of worldly people, they do not let conjugal love degenerate into hatred, and into the bitterness that springs from hatred. For this bitterness fights directly against the will of God, who joined male and female into one flesh, and greatly disgraces the marriages of Christians.

units.la: Pugnat etiam contra præceptum Apostolicum, quod viris mandat, ut uxores suas diligant, quemadmodum Christus dilexit Eccle-siam. Dilexit autem hanc ille quidem amore gratuito, recto, discreto, vehement, fructuoso & perseveranti. Gratuito, quia non præcedentibus ipsius Ecclesiæ meritis. Unde in prima epistola Ioannis cap.quarto: In hoc est charitas, non quod nos dilexerimus Deum, sed quod ipse dilexerit nos, & cæt. Recto vero, quia non propter utilitatem suam, sed Ecclesiæ: non enim aliquo indiget, qui ipse det omnibus vitam & halitum per omnia, &c. Actor. 17. Discreto, quia ipsam amat, & vitia illius odio habet & persequitur, Ioann.1. Psalm.45. Vehementi, quia non aurum, non argentum, non gemmas, sed semetipsum exposuit pro ea. Majorem autem hac dilectionem nemo habet, quam ut animam suam ponat quis pro amicis suis, Ioann.15. 1 Ioann.3. Fructuoso & non vocali solum, quia probavit dilectionem suam exhibitione operis, Rom.5. Perseveranti deniq; Cum enim dilexisset suos, qui erat in mundo, in finem dilexit illos, Ioann. 13[?]. Sic ergo etiam viri debent diligere uxores suas: imo unusquisque proximum suum. Quod ut facere possimus, & Deum ipsum ante omnia diligere ex corde, & tota anima, & ex omnibus viribus nostris, largiatur nobis spiritum suum bonum & sanctum, qui est spiritus δυνάμεως, & ἀγάπης, & σωφρονισμοῦ[?], is de quo dicitur Ioann.1. Hic est qui baptizat spiritu sancto, Amen.
units.tr: It also fights against the apostolic precept which commands husbands to love their wives, just as Christ loved the Church. He loved her with a love that was free, right, discerning, vehement, fruitful, and persevering. Free, because it did not rest on any prior merits of the Church itself. Hence in the first epistle of John, chapter 4: "Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us," and so on. Right, indeed, because he sought not his own advantage but the Church's; for he who gives life and breath to all things in all ways needs nothing (Acts 17). Discerning, because he loves her and hates and pursues her vices (John 1; Psalm 45). Vehement, because he gave up not gold, not silver, not gems, but himself for her. "Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends" (John 15; 1 John 3). Fruitful, and not merely verbal, because he proved his love by the performance of a deed (Rom. 5). Lastly, persevering: "Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end" (John 13). So husbands too ought to love their wives, indeed each one his neighbour. That we may be able to do this, and to love God himself above all things with our whole heart, soul, and all our strength, may he grant us his good and holy Spirit, who is the spirit of power [δυνάμεως], and of love [ἀγάπης], and of sound discipline [σωφρονισμοῦ], he of whom it is said in John 1: "This is he who baptizes with the Holy Spirit." Amen.

units.la: CONCIO LIIII.
units.tr: CONCIO LIIII.

units.la: 1. Thessal. 4.
units.tr: 1 Thessalonians 4.

units.la: HAEC enim est voluntas Dei, sanctificatio vestra, ut abstineatis a scortatione, & sciat unusquisque vestrum suum vas possidere cum sanctificatione & honorē[?], non cum affectu concupiscentiæ, quemadmodum & gentes, quæ non noverunt Deum. Ne quis opprimat ac fraudet in negocio fratrem suum, propterea quod ultor est Dominus de omnibus his, quemadmodum & ante diximus vobis, ac testati sumus. Non enim vocavit nos Deus immundiciæ causa, sed ad sanctificationem. Proinde qui rejicit, non reijcit hominem, sed eum qui dedit spiritum suum sanctum in vos. 1[?] Apostolus Paulus hoc loco de nova obedientia loquitur, in qua omnes justificati & adoptati omni studio contendere debent, ut sese,suosque mores & actiones Deo patri approbent. Adhortatur autem ad quasdam virtutes, ut sanctimoniam ac innocentiam: & dehortatur a quibusdam vitiis, veluti scortatione & avaritia. Quæ duo vitia tametsi omnis conditionis hominibus adhæreant: tamen scortatio magis videtur tentare eos qui sunt cęlibes[?]: avaritia autem eos qui sunt in matrimonio collocati. Hi enim plerunque solent prætexere huic vitio multitudinem liberorum, propter quam omnino cogantur attentiores esse ad rem: cum tamen videamus sæpissimè eos longè omnium esse avarissimos, qui carent liberis. Illi verò putant sibi impunè licere scortari, quum nō sint angeli, sed homines: quemadmodum loquuntur. Utrique verò audiant hoc loco quid Apostolus præcipiat ac doceat, non ex proprio cerebro, sed ex doctrina Christi. Neenim quis obmurmurans objiceret: Quid mihi cum præceptis Apostolicis negocii? Quis verò Paulus, quis Petrus erat? An non homines & miseri & mortales erat? Respondet Paulus statim in principio: Hæc enim est voluntas Dei, &c. q. d. Quod vobis nonnulla designavi per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum, quæ custodire debeatis: non feci meopte consilio, sed ex voluntate Dei. Vult enim ille, ut sitis sancti. Deinde in fine præleti[?] contextus:Itaque qui(nos,vel hæ[?]; id est, vocationem hanc ad sanctificationem, vel nostram conte-statio-nem & adhortationem) repudiat, non hominem repudiat, sed Deum, qui vos suo sancto spiritu donat. Q.d. Quæ proferimus contra scelera, & de judicio Domini, non ex nobismetipsis, sed oraculis Dei proferimus. Deus enim dedit nobis spiritum suum, ut jam non ipsi, sed spiritus patris illa quæ audistis per nos ceu instrumenta pronunciarit. Proinde qui aspernatur doctrinam nostram, aut ministerium nostrum, non nos aspernatur, qui sanè homines sumus miseri atq; mortales: sed ipsum Deum, qui per nostrum ministerium operatur in vobis, & cujus authoritate & jussu nos hæc in medium proferimus. Huc vero pertinet Domini verba, Luc.10. Qui vos audit, me audit. Item Ioan. 20. Quorum remiseritis peccata, remittuntur eis: & quorum retinueritis, retenta sunt. Item illud Exod.16. Et dixit Moses: Audivit Dominus murmur, quo contra eum murmuratis. quid enim nos sumus? Non contra nos sunt murmurationes vestræ, sed contra Dominum.
units.tr: For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication, and that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honour, not in the passion of lust, like the Gentiles who do not know God. Let no one oppress or defraud his brother in business, because the Lord is an avenger in all these things, as we also told you before and solemnly declared. For God did not call us for the sake of uncleanness, but to sanctification. Therefore whoever rejects this does not reject a man, but God, who gives his Holy Spirit to you. The Apostle Paul in this place speaks of the new obedience, in which all who are justified and adopted ought to strive with every zeal to approve themselves, their morals and their actions, to God the Father. He exhorts them to certain virtues, such as holiness and innocence, and dissuades them from certain vices, such as fornication and avarice. Although these two vices cling to people of every condition, fornication seems chiefly to tempt the unmarried, and avarice those who are settled in marriage. For the latter very often put forward the number of their children as a pretext for this vice, saying that because of them they must be more careful about money; yet we very often see that those who have no children are by far the most greedy of all. The former think that they may fornicate with impunity, since they are not angels but men, as they put it. Let both groups hear here what the Apostle directs and teaches, not from his own brain but from the teaching of Christ. For someone grumbling might object: "What business do I have with apostolic precepts? And who was Paul, or who was Peter? Were they not men, wretched and mortal?" Paul answers at once at the beginning: "For this is the will of God," and so on, as if to say: "What we have set before you through our Lord Jesus Christ, which you ought to keep, we did not do on our own counsel, but by the will of God, for he wishes you to be holy." Then at the end of the passage: "Therefore whoever rejects" (us, or this, that is, this calling to sanctification, or our testimony and exhortation) "rejects not a man but God, who gives you his Holy Spirit." That is: what we put forward against wickedness and concerning the judgment of the Lord, we put forward not from ourselves but from the oracles of God. For God has given us his Spirit, so that the things you have heard through us as instruments are no longer ours but spoken by the Spirit of the Father. Therefore whoever scorns our teaching or our ministry does not scorn us, who are indeed wretched and mortal men, but God himself, who works in you through our ministry, and by whose authority and command we set these things forth. To this pertain the words of the Lord in Luke 10: "He who hears you hears me." Likewise John 20: "Whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them, and whose you retain, they are retained." Likewise Exodus 16: "And Moses said: The Lord has heard your murmuring, with which you murmur against him. For what are we? Your murmurings are not against us, but against the Lord."

units.la: 2 Sed videamus quæ sit voluntas Dei (teste Apostolo) in reformanda vitę nostræ conversatione. Hæc enim est voluntas Dei, sanctificatio vestra: ad hanc vos, qui prius vivebatis in immunditia, vocavit is qui sanctus est: non ad immunditiam, quia non est author peccati. Mira autem cum gratia: Hæc, inquit, est voluntas Dei, non: Hoc est praeceptum Dei: illud enim plus gratiæ & paterni amoris habet, & quodammodo officium excitat postulatiue filiorum, qui non possunt non magnificare, & cum amore revereri voluntatem Patris. Quid vero etiam populo Dei proponi potest, quod plus apud illum authoritatis habere debeat, quam voluntas Dei? ubi illa cognoscitur: nihil relinquitur amplius, quod tergiversationis excusatione recipiat. Non est quaerenda nobis alia obedientiæ præstandæ ratio, ubi de voluntate Dei constat, sed omnino valet illud: Sit pro ratione voluntas. Vult autem ille, ut simus sancti animo & corpore, hoc est, operâ demus, quo incontaminati & casti simus. Hominum sanctificatio est, quum prorsus homines in Dei voluntate acquiescunt, mundo renunciant, & carnis inquinamentis exuti, se Deo velut in sacrificium offerunt. Nihil enim offerri decet nisi purum & sanctum. Ita hac ratione pii sancti sunt, id est, soli Deo consecrati, à cujus verbo ne latum quidem digitum volentes discedunt: & satagunt pro virili, & auxilio spiritus sancti anhelant, quo Dei præceptis obsecundent, auscultent, & se totos accommodent. Græca vox ἁγιος, ut author est Plato in Cratylo, dicitur ab α particula privativa, & γαῖα[?], terra: quod illi dicantur sancti, qui à terrenis maculis & sordibus purgati sunt, & soli Deo consecrati. Theophylactus & Oecumenius[?] ñius[?] per sanctificationem hic intelligunt temperantiam & pudicitiam. Ubiq; autem (inquiunt) de hac admonet, Timotheo nimirum scribens, Corinthiis & Hebraeis, ac ejus potissimum magnam habet rationem. Novit enim tyrannidem affectuum ac operis difficultatem. Tyrannicum enim malum est impuritas, unde & multis & continuis pharmacis indiget. Verum Apostolus ipse met exponit, quid per sanctificationem intelligat, quum ait, Ut abstineatis a fornicatione, id est, ab omni immunditia, libidine, fornicatione, adulterio, petulantia, omni re Venerea, omniq; quod his adjacet & cognatum est. Siquidem multae & variae hujus malifpecies sunt, quas ne dicere quidem sustinuit. Quando autem scortationem, tanquam quae minus videatur habere vitii, vitandam esse monet, admonemur, multo magis vitandae esse adulteria, stupra, incestum & Sodomiam, quod ea communi quoq; sensu plus habere peccati censeantur. Ac quoniam sic comparata est omnis puritatis ratio, ut ubi de illa praecipitur, mox quaecunque eam inquinare possunt prohibeantur: ideo & Paulus hoc loco, ubi de custodienda sanctificatione admonuit, statim de vitanda fornicatione subjecit. Illa namque sanctificationem polluit[?], & inter gentes invaluerat: ob quam causam Apostoli Christianos ex gentibus cumprimis ut fornicationem fugerent adhortabantur. Vide Actorum decimo quinto, 1. Corinthiorum 5.6.7. Galat.5. & Ephefiorum 5.
units.tr: 2 But let us see what the will of God is (as the Apostle testifies) in the reform of our conduct of life. For this is the will of God, your sanctification: he who is holy called you, who before lived in uncleanness, to this, not to uncleanness, because he is not the author of sin. The wording is remarkable in its grace: "This," he says, "is the will of God," not "This is the command of God." For that carries more grace and paternal love, and in a manner stirs up the duty of sons, who cannot but magnify and reverence with love the will of the Father. Indeed, what can be set before the people of God that ought to have more authority with him than the will of God? Where that is known, nothing further remains that could admit the excuse of evasion. No other reason for rendering obedience is to be sought where the will of God is certain, but that saying holds wholly true: "Let the will be the reason." Now he wishes us to be holy in soul and body, that is, that we should take care to be uncontaminated and chaste. Sanctification of men is when men fully acquiesce in the will of God, renounce the world, and, stripped of the pollutions of the flesh, offer themselves to God as a sacrifice. For nothing ought to be offered except what is pure and holy. Thus in this way the godly are holy, that is, consecrated to God alone, and from whose word they do not willingly depart even by the breadth of a finger; they labour as best they can, and long for the help of the Holy Spirit, so that they may obey, listen to, and wholly adapt themselves to the precepts of God. The Greek word for holy [ἁγιος], as Plato in the Cratylus is the authority for saying, is derived from the privative particle α and from earth [γαῖα], because those are called holy who have been cleansed from earthly stains and filth and are consecrated to God alone. Theophylact and Oecumenius understand sanctification here as temperance and chastity. And everywhere (they say) he gives this admonition, certainly in writing to Timothy, to the Corinthians and to the Hebrews, and he takes especially great account of it. For he knew the tyranny of the passions and the difficulty of the work. For impurity is a tyrannical evil, and therefore needs many and continual remedies. But the Apostle himself explains what he means by sanctification, when he says: "That you abstain from fornication," that is, from all uncleanness, lust, fornication, adultery, wantonness, every venereal matter, and whatever lies close to these and is akin to them. For there are many and varied species of this evil, which he did not even think it right to name. Moreover, when he warns that fornication, as one that seems to have less of vice, is to be avoided, we are taught that adulteries, rapes, incest and sodomy are to be avoided much more, since in common opinion too they are judged to carry more guilt. And since the whole method of purity is so arranged that, where something is commanded about it, whatever can defile it is forthwith forbidden, therefore Paul also in this place, where he admonished about keeping sanctification, at once added the avoidance of fornication. For that pollutes sanctification, and it had grown strong among the Gentiles; for this reason the Apostles especially exhorted the Christians from among the Gentiles to flee fornication. See Acts 15, 1 Corinthians 5, 6 and 7, Galatians 5, and Ephesians 5.

units.la: Pergit Paulus in præcepto de puritate & sanctimonia: quodq; modo privativè dixerat de fuga scortationis, hoc jam positivè dicit, servandam esse castitatem corporis.
units.tr: Paul continues in the precept about purity and holiness: what he had said in a privative way about fleeing fornication, he now says positively, namely that chastity of the body is to be kept.

units.la: Addit verò quandam pleniorem periphrasin hujus sententiæ, ut indicet magnam prudentiam, cautionemque in hoc præcepto Dei adhibibendam esse, cùm mille occasiones turpitudinum, in sermonibus & gestibus, aliisque rationibus, vel invitis piorum animis obtrudantur, præsertim in illa tanta Gentilium licentia libidinum. Verba ejus sunt hæc: Sciatq; quisq; vestrùm suum vas cum sanctimonia ac honestate possidere.
units.tr: Moreover, he adds a somewhat fuller periphrasis of this sentence, to indicate that great prudence and caution must be applied to this command of God, since a thousand occasions of shameful conduct, in speech and gestures and other ways, are forced upon even unwilling godly minds, especially in that great licence of lusts among the Gentiles. His words are these: "And let each of you know how to possess his own vessel with holiness and honour."

units.la: Sunt qui per vas uxorem intelligunt (ut & 1.Petr.3.intelligitur) præcipiúque ab Apostolo, ut quilibet uxore sua pudicè & moderatè utatur, non abutatur per affectum concupiscentiæ. Et sanè convenit Christianas uxores sanctè & castè diligere, non impudenter, & quasi ferina rabie illas ardere, ac perditè amare. Honorabile enim connubium, & thorus immaculatus in omnibus, Hebr. 13.[?] Unde & poeta Martialis:
units.tr: There are those who understand by the vessel a wife (as is also understood in 1 Peter 3), and the Apostle especially commands that each should use his wife chastely and with moderation, not abuse her through the passion of lust. And indeed it is fitting to love Christian wives holily and chastely, not shamelessly, and not to burn for them with a kind of savage rage or to love them to ruin. For "marriage is honourable, and the bed undefiled in all things," Hebrews 13. Hence also the poet Martial:

units.la: Non tristis thorus, attamen pudicus.
units.tr: Not a sad marriage bed, yet chaste.

units.la: Christi etiam charitas, qua Ecclesiam suam amat & honestissimè & ardentissimè, conjugalis amoris typus sive exemplar esse debet, Ephes. 5. Verùm quum promiscuè Paulus hîc alloquatur viros ac mulieres, legemque ponat non solùm illis, qui uxores habent, verùm etiam innuptis ac viduis, non dubium est, quin vas pro corpore accipiat, usitato Hebræis more (1. Reg.21. Actor.9.) ipsa quoq; voce alludens ad rem figulinam, primamq; hominis conditionem. Vt enim homo se fragilem esse nosset, & rebus caducis se minimè crederet, vel nimis testà hanc fictilem curaret, genioque indulgeret, de terra conditus legitur. Et Iefaias cap.52. hoc ipso loquendi genere, Exite, inquit, de medio ejus, mundemini qui portatis vasa Domini, id est, vos ipsi qui estis Deo consecrati & templa sancti spiritus mundemini. Hanc metaphoram illustrat Cicero Tusculan.1. inquiens: Corpus est quasi quoddà vas & receptaculum animi. Præcipit ergo Apostolus vt quilibet nostrùm corpus suum proprium quod à Deo accepit, & quod sibi ipse Deus in templũ delegit, quodq; nunc membrum Christi est (1. Cor.6.) cum sanctificatione & honore possideat, i.honestè, mit sucht[?] vnnd ehr[?]. Quia corpus suum probro & macula aspergit, qui ipsum prostituít ad scortatioēm, Roman.1. Quare etiam 1. Corinth.6. dicit, scortatorem in proprium corpus peccare. Hoc enim totum inquinat atque dehonestat. Quoniam autem ad possessionem vasorum & instrumentorum (σκευος[?] enim & vas, & instrumentum, seu quodcunq; organum significat) præsertim preciosorũ simul & fragilium, requiritur scientia, ad compe-tencentem usu'n pertinens:quæritur,quídnam ho ioris[?] debeatur corporibus nostris, ut iis legitimè utamur: id quod magnæ scientiæ res est.'Respondetur.Legitimus eorū honor est, primò,si pro sua infirmitate serviant gloriæ Dei,à quo sunt condita:deinde,si necessitatibus nostris famulentur, secundū quod à Deo sunt disposita: tertiò,si nullis peccatorum inquinamentis polluantur: postremò, si necessariis alimentis ac curis non destituantur,sed eorum valetudo viresq; confervantur,de quo corporali honore corporum, Rom.13.Colof.2. 1.Tim.5.
units.tr: Christ's own love, by which he loves his Church most honourably and most ardently, ought to be the type or pattern of conjugal love, Eph. 5. But since Paul here addresses men and women together, and lays down the law not only for those who have wives but also for the unmarried and widows, there is no doubt that he takes "vessel" to mean the body, in the common Hebrew manner (1 Kings 21; Acts 9), alluding by the very word to the potter's craft and to man's first condition. For so that man might know he is frail, and not trust himself to passing things, or give too much care to this earthen vessel and indulge the flesh, we read that he was made from earth. Isaiah 52 uses this very way of speaking: "Depart from the midst of her," he says, "be clean, you who carry the vessels of the Lord," that is, you yourselves who are consecrated to God and are temples of the Holy Spirit, be clean. Cicero, Tusculan Disputations 1, illustrates this metaphor, saying: "The body is as it were a certain vessel and receptacle of the mind." The Apostle therefore instructs that each of us should possess his own body, which he received from God, which God himself has chosen as his temple, and which is now a member of Christ (1 Cor. 6), with sanctification and honour, that is, honourably. For he who prostitutes his body to fornication stains and blemishes it with disgrace, Rom. 1. Hence also 1 Cor. 6 says that the fornicator sins against his own body, for this defiles and dishonours the whole. Since, moreover, the possession of vessels and instruments (for the Greek skeuos [σκεῦος] means vessel, instrument, or any organ), especially precious and fragile ones, requires knowledge of their proper use, the question is asked what honour is owed to our bodies, so that we may use them lawfully; and this is a matter of great knowledge. The answer is this. Their lawful honour is, first, if according to their weakness they serve the glory of God who made them; second, if they minister to our needs, as God has ordained; third, if they are polluted by no stains of sin; last, if they are not deprived of necessary food and care, but their health and strength are preserved. Concerning this bodily honour of bodies, see Rom. 13, Col. 2, 1 Tim. 5.

units.la: Paulus, quia opposita juxta se posita,magis elucescunt, subjungit: Non cum affectu concupiscentię,seu cupiditatis libidine:quæ particula per oppositum sanctificationis & honoris declarat, quomodo unusquisq; vas suum cum sanctificatione & honore possidere debeat. Contrarii sunt inter se affectus sanctificationis,& affectus desiderii seu concupiscentiæ,quæ est in carne corporum nostrorum, & gignit scortationem, adulteria,& omnis generis immundam libidinem. Est itaque corpora nostra possidere cum sanctificatione, non indulgere concupiscentiis carnis, sed affectus & passiones illarum internasq; ustiones reprimere ac mortificare, quo serviant non peccato,sed voluntati Dei.
units.tr: Paul, because opposites placed side by side stand out more clearly, adds: "not in the passion of lust," or the lust of desire. This clause, by contrast with sanctification and honour, shows how each one ought to possess his vessel with sanctification and honour. The feeling of sanctification and the feeling of desire or lust are opposed to each other; lust lies in the flesh of our bodies and begets fornication, adultery and every kind of impure lust. To possess our bodies with sanctification is therefore not to indulge the lusts of the flesh, but to restrain and mortify their emotions, passions and inner burnings, so that they serve not sin but the will of God.

units.la: Et adddit exemplum non imitandū, sed fugiendum,dicens: Quemadmodum & gentes,quę non noverunt Deū,scil.vera & recta notitia, de qua Ioann. 17. Qui Deum porrò non noverunt, neque retributionis spem habent: itaque omnia ad voluptatem faciunt. Quam vero inconveniens est Christianis, si similes sint gentibus immundis ac Deum ignorantibus, cùm ipsi sint per sanguinem Christi mundati, & ad cognitionem Dei perducti. Docet ergo Paulus hoc loco, ubi regnat vera Dei cognitio, domari oportere concupiscentias: & quia sanctitati nihil magis contrarium, quàm scortandi fœditas, hanc omnibus modis esse fugiendam: id quod etiam hoc Decalogi præcepto, Non mœchaberis, mandatur.
units.tr: And he adds an example not to be imitated but to be fled from, saying: "Just as the Gentiles also, who do not know God" (namely, with true and right knowledge, of which John 17 speaks), "who do not know God, have no hope of reward; so they do everything for pleasure." How unfitting it is for Christians to be like the unclean Gentiles who ignore God, since they have been cleansed through the blood of Christ and brought to the knowledge of God. Paul therefore teaches in this place, where the true knowledge of God reigns, that lusts must be tamed; and since nothing is more contrary to holiness than the foulness of fornication, it must be fled in every way. This is also commanded by the precept of the Decalogue: "You shall not commit adultery."

units.la: 3 Hoc præceptum, quemadmodum & alia, tametsi non possimus perfectè implere in hanc carne: tamen propositæ sunt nobis aliquot rationes, quibus illud sic implere possumus, ut coram Deo verè pudici, casti & sancti judicemur. Primùm agenda est pœnitentia, quæ duabus partibus constat. Una est, quòd debemus agnoscere nostram impuritatem & impudicitiam, & fateri quòd propter eam simus meriti æternam internecionem. Altera est, quòd debeamus agnoscere Iesum Christum, & credere, quòd expiaverit nostram impuritatem, & reconciliaverit nos cum Deo. Hac fide, Christus filius virginis, qui nullam unquam ne cogitationem quidem impudicam habuit, donatur nobis cum omni sua justicia & pudicitia. Quare cùm credimus in eum, reputat nos Deus propter ipsum tam castos & pudicos, quàm si nos hanc legem perfectè implevissemus.
units.tr: 3 This precept, like the others, although we cannot fulfil it perfectly in this flesh, nevertheless several reasons are set before us by which we can fulfil it so that we are judged truly chaste, pure and holy before God. First, repentance must be undertaken, which consists of two parts. One is that we must acknowledge our impurity and unchastity, and confess that on account of it we deserve eternal destruction. The other is that we must acknowledge Jesus Christ and believe that he has expiated our impurity and reconciled us to God. By this faith, Christ, the son of the virgin, who never had even an unchaste thought, is given to us with all his righteousness and chastity. Therefore, when we believe in him, God reckons us as chaste and pure on his account, as if we had perfectly fulfilled this law.

units.la: Deinde non est sentiendum, quòd Deus donet nobis pudicitiam Christi in hunc usum, ut liceat nobis deinceps impudicè vivere, sed ut operam demus (quemadmodū Brentius scribit) quo naturalem nostram impudicitiam spiritu Christi compescamus, & non præbeamus membra nostra serva immundiciei. Etsi enim talis compescentia non est per se perfecta impletio hujus legis, tamen Deus exigit eam, & delectatur ea propter Christum filium suum. Cùm enim ipse sit mens castissima, vult etiam ut nos castitati studeamus. Quare necessitas urget, ut exhibeamus nosipsos organa Spiritui sancto, quo compescat impudicos motus cordis, & excitet in nobis pudicitiam.
units.tr: Next, it must not be thought that God gives us the chastity of Christ for this purpose, that it may be lawful for us henceforth to live impurely; rather, we should take pains (as Brenz writes) to restrain our natural impurity by the Spirit of Christ, and not offer our members as servants of uncleanness. For although such restraint is not in itself the perfect fulfilment of this law, God nevertheless requires it and takes pleasure in it on account of Christ his Son. Since he himself is the most chaste mind, he also wills that we strive for chastity. Therefore necessity urges us to offer ourselves as instruments to the Holy Spirit, so that he may restrain the impure movements of the heart and stir up chastity in us.

units.la: Recensemus ergo, quę nobis facienda videantur, ut Spiritus sanctus habeat organa excitádæ in nobis pudicitiæ. Quanquam nō ignoramus fore, ut non omnes huic doctrinæ obediant. Scimus enim multos conqueri se his doctrinis redigi in ordines Monasticos. Sed sciamus etiam non omnes consequi hæreditatem cœlestis regni. Multi, inquit Christus vocati, sed pauci electi. Et iterum, Lata est via & spaciosa, quæ abducit in exitium, multique sunt qui ingrediuntur per illam. Et Paulus: Non est omnium fides. Etsi enim lex Domini & evangelion filii ejus prædicanda sunt universæ creaturæ: tamen hi foli capiunt verum & cœlestem fructum ejus, qui ex fide in Christū filium Dei resipiscunt, & ad cœlestem hæreditatem tota mente atque omni animo aspirant. Et hi, sicut necessarium est eis, ut obediant huic legi, & ducant semper honestam ac pudicam vitam: ita etiam omne studium suum in hoc conferent, ut obedientiam suam Domino servatori ipsorum probent. Reliqua turba præceps in suum ipsa exitium, furioso impetu ruit. Quare in tanta hominum, inter quos & aliquot hæredes cælestis regni admixti sunt, colluvie & impudicitia, danda nobis est opera, ut cùm non possimus omnes eripere, saltem eos, qui verè & ex animo tenentur studio pietatis, eripiamus.
units.tr: Let us therefore list what seems to us to be done, so that the Holy Spirit may have instruments for stirring up chastity in us. Yet we are not unaware that not all will obey this teaching. For we know that many complain that these teachings drive them into monastic orders. But let us also know that not all obtain the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. "Many are called," says Christ, "but few are chosen." And again: "Wide and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many are those who enter by it." And Paul: "Not all have faith." For although the law of the Lord and the gospel of his Son must be preached to every creature, yet only these take its true and heavenly fruit, who by faith repent in Christ the Son of God, and aspire with their whole mind and every soul to the heavenly inheritance. Just as it is necessary for these to obey this law and always lead an honest and chaste life, so too they will direct all their effort to this, that they may prove their obedience to the Lord their Saviour. The rest of the crowd, headlong to their own destruction, rush on with furious onslaught. Therefore, amid such a mass of men, among whom some heirs of the heavenly kingdom are also mixed, and such unchastity, we must take pains that, although we cannot rescue all, we rescue at least those who are truly and sincerely held by zeal for piety.

units.la: Propheta Amos cap. 3. dicit: Quomodo si servat pastor de ore leonis duo crura, & extremum auriculæ, sic eruentur filii Israel. Et iterum cap. 4. Facti estis sicut torris raptus ab incendio. Sic & nobis nostro ministerio conandum est, ut in tanta morum corruptione, si non omnes, at saltem aliquos ex incendio, & ab ore leonis rapiamus.
units.tr: The prophet Amos, chapter 3, says: "As a shepherd rescues from the lion's mouth two legs, or a piece of an ear, so shall the children of Israel be rescued." And again, chapter 4: "You have become like a brand snatched from the fire." So also we must strive by our ministry that, in such corruption of morals, if not all, at least some may be snatched from the fire and from the lion's mouth.

units.la: Ante omnia igitur credamus & sciamus, nos debere scortationem atq; adulterium sugere, & pudicitiam, castitatemq; sectari: item necesse habere, ac posse. Debere quidem, quoniam æquum, justum & legitimum est. Nam Deus, qui noster creator, pater, Dominus, maritus, pastor & caput est, hoc mandadavit & præcepit nobis, qui fumus ejus creatura, filii, servi, sponsa, oves, corpus atque subditi. Necesse autem habere:ut ne videlicet fidem perdamus, iram Dei provocemus, in stagnum ignis deijciamur. Posse vero, non sanè propriis viribus sine Dei auxilio, verum ejus ope, apud quem omnia possibilia, & cujus præcepta natis ex ipso non modo non impossibilia, sed nec gravia sunt, Matthæi 19. 1. Ioannis 5. Si enim impossibile esset homini fideli se castum & continentem præbere, non potuissent Iosephi, Booz, Iob, Iudith, Sara, Sufanna, Corinthii, de quibus Genef. 39. Ruth. 3. Iob. 31. Iudit. 13. Tob. 3. Dan. 13. 1. Corinthior. 6. Et tales (nimirum impudici, scortatores, adulteri, molles, cinædi, &c.) quidem nonnulli eratis (inquit Apostolus) sed abluti estis, sed sancti, sed iusti facti, per nomen Domini Iesu, perque Dei nostri spiritum. Quid dicam de Socrate, qui non fuit Christianus, sed Ethnicus? Hunc cum Phyliognomus [?] quidam hominem incontinentissimum & libidinosissimum esse dixisset, cæteris illum, ut arte sua turpiter deceptum deridentibus, illum verissimè hoc dixisse Socrates quidem confessus est: talem enim se omnino esse natura, qualem ille ex facie indicavit: sed addidit, mores naturæ similes futuros fuisse, nisi hos philosophiæ studium emendasset. Quid de Augusto Cæsare, qui cupidissimus mulierum erat, & praesentim earum, quæ maritis nupsissent. Hunc enim Athenodorus gladio vibrato eo adegit, ut sacramento præstito polliceretur, nunquam se deinceps toros alienos contaminaturum: ut refert Michael: Glycas Annal. par.3. Cæterum, ut idem dicit, mirari defuisse barbaros quosdam, qui virtutis & honesti amore ducerentur. Nam quum hominem fingeret Deus, eidem honesti & pravi discrimen indidit. Quo factum est, ut non Platonis modo sectatores vitam injustam & sceleratam odio prosequuti sint, verum etiam homines barbari non pauci. Anacharsis natione Scytha tanto castitatis & exercitiorum virtutis amore tenebatur, ut etiam cubans labra verendaque suis ipsemet manibus comprimeret. Nimirum non vigilans modo, verum etiam dormiens ostendebat, quàm accurata custodia duo istæc corporis membra indigeant. Ergo, ut Oecumenius cum Theophylacto scribit in hæc verba Pauli, Ut sciat unusquisque vestrûm, &c. castitas & continentia opus habet exercitio & disciplina.
units.tr: Above all, then, let us believe and know that we ought to flee fornication and adultery, and pursue purity and chastity; likewise that we are bound to do so, and are able. We ought, indeed, since it is fair, just and lawful. For God, who is our creator, father, Lord, husband, shepherd and head, has commanded and enjoined this upon us, who are his creatures, sons, servants, bride, sheep, body and subjects. We are also bound, lest we lose faith, provoke the wrath of God, and be cast into the lake of fire. We are able, indeed not by our own strength without the help of God, but by his aid, with whom all things are possible, and whose precepts are not only not impossible for those born of him but not even burdensome, Matt. 19; 1 John 5. For if it were impossible for a believing man to show himself chaste and continent, Joseph, Boaz, Job, Judith, Sarah, Susanna and the Corinthians, of whom we read in Gen. 39; Ruth 3; Job 31; Judith 13; Tobit 3; Dan. 13; 1 Cor. 6, could not have done so. "And some of you were such" (impure, fornicators, adulterers, effeminates, catamites and so on), says the Apostle, "but you have been washed, you have been sanctified, you have been made righteous, through the name of the Lord Jesus and through the Spirit of our God." What shall I say of Socrates, who was not a Christian but a heathen? When a certain physiognomist had said that this man was most incontinent and lustful, the others mocked him as shamefully deceived by his art; but Socrates admitted that the man had spoken most truly, for he was altogether such by nature as the man had indicated from his face. He added, however, that his morals would have been like his nature, had not the study of philosophy corrected them. What of Augustus Caesar, who was most eager for women, especially those who were married? For Athenodorus, brandishing a sword, compelled him to promise by a sworn oath that he would never again defile another's marriage bed, as Michael Glycas reports in the third part of his Annals. Moreover, as the same writer says, he marvelled that there were some barbarians who were led by love of virtue and honesty. For when God fashioned man, he implanted in him the distinction between the honourable and the wicked. Hence it came about that not only the followers of Plato pursued an unjust and wicked life with hatred, but also not a few barbarian men. Anacharsis, a Scythian by nation, was held by such love of chastity and of the practice of virtue that, even while lying down, he pressed his lips and private parts with his own hands. Surely he showed, by watching not only when awake but even when asleep, how carefully these two members of the body need guarding. Therefore, as Oecumenius with Theophylact writes on these words of Paul, "That each of you may know," etc., chastity and continence need exercise and discipline.

units.la: Quid igitur faciendum est, qui voluerit se castum exhibere? Nullus autem non volet, qui serio cogitaverit, quàm id sit non solùm honestum & laudabile, jucundum & suave, utile ac bonum: verùm etiam, ut dictû est, legitimum ac justû, necessarium & haud quaquam impossibile.
units.tr: What, then, must be done by one who wishes to show himself chaste? Hardly anyone who has seriously considered it will not want to, for chastity is not only honourable and praiseworthy, pleasant and sweet, useful and good, but also, as has been said, lawful and right, necessary, and by no means impossible.

units.la: Initiò, diligenter incumbendum est preeationi. Orandus est Deus, ut spiritu sancto suo nos adjuvet, ad compescendos impuros motus cordis, & gubernet universam vitam nostram. Pudicitia enim est singulare donum Dei, Sapient.8.Paulus ad Galat.5. numerat ἐγκράτειαν[?], hoc est, continentiam, quæ est genus pudicitiæ, inter fructus spiritus. Dona autem Dei impetranda sunt ab ipso precibus, Iacob.1. & 4. Luc.11. Quare cùm tentamur affectu impudicitiæ, properandū est ad preces, & orandum, ne in tentationem inducamur. Iam & hoc affectu in nobis exardescente, non minus nobis periculi instat, quàm si capitalis hostis staret ante nos vibrato gladio, & minaretur nobis præsente morte. Sicut ergo in tali periculo opportunissimum tempus est exclamandi ad Deum, & invocandi cœleste auxilium: ita etiam in exardescente impudicitiæ affectu necessitas urgere nos debet, ut attollamus oculos nostros ad Deum Patrem domini nostri Iesu Christi, & petamus, ut inter hæc Satanæ jacula nos illæsos conservet. Oremus cùm David Psalm.51. & Siracide cap.21[?]. & cùm discipulis Christi ac tota Ecclesia, Matth.6. Luc.11. Corda munda crea in nobis Deus, & innova spiritum rectum in visceribus nostris. Ne proijcias nos à facie tua, & spiritum sanctum tuum ne auferas à nobis. Omne desiderium pravum averte à nobis. Aufer à nobis ventris concupiscentias, & concubitus concupiscentiæ ne apprehendant nos.
units.tr: First, one must apply oneself diligently to prayer. God must be called upon to help us by his Holy Spirit, to restrain the impure movements of the heart and to govern our whole life. For chastity is a singular gift of God (Wisd. 8). Paul in Galatians 5 counts self-control [ἐγκράτεια], that is, continence, which is a kind of chastity, among the fruits of the Spirit. Gifts of God, however, are to be obtained from him by prayer (James 1 and 4; Luke 11). Therefore, when we are tempted by the desire of impurity, we must hasten to prayer and pray that we be not led into temptation. Moreover, when this desire blazes up within us, the danger is no less than if a deadly enemy stood before us with a brandished sword and threatened us with present death. Just as in such peril the most fitting time is to cry out to God and call for heavenly help, so in the blaze of lust necessity ought to urge us to lift our eyes to God the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ and to ask that he keep us unharmed amid these darts of Satan. Let us pray with David (Psalm 51), with the son of Sirach (chap. 21), and with the disciples of Christ and the whole Church (Matt. 6; Luke 11): "Create in us a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within us. Cast us not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from us. Turn away from us every wicked desire. Take from us the lusts of the belly and the desires of the flesh, that they may not take hold of us."

units.la: Fiat voluntas tua, ô Pater cœlestis, ut in cœlo, & in terra. Voluntas tua sanctificatio nostra est, ut abstineamus à scortatione. Libera nos à malo, cum primis verò spiritu fornicationum, vom buren[?] Teuffel. Wehr vnd steus[?] allem fleisch vnnd blut/ Das wider Deinen willen thut/Amen.
units.tr: "Your will be done, O heavenly Father, on earth as it is in heaven. Your will is our sanctification, that we abstain from fornication. Deliver us from evil, and above all from the spirit of fornication." Defend us from the devil, and keep from all flesh and blood whatever acts against your will. Amen.

units.la: Secundò fugiendæ atq; vitandæ sunt causæ impellentes & allicientes ad immundiciem, libidinem & scortationem, eamq; foventes. Qua de re etiam Erasmus Roterodamus scripsit in Enchiridio militis Christiani, circa finem fere, ubi agit de remediis contra specialia quædam vitia, & primùm contra libidinem & libidinis incentivum.
units.tr: Secondly, the causes that drive and entice to uncleanness, lust and fornication, and that foster it, must be fled and avoided. On this matter Erasmus of Rotterdam also wrote in the Enchiridion of the Christian Soldier, near the end, where he treats of remedies against certain special vices, and first against lust and the incitement of lust.

units.la: Ac cùm luxuria fit ignis(Iob.31.)necessarió erit triplex remedium contra eam, sicut contra ignem nimium, cin[?] grosse vnd grausame Brunst. Nam si olla, quæ juxta ignem est, adeò ebulliat, ut effundatur quod in ea continetur, aliquod horum trium fieri consuevit: vel aqua frigida ollæ infunditur, vel de lignis subtrahitur, vel olla ab igne elon-gatur.
units.tr: And since lechery is a fire (Job 31), there will necessarily be a threefold remedy against it, just as against an excessive fire, that is, a great and cruel burning. For if a pot standing near the fire boils so violently that what is inside spills over, one of three things is usually done: cold water is poured into the pot, or wood is taken away from the fire, or the pot is moved away from the fire.

units.la: Primò igitur, si quis se uri sentit igne luxuriæ, ad aquam recurrat, & aquam infundat. Quemadmodum enim merito domum suam amitteret, qui videns domum suam comburi, aquam non quæreret: sic merito ignis luxuriæ eos cōsumit, qui ad aquā, quæ talem ignem extinguere valet, non currunt, tàm videant ignem hunc non vestes, non supellectilem, non domum, sed seipsos consumere. Quæ est autem illa aqua, quæ in istiusmodi incendio quæreda & haurienda est? Non ista furtiva, quæ ex puteo angusto hauritur, de qua Proverb. 9. & 23. Sed illa, de qua Prov. 5. Bibe aquâ de cisterna tua: & 1. Cor 7. Propter stupra vitanda, suam quisque uxorem habeat: & suum quæq; virum habeat. Fons miraculosus in Epiro est, ut Augustin. scribit lib. 21. de Civ Dei, cap. 5. qui faces accensas extinguit quidē sicut alii fontes, verùm extinctas redaccendit, quod cum aliis commune non habet. Tale quid habet & scortatio, ut non tam extinguat, quàm redaccendat libidinis incendium.
units.tr: First, then, if anyone feels himself burning with the fire of lust, let him run to water and pour it on. For just as a man would rightly lose his house if, seeing it on fire, he did not seek water, so the fire of lust rightly consumes those who do not run to the water that can quench such a fire. Let them see that this fire consumes not their clothes, not their furniture, not their house, but themselves. What, then, is that water which must be sought and drawn in such a fire? Not the stolen water drawn from a narrow well, of which Proverbs 9 and 23 speak, but that of which Proverbs 5 speaks: "Drink water from your own cistern"; and 1 Cor. 7: "To avoid fornication, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband." There is a miraculous spring in Epirus, as Augustine writes in On the City of God, book 21, chapter 5, which quenches lit torches just as other springs do, but rekindles them once they are put out, something it does not share with others.
