Fornication has something of this kind: it does not so much quench as rekindle the fire of lust.

units.la: Non igitur talis aqua quærenda est, à Satana demonstrata, <bl>Des</bl> <bl>Teuffels Fül[?] und lösch wasser</bl>: sed ea quæ à Deo in ejus verbo ostenditur. Legitur de Benedicto, quòd semel immerserit se in gelidam aquam, propter vehementè tentationem carnis. Idem Bonavent. scribit de Francisco, cap. 5. in ejus Legenda. Item de Bernardo, quòd propter ardorem luxurię inter spinas projecerit se, ac vulnerarit corpus suum, & sic per vulnera carnis extinxerit ardorem libidinis. Et de alio quodam, qui tentatus à luxuria dixit: Si hoc egero, æternum ignem merebor. Ergo probare volo, utrum possim sustinere, & sic combusit sibi digitos, ac ita compescuit in se luxuriam. Hoc aliquo modo est in ebullientem ollam, seu testaceum vas, hoc est, corpus sive carnem suam libidinosam, infundere aquam tribulationis afflictionisque. Sed aqua tribulationis potest etiam alio modo usurpari, si quando contingit aliquem luxuriæ peccato tentari: nempe sic, ut quis cogitet de pœnis corporalibus & æternis, quæ debentur peccato luxuriæ, cujus oblivionem facit malitia unius horæ, teste Siracida cap. 11. Dolor enim vulneris absterget mala, Proverb.20. Luc.7.Repetendum ergo est memoria, quanto odio Deus hoc impudicitiæ peccatū prosequatur. Cùm enim Deus omnia peccata odio habeat, hoc peccatum ita detestatur & abominatur, ut puniat ipsum tam corporalibus, in hoc seculo, quàm spiritualibus & æternis, in altero seculo supplicitis. Itaq; Deus punit hoc peccatum, morbis, inopia, infamia, & multis id genus aliis malis. Homines ante diluvium, cum designarent varia scelera, magnam dabant operam impudicitiæ. Itaque necesse habuerunt diluvio perire, Genes. 6. In Sodoma cives erant impurissimi: perierunt igitur incendio, Genes.19. Israelitæ propter fornicationem prostrati sunt in deserto, nec intrare potuerūt in terram promissionis, Num.25. 1.Corinth.10. Sacerdotis filia in stupro deprehensa, flammis exurebatur, secundum legem, Levit.21. Fornicans virgo in domo patris à populo lapidabatur, Deuteronom.22. Fornicator Zambri occiditur à Phinees, Numer.25. Samson studuit impudicitiæ: quare non solùm sortitu-dinem dinem suam amisit, verùm etiam captus est ab hostibus & cæcatus, Iud.16. Beniamitæ defendunt impudicos adolescentes, qui concubina Levitæ turpissimè abusi fuerât. Quare universa penè tribus deleta est, Iud.19. Vide mihi Davidem: quàm horribiliter punitum est divinitus adulterium ejus. Nec tantùm in populo Dei extant talia exempla, verùm etiam in historiis gentium, quæ testantur sæpe politias, & regna propter impudicitiam non solùm mutata esse, verùm etiam omnino deleta.
units.tr: Therefore one should not seek such water, the devil's fire and extinguishing water shown by Satan, but that which is shown by God in his Word. It is read of Benedict that, on account of a violent temptation of the flesh, he once plunged himself into cold water. Bonaventure writes the same of Francis, chapter 5 of his Legend. Likewise of Bernard, that because of the burning of lust he threw himself among thorns and wounded his body, and so quenched the ardour of lust through the wounds of the flesh. And of another man who, tempted by lust, said: "If I do this, I shall deserve eternal fire. I want to test whether I can endure it," and so burned his own fingers, and thus restrained lust in himself. In some way this is pouring the water of tribulation and affliction into the boiling pot, that is, into one's own lustful body or flesh. But the water of tribulation can also be used in another way, when someone happens to be tempted by the sin of lust: namely, by thinking of the bodily and eternal punishments owed to the sin of lust, whose forgetfulness is caused by an hour of wickedness, as Sirach 11 attests: "For the pain of a wound drives out evils" (Prov. 20; Luke 7). Therefore one must recall how greatly God hates this sin of impurity. For since God hates all sins, he so detests and abominates this sin that he punishes it with bodily punishments in this age, and with spiritual and eternal ones to be suffered in the next. So God punishes this sin with diseases, want, infamy, and many other evils of this kind. Before the flood, when men were committing various crimes, they were especially devoted to impurity; therefore they had to perish in the flood (Gen. 6). The citizens of Sodom were most impure; therefore they perished in fire (Gen. 19). The Israelites, struck down in the desert because of fornication, could not enter the promised land (Num. 25; 1 Cor. 10). A priest's daughter caught in whoredom was burned with fire, according to the law (Lev. 21). A fornicating virgin in her father's house was stoned by the people (Deut. 22). The fornicator Zimri was slain by Phinehas (Num. 25). Samson pursued impurity; therefore he not only lost his strength but was also taken captive by his enemies and blinded (Judg. 16). The Benjamites defended the impure young men who had shamefully abused the Levite's concubine; therefore almost the whole tribe was destroyed (Judg. 19). Look at David: how horribly his adultery was punished by God. Such examples exist not only among the people of God, but also in the histories of the nations, which often attest that commonwealths and kingdoms have been not only changed but utterly destroyed on account of impurity.

units.la: Olim apud Cumanos erat mos, ut adulterae imponerentur asinis, & per civitatem, illis in ignominiam, ducebantur, de quo Plutarchus. Apud Germanos veteres ante natum Christum, maritus adulterae tondebat comam, & expellebat domo, tundebatque illam per plateas civitatis, ut Cornelius Tacitus scribit. Dionysius quum intellexisset filium cui principatum relicturus erat, ingenui viri conjugem adulterasse, iratus interrogavit, an unquam tale quicquam in patre comperisset? Hic adolescens: Tu enim, inquit, non habebas patrem regem. Nec tu, inquit Dionysius, filium regem habiturus es, ni talia perpetrare desinas. Tyrannus in filio dignum exhæredatione crimen judicabat adulterium, qui hodie magnatum ludus est. Severitatem legis divinæ, quæ adulterum corpore & vita privat, Levit. 20. Deut. 22.imitata est lex Iulia apud Romanos. Per[?]missum etiam legibus est, occidere adulterum in uxore deprehensum.
units.tr: Once among the Cumaeans it was the custom that adulteresses were placed on asses and led through the city for their shame, as Plutarch reports. Among the ancient Germans, before the birth of Christ, a husband cut off the hair of his adulterous wife, drove her from the house, and beat her through the streets of the town, as Cornelius Tacitus writes. When Dionysius learned that his son, to whom he was going to leave the principate, had committed adultery with the wife of a free man, he asked angrily whether he had ever found any such thing in his father. The young man replied: "Yes, for you did not have a king as your father." "And you," said Dionysius, "will not have a king as your son, unless you stop committing such deeds." A tyrant judged adultery in a son a crime worthy of disinheritance, whereas today it is a game of great men. The Roman Julian law imitated the severity of the divine law, which deprives the adulterer of body and life (Lev. 20; Deut. 22). By the laws it is also permitted to kill an adulterer caught with one's wife.

units.la: · Proverb. 7. comparatur adulter bovi ad victimam ducto, & avi ad laqueum festinanti: eo quod nescias, quod de periculo animae illius agitur. Quomodo enim sciret, cum adulterium hominem excaecet, dementet, cor & rationem ei auferat, fitque opus tenebrarum. Hof.4. Ecclesi.19 Dan.3. 2.Reg.11. Romanos 1. Iob.24. Hujus admonere voluerunt quosvis, qui Cupidinem, Veneris filium caecum pinxere.
units.tr: Proverbs 7 compares the adulterer to an ox led to the slaughter and a bird hurrying into a snare, because he does not know that his soul's life is at stake. For how would he know? Adultery blinds a man, drives him out of his mind, takes away his heart and his reason, and becomes a work of darkness. Hosea 4; Ecclesiastes 19; Daniel 3; 2 Kings 11; Romans 1; Job 24. Those who painted Cupid, the blind son of Venus, meant to warn everyone of this.

units.la: 1. Corinth.5. dicit Apostolus: Si quis cum frater appellatur, fuerit fornicator, cum ejusmodi ne cibum quidem capiatis: <bl>wirtig vnd wert/daß ein Bürgermann oder Edelmann mit jhm esse oder trincke.</bl>
units.tr: 1 Corinthians 5: The Apostle says: "If anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator, do not even eat with such a one." It is so shameful and unworthy that a citizen or nobleman should eat or drink with him.

units.la: Sed nec hoc praetereundum est, quod scribitur Prover. 6. Precium scorti, vix est unius panis: hoc est, scortatio tam maledicta est, ut scortatori, quamvis diviti, vix relinquat panem, sed conijciat eum in extremam paupertatem. Et cap. 29. Socius scortorum perdet substantiam.
units.tr: But this too must not be passed over, what is written in Proverbs 6: "The price of a harlot is scarcely a loaf of bread." That is, whoring is so cursed that it leaves the whoremonger, however rich he is, scarcely a loaf, and casts him into extreme poverty. And ch. 29: "The companion of harlots will waste his substance."

units.la: Deinde (quod maximum est) impudicitia punitur supplicio aeterni ignis, nisi in Christo resipiscas. Ita enim scriptum est: 1. Corinth. 6. Neque fornicatores, neque adulteri, neque molles accipient regni Dei haereditatem.
units.tr: Then (and this is the greatest thing) impurity is punished with the torment of eternal fire, unless you repent in Christ. For it is written: 1 Corinthians 6: "Neither fornicators, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate will inherit the kingdom of God."

units.la: Eph. 5. Scortatio & omnis immunditia, aut avaritia ne nominetur quidem inter vos, sicut decet sanctos. Nam hoc scitis, quod omnis scortator, aut immundus, aut avarus, qui est simulachrorum cultor, non habet hæreditatem[?] in regno Christi & Dei. Ne quisquam vos decipiat inanibus sermonibus. Propter hæc enim venire solet ira Dei in filios inobedientes, Colos.3. Rom.1.
units.tr: Ephesians 5: "Let fornication and all uncleanness, or covetousness, not even be named among you, as becomes saints. For you know this, that every fornicator, unclean person, or covetous man, who is a worshipper of idols, has no inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and God. Let no one deceive you with empty words. For because of these things the wrath of God is wont to come upon the disobedient sons." Colossians 3; Romans 1.

units.la: Galat.5. Manifesta sunt opera carnis, adulterium, fornicatio, immunditia: de quibus prædico vobis, quemadmodum & prædixi, quod qui talia agunt, regni Dei hæredes non erunt.
units.tr: Galatians 5: "The works of the flesh are manifest: adultery, fornication, uncleanness. Of these I forewarn you, as I have also forewarned, that those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God."

units.la: Hebr.13. Scortatores & adulteros judicabit Deus.
units.tr: Hebrews 13: "God will judge fornicators and adulterers."

units.la: Apoc.21. Scortatoribus & veneficis, & omnibus mendacibus, pars illorum erit in stagno ardenti igne & sulphure, quod est mors secunda. Et hoc loco: Dominus ultor est de omnibus his.
units.tr: Revelation 21: "For fornicators and sorcerers and all liars, their portion will be in the burning lake of fire and sulphur, which is the second death." And in another place: "The Lord is an avenger in all these things."

units.la: Hæc diligenter sunt meditanda, ut commonefaciamus nos, quam stultum, quam infanū, quam furiosum sit (utinam crederemus) propter voluptatulam nō admodum diuturnam abijcere felicitatem æternā. Lysimachus in Thracia superatus à Dromacheta, quum ob sitis impatientiam tum se tum exercitum dedidisset, posteaquam bibit jam factus captivus, dicebat: O dii, quàm brevis voluptatis gratia me ex rege feci servum! Quid ergo dicturos putamus eos, qui propter fornicationem non poterunt introire in regnum Dei? Inhonestæ enim voluptati paratam esse comitem poenitentiam significavit etiam Demosthenes, cùm diceret Laidi, quæ pro una nocte stipulabatur drachmarum decem millia, ὡς ἀλογιστῷ[?] τοιούτου[?] μετανοήσω[?]. i. Ego poenitere tanti non emo. autor est A.Gellius in 1.noct.Attic.lib.cap.8. Videris cap.5.Sap. Atq; hæc de primo remedio.
units.tr: These things must be carefully meditated on, so that we may remind ourselves how foolish, how insane, how frenzied it is (would that we believed it) to cast away eternal happiness for a pleasure that does not last very long. Lysimachus, defeated in Thrace by Dromachetes, when through impatience of thirst he had given himself and his army up, after he drank, now a captive, said: "O gods, how briefly, for the sake of a pleasure, have I made myself a slave from a king!" What then do we suppose they will say who, because of fornication, will not be able to enter the kingdom of God? Demosthenes too showed that repentance is the companion attending dishonourable pleasure, when he said to Lais, who demanded ten thousand drachmas for one night: I will not repent at such a price [ὡς ἀλογιστῷ τοιούτου μετανοήσω]. That is: "I do not buy repentance at such a price." The authority is Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, book 1, chapter 8. See Wisdom ch. 5. And so much for the first remedy.

units.la: Secundum remedium contra ignem luxuriæ est lignorum subtractio. Nam fecundum sylvæ ligna exardescit ignis, Eccles.28. Qui vult ergo caste vivere, subtrahat sibi de cibo & potu, præsertim tali, qui inflammat ad luxuriam, ut est forte vinum, cibus acuti saporis, &c. Si enim ebrietas Lothum, tam sanctum virum, in tam detestandum vitium traxit, ut Genef.19. legitur, quis securè posset operam dare ebrietati? Ac quemadmodum deridendus esset ille, qui faculis ardentibus domum suam accenderet, si diceret, quod combustio ejus sibi displiceret: sic deridendi sunt, qui dicunt se velle continere, cum talibus cibis & potibus domos suas incendant. Sicut autem ebrietas subministrat impuritati alimenta(Prover.23.) sic vita parca & sobrietas libidinem extinguit: id quod exemplum adolescentis illius etiam oftendit, qui per triduum inclusus fuit à muliere honesta, quam concupiverat, & postea proposita optione, potius comedere voluit, quàm suam libidinem explere. Nomine subtrahendorum lignorum intelligi possunt, & cætera irritamenta luxuriæ, veluti sunt ocium eium & mollicies. Multam enim malitiam docet ociofitas, Ecclesi.33.Ezechiel.16.2.Regum 11. Item, contubernia & colloquia hominum impudicorum, Proverb.7. Ecclesi. 42.Corrumpunt enim bonos mores, colloquia prava,1. Corint.15.Et vetus dictum est, Si juxta claudum habitaveris, discès & ipse claudicare. Dina filia Iacob, non continet se domi suæ, sed evagatur ad alienas mulieres: itaque amittit suam pudicitiam, Genef.34. Præterea oculorum jactus, Ecclesi.9. Iob.31. auditus obscoenarum cantilenarum, contactus externus, impura lectio, & occasio, &c.
units.tr: The second remedy against the fire of lust is the removal of fuel. For the fire blazes up with the wood of the forest, Ecclesiasticus 28. Whoever wishes to live chastely should therefore withdraw from himself food and drink, especially such as inflame to lust, such as strong wine, food of sharp flavour, and so on. For if drunkenness drew Lot, so holy a man, into so detestable a vice, as Genesis 19 relates, who could safely give himself to drink? Just as one would be mocked who set fire to his own house with burning torches and then said that its burning displeased him, so are they mocked who say they wish to be continent while they set their houses on fire with such foods and drinks. And just as drunkenness supplies nourishment to impurity (Proverbs 23), so a sparing life and sobriety quench lust. The example of that young man also shows this, who was shut up for three days by an honourable woman whom he had desired, and afterwards, when the choice was offered him, preferred to eat rather than satisfy his lust. By the removal of fuel may also be understood the other incitements to lust, such as idleness and softness. For idleness teaches much wickedness, Ecclesiasticus 33; Ezekiel 16; 2 Kings 11. Likewise the companionship and conversation of impure men, Proverbs 7; Ecclesiasticus 42. For "evil conversations corrupt good morals," 1 Corinthians 15. And there is the old saying: "If you live beside a lame man, you will learn to limp yourself." Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, did not restrain herself at home but wandered among foreign women, and so lost her chastity, Genesis 34. Further, the casting of the eyes, Ecclesiasticus 9; Job 31; hearing obscene songs; outward touch; impure reading; and occasions, and so on.

units.la: Tertium remedium est, ut homo elongetse ab igne luxuriæ, i.à præsentia mulieris, cuius species gladius igneus est, teste Hieron. Hoc remedium docet Paulus 1. Corinth. 6. inquiens: Fugite scortationem. Hoc usus est Joseph, Genef. 39. Item Antiochus tertius, qui cum Dianæ sacerdotem vidisset supra modum eleganti forma, continuo solvit Ephesio[?], veritus ne vis amoris aliquid ipsum facere compelleret, quod phas non esset. At Israelitæ conveniunt cum filiabus Moab. quare primum scortantur cum eis, deinde abducuntur ab ipsis in idolatriam. Et statim sequitur supplicium, quia multa millia interficiuntur, Num.25.
units.tr: The third remedy is that a man keep far from the fire of lust, that is, from the presence of a woman, whose appearance is a fiery sword, as Jerome testifies. Paul teaches this remedy in 1 Corinthians 6, saying: "Flee fornication." Joseph used this, Genesis 39. Likewise Antiochus the Third, who, when he had seen a priestess of Diana of extraordinary beauty, at once left Ephesus, fearing that the force of love might compel him to do something unlawful. But the Israelites consorted with the daughters of Moab: first they whored with them, then they were led by them into idolatry. And punishment immediately followed, because many thousands were slain, Numbers 25.

units.la: Quæritur autem cur fugiendo pugnandum sit cum hoc peccato, & cur non possit aliter melius vinci, quàm hac ratione, quemadmodum Ambrosius dicit? Responsio: Quia luxuria ignis est: homo autem fœnum arıdum ac stipula, Ief. 40. Eccles. 21. Et quia luxuria peccatum est valde immundū ac lutofum, cum quo luctari sine inquinamento, securum non est, Eccles. 1ȝ. Item quia nō est bonum cominus pugnare cum hoste illo, qui ex propinquitate sumit ac colligit vires. Talis est luxuria. Corpus enim nostrū, quod prius erat pacificum, convertitur in hostem. Si c[illegible, ~3 letters]erit forsitan aliquis, se non fœnum, sed ferrum, non stipulam sed lapidem esse, atque ideo non oportere se timere familiaritatem mulierum: hic sciat, quod ignis etiam ferrū ipsum immutet: & quod ignis ex lapidibus quoq;, si invicem collidantur, exeat: quod de niq; lapideus murus à candela juxta se posita denigretur. De Augustino legitur, quod nec cum sorore habitare consenserit. Hieronymus ait, Memento semper, quod paradisi colonum mulier de possessione sua ejecerit. Ne confidas propria castitate, Nec Davide sanctior, nec Samsone fortior, nec Salomone potes esse sapientior. Et Franciscus Seraphicus, ut Bonavent. refert cap. 5. sedulò hortatus est suos, ut mulierum consortia & colloquia vitarent, & ne quidem intuerentur: siquidem hoc pacto infirmos frangi,firmiores infirmari diceret. Hinc Apostolus necessarium duxit etiam Thessalonicenses rogare, adhortari, admonere, obtestari ad sanctimoniam vitæ custodiendam. Acceperant autem illi (in Christum credentes ac baptizati) à Deo Spiritum sanctum. Id enim Apostolus ipse testatur, quum ait: Qui dedit Spiritum suum sanctum in vos. Non est igitur ut dicamus: Cùm haberent in se Spiritum Dei sanctum (quem impuritate persequi, & injuria afficere ac contristare minimè decet,Ephes.5.)quorsum opus erat Apostolicis adhortationibus ad hoc, ut vas suum quisque cum sanctificatione & honore posideret? Agit quidem Spiritus Dei in credentibus: verùm non semper solo interno[?] actu, sed communiter utitur externo verbi ministerio, ob quam causam Apostoli ministri spiritus vocantur.
units.tr: But it is asked why one must fight this sin by flight, and why it cannot be conquered better in some other way than by this method, as Ambrose says. The answer: because lust is fire, and man is dry hay and stubble, Isaiah 40; Ecclesiasticus 21. And because lust is a very unclean and miry sin, with which it is not safe to struggle without being defiled, Ecclesiasticus 13. Also because it is not good to fight at close quarters with that enemy, who draws and gathers strength from proximity. Such is lust. For our body, which at first was peaceful, is turned into an enemy. If perhaps someone says that he is not hay but iron, not stubble but stone, and so need not fear the familiarity of women, let him know that fire even changes iron itself; that fire comes out even of stones, if they are struck against one another; and that a stone wall is blackened by a candle placed beside it. It is read of Augustine that he did not consent even to live with his sister. Jerome says: "Always remember that a woman drove the colonist of paradise from his possession. Do not trust in your own chastity: you can be neither holier than David, nor stronger than Samson, nor wiser than Solomon." And Francis the Seraphic, as Bonaventure relates in ch. 5, earnestly urged his followers to avoid the company and conversation of women, and not even to look at them, since he said that by this method the weak are broken and the stronger made weak. Hence the Apostle thought it necessary to beg, exhort, admonish and adjure the Thessalonians also to keep the holiness of life. Yet they, believing and baptized in Christ, had received the Holy Spirit from God. For the Apostle himself bears witness to this when he says: "Who gave his Holy Spirit into you." It is not therefore to be said that, since they had the Holy Spirit of God within them (whom it is by no means fitting to pursue with impurity, to wrong, or to grieve, Ephesians 5), there was no need of apostolic exhortations to the end that each should possess his own vessel in sanctification and honour. The Spirit of God indeed works in believers, but not always by inward action alone; he commonly uses the outward ministry of the Word, and for this reason the Apostles are called ministers of the Spirit.

units.la: 4 Sequitur in Apostolo alterum præceptum, de innocentia videlicet, ne noceamus proximis nostris fraude, deceptione, avaritia, rapacitate, contra illud, Exod. 20. Non furtu facies: sed potius eos juvemus aut sublevemus. Dicit enim: Ne quis opprimat ac fraudet in negocio fratrem suum. Laborant nonnulli, quomodo particulam hanc cum præcedenti conjungant. Conjungendam enim illi esse obid putant, quod sequitur: Non enim vocavit nos Deus immunditiæ causa, vel ad immunditiam, sed ad sanctificationem. Ex his est Chrysostomus, qui sic exponit: Bene dixit, Ne quis supergrediatur (<bl>Daß Keiner vbers</bl> <bl>Bögleins/oder/mit dem einem fuß in bad trette</bl>) unicuiq; Deus uxore deputavit, terminos posuit naturæ, commixtionem illam quæ est cum una. Itaque si quis misceatur alteri, transgressio est, & latrocinium & nimia cupiditas, seu fraudulentia: vel ut ipse loquitur, πορνείας[?] ἵστι ἐ λαγνεία, ἐ πλεονεξία. Et paulò pòst: Hic de adulterio loquitur, suprà vero de omni fcortatione. Sententiam hanc Theophylactus & Oecumenius sequuntur, & hanc particulam quoque de alienis uxoribus non appetendis exponunt. Sed hoc nimis coactum esse videtur.
units.tr: 4 Next in the Apostle comes another precept, namely concerning innocence: that we not harm our neighbours by fraud, deceit, covetousness or rapacity, against that commandment, Exodus 20, "You shall not steal." Rather we should help and relieve them. For he says: "That no one oppress or defraud his brother in business." Some struggle over how this clause is joined to the preceding one. For they think it should be joined to what follows: "For God has not called us for the sake of uncleanness, or to uncleanness, but to sanctification." Among these is Chrysostom, who expounds it thus: "Well did he say, 'that no one go beyond' (that no one step over the line, or put one foot into another's bed). God assigned each man a wife and set the bounds of nature, that intercourse which is with one. So if anyone mixes with another, it is transgression, and theft, and excessive lust, or fraud; or, as he himself puts it, a fornication, a lust, a covetousness." And a little later: "Here he speaks of adultery, but above he spoke of all fornication." Theophylact and Oecumenius follow this view, and they expound this clause also as a prohibition against desiring other men's wives. But this seems too forced.

units.la: Verba Pauli nihilominus optime cohærent. Docet enim sanctitatis partem esse, ut juste & innocenter agamus cum proximo. Ac ducitur hæc adhortatio tanquam rivus ex sanctificationis doctrina. Deinde quod in præcedenti denunciatione dixit: Hæc est voluntas Dei, id hic quoque subintelligendum est. Illic, Hæc est voluntas Dei, inquit, ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν. Hic repete, Hæc est voluntas Dei, τὸ μὴ ὑπερβαίνειν & πλεονεκτεῖν τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὐτοῦ ἐν τῷ πράγματι. Non simpliciter dicit, μὴ ὑπερβαίνειν: sed quemadmodum illic, ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν: ita hic, τὸ μὴ ὑπερβαίνειν: ut intelligas alteram denunciationem subijci præcedenti, quæ & ipsa profecta sit ex voluntate Dei.
units.tr: The words of Paul agree very well nonetheless. For he teaches that it is part of holiness that we act justly and blamelessly towards our neighbour, and this exhortation flows like a stream from the doctrine of sanctification. Then, what he said in the preceding declaration, "This is the will of God," must be understood here as well. There he says, "This is the will of God, your sanctification" [ὁ ἁγιασμὸς ὑμῶν]; here repeat, "This is the will of God, that one should not overstep and defraud his brother in the matter" [τὸ μὴ ὑπερβαίνειν καὶ πλεονεκτεῖν τὸν ἀδελφὸν αὐτοῦ ἐν τῷ πράγματι]. He does not simply say "not to overstep," but, as there "your sanctification," so here "not to overstep," so that you may understand that the second declaration is subordinate to the preceding one, and that it too proceeds from the will of God.

units.la: Est autem fratrem in negocio ὑπερβαίνειν & πλεονεκτεῖν, modum æquitatis ad detrimentum illius excedere, plus ab illo petere vel extorquere, quàm per æquitatem liceat: vel, superbè premere fratrem ( à Græco enim ὑπερβαίνειν vox superbus venit, mutato densò in S literam ) & defraudare eum plus nobis commodi rapiendo, quàm nobis jure debe<bl>tur:mit füffen vberein geben/ vnd mehr wol- len haben dann billich ist / oder jemand vber- trengen vnd verfoithalten.</bl> Cùm igitur negotiatio in rebus mortalium fit necessaria, & licita Christianis inter se, & cùm ἐπιεικείας[?]: praecipit Apostolus, ut in ea omnis absit fraus, vis, ars, mendacium, avaritia, atque dolus malus, ut juste & secundum aequas leges contrahamus, elocemus, omniaque negotia nostra instituamus. Sub negocia enim referimus venditionem, emptionem, mutuum, locationem, & si quae hujus generis alia sunt, quae pertinent ad commertia hominum.
units.tr: To overstep and defraud a brother in business means to go beyond the measure of fairness to his loss, to demand or extort from him more than fairness allows; or, to press down a brother with arrogance (for the word "arrogant" comes from the Greek ὑπερβαίνειν, with the dense letter changed into S) and to cheat him by seizing more advantage for ourselves than is rightly due to us; to agree to terms and wish to have more than is fair, or to overreach and defraud someone. Since, therefore, trade among mortals is necessary and lawful among Christians, and since [...] the Apostle commands that in it there be no fraud, force, cunning, lying, greed or wicked deceit, so that we may contract, sell and conduct all our business justly and according to equitable laws. For we include under business the sale, purchase, loan, lease, and whatever other things of this kind there are that pertain to the dealings of men.

units.la: Regula verò agendi sanctè & juste in negociis est, Quod tibi nolis fieri, alteri ne feceris: & proximum tuum sicut temetipsum dilige. Propheta David Psalm. 15. hominem illum qui cum proximo suo aperte, & sine damno & dolo egerit, beatum praedicat. Cæterum si quis non hoc nomine voluerit studere sanctimoniae & innocentiae, neque idcirco quod audit Deum hoc velle esseque id honestum, pulchrum, & consentaneum vocationi nostrae: contrarium autem turpe & illaudatum: is saltem damno poenisque perterreatur, & à peccatis absterreatur. Addit enim minas, seu rationem, aut demonstrationem ab ira & vindicta Dei, cujus manum ac virgam nemo poterit effugere, & in cujus manus incidere horrendum est, teste Scriptura, Hebr.10. Propterea quòd ultor est (inquit) Dominus omnium istorum. q.d. Etiamsi impunè iuxta seculum fieri potest, ut quis scortetur, aut in negotio circumveniat fratrem, non fiet tamen impunè coram Deo, qui omnia videt atq; ultor est non modò potestate, sed & ipso opere, & qui in fine mundi iudicabit vivos & mortuos, atq; reddet unicuique fecundum quod gessit in hac vita, five bonum, five malum,
units.tr: The rule for acting holily and justly in business is: "What you would not have done to you, do not do to another," and "love your neighbour as yourself." The prophet David in Psalm 15 pronounces blessed the man who deals openly with his neighbour, without loss or deceit. Moreover, if anyone will not for this reason strive after holiness and innocence, nor because he hears that God wills this, and that it is honourable, beautiful, and in harmony with our calling, while the opposite is shameful and unpraised, let him at least be terrified by loss and punishments, and be turned away from sins. For the Apostle adds threats, or the demonstration of the anger and vengeance of God, whose hand and rod no one can escape, and into whose hands it is dreadful to fall, as Scripture witnesses, Heb. 10: "Because the Lord is an avenger of all these things." That is to say: even if one can commit fornication or defraud a brother in business with impunity according to the world, it will not be done with impunity before God, who sees all things and is an avenger not only in power but also in deed, and who at the end of the world will judge the living and the dead, and will render to each one according to what he has done in this life, whether good or evil.

units.la: Quemadmodum & ante diximus vobis, ac testati fumus) hoc est, ferió & additis comminationibus hęc vobis prædiximus. Quod inprimis notandum nobis est. Tanta enim est hominum tarditas, ut nisi acriter perculfi, nullo divini judicij sensu tangantur: Non ergo frigidè ac defunctoriè debet pastores in hominum scelera invehi, sed constanter & intrepidè, non fine comminationibus in verbo Dei contentis adversus improborum flagitia vindictam Dei opponere. Rursus vero auditores, ejusmodi admonitiones & objurgationes amicè accipere debent, ac boni consulere, juxta illud Hebr.ult. Obsecro vos fratres, sufferte sermonem exhortationis:&c, Parete iis qui præsunt vobis. Hoc autem eò & libentius & diligentius facturi sunt fine dubio, fi cogitaverint, fe à Deo vocatos & electos esse ad sanctitatem & justitiam, & miniftros Dei ac verbi ejus, nō esse qui loquuntur, sed spiritum Patris cœlestis, qui loquitur in illis, five per os illorū. Sanctus Deus, qui vocavit nos, sanctificet nos totos integri que nostri spiritus & animæ, & corpora criminis expertia conserventur in adventum Domini nostri Iesu Christi, qui nos de manu inimicorum nostrorum liberavit, ut sine timore serviremus ipsi cum sanctitate & justitia coram ipso, cunctis diebus vitæ nostræ: cui sit honor in secula, Amen.
units.tr: As we also said before and testified to you, that is, earnestly and with added threats we foretold these things to you. This must be noted above all. For men are so slow that unless they are sharply struck, they are touched by no sense of divine judgement. Therefore pastors ought not to inveigh against the crimes of men coldly and perfunctorily, but steadfastly and fearlessly, and to set the vengeance of God against the shameful deeds of the wicked, not without threats contained in the Word of God. Again, hearers ought to receive such admonitions and rebukes kindly and take them in good part, according to that passage in Heb. last chapter: "I beg you, brothers, bear with the word of exhortation," etc.; "Obey those who rule over you." They will undoubtedly do this the more willingly and diligently if they reflect that they have been called and chosen by God to holiness and righteousness, and that the ministers of God and of his Word are not the ones who speak, but the Spirit of the heavenly Father who speaks in them, through their mouth. May the holy God, who called us, sanctify us wholly, and may our whole spirit and soul and bodies be preserved blameless until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, who delivered us from the hand of our enemies, so that we might serve him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before him, all the days of our life: to whom be honour for ever, Amen.

units.la: CONCIO LV.
units.tr: SERMON LV.

units.la: 1. Timot. 2.
units.tr: 1. Timot. 2.

units.la: O[?]olo igitur orare viros in omni loco sustollentes puras manus, absque ira & disceptatione. Consimiliter & mulieres in amictu modesto, cum verecundia & castitate ornare semetipsas, non tortis crinibus, aut auro, aut margaritis, aut vestitu sumptuoso, sed quod decet mulieres profitentes pietatem per bona opera. Mulier in silentio discat cum omni subjectione. Caterum mulieri docere non permitto, neque authoritatem usurpare in viros, sed esse in silentio. Adam enim prior formatus est, deinde Eva. Et Adam non fuit deceptus, sed mulier seducta, obnoxia facta est transgressioni: salva tamen fiet per generationem
units.tr: I will therefore that men pray in every place, lifting up pure hands, without wrath and disputing. Likewise also that women adorn themselves in modest apparel, with shamefastness and chastity, not with broided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly clothing, but (as becomes women professing godliness) with good works. Let the woman learn in silence with all subjection. But I do not permit a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence. For Adam was formed first, then Eve. And Adam was not deceived, but the woman, being deceived, was made liable to transgression: yet she shall be saved through childbearing

units.la: liberorum, si manserint in fide ac di- lectione & sanctificatione cum casti- tate.
units.tr: of children, if they continue in faith and love and holiness with chastity.

units.la: I Quemadmodum universi mortales ante omnia pro omnibus orare debent: sic etiam conjuges (Genes. 25. Tob. 8. 1.Corinth.7. 1.Petr.3.) non tam pro aliis, quàm pro se invicem, idque omni tempore, & omni loco: ut nimirum benedictionem à Deo consequantur. Sicut enim domus multum jurantis maledictionem habet, (Eccles. 3. & 24.) sic domus rectè orantis benedictione. Nam propè est Dominus omnibus invocantibus eum in veritate, Psal. 145. Tollitur autè hisce Pauli verbis, In omni loco) superstitio loci: docetúrque sublatam esse illam Iudaicam, olimque mandatam observationem de adorando Hierosolymæ, aut versus Hierosolymam, Ioann. 4. Reliquis verbis ostenditur, qualis debeat esse oratio . Elevandæ enim sunt manus ad cœlum, elevandæ & mentes, juxta illud Thren. 3. Levemus corda nostra cum manibus ad Dominum in cœlos. Gestus est feriò ad Deum orantium, & ceremonia usitata omnibus seculis, manus extendere ac levare in sublime, cœlum versus; quia natura nobis hic ingenitus est sensus, quum Deum quærimus, sursum aspicere, ut & Christus fecit, Marc. 7. Ioann. 11. & 17. Sic Moses Exod. 17. & David in Psalmis, & Salomon in dedicatione templi, manus suas inter orandum ad Deum levasse leguntur. Sed & idololatrae, quum alioqui Deum affigerent lignèis & lapideis simulachris, morem tamen in coelum tollendi manus retinebant. Ceremonia est verae pietati congruens, modo respondeat veritas, quae per eam significatur: nempe ut admoniti Deum in coelo quaerendum esse (quo & Christus Iesus nos remittit, quum ait: Sic igitur orate vos: Pater noster, qui es in coelis, &c. Matt.6.) primum de ipso terrenum vel carnale nihil imaginemur: deinde exuamus affectus carnales: ne quid impediat quominus animi nostri supra mundum assurgant. Obliviscamur rerum terrenarum, ut coelestia tantum cogitemus. Praeterea suppliciter gratiam Dei imploremus, ac toti à coelesti ope pendeamus. Quoniam vero & facilis est hic gestus, & saepenumero simulatur ab hypocritis, non simpliciter dicit Apostolus, Suftollentes manus: sed, Sustollentes puras. Innocentes[?] manus, mundas à sanguine, Iac.1.[?] ab ira.i. impatientia, vel injuriarum recordatione, & vindictae cupiditate, Matth.5. & disceptatione, id est, dubitatione, vel haesitatione, Iacob.1. vel mundas ab avaritia, à rapina, à caede, à verberibus, eleemosyna florentes ac plenas. Atq; hoc virorum est.
units.tr: Just as all mortals must above all pray for all people, so also spouses (Gen. 25; Tob. 8; 1 Cor. 7; 1 Pet. 3) should pray not so much for others as for one another, and this at all times and in every place, so that they may obtain a blessing from God. For as the house of one who swears much has a curse (Eccles. 3 and 24), so the house of one who prays rightly has a blessing. For the Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth, Psalm 145. By these words of Paul (In every place) the superstition of place is removed, and it is taught that the Jewish observance, once commanded, of worshipping at Jerusalem, or toward Jerusalem, is abolished (John 4). By the remaining words it is shown what prayer ought to be. For hands must be lifted up to heaven, and minds too, according to that in Lamentations 3: Let us lift up our hearts with our hands to the Lord in the heavens. The gesture of those praying to God is a common one, and a ceremony in use in every age: to stretch out and raise the hands on high, toward heaven, because nature has implanted in us this sense, that when we seek God we look upward, as Christ also did (Mark 7; John 11 and 17). Thus Moses (Exod. 17), David in the Psalms, and Solomon at the dedication of the temple are read to have lifted their hands to God while praying. But even idolaters, although they otherwise fastened God to wooden and stone images, nevertheless kept the custom of lifting up the hands to heaven. It is a ceremony congruent with true piety, provided that the truth which it signifies corresponds: namely, that, reminded that God is to be sought in heaven (to which Christ Jesus also directs us when he says: "Thus therefore pray you: Our Father, who art in heaven," etc., Matt. 6), we first imagine nothing earthly or carnal about him; then we strip off carnal affections, so that nothing hinders our minds from rising above the world. Let us forget earthly things, so that we think only of heavenly ones. Besides, let us humbly implore the grace of God, and depend wholly on heavenly help. But since this gesture is easy and is often feigned by hypocrites, the Apostle does not simply say "lifting up hands," but "lifting up pure" hands: innocent hands, clean from blood (James 1), from wrath, that is, impatience, or the recollection of injuries and desire for revenge (Matt. 5), and from disputing, that is, doubting or hesitation (James 1); or hands clean from avarice, from rapine, from murder, from blows, and rich and full of almsgiving. And this is the duty of men.

units.la: 2 Consimiliter autem & mulieres, scilicet in publicis conventibus orent, sicut viri, attolletes manus sine ira & disceptatione, manus, inquam, sanctas, non rapaces, non avaras. Cùm enim maritum cogit uxor geminas ei præbere & ornamenta aurea, is autè aliena rapit, ipsa omnino rapinæ est obnoxia.
units.tr: 2 Likewise, however, the women too, namely when they pray in public assemblies, as the men do, should lift up their hands without wrath and disputing: hands, I say, holy, not grasping, not greedy. For when a wife compels her husband to give her gold ornaments twice over, and he then seizes what belongs to others, she herself is altogether liable to the guilt of rapine.

units.la: Præscribit ergo Apostolus mulieribus ituris in sacrum cœtum, quomodo ibi se gerere debeant, nempe ne nimium sese ornent, sicut solent plerunque illæ in templum omnesque publicos cœtus convenire, potius ostentandæ formæ & ornamentorum quàm pietatis causa, sicut Poeta inquit:
units.tr: The Apostle therefore prescribes to women who are going to the holy assembly how they ought to conduct themselves there: namely, that they should not adorn themselves excessively, as they commonly do when they gather in the temple and in all public assemblies, for the sake of displaying their beauty and ornaments rather than of piety, as the poet says:

units.la: Spectatum veniunt, veniunt spectentur ut ipsæ.
units.tr: They come to be seen; they come that they themselves may be looked at.

units.la: Primum igitur affirmativè earum honestum ornatum describit: ponitq; duplicem Christianarum mulierum ornatum. unum qui sit in amictu honesto (& pro decoro perfonæ composito) cum verecundia & castitate, seu modestia, seu frugalitate, quæ virtutes vel maximè muliebrem sexum decent. Alterum qui sit ex bonis operibus. Honestus amictus (qui Græcè καλ[?]ὸς [illegible, ~6 letters] κόσμιος vocatur) est, quo mulieres honestè circumquaque ad pedes usq; amiciuntur. Non vult ergo mulieres feminulas coparere in conventibus ecclesiasticis, sed honestè ac decenter opertas.
units.tr: First, then, he describes positively their honest adornment, and he sets forth a twofold adornment of Christian women: one, which consists in honest apparel (arranged for the decorum of the person) together with shamefastness and chastity, or modesty, or frugality, virtues which especially befit the female sex; the other, which consists of good works. Honest apparel (called in Greek [καλὸς κόσμιος]) is that by which women are decently clothed all round, down to the feet. He does not want women to appear in church assemblies as flighty creatures, but modestly and decently covered.

units.la: Bona verò Christianæ mulieris opera sunt, si sit observans mariti, si liberos gignat & educet, si domum fideliter administret, si sit hospitalis, si sanctorum pedes lavet, si affligentibus subministret: & in summa, si sit in quolibet opere bono assidua. Hoc genus bona opera maximo sunt ornamento Christianæ & honestæ mulieri, redduntq; eam multo illustriorem, quàm si omnia illius auro, margaritis ac vestitu holoserico splendeant. Rectè igitur Phocionis cognomèto Probi uxor (frugalitatem suam excusatura aliis matronis obijcientibus quòd parum pro dignitate culta esset) dicere solebat, suum mundum esse præclara gesta mariti. Restius autem Cornelia Gracchorum mater, quum Campana matrona illius hospitio utens, ornamenta sua, quibus illud seculum nihil habebat pulchrius, ipsi ostenderet, traxit eam sermonē[?], donec liberi redirent è schola: Tum & hæc, dicebat, ornamenta mea sunt. Sentiens matronæ nihil esse pulchrius neque pretiosius, quàm liberos rectè educatos.
units.tr: The good works of a Christian woman are these: if she is obedient to her husband, if she bears and brings up children, if she faithfully manages the household, if she is hospitable, if she washes the feet of the saints, if she ministers to the afflicted; and in sum, if she is diligent in every good work. Good works of this kind are the greatest ornament to a Christian and honest woman, and make her far more illustrious than if all her possessions shone with gold, pearls and silk. Rightly, therefore, the wife of Phocion, surnamed the Upright, when other matrons objected to her that she was poorly dressed for her rank, used to say, in defending her frugality, that her adornment was her husband's splendid deeds. Likewise Cornelia, mother of the Gracchi, when a Campanian matron, staying at her house, showed her own ornaments, which that age had nothing finer than, drew her into conversation until her children came back from school; then, she said, "these too are my ornaments." Thus she showed that the matron had nothing more beautiful or precious than children rightly brought up.

units.la: Non est autē præter rationem, quòd mulierib.de honestate amictus præscribit. Solet enim illæ natura sua studiosiores esse ornandi corporis, & appetetiores intemperati, vani, & inhonesti, quàm decentis & honesti ornatus: haud memores justarū casarum[?] vestimentorum, quæ sunt necessitas, utilitas & honestas. Et quoniā solenne est mulierculis, ut seipsas ornēt: nō vetat hoc Apostolus, sed corrigit abusum: & docet quomodo seipsas ornare debeant. Admittit ille quidem, ut habitu ornato sint pro ingenio muliebri, non deniq; sordido amictu, quo abominatio sint maritis, & occasio forsitan exteros adamandi: sed modum præscribit, idque non solùm affirmativè, dum jubet, ut ornentur eo amictu, qui pudorem, qui pudicitiam vitæquę integritatem testetur, & muliebrem verecundiam deceat, sed etiam negativè-dum addit: Non cincinnis, aut auro, aut margaritis, aut sumptuoso vestitu. Quibus verbis vanitas & luxus, fastus & excessus in cultu muliebri reprehenditur & damnatur: sicut & Iesai.3. 1.Pet.3. Porrò si quæ divitiarum tantum sunt indicia, prohibet Paulus, multò magis curiosa & perversa, veluti sunt infeCtiones genarum, pictūræ oculorum, &c. quibus Iezabel se ornavit, 4.Reg.9. ignorans pulcherrimum colorem eum esse, ut Pythias Aristotelis filia dicebat, quem in ingenuis gignit pudor.
units.tr: Nor is it beside reason that he prescribes to women honesty in apparel. For women, by their nature, are more eager to adorn the body, and more inclined to what is immoderate, vain and dishonest than to decent and honest ornament, being mindful not at all of the just uses of clothing, which are necessity, usefulness and decency. And since it is customary for silly women to adorn themselves, the Apostle does not forbid this, but corrects the abuse, and teaches how they ought to adorn themselves. He allows indeed that they be dressed with an ornament suited to the feminine nature, not in squalid clothing, which might be an abomination to their husbands and perhaps an occasion for outsiders to fall in love with them; but he prescribes a measure, and this not only positively, when he commands that they be adorned with that dress which bears witness to modesty, chastity and the integrity of life, and becomes womanly shamefastness, but also negatively, when he adds: not with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly clothing. By these words vanity and luxury, pride and excess in women's dress are rebuked and condemned, as also in Isaiah 3 and 1 Peter 3. Moreover, if Paul forbids only the signs of wealth, much more does he forbid the curious and perverse things, such as the painting of cheeks, the colouring of eyes, and so on, with which Jezebel adorned herself (2 Kings 9), not knowing that the most beautiful colour is that which modesty produces in the freeborn, as Pythias, daughter of Aristotle, used to say.

units.la: Legitur cap.12.Exodi: Qui aperuerit cisternam, aut foderit, & non operuerit eam, & ceciderit què bos aut asinus in eam, reddet Dominus cisternæ pretium iumentorum.
units.tr: It is read in Exodus, chapter 12: If a man open a cistern, or dig one, and does not cover it, and an ox or an ass falls into it, the lord of the cistern shall make good to the beasts' owner the price of the animals.

units.la: Et dicit ibi Glossa: Cisterna aperitur, quando mulier ornatur. Tunc bos vel asinus incidit in eam, quando homo per ornatum illum illaqueatur: tunc mulier illa reddet rationem de anima illa. Si quis faceret foveam in via (inquit ille) & eam non cooperiret, non toleraretur. Mirum ergo est, quomodo hoc toleratur inter fideles (qui [illegible, ~8 letters] & Christianam pietatem profitentur) quòd mulieres sic præparent se ad interfectionem animarum. Memorabile est exemplum S. Agathæ, quæ cùm esset ex nobili genere, in servili veste incessit, & de hoc reprehensa, gloriabatur sese ancillam Christi.
units.tr: And the Gloss says there: the cistern is opened when a woman adorns herself. Then an ox or an ass falls into it when a man is ensnared by that adornment; then that woman will give an account of that soul. If someone made a pit in the road (it says) and did not cover it, he would not be tolerated. It is wonderful, therefore, how this is tolerated among the faithful (who [...] and profess Christian piety), that women prepare themselves in such a way for the destruction of souls. The example of St. Agatha is memorable: although she was of noble birth, she walked about in servile dress, and when rebuked for this, she boasted that she was a handmaid of Christ.

units.la: ¶[?] Cæterum quoniam Apostolus in oratione non discernit inter mulieres & viros, ne in omnibus etiam reliquis pares illas viris facere videatur: duo jam subjicit, in quibus à viris discerni debeant: quorum unum ecclesiasticum est, alterum domesticum, & ad conjugii statum pertinens. Ecclesiasticum est, quod dicit: Mulier quietè discat, summa cū obedientia. Mulieri verò docere non permittit to. Domesticum verò, quod mox subjicitur: Nec authoritatem sibi vendicare in virum, sed quietam, seu in silentio esse, id est, se continere intra suum ordinem. Nomen silentii repetit, quia hoc genus hominum natura garrulum est (1. Timoth. 5.) fastuosum & recalcitrans, volens habere novissimum verbum. Non solum ergo expetit honestas esse mulieres, sed & taciturnas ac subjectas. Æqualitas viri & mulieris erat quidem ante lapsum in summis rebus, par splendor & dignitas: id quod inde liquet, quia perpetrato peccato Eva inferior constituitur, hanc ob causam potissimum, quod primum aures serpenti præbuisset. Ipsum lapsum autem dignitatis muliebris imminutio subsequuta est. Nam Deus inquit Genef. 3. Sub viri potestate eris, ipseque dominabitur tui, eaque res pœnæ loco mulieri imponitur: ut postea quoque dicetur.
units.tr: But since the Apostle, in this passage, does not distinguish between women and men, lest he seem to make women equal to men in all other respects too, he now adds two points in which women ought to be distinguished from men. One is ecclesiastical, the other domestic and belonging to the state of marriage. The ecclesiastical point is what he says: "Let the woman learn quietly, with all submission." The domestic point, which follows at once, is: "Nor to usurp authority over the husband, but to be quiet, or in silence," that is, to keep herself within her own rank. He repeats the word "silence" because this kind of person is by nature talkative (1 Tim. 2.), proud and kicking against restraint, wanting to have the last word. So he requires that women be not only respectable but also quiet and subject. Before the fall, the equality of man and woman in the highest matters was indeed real, with equal brightness and dignity. This is clear from the fact that, once sin was committed, Eve was made inferior, chiefly for this reason, that she had first lent her ears to the serpent. The fall itself was followed by a diminishing of women's dignity. For God says in Genesis 3: "You shall be under the power of your husband, and he shall rule over you," and this condition is laid on the woman as a punishment, as will be said again later.

units.la: Sed quomodo mulier in silentio discere debet cum omni subjectione? In 1. ad Corinth. 14. sic legimus: Mulieres vestræ in ecclesiis sileant: Nec enim permissum est illis, ut loquantur, sed ut subditae sint, quemadmodum & lex dicit. Quod si quid discere volunt, domi suos viros interrogent. Nam turpe est mulieribus in coetu loqui. Quibus versibus idem quod hic tractat. Non quod auferat Paulus mulieribus munus docendi familiæ, aut seorsim instruendi alios, id quod Priscilla fecit, (A[?]tor.i8.) sed tantum hoc vult, ut eas a munere docendi publice aut in coetu arceat, quod solis viris Deus mandavit. Si quis autem Deboram, & similes objiciat, quas aliquando gubernando populo Dei mandato præfectas legimus (Iud.4.) responsio est facilis, extraordinariis Dei factis non everti communem politiam, cui nos voluit alligato. Ergo si aliquando prophetandi & docendi locum tenuerunt mulieres, idque Dei spiritu excitatæ, potuit hoc qui ab omni lege immunis est: sed quia hoc singulare est, non pugnat cum perpetua & usitata politia. Docere non est eorum, qui aliis sunt subjecti. tales autem sunt mulieres. Quare non convenit illis ut loquantur ac doceant in ecclesia: sed ut pro conditione subjectorum silentium teneant, silendoque audiant, & audiendo discat, cum omni subjectione, quæ requiritur a discentibus. Nisi enim illa fit, audientis animus doctrinæ capax esse non poterit. Quemadmodum enim in vasculū infundi poterit nihil, nisi fit submissum ac subjectū: ita nec in animum audientis doctrina poterit infundi, si non sit erga doctorem submissus, sed elatus. Et ipse cœlestis doctor spiritus sanctus, non amat elatos, sed humiles: ideoq; non illuminat nisi humiles ac summissos. Deniq; qui elati sunt, non appetunt veritatis cognitionē, sed vel alias illam sibi vendicant, vel superbè fastidiunt.
units.tr: But how is a woman to learn in silence and with all subjection? In 1 Corinthians 14 we read: "Let your women keep silence in the churches. For it is not permitted to them to speak, but to be subject, as the law also says. If they want to learn anything, let them ask their own husbands at home. For it is shameful for women to speak in the assembly." In these verses Paul treats the same matter as here. He does not mean that Paul takes away from women the task of teaching the household, or of instructing others privately, as Priscilla did (Acts 18.). He wants only this: that he keep them from the office of teaching publicly or in the assembly, which God has committed to men alone. If someone objects Deborah and others like her, whom we read were set over the people of God at some time by God's command (Judg. 4.), the answer is easy: extraordinary works of God do not overturn the common order, to which he wished us to be bound. So if women have at some time held a place of prophesying and teaching, and were roused by the Spirit of God, this could be done by him who is free from every law. But because this is an exception, it does not conflict with the constant and customary order. Teaching does not belong to those who are subject to others, and women are such. Therefore it is not fitting for them to speak and teach in the church, but to keep silence, as befits those who are subject, and by keeping silence to listen, and by listening to learn, with all the subjection required of learners. For unless that is present, the mind of the hearer cannot be capable of doctrine. For just as nothing can be poured into a little vessel unless it is lowered and set beneath, so teaching cannot be poured into the mind of the hearer if it is not humble toward the teacher, but proud. And the heavenly Teacher, the Holy Spirit himself, does not love the proud but the humble, and therefore he does not enlighten any but the humble and lowly. Finally, those who are proud do not seek the knowledge of the truth, but either claim it for themselves in some other way or disdainfully despise it.

units.la: Quid vero est autoritate usurpare in viros? Græcè est αὐθεντεῖν ἀνδρός[?], quod verti potest, dominari in virum, nec modo autoritate & potestate, sed propria potestate uti, id quod est dominorum. Non convenit autem mulieri imperitare, ac suapte potestate quicquam agere more dominantium. Esset enim hoc ordinem à Deo institutum pervertere, quo juberetur mulier esse sub potestate viri, unde & intolerabilis confusio ordinis domestici nascitur.
units.tr: What, then, is it to usurp authority over men? In Greek it is "authentein andros" [αὐθεντεῖν ἀνδρός], which may be rendered "to rule over a man," and not merely to use authority and power, but to exercise one's own power, which is the mark of masters. It is not fitting, however, for a woman to command, or to act by her own power in the manner of those who rule. For this would be to overturn the order instituted by God, by which the woman is commanded to be under the power of her husband, from which also comes the intolerable confusion of domestic order.

units.la: Illud quoq; vel maximè repugnat obedientiæ (ut Io. Iovianus ait) conjugali q concordiæ, velle id uxorem, ut consilio arbitrioque suo vivatur à viro, quod arrogantis est, penitusque intolerabilis. Satis sit mulieri, si sit sub tutela ac protectione mariti sui: gubernationem rerum permittat marito tanquam capiti & superiori. Illud tamen observa, quod non simpliciter dicit, neque autoritatem usurpare, sed addit, in virū. Licet sub viro in silentio esse debeat uxor, neque quicquam præsumere illo invito, nec imperium in illū rapere: quatenus tamen materfamilias est, & [illegible, ~3 letters] recte supra liberos & familiam potestate utitur, præsertim absente marito, perinde atque lunam videmus præsente sole esse in silentio: absente vero dominari nosti[?] ac stellis. Sicut enim illa socia est solis, sic & uxor socia est mariti sui, ad hoc illi conjuncta, ut adjuvet eum, nō ut imperio suo subjectum habeat.
units.tr: This also, as John Jovianus says, is above all contrary to the obedience and harmony of marriage: for a wife to wish that she be ruled by her husband according to her own counsel and judgment is arrogant and utterly intolerable. It is enough for the woman if she is under the guardianship and protection of her husband; let her leave the management of affairs to her husband as head and superior. Notice, however, that the Apostle does not simply say "nor to usurp authority," but adds "over the man." Although a wife ought to be silent under her husband, and not presume anything against his will, nor seize rule over him, nevertheless, insofar as she is the mistress of the household, and rightly uses authority over the children and household, especially when her husband is absent, we see the moon in silence while the sun is present, but when it is absent, ruling the stars. For as she is the sun's companion, so the wife is the companion of her husband, joined to him for this purpose, that she may help him, not that she may keep him subject to her command.

units.la: Deinde non dicit: Nec loqui viro, si quid in illo desideret. Notum est exemplum Sarae Admonere virum, si opus est, & si quæ facienda sunt, non fecerit, non est illicitum uxori, modo id fiat non imperiosè, sed cum debita modestia ac reverentia: quemadmodum Sunamitis maritum suum monet, ut Elisæum hospitio excipiat, eique cœnaculum ædificet, 4. Reg. 4. Et Esther Ahasuerum regem & maritum orat ut parcat Iudæis innocentibus, & crudelia edicta aboleat,cap.7.
units.tr: Next, he does not say: "Nor to speak to her husband if he lacks anything." The example of Sarah is well known. To admonish her husband, if there is need, and if he has not done what should be done, is not unlawful for a wife, provided this is done not domineeringly, but with due modesty and reverence. So the Shunammite woman admonishes her husband to receive Elisha as a guest and to build him a little upper room (2 Kings 4.). And Esther asks King Ahasuerus, her husband, to spare the innocent Jews and to abolish the cruel edicts (chap. 7.).

units.la: 4 Porrò mulieres silentium ac subjectionem decere, Paulus duplici argumento probat: altero, ratione creationis, quod scil. Adam prior formatus sit Heva: ergo vir est præstantior muliere. Videtur respicere ad jus primogenituræ, quo qui primogeniti sunt, reliquorum sunt fratrum suorum domini. Sic Adam, quoniam prior formatus erat, dominus erat Hevæ: ideoque non licebat Hevæ, ἀνδρὶ[?] in ipsum. Hoc argumentum 1. Corint. 11. in duo resolvitur: quia vir non fit ex muliere, non etiam propter mulierem, sed contrà. Propter hoc, inquit, mulier debet habere potestatem in capite(.i.veJamen, quod significet eam sub potestate viri esse) propter angelos. Nobilius vero praestantiusque tum, id est, ex quo tanquam origine aut causa aliud oritur, tum id propter quod, tanquam ultimum finem, aliud veluti famulans subserviensque illi conditur. Alioqui in nuda temporis ratione nō ita multum situm fuisset: nam & plantae ac bruta sunt ante hominem creata.
units.tr: Moreover, Paul proves with a double argument that women should keep silence and be subject. The first is from the order of creation, namely that Adam was formed before Eve; therefore the man is superior to the woman. He seems to refer to the right of the firstborn, by which those who are firstborn are lords over their brothers. So Adam, because he was formed first, was lord of Eve, and therefore it was not lawful for Eve to usurp authority over the man [αὐθεντεῖν ἀνδρί]. This argument is resolved into two parts in 1 Corinthians 11: man is not made from woman, but woman from man; and man was not created for woman, but woman for man. "For this reason," he says, "the woman ought to have power on her head" (that is, though it may signify that she is under the power of the man), "because of the angels." But that is more noble and excellent which is the origin or cause from which something else arises, and that for which something else is made, as its ultimate end, serving and subservient to it. Otherwise, the mere order of time would not count for much, for plants and beasts were also created before man.

units.la: Posterior causa est, quia non Adam, sed mulier fit prior seducta, Ecclesi. 25. quod tum ex quadam majore mulieris imbecillitate provenit: nam mulier postea adjuvit satanam in seducendo viro, siquidem ipsa ei dedit non sine aliquibus verborum illecebris: tum etiam idipsum meretur eam poenam, ut sit viro subjecta, sicut Deus ei disertè tunc hanc multam servitutis imponit, Genes.3. Cùm igitur initio ei munus docendi virum malè successerit, negat permittendum, ut mulier porrò doceat publicè. Semel docuit, & omnia subvertit. Ipsa experientia docuit, quàm sit noxium, si mulier praesumat habere potestatem in virum. Quia ergo mulier exitiale consilium dederat, digna suit, quae ab alieno jure & arbitrio pendere diceret: quia virum abduxerat à Dei imperio, digna fuit, quae omni libertate privata sub jugum redigeretur. Sic Anshelmus inquit in 14.cap. 1. ad Corint. Duabus de causis jubetur mulier esse subjecta: quia ex viro est, & per ipsam intravit peccatum. Iure enim taçeat[?]: inter viros, quæ cum loqueretur viro suo, suasit peccatum. Hoc agnoscens S. Monica viro suo tacuit & cessit. Aliis vero mulieribus, quæ à viris verberabantur, dicebat, Oportere memores conditionis suæ, non superbire contra dominos suos, quando recitatis tabellis matrimonialibus intelligere debuerant, se ancillas esse factas.
units.tr: The second cause is that it was not Adam but the woman who was first seduced (Ecclus. 25.), which arose partly from a greater weakness of the woman, for afterwards she helped Satan in seducing the man, since she herself gave him the fruit, not without some enticing words; and partly because she deserved that punishment, that she should be subject to the man, just as God then expressly laid upon her this penalty of servitude (Gen. 3.). Since, therefore, at the beginning her task of teaching the man turned out badly, he denies that it should be permitted for a woman to teach publicly any further. She taught once, and overturned everything. Experience itself has shown how harmful it is if a woman presumes to have power over a man. Because the woman had given a deadly counsel, she was worthy to depend on another's right and judgment; because she had drawn the man away from God's command, she was worthy to be deprived of all freedom and brought under the yoke. So Anselm says in his commentary on 1 Corinthians 14: "For two reasons the woman is commanded to be subject: because she is from the man, and because sin entered through her. For she should indeed be silent among men, since she persuaded sin when she spoke to her husband." Recognizing this, St. Monica was silent before her husband and yielded. But to other women who were beaten by their husbands she used to say that they ought to remember their condition, not to be proud against their masters, since, when the marriage documents were read, they should have understood that they had been made maidservants.

units.la: Ne autem nimium mulierum statum extenuasse, & quasi omne spem salutis eis admisse videretur Apostolus: dicit eas nihilominus servatum iri, utcunque sustineant poenam temporalem, & simul eis genus vitæ aut mores sanctos, in quibus potissimum versari, Deoque servire debeant, præscribit. Q.d. Audistis quantam muliebris sexus sibi inufferit maculam: sed hæc non ideo dicuntur, quo in desperationem aut suspicionem pertrahantur mulieres, quasi à salutis consortio dejectæ & exclusæ sint. Nam etsi ut in concione quid agant non permitto: habent tamen domi suæ functionem, in qua Deo placere possunt, si scilicet officio non defuerint: quod est liberos gignere & educare, fide erga Deum & maritum servare, utrunque diligere, sancte, caste & pudice vivere. Non est ergo ut de salute sua dubitent. Transgressio nanque Hevæ non sic facit ad condemnationem muliebris sexus, sicuti ad subjectionem illius fuit. Præterea lapsus ille non Hevæ tantum, sed & Adæ per mediationem Christi sublatus est, ne faciat ad condemnationem credentibus in Christum: qui Christus & virorum & fœminarum servator est. Hominis autem liberatio (teste Augustino lib. 83[?]. Quæst[?], q.xj.) in utroq; sexu debuit apparere. Ergo, quia virum oportebat suscipere, qui sexus honorabilior est, consequens erat, ut fœminei sexus liberatio hinc appareret, quòd ille vir de fœmina natus est. Huic viro & forti Deo, sit honor, benedictio,& gloria in omne ævum,Amen.
units.tr: Lest the Apostle should seem to have diminished the state of women too much, and to have cut off every hope of salvation for them, he says that they will nevertheless be preserved, however much they endure temporal punishment. At the same time he prescribes for them a holy way of life and good conduct, in which they above all ought to dwell and serve God. That is to say: you have heard how great a stain the female sex has brought upon itself, but these things are not said so that women should be driven into despair or suspicion, as if they were cast down and excluded from fellowship in salvation. For although I do not permit them to act in the sermon, they nevertheless have a function at home in which they can please God, provided they do not fail in their duty. This duty is to bear and bring up children, to keep faith towards God and their husband, to love both, and to live holily, chastely and modestly. So there is no reason for them to doubt their salvation. For the transgression of Eve does not count so much towards the condemnation of the female sex as it did towards its subjection. Moreover, that fall was removed not only from Eve but also from Adam through the mediation of Christ, so that it does not count towards condemnation for those who believe in Christ, who is the Saviour of both men and women. Now the deliverance of man (as Augustine witnesses in book lib. 83 Quaest., q. 11) ought to appear in both sexes. Therefore, since it was fitting that he who is the more honourable sex should take on the man, it followed that the deliverance of the female sex should appear from this, that this man was born of a woman. To this man and mighty God be honour, blessing and glory for ever. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO LVI.
units.tr: SERMON LVI.

units.la: 1. Timot. 3.
units.tr: 1. Timot. 3.

units.la: Indubitatus[?] ferme: si quis Episcopi munus appetit, honestum opus desiderat. Oportet igitur Episcopum irreprehensibilem esse, unius uxoris maritum, vigilantem, sobrium, modestum, hospitalem, aptum ad docendum, non vinolentum, non percussorem, non turpiter lucri cupidum: sed æquum, alienum a pugnis, alienum ab avaritia, qui suæ domui bene præsit, qui liberos habeat in subjectione cum omni reverentia. Quod si quis propriæ domui præesse non novit, quomodo Ecclesiam Dei curabit? Non novitium, ne inflatus in condemnationem incidat calumniatoris. Oportet autem & bonum habere testimonium ab extraneis, ne in probrum incidat & laqueum calumniatoris.
units.tr: It is almost certain: if anyone desires the office of bishop, he desires a noble work. A bishop must therefore be blameless, the husband of one wife, watchful, sober, modest, hospitable, apt to teach, not given to wine, not a striker, not greedy for base gain, but gentle, not quarrelsome, not avaricious, one who rules his own house well and keeps his children in subjection with all reverence. But if anyone does not know how to rule his own house, how will he care for the Church of God? He must not be a novice, lest being puffed up he fall into the condemnation of the slanderer. He must also have a good testimony from outsiders, lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the slanderer.

units.la: 1 Non incongruè posset hæc Epistola Pauli, vocari Christiana disciplinæ ecclesiasticæ ordinatio: quia in ea, non solùm in genere quid credendum & agendum omnibus Christianis sit, verùm etiam quid singulariter cuique in sua vocatione, docetur. Quemadmodum in hoc Capite primùm describitur officium Episcopi seu speculatoris, i. ministri, vel pastoris, vel presbyteri: deinde diaconorum: tertiò uxorum, &c. Nam quoniam mulieribus interdixerat officium docendi cap. præcedente, sumpta inde occasione de Episcopatu ipso disserit: primò quò melius appareat, quàm non sine causa mulieres admittere noluerit ad ipsum exercendum; deinde ne solas mulieres arcendo, viros omnes promiscuè admittere videatur. Tertiò quia expediebat Timotheum, & alios admoneri quanta in eligendis episcopis religio servanda esset. Episcopatus est opus eximium & arduum atque officium præclarissimum. Neque enim leve est, in tanta administratione sustinere personam Filii Dei, ubi agitur de regno Dei erigendo ac propagando, ubi de animarum salute curanda, quas sanguinis fui pretio Dominus ipse dignatus est, de regenda Ecclesia, quae est Dei hæreditas. Igitur oportet etiam personam ad illud deligendam, esse prorsus præstantem, & omnibus virtutibus ornatissimam. Quia quod honestum est, honestè quoque peragi debet. Non potest autem honestè peragi, quod ab inhonestis, infamibus & multis modis culpabilibus peragitur. Quemadmodum enim impura manus res puras contrectando inficit, ita & vir inhonestus gerendæ rei honestatem obscurat. Etsi vero liberum sit iis, qui se idoneos arbitrantur, suam operam Ecclesiæ modestè deferre: tamen eosdem maximè decet, ut se examini & judicio Ecclesiæ subijciant. Ait enim Apostolus: Si quis Episcopatum desiderat, bonum opus appetit (modò plurium juvandorum gratia, & non propter gloriam appetat) Sed addit:
units.tr: 1 This Epistle of Paul could not inappropriately be called an ordinance of Christian ecclesiastical discipline, because in it is taught not only what all Christians in general must believe and do, but also what each person must do in his own calling. In this chapter, first, the office of the bishop (overseer, that is, minister, or pastor, or presbyter) is described; then that of the deacons; third, that of wives, and so on. For since in the preceding chapter he had forbidden women the office of teaching, he takes up the matter of the episcopate itself on that occasion: first, so that it may more clearly appear that he was not without reason unwilling to admit women to exercise it; second, so that by excluding only women he does not seem to admit all men indiscriminately. Third, because it was fitting that Timothy and others be warned how great a scrupulousness must be observed in choosing bishops. The episcopate is a distinguished and arduous work and a most excellent office. For it is no small thing, in so great an administration, to sustain the person of the Son of God, where the kingdom of God is to be raised up and spread, where the salvation of souls is to be cared for, which the Lord himself deigned to redeem with the price of his blood, and where the Church, which is God's inheritance, is to be governed. Therefore the person chosen for that task must also be altogether outstanding and adorned with all virtues. For what is honourable must also be carried out honourably. But what is done by dishonourable, infamous and in many ways blameworthy men cannot be carried out honourably. For just as an unclean hand defiles pure things it handles, so a dishonourable man obscures the honour of the business he conducts. Although it is indeed free for those who think themselves fit to offer their service to the Church with modesty, nonetheless these men above all ought to subject themselves to the examination and judgment of the Church. For the Apostle says: If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good work (provided he seeks it for the sake of helping many and not for glory). But he adds:

units.la: Oportet ergo episcopum esse ἀνεπίληπτον[?]: vel, ut ad Titum cap. 1. dicit (ubi similis descriptio personæ Episcopi habetur) ἀνέγκλητον, ὡς θεοῦ οἰκονόμον[?], hoc est, irreprehensibilem & inculpatum seu inculpabilem: non ita, ut non reprehendi debeat, si quid peccat (1.Timoth.5.) aut ut neminem prorsus habeat, qui ei maledicat (impii enim vel optimè meritos de pietate calumniis gravare consueverunt) aut ut coram Deo etiam sit prorsus immunis à peccatis (1.Ioan.1.) sed tam sit vitæ inculpatæ coram hominibus, ut nullo jure reprehendi, nec ut manifestè flagitiosus in jus vocari queat. De criminibus enim seu sceleribus, & impudentiore conversatione hic Pauli locus intelligendus est, ut videlicet in Episcopo exigat summum innocentiæ studium, ne quod recte & sanctè docet, prava & impura vita destruat. Qua enim fronte, aut etiam fructu is alios reprehendet, cui dici poterit, Medice cura teipsum? Turpe enim valde est doctori, cùm culpa redarguit ipsum. Atque hoc quidem generaliter dictum est à Paulo. Subijcit autem specificationem quandam, cùm vitiorum, tum virtutum, quæ habendæ sunt & exercendæ ab Episcopo. Neque verò omnia vitiorum genera recenset, sed ea tantùm, quæ apud eas gentes præ cæteris invaluerant, & vulgariora erant.
units.tr: A bishop must therefore be ἀνεπίληπτον [blameless]; or, as he says to Titus in chapter 1 (where a similar description of the person of the bishop is given), ἀνέγκλητον, ὡς θεοῦ οἰκονόμον [blameless, as God's steward]; that is, irreproachable and unaccused, or inculpable. Not so that he should not be rebuked if he sins (1 Tim. 5), nor so that he has absolutely no one who speaks ill of him (for the impious are wont to slander with calumnies even those who have deserved best of piety), nor so that he is altogether free of sins before God (1 John 1), but so that his life is so blameless before men that he cannot rightly be reproached, nor be summoned to court as manifestly disgraceful. For this passage of Paul is to be understood of crimes or wickedness and of a more shameless way of life, namely so that he requires in a bishop the highest zeal for innocence, lest a perverse and impure life destroy what he teaches rightly and holily. For with what face, or even with what result, will he rebuke others, to whom it can be said: Physician, heal yourself? For it is very shameful for a teacher to be refuted by his own fault. And this, indeed, is what Paul said in general. He then adds a certain specification, both of the vices and of the virtues which a bishop must have and practise. Nor does he list all kinds of vices, but only those which among those nations had prevailed above the others and were more common.

units.la: Notandum simul quod pleraque omnia, quæ hic exiguntur ab Episcopo, exigantur quoq; alibi nō solùm à patrefamiliâs (qui id est in sua domo, quod Episcopus in ecclesia: Nihil enim, juxta Theophylactum, aliud est domus, quàm parva ecclesia) sed etiam ab omnibus fidelibus, quorum singuli suas animas habet, pro quibus vigilare[?] debet. Dum enim ea quæ damnabilia sunt, singulariter quibusdam prohibentur, haud sic prohibentur, ut solis illis illicita censeri debeant: sed ut certis de causis potissimum illis vitanda esse significetur. Magna ratione potissimum & magistratu requiritur, Exod.18.[?] quod in genere requiritur ab omnibus. Consimili modo[?] sentiendum est de iis, quæ hic Episcopo præcipiuntur.
units.tr: It should be noted at the same time that nearly all the things required here of a bishop are also required elsewhere, not only of the head of the household (who is in his house what the bishop is in the church; for, according to Theophylact, a house is nothing other than a small church), but also of all the faithful, each of whom has his own soul for which he must watch. For when things that are damnable are forbidden to certain persons individually, they are not forbidden in such a way that they ought to be considered unlawful only for those persons; rather, it is signified that for certain reasons they are to be avoided above all by those persons. For a great reason, and especially for magistracy, is required in Exodus 18, which is required in general of all. In a similar way must we think about those things which are here commanded of the bishop.

units.la: 2 Requiritur autem ut eligendus in Episcopum fit unius uxoris maritus. Quem locum quidam (sed ut Theophylactus scribit, citra omnem rationem) non de conjugio Episcoporum, sed de Ecclesia potius & sacerdotio exponunt, quòd videlicet Paulus noluit episcopo uni plures comitti ecclesias, aut illū ab una migrare ad aliam. At hic & mox in Diaconorum descriptione, item Tit.1. nominatur etiam filii, & præfens uxor, quæ jubetur esse honesta. Ex quo manifestè apparet non agi hìc de metaphorica aut spirituali uxore, sed carnali sanctaq;. Iam quod obijciunt, Apostolos quidè habuisse uxores, sed nō circumduxisse secum[?] in ministerio, cōfutatur ex hoc loco, qui palàm quid fieri debeat præscribit, nō quid gestū sit exponit. Episcopus verbi Dei minister est. At hunc oportet unius uxoris maritū esse, eò scil. quia Episcopus est, sanctumq; connubium aliis commendare, & à fornicatione absterrere debet. Deinde clarissimis verbis ipse Apostolus 1.Corin.9. An non habemus, ait, potestatem sororem mulierem circumducendi, quemadmodum & ceteri Apostoli Domini, & Cephas:'Hunc in modū convicti cōminiscuntur aliud, quibus contendere, quàm veritati obsequi jucundius est. Primum enim matrimonium admittunt, repetitum damnant, vel improbant: hinc à Paulo diserte unius uxoris maritū, unius,inquam dictum putant. Quasi vero secundae nuptiae primis sint pollutiores, & Paulus verum non dixerit, cum 1. Corinth. 7.inconjugatis & viduis praescripsit bonum esse si sic manserint: caeterum si se non contineant, contrahant matrimonium. Vide Hieron. ad Oceanum.
units.tr: 2 It is required, moreover, that the one to be chosen as bishop be the husband of one wife. Some interpret this passage (but, as Theophylact writes, without any sound reason) not of the marriage of bishops but rather of the Church and the priesthood, namely that Paul did not want many churches to be entrusted to one bishop, or that he should pass from one to another. But here, and soon after in the description of the deacons, and likewise in Titus 1, children and a present wife are also named, and she is commanded to be honourable. From this it clearly appears that what is meant here is not a metaphorical or spiritual wife, but a carnal and holy one. As for the objection that the Apostles indeed had wives but did not lead them about with them in the ministry, it is refuted by this passage, which plainly prescribes what ought to be done, not what was done. The bishop is a minister of the Word of God. But he must be the husband of one wife, namely because he is a bishop, and must commend holy wedlock to others and deter them from fornication.
