Next, the Apostle himself, in very clear words, 1 Cor. 9: Have we not, he says, the power to lead about a sister, a wife, as also the other Apostles of the Lord and Cephas do? Those who are refuted in this way devise something else, since it is more pleasant for them to contend than to obey the truth. For they admit the first marriage but condemn or disapprove of a repeated one; hence they think that by Paul's words "husband of one wife" is plainly meant "one" in the sense of only one. As if second marriages were more polluted than first ones, and Paul had not spoken the truth when, in 1 Cor. 7, he prescribed for the unmarried and widows that it is good if they remain so, but if they cannot contain themselves, let them marry. See Jerome to Oceanus.

units.la: Vnius ergo uxoris maritum esse debere ait, ut, testibus Chrysostomo, Cajetano, Bullingero, Flacio, excludat eos, qui vel simul habuerunt plures uxores, quod in Asia semper fuit usitatissimum, non solum apud Iudaeos, sed etiam multo magis apud Gentiles: tum ut etiam illos excludat, qui una extra casum adulterii dimissa, temere aliam duxerunt, tum qui concubinas habuerunt, aut alioqui impure vixerunt, ut fuit tunc ingens horum vitiorum licentia & frequentia, tum denique ut sanctum & iustum matrimonium stabiliat, quod non inter plures, sed duos tantum confit. Id quod & Dominus Matth.19.docuit: & Paulus 1.Corinth.6. Ephes.5. Itaque Polygamia (cujus primum exemplum Lamech, qui exposteris Caini suit,contra institutum Dei, vel ex libidine vel cupiditate dominandi invexit, Gen.4.)hic nominatim a Paulo damnatur, quae tunc apud Iudaeos pro lege fere obtinuerat, ut hodie apud Turcas. Partim hoc habebant ex perversa patrum imitatione (nam legebant Abraham, Iacob, Davidem, & similes pluribus simul uxoribus fuisse conjugatos, idem sibi quoque licere arbitrabantur: contra quā κακοζηλίαν[?] quid scripserit D. Augustʼ videris cap. 12. libri 3. de doct. Christ.) partim hanc corruptelam ex vicinis gentibus traxerant. Nunquam enim apud Orientales, qua decebat religione & fide culta fuerunt conjugia.
units.tr: He says, therefore, that a man must be the husband of one wife, in order, as witnessed by Chrysostom, Cajetan, Bullinger and Flacius, to exclude those who at the same time had several wives, which was always very common in Asia, not only among the Jews but much more among the Gentiles; then to exclude those who, having dismissed one wife for no reason other than adultery, rashly took another; then those who kept concubines or otherwise lived impurely, since at that time there was an enormous licence and frequency of these vices; and finally, that he might establish holy and just marriage, which is made not between many but only two. This the Lord also taught in Matthew 19, and Paul in 1 Cor. 6 and Eph. 5. Thus polygamy, whose first example was Lamech, a descendant of Cain, who introduced it against the institution of God, either from lust or from a desire to dominate (Gen. 4), is here expressly condemned by Paul; at that time it had almost acquired the force of law among the Jews, as it has today among the Turks. Partly they had this from a perverse imitation of the fathers (for they read that Abraham, Jacob, David and such men were married to several wives at once, and believed it was likewise permitted to them; on this bad zeal, see what Augustine wrote in chapter 12 of book 3 of On Christian Doctrine), and partly they had taken up this corruption from neighbouring nations. For marriages among the Orientals were never conducted with the religion and fidelity that befits them.

units.la: Quicquid fit, Polygamia vulgò invaluerat, & in usu erat tam inter Iudæos, quàm inter gentes (ut testis est Athenæus lib. 13. δειπνοσοφιστῶν[?]) ex quibus colligebatur ecclesia: & probabile est, multos polygamos perinde atque monogamos fidem in Christum recepisse, & ecclesiæ fuisse conjunctos. Neque enim legimus fuisse eos ab Apostolis repulsos. Cùm igitur essent in ecclesia non solùm nogami, sed & polygami, nec in ea adhuc detestatione esset polygamia inter fideles, in qua postea esse cœpit: ideoque fieri poterat, ut perinde polygami in Episcopos eligerentur, atque monogami, diserté hic prescribere voluit, eligi debere Episcopum non polygamum, sed monogamum, h. e. non plurium, sed unius tantum uxoris maritum. Quare hoc[?] Ne sit suspectus de impudicitia. Deinde quia Polygamia secundum pluralitatem uxorum œconomiam requirit multis curis, sumptibus, negociis impeditiorem, quàm convenire possit Episcopo, cujus humeris omnis est Ecclesiasticarum rerum imposita gubernatio. Adhæc non sunt gravandæ ecclesiæ sumptibus, quos Episcopalis domus jure officii postulat, non mediocres ac tolerabiles, si polygamus sit Episcopus, sed multo majores quam si sit monogamus.
units.tr: Whatever the case, polygamy had become widespread and was practised both among the Jews and among the nations from whom the church was gathered (as Athenaeus witnesses in book 13 of his Deipnosophists). It is probable that many polygamists, just as monogamists, received the faith in Christ and were joined to the church. For we do not read that they were rejected by the Apostles. Since, therefore, there were in the church not only unmarried men but also polygamists, and since polygamy was not yet held in that abhorrence among the faithful which it later began to incur, it could happen that polygamists were chosen as bishops just as monogamists were. That is why the Apostle wished to prescribe plainly here that a bishop must be chosen who is not a polygamist but a monogamist, that is, the husband of one wife only, and not of several. The reason is, first, that he should not be suspected of immorality. Second, because polygamy, with its plurality of wives, requires a household that is more burdened with cares, expenses and business than can fit a bishop, on whose shoulders the whole governance of church affairs is laid. Moreover, the church should not be burdened with the expenses which the bishop's household demands by the right of his office. These are not small or tolerable if the bishop is a polygamist, but far greater than if he is a monogamist.

units.la: Videtur autem plane feriò exigere Apostolus ut pius presbyter sit uxoratus, sicut & Tit. 1. Hic enim ait: Oportet, ibi vero dicit: Sit imperativè, nempe vitandi scandali causa, & ne tentet eum Satan 1. Cor. 7. prefertim cum ministri ecclesiae multum etiam cum mulierculis coferre & agere in functione cogantur. Sic Flacius annotavit. Haud dissimilia his quoque Musculus scribit. Et Vvigandus probat in Levit. 21, sacerdotibus & summo pontifici non modo coceffum, sed etiam imperatum esse conjugium à Deo. Potest quidem (inquit ille) etiam sine uxore inculpatè vivere episcopus in domo Dei: verum multis interea commodis & adminiculis destituitur, quibus adjuvatur ille qui uxorem habet, in suscipiendis peregrinis, invisendis ac curandis aegrotis, juvandis pauperibus, viduis & orphanis, ubi multa sunt, quæ negligi non debent, & tamen longè melius per uxorem, quàm per seipsum peraget Episcopus. Neq; enim talium Episcoporum domus sic erant opibus & famulitio instructæ, quemadmodum sunt Episcoporum Papæ, in quibus quæ bona pauperum sunt inutilium hominum ventres, canes, asini, equi, nunnunquâ & leones & ursi magno numero absumunt. Deinde quoniam Episcopus liberâ habet potestate convenindi singulos, non viros tantum, sed & mulieres, domusq; illarum visendi: ne libertâtas hæc occasionem, vel certè suspicionem mali gignat, si sit sine uxore, atq; ita Christiana honestas labefactetur: diserte statuit, eligi oportere Episcopum, non hominem ἀ[?]νέγκλητον, qui sine uxore vivat, sed unius uxoris maritum, quo omnis occasio auferatur Satanæ, Episcopos ecclesiarum Dei ad intolerabile scandalum in turpia flagitia precipitandi. Cura hæc longè majore serio pectus Apostoli sollicitavit, quàm posterorum Episcoporum animos, unde cœperunt ordines Ecclesiastici usque adeò corrumpi fornicationibus, adulteriis, stupris, & aliis libidinum generibus, ut jam olim graveolentiam turpitudinis suæ ipsi non sentiant. Bene institutæ Respublicæ, in quibus publicæ honestatis habetur condigna ratio, non eligunt in consules eos, qui honestum conjugium fastidientes sine uxoribus vivunt. Prudenter enim cavent, ne publica potestas oblatis occasionibus ad follicitandum matronarum virginum ac viduarum pudicitiam permoveatur: cujus rei exempla in medium adferre possemus, si necessarium efset. Quanto magis hæc cautio necessaria est Ecclesiis Christi?
units.tr: Indeed the Apostle plainly and earnestly requires that a godly elder be married, as also in Titus 1. There he says, "It is necessary," and here he speaks in the imperative, clearly for the sake of avoiding scandal, and "lest Satan tempt him" (1 Cor. 7), especially since ministers of the church are compelled in their office to deal and associate much even with women of humble rank. So Flacius has noted. Musculus writes things not unlike these. And Wigand proves, on Leviticus 21, that marriage was not only permitted but even commanded by God to priests and to the high priest. "A bishop," he says, "can indeed live blamelessly in the house of God without a wife; yet meanwhile he is deprived of many advantages and helps which he who has a wife enjoys: in receiving strangers, visiting and caring for the sick, helping the poor, widows and orphans, where there are many things that must not be neglected, and yet a bishop accomplishes them far better through a wife than through himself. For the houses of such bishops were not furnished with wealth and servants as are the houses of the Papal bishops, in which the goods of the poor are consumed by the bellies of useless men, dogs, asses, horses, and sometimes lions and bears in great numbers." Further, since a bishop has free power to meet individuals, not only men but also women, and to visit their homes, lest this liberty give rise to an occasion or at least a suspicion of evil, if he is without a wife, and so Christian honour be weakened, the Apostle expressly ordained that a bishop be chosen not as a man "blameless" who lives without a wife, but as the husband of one wife, so that every occasion is taken away from Satan of hurling the bishops of God's churches into intolerable scandal and shameful crimes. This concern troubled the Apostle's heart with far greater earnestness than it troubled the minds of later bishops, from whom the ecclesiastical orders began to be so corrupted by fornications, adulteries, debaucheries and other kinds of lust that by now they no longer perceive the foul stench of their own shamefulness. Well-ordered commonwealths, in which a proper regard for public decency is maintained, do not elect as consuls those who, scorning honourable marriage, live without wives. For they wisely take care that public power should not be moved, by opportunities offered, to solicit the chastity of matrons, virgins and widows; we could bring forward examples of this if it were necessary. How much more necessary is this caution for the churches of Christ?

units.la: Cæterum cui divinitus datum est, ut cœlibem & puram vitam vivat(quemadmodum rectè Iodo. Vvilichius monet) non est propterea reijciendus, sed magis diligedus: modo caveatur ne quis πορνεία[?] fit locus: quo nomine fœdas & vagas libidines quaslibet comprehendimus. Alioqui Episcopi designati fornicationis insimularentur, & effent reprehenfibiles. Illis quoque dictum est, ut quisque suam ducat uxorem, ad vitandam fornicationem. Item, Melius est nubere, quam uri,1. Corint.7. Et, Honorabile connubium, & thorus immaculatus in omnibus, Hebr. 13[?]. Id tamen semper excipiendum est, nisi quis singulari fuerit dono continentiae. Non enim reiiciendi sunt, qui vel ex utero matris nati eunuchi, vel ab hominibus, vel a seipsis propter regnum Dei castrati, nuptiis abstinent, & tamen ecclesiis Christi utiliter serviunt, Matt.19. Unde Theophylactus Chrysostomi abbreviator ait: Porro non ut legem sanciat, hoc dicit, quod omnino oporteat Episcopum uxoratum esse. Qui enim istuc statuerit, cum alias dicat, Volo vos omnes esse sicut meipsum[?] verum quia tempus ita tum postulabat. At si contingat, inquit, sit[?] unius uxoris vir, seu maritus.
units.tr: Moreover, to one to whom it has been given by God to live a celibate and pure life (as Jodocus Willich rightly observes), he is not therefore to be rejected but rather to be esteemed, provided only that no place is given to fornication, by which name we comprehend all foul and wandering lusts whatever. Otherwise bishops designated would be accused of fornication and would be open to reproach. To them too it was said that each should have his own wife, to avoid fornication. Likewise, "It is better to marry than to burn" (1 Cor. 7), and, "Marriage is honourable, and the bed undefiled in all things" (Heb. 13). Yet this must always be excepted, unless someone has been given the special gift of continence. For those are not to be rejected who, born eunuchs from their mother's womb, or made eunuchs by men, or who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of God, abstain from marriage and yet serve the churches of Christ usefully (Matt. 19). Hence Theophylact, the abridger of Chrysostom, says: "Furthermore, he does not say this to lay down a law, that a bishop must of necessity be married. For one who would establish that would not elsewhere say, 'I wish you all to be as I myself am'; but because the time then demanded it. But if it happens," he says, "that he is a man of one wife, or a husband."

units.la: Hinc vero manifestum est (diserte enim mariti mentionem facit Apostolus) conjugium non pugnare cum sacerdotio, neque illud prohiberi ministris Evangelii, & conjugium horum esse non solum honestum, sed & Apostolica sanctione sacrosanctum. Quare tyrannicum est, quod Episcopis conjugium interdicitur, & eisdem caelibatus perpetuus injungitur, etiamsi impurissime vivatur: ut Gratianus, & post eum plures pontifices contra omnia jura divina & humana, contra consuetudinem, sine ullo discrimine sanxerunt. Quorum veftigiis etiam nunc quidam infiftunt, atq; hodie in quibufdam locis in maritos facerdotes ita graffantur, ut nihil fupra: quafi Græca ecclefia & Latina idem jus non femper confirmaffent: quarũ posterior ufque ad tempora Gregorii quàm diligentifsimè confervavit. Poftea tamen nihil non mutatum eft contra omnia jura, ut ab officio mariti facerdotes femoverentur. Eò amentiæ tyrannis pontificia venit. Ignoratur enim id decretum de cœlibatu effe diabolicum, ficut in hac epiftola Paulus cap.4.eofdem autores fore prædixit. Neque dubitavit doctrinam dæmoniorum pronunciare, ut qui tam turpes libidines fumma opera defenfuri effent.
units.tr: From this it is clearly evident (for the Apostle expressly mentions a husband) that marriage does not conflict with the priesthood, nor is it forbidden to ministers of the Gospel, and that the marriage of these men is not only honourable but also consecrated by apostolic sanction. Therefore it is tyrannical that marriage is forbidden to bishops and perpetual celibacy is enjoined upon them, even if they live most impurely; as Gratian, and after him many pontiffs, decreed without any distinction, against all divine and human laws and against custom. Some still tread in their footsteps, and today in certain places they so rage against married priests that nothing could be more so, as if the Greek church and the Latin church had not always confirmed the same law, the latter of which preserved it most diligently until the times of Gregory. Afterwards, however, nothing was left unchanged, against all laws, so that priests might be removed from the duties of husbands. To such madness the papal tyranny came. For it is not known that this decree on celibacy is diabolical, as Paul in this epistle, chapter 4, foretold that these same authors would be. Nor did he hesitate to call it a doctrine of demons, since they would defend such shameful lusts with the greatest effort.

units.la: Quo confilio addû ctus Siricius ejufmodi conjugia in Hifpania dirimere ftuduit, ficut in Sicilia Gregorius. I[illegible, ~2 letters] in Germania quoque tentatum eft: fed Epifcopi Augustanus, Moguntinus & Curiensis Hildebrandi edicto reclamaruntur, & legem de cœlibatu nunquam approbarunt, fed Epifcopis licere effe maritos femper permiferunt.
units.tr: Led by this purpose, Siricius tried to dissolve such marriages in Spain, as Gregory did in Sicily. [Something similar was attempted] in Germany too, but the bishops of Augsburg, Mainz and Chur protested against Hildebrand's edict, and never approved the law on celibacy, but always allowed bishops to be husbands.

units.la: Sanè planum eft non modo ex monumentis veterum, fed neoteri corum quoq;, omnes Galliarum & Germaniæ Epifcopos fero tandem profefsionem cœlibatus recepiffe, feciffeq;. Ab antiquo enim uxores habuiffe longè certifsimum eft. Id quod & Lambertus Schaffnaburgensis hiftoricus in rebus Germanicis luculenter exponit, eo præcipuè in loco ubi gefta præclara anni 1074. describit. Mira tum erat in Episcopis ejus temporis constantia. Confidenter enim & negligebant & damnabant sanctiones & decreta Romani praesulis, uxoresque secundum verbum Domini retinebant. Gangrensis anno Domini 333[?]. & sexta tum vertialis synodus, ut citatur Dilti.31. can. acriter defendit[?] conjugium sacerdotum: sic-u& Nicaena pro eo contra necessitatem cęlibatus conclusit anno salutis 313. His & Panormitanus insignis jurisconsultus assen[?]tit. c. cum olim, de Cleri. conjug. Chrysostomus in Epistolam ad Titum verba Apostoli, Si quis est sine crimine unius uxoris vir, sic exponit: Obstruere prorsus intendit haereticorum ora, qui nuptias damnant: oltendes eam rem culpa carere, imo ita esse precio sam, ut cum ipsa etiā possit quispiam ad sanctum Episcopatus folium subvehi, Pius secundus, priusquam Pontifex factus calicem Icortationis[?] Babylonicæ Regibus porrigendum in manus sumpsisset, palam dixit: Sacerdotibus magna ratione sublatas nuptias, majori restituendas videri. Quare ergo cum pontificatum esset adeptus, non restituit Ecclesiis, quod tam gravibus de causis restituendum esse sciebat? Scilicet, non est hoc Romanorum pontificum, ut quod justum & æquum est, imò necessarium ecclesiis[?], statuant: sed ut neab aliis tale quid tentetur, totis viribus, igne, gladio, &c. impediant.
units.tr: It is clear not only from the records of the ancients but also from those of more recent times that all the bishops of Gaul and Germany at last reluctantly received and made a profession of celibacy. For it is most certain that from ancient times they had wives. Lambert of Hersfeld, the historian, sets this out brilliantly in his history of German affairs, especially in the place where he describes the famous deeds of the year 1074. At that time there was wonderful constancy among the bishops of that age. For they confidently both neglected and condemned the decrees and ordinances of the Roman prelate, and kept their wives according to the word of the Lord. The Synod of Gangra, in the year of the Lord 333 (?), and the sixth council in Trullo, as cited in Dist. 31 can. ..., strongly defended the marriage of priests; so too the Nicene council concluded in favour of it against the necessity of celibacy, in the year of salvation 313 (?). The famous jurist Panormitanus also agrees with these, on c. cum olim, de Cleri. conjug. Chrysostom, in his commentary on the Epistle to Titus, expounds the Apostle's words, "If anyone is blameless, the husband of one wife," thus: "He intends entirely to stop the mouths of heretics who condemn marriage, showing that this matter is free from fault, and indeed so honourable that one may be raised to the holy seat of the episcopate even with a wife." Pius II, before he became pontiff, when he had taken in hand the cup of Babylonian fornication to be handed to kings, openly said that marriage taken away from priests seemed for great reason to be restored with greater reason. Why then, when he had obtained the pontificate, did he not restore to the churches what he knew must be restored for such grave causes? Certainly it is not the custom of the Roman pontiffs to decree what is just and fair, indeed necessary for the churches; rather, that anyone else who attempts such a thing be hindered with all their strength, by fire, sword, and so on.

units.la: Sed videamus, qualem praeterea esse oporteat Episcopum. Vigilantem esse vult, qui in omnibus suae functionis partibus advigilet, ne quicquam mali ecclesiae Christi sibi committi contingat, neve insidiator ille obrepat, ac de Christi castris quid intercipiat. Itē [?] Sobrium, vel potius temperantem, & sana mente praeditum. Est enim σωφροσύνη [?], sive σωτηρία [?] ἢ φρονήσεως [?], sive σώφρονα φρόνησις [?], integra & illaesa mentis constitutio, ne qua fit parte vel odio, vel invidentia, vel pravo aliquo studio, aut aliàs incurabili defectu intelligentiae ac judicii vitiata.
units.tr: But let us see what else a bishop ought to be. He must be vigilant, watching over every part of his office, so that no harm comes to the church of Christ committed to him, and that that treacherous enemy does not creep in and seize anything from Christ's camp. He must also be sober, or rather temperate, and of sound mind. For temperance [σωφροσύνη], or [σωτηρία ἢ φρονήσεως], or [σώφρονα φρόνησις], is an integral and unimpaired constitution of the mind, not vitiated in any part by hatred, envy, some perverse zeal, or any other incurable defect of understanding and judgment.

units.la: Modestum, vel compositū, bonis scil. moribus decoratum, qui & frugalibus atque decoris utatur vestibus.
units.tr: Modest, or composed, that is, adorned with good morals, and one who wears simple and decent clothing.

units.la: Hospitalem, vel potius amantem hospitium, id est, qui hospites ac peregrinos amanter complectatur, & omnibus modis foveat.
units.tr: Hospitable, or rather one who loves hospitality, that is, one who warmly welcomes guests and strangers and cherishes them in every way.

units.la: Porro sobrietatem, modestiam & hospitalitatem etiam eos habere oportet, quibus praeest (quemadmodum Oecumenius annotavit.) Addidit ergo Apostolus, quod magistri proprium est:
units.tr: Furthermore, the bishop ought also to have sobriety, modesty and hospitality in those over whom he presides (as Oecumenius observed). The Apostle therefore added what belongs to a teacher:

units.la: Aptum ad docendum, qui videl.sciat quid, quibus, quatenus & quomodo docenda sint quelibet, ut scite ad usum populi accommodetur Dei verbum: quique non tantum artibus ad id necessariis sit excultus, sed etiam donum Dei tale habens, denique in hoc diligentiam adhibens. Non violentum, seu obnoxium vino, qui vino potando impensius delectetur, illiq; frequentius ac diutius assideat. Vinum enim dementat & pervertit sensum, adeo ut ne membra quidem corporis suo fungantur officio. Hac ratione vetuerunt Canones, ne ministri Ecclesiæ tabernas vinarias ingrediantur. Vide in concilio Loodicensi can. 24.
units.tr: Apt to teach: one who knows what, to whom, how far and in what manner anything is to be taught, so that the Word of God is skilfully adapted to the use of the people; who is not only trained in the arts needed for this, but also has such a gift from God, and who applies diligence to it. Not violent, or addicted to wine: one who takes more pleasure in drinking wine and sits with it more often and for longer. For wine makes a man mad and perverts his judgment, so that even the members of the body do not perform their function. For this reason the canons forbade ministers of the Church to enter wine taverns. See the Council of Laodicea, canon 24.

units.la: Non percussorem, hoc est, vel acerbum & sævum objurgatorem & minacem, qui fit Martii caloris, aut qui fratrũ percutiat conscientiam. Quanto enim ludibrio se exponant, notum est, qui ad infligendum pugni ictum (ne dicamus ad gladium exerendum) sunt promptiores, quàm ad pacandas sua gravitate aliorum lites.
units.tr: Not a striker, that is, not one who is harsh and cruel in rebuke, threatening, hot with the heat of March, or one who strikes the consciences of his brothers. How much they expose themselves to ridicule is well known, those who are quicker to deliver a blow with the fist (not to say draw the sword) than to settle the quarrels of others by their dignity.

units.la: Non turpis lucri cupidum, vel nimium avidè lucra captantem. Nam tametsi hospitalitas ab Episcopo requiratur, attamen hujus prætextu nullum sectabitur lucrum inhonestum: quod faciunt, qui cum pietatis & religionis detrimento munera accipiunt, deinde rebus turpibus, inhonestis, illiberalibus & Episcopo indecoris quærunt victū.
units.tr: Not greedy for shameful gain, nor one who grasps at profit too eagerly. For although hospitality is required of a bishop, he must not, under that pretext, pursue any dishonourable gain. This is what those do who accept gifts to the detriment of piety and religion, and then seek their living from base, disreputable and illiberal things, unbecoming to a bishop.

units.la: Sed æquum, qui de suo jure multum remittat, consideratâ proximi conditione, tenuitate, necessitate, impossibilitate: non rixas nec turbas dantem, non pertinaciter suum debitum, aut jus efflagitantem, etiam convitiis quotidianis. Est enim ἐπιεικὴς[?], homo sic moderatus, ut in rebus gerendis nihil tribuens affectibus, id sequatur, quod videtur esse decens, æquum & probabile.
units.tr: But equitable, one who gives up much of his right, having regard to the neighbour's circumstances, poverty, necessity and inability; not one who stirs up quarrels and disturbances, nor who stubbornly demands his due or right, even with daily abuse. For the equitable [ἐπιεικής] man is so moderate that in conducting affairs he yields nothing to the passions, but follows what seems fitting, fair and reasonable.

units.la: Alienum à pugnis, id est, absque jurgio, & litigandi contendendive ardore, 2. Timoth. 2. quique fugiat contentiones & certamina, dirimat potius ea & pacificus sit. Veritas enim nimia contentione amittitur.
units.tr: Not given to fighting, that is, without wrangling and without the ardour of litigating and contending (2 Tim. 2), one who avoids quarrels and disputes, rather settles them, and is peaceable. For truth is lost through excessive contention.

units.la: Alienum ab avaritia, id est, ab argenti amore & cupiditate alienum. Avaritia enim præcipuè nocet iis, qui versantur in administratione: & quidem nocet multis modis. Hæc ex Apostolo Christi, fecit proditorem Christi. Hæc est radix omnium malorum. Avari facilè expugnantur pecunia in judiciis: item studio cumulandi privatas facultates negligunt ministerium, negligunt studia doctrinæ (sicut nunc sæpe apparet, pastores magis servire rei familiari, quàm Ecclesiæ) quo fit ut avarus Episcopus & alios & seipsum defraudet. Itaque duplici nomine fuerit iniquus.
units.tr: Not greedy, that is, free from love of money and the desire for silver. For avarice harms especially those who are engaged in administration, and it harms them in many ways. This vice, from the Apostle of Christ, made a betrayer of Christ; it is the root of all evils. The avaricious are easily overcome by money in lawsuits; likewise, from eagerness to pile up private wealth, they neglect the ministry and neglect the study of doctrine (as is often now apparent, ministers serve their household affairs more than the Church), with the result that the greedy bishop defrauds both others and himself. Thus he is unjust on a double account.

units.la: Bonum ac frugi œconomum, qui (ut inquit Apostolus) suæ domui bene ac honestè præsit, eamque recte gubernet. Nam quemadmodum avaritia vitio datur Episcopis, ita & profusio & rei familiaris neglectus. Uterque enim in extremis hæret, & culpabilis est: qui verò medium tenet, is justè ambulat.
units.tr: A good and thrifty steward, who (as the Apostle says) presides well and honourably over his own house and governs it rightly. For just as avarice is a fault in bishops, so too are extravagance and neglect of household affairs. Both cling to extremes and are blameworthy; but the one who keeps to the middle walks justly.

units.la: Bonum item & probatum patrem familias, qui liberos (qui parentum sunt, quasi vivæ simulachra) habeat in subjectione cum omni reverètia, seu gravitate. i.familiam tum obedientem, tum & omnibus modis honestam. Hoc duplici de causa requiritur in Episcopo, tum ne ejus familia sit aliis malo exemplo aut scandalo, tum ut inde ingenium ejus cognoscatur ac judicetur, an videatur recte præfuturus domui Domini, qui suæ bene male præfuerit. Nam si quis (inquit) domui propriæ præesse non novit, quomodo Ecclesiam Dei curabit? Qui non potest facilora, quomodo is curabit majora? Qui sua propria negligit, multo magis aliena negligit. Qui liberos non amat, quos natura charissimos, conjunctissimosque esse voluit, quomodo alios amabit? Qui suos non coercet, multo minus coercebit alienos. Interea tamen satendum est, nonnunquam usuvenire, ut curam ac diligentiam patrisfamiliás invincibilis quædam liberorum protervia (taceo nunc superbam -contumaciam nonnullarum-uxorum) vincat, illis præsertim locis, ubi communi corruptione juventus perit & obrutescit. Sed quod rarum & extraordinarium est, communem legem atque regulam non infringit.
units.tr: Likewise, a good and approved father of a family, who keeps his children (who are, as it were, living images of their parents) in subjection with all reverence and seriousness; that is, a household both obedient and honourable in every way. This is required of a bishop for two reasons: first, that his household not be a bad example or a scandal to others; second, that his character may be known and judged, to see whether he seems likely to govern the house of the Lord rightly, if he has governed his own badly. For (he says) if a man does not know how to preside over his own house, how will he care for the Church of God? He who cannot manage smaller things, how will he manage greater ones? He who neglects his own affairs will much more neglect those of others. He who does not love his children, whom nature wished to be dearest and closest to him, how will he love others? He who does not restrain his own will much less restrain others. Meanwhile, it must be admitted that it sometimes happens that the care and diligence of the father of a family is overcome by an invincible wilfulness of children (I say nothing now of the proud obstinacy of certain wives), especially in those places where the young perish and are overwhelmed by common corruption. But such a case, being rare and exceptional, does not break the common law and rule.

units.la: Non novitium, seu recens plantatum vel insitum, intellige, in fidem & ecclesiam Dei, vel recens in Catechesi institutum. Ratio hujus consilii est, Ne inflatus, & quasi saltu dementatus (sufitatum enim est, ut inexperti, subitoque in summam dignitatem elati insolescant, juxta illud, Honores mutant mores) in judicium incidat diaboli, hoc est, ne perinde ruat, sicut diabolus, qui per superbiam ex angelo Dei factus est hostis & adversarius Dei, & calumniator fratrum: aut ne in ejus quasi jus, laqueos, potestatemque incidat. Superbi enim non quaerunt a Deo opem, eoque ab illo deferuntur, & transeunt in potestatem Satanae. Est hoc ingenium superbiae, ut ex Episcopis faciat Diabolos, ex pastoribus lupos, ex patribus oppressores ac tyrannos.
units.tr: Not a novice, or recently planted or grafted, understand: into the faith and Church of God, or recently instructed in the catechism. The reason for this counsel is that, puffed up and as if made giddy by a sudden leap (for it is commonly observed that the inexperienced, suddenly raised to the highest dignity, become insolent, according to the saying, "Honours change manners"), he may fall into the judgment of the devil, that is, fall in the same way as the devil, who through pride from an angel of God became an enemy and adversary of God and a slanderer of the brothers; or lest he fall into the snares and power of the devil, as if under his jurisdiction. For the proud do not seek help from God, and so are abandoned by him and pass into the power of Satan. It is the nature of pride to make devils out of bishops, wolves out of ministers, and tyrants and oppressors out of fathers.

units.la: In summa D. Paulus adeo illustre ac conspicuam innocentiam vitae Episcopi esse vult, ut ne gentes quidem.i.infideles ac impii habeant, quod de eo blaterent, aut jure objiciant flagitium. Oportet, inquit, illum habere bonum testimonium ab extraneis, seu alienis[?] a religione. Additur autem ratio: Ne in probrum incidat, & laqueum calumniatoris, seu diaboli: h.e. Ne fiat infamis, atq; ita habeat diabolus, quo eum reddat contemptibilem, omniaque ejus recte facta conatusque, tanquam laqueo quodam infamia suffocet: vel etiam ne turpiter lapsum subinde ex alio peccato in aliud pertrahat, ut ille solet, ubi aliquem semel in aliquod tetrum facinus pertraxit.
units.tr: In sum, St Paul wants the bishop's innocence of life to be so illustrious and conspicuous that even the Gentiles, that is, the unbelieving and impious, have nothing to babble about him or to object to him as a disgrace. "He must," he says, "have a good testimony from outsiders," that is, from those alien to religion. A reason is added: lest he fall into reproach and the snare of the slanderer, or devil; that is, lest he become infamous, and the devil have something by which to make him contemptible, and choke all his right deeds and efforts with infamy as with a noose; or even lest, having fallen shamefully, he draw him from one sin into another, as the devil is wont to do once he has drawn someone into some foul crime.

units.la: Haud ab re porro fuerit hic quaerere (juxta Theophyl.) cujus rei causa, qui a vulgaribus & laicis postulet, Col. 3[?]. Occidite membra vestra, quae super terram sunt: & iterum Gal. 5. Qui vero sunt Christi, carnem suam crucifixerunt; nunc vero ab episcopo requirit exigua quædam, ac tanto fastigio indigna, Ne fit vinolentus, neque percussor, &c. Atqui Christus etiam jubet, ut crucem tollamus, Luc.9.Et,Pastor,inquit,bonus,anima suam ponit pro ovibus suis,Ioan.10. Debebat igitur Paulus ab Episcopo potius, ut angelicam viveret vitam, exigere, quæ affectibus careret, quantum ad dignitatis summitatem attinet. Audi igitur, Quoniam paucos exactæ hujusmodi vitæ liceat invenire: Episcopis autem multis in quavis urbe opus erat, qui aliis præessent, propterea moderatam ab eis virtutem postulavit, quæ in multis inveniri potuit. At nunc, proh dolor, quo excidimus Episcopi, ut adeo ne umbram quidem adeo moderatę virtutis in nobis deprehendi liceat? O parce nobis Domine. Hæc ille.
units.tr: It is not beside the point here to ask (following Theophylact) why he requires of ordinary people and laymen, "Mortify your members which are upon the earth" (Col. 3), and again, "Those who are Christ's have crucified their flesh" (Gal. 5); yet now from the bishop he demands certain small things, unworthy of so high a station: that he not be a drunkard, nor a striker, and so on. Yet Christ also commands us to take up the cross (Luke 9), and "the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep" (John 10). Paul ought therefore to have required of the bishop that he live an angelic life, free from the passions, as far as the height of his dignity is concerned. Hear then: since few can be found of such exact life, and yet many bishops were needed in every city to preside over others, he demanded from them a moderate virtue, which could be found in many. But now, alas, into what have we bishops fallen, that not even a shadow of such moderate virtue can be detected in us? O Lord, spare us. So he.

units.la: Quid verò nos hodie dicemus Domino Deo nostro, cujus gloria & Evangelium propter nos male audit, & propter quorum flagitiosam & scandalis plenam vitam plurimorum salus impeditur, quæ per nos promoveri debebat? O Christe Iesu, pastorum princeps, ac magne ovium pastor, miserere tum nostri, tum gregis tui, preciofo sanguine tuo redempti: pasce & custodi tu nos & gregem tuum, qui in nobis est, & emunda nos ab omni peccato, & da nobis omnibus & singulis spiritum tuum sanctum, qui nos ducat in omnem veritatem, regat in omnibus actionibus, sermonibus, cogitationibus:consoletur in omni tentatione & afflictione: suscipe animas nostras nunc & in hora mortis, Amen.
units.tr: What then shall we today say to our Lord God, whose glory and Gospel are ill spoken of because of us, and through whose shameful and scandal-filled lives the salvation of many is hindered, which through us ought to have been advanced? O Christ Jesus, prince of shepherds and great shepherd of the sheep, have mercy both on us and on your flock, redeemed by your precious blood: feed and keep us and your flock that is among us, cleanse us from every sin, and give to us all and to each one your Holy Spirit, who may lead us into all truth, rule us in all our actions, words and thoughts, comfort us in every temptation and affliction; receive our souls now and in the hour of death. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO LVII.
units.tr: SERMON LVII.

units.la: 1. Timot. 4.
units.tr: 1. Timot. 4.

units.la: Spiritus autem certò loquitur, quòd in posterioribus temporibus desciscent quidam à fide, attendentes spiritibus impostoribus, ac doctrinis daemoniorum, per simulationem falsiloquorum, cauterio notatam habentium conscientiam, prohibentium contrahere matrimonium, jubentium abstinere à cibis, quos Deus creavit ad sumendum cum gratiarum actione fidelibus, & iis qui cognoverunt veritatem, quòd quicquid creavit Deus, bonum est: & nihil rejciendum, si cum gratiarum actione sumatur. Sanctificatur enim per sermonem Dei ac precationem.
units.tr: Now the Spirit speaks expressly, that in the latter times some will fall away from the faith, giving heed to deceiving spirits and doctrines of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose conscience is branded as with a hot iron; forbidding marriage, and commanding abstinence from foods which God created to be received with thanksgiving by the faithful and by those who have known the truth. For everything God created is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving. For it is sanctified by the word of God and by prayer.

units.la: 1 Apostolus Paulus his verbis in genere praedicit venturos prophetas falsos, sicut & Christus Matth. 24. Et Petrus cap. 2. Epist. 2. id quod signum erit praecurrens adventum Domini: qui non adveniet, nisi venerit defectio prius, 2. Thessal. 2. Animadvertere ergo hic licet, quantam Ecclesiae suae curam agat Deus, dum ita mature occurrit periculis.
units.tr: In these words the Apostle Paul predicts in general that false prophets will come, just as Christ also does (Matt. 24), and Peter in chapter 2 of his second epistle. This will be the sign going before the coming of the Lord, who will not come unless the falling away has come first (2 Thess. 2). Here we may notice how great a care God takes for his Church, since he meets dangers so early.

units.la: De Apostasia autem, seu defectione ita hoc loco scribit Apostolus.
units.tr: The Apostle writes thus in this place concerning apostasy, or defection.

units.la: Spiritus autem) scil. Dei, cujus oculis oin[?] nia patent.
units.tr: "But the Spirit": namely of God, to whose eyes all things lie open.

units.la: Certò loquitur) i.diserte, clarè, palàm, & non adumbratè nec ambiguè, per eos quos afflavit: qui audiendi sunt tanquam Christus, Luc.10.sicut fugiendi pseudoprophetę, Matth.7. Suntque hęc verba instar praefationis, authoritatem aut certitudinem vaticinii de ventura apostasia indicantis: quae ipsa certitudinis inculcatio gravem admonitionem de cavendis istis erroribus continet. Igitur author indicatur Spiritus sanctus, qui per Paulum loquutus est: certitudo est, quod diserte id, non obscurè testetur.
units.tr: "Clearly speaks": that is, plainly, clearly and openly, not obscurely or ambiguously, through those whom he inspired. They are to be heard as Christ is (Luke 10), and the false prophets are to be fled (Matt. 7). These words serve as a preface, indicating the authority and certainty of the prophecy of the coming apostasy; and this very insistence on certainty contains a grave warning to beware of these errors. So the author is shown to be the Holy Spirit, who spoke through Paul. The certainty lies in this, that he testifies plainly and not obscurely.

units.la: Non est quidem dubium quin reliqua ex eodem spiritu hauserit Paulus: quemadmodum passim non ex se, sed ex spiritu Dei loqui affirmat, 1.Corinth.7. 1.Thess.4.
units.tr: There is no doubt that Paul drew the rest also from the same Spirit, just as he asserts throughout that he speaks not from himself but from the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 7; 1 Thess. 4).

units.la: Verùm, utcunque semper audiendus sit tanquam Christi organû, tamen in causa magni ponderis peculiariter voluit hoc testatû, nihil se profere quàm ex spiritu prophetiae. Sequitur jam ipsum vaticinium, complectens circumstantias, tempus, defectionem à fide, seductores & errores, eorumq; primarium inventorem.
units.tr: However, although he is always to be heard as an instrument of Christ, in a matter of such great weight he wished this especially to be testified: that he puts forward nothing except from the Spirit of prophecy. There now follows the prophecy itself, comprising its circumstances: the time, the defection from the faith, the seducers and their errors, and the chief inventor of them.

units.la: Quod in posterioribus temporibus) sequentibus Apostolorum videlicet seculum, & ad judicii usq; diem procurrentibus: quæ tempora etiamnum hodie durant regnante Antichristo,1.Ioann.2.Ergo posteriora tempora non tam significat illud tempus, quod mox Apostolos confecutū est, quàm quod aliquot seculis postea, ut vox ipsa sonat. Quare perperam hæc Papistæ exponunt de illis primis hæreticis, ut mentes piorū avertant, ne quid tale de ipsorum abominationibus suspicentur. Licet autem semper fuerint hæreses, tamen insurgente Antichristo & plures & periculosiores & diuturniores, ac deniq; latius sævientes exorti sunt, idq; in ipso Dei templo, & sub prætextu summæ pietatis. Illa etiam ipsa vox in plurali numero postremis temporibus videtur indicare durationē erroris per plura secula: quòd nō uno breviq; tempore, sed multis temporibus existent, quod ipsum quoq; indicat ista non de primis illis fanaticis (tantùm) sed (&) de Papatu prædicta esse. Quocirca vigilandum ac diligenter circumspiciendum, ne seducamur.
units.tr: "In later times": that is, in the following age of the Apostles, running on to the day of judgment; these times still endure today, under the reign of Antichrist (1 John 2). So the phrase "later times" signifies not so much that time which closely followed the Apostles, as that which came some centuries afterwards, as the very word sounds. Hence the Papists wrongly explain these words of those first heretics, in order to turn the minds of the godly away from suspecting anything of this kind about their own abominations. Although there have always been heresies, yet with the rise of Antichrist there arose more of them, more dangerous and more lasting, and at last raging more widely, and this in the very temple of God and under the pretext of the highest piety. That very expression, in the plural "in later times", seems also to indicate the duration of the error over many centuries, since it would exist not for one brief time but for many ages; and this too shows that the prophecy concerns not only those first fanatics but also the Papacy. Therefore we must be watchful and look about carefully, lest we be seduced.

units.la: Desciscent quidam) imò multi (quod horrendum est auditu) Matth.24. At non omnes, quod consolatione plenum est. Novit enim Dominus pios è tentatione eripere, 2. Petr.2.
units.tr: "Some will fall away": indeed many (which is horrible to hear; Matt. 24). But not all, which is full of comfort. For the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation (2 Pet. 2).

units.la: A fide) à vera religione & doctrina Apostolorum: seu fiducia & vera noticia Christi, quae statuit, quod propter Christum habeamus remissionem peccatorum fide, quod Deus velit coli fide,& invocari,non externis observationibus, quod regnum Christi sit in spiritu, nova justicia & nova vita, non sit foris dissipatio conjugiorum, & similium ordinationum corporalium. Vbi autem femel vitiatus est cultus Dei,nihil amplius integrum aut sanum:imo tota fides periit,quae non nisi cum puro Dei verbo retineri poteft. Quemadmodum enim fides ex auditu verbi Dei oritur, Roman. 10.ita ex neglectu verbi patitur naufragium. Quoniam igitur omnium malorum causa est (teste Chryfoft.) a fide discedere:maneamus nos fideles usque ad mortem,Apoc.2.
units.tr: "From the faith": from the true religion and the teaching of the Apostles; or the trust in and true knowledge of Christ, which holds that for Christ's sake we have remission of sins through faith, that God wishes to be worshipped and invoked in faith and not by external observances, that the kingdom of Christ is in the Spirit, in new righteousness and new life, and does not consist in outward dissolution of marriages and similar bodily ordinances. But once the worship of God has been corrupted, nothing remains whole or sound; indeed the whole faith perishes, which cannot be kept except with the pure Word of God. For just as faith arises from hearing the Word of God (Rom. 10), so it suffers shipwreck when the Word is neglected. Since, then, as Chrysostom testifies, falling away from the faith is the cause of all evils, let us remain faithful even unto death (Rev. 2).

units.la: Attendentes spiritibus impostoribus) avertentes aures a veritate, & convertentes ad fabulas(2. Timoth.4.) & patefactiones daemoniorum , auscultantesque pseudoprophetis spiritum jactantibus. At non omnes spiritus idem instigat:igitur probandi sunt spiritus an ex Deo sint.1.Ioan.4.
units.tr: "Paying attention to deceiving spirits": turning their ears away from the truth and turning them to fables (2 Tim. 4), and to revelations of demons, listening to false prophets who boast of the Spirit. But the same spirit does not drive all men; therefore the spirits must be tested whether they are from God (1 John 4).

units.la: Ac doctrinis daemoniorum) Exponit ipsum Paulus.q.d.Attendentes pseudoprophetis & diabolicis eorum dogmatibus,a quibus ut seducatur omnino digni sunt,qui Christum.i.veritatem audire nolunt.2.Thessal. 2. Observandum autem , quod clarè & nominatim testatur, quod diabolus sit author malarum opinionum, & traditionum, seu fictitiorum cultuum, quibus vera pietas obruitur. Quantopere attenderint Papistæ spiritibus seductoribus, apparet ex eorum propriis infinitisque historiis. Ut quamprimum aliqua spectra apparuerunt, sive misfas aut quippiam simile præceperunt, mox eis obtemperatum est, neglecto penitus viventis Dei verbo ac expresso mandato, id prohibente, & contraria præcipiente. Sequuntur porro notæ quædam & proprietates antichristi & ejus seductorum.
units.tr: "And to the teachings of demons": Paul himself explains it: that is, to the false prophets and their diabolical dogmas, by which those are rightly deceived altogether who are unwilling to hear Christ, that is, the truth (2 Thess. 2). It must be noted that he clearly and by name testifies that the devil is the author of evil opinions and traditions, or of fictitious worships, by which true piety is crushed. How greatly the Papists have paid heed to seducing spirits appears from their own countless stories. As soon as some apparitions appeared, or ordered something like masses, they were at once obeyed, the living Word of God and its express command being utterly neglected, which forbade such things and commanded the contrary. Further, certain marks and properties of Antichrist and of his seducers follow.

units.la: Per simulationem falsiloquorum) Malo enim spiritu imbuti doctores in hypocrisi & data opera loquuntur ac docent mendacia, id est, à scripturis aliena, quæ videlicet in spirat impostor satanas, qui & ipse in lucis angelum se transfigurare potest. 2. Corint. II. Quantum vero omnibus seculis fucata illa simia hypocrisis & simulata religio potuerit in veritatem, ab ipso Caino Adæ filio usque ad præsens facilè videmus. Quare diligenter caveamus, ne sinamus nos seduci ab illis, qui apud simplices quidem se venditant personam sanctimoniæ, sed interim nugas pro fidei doctrina obtrudunt, & totam sanctitatem in externis exercitiis collocant[?] cùm tamen Deus nunquam ritè illis colatur, Matth.15. Rom.14. Col.2. Nam veri cultores eum adorant in spiritu & veritate, Ioan.4. D. August. lib. quæst. nov. & vet. Testa. quæst.127. egregiè de hypocritarum istiusmodi versutia scribit: Talis est enim (inquit) quorundam versutia: quia ut sanctitatis & castimoniæ amatores esse se simulent, nupœnas esse dicunt damnandas, ut per hoc commendentur, & populum à veritate avertant: & ut abstinentiæ se studere fingant, temperandum à cibis tradunt, ut per hoc se alienos à mundo ad cœlestia regna festinare ostendant, per quod mentes hominum illicientes, deinceps illicita doceant licere, & licita quasi inconcessa damnare. Hæc sunt præstiga Satanæ, &c.
units.tr: "Through the hypocrisy of liars": For teachers imbued with an evil spirit speak and teach lies in hypocrisy and deliberately, that is, things alien to the Scriptures, which the impostor Satan breathes in, he who can also transform himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11). How easily we see that, through all ages, that counterfeit ape hypocrisy and feigned religion could prevail over the truth, from Cain, the son of Adam, down to the present. Therefore let us take care not to allow ourselves to be seduced by those who present themselves to simple folk in the guise of holiness, but meanwhile foist trifles upon them as the doctrine of faith, and place all holiness in external exercises, when yet God is never rightly worshipped by such men (Matt. 15; Rom. 14; Col. 2). For true worshippers adore him in spirit and in truth (John 4). Augustine, in his Questions on the Old and New Testaments, question 127, writes admirably about this kind of cunning of hypocrites: "For this is the cunning of certain men: that, pretending to be lovers of holiness and chastity, they say that marriages are to be condemned, so that they may thereby be commended and turn the people away from the truth; and, feigning to devote themselves to abstinence, they teach abstaining from foods, so that by this they may show themselves to be strangers to the world and hasten to the heavenly kingdom; by which, enticing men's minds, they then teach that unlawful things are lawful, and condemn lawful things as if they were not permitted." These are the deceits of Satan, etc.

units.la: Cauterio notata habentium conscientiâ) Hoc est, qui male sibi conscii sunt, tanquam malefici coram Deo, ut foris sanctimoniam simulent. Nam apud nos candenti ferro notatur malefici stigmatis impressis cuti, quæadmodum olim servis fugitivis notæ inurebantur. Ambrosius cauteriatâ conscientiam exponit, simulatione corruptam: alii infynceram & compunctam: alii ita adustam & corruptam, ut male judicet: alii proi sus amputatam (ut candête ferro testiculi equorũ, boum & arietũ castrâtur) ut nihil sentiat, aut judicet. Solent etiam illa adusta loca aut partes crustâ quandam cócipere sensu omni carente, quæ etiâ metaphora nô male conveniret impiis, sensu omnis cosciẽtiæ caretibus.
units.tr: "Having consciences branded with a cautery": that is, those who are badly conscious of themselves, as evildoers before God, so that they feign holiness outwardly. For among us a criminal is marked with a glowing iron, the stigma impressed on the skin, just as runaway slaves were once branded. Ambrose explains "branded conscience" as one corrupted by pretence; others as one seared and corrupted, so that it judges badly; others as one utterly cut off (as horses', oxen's and rams' testicles are castrated with a hot iron), so that it feels or judges nothing. Such burnt places also commonly take on a kind of crust that has no sensation, which metaphor fits the impious not badly, those who are devoid of all sense of conscience.

units.la: 2 Prohibentium matrimonium) Iam speciatim subjungit quædam dogmata, ex quibus quæ jam proposuit, manifesta fiant, & reliquæ prophetarum doctrinæ æstimentur. Bina autem (secundum Bullingeri sententiam) exempla proponit: alterum quidem, quòd conjugio,&c alterum quòd cibis interdicturi sint. His tertium addit Flacius,quia (inquit) Apostolus nomine ciborum etiam dierum obseruationem praedixit & damnavit,sicut & alibi in Epist.ista cōjungit. Sunt enim illa ex hypocrisi, quae relicta vera sanctitate,alienos colores in fucū accersit. Nam qui ab ambitione, odio,avaritia,crudelitate, aliisq; similibus non abstinent, earum rerū abstinentia , quarum libertatem permisit Deus,justiciam acquirere sibi tentát. Quorsum enim istis legibus onerantur conscientiæ,nisi quia perfectio extra Dei legem quæritur? Hoc autem non fit,nisi ab hypocritis, qui ut impune transgrediantur cordis justiciam,quā lex requirit,interiore suam nequitiam observatiunculis istis tegere: quasi velis oppositis,tentant. Ac quod ad primum attinet, scimus non multò post Apostoli mortem extitisse Encratitas, qui nomen sibi à continentia indiderunt,Tatianos, Catharos cum sua secta, & tandem Manichaeos, qui teste Augustino nuptias & damnarunt, & has omnino pares fecerunt fornicationibus. Idem & Apotactici, id est, Extraordinarii fecēre. Accesit & Hierax, qui usus est hoc argumento : Evangelium debet habere aliquod proprium praeceptum supra Decalogum. Nullum repetitur proprium praeceptum supra Decalogum , nisi de Castitate : ergo Evangelium præcipit coelibatum. Denique Papa prohibuit conjugium suis spiritualibus prorsus. In Laicis autem id horribiliter insectatur, ut impurum ac carnale, immundumque vitae genus, sicut Syricius dicit, istud esse in carne vivere. dist.82[?]
units.tr: "Forbidding marriage": Now he specifically adds certain doctrines, from which what he has already proposed becomes clear and the rest of the prophets' teaching is judged. Two examples (according to Bullinger's opinion) he sets forth: the first, that they will forbid marriage, and the second, that they will forbid foods. Flacius adds a third to these, because (he says) the Apostle, by the name of foods, also foretold and condemned the observance of days, as he joins elsewhere in this Epistle. For these come from hypocrisy, which, leaving aside true holiness, brings in alien colours as paint. For those who do not abstain from ambition, hatred, avarice, cruelty and the like, try to acquire righteousness for themselves by abstaining from those things whose liberty God has granted. For why are consciences burdened with these laws, unless perfection is sought outside the law of God? But this happens only with hypocrites, who, so that they may transgress with impunity the righteousness of the heart that the law requires, try to cover their inner wickedness with these little observances, as if setting up sails against the wind. As for the first example, we know that not long after the death of the Apostles there arose the Encratites, who took their name from continence, and Tatians, Cathari with their sect, and finally the Manichaeans, who, as Augustine testifies, both condemned marriages and made them altogether equal to fornications. The Apotactites, that is, the "Extraordinary" ones, did the same. Hierax also arose, who used this argument: the Gospel must have some special precept above the Decalogue. No special precept above the Decalogue is repeated except concerning chastity; therefore the Gospel commands celibacy. Finally, the Pope has forbidden marriage altogether to his spiritual men. Among the laity, moreover, he attacks it horribly, as an impure, carnal and unclean way of life; as Siricius says, to live in the flesh is that (dist. 82).

units.la: Quid autem veritas de hoc sentit atque pronunciat? Honorabile est, inquit Heb.13. inter omnes conjugium, & cubile impollutum. igitur prohibere conjugium seu matrimonium (quod ex eo sic appellatum esse Augustinus dicit, quod non ob aliam causam debeat foemina nubere, quàm ut mater fiat) non solùm est contra permissionem Dei, sed etiam contra ejusdem institutionem & approbationem. Conjugium enim Deus ipse per se instituit & benedixit, idque in paradiso, & in statu innocentiae. Conjugium enim Deus suo verbo in quinto praecepto (in quo omnis potestas humana superior, qualis & maritorum est, praecipitur honorari) confirmavit: & in septimo probè munivit, ac quasi muro quodam sepivit. Christus Iesus Dei filius de Beata quidem Virgine, sed quae esset in statu matrimonii, nasci voluit. Idem praesens esse voluit nuptiis unà cum matre & discipulis suis, atq; ibi primum signum, quo suam divinitatem ostendit, edere: & , ut Cyrillus ait, nativitatis nostrae principium, quantum ad carnem attinet, sanctificare. Idem se & Ecclesiam suam conjugibus comparavit: & regnum coelorum nuptiali ac regio convivio simile esse pronunciavit. Usus est etiam comparatione de mulieris partu: amplexatusque est pueros, & jusit eos ad se venire. Spiritus sanctus per organa sua & ministros & Apostolos, praescribit conjugibus praecepta & regulas vivendi in hoc statu: quo manifestè declarat se non improbare, sed approbare conjugium. Idem multis egregiis testimoniis & historiis in sacris Bibliis illustravit. Quocirca sancti patriarchae etiam post lapsum hominis sanctè matrimonium conservarunt usque ad tempus Mosis: quo tempore etiam aliquot leges de hoc latae sunt, ut videremus Deo cum primis curae esse, quomodo in eo vivamus. Videris Exod. 20.22.24. Levit.12.15.18. 20. Numer.5.30.36. Deuteron.20.21.22.24. 25. In novo deniq; Testamento conjugium manifestissimè approbatur, commendatur, instruitur, idque plurimis in locis; ut Matt. 19.1. Corinth.7. Ephes.5. Col.3.&c. Petrus 1. Epist.3.non solùm conjugibus sua bona opera praescribit, sed etiam mulieres patriarcharum sanctas appellat, & uxores cohaeredes gratiae dicit.
units.tr: What, however, does the truth think and declare about this? "Marriage is honourable among all, and the bed undefiled," says Heb. 13. Therefore to forbid marriage or wedlock (which Augustine says is so called because a woman ought to marry for no other reason than to become a mother) is not only contrary to God's permission but also contrary to his own institution and approval. For God himself instituted marriage and blessed it, and that in paradise, in the state of innocence. God confirmed marriage by his word in the fifth commandment, in which every human authority, such as that of husbands, is commanded to be honoured, and in the seventh he well fortified it and fenced it in, as with a wall. Christ Jesus, the Son of God, willed to be born of the blessed Virgin, who was, however, in the state of marriage. He himself willed to be present at a wedding together with his mother and disciples, and there to work the first sign by which he showed his divinity; and, as Cyril says, to sanctify the beginning of our birth as far as the flesh is concerned. He likewise compared himself and his Church to spouses, and declared the kingdom of heaven to be like a nuptial and royal feast. He also used the comparison of a woman's labour; he embraced the little children and bade them come to him. The Holy Spirit, through his instruments, his ministers and the Apostles, prescribes to spouses precepts and rules for living in this state, by which he plainly declares that he does not disapprove but approves of marriage. He has illustrated the same in the holy Bible with many excellent testimonies and histories. Hence the holy patriarchs, even after the fall of man, kept marriage holy until the time of Moses, at which time also several laws concerning it were enacted, so that we might see that God has especially cared how we live in it. See Exod. 20.22.24. Levit. 12.15.18.20. Numer. 5.30.36. Deuteron. 20.21.22.24.25. Finally, in the New Testament marriage is most clearly approved, commended and taught, and that in very many places: as Matt. 19.1. Corinth. 7. Ephes. 5. Col. 3. etc. Peter, 1 Epist. 3, not only prescribes good works to spouses but also calls the holy wives of the patriarchs wives and says they are fellow heirs of grace.

units.la: Nullum igitur dubium est, prohibitione conjugii (sicuti & ciborum, de qua mox) do[?] ctrinam esse daemoniorum: id quod novem rationibus Apostolus hoc loco probat, quemadmodum Flacius Illyricus collegit. 1. Quia isti, qui hoc faciunt, de re aliena Dei creatoris sui arbitrio statuunt. 2. Quia contra ejus voluntate ordinant. 3. Quia hoc facto damriant ipsum opificem omnium. 4. Quia còl[?] locant cultum in rebus externis. 5. Quia invertunt finalem causam creationis in summam creatoris contumeliam. 6. Quia libertatem Christianam restringunt, atque adeò in servitutem commutant, quam Christus suo sanguine acquisivit. 7. Quia Deum spoliant debita laude gratiarum actionis, quam ex usu ciborum exigit. 8. Quia spoliant fideles necessario usu rerum. 9. Quia veram notitiam fidelium invertunt, eosque à vera fide abducunt in meram apostasiam.
units.tr: There is therefore no doubt that the forbidding of marriage (as also of foods, of which presently) is a doctrine of demons. The Apostle proves this in this place by nine reasons, as Flacius Illyricus has gathered: (1) because those who do this decide by their own will about something that belongs to another, namely the creation of their Creator; (2) because they ordain against his will; (3) because by this deed they condemn the maker of all things; (4) because they place worship in external things; (5) because they invert the final cause of creation to the highest insult of the Creator; (6) because they restrict Christian liberty and so change it into the servitude which Christ acquired with his blood; (7) because they rob God of the due praise of thanksgiving, which he requires from the use of foods; (8) because they deprive the faithful of the necessary use of things; (9) because they invert the true knowledge of the faithful and lead them away from the true faith into mere apostasy.

units.la: 3 Iubentium abstinere à cibis) Alterum exemplum est de cibis, seu ciborum delectu, quem non semel Apostolus contra Iudaeorum constitutionem, vel apud D. Petrum (qui Legis Mosaicae servitutem nondum plane exuerat) reliquum damnare & reprehendere summo studio conatus est. Attamen Manichaei, Apotactitae & Effeni (quorum haud dissimiles sunt Carthusiani) eundem non fine magno conscientiarum detrimento repetebat, & tanquam necessarium urgebant.
units.tr: Commanding abstinence from foods. The second example concerns foods, or the choice of foods, which the Apostle more than once strove with the utmost zeal to condemn and rebuke, both against the Jewish regulation and in the case of St Peter, who had not yet fully cast off the servitude of the Mosaic law. Yet the Manichaeans, Apotactites and Essenes (to whom the Carthusians are not very unlike) kept demanding the same, not without great harm to consciences, and urged it as necessary.

units.la: Neque etiamnum in pontificum decretis & diplomatibus intermittitur, quum neutiquam is in Ecclesia Dei, tanquam Antichristianae doctrinae symbolum, tolerandus esset. Quare non immerito Papistis hodie objicimus hanc prophetiam, quando coelibatum & ciborum abstinentiam severius urgent, quam ullum Dei praeceptum. Nam omnino in his rebus sanctimoniam locant:
units.tr: Nor is it even now discontinued in the decrees and bulls of the pontiffs, although it ought by no means to be tolerated in the Church of God as a symbol of anti-Christian doctrine. Therefore we rightly object this prophecy today to the Papists, since they urge celibacy and abstinence from foods more strictly than any command of God. For in these things they place holiness altogether:

units.la: deinde falsum & adulterinum Dei cultū instituunt: postremo conscientias alligant necessitati, à qua debebant esse liberæ. Nam fides & religio sincera tradit liberum esse homini cuilibet ducere uxorem, aut nubere viro, hoc vel illo cibi vesci. Sed videamus quomodo ipse Paulus refutet prædictos errores, eorumque similes, simulq; probet illas verè esse doctrinas dæmoniorum, ut dixit.
units.tr: then they institute a false and adulterous worship of God; lastly, they bind consciences to a necessity from which they ought to be free. For sincere faith and religion teach that it is free for any man to take a wife, or for a woman to marry a husband, and to eat this or that food. But let us see how Paul himself refutes the aforesaid errors and their like, and at the same time proves that they are truly doctrines of demons, as he said.

units.la: Quos Deus creavit ad sumendum) vel participandum, id est, ut illis fruantur homines in usum nutricationis, non voluptatis. Participatio enim (inquit Oecumenius) mediocrem acceptionem significat. Neq; ex hoc statim (ut rectè Tertullianus lib. de jejunio scribit) quia libertas ciborum concessa, luxuria permissa est: nec quia liberalius nobiscum Evangelium gesit, continentiam suffulit. Argumentatur Paulus ab efficiente & finalibus causis. Cibi enim sunt creaturæ Dei, conditæ ad usum fidelium: id quod piis omnibus inæstimabile gaudium est, quum sciant alimenta omnia, quibus vescuntur, sibi de manu in manum à Domino porrigi: ut purus sit ac legitimus illorum usus.
units.tr: Which God created to be taken, or partaken of: that is, that men may enjoy them for the sake of nourishment, not pleasure. For participation (says Oecumenius) signifies a moderate reception. Nor for this reason (as Tertullian rightly writes in his book on fasting), because freedom in foods is granted, is luxury permitted; nor, because the Gospel has treated us more generously, has it therefore supported continence. Paul argues from the efficient and final causes. For foods are creatures of God, created for the use of the faithful, a thing which is an inestimable joy to all the pious, since they know that all the nourishment they eat is handed to them by the Lord from hand to hand, so that their use of it is pure and lawful.

units.la: Quanta vero hominum arrogantia est, eripere quod Deus largitur? An cibos ipsi crearunt? An Dei creationem possunt irritam facere? Semper itaq; nobis in mente veniat, eum qui creavit liberum quoque usum fecisse, quem frustrà impedire conantur homines. Hanc libertatem probè intellexit Spiridion Tremithuntis Cypriorum Episcopus, de quo libro 1. Histor. Ecclesiast. Tripartit. cap. 10. sic legimus: Qualis autem circa peregrinorum susceptiones fuerit hinc appareat. Instante jam quadragesima, quidam ex itinere venit ad eum, quibus diebus consuerat cum suis continuare jejunia, & die certo comedere, medio die fine cibo consistens. Videns itaque peregrinum valde defessum: Perge (inquit filiæ suæ) lava peregrini pedes, & cibos appone. Cumque virgo dixisset, nec panè esse, nec ἀλφὸς[?] id est, farinas (quarum rerum folebat nihil habere reconditum propter jejunium) orans primùm, veniamque petens, filiæ jussit ut porcinas carnes, quas domi salitas habebat, coqueret. Quibus coctis, sedens cum peregrino positis carnibus comedebat, & rogabat, ut unà cum eo ederet peregrinus. Quo refutante, Christianumque se profitente: propterea magis, inquit, refutare non debes. Omnia enim munda mundis, sicut sermo divinus edocuit.
units.tr: But how great is the arrogance of men, to snatch away what God bestows! Did they create foods themselves? Can they make God's creation void? Let us therefore always bear in mind that he who created things also made their free use, which men try in vain to hinder. Spyridon, bishop of Tremithus in Cyprus, understood this liberty well, of whom we read in book 1 of the Tripartite Ecclesiastical History, chapter 10, as follows: "What sort of man he was in receiving strangers appears from this. When the fast was now at hand, a certain man came to him from a journey, on days when he was accustomed to continue his fasts with his own people and to eat on a fixed day, standing at midday without food. Seeing therefore that the stranger was very weary, he said to his daughter: 'Go, wash the stranger's feet and set out food.' And when the virgin said that there was neither bread nor [ἀλφὸς], that is, meal (things which he was accustomed to keep in reserve on account of the fast), he first prayed and asked pardon, and then ordered his daughter to cook the pork which he had at home, salted. When these were cooked, he sat down with the stranger, the meat having been set out, and ate, and asked that the stranger eat along with him. When he refused, professing himself a Christian, he said: 'For that reason you ought not to refuse all the more. For all things are clean to the clean, as the divine word has taught.'"

units.la: Altera historia etiam huc faciens apud Eusebium lib. 5. cap. 3. recitatur. Fuit Alcibiades de numero martyrum eorum, qui sub M. Antonino Vero in Galliis passi sunt. Is cum antea nimium parce vixisset, pane solo & aqua in cibum utens, ne in carcere quidem aliam servare victus rationem voluit. Attalus vero Romanus, nobilis, martyr, post supplicia quæ in amphitheatro multa & varia miraculosè sustinuerat,in carcerem reductus,vi* fione monitus est, peccare Alcibiadè, quòd à creaturis Dei abstineret, aliisque occasionem offendiculi præberet. Ita igitur per Attalum Alcibiades admonitus,& meliora doctus,eò tandem perductus est, ut sine formidine & cum gratiarum actione creaturis Dei indifferenter usus in posterum fit. Audet porrò Ignatius ad Philad[?]ph. scribere: Si quis aliquam escam putat execrabilem, cohabitatorem habet Draconem apostatam.
units.tr: Another story bearing on this is related in Eusebius, book 5, chapter 3. Alcibiades was of the number of martyrs who suffered under Marcus Antoninus Verus in Gaul. Having previously lived too sparingly, using only bread and water as food, he did not wish to keep any other manner of diet even in prison. But Attalus, a noble Roman martyr, after the tortures which he had miraculously endured in the amphitheatre, was led back into prison and was warned in a vision that Alcibiades was sinning, in that he abstained from God's creatures and gave occasion of stumbling to others. Thus Alcibiades, admonished through Attalus and taught better things, was at last brought to this point: that thereafter he used God's creatures without distinction, without fear and with thanksgiving. Moreover Ignatius dares to write in his letter to the Philadelphians: "If anyone thinks any food accursed, he has a dragon, an apostate, as his housemate."

units.la: Cum gratiarũ actione) hoc est, ut cognos-scamus cibos esse veré ipsius Dei dona, & à Deo petamus & expectemus, & vicissim glorificemus eum tanquam authorem & datorem. Nihil enim Deo pro sua liberalitate rependere possumus,quàm gratitudinis testimonium. Porrò non potest esse gratiarum actio sine sobrietate & temperantia. Neque enim Dei beneficentiam verè agnoscit, qui ea perperam abutitur.
units.tr: With thanksgiving: that is, that we may acknowledge that foods are truly the gifts of God himself, and ask for them and expect them from God, and in turn glorify him as their author and giver. For we can render nothing to God for his bounty except a testimony of gratitude. Moreover, thanksgiving cannot exist without sobriety and temperance, for he does not truly acknowledge God's kindness who abuses those things amiss.

units.la: Fidelibus ) quibus solis, proprié loquendo,Deus tanquam filiis suis,creaturarum usum, imò totum mundum, & quicquid in mundo est,destinavit,Roman.4. non impiis ac infidelibus, qui velut alienum furantur aut prædantur, quodcunq; usurpant. Quoniam insalutato creatore ea usurpant, & rapiunt cum ejus contemptu. Ac quòd impij & infideles sine omni jure abutantur creaturis Dei, & quòd eæ aliquádo exturbatis impiis, filiis Dei tantum servituræ sint, Paulus Roman.8.docet.
units.tr: To the faithful: to whom alone, properly speaking, God has assigned the use of creatures, indeed the whole world and whatever is in it, as to his own sons (Rom. 4), and not to the impious and unbelievers, who steal or plunder as if it were another's property, whatever they seize. For they seize and snatch these things without acknowledging the Creator, and with contempt for him. And that the impious and unbelievers abuse the creatures of God without any right, and that these creatures will at some point, when the impious have been driven out, serve only the sons of God, Paul teaches in Romans 8.

units.la: Et iis qui cognoverunt veritatem) Definit hic quos vocet fideles, nempe qui notitiam habent sanæ doctrinæ. Neq; enim fides nisi ex verbo Dei, Roman.10. Porrò veritas est, quòd quicquid creavit Deus, per se suaq; natura bonum fit, quòd fidelibus omnia sint licita, quòd legis umbræ adveniente Christo cessaverit[?], &c. Qui igitur hanc veritatem cognoscit, potest tranquilla conscientia quibuslibet cum gratiarum actione vesci.
units.tr: And to those who have known the truth: Here he defines whom he calls the faithful, namely those who have knowledge of sound doctrine. For faith comes only from the Word of God (Rom. 10). Moreover, the truth is this: whatever God has created is good in itself and by its nature; to the faithful all things are lawful; and with the coming of Christ the shadows of the law have ceased, etc. He who knows this truth can therefore eat anything with a quiet conscience, giving thanks.

units.la: Nam quicquid creavit Deus) & vero etiam ordinavit, ut conjugium (Creatura enim pro ordinatione etiam capitur, 1. Petr. 2.) bonum est, & nihil reijciendum: si cum gratiarum actione sumatur) cujus semper meminisse debemus, 1. Corinth. 10. Ioann. 6.
units.tr: For whatever God has created, and indeed has ordained, such as marriage (for "creature" is also taken for ordinance, 1 Pet. 2), is good, and nothing is to be rejected, if it is received with thanksgiving, which we must always remember (1 Cor. 10; John 6).

units.la: Sanctificatur enim) Id est, ita purum & sanctū fit, ut eo uti possimus bona confcientia, tanquam de manu patris nostri coelestis, cum ejus benedictione, rite accepto.
units.tr: For it is sanctified: that is, it is made so pure and holy that we may use it with a good conscience, as received from the hand of our heavenly Father, with his blessing, duly taken.

units.la: Per sermonem Dei) scilicet nō pronunciatum tantùm, sed etiam creditum: vel per filium Dei, per quem omnia nobis benedicuntur. vel per institutionem Dei.
units.tr: Through the word of God: understood not only as spoken but also as believed; or through the Son of God, through whom all things are blessed for us; or through the institution of God.

units.la: Ac precationem) id est, tum petitionem favoris Dei benedictionisq; alimenti, tum celebrationem Dei & gratiarum actionem, ufumq; fidelem. Ita sententia erit. Ipsum enim Domini verbum,ipsa inquam Dei concessio, & sententia, qua pronunciat omnia esse puris pura, fides item recipientis, & gratiarum actio fidelis, facit ut nihil impuritatis habeat cibus Christianorum.
units.tr: And prayer: that is, both the request for God's favour and blessing upon our food, and the celebration of God and the giving of thanks, and the faithful use of it. The sense will therefore be this: the very word of the Lord, indeed God's own grant and sentence by which he pronounces that all things are pure to the pure, together with the faith of the one receiving and the faithful thanksgiving, makes the food of Christians free of any impurity.

units.la: Concidunt ergo hic seinel[?] quęcunq; mercatores Romani præceperunt de ciborum delectu, de temporum & dierum discrimine. Christiano enim licet quovis tempore vesci cibis, Matth.15. Actor.10. Colos.2. Discimus præterea quanta cum reverentia ad mensam accedere, & ab eadem debeamus recedere. Est enim belluinus vescendi mos, quum homines sine ulla precatione ad mensam se ingerunt (qui mos tamen valde usitatus est in nuptiis, quibus nullus verbi minister interest)ac bene saturi, sepulta Dei mentione alio se proripiunt: illorumve imitatores fiunt, de quibus scriptum est: Sedit populus ut ederet ac biberet, & surrexerunt ad ludendum. Atqui convivæ Domini sumus, Dominus pascit nos, in hujus oculis versamur, illius munificentia alimur. Precandum ergo & gratias agendas esse ante & post cibum, nemo est qui nō videat, sed &ita in mensa, ut in oculis Dei versandum, quemadmodū piè M. Heinrychus Bullingerus pię memoriæ, monet. Aberit itaq; omnis amaritudo, contumelia, calumnia, rixa, obtrectatio, denique luxus & ebrietas, obscœnitas & intemperantia omnis: nihil fœdum dictu, aut auditum turpe in mensa proponatur, sed quod honę-[?] stum, pium ac jucundum sit. Reverentia hospitis, qui præsens est, & nos alit perpetuò, retineat in officio & disciplina sanƈta. Idem nobis adsit sua gratia, suoque spiritu, ut possimus omnia, sive edamus, sive bibamus, sive matrimonium contrahamus, sive quid faciamus, in gloriam ejus facere, per Christum Jesum Dominum nostrum. Amen.
units.tr: Therefore the rules the Roman merchants laid down about the choice of foods, and the distinction of times and days, fall away here at once. For a Christian may eat foods at any time (Matt. 15; Acts 10; Col. 2). We learn further with how much reverence we ought to come to the table and how we ought to leave it. For it is a beastly manner of eating when people throw themselves at the table without any prayer (a custom indeed very common at weddings, where no minister of the Word is present), and, being well filled and having buried the mention of God, rush off elsewhere; or they become imitators of those of whom it is written: "The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play" (Exod. 32). Yet we are guests of the Lord; the Lord feeds us, we live before his eyes, and we are nourished by his bounty. That we must pray and give thanks before and after food no one fails to see; but also that we must so conduct ourselves at table as those who are under God's eyes, as the pious Heinrich Bullinger of blessed memory advises. Therefore all bitterness, insult, slander, quarrelling, detraction, and finally luxury and drunkenness, obscenity and all intemperance, shall be absent; nothing foul to say or shameful to hear shall be put forward at the table, but what is honourable, pious and pleasant. Let reverence for the guest, who is present and nourishes us continually, keep us in holy duty and discipline. May he himself be present with his grace and his Spirit, so that we may be able to do all things, whether we eat, or drink, or contract marriage, or do anything else, to his glory, through Christ Jesus our Lord. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO LVIII
units.tr: SERMON LVIII

units.la: Tit. 2.
units.tr: Titus 2.

units.la: Tu vero loquere quæ decent sanam doctrinam. Senes ut sobrii sint, graves, modesti, sanæ fide, charitate, patientia. Anus itidem, ut in habitu sint qui religionem deceat, non calumniatrices, vino multo servientes, ut honesta doceant, quæ possint modestas reddere adolescentulas, ut maritos suos diligant, ut liberos ament, ut sobriæ sint, pura, domus custodes, bonæ, subditæ suis viris, ne sermo Dei male audiat. Adolescentes similiter adhortare, ut sobrii sint, per omnia temetipsum præbens formam bonorum operum in doctrina, integritatem, gravitatem, sermonem sanum, irreprehensibi-lem: lem:ut[?] is qui repugnat, rubore suffundatur, nihil habens, quod de vobis dicat mali.
units.tr: But you, speak the things that befit sound doctrine. That the aged men be sober, grave, temperate, sound in faith, in charity, in patience.
