The aged women likewise, that they be in such behaviour as becomes holiness, not false accusers, not given to much wine, teachers of good things; that they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children, to be discreet, chaste, keepers at home, good, obedient to their own husbands, that the word of God be not blasphemed. Young men likewise exhort to be sober-minded; in all things shewing thyself a pattern of good works: in doctrine, in incorruptness, in gravity, sound speech that cannot be condemned: that he who is of the contrary part may be afraid, having no evil thing to say of you.

units.la: Etsi Apostolus hoc loco videtur duntaxat officium evangelici concionatoris (si referatur [illegible, ~6 letters] ad [illegible, ~4 letters]) praescribere, quemadmodum & principium & finis contextus indicare videntur: tamen interim quoq; de aliarum personarum officiis agit, veluti senum vetularum, juvencularum & juvenum. Est autem Doctoris Evangelici, sanam doctrinam de fide in Christum & bonis moribus urgere apud omnes ordines & aetates: & optimo exemplo sanctae vitae aliis praelucere, malosque refutare. Inquit enim: Tu verò loquere, quae decent sanam doctrinam, h. e. non nugas, non fabulas Iudaicas, non somnia propria, in tui & aliorum perditione, non humanas constitutiones, non speculationes, quae ostentationi serviunt magis, quàm aedificationi, sed sermonem Dei, qui animas verè pascit, & sanat atque salvat omnem credentem, eumque ad veram pietatem erudit, Matth.4.8. Psalm.107. Rom.1. 2.Tim.1. Tametsi nullam dictis tuis adhibeant fidem, & reprobi sint, tu tamen quod tua interest, facito, nihil obticeas, Ezech.3. Sed quoniam nihil prodest aliquem (ut ait Hieron.) exercitatum esse in dicendo, & ad loquendum trivisse linguam, nisi plus exemplo docuerit quàm verbo: vult insuper Apostolus[?], ut Titus & quilibet episcopus sese[?] τύπον, id est, formam & exemplar aut speculum praebeat omnis virtutis ad doctrinam, ut scilicet inter docendum praestet integritatem animi nullis corrupti cupiditatibus, gravitatem quoque morum, non illa nimis austeram & tetricam, quae arceat auditores & doctorem reddat exosum, sed conjunctam lenitati ac humanitati, quae eum efficiat venerandum simul & amabilem. Ita quoq; sermonem & colloquia instituat omnia, ut nihil in his omnibus reprehendi possit, imo ne hostis quidem quod sugillet inveniat, sed rubore potius suffundatur, si optimo viro male loqui & obtrectare coeperit,1.Petr.2.3. Et sanè, si pastores omnes vitam viverent vocatione sua dignam, etiam hostibus terrori essent. Verumenimvero tales non multi reperiuntur. Quare autem hoc? Si mihi licet dicere quod sentio, duas referam rationes haud postremas, ob quas ejusmodi non habemus. Quarum prior colligi potest ex verbis Iacobi,cap.4. ubi ait: Non habetis, propterea quod non postulatis: Altera ex verbis Pauli 1. Thessalon. 5. ubi dicit: Rogamus autem vos fratres, ut agnoscatis eos qui laborant inter vos, & qui praesunt vobis in Domino, & admonent vos, ut habeatis illos in summo precio, per charitatem propter opus illorum, pacem habete cum illis, &c. Si enim Ecclesiae rogarent dominum messis, ut extruderet operarios in messem suam: & si fideles ac prudentes operarios ad fe missos agnoscerent, iisque parerent: utique res earum optime fe haberent. Sed de his satis.
units.tr: Although the Apostle in this place seems only to prescribe the duty of the evangelical preacher (if it is referred to ...), as both the beginning and the end of the context seem to indicate; yet meanwhile he also deals with the duties of other persons, namely of old men, old women, young women and young men. It is, however, the duty of the evangelical teacher to press sound doctrine concerning faith in Christ and good morals upon all orders and ages, and to shine before others with the best example of a holy life, and to refute the wicked. For he says: But you, speak the things that befit sound doctrine, that is, not trifles, not Jewish fables, not private dreams to the ruin of yourself and others, not human constitutions, not speculations which serve display more than edification, but the word of God, which truly feeds souls, heals and saves every believer, and instructs him in true piety (Matt. 4.8; Ps. 107; Rom. 1; 2 Tim. 1). Although they give no faith to your words and are reprobate, you nevertheless, as it concerns you, do it; conceal nothing (Ezek. 3). But since it profits nothing (as Jerome says) for someone to be practised in speaking and to have worn down his tongue for talking, unless he has taught more by example than by word, the Apostle further wills that Titus and every bishop should present himself as a type, that is, a form, exemplar or mirror of every virtue for doctrine; so that, namely, while teaching he may show integrity of mind, uncorrupted by any lusts, and also gravity of manners, not that too severe and harsh gravity which repels the hearers and makes the teacher hateful, but gravity joined with gentleness and humanity, which makes him at once venerable and lovable. Likewise let him so order all his speech and conversations that nothing in all these can be found fault with, and not even an enemy may find anything to carp at, but rather be put to shame if he begins to speak evil of an excellent man (1 Pet. 2.3). And truly, if all ministers lived lives worthy of their calling, they would even be a terror to enemies. But truly such are not many to be found. Why is this? If I may say what I think, I will set forth two reasons, not the least, on account of which we do not have such men. The first of these can be gathered from the words of James, ch. 4, where he says: You have not, because you ask not. The other from the words of Paul, 1 Thess. 5, where he says: We beseech you, brethren, that you know them who labour among you, and who are over you in the Lord, and admonish you, that you esteem them very highly in charity for their work's sake, and be at peace with them, etc. For if the churches asked the Lord of the harvest to thrust labourers into his harvest, and if the faithful recognised the prudent labourers sent to them and obeyed them, surely their affairs would go on very well. But enough of these things.

units.la: 2 Videamus nunc quid unamquamque aetatem & sexum deceat. Generalis enim doctrina minus afficit: ubi autem paucis exemplis propositis singuli vocationis suae admonentur, nemo est cui non promptum sit colligere, sibi a Domino satis mandari negocii, in quo se exerceat: adeo ut non opus sit vel hunc monachum, vel illam nonnam fieri.
units.tr: 2 Let us now see what befits each age and sex. For general teaching affects less; but when a few examples are set forth and each is reminded of his calling, there is no one who cannot readily gather that enough business has been entrusted to him by the Lord in which he may exercise himself; so that there is no need for this one to become a monk or that one a nun.

units.la: Est igitur Evangelicorum senum munus, primum ut sobrii sint, & ad officia pietatis advigilantes, non temulenti, non somnolenti: ut eorum consilio juventus uti, & exemplo ad virtutis amorem induci possit. Omnibus quidem prohibetur crapula & ebrietas (Luc. 21.Ephef.5.) sed senum hic mentionem fecit Apostolus, quos jubet esse [?]νηφαλίους: quia plerunque sunt bibaculi, & torpidi: sicut proverbium [?]Αστοῦ γῆρας, cujus & Terentius in Heautont. meminit, ubi Syrus ait, Visavero est, quod dici solet, aquilae senectus, non frustra usurpatur, & exemplum Noachi & Loti testatur.
units.tr: It is therefore the office of evangelical old men, first, that they be sober, and watchful over the duties of piety, not drunken, not drowsy; so that the young may use their counsel and be led by their example to love virtue. Excess and drunkenness are indeed forbidden to all (Luke 21; Eph. 5); but the Apostle has made mention here of old men, whom he bids to be sober [νηφαλίους], because they are for the most part tipplers and sluggish; just as the proverb "the old age of a city" [ἀστοῦ γῆρας], which Terence also mentions in the Heautontimorumenos, where the Syrian says, is what is commonly said: "the old age of an eagle". It is not used without reason, and the example of Noah and Lot bears witness to it.

units.la: Deinde, ut sint graves, honestatem prę se ferentes, ut sint venerandi omnibus, non leves, & contra aetatis decorum juveniliter ineptientes, ut sint ridiculi, atque ita juventutem omni verecundia solvant: quod malum ex vinositate multum oriri solet. Tum eorum est, ut sint temperantes, vel modesti sive moderati, ne sint nimium Demeq, id est, severi & morosi, vel iracundi. Alii vertunt pudici, ut Hieronymus: ne videlicet in aliena ætate luxurient, id est, ne frigido jam ad libidinem sanguine exemplo sint adolescentibus ad ruinam. Tales enim odit sapientia, Sira.25. Alii prudentes. Græcè vocatur σωφρονες, παρὰ τοῦ σώματος ἔχειν τὰς φρένας [?], ut Theo-phylactus ait, id est, eo quod salvas & incolumes mentes habeant. Sunt enim inter fenes etiam qui insaniant ac dementes sint: alii quidem ex vino: alii vero ex pusillanimitate.
units.tr: Next, that they be grave, bearing honesty before them, so that they may be venerable to all, not light, and, contrary to the decorum of their age, playing the fool youthfully, so that they become ridiculous and thus loosen the young from all shame; a evil which is commonly much produced by intoxication. Then it is their duty to be temperate, or modest and moderate, lest they be too severe and morose, that is, harsh and sour, or irascible. Others translate "chaste", as Jerome does: namely, lest they run riot in the age of others, that is, lest, with blood now cold for lust, they become a ruinous example to the young. For wisdom hates such men (Sirach 25). Others "prudent". In Greek it is called "sensible" [σωφρονες], as if from "having sound minds" [παρὰ τοῦ σῴζειν τὰς φρένας], as Theophylact says, that is, because they have their minds safe and whole. For there are also among old men some who rave and are demented: some indeed from wine, others from pusillanimity.

units.la: Præterea, ut sint sani fide erga Deum, charitate erga proximum, ita ut etiam inimicos diligant: patientia in communi vita & variis injuriis ac difficultatibus, ita ut perduret in omni tentatione usque in finem, nullis cedentes adversis. Senibus vero hoc præcipitur non solum, quia plerunque sunt superstitiosi, attenti ad rem, & morosi: sed etiam, ut ipsi reliquos sanitatem fidei, quæ sit in Deum per Christum, doceant.
units.tr: Moreover, that they be sound in faith towards God, in charity towards their neighbour, so that they love even their enemies; in patience in common life and under various injuries and difficulties, so that they persevere in every temptation to the end, yielding to no adversities. This is enjoined on old men not only because they are for the most part superstitious, anxious about property, and morose; but also so that they may themselves teach the rest the soundness of faith which is towards God through Christ.

units.la: 3 Anuum & provectæ ætatis matronarum idem officium est. Et insuper quoniam illæ (ut plurimum videre est) aut lascivé adhuc se colunt, aut aliquid habent in vestitu superstitiosum: raro medium tenent: utrique vitio occurrere Paulus voluit, modum præscribens, qui & decoro & religioni congruat, aut (si mavis simplicius) quo sanctas pias se esse testentur: unde Lutherus vertit: <bl>Daß sie sich stellen / wie den heiligen ʒimer[?].</bl> Quod genus per species quasdam declarat: quarum prima est, ne sint calumniatrices, ut plerunque solent malevolè pravos sermones de aliis spargere. Ita fit ut sæpenumerò calumniosa garrulitate quasi face ardenti multas domos inflamment.
units.tr: 3 The same duty belongs to old women and matrons of advanced age. And moreover, since these (as is most often seen) either still adorn themselves wantonly, or have something superstitious in their dress, they seldom keep the middle way; Paul wished to meet both faults, prescribing a measure which agrees both with decorum and with religion, or (if you prefer a plainer way of saying it) by which they show themselves to be holy and pious; whence Luther translates: that they conduct themselves as holy women. He declares this kind by certain species: of which the first is that they not be false accusers, since they are wont for the most part to spread evil talk about others out of malice. Thus it comes about that very often, with calumnious chatter, like a blazing torch, they set many houses on fire.

units.la: Secunda, ne sint multo vino deditæ, sed sobriæ. Frigida res est senectus, quare vinum desiderat: deinde cum non possit sustinere, ut imbecilla, succumbit & vincitur, non ex moderato vino, sed à multo: ex hoc autem & ad calumnias & criminationes fiunt propensiores[?].
units.tr: The second: that they not be given to much wine, but sober. Old age is a cold thing, therefore it desires wine; then, since it cannot bear it, being feeble, it succumbs and is overcome, not by moderate wine but by much; and from this they become more prone to calumnies and accusations.

units.la: Tertia, ut doceant, non in templo aut cœtu (1. Corinth. 14. 1.Tim. 2.) sed domi & privatim, virgines & juvenculas mulierculas, non aniles fabulas, somnia, deliria, carmina amatoria, nugas de observationibus superstitiosis, de miraculis, benedictionibus & exemplis nescio quibus: sed pia & salutaria præcepta, quæ ad morum honestatem pertinent: ut sint temperantes, modestæ & graves.
units.tr: The third: that they teach, not in the temple or assembly (1 Cor. 14; 1 Tim. 2), but at home and privately, the young virgins and little women, not old wives' fables, dreams, delirious fancies, love songs, trifles about superstitious observances, miracles, blessings and I know not what examples; but holy and salutary precepts, which pertain to the honesty of manners: that they be temperate, modest and grave.

units.la: 4 Virtutes autem junioribus mulierculis præscribendæ, tum à vetulis, tum & à pastore, sunt illæ. Prima, ut sint amantes maritorum: id quod caput est domesticorum bonorum. Nam si hoc affuerit, sequuntur etiam reliqua, nempe prosperitas domus, facultatumque copia & abundantia: quemadmodum è diverso, si absit amor maritalis, omnia quæ affuerint, diffluent ac pessum ibunt. Exemplū Abigail docet [?] etiam stultos maritos amandos esse. Ita enim ad Davidem ait, 1. Reg 25. Ne ponat oro, dominus meus rex cor suum super virum istum iniquum Nabal: quia secundū nomen suum stultus est, & stultitia est cum eo. Hieronymus Vvellerus in Libello de officio Oeconomico, &c. loquens de officio Conjugis, ostendit duobus exemplis quomodo Satan hanc dulcifsimam [illegible, ~6 letters] & benevolentiam uxoris erga maritum multis & variis modis ac technis impedire conetur.
units.tr: 4 The virtues to be prescribed to younger women, both by the older women and by the minister, are these. First, that they love their husbands, which is the head of all domestic blessings. For if this is present, the rest follow as well: prosperity in the household, and plenty and abundance of possessions. Conversely, if marital love is absent, everything that is present will dissolve and come to ruin. The example of Abigail [?] teaches that even foolish husbands are to be loved. For she says to David (1 Sam. 25.): "Let not my lord the king, I pray, set his heart on this wicked man Nabal, for as his name is, so he is: a fool, and folly is with him." Hieronymus Wellerus, in his little book on the duty of the household, etc., speaking of the duty of the wife, shows by two examples how Satan tries to hinder this sweetest [illegible] and goodwill of the wife toward her husband in many and various ways and devices.

units.la: Secunda, ut ament liberos. Nam quæ radicem seu patrem amat, etiam & ramos & fructus, sive filios amabit. Amant autem, qui liberos probè curant, & in pietate disciplina Dei sanctè erudiunt. Nam nolle eos contristare (ut ait Hieronym.) docendo quæ bona sunt, & libertatem tribuere peccandi, non est amare filios, sed odisse.
units.tr: Second, that they love their children. For she who loves the root or the father will also love the branches and fruits, that is, the sons. Those love them who look after their children well and bring them up in piety and in the discipline of God. For not to wish to grieve them (as Jerome says) by teaching them what is good, and to grant them freedom to sin, is not to love children but to hate them.

units.la: Tertia, ut sobriæ sint. Nam temulentæ facile sui copiam faciunt, & sese prostituunt.
units.tr: Third, that they be sober. For drunken women readily make themselves available and prostitute themselves.

units.la: Quarta, ut puræ seu castæ, fideique conjugalis observatissimæ, tam in verbis, quàm corporis gestibus pudicæ sint. Quid enim salvi est in muliere amissa pudicitia? Ita olim dicebat Lucretia.
units.tr: Fourth, that they be pure or chaste, most faithful to the marriage bond, and modest both in words and in bodily gestures. For what is left of a woman once her chastity is lost? So Lucretia once said.

units.la: Quinta, ut domus custodes. Non enim debet domesticatim vagari mulieres (quod vitium etiam 1. Timoth. 5. notatur) sed se dodomi continere, & ut inquit Homerus) telam columque tractare: vel(ut Theophyl. exponit) optimè rem domesticam dispensare, nil prorsus vel luxui, supervacaneis sumptibus, & ornamentis impendere. Atque huc pertinet, quod veteres (ut Phidias Eliensibus, referente Plutarcho in praeceptis conjugalibus) matremfamilias descripturi, pinxerunt Venerem nudam, insistentem testudini, admonentes convenire matribus familias, domum curare, neq; publicis se immiscere negociis. Quemadmodum enim summa testudini voluptas est in sua delitescere cavea: ita proba materfamilias domus custodia nihil habet antiquius. Et ut testudo caput, summitatemque pedum non exerit è corte, nisi hoc corporis cura flagitet: ita proba materfamilias non nisi ob domesticas res excedit in publicum. Et sanè vera matronarum probitas longinquas à domo peregrinationes, choreas, compotationes, discursus frequentiores & confabulationes privatas nedum odit, sed abominatur etiam.
units.tr: Fifth, that they be guardians of the house. For women ought not to wander about from house to house (a fault also noted in 1 Tim. 5.), but should keep themselves at home and, as Homer says, handle the loom and the distaff; or (as Theophylact explains) manage household affairs very well, spending nothing at all on luxury, superfluous expenses and ornaments. To this pertains also what the ancients did (as Phidias did for the Elians, as Plutarch reports in the Precepts of Marriage) when they wished to depict the mistress of the household: they painted Venus naked, standing on a tortoise, reminding us that it befits matrons to care for the house and not to meddle in public affairs. For just as the tortoise's greatest pleasure is to lie hidden in its shell, so a good mistress of the household considers nothing more important than guarding her home. And just as the tortoise does not put out its head and the tips of its feet from the shell unless the care of its body demands it, so a good mistress goes out in public only for domestic business. Indeed, the true honesty of matrons not only dislikes but even abhors long journeys away from home, dances, drinking parties, frequent gadding about and private gossip.

units.la: Apud Ægyptios patrius mos fuit, ne calceis uterentur mulieres, ut ipsa quasi necessitas illas domi manere cogeret. Neque ista fine gravi ratione homines sapientissimi instituerunt. Quàm facilè enim pudicitiæ & honoris sui jacturam faciant, quæ licentiosius vagantur, exemplum Dinæ Iacobi filiæ docet, quam ea occasione constupravit Sichemi princeps, quòd ut filias Chananitides spectaret, incautius egressa fuerat, Genes.34.
units.tr: Among the Egyptians it was the ancestral custom that women did not wear shoes, so that necessity itself would compel them to stay at home. Nor did the wisest men establish this without a serious reason. For how easily do those who wander too freely lose their chastity and honour! The example of Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, teaches this, whom the prince of Shechem violated on the occasion when she had gone out too carelessly to see the daughters of the Canaanites (Gen. 34.).

units.la: Sexta, ut sint bonæ, hoc est, suaves, commodæ, benignæ, placidæ, mites, non acerbæ, rixosæ, responsatrices, pro imperio decertantes, maritis suis obstrepentes. Valeat Xantippe. Debent & in maritis vitia quædam tolerare aut dissimulare, si qui ipsis inciviliores & parum humani contigerint. Exemplo fit Abigail[?] uxor Nabal, de qua 1.Reg.25.
units.tr: Sixth, that they be good, that is, agreeable, accommodating, kind, gentle, mild, not bitter, quarrelsome, contradicting, contending for mastery, or nagging at their husbands. Farewell to Xanthippe! They ought also to tolerate or overlook certain faults in their husbands, if they have been given husbands who are rather rude and less humane. An example is Abigail, the wife of Nabal, of whom we read in 1 Sam. 25.

units.la: Septima, ut subditæ sint suis viris, ne divitiis & nobilitate inflatæ Dei non meminerint sententiæ, per quam subjectæ sunt viris, qui illarum dominentur ex Dei mandato, Genes. 3. Quod mandatum si mulieres diligenter perpenderent, & cogitarent hoc præstando, se non hominibus, sed Deo servire, & eundem Deum in viris (nam vir imago & gloria Dei est, 1. Corinth. ii.[?]) agnoscerent, haud difficile esset illis morem gerere maritis suis.
units.tr: Seventh, that they be subject to their husbands, lest, puffed up with riches and nobility, they forget the sentence of God by which they are made subject to men, who rule over them by God's command (Gen. 3.). If women weighed this command carefully, and reflected that in performing it they serve not men but God, and recognised the same God in their husbands (for the man is the image and glory of God, 1 Cor. 11.), it would not be difficult for them to comply with their husbands.

units.la: Addit autem Apostolus & aliam rationem præscriptorum officiorum: quæ omnes & singulos Christianos impellere debet ad officium suum faciendum. Nam gloriæ divini nominis nosmetipsos & nostra omnia debemus. Et, si curæ nobis est salus nostra, studebimus illam per omnia & in omnibus promovere & ornare. Dicit enim: Ne sermo Dei male audiat, i. ne detur scandalum, & præbeatur impiis occasio calumniandi veram doctrinam. Moxenim impii solent personarum vitia religioni, Deoque vero imputare. Hanc rationem etiam Christus proponit Matth.5. Sic luceat lux vestra coram hominibus, ut videntes vestra bona opera, glorificent patrem vestrum coelestem.
units.tr: The Apostle also adds another reason for the duties prescribed, one which ought to impel all and each Christian to perform their duty. For we owe ourselves and all that is ours to the glory of the divine name. And if our salvation is a concern to us, we will strive to advance and adorn it in all things and in every respect. For he says: that the word of God not be ill spoken of, that is, that no scandal be given and no occasion be offered to the impious for slandering the true doctrine. For soon the impious are wont to impute the vices of individuals to religion and to God himself. Christ also sets out this reason in Matt. 5.: "Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven."

units.la: 5 Porrò adolescentium & juvenum virorum est, ut sobrii sint, pudici in omnibus, tam secundum mentem quàm corpore, tam opere, quàm cogitatione, ut nulla sit in adolescente suspicio turpitudinis. vel, temperantes, non solùm nempe à potu & cibo, sed etiam ab affectibus & cupiditatibus pravis. Possunt ergo superiora quæ de senibus dicta sunt, & ipsis juvenibus accommodari. Nisi quis dicere malit, Apostolum præcipere ut juvenes tantùm ad temperantiam instituantur: quia hæc virtus (ut docet Plato) totam hominis mentem sanat. & in hac virtute facilè omnes aliæ comprehendi queunt, quemadmodum & Cicero eam valde latè expandit. Ergo perinde est, ac si diceret, bene compositos & rationi obtemperantes: <bl>mefig[?] vnd vernünff-</bl> <bl>tig[?]</bl>. Theophyl. hanc rationem reddit, quòd juvenes hujus potissimum admoneri Apostolus velit, ut sint sobrii: quia juvenilem, inquit, ætatem ignis absurdarum voluptatum maximè interturbat, quem oportet extinguere, & ad sobrietatem & temperantiam festinare. Oecumen. ait: Nihil adeò hostile est juventuti, sicut amor corporum. Idem autores scribunt: Adolescentulis senio consectas doctrices attribuit, fœminas fœminis: junioribus autem viris ipsum Titum præficit,virum viris: decorum enim ubique fervat. Vt autem & viri & fœminæ, tam juvenes, quàm senes officio suo fungi queant, atque ita doctrinam servatoris nostri Dei ornare in omnibus, largiatur nobis gratiam suam, qui plenus est gratia & veritate, quæ id nos doceat, propter nominis sui gloriam. Amen.
units.tr: 5 Moreover, it is the duty of young men and adolescents to be sober, and chaste in all things, both in mind and body, in deed and in thought, so that there be no suspicion of baseness in a young man; or, temperate, not only from drink and food but also from evil passions and desires. What was said above about the old men can therefore be applied also to the young men themselves. Unless someone prefers to say that the Apostle prescribes only that the young be trained in temperance, because this virtue (as Plato teaches) heals the whole mind of man, and because all other virtues can easily be comprehended within it, as Cicero also expounds it very widely. So it is as if he said: well ordered and obedient to reason, wise and sensible (a German marginal gloss). Theophylact gives this reason: the Apostle wishes especially the young to be admonished to be sober, because, he says, the fire of absurd pleasures most of all disturbs youthful age, and this fire must be extinguished, and one must hasten to sobriety and temperance. Oecumenius says: nothing is so hostile to youth as love of bodies. The same authors write: he assigns the older teaching women to the younger women, women to women; but he sets Titus himself over the younger men, a man over men, for he keeps decorum everywhere. May he who is full of grace and truth grant us his grace, so that both men and women, young as well as old, may be able to perform their duty, and so adorn in all things the teaching of our Saviour God; and may he teach us this for the glory of his name. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO LIX.
units.tr: SERMON 59.

units.la: Hebr. 13.
units.tr: Heb. 13.

units.la: Onorabile est inter omnes conjugium, & cubile impollutum. Scortatores autem & adulteros judicabit Deus, &c.
units.tr: Marriage is honourable among all, and the bed undefiled. But God will judge whoremongers and adulterers, etc.

units.la: 1 Quid sentiendum fit tum de conjugio sive nuptiis, tum de scortatione & adulterio, docet etiá hic sacra scriptura, idq; brevibus quidé, sed gravissimis verbis. Disserit enim Apostolus de castimonia adversus incontinentiam. Illius dignitatem laudibus effert: hujus vero fœditatem indicat. Ac quo tanto efficacius à vagis libidinibus auditores dehortetur, collationem instituit inter ordinationem divinam conjugii, & turpitudinem à diabolo profectam.
units.tr: 1 Holy Scripture also teaches here what must be thought both about marriage, or wedlock, and about fornication and adultery, and it does so in brief but very weighty words. The Apostle is discussing chastity over against incontinence. He extols the dignity of the one and points out the foulness of the other. And so that he might more effectively turn his hearers away from wanton lusts, he sets up a comparison between the divine ordinance of marriage and the filthiness that has its origin in the devil.

units.la: Quale igitur est conjugium? Bonum & sanctum, utile & necessarium: neque hoc solum, verumetiam, ut hic scriptum est, honorábile[?], sive honestum: Non enim criminis maculam, sed virtutem habet adjunctam.
units.tr: What, then, is marriage? It is good and holy, useful and necessary. Not only that, but, as is written here, it is honourable [?], or honest: for it carries with it not the stain of crime but the mark of virtue.

units.la: Quomodo aut quare bonum? quia à Deo ipso institutum, Gen. 2. Matt. 19. Sed & præceptum quintum, Honora patrem tuum & matrem tuam: & septimum, Non mœchaberis, docent conjugium esse ordinatione Dei. Cùm igitur conjugium sit ordinatio divina, necesse est in piis hoc genus vitæ esse castum & sanctum, & consuetudinem conjugalem, & totam illam maris & fœmellæ consociationem placere Deo. Sic enim inquit Scriptura: Masculum & fœminam creavit eos. Bene dixitque illis Deus, & ait: Crescite & multiplicamini. Quia igitur benedicit, & jubet crescere & multiplicari, adprobat hoc vitæ genus. Unde & Apostolus hoc loco dicit thorum conjugalem esse impollutum, id est, moderatum in connubio coitum non reputari pro peccato. Ignatius ad Philadel. inquit: Si quis corruptionem & coinquinationem vocat legitimam commixtionem, & filiorum procreationem, hujusmodi habet cohabitatorem Draconé apostatam. Et Paphnutius in concilio Niceno castitatem esse dixit, concubitum cum propria conjuge. Magna igitur consolatio proposita est piis conjugibus, cùm sciunt se versari in tali genere vitæ, quod & à Deo ipso institutum est, & cui benedicit, quod approbat, tuetur & conservat, sicut & Psalm. 128. inquit: Ecce sic benedicetur homo qui timet Dominum.
units.tr: How and why is it good? Because it was instituted by God himself (Gen. 2; Matt. 19). Moreover, the fifth commandment, "Honour your father and your mother," and the seventh, "You shall not commit adultery," teach that marriage is by the ordinance of God. Since marriage is therefore a divine ordinance, it must be that for the godly this kind of life is chaste and holy, and that conjugal intercourse, and that whole partnership of male and female, pleases God. For Scripture says: "He created them male and female. And God blessed them and said: Increase and multiply." Because he blesses and commands them to increase and multiply, he approves this way of life. Hence the Apostle here also says that the marriage bed is undefiled, that is, that intercourse within marriage, kept within due bounds, is not counted as sin. Ignatius, in his letter to the Philadelphians, says: "If anyone calls the lawful union and the begetting of children corruption and defilement, such a man has as his housemate the apostate dragon." And Paphnutius at the Council of Nicaea said that chastity is the coming together of a man with his own wife. Great comfort, then, is set before godly spouses, when they know that they live in a kind of life which God himself has instituted, which he blesses, which he approves, protects and preserves, just as Psalm 128 says: "Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord."

units.la: Cur aut quomodo utile & necessarium? Quia ideo institutum est à Deo, primùm, ne homo fit solus, sed habeat sociam & adjutricem conjunctam in tota vita, nec solùm in procreatione, sed etiam in educatione liberorum, in regenda familia, in parandis & tuendis rebus ad hanc vitam necessariis, ut partem laborum & molestiarum sustineat, & ut omnis fortunæ sociam, & quasi solatium & levamen multarum miseriarum hujus ærumnosæ vitæ habeat. Genef.2. Ecclef. 4.9. Neque enim in ærumnis remedium ullum suavius & dulcius est, quàm præsentia & consociatio piæ & prudentis conjugis: Sicuti & Proverb.31. dicitur: Cui contigit proba uxor, ea præstat gemmis, confidit ea cor mariti, & res familiaris non deficiet. Et Eccles.26. Mulier comis exhilarat maritum: & cùm humaniter eum tractat, recreat cor ejus. Item cap.37. Mulier formosa exhilarat maritum suum. Et cap.40. Ut amicus commodè congruat cum amico, vir tamen & uxor concordes utriq; præferendi sunt. Hinc Augustinus de bono Conjugali cap.3. ait: Quod (bonum conjugii bonum) mihi non videtur propter solam filiorum procreationem, sed propter ipsam naturalem in diverso sexu societatem. Alioqui non jam diceretur conjugium in senibus, præsertim si vel amississent filios, vel minimè genuissent. Nunc verò in bono licet annoso conjugio, etsi emarcuit ardor ætatis inter masculum & fœminam, viget tamen ordo charitatis inter maritum & uxorem, &c. Est autem & esse debet legitima conjunctio maris & fœminæ talis,in qua(ut Theogena Agathoclis regis conjunx dicebat)non prosperæ tantúm,sed omnis fortunæ contrahatur societas. Unde merito laudatur Tefcha Dionysii Syracusani soror nupta Polyxeno,quæ posteaquâ maritus metu tyranni profugerat, & rex sororem accusaret,quòd conscia fugæ mariti non indicasset : Adeone, inquit,Dionysiine[?] vilem, abjectíque animi fœminam judicas, ut si sensissem illum moliri fugam, non me illi navigationis & omnium fortunarum comitem additura fuerim? Talem etiam fidem promittebant ac præstabant olim uxores Germanorum suis maritis,quemadmodum Chronographi referunt in recensendis Germanorum moribus ante nativitatem Christi,ut Sebast. Franck, Iacobus Uvimphelingius,&c. Præterea cùm muliebris sexus perse sit imbecillis,maximè opus habet duce ac capite, hoc est, viro, ex quo defensionem & præsidium habeat.
units.tr: Why and how is it useful and necessary? Because God instituted it, first, so that man should not be alone, but should have a companion and helper joined to him throughout his whole life, not only in procreation but also in the upbringing of children, in governing the household, in providing and guarding the things necessary for this life; so that she may share his labours and troubles, and be his companion in every kind of fortune, and as it were his solace and relief in the many miseries of this burdensome life (Gen. 2; Eccles. 4:9). For there is no remedy in hardships more sweet and pleasant than the presence and fellowship of a godly and prudent wife. As Proverbs 31 says: "He who has found a good wife has a treasure above jewels; the heart of her husband trusts in her, and his household will not lack." And Ecclesiasticus 26: "A gracious woman gladdens her husband, and when she treats him kindly she refreshes his heart." Likewise chapter 37: "A beautiful woman gladdens her husband." And chapter 40: "As a friend agrees well with a friend, yet husband and wife, being in harmony, are to be preferred to both." Hence Augustine, in On the Good of Marriage, chapter 3, says: "The good of marriage seems to me to lie not merely in the procreation of children, but in the natural partnership of the two sexes. Otherwise there would not be talk of marriage among old people, especially if they had lost their children or had never begotten any. But now, even in a long-lasting marriage of good quality, although the ardour of youth between man and woman has faded, the order of charity between husband and wife still flourishes, etc." The lawful union of man and woman is and ought to be of such a kind that (as Theogena, the wife of King Agathocles, used to say) a partnership is entered into not only for prosperity but for every kind of fortune. Hence Tefcha, the sister of Dionysius of Syracuse, who was married to Polyxenus, is rightly praised: when her husband had fled in fear of the tyrant, and the king accused her of not disclosing his flight though she knew of it, she said: "Do you judge me, Dionysius, to be so base and a woman of so abject a spirit, that if I had perceived him planning flight, I would not have added myself as his companion in the voyage and in all his fortunes?" The wives of the Germans once promised and practised such fidelity to their husbands, as the chroniclers report in describing the customs of the Germans before the birth of Christ, as Sebastian Franck, Jacob Wimpheling, etc. Moreover, since the female sex is by nature weak, it especially needs a leader and head, that is, a husband, from whom it may have defence and protection.

units.la: Deinde institutum est matrimonium, ut ex legitima conjunctione propagetur genus humanum,ex quo Ecclesia colligatur & excerpatur in omnem æternitatem victura cum Deo, quæ ei sit copulata & conjuncta indissolubiliter. Quòd matrimonium non cessabit, nisi priùs impleatur numerus elestorum & vocatorum ad nuptias filii Dei: quo impleto demum, amplius non nubent, neque ducent, sed erunt sicut angeli Dei in coelo, Matth.22.Luc.14. Generant & concubinarii & scortatores, sed de hujusmodi generatione glorientur spurii & conjugii contemptores. Nec voluit Deus per inordinatam hanc & liberam libidinem & turpitudinem propagari genus humanum [?]. Et fures, satiantur, de pane furto acquisito, & veste furto ablata refocillantur. Nemo tamen dixerit, furto quaerendum esse victum & amictum;
units.tr: Next, marriage was instituted so that the human race might be propagated by lawful union, and out of it the Church might be gathered and chosen, to live with God for all eternity, being joined and united to him indissolubly. Marriage will not cease until the number of the elect and called to the wedding of the Son of God has been completed; and when that is complete, they will no longer marry or be given in marriage, but will be like the angels of God in heaven (Matt. 22; Luke 14). Concubines and whoremongers also beget children, but spurious children and the despisers of marriage may boast of such begetting. Nor did God will that the human race be propagated through this disorderly and unrestrained lust and filthiness. Thieves also are satisfied with bread obtained by theft, and are refreshed with clothing taken by theft. Yet no one would say that food and clothing are to be sought by theft.

units.la: Tertiò institutum est, ut hoc modo vagæ libidines, adulteria, stupra, fornicationes, & omnes immunditiæ, quas Deus ut mens casta & sancta extremè abominatur, vitentur, sicut scriptum est, 1.Corinth.7. Nam sine conjugii remedio, promiscuæ & vagæ libidines coerceri nequeunt. Unde & Theophyl. Ecce, inquit, preciosas nuptias, honorabile matrimonium nominat, quod in temperantia hominem conservet. Et Metellus Numidicus, A. Gellio teste in 1.cap.6. Si (inquit) sine uxoribus possemus esse, omnes ea molestia careremus (ac, ut Cato dicebat, vita nostra non esset absq; diis) sed quoniam ita natura tradidit, ut nec cum illis satis commodè, nec sine illis ullo modo vivi possit, saluti perpetuæ potius, quàm in brevi voluptati consulendum est. Multos hodie à conjugio abster ret domestica cura, & tribulatio quæ conjuges comitatur. Sed si saperent, multo melius esse judicarent conjugium cum molestia temporali conjunctum, quàm scortationem æterna morte & privatione regni cœlestis dignam. Adde quod contra tentationem de victu & amictu, & timorem afflictionum. Apostolus hoc loco præclarè loquitur: Sint mores alieni ab avaritia, contenti iis, quæ adsunt. Siquidem ipse dixit: Non te defero, neque derelinquo, ut fidentes dicamus: Dominus (qui matrimonium instituit & benedixit: & scortationem prohibuit & maledixit) mihi auxiliator, nec timebo quid faciat mihi homo.
units.tr: Thirdly, it was instituted so that in this way wanton lusts, adulteries, debaucheries, fornications, and all the impurities, which God, as a chaste and holy mind, utterly abominates, might be avoided, as it is written in 1 Corinthians 7. For without the remedy of marriage, promiscuous and wandering lusts cannot be restrained. Hence Theophylact also: "Behold," he says, "he calls marriage precious and honourable, because it keeps a man in self-control." And Metellus Numidicus, as Aulus Gellius witnesses (in book 1, chapter 6): "If," he says, "we could be without wives, we would all be free of that trouble (and, as Cato used to say, our life would not be without the gods); but since nature has so arranged it that one can live neither comfortably with them nor in any way without them, we must look to lasting well-being rather than to brief pleasure." Many today are held back from marriage by domestic care and the tribulation that accompanies spouses. But if they were wise, they would judge far better that marriage, joined with temporal trouble, is preferable to fornication, which deserves eternal death and the loss of the heavenly kingdom. Add that marriage is also the answer to the temptation concerning food and clothing, and to the fear of afflictions. The Apostle speaks admirably here: "Let your manners be free from avarice, content with what you have. For he himself has said: I will not fail you, nor forsake you; so that we may confidently say: The Lord is my helper (he who instituted marriage and blessed it, and forbade and cursed fornication), and I will not fear what man may do to me."

units.la: Quartò institutum est, ut unius maris & unius fœmellæ corporalis conjunctio in hac vita sit imago aut typus, & cominonefactio illius mirandi fœderis, quo Deus sibi ecclesiam copulavit, & summi ac inenarrabilis amoris divini erga sponsam ecclesiam, de quo Hebr.2.Ioann.1.15.Ephes.5. Hof[?] 2.Ezech.16. Ierem. [?]. & 3.Psalm.45. & in Cant. canticor. Hoc enim mysterium statim in creatione hominis & conjunctione Adæ & Evæ significatum fuit. Quemadmodum enim Adam obdormiscit, & ex dormientis latere, sicut costa ex latere sumpta, ædificatur mulier; quæ cum sit os ex ossibus eius, & caro de carne ejus, ita arctè illi copulatur, ut una sint caro: ita Christus sponsus Ecclesiæ obdormiscit in cruce, & ex dormientis latere profluit sanguis & aqua, quo sanguine primum Ecclesia ædificatur & redimitur, quæ antea sub peccato, sub ira Dei & regno Satanae erat: deinde mundatur & sanctificatur per verbum & aquam: Sicque Ecclesia ex latere Christi ædificata, & mundata per verbum & aquam, sincera sponsione, & fide copulatur sponso Christo.
units.tr: Fourthly, it was instituted so that the bodily union of one man and one woman in this life should be an image or type, and a reminder of that wonderful covenant by which God joined the Church to himself, and of the highest and inexpressible love of God towards his bride, the Church (on which see Heb. 2; John 1:15; Eph. 5; Hos. 2; Ezek. 16; Jer. [?]; Ps. 45; and in the Song of Songs). For this mystery was signified at once in the creation of man and in the joining of Adam and Eve. For just as Adam falls asleep, and from the side of the sleeping man the woman is built from a rib taken from his side, and she is bone of his bones and flesh of his flesh, and so closely joined to him that they are one flesh; so Christ, the bridegroom of the Church, falls asleep on the cross, and from the side of the sleeping one there flows blood and water, by which blood the Church is first built and redeemed, she who before was under sin, under the wrath of God and the kingdom of Satan; then she is cleansed and sanctified through the Word and water. And so the Church, built from the side of Christ, and cleansed through the Word and water, is joined to Christ her bridegroom in sincere betrothal and faith.

units.la: Sicut autem Deus unam costarum tulit ex Adæ latere: sic una tantum est Ecclesia, unumque corpus, Ephes. 4. 1. Corint. 12. Galat. 3. Et sicut unam de costis Adæ tulit, & pro ea carnem replevit: sic ecclesia fortitudinis, justitiæ & sapientiæ Christi particeps facta est. 1. Corinth. 1. & Christus languores ac dolores Ecclesiæ portavit, proque ea Dei iram, poenam & mortem in se transtulit, Iesa. 53[?]. Matth. 8.
units.tr: Just as God took one rib from Adam's side, so there is only one Church and one body (Eph. 4; 1 Cor. 12; Gal. 3). And just as God took one of Adam's ribs and filled the place with flesh, so the Church has been made a partaker of Christ's strength, righteousness and wisdom (1 Cor. 1). Christ bore the languors and pains of the Church, and in her place took upon himself God's wrath, punishment and death (Isa. 53[?]; Matt. 8).

units.la: Ut vera Eva dicitur ædificata: sic Ecclesia domus, templum & ædificatio Dei dicitur, 1. Corinth. 3. Hebr. 3.
units.tr: Just as the true Eve is said to have been built up, so the Church is called God's house, temple and building (1 Cor. 3; Heb. 3).

units.la: Sed quemadmodum adducta dicitur Eva ad Adam: sic nemo venit ad filium, nisi pater traxerit eum, Ioan. 6.
units.tr: But just as Eve is said to have been brought to Adam, so no one comes to the Son unless the Father draws him (John 6).

units.la: Ut porro Adam agnovit Evam pro carne sua: ita Christus Dominus seipsum persecutionem pati dicit, quando patitur ecclesia, Actor. 9. Zach. 2. Matth. 25.
units.tr: As Adam acknowledged Eve as his own flesh, so Christ the Lord says that he himself suffers persecution when the Church suffers (Acts 9; Zech. 2; Matt. 25).

units.la: Ut enim ab Adam viro denominatur Eva virago: sic a Christo filio Dei, ecclesia Christiana.
units.tr: For just as Eve is named "virago" from her husband Adam, so the Christian Church is named from Christ, the Son of God.

units.la: Quemadmodum denique homo relinquit patrem & matrem, & adhæret uxori suæ: ita etiam Christus. Patrem enim relireliquit,teste Augustino, Tractat.9.in Evangel.Ioann.non quia deferuit & recessit à patre,sed quia non in ea forma apparuit hominibus,in qua æqualis est patri:matrem verò, dum synagogam deferuit Iudæorum,de qua secundum carnem natus est. Vxori adhæsit, in hærendo Ecclesiæ,quam ex omnibus gentibus congregavit. vel, dum assumpsit humanitatem. In hac assumptione humanæ naturæ, & sancto fœdere, quo sibi ecclesiam copulavit,egregiè cernere licet illa quinque, quæ in conjugio esse debent, videlicet, Amor mutuus,Fides, Societas bonorum & ç[?]rumnarum, Generatio & Defensio : de quibus Georg. Major in Enarr. Epist. Pauli ad Ephes.
units.tr: Just as a man leaves father and mother and cleaves to his wife, so also Christ did. For he left the Father, as Augustine testifies (Tractate 9 on John's Gospel), not because he deserted or withdrew from the Father, but because he did not appear to men in that form in which he is equal to the Father. He left the mother when he forsook the synagogue of the Jews, from which he was born according to the flesh. He cleaved to his wife in cleaving to the Church, whom he gathered from all nations; or, when he took on our humanity. In this assumption of human nature and in the holy covenant by which he joined the Church to himself, one can clearly see those five things which ought to be present in marriage: mutual love, faithfulness, partnership of goods and hardships, begetting, and defence. Georg Major treats these in his exposition of Paul's Epistle to the Ephesians.

units.la: 2 Quæ cùm ita se habeant:quis negare poterit, conjugium esse rem & ordinationem non solùm sanctam,sed etiam cumprimis utilem & necessariam;[?] adde & honorabilem, quemadmodum hoc loco Apostolus testatur. In conjugio enim non tantùm opera honesta laudeque digna,tam à viris,quàm à fœminis fieri possunt, ut sunt opera dilectionis,patientiæ,& reliqua,de quibus modò dictum est: verumetiam in eo vivere, & à sanctis & à gentibus, jam olim honestum & laudabile judicatum est. Honorem quidem matrimoniis apud gentes habitum esse, idque ob favorem publici commodi, liquet ex historiis,poetis & legibus : apud sanctos verò, ex vetere & novo Testamento. In hoc statu vixerunt patriarchæ, prophetæ, sacerdotes, Apostoli, Evangelistæ, &c. Omnibus enim hominibus est concessus, non vulgo hominum tantummodo permissus. Clarè enim pronunciat Apostolus: Honorabile est in omnibus, aut inter omnes, conjugiū & cubile impollutum. Adeò preciosa res est matrimonium (ut Theophyl. scribit in Epist. Pauli ad Tit. cap. 1.) ut possit cum eo ad sanctum thronum Episcopalemq; sedem ascendere.
units.tr: Since these things are so, who can deny that marriage is an institution and ordinance not only holy, but also especially useful and necessary, and honourable as well, as the Apostle here testifies? In marriage, men and women alike can do honest works worthy of praise, such as works of love, patience and the rest, which have just been mentioned. Moreover, to live in marriage has long been judged honourable and praiseworthy both by the saints and by the nations. That marriage was held in honour among the nations, on account of the public advantage it brings, is clear from histories, poets and laws; among the saints it is clear from the Old and New Testaments. In this state lived the patriarchs, prophets, priests, Apostles, Evangelists, and so on. For it is granted to all men, not merely permitted to the common crowd. The Apostle declares it clearly: "Marriage and the bed undefiled is honourable in all, or among all." So precious a thing is matrimony (as Theophylact writes on Paul's Epistle to Titus, chapter 1) that with it one may ascend to the holy throne and episcopal see.

units.la: Quod conjugati fuerint Apostoli testantur ipsorum discipuli, Ignatius in Epist. ad Philadelphicum, & Clemens quem Eusebius citat in Eccles. hist. lib. 3. cap. 30. Valeat igitur iniquum atque impium pontificis Romani decretum, quo connubia sacerdotibus inhibuit, & fornicationem admisit. Paulus enim Christi servus ad suam prophetiam (1. Tim. 4.) respiciens, opponit hic ordinationem Dei, ad omnes ordines extensam, doctrinis dæmoniorum: atque ut prævertat feductorū objectione jactantium suam virginitatē & castitatem, dicit hanc quoque Dei ordinationē esse castitatē. D. Chrysost. ait quidē synceram virginitatē esse primum gradū castitatis, sed addit, secundum gradū esse fidele conjugium. Sed & Theano Pythagorę uxor rogata quando mulier esset munda à viro, respondit: A suo semper, ab alieno nunquam.
units.tr: That the Apostles were married is attested by their own disciples: Ignatius in his epistle to the Philadelphians, and Clement, whom Eusebius cites in his Ecclesiastical History, book 3, chapter 30. Let the unjust and impious decree of the Roman pontiff, by which he forbade marriage to priests and admitted fornication, be done away with. For Paul, the servant of Christ, looking to his own prophecy (1 Tim. 4), sets the ordinance of God, extended to all orders, against the doctrines of demons. And to forestall the objection of deceivers who boast of their virginity and chastity, he says that this ordinance of God is chastity too. Chrysostom indeed says that pure virginity is the first degree of chastity, but he adds that faithful marriage is the second degree. And Theano, the wife of Pythagoras, when asked when a woman is clean from a man, replied: "Always from her own; never from another's."

units.la: Sunt qui particulam, ἐν σαρκὶ[?], variè exponant, ut fit perinde quasi dicatur vel in omnibus ætatibus, id est, non in solis provectioris ætatis hominibus, sed etiam in juvenibus: vel in omni tempore, id est, in afflictione & relaxatione: vel omnibus modis, id est, non in hac quidem parte preciosum & honoratum, in illa vero secus: sed integrè, persectè, & totum per omnia preciosum, honorabile & impollutum est. At simplex sensus est, nullum esse ordinem, qui à conjugio prohibeatur. Nam quod Deus generi humano in universum concessit, omnes sine exceptione decet, omnes (inquam) qui conjugio apti sunt, eoque opus habent. Hoc autem disertis verbis exprimi oportuit, ut superstitioni[?] occurreret, cujus tunc jam forte femina occultè jaciebat Satan, conjugium rem profanā esse, aut certè à Christiana prosessione procul remotam. Nam spiritus illi impostores, de quibus vaticinatus erat Paulus in Epistola ad Timotheum, mox extiterunt, prohibentes conjugium. Ergo ne quis stultè imaginaretur conjugium vulgo duntaxat hominum permitti: qui autem in ecclesia excellunt, debere eos abstinere, omnem exceptionem tollit Apostolus: neque tantùm docet per indulgentiam concedi (ut quidam cavillantur) sed honore dignum esse asserit.
units.tr: Some explain the particle "in the flesh" in various ways: as if it said "in all ages", that is, not only in men of more advanced age but also in young men; or "at all times", that is, in affliction and in relaxation; or "in all respects", that is, not that marriage is precious and honourable in one respect and otherwise in another, but that it is wholly, perfectly and in every way precious, honourable and undefiled. But the plain sense is that no order is excluded from marriage. For what God granted to the human race in general applies to all without exception: all, I say, who are fit for marriage and need it. This however had to be stated in plain words, to meet a superstition which Satan was perhaps already secretly sowing among women: that marriage is a profane thing, or at least far removed from the Christian profession. For those impostor spirits, of whom Paul had prophesied in his epistle to Timothy, soon appeared, forbidding marriage. Therefore, lest anyone foolishly imagine that marriage is permitted only to the common people, while those who excel in the Church ought to abstain, the Apostle removes every exception. He not only teaches that it is granted by indulgence, as some sneer, but asserts that it is worthy of honour.

units.la: Interim autem discamus, matrimonium, quoniam licitum, honorabile & sanctum est, sanctè etiam esse colendum, & ideo officium conjugum esse, nuptias honestè agere, & hac ordinatione Dei in ejus timore, sanctè, & in gloriam ipsius, alteriusque conjugis ac liberorum utilitatem uti. Ab honestis nuptiis omnia turpia & obscœna (qualia sunt cantiones, tibiæ, choreæ, ebrietates, verba lasciva) tollenda esse, censet Chrysostomus in 1. Corinth. 4. Hom. 12. & in 5. cap. ad Ephef. Modum servandum esse in sumptibus nuptiarum docere nos debet juxta scripturas, exemplum Henrici Tertii, qui ut habetur in Chron. Magdeburg. in nuptiis suis Ingelheim actis prohibuit, tibicinibus, mimis & scurris, quorum ingens caterva confluxerat, cibos, vestes & pecuniâ aut alia munera dari: sed ciborum reliquias pauperibus distribui jussit. Dicitur enim, honorabile conjugium inter omnes (ubi quidem intelligi potest non solùm, Est, sed etiam, Esto) & cubile impollutum: vel, intemeratus lestus:q. d. Honorabiles quidem erunt nuptiæ, si thorus confervetur immaculatus, id est, si non serviatur voluptati, si custodiatur pudicitiæ fides, si charitas & concordia. Nam propter hæc omnia, scil. generandi ordinationem, fidem & connubii sacramentum, honorabiles sunt nuptiæ, ut dicit Augustinus. Sciant itaque conjugati non quidvis sibi licere, sed usum thori legitimi debere esse moderatum, ne quid alienum à conjugii pudore & castimonia admittant. Vnde Aben Ezra illud Proverb. 5. (ubera ejus inebriabunt te, &c.) putat sic intelligendum, ut etiam amor uxoris sit restringendus, ne erres in præceptis Dei, si nimium uxori animus tuus sit assixus. Rabi Levi quoque in eundem forè sensum exponit: Si errare, inquit, poteris in uxore, quantus erit error, si alienæ sis affixus?
units.tr: Meanwhile let us learn that marriage, since it is lawful, honourable and holy, is also to be holily cherished, and therefore the duty of spouses is to conduct their wedding honourably and to use this ordinance of God in the fear of him, holily, to his glory, and for the benefit of the other spouse and of the children. Chrysostom holds that all shameful and obscene things (such as songs, pipes, dances, drunkenness and wanton words) must be removed from honourable weddings (on 1 Corinthians, homily 12, and on Ephesians, chapter 5). The moderation to be kept in the expenses of weddings should teach us, according to the Scriptures, the example of Henry III. As is recorded in the Magdeburg Centuries, at his wedding held at Ingelheim he forbade food, clothing, money or other gifts to be given to the flute-players, mimes and jesters, of whom a huge crowd had gathered, and he ordered the leftover food to be distributed to the poor. For it is said: "Marriage is honourable among all" (where it can be understood not only as "is" but also as "let it be"), "and the bed undefiled," or "untainted couch." It is as if to say: weddings will indeed be honourable if the marriage bed is kept undefiled, that is, if it is not given over to pleasure, if the faith of chastity is guarded, and if there is love and concord. For on account of all these things, namely the ordinance of begetting, the faith and the sacrament of marriage, weddings are honourable, as Augustine says. Let spouses therefore know that they may not do just anything they please, but that the use of the lawful bed must be moderate, lest they admit anything foreign to the modesty and chastity of marriage. Hence Aben Ezra thinks that Proverbs 5 ("her breasts will inebriate you," etc.) should be understood to mean that even love for one's wife must be restrained, lest you go astray in God's precepts if your mind is too attached to your wife. Rabbi Levi also expounds it in much the same sense: "If you can go astray with your wife, how great will the error be if you are attached to another's?"

units.la: Porrò sicut conjugium tanquam divinâ ordinationem & rem honestam Apostolus laudat: ita contrà omnes vagas libidines tam quâ opera diaboli atq; res turpes vituperat, & ab eis dehortatur, proponens etiâ divinas minas. Cùm enim societatem viri & uxoris àse institutam Deus benedixerit, sequitur quamlibet ab ea diversam ab eo damnari & maledici. Ait igitur: Scortatores autem & adulteros puniet Deus. Et merito, ut dicit Oecumenius. Nam si conjugium permissum est, & sine peccato licet ad explendam cupiscentiam, quis erit excusationis prætextus scortatoribus & adulteris? quorum illos quidem non injuria quis contemptores nuptiarum: hos verò thori temeratores appellarit.
units.tr: Moreover, just as the Apostle praises marriage as a divine ordinance and an honourable thing, so on the contrary he condemns all wandering lusts, as works of the devil and shameful things, and dissuades from them, also setting out divine threats. For since God blessed the partnership of man and wife which he himself instituted, it follows that whatever differs from it is condemned and cursed by him. So he says: "But God will punish fornicators and adulterers." And rightly so, as Oecumenius says. For if marriage is permitted, and it is lawful without sin to satisfy desire, what pretext of excuse will fornicators and adulterers have? Of these, one might rightly call the former despisers of marriage, and the latter violators of the marriage bed.

units.la: Vtrique à sancto Dei instituto[?] discedunt, imò illud violant atque evertunt, promiscuè se miscendo: quùm una fit conjunctio legitima, quæ Dei nomine & auspiciis sancitur. Quàm verò fœda res sit omnis vaga Venus, abundè monstrat Apostolus 1. Corinth. 6. Etsi enim alia quædam peccata (veluti homicidium, &c.) majora sunt hæc: tamen hæc totum etiam corpus inquinat, adeò ut qui scortatus est, ad se lavandum properet (ut ille ait) quod avarus aut raptor non facit. Quare non adulteris tantum,sed fcortatö ribus quibuslibet pœna denunciatur. Verbum enim Dei per copulam,&,hoc loco eos in pœna conjungit.Licet autem omnes pœnę,quæ etiam per magistratum infliguntur, divinæ pœnæ sint: tamen hoc non finefingulari quadam emphasi dicitur, quòd talia peccata Deus ipse judicabit,id est,damnabit ac puniet.q.d.quem omnino nihil latet,quique solus verè & perfectè punire potest. Cujus denique judicia minimè cessant, etsi nemo hominum manum admoveat. Fortè etiam simul respicit summam negligentiam in magistratus in puniendis talibus flagitiis,ac si diceret: Nolite propterea securi esse,quòd non punimini à magistratu,ob turpitudines, aut quia etiam ipsimet magistratus sese eis contaminant,easque non improbant.
units.tr: Both depart from God's holy institution; indeed they violate and overturn it by mixing promiscuously, since there is one lawful union, which is sanctioned in God's name and under his auspices. How foul a thing all wandering lust is, the Apostle shows abundantly in 1 Corinthians 6. For although some other sins (such as murder, etc.) are greater, yet this sin defiles the whole body as well, so that the fornicator hurries to wash himself (as he says), which the covetous man or the robber does not do. Therefore punishment is announced not only for adulterers but for fornicators of every kind. For the word of God joins them together in punishment by the conjunction "and." Although all punishments, even those inflicted by the magistrate, are divine punishments, yet this is said with a particular emphasis: God himself will judge such sins, that is, condemn and punish them, as if to say: he from whom nothing is hidden, and who alone can punish truly and perfectly. Finally, his judgments by no means cease, even if no human hand is raised. Perhaps he also at the same time looks upon the great negligence of magistrates in punishing such disgraceful acts, as if he said: Do not therefore be secure because you are not punished by the magistrate for these shameful deeds, or because the magistrates themselves defile themselves with them and do not disapprove of them.

units.la: Erit enim profecto, qui tales omnes feveriffimè puniat: juxta illud πολυθεύκτος[?], <bl>Gott richtet/wenn niemand</bl> <bl>spricht,</bl> 1.Corinth.11.Sic Ephes.5. inquit: Propter talia venit ira Dei super filios inobedientiæ. Et Propheta Malac.2.ait, Excindet Dominus virum,qui hoc fecerit,&c. Sic olim diluvii aquis conjugii prophanationem, & quæ ex illa enata fuerunt scelera,eluit, cum nemo esset, qui de illis tollendis cogitaret. Idem suam manum illis intulit, qui Madianitarum filiabus commixti fuerant. Taceo quæ ex prophanis historiis adduci possent exempla, & quæ ipsi adulteris & fœdis conjugii prophanatoribus indies accidere videmus. Punit illos Deus, conjugii vindex, morbis, egestate, orbitate, & fere illorum posteritas extinguitur, qui spuriis suis urbes totas replere videbantur. Misericors & omnipotens Deus convertat nos ab omni immunditia ad veram sanctimoniam, sine qua nemo videbit Dominum (Hebraeorum duodecimo) ut liberemur ab ira ventura, per Iesum Christum Dominum, & castissimae virginis filium, Amen.
units.tr: There will surely be one who punishes all such people most severely, according to the saying: God judges when no one speaks (1 Corinthians 11). So Ephesians 5 says: "Because of such things the wrath of God comes upon the sons of disobedience." And the prophet Malachi 2 says: "The Lord will cut off the man who does this," etc. Thus of old he washed away with the waters of the flood the profanation of marriage and the crimes born from it, when no one was there who thought of removing them. He likewise laid his hand upon those who had mingled with the daughters of Midian. I pass over the examples that could be drawn from profane histories, and what we see happening daily to adulterers and foul profaners of marriage themselves. God, the avenger of marriage, punishes them with disease, poverty and childlessness, and their posterity is almost wiped out, those who seemed to fill whole cities with their bastard children. May the merciful and almighty God turn us from all uncleanness to true holiness, without which no one will see the Lord (Hebrews 12), so that we may be delivered from the wrath to come, through Jesus Christ the Lord, son of the most chaste virgin. Amen.

units.la: CONCIO LX.
units.tr: SERMON LX.

units.la: 1. Petri 3.
units.tr: 1 Peter 3.

units.la: Similiter uxores subdita sitis vestris viris, ut etiam qui non obtemperant sermoni, per uxorum conversationem absque sermone lucrifiant: dum considerant cum reverentia conjunctam castam conversationem vestram, quarum ornatus sit non externus, qui situs est in plicatura capillorum, et additione auri, aut in palliorum amictu: verum occultus, qui est in corde homo, si is careat omni corruptela, ita ut spiritus pla[?] cidus [?] fit ac quietus, qui spiritus in oculis Dei magnifica ac sumptuosa res est. Nam ad eum modum olim & sanctae illae mulieres sperantes in Deo, comebant sese, & subditae erant suis viris, quemadmodum Sara obedivit Abrahae, dominum illum appellans, cuius factae estis filiae, dum benefacitis, & non terremini ullo pavore.
units.tr: Likewise, ye wives, be in subjection to your own husbands, so that even those who do not obey the word may be won over without a word by the conduct of their wives, while they behold your chaste conversation coupled with fear. Let your adorning not be the outward kind, which lies in the plaiting of the hair, the putting on of gold, or the wearing of fine clothes, but the hidden man of the heart, if it is free from all corruption, so that the spirit is gentle and quiet, which in the sight of God is a precious and costly thing. For after this manner in former times the holy women also, who trusted in God, adorned themselves and were subject to their own husbands, as Sara obeyed Abraham, calling him lord, whose daughters you are, so long as you do well and are not terrified by any fear.

units.la: Viri similiter cohabitent secundum scientiam, velut infirmiori vasi muliebri impartientes honorem, tanquam etiam coheredes gratiae vitae, ne interrumpantur preces vestrae.
units.tr: Likewise, husbands, dwell with your wives according to knowledge, giving honour to the woman as to the weaker vessel, as being heirs together of the grace of life, so that your prayers are not hindered.

units.la: 1 D. Petrus postquam tradita fide bona opera ceu fidei fructus & signa docere coepisset, & singulorum ordinum officia praescribere: nunc ostendit quid conjuges facere debeant. Quandoquidem multum bonae frugis in matrimonio est, si recte instítutum sit in timore Dei. Nam & calamitates variae, & scelera innumera oriuntur ex conjugio malo. Qui hactenus de operibus bonis ex pontificiorum parte scripserunt, vere bona opera neglexerunt, fictitia quaedam laudibus extulere. Nam monachismum, ceremoniarum studium, jejunia, stolida, & preculas superstitiosas laudavere: interim vera Christianorum officia neglexere prorsus. Neque putaverunt eos labores, quos perferunt serviui,vel conjugati,ullum inter opera bona habere locum. At D. Petrus his primum assignat. Sed & Christus ipse hæc officia vel maxime ornat, cum mandatum de dilectione proximi ait esse simile primo, h. e. Deum obedientiam in utroque genere simul postulare, & utriusque generis officia cultus Dei esse. Est enim Dei cultus, opus mandatum a Deo, quod principaliter eo fit, ut Deo præstetur obedientia & honos: ac fit cum agnitione Christi hac fide, quod propter eum Patri placeas, 1.Pet.2.
units.tr: 1 After St Peter had taught faith and good works as the fruit and signs of faith, and had prescribed the duties of each order, he now shows what married people ought to do. For there is much good fruit in marriage when it is rightly ordered in the fear of God, while many calamities and countless crimes arise from a bad marriage. Those who until now have written about good works on the Papists' side have indeed neglected true good works and praised certain fictitious things instead. For they have extolled monasticism, the study of ceremonies, fasts, foolish and superstitious little prayers, and meanwhile have utterly neglected the true duties of Christians. Nor have they thought that the labours which servants or married people endure have any place among good works. But St Peter assigns the first place to these. Christ himself also greatly honours these duties, when he says that the commandment about love of neighbour is like the first, that is, that God demands obedience in both kinds at once, and that the duties of both kinds are the worship of God. For the worship of God is a work commanded by God, which is done chiefly so that obedience and honour may be rendered to God; and it is done with the knowledge of Christ, by this faith, that you please the Father for his sake (1 Pet. 2.).

units.la: Quia ergo Deus verbo suo instruit conjuges, certum est, non solum quod conjugium fit honorabile, & status Deo placens, atque minime vituperandus aut prohibendus, Heb.13.1.Tim.4. item, quod & conjuges pertineant ad vitam æternam: sed etiam quod ea opera quæ faciunt ex præscripto Dei, sint cultus Dei, si fiant propter mandatum Dei.
units.tr: Therefore, since God instructs married people by his word, it is certain not only that marriage is honourable, a state pleasing to God, and in no way to be disparaged or forbidden (Heb. 13; 1 Tim. 4.), and that married people also belong to eternal life, but also that those works which they do according to the prescription of God are the worship of God, if they are done because of the command of God.

units.la: Ut autem qui medicus fieri vult, ea quæ de re medica & medicorum officio scripta sunt, diligenter legit atque discit: sic & qui conjux fieri cupit, ea quæ ad Christianum conjugem pertinent, scire debet. Nam si monachi suorum ordinum regulas non solum noverunt, sed etiam servant: multo magis qui in conjugio, à Deo instituto sunt, suam regulam & nosse & servare debent.
units.tr: Just as one who wishes to become a physician diligently reads and learns what has been written about the medical art and the physician's duty, so one who wishes to become a spouse ought to know what pertains to a Christian spouse. For if monks not only know but also keep the rules of their orders, much more ought those who are in the marriage instituted by God both to know and to keep their rule.

units.la: 2 Audiant igitur primum fœminæ (istæ enim doctrina & admonitione cumprimis indigent: nàm mater earum Eva prior peccavit, (Genes.3. Ecclesi.25. 1.Timoth.2.) quid Deus ipsas facere jubeat per eximium servu & apostolum suum Petrum. Similiter, inquit, uxores subditæ sint suis viris. Adverbium, Similiter, respicit ad præceptum suprà cap.2. datum subditis erga gubernatores, & porro servis erga heros, ac si diceret: Sicut illis præcepi subjectionem erga suos superiores: ita & vobis uxoribus similiter præcipio, quia & vos pecies subditarum personarum eitis. Loquitur autem Petrus in præsentiarum de uxoribus, quæ eo tempore adhuc insideles habebant maritos, adeoque plus coloris ad excutiendum jugum habere videbantur: sicut rursum de fidelibus maritis, qui Ethnicas etiamnum habebant uxores.
units.tr: 2 Let women hear first (for they especially need this teaching and admonition, since their mother Eve sinned first; Gen. 3; Eccl. 25; 1 Tim. 2), what God commands them to do through his outstanding servant and apostle Peter. "Likewise," he says, "let wives be subject to their own husbands." The adverb "likewise" refers to the precept given above in chapter 2 to subjects towards rulers, and again to servants towards masters, as if he said: as I commanded them to be subject to their superiors, so likewise I command you wives, since you too are of the sex of subject persons. Peter speaks at present about wives who at that time still had unbelieving husbands, and so seemed to have more reason to shake off the yoke; likewise about believing husbands who still had heathen wives.

units.la: Sæpenumero enim eo tempore usuveniebat, ut inter Ethnicos Apostoli evangelion prædicarent, apud quos unus conjugum ad Christum convertebatur, altero in errore perseverante. Si igitur tum præcipiebatur hoc, ut uxores maritis essent subditæ, quanto magis convenit id hodie præstare? Si eterum maritis impiis mulieres obedientiam debent, multo promptiores ad obsequium esse convenit, si maritos habeant fideles. Atque hoc & Lex dicit, & Evangelium docet, Genes.3 1.Corinth.14. Ephes 5. Colos.3. Imo hoc præcepit, ut morigera marito uxor fit, Deus tam firmiter voluit observari, ut maritis potestatem fecerit uxorum vota, si difdisplicuissent, dissolvendi cassandiq;, Num. 30. nulla alia de causa, quàm ut domi tranquille & in pace viveretur. Vnde & Ioann. Iovianus Pontanus lib. 3. de obedient. cap.
units.tr: For in that time it often happened that among the heathen the apostles preached the gospel, and one of the spouses was converted to Christ while the other persisted in error. If therefore it was commanded then that wives be subject to their husbands, how much more fitting is it to do this today? If women owe obedience even to ungodly husbands, it is fitting that they be much more ready to obey if they have believing husbands. This both the Law teaches and the Gospel proclaims (Gen. 3; 1 Cor. 14; Eph. 5; Col. 3). Indeed God willed this, that a wife be compliant with her husband, to be observed so firmly that he gave husbands the power to annul and cancel their wives' vows if they had displeased them (Num. 30), for no other reason than that people might live quietly and peacefully at home. Whence also Giovanni Gioviano Pontano, in book 3 of On Obedience, chapter ...

units.la: 2. Cum, inquit, conjugium ex viro constet & uxore, fitque uxor in re præsertim domestica (in alienam enim concessit domum.) viro suo inferior, & propter naturæ excellentiam, & propter leges, quæ hoc jubent, erit maritis jus potestasque præcipiendi uxoribus. Quę si utilibus & honestis illorum præceptis parérent semper, & genialis tori legibus adversari nollent, nunquam sapientes quidam viri de ducenda uxore dubitassent, nec fortunatum putassent illam non habere. Ex inobedientia enim & contumacia lites oriuntur, ac pleraque conjugiorum mala, quibus utinam ne essent etiam fortunatissimæ domus oppletæ. Et paulò post: Omnis igitur pene rei uxoriæ molestia ortum habet ab inobedientia, quæ totam sæpisime rem familiarem intervertit, conijcitque ipsos patresfamilias in ærumnas quàm gravissimas.
units.tr: 2 "Since marriage," he says, "consists of a husband and a wife, and the wife, especially in domestic matters (for she has gone into another's house), is inferior to her husband, both because of the excellence of nature and because of the laws which command this, it will be the right and power of husbands to command their wives. If wives always obeyed their husbands' useful and honourable precepts, and were unwilling to oppose the laws of the marriage bed, wise men would never have hesitated to take a wife, nor would they have thought a man fortunate who did not have one. For quarrels arise from disobedience and contumacy, and most of the evils of marriage, with which I wish the most fortunate households were not filled." And a little later: "Almost all the trouble of a wife's affairs therefore arises from disobedience, which very often overturns the whole household and throws the heads of families themselves into the most grievous distress."

units.la: Officium itaque uxoris, inquit D. Petrus, est, ut subdita sit marito suo, etiamsi infidelis & ethnicus existat: nimirum in iis quæ religioni Christianæ prorsum adversa non sunt. Paulus enim 1. Corinth. 7. loquens de impari connubio, Si quæ mulier (inquit) maritum habet infidelem, & hæc assentitur ut habitet cum ea, ne dimittat eam: item, Si quis frater uxorem habet infidelem, & haec assentitur ut habitet cum illo, ne dimittat eam. Causam cur id fieri oporteat, Petrus reddit, inquiens: Ut etiam ij qui verbo non credunt, per conversationem uxorum, sine verbo lucrifiant. Revera magnum lucrum obedientiae: nimirum bona aemulatio eorum, qui alieni sunt a fide (quae etiam ex nostri subjectione erga principes generatur) & Dei laudatio propter nos ab ipsis profecta: quod etiam in magnam cedit laudem Christianorum, nempe quod propter nos non male audiat: sed benedicatur nomen Dei.
units.tr: The duty of a wife, says St Peter, is to be subject to her husband, even if he is unbelieving and a heathen; namely in those matters which are not wholly opposed to the Christian religion. For Paul, speaking in 1 Corinthians 7 about an unequal marriage, says: "If any woman has an unbelieving husband, and he is content to dwell with her, let her not leave him"; likewise: "If any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she is content to dwell with him, let him not leave her." Peter gives the reason why this ought to be done, saying: "that even those who do not believe the word may be won over by the conduct of their wives, without a word." Truly a great gain of obedience: namely the good emulation of those who are alien to the faith (which is also produced by our subjection to rulers), and the praise of God, spoken by them on our account; which also redounds to the great praise of Christians, namely that on our account the name of God is not ill spoken of, but blessed.

units.la: Quod dicit, Absque sermone lucrifiant, non id vult, fidem cuiquam sine doctrina coelesti contingere posse (fides enim ex auditu, Rom.10.) sed quod prima occasio conversionis & inclinatio animi illorum non proprie a doctrina, sed ab honesta sanctaque uxorum conversatione exorta fit, accedentibus earum piis colloquiis & admonitionibus: Intelligit ergo per sermonem potissimum publicam praedicationem, quam infideles non facile adibant: tali tamen piarum uxorum vitae sanctitate, piisque admonitionibus primum nonnihil flectebantur, ut postea etiam publicas conciones adirent, atque ita plene converterentur: huc etiam nonnihil appellente affectu maritali, ut qui thori consortes sunt, velint & professionis esse socii. Significat ergo Petrus, mulieres sancte & honeste vivendo hoc posse consequi, ut etiam tacentes præparent maritos ad amplexandam Christi fidem, quam vident tantarum virtutum esse altricem. Et sané perquá acres stimulos habet sincera probitas, quæ plus feré potest apud adversarios non omnino perversos, quàm docta disputatio. Sed & vita improba plus nonnunquam diruit, quàm sana doctrina ædificare possit. Legimus de D. Monica matre D. Augustini, quod sua innocentia ac pietate, maritum suum ante mortem ad Christum perduxerit, postea etiam filium Augustinum. Extant & alia exempla, quæ docent uxorum prudentia & pietate viros vel Deo adduc-tos, vel saltem commodiores factos esse.
units.tr: When he says "they may be won without a word," he does not mean that faith can come to anyone without heavenly doctrine (for faith comes by hearing, Rom. 10), but that the first occasion of conversion and the inclination of their minds does not properly arise from doctrine, but from the honest and holy conduct of the wives, to which their pious conversations and admonitions are added. By "word" he therefore understands chiefly public preaching, which unbelievers did not readily attend. Yet by the holiness of the pious wives' lives and their pious admonitions they were first somewhat moved, so that afterwards they also went to the public sermons and were thus fully converted; in this also the affection of the husband played some part, since those who share a marriage bed want to share the profession as well. Peter therefore signifies that women, by living holy and honest lives, can achieve this: that even while silent they prepare their husbands to embrace the faith of Christ, which they see to be the nurse of such great virtues. Indeed sincere integrity has very sharp goads, which can do more, almost, with adversaries who are not wholly perverse, than learned disputation. But a wicked life sometimes also overturns more than sound doctrine can build up. We read of St Monica, the mother of St Augustine, that by her innocence and piety she led her husband to Christ before his death, and afterwards her son Augustine as well. There are also other examples which teach that husbands have been brought to God, or at least made more tractable, by the prudence and piety of their wives.

units.la: Pertinet huc quod de Helthere in sacris literis traditur. Et in Francorum historiis legimus, Clodoveum Magnum (qui postea Ludovicus primus dictus est) uxoris suæ Gothildis Burgundicæ colloquiis eruditum suisse, ut in ancipiti contra Alemannos præ lio Christi opem implora-ret, seq; Christianum fore voveret, si victoria potiretur. Neque irritum fuit votum hoc, quando & victoriam ab hostibus retulit, & idem Francis recipiendæ Christianæ religionis author fuit.
units.tr: This applies to what is handed down about Helthere in the sacred writings. Also, in the histories of the Franks we read that Clovis the Great (who was later called Louis I) was instructed by the conversations of his wife Clotilde of Burgundy. In a doubtful battle against the Alemanni, he implored the help of Christ and vowed that he would become a Christian if he won the victory.
